We prove the two implications after setting up the three ingredients: (1) K/k is a cyclic Galois field extension of degree p with generator σ; (2) A is a central simple k-algebra of degree p, split by K; (3) for a central simple algebra of prime degree p, "division" is equivalent to "not split".

STEP 1: K/k is cyclic Galois of degree p, generated by σ.
Let f(T) = T^p - T - a ∈ k[T]. Since f is irreducible and x^p - x = a, the k-algebra homomorphism ev_x : k[T] → K, T ↦ x, is surjective (its image is k[x] = K) and its kernel is the maximal ideal (f). Hence K ≅ k[T]/(f) is a field and [K : k] = deg f = p, with k-basis 1, x, …, x^{p-1}.

Roots of f inside K: the prime field F_p lies in k. For each i ∈ {0,1,…,p-1} ⊂ F_p, using the characteristic-p binomial theorem ((u+v)^p = u^p + v^p) and Fermat's identity i^p = i in F_p,
  (x+i)^p - (x+i) = (x^p + i^p) - x - i = (x^p - x) + (i^p - i) = a + 0 = a.
So each x+i is a root of f. They are pairwise distinct: (x+i) - (x+j) = i - j ≠ 0 for 0 ≤ i < j ≤ p-1. Thus f has p distinct roots in K, all lying in K, and since deg f = p we have the factorisation f(T) = ∏_{i=0}^{p-1} (T - (x+i)) in K[T]. Moreover f'(T) = pT^{p-1} - 1 = -1 ≠ 0, so f is separable. Therefore K is the splitting field over k of a separable polynomial, i.e. K/k is Galois, and |Gal(K/k)| = [K:k] = p.

Existence and order of σ: since x+1 is another root of the minimal polynomial f of x over k, the assignment x ↦ x+1 extends (uniquely) to a k-embedding σ : K → K. Being a k-linear injection of the p-dimensional k-vector space K into itself, it is surjective, hence a k-automorphism. By induction σ^i(x) = x + i for 0 ≤ i ≤ p-1 (σ^{i+1}(x) = σ(x+i) = σ(x)+i = x+i+1, as σ fixes k ⊃ F_p). Hence σ^i ≠ id for 1 ≤ i ≤ p-1, and σ^p(x) = x + p = x + 0 = x since p = 0 in k, so σ^p = id on K = k(x). Thus σ has order p and, since |Gal(K/k)| = p, Gal(K/k) = ⟨σ⟩ ≅ Z/p. In particular K/k is a cyclic field extension of degree p with generator σ, exactly as required to apply the theory of cyclic algebras.

(The norm map N_{K/k} : K^× → k^× is the homomorphism N(y) = ∏_{i=0}^{p-1} σ^i(y); its image N_{K/k}(K^×) is a subgroup of k^×, so the quotient k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) and the order of the class of b in it are well defined.)

STEP 2: A is a central simple k-algebra of degree p, split by K.
By the reference ref_22, part (i), applied to the cyclic Galois field extension K/k of degree n = p with generator σ and the element b ∈ k^×: the algebra (K/k, σ, b) with basis 1, u, …, u^{p-1} over K, relation u c = σ(c) u for all c ∈ K and u^p = b, is a central simple k-algebra of degree p; since K is a field, it is split by K (i.e. [A] lies in the relative Brauer group Br(K/k) = ker(Br(k) → Br(K))). Concretely dim_k A = [K:k]·p = p^2, so deg A = p. Note also that u is a unit of A, with inverse u^{p-1} b^{-1}, since u^p = b ∈ k^×.

STEP 3: for deg A = p, "A is a division algebra" ⇔ "A is not split".
By the Wedderburn structure theorem for central simple algebras, A ≅ M_r(D) for an integer r ≥ 1 and a central division k-algebra D, uniquely determined up to isomorphism, and deg A = r · deg D. Since deg A = p is prime, exactly one of the following holds:
 (a) r = 1 and deg D = p: then A ≅ D is a division algebra (no zero divisors);
 (b) deg D = 1 and r = p: then D = k and A ≅ M_p(k), which is NOT a division algebra, because p ≥ 2 and M_p(k) contains non-zero zero-divisors, e.g. the matrix units E_{11} ≠ 0 and E_{22} ≠ 0 satisfy E_{11}E_{22} = 0.
Case (b) is precisely the case in which A is split, i.e. [A] = 0 in Br(k). Hence: A is a division algebra ⇔ [A] ≠ 0 in Br(k) ⇔ A is not split. (Equivalently, exp(A) = 1 ⇔ [A] = 0 ⇔ A split, since the exponent of a central simple algebra is by definition the order of its Brauer class.)

STEP 4: exponent of A = order of b modulo norms, and this order is 1 or p.
By ref_23, applied to the cyclic extension K/k of degree n = p with generator σ and parameter b: exp(A) = exp((K/k, σ, b)) equals the order of the class of b in k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×).
By the proved lemma lemma_cyclic_norm_quotient_exponent_divides_degree (user eoinm), applied to the cyclic extension K/k of degree n = p, the quotient group k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) has exponent dividing p. Since p is prime, every element of this quotient — in particular the class of b — has order exactly 1 or exactly p. Moreover the class of b has order 1 if and only if b ∈ N_{K/k}(K^×).

STEP 5: conclusion.
(⇐) Assume b ∉ N_{K/k}(K^×). By Step 4 the order of b in k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) is not 1, hence is p. By ref_23, exp(A) = p ≠ 1, so [A] ≠ 0 in Br(k), i.e. A is not split. By Step 3, A is a division algebra. (This also matches the "in particular" clause of ref_23: order p gives a division algebra of exponent p.)
(⇒) Assume A is a division algebra. Suppose for contradiction that b ∈ N_{K/k}(K^×). Then the class of b in k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) is trivial, of order 1, so by ref_23 exp(A) = 1, hence [A] = 0 in Br(k) and A is split; by Step 3, A ≅ M_p(k), which has zero divisors (E_{11}E_{22} = 0 with E_{11}, E_{22} ≠ 0, as p ≥ 2). This contradicts A being a division algebra. Therefore b ∉ N_{K/k}(K^×).

Combining Steps 5(⇐) and 5(⇒) gives: A is a division algebra if and only if b ∉ N_{K/k}(K^×). ∎

lemma_69.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$ be the field of Laurent series in $u$ over $\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$, with its $u$-adic valuation $v$ normalized by $v(u)=1$. Then $k$ is a complete, hence henselian, discretely valued field of characteristic $p$ whose residue field is $\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$, and the classes of $s$, $t$ and $u$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_p$ in $k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^p$; in particular the residue field has $p$-rank $2$, i.e. $[\mathbb{F}_p(s,t):\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)^p]=p^2$.
lemma_69.proof:
Put F := \mathbb{F}_p(s,t), the rational function field in two indeterminates over the prime field \mathbb{F}_p, so that k = \mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u)) = F((u)). We argue in steps.

STEP 0 (the field of Laurent series). By definition k consists of all formal sums x = \sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} a_i u^i with a_i \in F and with support supp(x) := \{i : a_i \neq 0\} bounded below; addition is termwise and the Cauchy product has coefficient (xy)_r = \sum_{i+j=r} a_i b_j, which is a finite sum (only i with M_x \le i \le r - M_y occur, where M_x, M_y are lower bounds for the supports), so the product is well defined and k is a commutative ring with 1 = (1 at i = 0).

STEP 1 (the valuation v). For 0 \neq x \in k set v(x) := min supp(x) \in \mathbb{Z}; thus x = u^{m}(a_m + u\xi) with m = v(x), a_m \in F^{\times}, and \xi \in F[[u]] (i.e. writing x = \sum_{i\ge m} a_i u^i with a_m \neq 0, we have a_m + u\xi the tail). For x,y \neq 0 with v(x)=m, v(y)=n we have xy = u^{m+n}(a_m b_n + u\eta), and a_m b_n \neq 0 because F is a field; hence v(xy) = m+n = v(x)+v(y). Also supp(x+y) \supseteq supp(x)\cap supp(y), so v(x+y) \ge \min(v(x),v(y)), with equality when v(x) \neq v(y) (the lowest-degree term of the one of smaller valuation cannot be cancelled). Thus v : k^{\times} \to \mathbb{Z} is a discrete (surjective, since v(u)=1) valuation, normalized by v(u)=1, and v(c)=0 for every c \in F^{\times} (constant series). We set v(0)=+\infty by convention.

STEP 2 (valuation ring, units, residue field). The valuation ring is O = \{x : v(x)\ge 0\} = F[[u]], and its set of nonunits is m := \{x : v(x)\ge 1\} = uF[[u]]: indeed every z \in 1 + m, z = 1 + \sum_{i\ge1} b_i u^i, is invertible by solving recursively c_0 := 1 and c_r := -\sum_{i=1}^{r} b_i c_{r-i} for r \ge 1; then the coefficient of u^r in z\cdot(\sum_{r\ge0} c_r u^r) is c_r + \sum_{i=1}^{r} b_i c_{r-i} = 0 for r\ge1 and equals 1 for r=0, so z is a unit. Since any nonzero x = u^{v(x)}\cdot a_{v(x)}\cdot(1 + u\xi'/a_{v(x)}) with the last two factors in O^{\times}, every nonzero element of k is a power of u times a unit of O; consequently k is a field, O^{\times} = \{v = 0\}, m = uF[[u]] is the unique maximal ideal of O, and v(k^{\times}) = \mathbb{Z} confirms that v is a discrete valuation. The constant-term map O \to F, x = \sum_{i\ge0} a_i u^i \mapsto a_0, is a surjective ring homomorphism (constant term of a sum/product is the sum/product of constant terms) whose kernel is exactly \{a_0 = 0\} = m. Hence the residue field is O/m \cong F = \mathbb{F}_p(s,t).

STEP 3 (characteristic). Since char F = p, p\cdot 1_F = 0, and 1_k is the series with a_0 = 1 and all other coefficients 0; coefficientwise, p\cdot 1_k has all coefficients p\cdot 1_F = 0, so p\cdot 1_k = 0 while 1_k \neq 0. Thus char k = p (and char of the residue field is p).

STEP 4 (completeness). Equip k with the ultrametric distance d(x,y) = 2^{-v(x-y)} (d(x,x)=0). Let (x_n)_{n\ge1} be Cauchy: for every N there is n_0(N) such that v(x_n - x_m) \ge N whenever n,m \ge n_0(N).
(a) Uniform lower bound: choose n_1 with v(x_n - x_{n_1}) \ge 0 for n \ge n_1; then v(x_n) \ge \min(v(x_{n_1}),0) for n \ge n_1, and setting M := \min\big(0, \min_{n<n_1} v(x_n)\big) gives v(x_n) \ge M for all n.
(b) Stabilisation of coefficients: choose the indices n_0(N) nondecreasing in N. For i \ge M and n,m \ge n_0(i+1) we have v(x_n-x_m)\ge i+1, i.e. x_n and x_m have the same coefficient of u^j for every j \le i; in particular the coefficient of u^i in x_n is independent of n for n \ge n_0(i+1). Define c_i to be that common value for i \ge M, and c_i := 0 for i < M. Then x := \sum_{i\ge M} c_i u^i is a legitimate element of k.
(c) Convergence: fix N and take n \ge n_0(N). For each i \le N and each m \ge n_0(N) (hence m \ge n_0(i+1) by monotonicity) the coefficients of u^i in x_n and x_m agree; letting m \to \infty in the sense that m ranges over indices \ge \max(n_0(N), n_0(i+1)), the coefficient of u^i in x_m is c_i by definition of c_i. Hence x_n - x has zero coefficients of u^i for all i \le N, i.e. v(x_n - x) \ge N. Thus x_n \to x, and k is complete.

STEP 5 (henselianity: Hensel's lemma from completeness). We prove Hensel's lemma for (k,v). Let P(X) = \sum_{k=0}^{d} c_k X^k \in O[X] and a_0 \in O satisfy v(P(a_0)) \ge 1 and v(P'(a_0)) = 0 (this is exactly the hypothesis that the reduction \bar P \in (O/m)[X] has a simple root \bar a_0). There is a polynomial Q(X,Y) \in O[X,Y] with P(X+Y) = P(X) + P'(X)Y + Y^2 Q(X,Y), because for each k, (X+Y)^k - X^k - kX^{k-1}Y = Y^2\sum_{j=2}^{k}\binom{k}{j}X^{k-j}Y^{j-2} and the integers \binom{k}{j} lie in O; similarly P'(X+Y) = P'(X) + Y R(X,Y) with R \in O[X,Y]. Define the Newton sequence a_{n+1} := a_n - P(a_n)/P'(a_n). We show inductively, writing e_n := v(P(a_n)), that e_n \ge 2^n e_0, that a_n \in O, and that v(P'(a_n)) = 0. For n=0 these hold with e_0 \ge 1. Assuming them for n: h_n := a_{n+1}-a_n = -P(a_n)/P'(a_n) has v(h_n) = e_n - 0 = e_n \ge 0, so h_n \in O and a_{n+1} \in O; then P(a_{n+1}) = P(a_n) + P'(a_n)h_n + h_n^2 Q(a_n,h_n) = h_n^{2}Q(a_n,h_n), and since a_n,h_n \in O and Q has coefficients in O we get Q(a_n,h_n) \in O, so e_{n+1} = v(P(a_{n+1})) \ge 2v(h_n) = 2e_n \ge 2^{n+1}e_0; finally P'(a_{n+1}) = P'(a_n) + h_n R(a_n,h_n) with v(h_nR(a_n,h_n)) \ge e_n \ge 1 > 0 = v(P'(a_n)), so by the strict ultrametric inequality v(P'(a_{n+1})) = 0. Hence v(a_{n+1}-a_n) = e_n \ge 2^n \to \infty: (a_n) is Cauchy and by Step 4 converges to some a \in O, with v(a-a_0) \ge 1. Finally P(a) = 0: using the Taylor identity with (X,Y) = (a_n, a-a_n) \in O\times O, P(a) = P(a_n) + P'(a_n)(a-a_n) + (a-a_n)^2 Q(a_n,a-a_n), and each of the three terms has valuation at least \min(e_n, v(a-a_n), 2v(a-a_n)) \to \infty as n\to\infty; since v(P(a)) is a fixed element of \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\} bounded below by arbitrarily large integers, v(P(a)) = \infty, i.e. P(a) = 0. This is Hensel's lemma, and a valued field satisfying Hensel's lemma is henselian (classically equivalent to the requirement that v extend uniquely to every algebraic extension of k). Hence k is henselian.

STEP 6 (the p-th powers and the p-rank of the residue field). We first identify F^p := \{x^p : x \in F\}, which is a subfield of F since Frobenius is an injective homomorphism. Because \mathbb{F}_p is perfect (a^p = a for all a \in \mathbb{F}_p), \mathbb{F}_p \subset F^p, and s^p, t^p \in F^p, so \mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p) \subseteq F^p. Conversely, for x = f/g \in F^{\times} with f,g \in \mathbb{F}_p[s,t] nonzero, Freshman's dream gives f^p = \sum c_{ij}^{p} s^{pi}t^{pj} \in \mathbb{F}_p[s^p,t^p] and likewise g^p, hence x^p = f^p/g^p \in \mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p). Thus F^p = \mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p).
Next we compute [F : F^p] = [\mathbb{F}_p(s,t) : \mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p)] = p^2. The ring A := \mathbb{F}_p[t^p][s^p] is a UFD and s^p is a prime element of it (A/(s^p) \cong \mathbb{F}_p[t^p] is a domain), with Frac(A) = \mathbb{F}_p(t^p)(s^p) = \mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p) = F^p. The polynomial X^p - s^p \in A[X] is Eisenstein at the prime s^p: the leading coefficient 1 is not divisible by s^p, all intermediate coefficients are 0, and the constant term -s^p is divisible by s^p but not by (s^p)^2 (the s^p-adic valuation of s^p is 1). Hence X^p - s^p is irreducible over F^p, and [F^p(s) : F^p] = p with basis 1, s, \dots, s^{p-1}.
Now F^p(s) = \mathbb{F}_p(s,t^p) = \mathrm{Frac}(\mathbb{F}_p[s][t^p]); in the UFD \mathbb{F}_p[s][t^p] the element t^p is prime (quotient \cong \mathbb{F}_p[s], a domain), and X^p - t^p is Eisenstein at t^p by the same check. Hence X^p - t^p is irreducible over \mathbb{F}_p(s,t^p) and [\mathbb{F}_p(s,t^p)(t) : \mathbb{F}_p(s,t^p)] = p with basis 1, t, \dots, t^{p-1}. Since \mathbb{F}_p(s,t^p)(t) = \mathbb{F}_p(s,t) = F, the tower law gives [F:F^p] = p\cdot p = p^2, and the products \{s^{i}t^{j} : 0 \le i,j \le p-1\} form an F^p-basis of F. This is exactly the statement that the residue field has p-rank 2.

STEP 7 (linear independence of the classes of s, t, u in k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^p). The quotient k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^p is an elementary abelian p-group, hence an \mathbb{F}_p-vector space with \lambda\cdot[\alpha] := [\alpha^{\lambda}] for \lambda \in \mathbb{F}_p represented by an integer in \{0,\dots,p-1\}. Suppose \lambda_1[s] + \lambda_2[t] + \lambda_3[u] = 0 with \lambda_i \in \mathbb{F}_p, and choose integer representatives 0 \le \alpha_i \le p-1. Then s^{\alpha_1} t^{\alpha_2} u^{\alpha_3} = a^{p} for some a \in k^{\times}.
Write a = \sum_{i\ge m} a_i u^{i} with m = v(a) and a_m \neq 0. Since char k = p and Frobenius is continuous for the u-adic topology (if x = y + z then x^p = y^p + z^p and v(z^p) = p\,v(z)), we get a^{p} = \sum_{i\ge m} a_i^{p} u^{pi}, with each a_i^p \in F^p. Comparing valuations in a^p = s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2}u^{\alpha_3}: v(s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2}u^{\alpha_3}) = \alpha_3 because v(s) = v(t) = 0 and v(u) = 1, while v(a^p) = p\,v(a). Hence p \mid \alpha_3 and, as 0 \le \alpha_3 \le p-1, we get \alpha_3 = 0.
Then a^{p} = s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2} is a nonzero constant series, so v(a) = 0 and a = \sum_{i\ge0} a_i u^i with a^p = \sum_{i\ge0} a_i^{p}u^{pi} equal to a series supported in degree 0. For every i \ge 1 the coefficient of u^{pi} gives a_i^{p} = 0, hence a_i = 0; so a = a_0 \in F^{\times} and a^p = a_0^{p} \in F^p = \mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p). Thus s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2} \in F^p. But \{s^{i}t^{j}\}_{0\le i,j\le p-1} is an F^p-basis of F by Step 6, so the relation s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2} - c = 0 with c := s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2} \in F^p expresses a basis element as an F^p-multiple of another basis element: if (\alpha_1,\alpha_2) \neq (0,0), then s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2} and s^0t^0 = 1 are distinct basis elements and 1\cdot(s^{\alpha_1}t^{\alpha_2}) + (-c)\cdot 1 = 0 is a nontrivial linear relation among basis vectors, impossible. Hence (\alpha_1,\alpha_2) = (0,0). Altogether \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambda_3 = 0, proving that [s], [t], [u] are linearly independent over \mathbb{F}_p in k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^p.

STEP 8 (conclusion). Steps 1-3 show that k is a discretely valued field of characteristic p, complete for its u-adic valuation with v(u)=1 and residue field \mathbb{F}_p(s,t); Step 5 shows it is henselian; Step 6 shows the residue field satisfies [\mathbb{F}_p(s,t):\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)^p] = p^2, i.e. has p-rank 2; and Step 7 shows the classes of s, t, u are \mathbb{F}_p-linearly independent in k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^p (in particular the p-rank of k itself is at least 3). This proves all the claims of the lemma.

lemma_70.statement: Let $k$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>0$ with valuation $v$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra whose residue division ring coincides with the residue field of $k$, and let $w$ be the valuation of $D^{\times}$ extending $v$. If $x\in D\setminus k$ satisfies $x^p-x\in k$, then $k(x)/k$ is a cyclic Galois extension of degree $p$ and $p\,w(x)=v(x^p-x)<0$.
lemma_70.proof:
Throughout, write v: k^× → Γ_v for the given discrete valuation, O_v = {λ ∈ k : v(λ) ≥ 0} ∪ {0} for its valuation ring, 𝔪_v for its maximal ideal, and k̄ = O_v/𝔪_v for the residue field. The centre of D is k, so every element of k (in particular every element of the prime field F_p ⊂ k) is central in D.

STANDING FACTS ABOUT w. By hypothesis w: D^× → Γ is a valuation of the division ring D extending v, where Γ is a totally ordered abelian group. We use:
 (w1) w(d₁d₂) = w(d₁) + w(d₂) for d₁,d₂ ∈ D^× (w is a group homomorphism);
 (w2) w(d₁+d₂) ≥ min{w(d₁), w(d₂)}, with EQUALITY whenever w(d₁) ≠ w(d₂). Indeed, if w(d₁) < w(d₂) and w(d₁+d₂) > w(d₁), then w(d₂) = w((d₁+d₂) − d₁) ≥ min{w(d₁+d₂), w(−d₁)} > w(d₁), while also w(d₂) < w(d₁) by assumption, contradiction; the other case is symmetric;
 (w3) w(λ) = v(λ) for all λ ∈ k^×.
Put O_D = {d ∈ D^× : w(d) ≥ 0} ∪ {0} and 𝔇 = {d ∈ D^× : w(d) > 0} ∪ {0}; O_D is a valuation ring of D with maximal ideal 𝔇, and D̄ = O_D/𝔇 is the residue division ring. For d,e ∈ O_D one has d̄ = ē in D̄ ⇔ d − e ∈ 𝔇 ⇔ w(d − e) > 0, by definition of the residue map (kernel 𝔇). The inclusion O_v ↪ O_D induces an injective homomorphism of fields k̄ → D̄; the hypothesis "the residue division ring of D coincides with the residue field of k" means this map is an isomorphism, and we shall use precisely its surjectivity: every element of O_D is congruent modulo 𝔇 to some element of O_v.
Since Γ is totally ordered it is torsion free and its order is translation invariant; in particular γ < 0 and n ∈ ℤ_{>0} imply nγ < 0 (else −γ > 0 would give −nγ = n(−γ) > 0 and nγ < 0 simultaneously is impossible, i.e. nγ > 0 would contradict nγ ≥ 0 failing; concretely γ < 0 ⇒ 0 < −γ ⇒ 0 < n(−γ) = −(nγ) ⇒ nγ < 0).
HENSEL FORM USED. Since k is henselian, we use the standard equivalent form of Hensel's lemma: if h(T) ∈ O_v[T] and c ∈ O_v satisfy v(h(c)) > 2·v(h'(c)), then there exists t ∈ O_v with h(t) = 0.

CLAIM 1 (the kernel of T^p − T inside D is F_p). Let z ∈ D satisfy z^p = z. The prime field F_p is central in D, so the subring F_p[z] ⊂ D is a commutative domain; z is integral over F_p (root of T^p − T), so F_p[z] is a finite F_p-algebra generated by one element, hence a field (a finite domain is a field). Let m_z ∈ F_p[T] be the minimal polynomial of z over F_p; the kernel of the evaluation map F_p[T] → F_p[z] is the prime ideal (m_z), and since z^p − z = 0 we have m_z | (T^p − T). Now T^p − T = ∏_{i ∈ F_p}(T − i) in F_p[T]: both sides are monic of degree p, and the p elements of F_p are roots of T^p − T (Fermat) and are all simple roots since the derivative is −1 ≠ 0; hence the two monic polynomials of degree p with the same p distinct roots coincide. Thus m_z is a product of distinct linear factors T − i, and being irreducible it is linear: m_z = T − i for some i ∈ F_p, i.e. z = i ∈ F_p. ∎

STEP 1 (k(x) is a field, finite Galois of degree p over k, with cyclic Galois group). Write a = x^p − x ∈ k and f(T) = T^p − T − a ∈ k[T]; f is monic, nonzero, and f(x) = 0, so x is algebraic over k and k[x] is spanned over k by 1, x, …, x^{p−1}; hence dim_k k[x] ≤ p. Since x commutes with k (k = Z(D)), k[x] is a commutative k-algebra, and being a subalgebra of the division ring D it is a domain. A finite-dimensional commutative domain over a field is a field: for 0 ≠ u ∈ k[x], multiplication by u is an injective k-linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space k[x], hence surjective, so u^{-1} ∈ k[x]. Therefore k[x] = k(x) is a field, finite over k, with [k(x):k] = deg m ≥ 2 (m the minimal polynomial of x over k; the inequality is because x ∉ k).
The evaluation homomorphism k[T] → D, T ↦ x, has kernel the principal ideal (m) (k[T] is a PID and the kernel is nonzero because x is algebraic); since f(x) = 0 we get m | f.
In the commutative ring k(x)[T] we now verify that f splits completely:
   ∏_{i ∈ F_p}(T − (x+i)) = (T − x)^p − (T − x) = (T^p − x^p) − T + x = T^p − T − a = f(T).
The first equality is the identity ∏_{i∈F_p}(U − i) = U^p − U (established in Claim 1) applied with U = T − x; the second is the binomial theorem in the commutative ring k(x)[T], where (T − x)^p = T^p − x^p because the characteristic is p. The p roots x + i (i ∈ F_p) are pairwise distinct, since (x+i) − (x+j) = i − j ≠ 0 for i ≠ j.
Since m | f, the minimal polynomial m of x splits over k(x) into distinct linear factors, and f'(T) = −1 shows f is separable. Hence k(x)/k is separable and normal, i.e. finite Galois.
Define θ: Gal(k(x)/k) → (F_p, +) by θ(σ) = σ(x) − x. Well defined: σ(x) is a root of f because f has coefficients in k and σ fixes k, so σ(x) = x + i for a unique i ∈ F_p, and then θ(σ) = i ∈ F_p. Homomorphism: if τ(x) = x + t with t ∈ F_p, then σ(τ(x)) = σ(x) + σ(t) = σ(x) + t, because t ∈ F_p ⊂ k is fixed by every k-automorphism; hence θ(στ) = σ(τ(x)) − x = (σ(x) + t) − x = θ(σ) + θ(τ) = θ(σ) + θ(τ). Injective: θ(σ) = 0 means σ(x) = x, and since k(x) = k[x] is generated over k by x, σ = id.
Thus Gal(k(x)/k) embeds in the additive group F_p, which has order p, so |Gal(k(x)/k)| ∈ {1, p}. Because k(x)/k is finite Galois, |Gal(k(x)/k)| = [k(x):k] ≥ 2; therefore |Gal(k(x)/k)| = p = [k(x):k], and Gal(k(x)/k) ≅ ℤ/pℤ is cyclic. (As a by-product m = f and f is irreducible over k, but this is never needed below.)

STEP 2 (a ≠ 0). If a = 0 then x^p = x, so x ∈ F_p ⊂ k by Claim 1, contradicting x ∉ k. Hence a ∈ k^× and v(a) is defined.

STEP 3 (w(x) < 0). Suppose for a contradiction that w(x) ≥ 0, i.e. x ∈ O_D. By the hypothesis D̄ = k̄, the reduction map O_v → D̄ is onto, so there exists c ∈ O_v with c̄ = x̄; equivalently, y := x − c satisfies w(y) > 0. Note y ≠ 0, for y = 0 would give x = c ∈ k. Since c ∈ k = Z(D), the elements x and c commute, so in characteristic p we have (x − c)^p = x^p − c^p, and therefore
   a − (c^p − c) = (x^p − x) − (c^p − c) = (x^p − c^p) − (x − c) = y^p − y.
By (w1), w(y^p) = p·w(y); since w(y) > 0 and p − 1 > 0, we have (p−1)·w(y) > 0 in the ordered group Γ, hence p·w(y) = w(y) + (p−1)w(y) > w(y). The two values w(y^p) and w(y) are unequal, so the strict-minimum case of (w2) gives
   w(a − (c^p − c)) = w(y^p − y) = min{p·w(y), w(y)} = w(y) > 0.
The element a − (c^p − c) belongs to k (as a ∈ k and c ∈ k), and it is nonzero, so by (w3), v(a − (c^p − c)) > 0.
Now consider h(T) = T^p − T − a ∈ O_v[T] (a ∈ k; in fact a ∈ O_v is not needed, only that h(c) makes sense, and h(c) = c^p − c − a ∈ k, which we have shown has positive valuation, so in particular a ∈ O_v). We have h(c) = c^p − c − a = −(a − (c^p − c)), so v(h(c)) > 0, while h'(T) = −1 gives v(h'(c)) = 0. Thus v(h(c)) > 0 = 2·v(h'(c)), and henselianity of k (Hensel's lemma in the form recalled above) yields t ∈ O_v with h(t) = 0, i.e. t^p − t = a.
Then, using that t ∈ k is central so that (x − t)^p = x^p − t^p,
   (x − t)^p − (x − t) = (x^p − t^p) − x + t = (x^p − x) − (t^p − t) = a − a = 0.
By Claim 1, x − t ∈ F_p ⊂ k, whence x ∈ k, contradicting the hypothesis x ∉ k. Therefore w(x) < 0.

STEP 4 (the valuation computation). Since w(x) < 0 and p > 0, we have (p−1)·w(x) < 0 in Γ, hence p·w(x) = w(x) + (p−1)w(x) < w(x). In particular w(x^p) = p·w(x) ≠ w(x), so by the strict-minimum case of (w2) and (w1),
   w(a) = w(x^p − x) = min{w(x^p), w(x)} = min{p·w(x), w(x)} = p·w(x).
Because a ∈ k^×, (w3) gives v(a) = w(a). Combining,
   v(x^p − x) = v(a) = p·w(x),
and this common value is strictly negative because w(x) < 0 and p > 0.

CONCLUSION. Steps 1–4 give exactly the two assertions: k(x)/k is a cyclic Galois extension of degree p, and p·w(x) = v(x^p − x) < 0. ∎

lemma_71.statement: Let k be a field and let D be a central simple k-algebra of degree p^2 for a prime p. If K is a subfield of D with [K:k]=p, then the centralizer C_D(K) of K in D is a central simple algebra over K of degree p whose Brauer class in Br(K) equals the image of the Brauer class [D] under the restriction homomorphism Br(k) -> Br(K).
lemma_71.proof:
SETUP AND NOTATION. Since D is a central simple k-algebra of degree p^2, its center is Z(D) = k and dim_k D = (deg D)^2 = (p^2)^2 = p^4. Let C := C_D(K) = { y in D : y*lambda = lambda*y for all lambda in K } be the centralizer of K in D. Because K is commutative, K subset C; and because k = Z(D), also k subset C. (The statement "K is a subfield of D with [K:k] = p" means k subset K subset D.) No hypothesis on char(k) is used anywhere below, and D is not assumed to be a division algebra; the only properties of p used are the arithmetic identities p^4/p = p^3, p^3/p = p^2 and sqrt(p^2) = p.

STEP 1 (double centralizer theorem, ref_1). A field is a simple ring, so K is a simple k-subalgebra of the central simple k-algebra D. Apply the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) with A = D and B = K. It gives:
 (1a) C = C_D(K) is a simple k-subalgebra of D;
 (1b) C_D(C_D(K)) = C_D(C) = K;
 (1c) dim_k(K) * dim_k(C) = dim_k(D), hence p * dim_k(C) = p^4, so dim_k(C) = p^3.

STEP 2 (the center of C, and its degree over K). For z in D we have, by the definition of the center and of the centralizer,
 z in Z(C)  <=>  z in C and z*c = c*z for every c in C  <=>  z in C intersection C_D(C).
By (1b), C_D(C) = K, so Z(C) = C intersection K. Since K subset C (K is commutative), C intersection K = K; hence Z(C) = K. Thus C is a simple ring whose center is the field K and which is finite dimensional over K. By definition this means C is a central simple K-algebra. Its K-dimension is dim_K(C) = dim_k(C)/[K:k] = p^3/p = p^2, and since for a central simple algebra the dimension over the center is the square of the degree, deg_K(C) = sqrt(p^2) = p. This is exactly the field-case clause of ref_1, deg_K C_D(K) = deg(D)/[K:k] = p^2/p = p.

STEP 3 (identification of the Brauer class with the restriction). By definition of the restriction (scalar-extension) homomorphism res_{K/k}: Br(k) -> Br(K), one has res_{K/k}([D]) = [D tensor_k K]. The Brauer-equivalence clause of ref_1, applied to A = D and to the subfield K, states precisely that C_D(K) is Brauer equivalent over K to D tensor_k K. We spell out the concrete content with an explicit dimension count. Write C congruent M_q(Delta) with Delta a central division K-algebra (so q * deg_K(Delta) = deg_K(C) = p, and Delta represents the class [C] in Br(K)). Brauer equivalence of the K-algebra D tensor_k K to C means D tensor_k K congruent M_r(Delta) for some integer r >= 1; in particular D tensor_k K is central simple over K of degree r * deg_K(Delta). Now compare K-dimensions:
   dim_K(D tensor_k K) = dim_k(D) = p^4  (extension of scalars: a k-basis {w_i} of D gives a K-basis {w_i tensor 1} of D tensor_k K),
   dim_K(C) = p^2 = q^2 * dim_K(Delta),
   dim_K(D tensor_k K) = p^4 = r^2 * dim_K(Delta).
Dividing the third equality by the second gives (r/q)^2 = p^4/p^2 = p^2, hence r/q = p, i.e. r = p*q. Therefore, as K-algebras,
   D tensor_k K congruent M_r(Delta) = M_{pq}(Delta) = M_p(M_q(Delta)) = M_p(C) = M_p(C_D(K)).
Passing to Brauer classes in Br(K), and using that a matrix algebra over a central simple algebra represents the same Brauer class as the algebra itself (both are matrices over the same division algebra Delta),
   res_{K/k}([D]) = [D tensor_k K] = [M_p(C)] = [Delta] = [C] = [C_D(K)].

CONCLUSION. C_D(K) is a central simple algebra over K of degree p, and [C_D(K)] = res_{K/k}([D]) in Br(K). This is exactly the assertion of the lemma.

REMARKS (the mechanism behind Step 3; these are explanatory and the conclusion above does not depend on them, and they also record the corrections to the previously rejected argument). 
(1) D is free of rank p as a right C-module. Indeed D_C is finitely generated: a k-basis {b_i} of D generates D over C because k subset C and k is central (d = sum b_i * alpha_i with alpha_i in k). Since C is simple and finite dimensional over its center K, C is a simple artinian ring, so by the Artin-Wedderburn structure theory C congruent M_s(Delta) for a division K-algebra Delta, every right C-module is semisimple, and D_C congruent S^m where S is the unique simple right C-module (the row module Delta^{1 x s}, with dim_k S = s * dim_k Delta) and m >= 0. As C_C congruent S^s we have dim_k C = s * dim_k S, while dim_k D = m * dim_k S; hence m/s = dim_k D / dim_k C = p^4/p^3 = p, i.e. m = p*s, and D_C congruent (S^s)^p congruent C_C^p.
(2) The K-algebra structure on End_C(D_C) must be defined through RIGHT multiplication: iota: K -> End_C(D_C), iota(lambda) = rho_lambda, x |-> x*lambda. Checks: (i) rho_lambda is right C-linear because rho_lambda(x*c) = x*c*lambda = x*lambda*c = rho_lambda(x)*c, using lambda in K = Z(C) from Step 2; (ii) iota is a ring map because (rho_lambda o rho_mu)(x) = (x*mu)*lambda = x*(mu*lambda) = rho_{mu*lambda}(x) = rho_{lambda*mu}(x), where the last step uses commutativity of K (this is the opposite-algebra convention point: composition of right multiplications reverses the order in the original algebra); (iii) iota(K) is central in End_C(D_C), since for right C-linear f one has (f o rho_lambda)(x) = f(x*lambda) = f(x)*lambda = (rho_lambda o f)(x), the middle equality being right C-linearity applied to the element lambda of C. With a right C-basis e_1,...,e_p of D and the convention f(e_j) = sum_i e_i a_{ij} (coefficients on the right), the map Psi: End_C(D_C) -> M_p(C), f |-> (a_{ij}), is a ring isomorphism preserving composition order: writing g(e_j) = sum_{j'} e_{j'} g_{j'j}, one computes (f o g)(e_j) = sum_{j'} f(e_{j'}) g_{j'j} = sum_{j'} (sum_i e_i a_{ij'}) g_{j'j} = sum_i e_i (sum_{j'} a_{ij'} g_{j'j}), so the matrix of f o g is the ordinary product A*G. Finally Psi(iota(lambda)) = lambda*I_p because rho_lambda(e_j) = e_j*lambda is already of the required form; hence Psi is an isomorphism of K-algebras once M_p(C) carries the K-structure lambda |-> lambda*I_p (legitimate because lambda in Z(C)). 
(3) The map Phi: D tensor_k K -> End_C(D_C), d tensor lambda |-> (x |-> d*x*lambda) = lambda_d o rho_lambda, is a K-algebra homomorphism: left and right multiplications commute ((lambda_d o rho_mu)(x) = d*(x*mu) = (d*x)*mu = (rho_mu o lambda_d)(x)), rho_lambda o rho_mu = rho_{mu*lambda} = rho_{lambda*mu} by commutativity of K, so Phi is multiplicative; its image lies in End_C(D_C) because lambda in K commutes with every element of C; and Phi(mu*(d tensor lambda)) = Phi(d tensor mu*lambda) = lambda_d o rho_{mu*lambda} = iota(mu) o Phi(d tensor lambda). The Brauer-equivalence clause of ref_1 used in Step 3 asserts exactly that this Phi is an isomorphism, i.e. D tensor_k K congruent M_p(C_D(K)) as K-algebras. Note in particular the error in the earlier argument: LEFT multiplication by lambda in K \ k is not right C-linear, since lambda_lambda(x*c) = lambda*x*c whereas lambda_lambda(x)*c = x*lambda*c, and these differ for some x, c unless lambda in Z(D) = k; so left multiplication cannot define the K-structure on End_C(D_C), and only rho_lambda may be used, as in (2).

lemma_no_separable_immediate_degree_p.statement: Let k be a field equipped with a henselian discrete valuation v, with valuation ring, maximal ideal and residue field \bar k, and let L/k be a separable field extension of degree p. Let w be the extension of v to L, with residue field \bar L. Then the index [w(L^\times):v(k^\times)] is greater than 1, or the residue field extension [\bar L:\bar k] is greater than 1.
lemma_no_separable_immediate_degree_p.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_no_separable_immediate_degree_p",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Notation. Let O = {a ∈ k : v(a) ≥ 0} be the valuation ring, m = {a ∈ O : v(a) > 0} its maximal ideal, k̄ = O/m the residue field, and normalise v so that v(k^×) = Z; fix a uniformiser π of O, so m = πO. Put n := [L:k] = p, and let B denote the integral closure of O in L. The whole argument is the proof of the fundamental equality [L:k] = e·f in this situation (following the reviser's route (1b)); no Hensel application to a polynomial with vanishing derivative is made, and no valuation is ever renormalised to Z.

STEP 1: B is a free O-module of rank n.
(1a) B ∩ k = O, because O is integrally closed in k. In particular 1/π ∈ L \ B, so B ≠ L and B is not a field.
(1b) Scaling into B: if x ∈ L has minimal polynomial T^m + c_{m-1}T^{m-1} + … + c_0 over k, choose d ∈ O \ {0} with v(d) ≥ max_{j<m, c_j≠0} ⌈−v(c_j)/(m−j)⌉ ≥ 0. Then T^m + d c_{m-1}T^{m-1} + d²c_{m-2}T^{m-2} + … + d^m c_0 is monic in O[T} and has root dx, so dx ∈ B. Starting from any k-basis of L we therefore obtain a k-basis y_1,…,y_n of L contained in B; M := ⊕_i O y_i is a free O-lattice of rank n with M ⊆ B.
(1c) Since L/k is separable, the trace pairing (u,v) ↦ Tr_{L/k}(uv) is non-degenerate; let y_1^*,…,y_n^* ∈ L be the dual basis of y_1,…,y_n. For b ∈ B, each b y_i lies in B (the integral closure is a ring), hence is integral over O; Tr_{L/k}(b y_i) ∈ k is a sum of conjugates of b y_i, so it is integral over O and lies in O. Writing b = Σ λ_i y_i^* gives λ_i = Tr_{L/k}(b y_i) ∈ O. Hence B ⊆ M^* := ⊕_i O y_i^*, a free O-module of rank n.
(1d) A DVR is a PID, hence Noetherian; a submodule of a free module of rank n over a PID is free of rank ≤ n. Thus B is free of rank ≤ n, and since B ⊇ M it has rank exactly n.

STEP 2: every nonzero prime ideal of B contains m.
Let q ≠ (0) be prime in B and 0 ≠ x ∈ q. Choose a relation x^m + a_1 x^{m-1} + … + a_m = 0 with a_i ∈ k and m ≥ 1 minimal. Then a_m ≠ 0: otherwise x·(x^{m-1} + a_1 x^{m-2} + … + a_{m-1}) = 0 in the field L with x ≠ 0, contradicting minimality of m. Now a_m = −x(x^{m-1} + a_1x^{m-2} + … + a_{m-1}) ∈ q ∩ k^×. Since x ∈ B is integral over O, so is a_m, and a_m ∈ k, hence a_m ∈ B ∩ k = O by (1a). A unit of O cannot lie in the proper ideal q, so v(a_m) ≥ 1; write a_m = uπ^s with s ≥ 1 and u ∈ O^×. As u^{−1} ∈ O ⊆ B, u is a unit of B, so π^s = u^{−1}a_m ∈ q, and q prime gives π ∈ q. Thus m = πO ⊆ q.
Consequences. (i) Every maximal ideal of B is nonzero (B is not a field, by 1a) and hence contains m; therefore mB ⊆ Jac(B). (ii) Max(B) = Max(B/mB) under the quotient map, since the maximal ideals of B are exactly those containing mB.

STEP 3 (idempotent lifting modulo mC; this is where henselianity is used).
Claim: if C is a commutative O-algebra that is free of finite rank over O, every idempotent of C/mC is the image of an idempotent of C.
Proof of the claim. Let ē ∈ C/mC be idempotent, c ∈ C a lift, and let χ(T) = T^N + γ_1T^{N-1} + … + γ_N ∈ O[T] be the characteristic polynomial of the O-linear endomorphism μ_c : z ↦ cz of the free O-module C (N = rank_O C). Reducing coefficients mod m, χ̄ ∈ k̄[T] is the characteristic polynomial of the induced operator on C/mC, which is μ_ē. Because ē² = ē, the operator μ_ē satisfies T² − T = 0; over the field k̄ its minimal polynomial divides T(T−1), which is separable, so μ_ē is diagonalisable with all eigenvalues in {0,1}. Hence χ̄(T) = T^a(T−1)^b with a + b = N.
• If b = 0, then χ̄ = (T−1)^N and diagonalisability forces μ_ē = id_{C/mC}; then ē = μ_ē(1) = 1, and e := 1_C is the required lift.
• If a = 0, similarly μ_ē = 0, so ē = μ_ē(1) = 0, and e := 0 works.
• Suppose a ≥ 1 and b ≥ 1. Since O is henselian and T^a, (T−1)^b are monic coprime polynomials in k̄[T], Hensel's lemma in factorisation form gives monic χ_1, χ_2 ∈ O[T] with χ = χ_1χ_2, χ̄_1 = T^a, χ̄_2 = (T−1)^b. The resultant Δ := Res(χ_1,χ_2) reduces to Res(T^a,(T−1)^b) = ∏_{α: T^a-root} (0−1)^b = (−1)^{ab} ≠ 0, so Δ ∈ O^×. The adjugate of the Sylvester matrix of (χ_1,χ_2), whose entries lie in O, yields p, q ∈ O[T] with pχ_1 + qχ_2 = Δ. Define e := p(c)χ_1(c)Δ^{−1} and e' := q(c)χ_2(c)Δ^{−1} in C. Evaluating the Bézout identity at c, and using Cayley–Hamilton in the form χ(c) = 0 in C (indeed μ_{χ(c)} = χ(μ_c) = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton, and z ↦ μ_z is injective since μ_z(1) = z), gives e + e' = Δ·1·Δ^{−1} = 1 and ee' = p(c)q(c)χ(c)Δ^{−2} = 0. Therefore e² = e(1 − e') = e − ee' = e: e is idempotent.
It remains to check that e reduces to ē. Write R := C/mC and bar for reduction. Reducing the Bézout identity and evaluating at ē ∈ R gives p̄(ē)χ̄_1(ē) + q̄(ē)χ̄_2(ē) = Δ̄ = (−1)^{ab}·1_R. Since a ≥ 1 and ē is idempotent, χ̄_1(ē) = ē^a = ē; since b ≥ 1, χ̄_2(ē) = (ē−1)^b = (−1)^b(1−ē)^b = (−1)^b(1−ē), as 1−ē is idempotent. Multiply the displayed identity by ē: the second term becomes q̄(ē)(−1)^b(1−ē)ē = 0 because (1−ē)ē = 0, and the first becomes p̄(ē)ē·ē = p̄(ē)ē. Hence p̄(ē)ē = (−1)^{ab}ē. The reduction of e is p̄(ē)χ̄_1(ē)Δ̄^{−1} = p̄(ē)ē·(−1)^{ab} = (−1)^{2ab}ē = ē. This replaces any cancellation step by an explicit multiplication by ē, and the degenerate cases a = 0, b = 0 were handled separately. The claim is proved.
(Remark: this hypothesis on O is exactly henselianity; the conclusion is false for non-henselian DVRs — e.g. the integral closure of Z_(5) in Q(i) is Z_(5)[i], a domain with two maximal ideals above 5, so the idempotents of Z_(5)[i]/5Z_(5)[i] ≅ F_5 × F_5 do not lift.)

STEP 4: B is local.
B/mB is a finite-dimensional k̄-vector space, hence an artinian (and noetherian) ring. By the structure theorem for artinian rings — every prime is maximal; there are only finitely many maximal ideals m̄_1,…,m̄_h (the primes of an artinian ring are minimal, and there are finitely many); Jac = ∩ m̄_i is nilpotent (its powers stabilise, and the determinant trick with Jac finitely generated gives J^k = J^{k+1} ⟹ J^k = 0); and CRT applied to the pairwise comaximal ideals m̄_i^{t_i} with ∩ m̄_i^{t_i} = 0 — we have B/mB ≅ ∏_{i=1}^h A_i with each A_i artinian local, and h is the number of maximal ideals of B/mB, which by Step 2(ii) is the number of maximal ideals of B. If h ≥ 2, then (1,0,…,0) is an idempotent of B/mB distinct from 0 and from 1; by Step 3 it lifts to an idempotent e ∈ B, which is then also distinct from 0 and 1 (as e ≡ ē mod mB). That is impossible in the domain B, whose only idempotents are 0 and 1. Hence h = 1, i.e. B is local; denote its maximal ideal by M_B.

STEP 5: B is a discrete valuation ring.
B is noetherian (finite over the noetherian ring O), local, integrally closed, a domain, and of Krull dimension 1: the only prime ideals are (0) and M_B, since every nonzero prime contains m by Step 2 and hence is a prime of the artinian ring B/mB, therefore maximal.
We prove M_B is principal. Pick 0 ≠ t ∈ M_B (M_B ≠ 0 as B is a local non-field). The only prime containing t is M_B, so √(tB) = M_B. If M_B = tB we are done. Otherwise M_B ⊄ tB, and taking r ≥ 2 minimal with M_B^r ⊆ tB (such r exists since √(tB) = M_B), choose a ∈ M_B^{r-1} \ tB and set x := a/t ∈ L. Then x ∉ B, and for every m ∈ M_B, xm = am/t with am ∈ M_B^{r-1}·M_B = M_B^r ⊆ tB, so xm ∈ B. Thus x ∈ M_B^{−1} \ B, where M_B^{−1} := {y ∈ L : yM_B ⊆ B} ⊇ B.
Next, (M_B : M_B) := {y ∈ L : yM_B ⊆ M_B} = B: for such y, multiplication by y is a B-linear endomorphism of the finitely generated faithful B-module M_B (faithful because B is a domain and M_B ≠ 0) whose image lies in M_B; the determinant trick then shows y satisfies a monic polynomial over B with coefficients in the powers of M_B, so y is integral over B, and since B is integrally closed in L, y ∈ B.
Now M_B·M_B^{−1} is an ideal of B (contained in B by definition). It is not contained in M_B, for otherwise M_B^{−1} ⊆ (M_B : M_B) = B, contradicting M_B^{−1} ⊋ B. Hence M_B·M_B^{−1} = B, so 1 = Σ_{i=1}^s x_i y_i with x_i ∈ M_B, y_i ∈ M_B^{−1}. Each x_i y_i ∈ B; if all lay in M_B then 1 ∈ M_B, absurd. Fix j with x_j y_j ∈ B \ M_B = B^×. For each i, x_i y_j ∈ B (as y_j M_B ⊆ B and x_i ∈ M_B), and in the field L, (x_i y_j)(x_j y_j)^{−1}x_j = x_i y_j x_j x_j^{−1} y_j^{−1} x_j = x_i, so x_i ∈ B x_j. Therefore M_B = Σ_i B x_i = B x_j is principal. Choose Π with M_B = ΠB.
Finally, B is a DVR: for 0 ≠ z ∈ B, Krull's intersection theorem (∩_{i≥0} M_B^i = 0 in the noetherian domain B) gives a unique i ≥ 0 with z ∈ M_B^i \ M_B^{i+1}, i.e. z = Π^i u with u ∉ M_B, hence u ∈ B^×. Consequently every element of L^× is uniquely of the form Π^n β with n ∈ Z and β ∈ B^×; write ord_B(Π^n β) := n.

STEP 6: the given extension w, and the invariants e and f.
Let w be the extension of v to L prescribed in the statement, and O_w its valuation ring.
(6a) B ⊆ O_w. If b ∈ B satisfies b^m + α_1 b^{m-1} + … + α_m = 0 with α_i ∈ O and w(b) < 0, then for each i ≥ 1, w(α_i b^{m-i}) = w(α_i) + (m−i)w(b) ≥ (m−i)w(b) > m w(b) = w(b^m). So the term b^m has a value strictly smaller than every other term of the sum, contradicting the ultrametric inequality applied to a sum equal to 0. Hence w(b) ≥ 0.
(6b) By Step 2, π ∈ m ⊆ M_B and π ≠ 0, so e := ord_B(π) ≥ 1; write π = uΠ^e with u ∈ B^×. Since B ⊆ O_w by (6a), both u and u^{−1} lie in O_w, so w(u) = 0; and since w extends v, w(π) = v(π) = 1. Hence e·w(Π) = 1 in the value group Γ_w. Ordered abelian groups are torsion-free, so there is a unique ξ ∈ Γ_w with eξ = 1, namely ξ = w(Π); note ξ > 0.
(6c) Take x ∈ L^× with x = Π^n β, n = ord_B(x), β ∈ B^×. Then β, β^{−1} ∈ B ⊆ O_w, so w(β) = 0, and w(x) = n w(Π) = nξ. Therefore O_w = {x : w(x) ≥ 0} = {x : ord_B(x) ≥ 0} = B. In particular: w(L^×) = Z·ξ; v(k^×) = Z·1 = Z·(eξ) = e·Z·ξ ⊂ Z·ξ; and the index [w(L^×) : v(k^×)] = [Zξ : eZξ] = e. Also the residue field of w is O_w/m_{O_w} = B/M_B = B/ΠB, and the induced embedding k̄ = O/m → B/ΠB is the natural one (M_B ∩ O = m, as m ⊆ M_B and M_B ∩ O is a prime of O contained in O_w's maximal ideal contracted to m). Thus f := [L̄ : k̄] = [B/ΠB : k̄].

STEP 7: the fundamental equality n = e·f.
Since B ≅ O^n as O-modules (Step 1), B/πB ≅ (O/πO)^n = k̄^n, so dim_{k̄}(B/πB) = n.
Considerthe filtration
B \supseteq \Pi B \supseteq \Pi^2 B \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \Pi^e B = \pi B.
The equality \Pi^e B = \pi B holds because \pi = u\Pi^e with u\in B^	imes. For i=0,\ldots,e-1 set Q_i = \Pi^i B/\Pi^{i+1}B.

First, each Q_i is a vector space over  ar L = B/\Pi B. Indeed, M_B=\Pi B annihilates Q_i, and mB=\pi B=\Pi^eB\subseteq \Pi^{i+1}B, so the image of m acts by zero; hence the action of O on Q_i factors through O/m= ar k, and the action of B factors through B/M_B= ar L.

Multiplication by \Pi^i gives a B-module isomorphism
B/\Pi B \longrightarrow Q_i, \quad b+\Pi B \mapsto \Pi^i b+\Pi^{i+1}B.
It is well defined, injective because B is a domain and \Pi^i
eq 0, and surjective by definition. It is O-linear, hence  ar k-linear after passing to the residue action. Therefore
\dim_{ ar k} Q_i = \dim_{ ar k}(B/\Pi B) = [ ar L: ar k] = f.

The short exact sequences
0 	o \Pi^{i+1}B/\Pi^eB 	o \Pi^iB/\Pi^eB 	o Q_i 	o 0
or simply additivity of dimension along the finite filtration of B/\piB give
\dim_{ ar k}(B/\piB) = \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} \dim_{ ar k} Q_i = e f.

On the other hand, B is a free O-module of rank n (Step 1), so
B/\piB \cong (O/\pi O)^n =  ar k^n,
and therefore \dim_{ ar k}(B/\piB)=n=[L:k]=p.

Thus p = e f, where
e=[w(L^	imes):v(k^	imes)] and f=[ ar L: ar k].
Both e and f are positive integers. Since p>1, it is impossible that e=f=1. Hence either [w(L^	imes):v(k^	imes)]>1 or [ ar L: ar k]>1, which is exactly the desired conclusion.
  "
}

lemma_72.statement: Let p>2 and let k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u)) with its u-adic valuation v normalized by v(u)=1. Let m be a positive integer with p\nmid m, let K=k(z) where z^p-z=s/u^m, let w be the unique extension of v to K, and let \sigma be the k-automorphism of K with \sigma(z)=z+1. Choose integers a,b with bp-am=1 and set \pi=z^a u^b. Then w(\sigma(\pi)/\pi-1)=m/p.
lemma_72.proof:
Throughout, $w$ denotes the (unique) extension of the $u$-adic valuation $v$ to $K$; it is a discrete valuation on the field $K$ with $w|_k=v$, so $w(u)=1$, $w(c)=0$ for every $c\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}$, and it satisfies the strict-minimum rule: $w(y_1+y_2)=\min(w(y_1),w(y_2))$ whenever $w(y_1)\neq w(y_2)$.

Step 1: $K$ is a field and $\sigma$ is a $k$-automorphism of it. By lemma_56 (Spark), for $k=\mathbb F_p(s,t)((u))$ and $m\ge 1$ with $p\nmid m$, the polynomial $T^p-T-s/u^m$ is irreducible over $k$ and $K=k(z)$ with $z^p-z=s/u^m$ is a totally ramified cyclic Galois extension of $k$ of degree $p$ whose Galois group is generated by $\sigma$ with $\sigma(z)=z+1$. Thus $K$ is a field, $\sigma$ fixes $k$ (in particular fixes $u$), and $w$ is a valuation on $K$ extending $v$.

Step 2: $w(z)=-m/p$. First, $v(s/u^m)=v(s)-m\,v(u)=0-m\cdot 1=-m$, since $s\in\mathbb F_p(s,t)^{\times}$ is a unit for the $u$-adic valuation. Next $z\neq 0$, for otherwise $s/u^m=z^p-z=0$, contradicting $v(s/u^m)=-m$. Hence, as $s/u^m\in k$,
  $w(z^p-z)=w(s/u^m)=v(s/u^m)=-m<0$.
If $w(z)\ge 0$ then $w(z^p-z)\ge\min(p\,w(z),w(z))\ge 0$, impossible; so $w(z)<0$. Since $p\ge 2$, we then have $w(z^p)-w(z)=(p-1)w(z)<0$, i.e. $w(z^p)=p\,w(z)<w(z)$; the two summands have distinct values, so by the strict-minimum rule
  $-m=w(z^p-z)=\min(p\,w(z),\,w(z))=p\,w(z)$.
Therefore $w(z)=-m/p$, and consequently
  $w(z^{-1})=m/p>0$.   (1)

Step 3: $\gcd(a,p)=1$. Reducing the chosen Bezout identity $bp-am=1$ modulo $p$ gives $-am\equiv 1\pmod p$. Since $p\nmid m$, $m$ is invertible mod $p$, so $a\equiv -m^{-1}\not\equiv 0\pmod p$. In particular $a\neq 0$ and the image of $a$ in $\mathbb F_p^{\times}\subset k^{\times}$ satisfies $w(a)=0$.

Step 4: simplifying $\sigma(\pi)/\pi$. Since $\sigma$ is a $k$-automorphism it fixes $u$, so $\sigma(u^b)=u^b$, and $\sigma(z)=z+1$. With $\pi=z^au^b$ and $z\neq0$,
  $\sigma(\pi)/\pi=\dfrac{(z+1)^a u^b}{z^a u^b}=\left(\dfrac{z+1}{z}\right)^{a}=(1+z^{-1})^{a}$.
Put $X=z^{-1}$; by (1), $w(X)=m/p>0$. Then $w(1+X)=0$ (strict minimum, since $w(1)>0=w(X)$ fails: $w(1)=0<w(X)$, so $w(1+X)=\min(0,m/p)=0$); in particular $1+X$ is a nonzero unit of the valuation ring of $w$.

Step 5: auxiliary claim. If $X\in K^{\times}$ satisfies $w(X)>0$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$ satisfies $p\nmid n$, then $w\big((1+X)^n-1\big)=w(X)$.
Proof of the claim.
(a) $n\ge 1$. In $\mathbb Z[T]$ one has the polynomial identity $(1+T)^n-1=T\,g(T)$ with
  $g(T)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{n}{i}T^{i-1}=n+\sum_{i=2}^{n}\binom{n}{i}T^{i-1}$
(the second sum being empty when $n=1$). Each $\binom{n}{i}$ is an integer, so its image in $k$ has $w$-value $\ge 0$ (it is $0\in\mathbb F_p$ when $p\mid\binom{n}{i}$, and an element of $\mathbb F_p^{\times}$ of value $0$ otherwise). Hence every term of $g(X)-n$ has $w$-value at least $(i-1)w(X)\ge 2w(X)>0$, so $w(g(X)-n)\ge 2w(X)>0=w(n)$ (using $p\nmid n$). By the strict-minimum rule applied to $g(X)=n+(g(X)-n)$, we get $w(g(X))=w(n)=0$. Therefore
  $w\big((1+X)^n-1\big)=w(X)+w(g(X))=w(X)$.
(b) $n\le -1$. Write $n=-n'$ with $n'\ge 1$; then $p\nmid n'$ as well. Since $1+X\neq0$,
  $(1+X)^n-1=(1+X)^{-n'}-1=-\big((1+X)^{n'}-1\big)\,(1+X)^{-n'}$.
By part (a), $w\big((1+X)^{n'}-1\big)=w(X)$, and $w\big((1+X)^{-n'}\big)=-n'\,w(1+X)=0$. Hence $w\big((1+X)^n-1\big)=w(X)$. This proves the claim. (Note that no infinite series is used, so no completeness argument is needed.)

Step 6: conclusion. Apply the claim with $n=a$ (which satisfies $p\nmid a$ by Step 3) and $X=z^{-1}$ (which satisfies $w(X)=m/p>0$ by Step 2). Using Step 4,
  $w\!\left(\dfrac{\sigma(\pi)}{\pi}-1\right)=w\!\big((1+z^{-1})^{a}-1\big)=w(z^{-1})=\dfrac{m}{p}$.
Since this value is finite, $\sigma(\pi)/\pi-1\neq0$, as required.

Step 7: consistency checks (not used above). The computation of Step 2 gives $w(\pi)=a\,w(z)+b\,w(u)=-am/p+b=(bp-am)/p=1/p$, so $\pi=z^au^b$ is indeed a uniformizer of $K$, in agreement with the value-group statement $w(K^{\times})=\tfrac1p\mathbb Z$ forced by total ramification of $K/k$ (lemma_56). Also, the argument only used $p\ge2$; the hypothesis $p>2$ is more than needed, and neither $b$ nor $t$ enters the final value.

lemma_73.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic p>0 equipped with a discrete valuation v: K^\times \to \mathbb{Z}. If c \in K satisfies v(c)<0 and p does not divide v(c), then c does not belong to wp(K)=\{x^p-x : x \in K\}.
lemma_73.proof:
We argue directly from the axioms of a discrete valuation. Write the valuation with the usual convention v(0) = +\infty, so that v : K \to \mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\} satisfies, for all a,b \in K,
  (i) v(a) = +\infty \iff a = 0,
  (ii) v(ab) = v(a) + v(b),
  (iii) v(a+b) \ge \min(v(a), v(b)),
and, moreover, whenever v(a) \neq v(b) one has equality in (iii): indeed, assuming v(a) < v(b), the relation a = (a+b) - b together with (iii) gives v(a) \ge \min(v(a+b), v(b)); if v(a+b) were strictly larger than v(a) = \min(v(a),v(b)), the right hand side would be > v(a), a contradiction. Hence v(a+b) = v(a) = \min(v(a),v(b)).

We must prove: if c \in K^\times with v(c) < 0 and p \nmid v(c), then there is no x \in K with x^p - x = c.

Suppose, towards a contradiction, that x \in K satisfies
  x^p - x = c.   (\ast)

Step 1: x \neq 0. Indeed, x = 0 would give c = 0^p - 0 = 0, contradicting v(c) < 0 (which in particular implies c \neq 0 by (i)).

Step 2: v(x) < 0. Assume instead that v(x) \ge 0. By (ii) applied repeatedly, v(x^p) = p\,v(x) \ge 0. Then by (iii),
  v(c) = v(x^p - x) \ge \min(v(x^p), v(-x)) = \min(p\,v(x), v(x)) \ge 0,
where we used v(-x) = v(x) (which follows from (ii), since v(-1)^2 = v(1) = 0 and v(-1) \in \mathbb{Z}, so v(-1) = 0). This contradicts the hypothesis v(c) < 0. Hence v(x) < 0.

Step 3: the two valuations v(x^p) and v(-x) are distinct. Since v(x) < 0 and p \ge 2, we have (p-1)\,v(x) < 0, i.e. p\,v(x) < v(x). Using (ii) and v(-x) = v(x) again,
  v(x^p) = p\,v(x) < v(x) = v(-x).

Step 4: compute v(c). By Step 3 the two summands x^p and -x have distinct valuations, so the equality case of (iii) applies:
  v(c) = v(x^p - x) = \min(v(x^p), v(-x)) = \min(p\,v(x), v(x)) = p\,v(x).

Step 5: contradiction. Since v(x) \in \mathbb{Z}, the integer v(c) = p\,v(x) is divisible by p, contradicting the hypothesis that p does not divide v(c).

The contradiction shows that (\ast) has no solution x \in K, i.e. c \notin \wp(K) = \{x^p - x : x \in K\}. This completes the proof.

(Remark on the hypotheses: the argument uses only p \ge 2 and that v is a discrete valuation taking the value v(c) < 0 with p \nmid v(c); no assumption on the residue field, on completeness/henselianness of v, or on p > 2 is needed. The edge case c = 0 is excluded by v(c) < 0, and the case x = 0 is handled in Step 1.)

lemma_75.statement: Let F be a discretely valued field of characteristic p>0 with valuation ring O_F and residue field F̄, and let E/F be a totally ramified extension of degree p. Then for every unit ε in O_E^× the residue of the norm N_{E/F}(ε) in F̄^× equals the p-th power of the residue of ε. In particular N_{E/F}(O_E^×) is contained in the subgroup of O_F^× consisting of units whose residue lies in F̄^{×p}.
lemma_75.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_75",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We fix notation. Let v: F^× → Z be the (normalized) discrete valuation of F, O_F = {x ∈ F : v(x) ≥ 0} its valuation ring, m_F = {x : v(x) ≥ 1} its maximal ideal, π_F a uniformizer, and F̄ = O_F/m_F the residue field. The field E carries a valuation w extending v (so w|_F = v); write O_E, m_E, Ē for its valuation ring, maximal ideal and residue field. The extension is totally ramified of degree p, so the ramification index is e = [w(E^×) : v(F^×)] = p.

Step 1 (Residue fields coincide; shape of the value group).
The natural homomorphism F̄ → Ē is injective because O_E ∩ F = O_F (for x ∈ F, w(x) ≥ 0 ⟺ v(x) ≥ 0). The fundamental inequality of valuation theory says that for a finite extension of valued fields, e·f ≤ [E:F] where f = [Ē : F̄]; (it follows from the standard linear-independence argument: elements of E whose values lie in distinct cosets of v(F^×), multiplied by lifts of an F̄-basis of Ē, are linearly independent over F, by the strict triangle inequality together with linear independence of the residues). Since e = p = [E:F], we get f = 1, so F̄ → Ē is an isomorphism; we identify Ē = F̄. (If one's definition of "totally ramified" already includes trivial residue extension, this step is immediate.)
Moreover w(E^×) is a subgroup of Q containing Z = v(F^×) with index p (any value group of an extension of a rank-one valuation embeds in R, and w(E^×)/v(F^×) has order p); Q/Z has a unique subgroup of order p, namely (1/p)Z/Z, hence w(E^×) = (1/p)Z. In particular there is Π ∈ E^× with w(Π) = 1/p; Π generates m_E, since x ∈ m_E means w(x) > 0, hence w(x) ≥ 1/p = w(Π), so x/Π ∈ O_E.

Step 2 (Structure of O_E as an O_F-module).
(a) E = F(Π). Indeed w(F(Π)^×) ⊇ w(F^×) + Z·w(Π) = Z + (1/p)Z = (1/p)Z, so e(F(Π)/F) = p, and the fundamental inequality gives [F(Π):F] ≥ p = [E:F]; hence F(Π) = E and (1, Π, …, Π^{p−1}) is an F-basis of E.
(b) For a_0, …, a_{p−1} ∈ F, not all zero, w(Σ_{i=0}^{p−1} a_i Π^i) = min_i (v(a_i) + i/p). Indeed, the numbers v(a_i) + i/p lie in pairwise distinct cosets of Z, because for 0 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ p−1 one has (i − j)/p ∉ Z (as 0 < |i−j| < p); hence they are pairwise distinct, and a finite sum of elements with pairwise distinct values has value equal to the minimum (by induction from: w(y)+w(z) with w(y) < w(z) implies w(y+z) = w(y)).
(c) O_E = ⊕_{i=0}^{p−1} O_F Π^i. If x = Σ a_i Π^i ∈ O_E then by (b), 0 ≤ w(x) = min_i(v(a_i) + i/p), so v(a_i) ≥ −i/p > −1 for every i; since v(a_i) ∈ Z, v(a_i) ≥ 0, i.e. a_i ∈ O_F. The reverse inclusion is clear since Π ∈ O_E. Thus O_E is free of rank p over O_F with basis (1, Π, …, Π^{p−1}), and O_E ⊗_{O_F} F = ⊕_i F Π^i = E.
(d) m_F O_E = m_E^p. Since w(π_F) = 1 = p·(1/p) = w(Π^p), the element η := π_F Π^{−p} has w(η) = 0, so η ∈ O_E^×, and therefore m_F O_E = π_F O_E = Π^p O_E = m_E^p (the last equality since m_E = Π O_E).

Step 3 (The norm as a determinant, and its reduction).
Let ε ∈ O_E^×. By Step 2(c), ε = Σ_{i=0}^{p−1} a_i Π^i with a_i ∈ O_F. Multiplication by ε is an O_F-linear endomorphism of the free O_F-module O_E of rank p; let M ∈ M_p(O_F) be its matrix in the basis (1, Π, …, Π^{p−1}). Since O_E ⊗_{O_F} F = E (Step 2(c)), the matrix M also represents the F-linear map m_ε : E → E, x ↦ εx, so
   det(M) = det_F(m_ε) = N_{E/F}(ε),
the last equality being the definition of the field norm as the determinant of multiplication. In particular N_{E/F}(ε) ∈ O_F, and since ε^{−1} ∈ O_E^× as well, N_{E/F}(ε)^{−1} = N_{E/F}(ε^{−1}) ∈ O_F; hence N_{E/F}(ε) ∈ O_F^× and its residue is defined.
Reducing the matrix entries modulo m_F gives the matrix of the induced F̄-linear endomorphism of O_E ⊗_{O_F} F̄ = O_E/π_F O_E. Because the determinant is a polynomial (hence compatible with the homomorphism O_F → F̄) in the entries,
   det_{F̄}(M̄) = det(M) mod m_F = N_{E/F}(ε) mod m_F = overline{N_{E/F}(ε)},
where M̄ is the reduction of M. Note dim_{F̄}(O_E/π_F O_E) = p, since O_E ≅ O_F^p.

Step 4 (The reduced operator is a scalar plus a nilpotent).
Let ā ∈ F̄^× be the residue of ε (a unit because ε · ε^{−1} = 1 gives ā · res(ε^{−1}) = 1). We claim ā = res(a_0): indeed ε − a_0 = Σ_{i≥1} a_i Π^i = Π·(Σ_{i≥1} a_i Π^{i−1}) ∈ Π O_E = m_E, so ε and a_0 have the same residue in Ē = F̄. Set V := O_E/π_F O_E and let T := multiplication by (ε − a_0) on V. Since ε − a_0 ∈ m_E, Step 2(d) gives (ε − a_0)^p ∈ m_E^p = π_F O_E, hence T^p = 0 on V: T is nilpotent. The operator of multiplication by ε on V decomposes as
   m_ε|_V = ā·Id_V + T,
because multiplication by a_0 on V is the scalar ā acting through O_F/m_F = F̄.
A nilpotent endomorphism of a vector space over F̄ is triangularizable over F̄ itself (its only eigenvalue is 0; e.g. take a basis adapted to the flag ker T ⊂ ker T^2 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ ker T^p = V), so in such a basis ā·Id_V + T is upper triangular with ā on all p diagonal entries. Therefore
   det_{F̄}(m_ε|_V) = ā^p.

Step 5 (Conclusion).
Combining Steps 3 and 4:
   overline{N_{E/F}(ε)} = det_{F̄}(m_ε|_V) = ā^p = (ε̄)^p,
which is the required identity: the residue of N_{E/F}(ε) in F̄^× is the p-th power of the residue ε̄ of ε. Since ā^p ∈ F̄^{×p} by definition, and since we showed in Step 3 that N_{E/F}(ε) ∈ O_F^×, it follows that
   N_{E/F}(O_E^×) ⊆ { u ∈ O_F^× : ū ∈ F̄^{×p} },
completing the proof.

(Remarks on the argument. (i) No separability hypothesis was needed: the structural description O_E = ⊕_{i<p} O_F Π^i of Step 2 holds for any totally ramified extension of degree p, whether E/F is separable, purely inseparable, or (for p prime) either alternative; correspondingly the purely inseparable case N(ε) = ε^p is automatically consistent with the formula. (ii) The characteristic p assumption was in fact not used either: exactly the same proof, replacing p by n = e = [E:F] and using m_E^n = m_F O_E, shows that for any totally ramified extension of degree n one has overline{N_{E/F}(ε)} = (ε̄)^n. (iii) All edge cases are covered: the case ε ∈ O_F^× is included (then ā = ε̄ and the formula reads ε̄^p = ε̄^p), and ε ∉ O_F is excluded by hypothesis since ε ∈ O_E^×.")
}

lemma_74.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic p>2 and let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p^2. Suppose that D contains no cyclic Galois subfield of degree p^2 over k, and that for every cyclic subfield K/k of D of degree p and every b in K with b not in wp(K) = {x^p - x : x in K} such that the Artin-Schreier extension K(b), generated by a root of T^p - T - b, splits the centralizer C_D(K), the continuous F_p-character of G_K associated to K(b)/K does not extend to a continuous character of G_k. Then D is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) for any group G of order p^2.
lemma_74.proof:
Throughout, for a field F of characteristic p write wp(F) = {x^p - x : x in F}.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose there are a group G with |G| = p^2, a G-Galois k-algebra L (i.e. L etale over k of dimension |G| = p^2, with G acting by k-automorphisms and L^G = k), and a 2-cocycle c, such that D is isomorphic as a k-algebra to the crossed product (L, G, c). Fix an isomorphism phi: (L,G,c) -> D, and identify L with its image phi(L*u_1) inside D; this image is a commutative unital k-subalgebra of D isomorphic to L.

=== Claim 1 (subfield bound in a division algebra) ===
Let Delta be a finite-dimensional division algebra with centre F and deg_F(Delta) = d (so dim_F Delta = d^2). Then every subfield E of Delta containing F satisfies [E:F] <= d; moreover, if [E:F] = d then E is a maximal subfield of Delta.
Proof of Claim 1. Delta is central simple over F and E is a simple F-subalgebra, so by the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), dim_F(E) * dim_F(C_Delta(E)) = dim_F(Delta) = d^2. The centralizer C_Delta(E) is a finite-dimensional F-subalgebra of the division ring Delta, hence itself a division ring: for 0 != x in C_Delta(E) the inverse x^{-1} lies in Delta, and xk = kx for all k in E implies kx^{-1} = x^{-1}k, so x^{-1} in C_Delta(E). Let Z = Z(C_Delta(E)) be its centre. Since every element of C_Delta(E) centralizes E by definition, E is contained in Z. As C_Delta(E) is a division algebra central over Z, its dimension over Z is a perfect square, say delta^2 with delta >= 1 (Wedderburn: a central simple algebra over a field has square dimension over its centre). Therefore
   d^2 = [E:F] * dim_F(C_Delta(E)) = [E:F] * [Z:F] * delta^2 >= [E:F] * [E:F] * 1 = [E:F]^2,
where we used Z superset E superset F, hence [Z:F] >= [E:F]. Taking square roots gives [E:F] <= d. If equality holds, then every inequality above is an equality, so delta = 1 and Z = E; thus C_Delta(E) = Z = E, and by the maximal-subfield criterion of ref_1 (K is a maximal subfield iff C_A(K) = K) E is a maximal subfield. This proves Claim 1.

=== Step 1: L is a field, Galois over k with group G ===
Since L is etale over k, L is a product of finitely many finite separable field extensions of k, say L = prod_{i=1}^r F_i. Its image in D has no zero divisors because D is a division ring; hence r = 1 and L is a field. Thus L/k is a field extension of degree dim_k L = |G| = p^2, with G acting by k-automorphisms and L^G = k. By the structure theorem for Galois algebras, ref_2 (i): the only primitive idempotent of the field L is 1, whose stabilizer is H = G, so m = [G:H] = 1 and L = M is Galois over k with Galois group H = G. Hence L/k is a Galois field extension with group G, contained in D.
Also [L:k] = p^2 = deg D, so L is a maximal subfield of D: any subfield E with L superset E superset k satisfies [E:k] <= deg D = p^2 by Claim 1 (applied with Delta = D, F = k, d = p^2), hence [E:k] = [L:k] and E = L. (Maximality is recorded for orientation; the argument below does not need it.)

=== Step 2: G is abelian, of type C_{p^2} or C_p x C_p ===
By the class equation, p^2 = |Z(G)| + sum_i [G : C_G(x_i)], where the sum runs over representatives of the noncentral conjugacy classes; each index [G:C_G(x_i)] is a divisor of p^2 strictly larger than 1, hence divisible by p. Therefore p divides |Z(G)|, so Z(G) != 1. If G/Z(G) were cyclic, say generated by gZ(G), then every element of G would be of the form g^i z with z in Z(G), and any two such elements commute; so G would be abelian, forcing Z(G) = G, contradiction unless |G/Z(G)| != p. Thus |Z(G)| != p, and consequently |Z(G)| = p^2: G is abelian.
An abelian group of order p^2 is either cyclic (if it contains an element of order p^2) or has all nonidentity elements of order p; in the latter case, taking a of order p and b not in <a>, the subgroup <a> + <b> has order p^2 (as <a> intersect <b> = 0) and equals G, so G = <a> oplus <b> ~ C_p x C_p. Hence G ~ C_{p^2} or G ~ C_p x C_p.

=== Step 3: the cyclic case contradicts hypothesis (H1) ===
If G ~ C_{p^2}, then L is a subfield of D which is cyclic Galois of degree p^2 over k, contradicting the hypothesis that D contains no cyclic Galois subfield of degree p^2 over k.

=== Step 4: the elementary abelian case, Artin-Schreier data ===
Assume henceforth G ~ C_p x C_p, and regard G as a 2-dimensional vector space over F_p. Choose a subgroup H <= G of order p (a line), and set K := L^H. By the Galois correspondence: [K:k] = [G:H] = p, [L:K] = |H| = p, K/k is Galois with group G/H ~ C_p (every subgroup of the abelian group G is normal), and Gal(L/K) = H. Thus K is a cyclic (Galois) subfield of D of degree p, exactly the kind of subfield quantified over in hypothesis (H2).
Since L/K is a Galois extension of degree p = char K, Artin-Schreier theory (ref_14 (a)) gives L = K(y) with y^p - y = b for some b in K \ wp(K). Explicitly, b not in wp(K): if b = x^p - x for some x in K, then the roots of T^p - T - b are x + j (j in F_p), all lying in K, so K(y) = K, contradicting [L:K] = p.

=== Step 5: L = K(b) splits the centralizer C_D(K) ===
The subalgebra L of D is commutative and contains K, so L subseteq C_D(K). By ref_1, C_D(K) is a central simple K-algebra of degree deg(D)/[K:k] = p^2/p = p; as a K-subalgebra of the division ring D it is a division ring (same inverse argument as in Claim 1). Applying Claim 1 with Delta = C_D(K), F = K, d = p and E = L, we get [L:K] = p = deg_K C_D(K), so L is a maximal subfield of C_D(K). By the embedding criterion ref_5 (the case m = n: a subfield whose degree equals the degree of the algebra embeds as a maximal subfield and splits it), L splits C_D(K), i.e. C_D(K) tensor_K L ~ M_p(L).
Summarising: K is a cyclic subfield of D of degree p, b in K \ wp(K), and the Artin-Schreier extension K(b) := K(y) generated by a root of T^p - T - b splits C_D(K). Hypothesis (H2) therefore applies to the pair (K, b) and yields:
   (*) the continuous F_p-character chi: G_K -> F_p associated to K(b)/K does not extend to a continuous character of G_k.

=== Step 6: the character chi does extend; contradiction ===
First identify chi concretely. Under the Artin-Schreier isomorphism K/wp(K) ~ H^1(G_K, Z/p) of ref_14, the class of b corresponds to the map gamma |-> gamma(y) - y: indeed gamma(y) is again a root of T^p - T - b, so gamma(y) - y in F_p; and this map is a homomorphism because (sigma tau)(y) - y = sigma(tau(y) - y) + (sigma(y) - y) = (tau(y) - y) + (sigma(y) - y), as tau(y) - y lies in F_p and is fixed by sigma. Its kernel is G_{K(y)} = G_L, so it is precisely the continuous F_p-character of G_K associated to the extension K(b)/K; i.e. chi(gamma) = gamma(y) - y.
Now use that L/k is Galois with group G. Restriction to L gives a continuous surjection res: G_k = Gal(k_s/k) -> G = Gal(L/k). Since K/k is Galois (Step 4), the image of G_K = Gal(k_s/K) under res is exactly Gal(L/K) = H.
The map iota: H -> F_p, tau |-> tau(y) - y, is a group isomorphism: it is a homomorphism by the computation above, injective because L = K(y) (an element of H fixing y is the identity), and |H| = p = |F_p|.
Since G is an F_p-vector space (elementary abelian of order p^2) and H is a 1-dimensional subspace, there exists an F_p-linear retraction pi: G -> H with pi|_H = id. Concretely, choose any degree-p subfield E of L with E != K (L/k being C_p x C_p-Galois contains p+1 such subfields); then Gal(L/E) and H = Gal(L/K) are distinct lines with Gal(L/E) intersect H = Gal(L/EK) = 1 since EK = L, and Gal(L/E) oplus H = G; the projection onto H along Gal(L/E) is the required pi.
Define
   chi~: G_k -> F_p,  chi~(gamma) = iota( pi( res(gamma) )),
i.e. chi~(gamma) is the unique j in F_p with pi(res gamma)(y) = y + j. Then chi~ is a continuous group homomorphism, being the composition of the continuous restriction map res with the homomorphism pi and the isomorphism iota. For gamma in G_K we have res(gamma) in H, hence pi(res gamma) = res gamma, and therefore
   chi~(gamma) = iota(res gamma) = gamma(y) - y = chi(gamma).
Thus chi~|_{G_K} = chi: the character chi extends to a continuous F_p-character of G_k. (This is exactly the general fact recorded in Spark's lemma_64: for a Galois extension E/k with group C_p x C_p, an intermediate field K of degree p, and E = K(y) with y^p - y in K, the character tau |-> tau(y) - y of G_K extends to G_k; our situation is that lemma with E = L.)
This contradicts (*).

=== Step 7: conclusion ===
Both possibilities for the group G of order p^2 lead to contradictions: the cyclic case contradicts the absence of cyclic Galois subfields of degree p^2 in D, and the elementary abelian case contradicts hypothesis (H2) via the extension of the Artin-Schreier character constructed in Step 6. Hence no isomorphism D ~ (L, G, c) exists for any group G of order p^2, i.e. D is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra for any group of order p^2.

lemma_76.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic p>2, let K/k be a cyclic Galois extension of degree p, and let b ∈ K with b ∉ wp(K) = {x^p - x : x ∈ K}. Let K(b) be the Artin–Schreier extension of K generated by a root of T^p - T - b, and let χ: G_K → F_p be the continuous character attached to K(b)/K. If χ extends to a continuous F_p-character of G_k, then K(b) is a Galois extension of k with Galois group C_p × C_p.
lemma_76.proof:
Fix a separable closure k_s of k containing K and containing a chosen root θ of T^p - T - b; then K(b) := K(θ) ⊂ k_s. Write G_k = Gal(k_s/k) and G_K = Gal(k_s/K) = Gal(k_s/K) (a normal subgroup of G_k, since K/k is Galois). We prove that K(θ)/k is Galois with group C_p × C_p in five steps.

STEP 1. The polynomial T^p - T - b is irreducible over K, and K(θ)/K is cyclic of degree p; χ is surjective with kernel G_{K(θ)}.

The derivative of f(T) = T^p - T - b is -1 ≠ 0, so f is separable. Its roots are exactly θ + i for i ∈ F_p (since (θ+i)^p - (θ+i) - b = θ^p - θ - b + (i^p - i) = 0, and the p elements θ + i, i ∈ F_p, are distinct). Let d = [K(θ):K] and let g ∈ K[T] be the monic minimal polynomial of θ over K; then g divides f in K[T], and the roots of g are θ + S for a subset S ⊆ F_p with |S| = d. Since g ∈ K[T], the coefficient of T^{d-1} in g, namely -(Σ_{i∈S}(θ+i)) = -(dθ + s) with s = Σ_{i∈S} i ∈ F_p ⊆ K, lies in K. If d < p, then d ∈ F_p^× ⊂ K, so θ = -d^{-1}(-(dθ+s)) - d^{-1}s ∈ K, which would give b = θ^p - θ ∈ wp(K), contradicting the hypothesis. Hence d = p and f is irreducible over K.

Since all p roots θ + i of f lie in K(θ) and [K(θ):K] = p, the extension K(θ)/K is Galois of degree p, and every K-automorphism is of the form θ ↦ θ + i; thus Gal(K(θ)/K) = {τ_i : θ ↦ θ + i}_{i ∈ F_p} ≅ (F_p, +) ≅ C_p.

The character of the statement is χ(γ) = γ(θ) - θ for γ ∈ G_K. This is well defined because γ(θ) ∈ {θ + i : i ∈ F_p}, and γ(θ) - θ ∈ F_p. It is a homomorphism: for γ, δ ∈ G_K, since δ(θ) - θ ∈ F_p is fixed by γ,
  χ(γδ) = γδ(θ) - θ = γ(δ(θ) - θ) + (γ(θ) - θ) = χ(δ) + χ(γ).
Its kernel is {γ : γ(θ) = θ} = Gal(k_s/K(θ)) =: G_{K(θ)}, and since the induced map Gal(K(θ)/K) → F_p is injective with |Gal(K(θ)/K)| = p, the character χ is surjective. In particular χ is nontrivial, so G_{K(θ)} ⊊ G_K.

STEP 2. The extension field E of k attached to χ̃.

By hypothesis there is a continuous homomorphism χ̃ : G_k → F_p with χ̃|_{G_K} = χ. Since χ is surjective, so is χ̃; hence ker(χ̃) is a normal subgroup of G_k of index p. Put U := ker(χ̃) and E := k_s^U. Then E/k is Galois (U ◁ G_k) with Gal(E/k) = G_k/U ≅ (F_p, +) ≅ C_p, and [E:k] = p. Also V := G_K = Gal(k_s/K) is normal in G_k, since K/k is Galois.

STEP 3. Identification K(θ) = EK.

Restricting the character gives ker(χ̃|_{G_K}) = ker(χ̃) ∩ G_K = U ∩ V. On the other hand ker(χ̃|_{G_K}) = ker(χ) = G_{K(θ)} by Step 1. An element of k_s fixed by both U and V fixes E and K, hence fixes the compositum EK, and conversely; therefore U ∩ V = Gal(k_s/EK). By the Galois correspondence, K(θ) = EK.

STEP 4. E ≠ K, E ∩ K = k, and EK/k is Galois of degree p^2.

If E = K then U = V, and Step 3 would give G_{K(θ)} = U ∩ V = V = G_K, contradicting the strictness G_{K(θ)} ⊊ G_K noted in Step 1. Hence E ≠ K.

Now U ◁ G_k and V ◁ G_k, so U ∩ V ◁ G_k, and therefore K(θ) = EK is Galois over k with Galois group G_k/(U ∩ V).

We compute its order. Since U ◁ G_k, the product UV is a subgroup of G_k, and its fixed field is E ∩ K; moreover UV ≠ V, for UV = V would give U ⊆ V, i.e. E ⊇ K, hence E = K by equal degrees — excluded. Since [G_k : V] = [K:k] = p is prime and V ⊊ UV ⊆ G_k, it follows that UV = G_k. Counting finite indices,
  [G_k : U ∩ V] = [G_k : U] · [U : U ∩ V] = p · [UV : V] = p · [G_k : V] = p · p = p^2,
where the middle equality [U : U ∩ V] = [UV : V] is the standard bijection u(U ∩ V) ↦ uvV between the coset spaces (valid because UV is a subgroup). Thus [K(θ):k] = [EK:k] = p^2 (and E ∩ K = k, the fixed field of UV = G_k).

STEP 5. The Galois group is C_p × C_p.

Restriction gives a homomorphism
  ρ : Gal(EK/k) → Gal(E/k) × Gal(K/k),   ρ(σ) = (σ|_E, σ|_K).
It is injective, because E and K generate EK over k, so an automorphism of EK over k restricting to the identity on both E and K is the identity. By Step 4, |Gal(EK/k)| = [EK:k] = p^2, while |Gal(E/k) × Gal(K/k)| = p · p = p^2. Hence ρ is an isomorphism, and
  Gal(K(b)/k) = Gal(EK/k) ≅ Gal(E/k) × Gal(K/k) ≅ C_p × C_p.

CONCLUSION. K(b)/k is Galois (Step 4) and its Galois group is C_p × C_p (Step 5). Note that the cyclic group C_{p^2} is automatically excluded here: the character χ̃ exhibits K(b) as the compositum EK of two (necessarily distinct) cyclic degree-p extensions of k, so the group splits as a direct product of two groups of order p.

(Remark on the mechanism: via Artin-Schreier theory the hypothesis that χ extends is equivalent to b lying in F_p^×·a + wp(K) for some a ∈ k; then replacing the root θ by θ - x with θ^p - θ = b and x^p - x = b - a gives K(b) = K(y) with y^p - y = a ∈ k, and the compositum description above is exactly E·K with E = k(y). The argument given avoids any reliance on that dictionary and proves the claim directly from Galois theory.)

lemma_77.statement: Let $p$ be a prime, let $k$ be a field, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. Suppose $D$ contains a subfield $K$ such that $K/k$ is cyclic Galois of degree $p$. Then the image of the Brauer class $p[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$ is trivial, and the index of the class $p[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ divides $p$.
lemma_77.proof:
Throughout, $p[D]\in \mathrm{Br}(k)$ denotes the $p$-fold sum $[D]+\cdots+[D]=[D]^{\otimes p}$, and for an extension $F/k$ we write $\operatorname{res}_{F/k}:\mathrm{Br}(k)\to \mathrm{Br}(F)$ for the homomorphism induced by scalar extension, $[A]\mapsto [A\otimes_k F]$. No hypothesis on $\operatorname{char} k$ is used; the argument is valid for every prime $p$ and every field $k$.

**Preliminaries: corestriction and its basic property.** We record the piece of Brauer-group formalism we need, and prove it, so that the argument is self-contained. Let $K$ be a field, $L/K$ a finite separable extension of degree $d$, fix a separable closure $K_s\supset L$, and put $G=G_K=\mathrm{Gal}(K_s/K)$, $H=G_L=\mathrm{Gal}(K_s/L)$; then $H$ is an open subgroup of $G$ of index $d$, and $M=K_s^{\times}$ is a discrete $G$-module. Work in the category of discrete $G$-modules.

(a) For every $n\geq 0$ there is a natural homomorphism (corestriction) $\operatorname{cor}_{L/K}=\operatorname{cor}_H^G:H^{n}(H,M)\to H^{n}(G,M)$, characterized as the unique morphism of $\delta$-functors in $M$ whose degree-$0$ component is the norm $N(m)=\sum_{s\in H\backslash G}s\cdot m$ (a sum over the finitely many left cosets of $H$ in $G$). Existence and uniqueness follow from the comparison theorem for universal $\delta$-functors: the functor $M\mapsto H^{n}(H,M)$ is universal, because it is effaceable — every discrete $H$-module embeds in a coinduced module $\operatorname{Coind}_{1}^{H}N=\mathrm{Map}^{\mathrm{cont}}(H,N)$, and Shapiro's isomorphism $H^{n}(H,\operatorname{Coind}_{1}^{H}N)\cong H^{n}(1,N)=0$ for $n\geq 1$ makes these modules acyclic; the same holds for $G$. Since $N:(\ )^{H}\to (\ )^{G}$ is a natural transformation of the degree-$0$ functors, it extends uniquely to a morphism of $\delta$-functors; we call it $\operatorname{cor}_H^G$.

(b) $\operatorname{cor}_H^G\circ\operatorname{res}_H^G=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^{n}(G,M)$ for all $n\geq 0$. Indeed, both $\operatorname{cor}_H^G\circ\operatorname{res}_H^G$ and multiplication by $d$ are morphisms of $\delta$-functors $H^{\bullet}(G,-)\to H^{\bullet}(G,-)$, and in degree $0$ they agree: for $m\in M^{G}$, $\operatorname{res}$ is the inclusion $M^{G}\subset M^{H}$ and $N(m)=\sum_{s\in H\backslash G}s\cdot m=\sum_{s\in H\backslash G}m=d\,m$. Since the target $\delta$-functor $H^{\bullet}(G,-)$ is universal, a morphism out of it is determined by its degree-$0$ component, so the two morphisms coincide in every degree.

(c) Under the standard functorial identification $\mathrm{Br}(F)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{2}(G_F,F_s^{\times})$ (a central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $r$ maps to the class of the $2$-cocycle measuring the failure of a chosen isomorphism $A\otimes_F F_s\simeq M_r(F_s)$ to be $G_F$-equivariant), the restriction map $\operatorname{res}_{L/K}:\mathrm{Br}(K)\to\mathrm{Br}(L)$ is exactly the group-cohomological restriction $H^{2}(G_K,K_s^{\times})\to H^{2}(G_L,K_s^{\times})$ (using $L_s=K_s$). This is immediate from the construction, since choosing an isomorphism over $K_s$ and restricting the equivariance data to $G_L$ is precisely scalar extension $A\mapsto A\otimes_K L$.

Combining (b) and (c): for every $\alpha\in\mathrm{Br}(K)$, $\operatorname{cor}_{L/K}(\operatorname{res}_{L/K}(\alpha))=d\,\alpha$; in particular, if $L$ splits $\alpha$ (i.e. $\operatorname{res}_{L/K}(\alpha)=0$), then $d\,\alpha=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$.

**Step 1: the centralizer of $K$ in $D$.** Put $C=C_D(K)$. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), $C$ is a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[K:k]=p^{2}/p=p$, and $\dim_K(C)=p^{2}$.

$C$ is in fact a division ring: if $0\neq c\in C$, then $c^{-1}$ exists in $D$ (as $D$ is division), and for $a\in K$ we have $c^{-1}a=c^{-1}(aca^{-1})a^{-1}=c^{-1}(ca)a^{-1}=c^{-1}(ac)a^{-1}=(c^{-1}a)(cc^{-1})\cdot\dots$; more explicitly, $ca=ac$ gives $c^{-1}a=c^{-1}ac\,c^{-1}=a\,c^{-1}$, so $c^{-1}$ commutes with $K$ and hence lies in $C$. Thus every non-zero element of $C$ is invertible in $C$, i.e. $C$ is a central division $K$-algebra of degree $p$.

By Spark's lemma_71 (equivalently, the Brauer-equivalence clause of ref_1), the Brauer class of $C$ in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$ is the restriction of $[D]$:
$$[C]=\operatorname{res}_{K/k}([D])\in\mathrm{Br}(K).$$

**Step 2: $p[C]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$.** By the Noether–Goethals theorem (ref_16), the division algebra $C$ contains a maximal subfield $L$ that is separable over $K$. Since $L$ is a maximal subfield of $C$, the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) gives $C_C(L)=L$ and $\dim_K(L)\cdot\dim_K(C_C(L))=\dim_K(C)$, hence $[L:K]^{2}=p^{2}$, i.e. $[L:K]=p$.

The field $L$ splits $C$: indeed $[L:K]=p=\deg(C)$, so by the maximal-subfield case of the embedding criterion (ref_5) applied to the central simple $K$-algebra $C$, the condition that $L$ embed in $C$ as a maximal subfield is equivalent to $L$ splitting $C$. Thus $\operatorname{res}_{L/K}([C])=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(L)$.

Applying the identity of the Preliminaries with the separable extension $L/K$ of degree $d=[L:K]=p$ and $\alpha=[C]$ gives
$$p\,[C]=\operatorname{cor}_{L/K}\bigl(\operatorname{res}_{L/K}([C])\bigr)=\operatorname{cor}_{L/K}(0)=0\quad\text{in }\mathrm{Br}(K).$$

**Step 3: the image of $p[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$ is trivial.** Since $\operatorname{res}_{K/k}$ is a group homomorphism,
$$\operatorname{res}_{K/k}\bigl(p[D]\bigr)=p\cdot\operatorname{res}_{K/k}([D])=p\,[C]=0$$
by Step 2. This proves the first assertion.

**Step 4: $\operatorname{ind}(p[D])$ divides $p$.** Let $\Delta$ be the central division $k$-algebra representing the class $p[D]$, so that $\operatorname{ind}(p[D]):=\operatorname{ind}(\Delta)$. By Step 3, $\operatorname{res}_{K/k}(p[D])=0$, which means exactly that $\Delta\otimes_k K$ is a split $K$-algebra, i.e. $\operatorname{ind}(\Delta\otimes_k K)=1$. Apply the index-reduction formula (ref_12) to the central division $k$-algebra $\Delta$ and the finite extension $K/k$:
$$\operatorname{ind}(\Delta)\ \big|\ [K:k]\cdot\operatorname{ind}(\Delta\otimes_k K)=p\cdot 1=p.$$
Hence $\operatorname{ind}(p[D])$ divides $p$ (it is $1$ if $p[D]=0$, and $p$ otherwise).

Both assertions are proved. (Remark: the argument shows more generally that whenever a division algebra of degree $p^{2}$ contains a cyclic subfield of degree $p$, the class $p[D]$ has index at most $p$; the only structural inputs are that the centralizer is a division algebra of degree $p$ — hence killed by $p$ in the Brauer group via corestriction — and the index-reduction formula.)

lemma_78.statement: Let k be a field, let G be a finite group, and let D be a central division k-algebra of degree |G|. If D is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) for a Galois G-algebra L over k, then L is a field, and its image in D is a maximal subfield of D that is Galois over k with Galois group G.
lemma_78.proof:
Write A := (L,G,c) = \bigoplus_{g\in G} L u_g for the crossed product, and fix a k-algebra isomorphism \Psi : A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} D.

Hypotheses recalled. By the definition of a Galois G-algebra: L is a commutative etale k-algebra, dim_k L = |G|, G acts on L by k-algebra automorphisms, and L^G = k. By the definition of the crossed product, A is the free left L-module with basis {u_g : g \in G}, with multiplication determined by u_g x = g(x) u_g and u_g u_h = c(g,h) u_{gh}; equivalently
   (x u_g)(y u_h) = x\, g(y)\, c(g,h)\, u_{gh}      (x,y \in L),
extended k-bilinearly (associativity is exactly the 2-cocycle condition c(g,h)c(gh,i) = g(c(h,i))c(g,hi)). In particular dim_k A = |G| \cdot dim_k L = |G|^2, which agrees with dim_k D = (deg D)^2 = |G|^2.
