(a) Structure constants. With the basis (e_i) of B and e_i*e_j = sum_k c_{ij}^k e_k, the basis (eps_i) of B^sigma satisfies
   eps_i*eps_j = (e_i*e_j) tensor 1 = sum_k iota(c_{ij}^k)*eps_k = sum_k sigma(c_{ij}^k)*eps_k,
where the last equality is exactly iota(mu) = sigma(mu)*1_{B^sigma} from 1(i). So B^sigma is precisely the algebra obtained from B by applying sigma to the structure constants in the basis (e_i); by 1(v) this is independent of the chosen basis (a change-of-basis matrix T is replaced by sigma(T)).

(b) Matrices. In M_r(K)^sigma the elements eps_{ij} := E_{ij} tensor 1 (E_{ij} the matrix units) form a K-basis by 1(iii), satisfy eps_{ij}*eps_{kl} = delta_{jk}*eps_{il} and sum_i eps_{ii} = (sum_i E_{ii}) tensor 1 = 1. Hence sum_{i,j} lambda_{ij}*eps_{ij} |-> (lambda_{ij}) is a K-algebra isomorphism M_r(K)^sigma -> M_r(K): multiplicativity holds because the structure constants delta_{jk} lie in F_p and are fixed by sigma, so (sum lambda_{ij} eps_{ij})(sum rho_{kl} eps_{kl}) = sum_{i,l}(sum_j lambda_{ij} rho_{jl}) eps_{il}. Using M_r(B) isomorphic to B tensor_K M_r(K) via b tensor (lambda_{kl}) |-> (b*lambda_{kl}) (a ring isomorphism since entries of M_r(K) are central in M_r(B)) together with (c) below, we get M_r(B)^sigma isomorphic to B^sigma tensor_K M_r(K)^sigma, hence to B^sigma tensor_K M_r(K), hence to M_r(B^sigma).

(c) Tensor products. Define Psi: (B tensor_K B')^sigma -> B^sigma tensor_K B'^sigma by Psi((b tensor b') tensor lambda) = (b tensor 1) tensor (b' tensor lambda). Well-defined: Psi((b*mu tensor b') tensor lambda) = (b*mu tensor 1) tensor (b' tensor lambda) = (b tensor sigma(mu)) tensor (b' tensor lambda) = (b tensor 1)*sigma(mu) tensor (b' tensor lambda) = (b tensor 1) tensor sigma(mu)*(b' tensor lambda) = (b tensor 1) tensor (b'*mu tensor lambda) (using sigma(mu)*(b' tensor 1) = (b'*mu tensor 1), which is 1(i) read backwards), and Psi((b tensor b') tensor sigma(mu)*lambda) = (b tensor 1) tensor (b' tensor sigma(mu)*lambda) = (b tensor 1) tensor (b'*mu tensor lambda): equal. Multiplicative: Psi of ((b tensor b') tensor lambda)((c tensor c') tensor lambda') = (b*c tensor b'*c') tensor lambda*lambda' is (b*c tensor 1) tensor (b'*c' tensor lambda*lambda'); the product of the images is (b*c tensor 1) tensor (b'*lambda*c' tensor lambda*lambda') = (b*c tensor 1) tensor (b'*c'*lambda tensor lambda*lambda') (lambda central in B') = (b*c tensor 1) tensor ((b'*c' tensor 1)*lambda)*lambda' = (b*c tensor 1) tensor (b'*c' tensor lambda*lambda'): equal. K-linear: Psi(((b tensor b') tensor lambda)*nu) = (b tensor 1) tensor (b' tensor lambda*nu) = Psi((b tensor b') tensor lambda)*nu. Surjective: (b tensor lambda) tensor (b' tensor mu) = (b tensor 1)*lambda tensor (b' tensor mu) = (b tensor 1) tensor lambda*(b' tensor mu) = (b tensor 1) tensor (b' tensor lambda*mu) = Psi((b tensor b') tensor lambda*mu). Since dim_K of source and target are both dim_K B * dim_K B', Psi is an isomorphism.

(d) Consequently sigma_*: Br(K) -> Br(K), sigma_*[B] := [B^sigma], is a well-defined group automorphism. Well-defined on Brauer classes: if B is similar to the division algebra D, B = M_r(D), then B^sigma = M_r(D)^sigma is isomorphic to M_r(D^sigma) by (b), so [B^sigma] = [D^sigma] depends only on the class of B. Homomorphism: (B tensor_K B')^sigma is isomorphic to B^sigma tensor_K B'^sigma by (c). Bijective: by 1(v), the composition B -> B^rho -> (B^rho)^sigma of a rho-semilinear and a sigma-semilinear ring isomorphism is a (sigma o rho)-semilinear ring isomorphism (it sends mu*beta to sigma(rho(mu)) times the image), hence (B^rho)^sigma is isomorphic to B^{sigma o rho}; therefore sigma_* o rho_* = (sigma o rho)_*, and sigma_* has inverse (sigma^{-1})_*.

This is exactly the standard meaning of the action of Aut(K) on Br(K) through its action on K: by 1(v), sigma_*[B] is the Brauer class of the central simple K-algebra obtained from B by transport of structure along the automorphism sigma of the ground field, equivalently (by (a)) by applying sigma to the structure constants. (As a consistency check only, and not used below: under Br(K) = H^2(G_K, K_s^x) this is the action obtained by extending sigma to K_s and setting (sigma.f)(gamma, delta) = sigma(f(sigma^{-1} gamma sigma, sigma^{-1} delta sigma)).)

=====================================================================
STEP 3. Extension of sigma to L -> L'.

By Step 0(b), L = K(w) and L' = K(w') are fields, Galois of degree p over K, generated respectively by tau (tau(w) = w + 1) and tau' (tau'(w') = w' + 1). The minimal polynomial of w over K is f_b(T) = T^p - T - b; applying sigma to its coefficients gives f_{sigma(b)}(T) = T^p - T - sigma(b), of which w' is a root. Define sigma~: L -> L' by sigma~(sum_{i=0}^{p-1} a_i w^i) = sum_{i=0}^{p-1} sigma(a_i) w'^i. This is well defined: if h(T) in K[T] satisfies h(w) = 0 then f_b divides h in K[T], so applying sigma to the coefficients gives f_{sigma(b)} dividing sigma(h) in K[T], hence sigma(h)(w') = 0. It is a ring homomorphism (multiplication in L is computed by reducing with w^p = w + b, and the same reduction in L' uses w'^p = w' + sigma(b), which is the sigma-image of the former), it is bijective with inverse defined using sigma^{-1}, it extends sigma (constants go to their sigma-image), and sigma~(w) = w'.
Now set tau'_0 := sigma~ o tau o sigma~^{-1}, an automorphism of L'. It fixes K pointwise: for nu in K, sigma~^{-1}(nu) = sigma^{-1}(nu) in K, tau fixes it, and sigma~ returns sigma(sigma^{-1}(nu)) = nu. And tau'_0(w') = sigma~(tau(w)) = sigma~(w + 1) = w' + 1. By Step 0(b) the automorphism of L' sending w' to w' + 1 is unique, so tau'_0 = tau'. Hence tau'^i o sigma~ = sigma~ o tau^i on L for all i >= 0.

=====================================================================
STEP 4. A^sigma is K-isomorphic to (L'/K, tau', sigma(x)) = A'.

Define Psi_0: A -> A' by Psi_0(sum_{i=0}^{p-1} l_i u^i) = sum_{i=0}^{p-1} sigma~(l_i) v^i. It is a bijection of abelian groups (sigma~ is a field isomorphism and both algebras are free of rank p over L resp. L' with the displayed bases). It is multiplicative: it suffices to check on homogeneous elements a = l*u^i, a' = m*u^j; write i + j = q*p + r with 0 <= r < p. Then aa' = l*u^i*m*u^j = l*tau^i(m)*u^{i+j} = l*tau^i(m)*x^q*u^r (as u^p = x in K^x), so Psi_0(aa') = sigma~(l*tau^i(m)*x^q) v^r = sigma~(l)*sigma~(tau^i(m))*sigma(x)^q v^r (using sigma~(x) = sigma(x) since x in K). On the other hand Psi_0(a)Psi_0(a') = sigma~(l)*v^i*sigma~(m)*v^j = sigma~(l)*tau'^i(sigma~(m))*v^{i+j} = sigma~(l)*sigma~(tau^i(m))*sigma(x)^q v^r, where we used v*lambda' = tau'(lambda')*v, the identity tau'^i o sigma~ = sigma~ o tau^i from Step 3, and v^{i+j} = v^{qp} v^r = sigma(x)^q v^r. The two expressions coincide. Also Psi_0(nu*a) = sigma(nu)*Psi_0(a) for nu in K, since sigma~ extends sigma. Thus Psi_0 is a sigma-semilinear ring isomorphism.

By Step 1(v), Psi_0 induces a K-algebra isomorphism Psi: A^sigma -> A', Psi(a tensor lambda) = Psi_0(a)*lambda. For completeness: Psi is well defined because Psi_0(a*mu)*lambda = sigma(mu)*Psi_0(a)*lambda = Psi_0(a)*sigma(mu)*lambda = Psi(a tensor sigma(mu)*lambda); it is multiplicative, Psi((a tensor lambda)(a' tensor lambda')) = Psi_0(aa')*lambda*lambda' = Psi_0(a)Psi_0(a')*lambda*lambda' = Psi(a tensor lambda)*Psi(a' tensor lambda') (lambda is central in A'), and K-linear, Psi((a tensor lambda)*nu) = Psi_0(a)*lambda*nu = Psi(a tensor lambda)*nu. It is surjective because Psi(w^i u^j tensor 1) = sigma~(w^i) v^j = w'^i v^j, which form a K-basis of A'; and dim_K A^sigma = dim_K A = p^2 = dim_K A' by Step 1(iii), so Psi is an isomorphism. Since A is central simple over K (Step 0(b), ref_22(i)), Step 1(iv) shows A^sigma is central simple over K as well.

Sanity check on conventions: applying sigma to the structure constants of A in the basis {w^i u^j} amounts to replacing the relations w^p = w + b, u^p = x, u*w = (w+1)*u by w'^p = w' + sigma(b), u'^p = sigma(x), u'*w' = (w'+1)*u', which is precisely the algebra (K(w')/K, tau', sigma(x)) = A'; this agrees with the explicit isomorphism just constructed.

=====================================================================
STEP 5. Conclusion.

By definition [b, x) = [A] in Br(K). Using Step 2 for the action of sigma on Br(K) through its action on K, then Step 4, then the definition of the symbol on the right,
   sigma([b, x)) = sigma_*[A] = [A^sigma] = [A'] = [(L'/K, tau', sigma(x))] = [sigma(b), sigma(x)).
All terms are defined thanks to Step 0: sigma(b) is not in wp(K) and sigma(x) is in K^x. This is the required identity. (Note that neither b nor x is assumed to satisfy anything beyond b not in wp(K) and x in K^x, and no additional hypothesis on K/k beyond sigma being a K-automorphism was used.)

lemma_89.statement: Let K/k be a finite field extension of degree n and let α be a class in the Brauer group Br(k). Then the index of the image of α in Br(K) divides the index of α, and the index of α divides n times the index of the image of α in Br(K). In particular, if p is a prime, [K:k] = p, and the image of α in Br(K) has index p, then α has index p or index p^2.
lemma_89.proof:
We write ind(β) for the index of a Brauer class β over a field F, i.e. the degree of the unique (up to F-isomorphism) central division F-algebra representing β; thus ind(0)=1. The proof uses only two standard facts about central simple algebras, which we recall and justify.

(Structure fact A: Wedderburn–Artin.) Every central simple F-algebra B is isomorphic to M_s(Γ) for some s ≥ 1 and some central division F-algebra Γ, unique up to isomorphism; by definition ind([B]) = deg Γ.

(Structure fact B: stability under scalar extension.) If B is central simple over k and K/k is any field extension, then B_K := B ⊗_k K is central simple over K. Indeed, let Ω be an algebraic closure of K. Then (B ⊗_k K) ⊗_K Ω ≅ B ⊗_k Ω. Since B is central simple over k, B ⊗_k Ω ≅ M_m(Ω) for some m (a splitting field argument), which is simple. If I ⊊ B_K were a nonzero two-sided ideal, then, Ω being free (hence faithfully flat) over K, I ⊗_K Ω would be a nonzero proper two-sided ideal of M_m(Ω), a contradiction; hence B_K is simple. For the center: Z(B)⊗_k K = k ⊗_k K = K is contained in Z(B_K); conversely, if z ∈ Z(B_K), its image in B ⊗_k Ω ≅ M_m(Ω) is central, so z = 1 ⊗ μ with μ ∈ Ω (the map B_K → B ⊗_k Ω is injective because Ω is free over K). Choose a k-linear form f: B → k with f(1)=1; applying f ⊗ id to z = Σ_i b_i ⊗ λ_i (b_i a k-basis of B) gives μ = Σ_i f(b_i)λ_i ∈ K. Hence Z(B_K) = K.

Now let n = [K:k], let D be the central division k-algebra representing α, and put d := deg D = ind(α). The image of α in Br(K) is the restriction res(α) = [D ⊗_k K] = [D_K].

Step 1 (ind(res α) divides ind(α)). By Structure fact B, D_K is central simple over K, and by Structure fact A there are an integer r ≥ 1 and a central division K-algebra Δ such that
    D_K ≅ M_r(Δ),      δ := deg Δ = ind(res α).
Compare K-dimensions. Since a k-basis of D is a K-basis of D ⊗_k K, we have dim_K D_K = dim_k D = d². On the other hand dim_K M_r(Δ) = r²·dim_K Δ = r²δ². Therefore
    d² = r² δ²,   whence   d = r δ.
In particular δ | d, i.e. ind(res_{K/k} α) divides ind(α). This is the first divisibility.

Step 2 (ind(α) divides n · ind(res α)). Keep the isomorphism φ: D_K → M_r(Δ) of Step 1, and let e_{11} ∈ M_r(Δ) be the matrix unit. Set
    P := M_r(Δ) e_{11} = { matrices in M_r(Δ) whose only possibly non-zero column is the first one }.
(a) As a K-vector space, P is a direct sum of r copies of Δ (one copy for each row), so
    dim_K P = r · dim_K Δ = r δ²,      hence      dim_k P = [K:k] · dim_K P = n r δ²,
where the k-vector space structure is the one obtained by restriction of scalars along k ⊂ K = Z(M_r(Δ)).
(b) Via φ^{-1}, P is a left ideal of D_K, hence a left D_K-module; restricting scalars along the k-algebra embedding ι: D → D_K, d ↦ d ⊗ 1, it becomes a left D-module, and the action is k-linear. Since D is a division ring, every D-module is free; P ≠ 0, so P ≅ D^{⊕ t} as left D-modules for some integer t ≥ 1, and therefore
    dim_k P = t · dim_k D = t d².
(c) Equating the two expressions for dim_k P gives t d² = n r δ². Using r²δ² = d² from Step 1, we have r δ² = d²/r, so
    t d² = n · d² / r,   i.e.   t = n / r.
Since t is an integer, r divides n; write n = r t.
(d) Finally, by Step 1, ind(α) = d = r δ. Multiplying by t and using n = r t and δ = ind(res α),
    n · ind(res α) = (r t) δ = t · (r δ) = t · ind(α).
Thus ind(α) divides n · ind(res_{K/k} α) = [K:k] · ind(res_{K/k} α). This is the second divisibility. (Note that the edge case n = 1, i.e. K = k, is covered: then r = 1, t = 1, and both divisibilities are equalities.)

Step 3 (the particular case). Suppose p is a prime, [K:k] = p, and ind(res_{K/k} α) = p. The two divisibilities proved in Steps 1 and 2 give
    p = ind(res α)  |  ind(α)  |  [K:k] · ind(res α) = p · p = p².
The positive divisors of p² are 1, p, p². Since p divides ind(α), the value 1 is excluded. Hence
    ind(α) ∈ { p, p² },
exactly as claimed. (Both values do occur in general: ind(α) = p when α itself has index p, and ind(α) = p² when a degree-p extension reduces the index from p² to p, e.g. when K embeds in the division algebra of degree p² representing α.) This completes the proof.

lemma_90.statement: Let k be a field, let n be a positive integer, and let D be a central division k-algebra of degree n. If D contains a maximal subfield L that is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group generated by σ, then there exists a ∈ k^× such that D is isomorphic to the cyclic k-algebra (L/k, σ, a) = ⊕_{i=0}^{n-1} L u^i with u^n = a and uλ = σ(λ)u for all λ ∈ L; in particular D is a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) for the cyclic group G of order n.
lemma_90.proof:
We fix notation. D is a central division k-algebra of degree n, so dim_k D = n^2 and Z(D) = k. L ⊂ D is a maximal subfield, Galois over k, with Gal(L/k) = ⟨σ⟩ cyclic of order n. We prove D ≅ (L/k, σ, a) for some a ∈ k^×, and then read off the crossed-product structure.

STEP 0 (the case n = 1). If n = 1 then dim_k D = 1, so D = k and L = k, σ = id_k, G = {1}. Taking a = 1 ∈ k^×, the cyclic algebra (k/k, id, 1) = ⊕_{i=0}^{0} k·u^0 = k equals D, and the crossed-product claim is trivial (c ≡ 1). Henceforth assume n ≥ 2; all arguments below also cover n = 1 but we keep n ≥ 2 for readability.

STEP 1 ([L : k] = n). Put m = [L : k]. By the double centralizer theorem for central simple algebras (ref_1), C_D(L) is a central simple L-algebra of degree deg(D)/[L:k] = n/m (so m | n) and dim_k L · dim_k C_D(L) = dim_k D, i.e. dim_k C_D(L) = n^2/m. If m < n then dim_k C_D(L) = n^2/m > n = dim_k L, so we may pick α ∈ C_D(L) \ L. The k-subalgebra L(α) ⊂ C_D(L) generated by L and α is commutative (it lies in the centralizer of L, and L(α) is generated by the commuting set L ∪ {α}), and it is a domain finite-dimensional over k, hence a field (every nonzero element of L(α) is invertible in D, and its inverse is a k-polynomial in α: if 0 ≠ β ∈ L(α), multiplication by β is an injective, hence surjective, k-linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional k-space L(α), so 1 = βγ for some γ ∈ L(α)). Thus L(α) is a field strictly containing L, contradicting the maximality of L as a subfield of D. Therefore m = n, i.e. [L : k] = n = deg D, and C_D(L) has L-dimension 1, so
(1)  C_D(L) = L.
Since L/k is Galois, it is finite separable, hence L is a commutative etale k-algebra of dimension n = deg D.

STEP 2 (Skolem–Noether for σ). Since L is a commutative etale subalgebra of the central simple k-algebra D with dim_k L = n = deg(D), part (iv) of ref_2 applies: every k-algebra automorphism of L is induced by an inner automorphism of D. Applying this to σ ∈ Gal(L/k), we obtain an element u ∈ D^× such that
(2)  u λ u^{-1} = σ(λ) for all λ ∈ L, equivalently u λ = σ(λ) u for all λ ∈ L.

STEP 3 (the powers of u act as the powers of σ). By induction on i ≥ 0: for i = 0 this is trivial; if u^i λ u^{-i} = σ^i(λ), then u^{i+1} λ u^{-(i+1)} = u σ^i(λ) u^{-1} = σ(σ^i(λ)) = σ^{i+1}(λ), using (2) with λ replaced by σ^i(λ). Hence for all i ≥ 0 and λ ∈ L,
(3)  u^i λ = σ^i(λ) u^i.

STEP 4 (Dedekind independence of 1, σ, …, σ^{n-1} inside D). Claim: if λ_0, …, λ_{n-1} ∈ L satisfy Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} λ_i u^i = 0, then all λ_i = 0. Proof: suppose some relation has a nonzero coefficient, and choose one with r = #{i : λ_i ≠ 0} minimal. Then r ≥ 2, because r = 1 would give λ_i u^i = 0 for some i, and multiplying on the right by u^{-i} (which exists since u ∈ D^×) gives λ_i = 0, contradiction. Choose distinct i_0, j ∈ {i : λ_i ≠ 0}. Since σ has order exactly n and 0 ≤ i_0 ≠ j ≤ n−1, the automorphisms σ^{i_0} and σ^j of L are distinct; hence there is μ ∈ L with σ^{i_0}(μ) ≠ σ^j(μ). Multiplying Σ λ_i u^i = 0 on the right by μ and using (3) gives Σ_i λ_i σ^i(μ) u^i = 0. Multiplying the original relation on the left by the scalar σ^{i_0}(μ) ∈ L (which commutes with each λ_i, L being commutative) gives Σ_i σ^{i_0}(μ) λ_i u^i = 0. Subtracting yields
  Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} λ_i (σ^i(μ) − σ^{i_0}(μ)) u^i = 0.
The coefficient of u^{i_0} in this relation is λ_{i_0}(σ^{i_0}(μ) − σ^{i_0}(μ)) = 0, whereas the coefficient of u^j is λ_j (σ^j(μ) − σ^{i_0}(μ)), a product of two nonzero elements of the division algebra D, hence nonzero. Thus we have produced a nontrivial relation with at most r − 1 nonzero coefficients, contradicting the minimality of r. The claim follows. ∎

STEP 5 (D is a free left L-module with basis 1, u, …, u^{n-1}). For each i, right multiplication by u^i is a k-linear isomorphism L →→ L u^i, so each L u^i is an n-dimensional k-subspace of D. By Step 4 the sum Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} L u^i is direct, hence it is a k-subspace of dimension n · n = n^2 = dim_k D, and therefore
(4)  D = ⊕_{i=0}^{n-1} L u^i,
every element of D being written uniquely as Σ_i λ_i u^i with λ_i ∈ L.

STEP 6 (the parameter a). We show a := u^n lies in k^×. Let x = Σ_i λ_i u^i ∈ D. Using (3) with i = n and σ^n = id_L (σ has order n),
  u^n x = Σ_i u^n λ_i u^i = Σ_i σ^n(λ_i) u^{n+i} = Σ_i λ_i u^{n+i} = Σ_i λ_i u^i u^n = x u^n.
So u^n ∈ Z(D) = k. Since u ∈ D^×, also u^n ∈ D^×, so u^n ≠ 0 and
(5)  a := u^n ∈ k^×.

STEP 7 (the isomorphism with the cyclic algebra). Let A := (L/k, σ, a) be the cyclic algebra: as a left L-vector space A has basis e_0 = 1, e_1, …, e_{n-1}, and multiplication is given on basis elements by
  (λ e_i)(μ e_j) = λ σ^i(μ) e_{i+j} if i + j ≤ n − 1,   (λ e_i)(μ e_j) = λ σ^i(μ) a e_{i+j-n} if n ≤ i + j ≤ 2n − 2;
equivalently A is the k-algebra generated by L and a symbol e with relations e λ = σ(λ) e (λ ∈ L) and e^n = a. Define
  Φ : A → D,   Φ(Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} λ_i e_i) = Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} λ_i u^i.
By Step 4/5, Φ is a well-defined k-linear bijection (basis to basis), and Φ(1) = 1 = u^0. We check multiplicativity on basis elements. Take 0 ≤ i, j ≤ n − 1. In D,
  (λ u^i)(μ u^j) = λ (u^i μ) u^j = λ σ^i(μ) u^{i+j}  by (3).
If i + j ≤ n − 1 this equals λ σ^i(μ) u^{i+j} = Φ(λ σ^i(μ) e_{i+j}) = Φ((λ e_i)(μ e_j)). If n ≤ i + j ≤ 2n − 2, then u^{i+j} = u^{i+j-n} u^n = a u^{i+j-n} (as a ∈ k ⊂ Z(D)), so
  (λ u^i)(μ u^j) = λ σ^i(μ) a u^{i+j-n} = Φ(λ σ^i(μ) a e_{i+j-n}) = Φ((λ e_i)(μ e_j)).
Thus Φ preserves products of basis elements, hence all products by k-bilinearity, and Φ is a k-algebra isomorphism
(6)  D ≅ (L/k, σ, a) = ⊕_{i=0}^{n-1} L u^i,  u^n = a,  u λ = σ(λ) u.

STEP 8 (D is a crossed product (L, G, c) for the cyclic group G of order n). Let G := Gal(L/k) = ⟨σ⟩, a group of order n. Then L is a Galois G-algebra over k in the sense of the definition: (i) L is etale over k (finite separable, Step 1); (ii) dim_k L = n = |G| (Step 1); (iii) G acts on L by k-automorphisms; (iv) L^G = k by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory. Define elements u_g ∈ D^× for g ∈ G by u_{σ^i} := u^i (0 ≤ i ≤ n − 1), and define c : G × G → L^× by
  c(σ^i, σ^j) := u^i u^j u^{-(i+j mod n)} =  1 if i + j ≤ n − 1,   a if n ≤ i + j ≤ 2n − 2,
which indeed takes values in k^× ⊂ L^×.

We verify the two defining relations of the crossed product (L, G, c). For g = σ^i and x = λ ∈ L,
  u_g x = u^i λ = σ^i(λ) u^i = g(x) u_g   by (3);
and for g = σ^i, h = σ^j, writing r ≡ i + j (mod n), 0 ≤ r ≤ n − 1, the definition of c gives u^i u^j = c(σ^i, σ^j) u^r = c(g, h) u_{gh} directly (both cases i + j ≤ n − 1 and i + j ≥ n are exactly the two branches of the definition of c). Finally, c is a 2-cocycle: for i, j, k ∈ {0, …, n − 1}, associativity in D gives (u^i u^j) u^k = u^i (u^j u^k), i.e.
  c(σ^i, σ^j) c(σ^{i+j mod n}, σ^k) u^{(i+j+k) mod n} = c(σ^j, σ^k) c(σ^i, σ^{j+k mod n}) u^{(i+j+k) mod n}.
Since u^{(i+j+k) mod n} ∈ D^× and the coefficients lie in k^× ⊂ Z(D), multiplying on the right by its inverse yields
  c(σ^i, σ^j) c(σ^{i+j mod n}, σ^k) = c(σ^j, σ^k) c(σ^i, σ^{j+k mod n}),
which is precisely the cocycle identity for c on G × G × G (identifying G with Z/n via σ^i ↔ i). Moreover c is normalized: u_{1_G} = u^0 = 1, so c(1_G, σ^i) = u^0 u^i u^{-i} = 1 and c(σ^i, 1_G) = u^i u^0 u^{-i} = 1.
By (4), D = ⊕_{g ∈ G} L u_g as a k-vector space, and the multiplication is governed by the two relations above; hence, by the definition of a crossed product algebra,
  D ≅ (L, G, c)
for the cyclic group G of order n and the cocycle c. Combined with (6), this completes the proof of the lemma.

lemma_crossed_p2_has_cyclic_subfield.statement: Let k be a field, let p be a prime, and let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p^2. If D is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) for a group G of order p^2 and a Galois G-algebra L over k, then D contains a subfield K such that K/k is a Galois field extension of degree p with cyclic Galois group.
lemma_crossed_p2_has_cyclic_subfield.proof:
Let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$, and suppose $D\simeq (L,G,c)$ where $G$ is a group of order $p^2$ and $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$.

**Step 1: $L$ is a Galois maximal subfield of $D$ with group $G$.**
We apply the proved lemma lemma_78 (Spark) to $D$: its hypotheses are that $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $|G|$ and that $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for a Galois $G$-algebra $L$ over $k$. Here $|G|=p^2=\deg D$, so the hypotheses hold. The conclusion is that $L$ is a field, that its image $L'$ in $D$ is a maximal subfield of $D$, and that $L'/k$ is a Galois field extension whose Galois group is $G$ (the isomorphism $\operatorname{Gal}(L'/k)\xrightarrow{\sim} G$ being the one transported from the crossed-product structure, in which $G$ acts on $L$ by $k$-automorphisms and $L^G=k$).
For readability we identify $L$ with its image $L'\subset D$. Thus:
\[
L\subset D \text{ is a maximal subfield},\qquad L/k \text{ is Galois with } \operatorname{Gal}(L/k)=G,\qquad [L:k]=|G|=p^2,\qquad L^G=k .
\]
(The equality $[L:k]=|G|$ holds because $L/k$ is Galois with group $G$.)

**Step 2: Every group of order $p^2$ is abelian.**
Write the class equation for the conjugation action of $G$ on itself:
\[
|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i [G:C_G(x_i)],
\]
where $x_i$ runs over representatives of the conjugacy classes of $G$ of size $>1$. Each index $[G:C_G(x_i)]$ divides $|G|=p^2$ and is $>1$, hence equals $p$ or $p^2$; in particular each is divisible by $p$. Reducing the class equation modulo $p$ gives $|Z(G)|\equiv |G|\equiv 0\pmod p$. Since $Z(G)$ is a subgroup, $|Z(G)|\in\{p,p^2\}$.
If $|Z(G)|=p$, then $G/Z(G)$ has order $p$ and is therefore cyclic; let $aZ(G)$ be a generator. Every element of $G$ is then of the form $a^iz$ with $z\in Z(G)$, and for $g=a^iz$, $g'=a^jz'$ we have
\[
 gg'=a^{i}z\,a^{j}z'=a^{i+j}zz'=a^{j+i}z'z=g'g,
\]
using that $z,z'$ are central and that powers of $a$ commute with each other and with central elements. Thus $G$ would be abelian, whence $Z(G)=G$, contradicting $|Z(G)|=p<p^2$. Therefore $|Z(G)|=p^2$, i.e. $Z(G)=G$ and $G$ is abelian.

**Step 3: $G$ has a subgroup $H$ of order $p$, and it is normal.**
We prove this special case of Cauchy's theorem directly. Let
\[
S=\{(x_1,\dots,x_p)\in G^p : x_1x_2\cdots x_p=1\}.
\]
The first $p-1$ entries may be chosen arbitrarily in $G$ and then $x_p=(x_1\cdots x_{p-1})^{-1}$ is forced, so $|S|=|G|^{p-1}=p^{2(p-1)}$, which is divisible by $p$ (since $2(p-1)\ge 1$ for every prime $p$). The cyclic group $C_p=\langle \rho\rangle$ acts on $S$ by the rotation $\rho(x_1,\dots,x_p)=(x_2,\dots,x_p,x_1)$; this preserves $S$ because $x_1\cdots x_p=1$ is equivalent to $x_2\cdots x_px_1=1$ (in a group, $ab=1\Rightarrow ba=1$). By orbit-stabiliser, each orbit has size $1$ or $p$ (the stabiliser is a subgroup of $C_p$, whose only subgroups are $1$ and $C_p$). Hence, modulo $p$, $|S|$ equals the number of fixed points of $\rho$. A tuple is fixed by $\rho$ exactly when all its entries are equal, say $x$, with $x^p=1$; so the number of fixed points is $N:=\#\{x\in G: x^p=1\}$. Thus $N\equiv |S|\equiv 0\pmod p$. Since $1^p=1$, $N\ge 1$, so $N\ge p$ and there exists $x\in G$, $x\neq 1$, with $x^p=1$. The order of $x$ divides $p$ and is $>1$, hence equals $p$, and $H:=\langle x\rangle$ is a subgroup of $G$ of order $p$. Because $G$ is abelian (Step 2), every subgroup is normal; in particular $H\trianglelefteq G$.

**Step 4: The fixed field $K:=L^H$ is a subfield of $D$, Galois over $k$ of degree $p$.**
Since $G$ acts on $L$ by $k$-automorphisms, every element of $H$ fixes $k$ pointwise, so $k\subseteq L^H=:K\subseteq L\subseteq D$; thus $K$ is an intermediate field of $L/k$ contained in $D$.

(i) Degree over $L^H$: by Artin's theorem on the fixed field of a finite group of automorphisms, $L/L^H$ is Galois with Galois group exactly $H$, so $[L:K]=[L:L^H]=|H|=p$. Consequently
\[
[K:k]=\frac{[L:k]}{[L:K]}=\frac{p^2}{p}=p .
\]

(ii) $K$ is $G$-stable: let $\sigma\in G$, $x\in K$ and $h\in H$. Since $H\trianglelefteq G$ we have $\sigma^{-1}h\sigma\in H$, which fixes $x$; hence $h(\sigma(x))=\sigma\big((\sigma^{-1}h\sigma)(x)\big)=\sigma(x)$. So $\sigma(x)$ is fixed by every $h\in H$, i.e. $\sigma(x)\in K$. Thus each $\sigma\in G$ restricts to a $k$-automorphism of $K$, giving a homomorphism (restriction) $\rho\colon G\to \operatorname{Aut}(K/k)$.

(iii) Kernel of $\rho$: $\ker\rho=\{\sigma\in G:\sigma|_K=\mathrm{id}\}=\operatorname{Gal}(L/L^H)=H$, the last equality being Artin's theorem again. Hence $|\rho(G)|=[G:H]=p$.

(iv) Normality of $K/k$: let $x\in K$ and let $f\in k[T]$ be its minimal polynomial over $k$. Consider $P(T)=\prod_{\sigma\in G}(T-\sigma(x))\in L[T]$. For any $\tau\in G$, the map $\sigma\mapsto\tau\sigma$ permutes $G$, so $\tau$ permutes the roots of $P$ and therefore fixes each coefficient of $P$; the coefficients lie in $L^G=k$, so $P\in k[T]$. Clearly $f\mid P$ in $k[T]$ (as $P(x)=0$ and $P$ is a polynomial over $k$), and $P$ splits into linear factors in $L$ with all roots $\sigma(x)$ belonging to $K$ by (ii). Hence $f$ splits over $K$, so $K/k$ is normal.

(v) Separability of $K/k$: $L/k$ is Galois, hence separable; every element of $K$ lies in $L$, so its minimal polynomial over $k$ is separable. Thus $K/k$ is separable.

From (iv) and (v), $K/k$ is a Galois extension, so $|\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)|=[K:k]=p$ by (i). The restriction map $\rho\colon G\to\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)$ has image of order $p$ by (iii), hence is surjective, and induces an isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)\;\cong\; G/H .
\]

**Step 5: The Galois group is cyclic.**
$G/H$ is a group of order $p$, where $p$ is prime. Any non-identity element of $G/H$ has order dividing $p$ by Lagrange's theorem and order $>1$, hence order exactly $p$, so $G/H$ is generated by it and is cyclic, isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

**Conclusion.** $K=L^H$ is a subfield of $D$ (as $k\subseteq K\subseteq L\subseteq D$), the extension $K/k$ has degree $p$, is Galois, and has cyclic Galois group $\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)\cong G/H\cong\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. This is exactly the required subfield.

(Remark on scope: no Brauer-group, valuation-theoretic, or cyclicity-of-$D$ input was used, and in particular no statement about degree $p^2$, exponent $p^2$ algebras being cyclic; the argument is purely Galois-theoretic, relying only on lemma_78 to promote the Galois $G$-algebra $L$ to a Galois maximal subfield of the division algebra $D$, together with the elementary group theory of groups of order $p^2$ proved in Steps 2 and 3.)

lemma_92.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, complete for a discrete valuation $v$ with uniformizer $\pi$ and residue field $\bar k$. Let $L/K$ be a totally ramified cyclic Galois extension of degree $p$ whose residue field is $\bar k$. If $\alpha\in K^\times$ lies in the norm group $N_{L/K}(L^\times)$ and $p$ divides $v(\alpha)$, then the residue of $\alpha\,\pi^{-v(\alpha)}$ in $\bar k^\times$ is a $p$-th power.
lemma_92.proof:
NOTATION. Write A = O_K = {a in K : v(a) >= 0} ∪ {0} for the valuation ring of K, m_A = πA for its maximal ideal (v(π) = 1), k̄ = A/πA for the residue field, and G = Gal(L/K), so |G| = p = [L:K]. Since L/K is Galois it is separable, and for t in L the trace is Tr_{L/K}(t) = Σ_{σ∈G} σ(t), while the norm is N_{L/K}(t) = ∏_{σ∈G} σ(t) (both identities hold because L/K is Galois of degree p = |G|, so the K-embeddings of L into an algebraic closure are exactly the elements of G).

STEP 1. THE INTEGRAL CLOSURE B OF A IN L IS A DVR; IT IS THE VALUATION RING OF THE UNIQUE EXTENSION w OF v TO L; ITS RESIDUE FIELD IS k̄.

1a. (Integral elements; a lattice inside B; Frac(B) = L.) Let x ∈ L and let T^m + c_{m-1}T^{m-1} + ... + c_1 T + c_0 ∈ K[T] be its minimal polynomial over K. Since v is discrete and there are only finitely many c_i, we can choose N ≥ 0 such that a := π^N ∈ A satisfies a·c_i ∈ A for every i. Put y := a x. Multiplying the equation x^m + c_{m-1}x^{m-1} + ... + c_0 = 0 by a^m gives
   y^m + (a c_{m-1}) y^{m-1} + (a^2 c_{m-2}) y^{m-2} + ... + (a^{m-1} c_1) y + a^m c_0 = 0,
and each coefficient a^{m-i} c_i = a^{m-i-1}(a c_i) lies in A. Hence y is integral over A, i.e. y ∈ B. (This replaces the incorrect parenthetical of the earlier attempt: no claim is made that a K-linear expression in a non-integral element is integral; integrality is obtained only after the substitution y = ax, where the coefficients genuinely lie in A.) Apply this to the elements x_1,...,x_p of any K-basis of L, producing nonzero a_i ∈ A with y_i := a_i x_i ∈ B. Since a_i ≠ 0, the y_i are again a K-basis of L. Thus M := Σ_i A y_i is a free A-submodule of rank p with M ⊆ B. Moreover Frac(B) = L: given z ∈ L write z = Σ μ_i y_i with μ_i ∈ K, take a common denominator s ∈ A\{0} for the μ_i; then s z = Σ (s μ_i) y_i ∈ B, so z = (s z)/s ∈ Frac(B).

1b. (B is finite free of rank p over A.) A K-automorphism of L preserves integrality over A, so σ(B) = B for all σ ∈ G. For b ∈ B and m ∈ M we have bm ∈ B (B is a ring), hence Tr(bm) = Σ_{σ∈G} σ(bm) ∈ B ∩ K = A; the last equality holds because A is integrally closed in K and elements of B ∩ K are integral over A. Thus B ⊆ M^# := {z ∈ L : Tr(zM) ⊆ A}. The trace pairing is non-degenerate (L/K separable), so z ↦ (m ↦ Tr(zm)) identifies M^# with Hom_A(M, A), a free A-module of rank p. A is a PID, B is torsion-free, so B is free of rank ≤ p; since M ⊆ B the rank is exactly p. In particular B is noetherian and B/πB is a finite-dimensional k̄-vector space.

1c. (B is local.) The prime ideals of B/πB are the primes of B containing π; since B is integral over A and dim A = 1, these are exactly the maximal ideals m_1,...,m_g of B (lying over (π)). Because B/πB is artinian, rad(B/πB) = (∩_i m_i)/πB is nilpotent: with m := ∩_i m_i we have m^t ⊆ πB ⊆ m. As a finite module over the complete noetherian local ring A, B is separated and complete for the (π)-adic topology; since πB ⊆ m ⊆ rad(B) and m^t ⊆ πB, the (π)-adic and m-adic topologies coincide, and the Chinese remainder theorem (the m_i are pairwise comaximal) gives
   B ≅ lim_t B/π^t B ≅ lim_t B/m^t B ≅ ∏_{i=1}^{g} (lim_t B/m_i^t B) =: ∏_{i=1}^{g} B_i,
with all B_i nonzero. If g ≥ 2, the product contains a non-trivial idempotent e (e = (1,0,...,0)); localising B ≅ ∏ B_i at B\{0} then gives 0 = e·(1-e) with 1-e ≠ 0 an inverted element, hence 1 = 0 in the localisation, contradicting Frac(B) = L ≠ 0 (Step 1a). Therefore g = 1: B is local. It is a noetherian local domain, integrally closed in its fraction field L (any element of L integral over B is integral over A, hence in B), of dimension 1 (integral over A, dim A = 1). Hence B is a discrete valuation ring.

1d. (Uniqueness of the extension; G-invariance of w.) Let w_B be the normalized valuation of B (w_B(B^×) = Z), let e := w_B(π) ≥ 1, and set w := w_B/e. Then w: L^× → (1/e)Z is a discrete valuation with w(π) = 1, hence w|_K = v; its valuation ring is B and its units are exactly {x ∈ L^× : w(x) = 0} = B^×. Let w' be any valuation of L extending v, with ring R. Then B ⊆ R, since elements integral over A are integral over R and a valuation ring is integrally closed. We first show m_B ⊆ m_{w'}. Take b ∈ m_B and n ≥ 1: then w_B(b^n) ≥ n ≥ e⌊n/e⌋, so b^n = π^{⌊n/e⌋} c_n with c_n ∈ B; therefore w'(b^n) = ⌊n/e⌋·v(π) + w'(c_n) ≥ ⌊n/e⌋, because c_n ∈ B ⊆ R. As w'(b^n) = n·w'(b) and ⌊n/e⌋ → ∞, we must have w'(b) > 0, i.e. b ∈ m_{w'}. Now if x ∈ R \ B then w_B(x) < 0, so x^{-1} ∈ m_B ⊆ m_{w'} ⊆ R, whence x ∈ R^×; but then in the residue field R/m_{w'} we would have 1 = overline{x·x^{-1}} = overline{x}·0 = 0, absurd. Thus R = B: the valuation v has a unique extension to L, namely w, with ring B. Uniqueness implies w∘σ = w for every σ ∈ G, because w∘σ is again a valuation of L extending v.

1e. (Residue field; G acts trivially on it.) The hypothesis that L/K is totally ramified of degree p with residue field k̄ means precisely that the natural map A/πA → B/m_B is an isomorphism; we identify both with k̄. For b ∈ B choose a ∈ A with b − a ∈ m_B; then σ(b) − a = σ(b − a) ∈ σ(m_B) = m_B (σ is an automorphism of the local ring B), so σ(b) ≡ a ≡ b (mod m_B). Thus G acts trivially on the residue field k̄ of B.

STEP 2. VALUATION OF A NORM. For x ∈ L^×,
   v(N_{L/K}(x)) = w(N_{L/K}(x))          (as N_{L/K}(x) ∈ K^× and w extends v)
                 = w( ∏_{σ∈G} σ(x) )
                 = Σ_{σ∈G} w(σ x)          (w is a valuation)
                 = p·w(x)                  (w is G-invariant, Step 1d).
(In particular, for a ∈ K^×, N_{L/K}(a) = ∏_σ a = a^p, giving v(N(a)) = p·v(a), consistent with the formula.) Note that nothing here uses the fundamental identity [L:K] = e·f, which can fail in the presence of a defect in characteristic p with imperfect residue field, nor do we need the value group w(L^×) beyond the fact that it contains v(K^×) = Z with w(π) = 1.

STEP 3. NORM OF A UNIT IS A UNIT WHOSE RESIDUE IS A p-TH POWER. This is exactly the content of Spark/lemma_75 (F = K, E = L: a totally ramified extension of degree p with the same residue field k̄); we spell out the short computation. Let η ∈ B^×. Each σ(η) ∈ B^×, so N(η) ∈ B^× ∩ K = A^× (equivalently, w(N(η)) = p·w(η) = 0 by Step 2). Passing to residues in k̄ = B/m_B and using Step 1e,
   overline{N(η)} = ∏_{σ∈G} overline{σ(η)} = ∏_{σ∈G} η̄ = η̄^p ,
so the residue of N(η) is the p-th power of the residue η̄ ∈ k̄^×. (Equivalently, and this is the argument of lemma_75: choose a lift ã ∈ A^× of η̄ — possible because A^× → k̄^× is surjective, which is exactly where the hypothesis 'the residue field of L is k̄' enters — write η = ã(1+δ) with w(δ) > 0; then N(1+δ) = ∏_σ (1+σδ) = 1 + Σ_{i≥1} e_i, where the elementary symmetric functions e_i of the σδ are G-invariant, hence lie in L^G = K, and satisfy v(e_i) = w(e_i) ≥ i·w(δ) > 0; thus N(η) ≡ ã^p mod m_A.)

STEP 4. REDUCTION TO A UNIT AND CONCLUSION. Let α ∈ N_{L/K}(L^×) with p | v(α), and choose x ∈ L^× with α = N_{L/K}(x). By Step 2, p·w(x) = v(α), so w(x) = v(α)/p =: n ∈ Z; this is the only use of the divisibility hypothesis. Set y := x π^{-n}. Then
   w(y) = w(x) − n·w(π) = n − n·1 = 0,
so y ∈ B^×. Furthermore, using N_{L/K}(π) = π^p,
   N_{L/K}(y) = N_{L/K}(x)·N_{L/K}(π)^{-n} = α·(π^p)^{-n} = α π^{-pn} = α π^{-v(α)},
which indeed lies in A^× since v(α π^{-v(α)}) = 0. Applying Step 3 to the unit y ∈ B^×, the residue of N_{L/K}(y) = α π^{-v(α)} in k̄^× equals ȳ^p. Under the identification B/m_B = A/πA = k̄ of Step 1e, the residue of α π^{-v(α)} computed in (B/m_B)^× is the same as its residue computed in (A/πA)^× = k̄^×, since α π^{-v(α)} ∈ A. Hence the residue of α π^{-v(α)} in k̄^× is the p-th power ȳ^p. ∎

REMARKS ON THE POINTS FLAGGED EARLIER. (i) The inconsistent Artin–Schreier presentation of L is not used anywhere: the only properties of L/K that enter are that it is Galois of degree p (for N = product of the p conjugates and for Tr = sum), that the residue field extension is trivial (Steps 1e, 3), and that K is complete (Step 1c, 1d). (ii) The false integrality assertion of the old Step 1a is replaced by the explicit denominator-clearing computation in Step 1a above, which simultaneously yields an integral K-basis, the lattice M ⊆ B, and Frac(B) = L. (iii) No claim such as Π^p ∈ K for a uniformiser Π of L is made, and v∘N = p·w is obtained in Step 2 purely from Galois invariance of the unique extension w, not from the ultrametric inequality; the fundamental identity ef = [L:K] is never invoked, so the argument is valid with imperfect residue field and in the presence of possible defect.

lemma_94.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, fix a separable closure $K_s$ of $K$, and write $\wp(K)=\{x^p-x:x\in K\}$. For $c\in K\setminus\wp(K)$ and $y\in K_s$ with $y^p-y=c$, define $\chi_c:G_K\to\mathbb{F}_p$ by $\chi_c(\gamma)=\gamma(y)-y$; this does not depend on the choice of $y$. Then for $c,c'\in K\setminus\wp(K)$ the characters $\chi_c$ and $\chi_{c'}$ are equal if and only if $c'-c\in\wp(K)$.
lemma_94.proof:
Throughout write $\wp(x)=x^p-x$, and give $G_K=\operatorname{Aut}(K_s/K)$ the Krull topology, whose basic open subgroups are $\operatorname{Gal}(K_s/F)$ for $F/K$ finite inside $K_s$. The proof is self-contained; no external result is cited.

**Step 0: $\wp$ is additive and $\ker\wp=\mathbb F_p$.** For $x,y$ in any field $E$ of characteristic $p$, the binomial theorem gives $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$, because $\binom{p}{i}$ is divisible by $p$ for $0<i<p$. Hence $\wp(x+y)=(x+y)^p-(x+y)=(x^p-x)+(y^p-y)=\wp(x)+\wp(y)$, so $\wp\colon(E,+)\to(E,+)$ is a group homomorphism (in particular $\wp(-x)=-\wp(x)$). Its kernel is the set of roots of $T^p-T$: this polynomial has at most $p$ roots, and all $p$ elements of the prime field $\mathbb F_p$ are roots (Fermat's little theorem), so $\ker\wp=\mathbb F_p$ inside both $K$ and $K_s$.

**Step 1: the roots of $T^p-T-c$.** Fix $c\in K$ and put $f(T)=T^p-T-c\in K[T]$. Then $f'(T)=pT^{p-1}-1=-1\neq0$, so $f$ is separable; since $K_s$ is separably closed, $f$ has a root $y\in K_s$. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$ one has $(y+\lambda)^p-(y+\lambda)=y^p-y+\lambda^p-\lambda=c+0=c$, so the $p$ distinct elements $y+\lambda$ ($\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$) are roots of $f$; as $\deg f=p$, they are exactly the roots of $f$ in $K_s$. Consequently, for $\gamma\in G_K$, the element $\gamma(y)$ is again a root of $f$ (the coefficients of $f$ lie in $K$ and are fixed by $\gamma$), hence $\gamma(y)=y+\lambda$ for a unique $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$, i.e. $\gamma(y)-y\in\mathbb F_p$. (Direct check of the last inclusion: with $\lambda=\gamma(y)-y$, one has $\lambda^p-\lambda=\gamma(y^p-y)-(y^p-y)=\gamma(c)-c=0$, so $\lambda\in\ker(\wp|_{K_s})=\mathbb F_p$.)

**Step 2: $\chi_c$ is well defined.** Define $\chi_c(\gamma):=\gamma(y)-y\in\mathbb F_p$. If $y'=y+\mu$ is another root, with $\mu\in\mathbb F_p$, then, because every $\gamma\in G_K$ fixes the prime field $\mathbb F_p$ pointwise,
$$\gamma(y')-y'=\gamma(y)+\gamma(\mu)-y-\mu=\gamma(y)-y.$$
Thus $\chi_c(\gamma)$ is independent of the chosen root $y$, exactly as the statement asserts. Note that the very same formula makes sense for *every* $c\in K$ (Step 1 needs no hypothesis on $c$), and we shall use it for arbitrary $c$ inside the proof; for $c\in K\setminus\wp(K)$ it is precisely the character of the statement. The normalisation $\chi_c(\gamma)=\gamma(y)-y$ is thus part of the definition and $\chi_c$ is canonical; nothing in the argument below is based on the kernel alone.

**Step 3: $\chi_c$ is a continuous homomorphism $G_K\to(\mathbb F_p,+)$ with kernel $G_{K(y)}$.**
*Homomorphism.* For $\gamma,\delta\in G_K$,
$$\chi_c(\gamma\delta)=\gamma\delta(y)-y=\gamma\bigl(\delta(y)-y\bigr)+\bigl(\gamma(y)-y\bigr)=\gamma\bigl(\chi_c(\delta)\bigr)+\chi_c(\gamma)=\chi_c(\delta)+\chi_c(\gamma),$$
since $\chi_c(\delta)\in\mathbb F_p$ is fixed by $\gamma$. As $(\mathbb F_p,+)$ is abelian, $\chi_c(\gamma\delta)=\chi_c(\gamma)+\chi_c(\delta)$; taking $\delta=1$ also shows $\chi_c(\gamma^{-1})=-\chi_c(\gamma)$ and $\chi_c(1)=0$.
*Kernel.* $\chi_c(\gamma)=0\iff\gamma(y)=y\iff\gamma$ fixes every element of $K(y)\iff\gamma\in\operatorname{Gal}(K_s/K(y))=:G_{K(y)}$. Hence $\ker\chi_c=G_{K(y)}$.
*Continuity.* $K(y)/K$ is finite, generated by one element algebraic of degree at most $p$, so $G_{K(y)}$ is open in $G_K$ by the definition of the Krull topology. The group $\mathbb F_p$ is discrete; for any subset $S\subseteq\mathbb F_p$, choosing for each attained value $s\in S\cap\operatorname{im}\chi_c$ one $\gamma_s\in G_K$ with $\chi_c(\gamma_s)=s$, one has $\chi_c^{-1}(S)=\bigcup_{s\in S\cap\operatorname{im}\chi_c}\gamma_s\ker\chi_c$, a union of open cosets. Hence $\chi_c$ is continuous.

**Step 4: $\chi_c\equiv0\iff c\in\wp(K)$.**
$(\Leftarrow)$ If $c=x^p-x$ with $x\in K$, then $\wp(y-x)=\wp(y)-\wp(x)=c-c=0$, so $y-x\in\ker(\wp|_{K_s})=\mathbb F_p\subseteq K$, whence $y\in K$. Then $K(y)=K$, $G_{K(y)}=G_K$, and Step 3 gives $\chi_c\equiv0$.
$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $\chi_c\equiv0$, i.e. $\gamma(y)=y$ for all $\gamma\in G_K$. We use the claim: *if $\alpha\in K_s$ is separable over $K$ and is fixed by all of $G_K$, then $\alpha\in K$.* Proof of the claim: assume $\alpha\notin K$ and let $m\in K[T]$ be its minimal polynomial; then $\deg m\ge2$, $m$ is separable, and $m$ splits in $K_s$, so $m$ has a root $\beta\in K_s$ with $\beta\ne\alpha$. The map $K(\alpha)\to K(\beta)$, $h(\alpha)\mapsto h(\beta)$, is a well-defined $K$-isomorphism. Since $K_s$ is separably closed and $K_s/K(\alpha)$ is separable algebraic ($K_s$ is separable over $K$ and separably closed, hence is a separable closure of $K(\alpha)$), a standard Zorn-lemma extension argument applies: any $K$-embedding of an intermediate field extends across a simple separable extension because the image of the minimal polynomial splits over the separably closed field $K_s$; thus the embedding $K(\alpha)\hookrightarrow K_s$ extends to a $K$-embedding $\iota\colon K_s\to K_s$. Because $K_s/K$ is normal, $\iota$ is a $K$-automorphism of $K_s$, i.e. $\iota\in G_K$, but $\iota(\alpha)=\beta\ne\alpha$, a contradiction. This proves the claim. Applying it to $\alpha=y$ (separable over $K$, being a root of the separable polynomial $f$) yields $y\in K$, and then $c=y^p-y\in\wp(K)$.
As a by-product: for $c\notin\wp(K)$ the character $\chi_c$ is non-zero, and since its image is a non-trivial subgroup of the group $(\mathbb F_p,+)$ of prime order $p$, $\chi_c$ is surjective; it induces an isomorphism $G_K/G_{K(y)}\simeq(\mathbb F_p,+)$ in which the class of $\gamma$ acts on $K(y)$ as $y\mapsto y+\chi_c(\gamma)$.

**Step 5: additivity $\chi_{a+b}=\chi_a+\chi_b$ for all $a,b\in K$.** Choose roots $y_a,y_b\in K_s$ of $T^p-T-a$ and $T^p-T-b$. Then $(y_a+y_b)^p-(y_a+y_b)=(y_a^p-y_a)+(y_b^p-y_b)=a+b$, so $y_a+y_b$ is a root of $T^p-T-(a+b)$. By Step 2 the value of $\chi_{a+b}$ may be computed with any root, so for every $\gamma\in G_K$,
$$\chi_{a+b}(\gamma)=\gamma(y_a+y_b)-(y_a+y_b)=\bigl(\gamma(y_a)-y_a\bigr)+\bigl(\gamma(y_b)-y_b\bigr)=\chi_a(\gamma)+\chi_b(\gamma).$$
Hence $\chi_{a+b}=\chi_a+\chi_b$ as maps $G_K\to\mathbb F_p$; that is, $c\longmapsto\chi_c$ is a homomorphism from $(K,+)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G_K,\mathbb F_p)$.

**Step 6: conclusion.** Let $c,c'\in K\setminus\wp(K)$.
If $c'-c\in\wp(K)$, then by Step 5 and Step 4$(\Leftarrow)$,
$$\chi_{c'}=\chi_{(c'-c)+c}=\chi_{c'-c}+\chi_c=0+\chi_c=\chi_c.$$
Conversely, if $\chi_{c'}=\chi_c$, then by Step 5,
$$\chi_{c'-c}=\chi_{c'}+\chi_{-c}=\chi_{c'}-\chi_c=0,$$
where $\chi_{-c}=-\chi_c$ because $\chi_c+\chi_{-c}=\chi_{c+(-c)}=\chi_0\equiv0$ (indeed $T^p-T$ has the root $0\in K$). Step 4$(\Rightarrow)$ applied to $c'-c$ now gives $c'-c\in\wp(K)$.
This establishes the equivalence for all $c,c'\in K\setminus\wp(K)$, which is exactly the statement.

**Step 7: remarks delimiting the result.** Equivalently, Steps 4--5 say that $c\bmod\wp(K)\mapsto\chi_c$ is an *injective* homomorphism $K/\wp(K)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G_K,\mathbb F_p)$; we do not assert surjectivity onto $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G_K,\mathbb F_p)$, and none is needed. The normalisation in Step 2 is essential when $p>2$: the kernel $G_{K(y)}$ alone determines only the line $\{\lambda\chi_c:\lambda\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\}$, whereas the formula $\chi_c(\gamma)=\gamma(y)-y$ picks out a single character, so the equality of characters appearing in the lemma is a well-posed assertion. The hypothesis $p>2$ is nowhere used: the argument is valid for every $p>0$.

lemma_93.statement: Let k be a field, let p be a prime, and let K/k be a cyclic Galois extension of degree p with generator σ. Let α be a class in Br(K) fixed by σ whose index is p, and let β be a class in Br(k) whose image under the restriction homomorphism Br(k) → Br(K) is α. Then the corestriction of α from K to k equals p·β in Br(k). In particular, if the corestriction of α is nonzero in Br(k), then β has index p^2.
lemma_93.proof:
We first prove the group-cohomological identity in full generality (Step 1), then transport it to Brauer groups (Step 2), and finish with the index computation (Steps 3-5). Throughout, all modules are LEFT modules, and Res denotes restriction of scalars.

=== STEP 1. For G a finite group, H a subgroup of index m, and M a ZG-module, cor^G_H \u2218 res^G_H = m\cdot id on H^n(G,M) for all n \ge 0. ===

1(a) Coset decompositions and the two sidedness facts. Write the disjoint union of RIGHT cosets G = \bigsqcup_{r\in R} H r (R a set of representatives of H\G) and of LEFT cosets G = \bigsqcup_{t\in T} t H (T a set of representatives of G/H); m = |T| = |R|.
(i) Every g \in G is written UNIQUELY as g = h r with h \in H, r \in R (take r the representative of the right coset Hg and h = g r^{-1}). Therefore ZG = \bigoplus_{r\in R} (ZH)\cdot r is a free LEFT ZH-module with basis R.
(ii) Every g \in G is written UNIQUELY as g = t h with t \in T, h \in H. Therefore ZG = \bigoplus_{t\in T} t\cdot (ZH) is a free RIGHT ZH-module with basis T.
These two statements are different and are used for different purposes below: (i) makes restriction of scalars preserve projectives, (ii) makes ZG \otimes_{ZH} - exact.

1(b) Resolutions. Let P_\bullet \to Z be a projective ZG-resolution.
\quad \bullet Res P_\bullet \to Z is exact (Res is an exact functor: it is only a forgetful functor of abelian groups) and each Res P_i is projective over ZH: P_i is a direct summand of a free ZG-module ZG^{(I)}, and Res(ZG^{(I)}) = (Res ZG)^{(I)} = (\bigoplus_{r\in R} ZH\cdot r)^{(I)} is a free left ZH-module by 1(a)(i); a direct summand of a projective is projective. Hence Res P_\bullet is a projective ZH-resolution of Z, so H^n(H,M) may be computed as H^n(Hom_{ZH}(Res P_\bullet, M)). The restriction map res = res^G_H: H^n(G,M) = H^n(Hom_{ZG}(P_\bullet,M)) \to H^n(Hom_{ZH}(Res P_\bullet,M)) = H^n(H,M) is induced by the identity of underlying abelian groups Hom_{ZG}(P_n,M) = Hom_{ZH}(Res P_n, M) (a map is ZG-linear iff it is ZH-linear after forgetting the G-action).
\quad \bullet By 1(a)(ii), ZG is free, hence flat, as a RIGHT ZH-module, so ZG \otimes_{ZH} - is exact. Each ZG \otimes_{ZH} P_i is a projective ZG-module: if P_i is a summand of ZH^{(J)}, then ZG \otimes_{ZH} P_i is a summand of ZG \otimes_{ZH} ZH^{(J)} \cong ZG^{(J)}, which is free. Thus ZG \otimes_{ZH} P_\bullet is a ZG-projective resolution of ZG \otimes_{ZH} Z. The map ZG \otimes_{ZH} Z \to Z[G/H], x \otimes 1 \mapsto xH, is a well-defined ZG-module isomorphism: it is well defined because x u \otimes 1 = x \otimes u\cdot 1 = x \otimes 1 for u \in ZH (Z has trivial ZH-action); its inverse gH \mapsto g \otimes 1 is well defined because gh \otimes 1 = g \otimes h\cdot 1 = g \otimes 1; ZG-linearity is clear. Hence H(Hom_{ZG}(ZG \otimes_{ZH} P_\bullet, M)) = Ext^n_{ZG}(Z[G/H], M).

1(c) The Shapiro isomorphism. Define, degreewise, Sh: Hom_{ZH}(P_n, M) \to Hom_{ZG}(ZG \otimes_{ZH} P_n, M) by Sh(\varphi)(x \otimes p) := x\,\varphi(p).
\quad Well-defined: Sh(\varphi)(xu \otimes p) = xu\,\varphi(p) = Sh(\varphi)(x \otimes up) for u \in ZH, using ZH-linearity of \varphi; so the formula descends from ZG \times P_n to the balanced tensor product.
\quad ZG-linearity: Sh(\varphi)(g\cdot(x\otimes p)) = Sh(\varphi)(gx\otimes p) = gx\,\varphi(p) = g\,Sh(\varphi)(x\otimes p).
\quad Cochain map: writing d for the differentials, Sh(d_{Hom}\varphi)(x\otimes p) = x\,(\varphi \circ d)(p) = (d_{Hom} Sh(\varphi))(x\otimes p).
\quad Isomorphism: the inverse is \psi \mapsto (p \mapsto \psi(1\otimes p)).
\quad Naturality in M: Sh is defined degreewise by formulas linear in M, so for every short exact sequence 0 \to M' \to M \to M'' \to 0 of ZG-modules, Sh is a degreewise isomorphism between the two short exact sequences of cochain complexes 0 \to Hom_{ZH}(Res P_\bullet,M') \to Hom_{ZH}(Res P_\bullet,M) \to Hom_{ZH}(Res P_\bullet,M'') \to 0 and 0 \to Hom_{ZG}(ZG\otimes_{ZH}P_\bullet,M') \to \dots \to Hom_{ZG}(ZG\otimes_{ZH}P_\bullet,M'') \to 0 (both exact because the modules P_i are projective for the respective group rings). Since the connecting homomorphism of a short exact sequence of cochain complexes is natural with respect to morphisms of short exact sequences, Sh commutes with the connecting homomorphisms. Thus Sh: H^\bullet(H,-) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Ext^\bullet_{ZG}(Z[G/H],-) is an isomorphism of cohomological \delta-functors in the second variable.

1(d) The two comparison maps on Z[G/H].
\quad \varepsilon: Z[G/H] \to Z, xH \mapsto 1, is ZG-linear since Z carries the trivial action: \varepsilon(g'\cdot xH) = 1 = g'\cdot 1 = g'\varepsilon(xH).
\quad \eta: Z \to Z[G/H], 1 \mapsto N := \sum_{t\in T} tH. This is independent of the choice of representatives T, because each summand tH is the basis element of Z[G/H] indexed by the coset. It is ZG-linear: for g \in G, gN = \sum_{t\in T} gtH = \sum_{t\in T} \overline{gt}\,H where t \mapsto \overline{gt} (the representative of the coset gtH) is a permutation of T, so gN = N = g\cdot N = \eta(g\cdot 1).
\quad Precomposition with a fixed ZG-map f: X' \to X induces f^*: Ext^n_{ZG}(X,M) \to Ext^n_{ZG}(X',M), a morphism of cohomological \delta-functors in M: for 0 \to M' \to M \to M'' \to 0 with extension class e \in Ext^1_{ZG}(M'',M'), the connecting homomorphism is Yoneda product \delta(\xi) = \xi \cup e, and splicing an extension with a fixed extension commutes with pulling the first extension back along f, i.e. f^*(\xi \cup e) = (\xi \circ f) \cup e = f^*(\xi) \cup e, so f^* \delta = \delta f^*. Also, precomposition is ADDITIVE in f: lifting f,g: X' \to X to chain maps \tilde f, \tilde g between projective resolutions, \tilde f + \tilde g is a chain map lifting f+g (differentials are additive), and \varphi\circ(\tilde f+\tilde g) = \varphi\tilde f + \varphi\tilde g; hence (f+g)^* = f^* + g^*.

1(e) Identification Sh \circ res = \varepsilon^*. We need a ZG-chain map \tilde\varepsilon: ZG \otimes_{ZH} P_\bullet \to P_\bullet covering \varepsilon. Define \tilde\varepsilon(x \otimes p) := x\,p (the action).
\quad Well defined: \tilde\varepsilon(xu\otimes p) = xup = \tilde\varepsilon(x \otimes up).
\quad ZG-linear: \tilde\varepsilon(g\cdot(x\otimes p)) = gx\,p = g\,\tilde\varepsilon(x\otimes p).
\quad Chain map: \tilde\varepsilon((1\otimes d)(x\otimes p)) = x\,dp = d(x\,p).
\quad Covers \varepsilon: if aug: P_0 \to Z is the augmentation and aug': ZG\otimes_{ZH}P_0 \to Z[G/H] is x\otimes p_0 \mapsto \overline{p_0}\,xH (where bar denotes aug), then \varepsilon\,aug'(x\otimes p_0) = \overline{p_0}, while aug\,\tilde\varepsilon(x\otimes p_0) = \bar{x p_0} = x\cdot\bar p_0 = \bar p_0 since G acts trivially on Z. So \varepsilon\,aug' = aug\,\tilde\varepsilon.
Now let x \in H^n(G,M) be represented by a cocycle \varphi \in Hom_{ZG}(P_n,M). Then res(x) is represented by the same \varphi viewed as a ZH-map, so Sh(res\,x) is represented by Sh(\varphi), while \varepsilon^*(x) is represented by \varphi \circ \tilde\varepsilon. For x \in ZG, p \in P_n:  Sh(\varphi)(x\otimes p) = x\,\varphi(p) = \varphi(x\,p) \ (\varphi is ZG-linear!) = \varphi(\tilde\varepsilon(x\otimes p)). Hence Sh(\varphi) = \varphi\circ\tilde\varepsilon as cochains, and Sh \circ res = \varepsilon^* as maps H^n(G,M) \to Ext^n_{ZG}(Z[G/H],M).

1(f) Definition of the corestriction and the key computation. Define cor := \eta^* \circ Sh: H^n(H,M) \xrightarrow{\sim} Ext^n_{ZG}(Z[G/H],M) \to Ext^n_{ZG}(Z,M) = H^n(G,M). By 1(c) and 1(d) this is a morphism of cohomological \delta-functors in M. Using 1(e):
   cor \circ res = \eta^* \circ \varepsilon^* = (\varepsilon \circ \eta)^*.
Now \varepsilon\eta(1) = \varepsilon(\sum_{t\in T} tH) = \sum_{t\in T} 1 = m, i.e. \varepsilon\eta = m\cdot id_{Z}. By the additivity of f \mapsto f^* proved in 1(d), (m\cdot id)^* = m\cdot id on Ext. Therefore
   cor \circ res = m\cdot id_{H^n(G,M)}   (\ast)
as maps on cohomology, for every n \ge 0.

1(g) This cor is the classical corestriction (transfer). Degree 0: for m_0 \in M^H = H^0(H,M), viewed as the ZH-map Z \to M, 1 \mapsto m_0, Sh(m_0): Z[G/H] \to M is xH \mapsto x\,m_0 (well defined precisely because m_0 is H-fixed), hence (\eta^* Sh(m_0))(1) = Sh(m_0)(N) = \sum_{t\in T} t\,m_0 = Tr^G_H(m_0), the classical trace M^H \to M^G, which is the classical corestriction in degree 0. The classical corestriction cor^G_{H,cl}: H^\bullet(H,-) \to H^\bullet(G,-) is a morphism of cohomological \delta-functors (it is constructed by an explicit formula on the standard bar resolution which is natural in M and commutes with the connecting homomorphisms; equivalently, it is the map induced by the transfer of the standard resolution). The functor H^\bullet(H,-) is the functor of right derived functors of the left exact functor (-)^H = Hom_{ZH}(Z,-); by Cartan-Eilenberg (Homological Algebra, Ch. III, Thm 1.1) a derived \delta-functor is UNIVERSAL, and by the comparison theorem in the direction "out of the universal \delta-functor" (CE Ch. III, Thm 1.3): if T^\bullet is a universal cohomological \delta-functor and U^\bullet any cohomological \delta-functor, a morphism of \delta-functors T^\bullet \to U^\bullet is uniquely determined by its degree-0 component T^0 \to U^0. Applying this with T^n(-) = H^n(H,-), U^n(-) = H^n(G,-), and the two morphisms a^\bullet = cor^G_{H,cl} and b^\bullet = \eta^*\circ Sh, which coincide in degree 0, we get a^n = b^n for all n. Hence the classical corestriction satisfies (\ast).

=== STEP 2. Transport to Brauer groups. ===
Let k_s be a separable closure of k. Since K/k is finite separable (Galois of degree p), k_s is also a separable closure of K. Put G := G_k = Gal(k_s/k) and H := G_K = Gal(k_s/K) \le G. By the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, [G:H] = [K:k] = p (H is normal with G/H = Gal(K/k), but normality is not needed for Step 1). For F \in \{k,K\} the Noether isomorphism (crossed products / factor sets, i.e. Br(F) = H^2_{\acute et}(Spec F, G_m) = H^2_{cont}(Gal(k_s/F), k_s^\times)) gives canonical isomorphisms \theta_F: Br(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^2(Gal(k_s/F), k_s^\times).
(2a) Restriction. \theta_K(res_{K/k}\,\gamma) = res(\theta_k(\gamma)) for every \gamma \in Br(k). Indeed, represent \gamma by a central simple k-algebra A of degree n split by k_s, choose a k_s-isomorphism f: A \otimes_k k_s \xrightarrow{\sim} M_n(k_s), and form the factor set (a_{\sigma\tau})_{\sigma,\tau \in G_k} as follows: the semilinear G_k-action id_A \otimes \tau on A \otimes_k k_s becomes, via f, the \tau-semilinear automorphism \varphi_\tau of M_n(k_s); composing \varphi_\tau with entrywise application of \tau^{-1} gives a k_s-algebra automorphism \psi_\tau of M_n(k_s), inner by Skolem-Noether, say \psi_\tau = Inn(U_\tau) with U_\tau \in GL_n(k_s); then a_{\sigma\tau} := U_\sigma\,\sigma(U_\tau)\,U_{\sigma\tau}^{-1} \in k_s^\times is a continuous 2-cocycle whose class is \theta_k(\gamma). The same f is also a k_s-isomorphism (A \otimes_k K) \otimes_K k_s = A \otimes_k k_s \to M_n(k_s), and the descent datum defining A \otimes_k K as a K-algebra split by k_s is precisely the restriction of the G_k-action to H = G_K. Hence the identical construction yields for res_{K/k}\,\gamma = [A \otimes_k K] the factor set (a_{\sigma\tau})|_{H\times H}, i.e. the group-theoretic restriction of \theta_k(\gamma).
(2b) Corestriction. For every finite separable extension F'/F the Witt corestriction cor_{F'/F}: Br(F') \to Br(F) is, under the identifications of this Step, the group-cohomological corestriction (transfer) of Step 1 for the inclusion G_{F'} \le G_F of index [F':F]: this is the standard comparison (Br = H^2_{\acute et}(-,G_m), and the corestriction attached to the finite locally free morphism Spec F' \to Spec F is computed on absolute Galois groups by the transfer; equivalently, this is the description of the Witt corestriction via factor sets). In particular, combined with Step 1, the Brauer-group corestriction and restriction satisfy
   cor_{F'/F} \circ res_{F'/F} = [F':F]\cdot id_{Br(F)}      (\ast\ast)
for every finite separable extension F'/F. Applying (\ast\ast) to F' = K, F = k (which is a cyclic Galois extension of degree p, as in the statement) gives the first claim of the lemma directly; note that the argument does not use cyclicity, nor the \sigma-invariance of \alpha (that hypothesis only guarantees, via the exactness properties of Br(k) \to Br(K)^\sigma, that some \beta with res\,\beta = \alpha exists).

=== STEP 3. Proof of cor_{K/k}(\alpha) = p\,\beta. ===
By hypothesis res_{K/k}(\beta) = \alpha. Applying (\ast\ast) to \beta \in Br(k) gives cor_{K/k}(\alpha) = cor_{K/k}(res_{K/k}\beta) = [K:k]\cdot\beta = p\,\beta in Br(k). This proves the first assertion. (Equivalently, in cohomological terms: with \hat\beta := \theta_k(\beta) \in H^2(G_k,k_s^\times), Step 1 with n=2, M = k_s^\times, m=p gives cor^{G_k}_{G_K}(res\,\hat\beta) = p\hat\beta, and 2a/2b translate this into Br.)

=== STEP 4. The index of \beta is p or p^2. ===
Apply lemma_89 (Spark) to the extension K/k of degree n = p and the class \beta \in Br(k): the index of the image of \beta in Br(K), which is ind(\alpha) = p, divides ind(\beta), and ind(\beta) divides [K:k]\cdot ind(\alpha) = p\cdot p = p^2. Hence ind(\beta) is a multiple of p dividing p^2, i.e. ind(\beta) \in \{p, p^2\}.

=== STEP 5. If cor_{K/k}(\alpha) \neq 0 then ind(\beta) = p^2. ===
Assume cor_{K/k}(\alpha) \neq 0. By Step 3, p\beta = cor_{K/k}(\alpha) \neq 0 in Br(k). Suppose, towards a contradiction, that ind(\beta) = p, and let D be the central division k-algebra representing \beta; then deg D = p. By the Noether-Koethe theorem (ref_16), D contains a maximal subfield L that is separable over k. Since L is a maximal subfield, C_D(L) = L (otherwise x \in C_D(L) \setminus L would generate with L the commutative finite-dimensional k-domain L(x), a field properly containing L, contradicting maximality); the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) then gives [L:k]\cdot[C_D(L):k] = [D:k], i.e. [L:k]^2 = p^2, so [L:k] = p. A maximal subfield splits the algebra (ref_5: a degree-n subfield of a degree-n central simple algebra splits it), so res_{L/k}(\beta) = [D \otimes_k L] = 0 in Br(L). As L/k is finite SEPARABLE of degree p, the identity (\ast\ast) of Step 2 applies to L/k (the subgroup G_L \le G_k has index p and need not be normal; Step 1 was proved for arbitrary subgroups), and since cor_{L/k} is a group homomorphism we obtain
   p\beta = [L:k]\cdot\beta = cor_{L/k}(res_{L/k}\beta) = cor_{L/k}(0) = 0,
a contradiction. (This is the standard argument proving exp \mid ind in this case: ind \beta = p would force p\beta = 0.) Therefore ind(\beta) \neq p, and by Step 4, ind(\beta) = p^2.

=== STEP 6. Conclusion. ===
Steps 1-3 give cor_{K/k}(\alpha) = p\,\beta in Br(k) for every \beta lifting the \sigma-invariant class \alpha, and Steps 4-5 show that cor_{K/k}(\alpha) \neq 0 forces ind(\beta) = p^2. Both assertions of the lemma are proved.

lemma_96.statement: Let (k,v) be a henselian discretely valued field with residue field k̄, and let L/k be a finite Galois field extension, endowed with the valuation w extending v and with residue field k̄_L. Then [L:k] = [w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[k̄_L:k̄]; equivalently, L has trivial defect over k, and both indices [w(L^\times):v(k^\times)] and [k̄_L:k̄] divide [L:k].
lemma_96.proof:
We prove: for a henselian discretely valued field (k,v) and a finite Galois extension L/k with (necessarily unique) extended valuation w, [L:k] = [w(L^x):v(k^x)]·[k̄_L:k̄]. Throughout we normalise v so that v(k^x) = Z. Write O, m, k̄ for the valuation ring, maximal ideal and residue field of k, and O_L, m_L, k̄_L for those of (L,w). We first collect the needed facts; each is proved (or, when it is a textbook characterisation of henselianity, stated with the reference chain we use).

PRELIMINARIES.
(P1) Completion. Let K̂ be the completion of (k,v). Then K̂ is a field: for x ≠ 0 in K̂ choose a ∈ k with v(x−a) > v(x) (density, tolerance v(x)+1); then v̂(x) = v(a) ≠ ∞, and the value v̂(x) := lim v(x_n) for any Cauchy sequence x_n → x is well defined because v takes values in the discrete group Z and v(x_n − x_m) → ∞ forces v(x_n) eventually constant. The extended valuation v̂ satisfies v̂(K̂^x) = v(k^x) = Z (the same approximation argument: every x ∈ K̂^x has v̂(x) = v(a) for some a ∈ k^x), so K̂ is again a discrete valuation ring with the same uniformiser π; and its residue field equals k̄: every x ∈ O_K̂ has v̂(x−a) > 0 for some a ∈ O, so a̅ is its residue, and injectivity is v̂(a) > 0 ⇒ v(a) > 0. The same two arguments hold for any valued field and its completion: the completion never changes the value group or the residue field.
(P2) Henselianity. A complete valued field is henselian: given f ∈ O[T], a ∈ O with v(f(a)) > 2v(f′(a)), the Newton iteration a_{n+1} = a_n − f(a_n)/f′(a_n) stays in O, satisfies v(a_{n+1} − a_n) ≥ v(f(a_n)) − v(f′(a_n)) → +∞ and converges to a root of f by completeness. We use the standard equivalent characterisation of henselianity (Bourbaki AC Ch. VI §5, Serre, Corps locaux Ch. II §5): (K,v) is henselian iff v extends uniquely to every algebraic extension; in particular every algebraic extension of a henselian field, with its unique extended valuation, is henselian, and the valuation w of the lemma (extending v to L) exists (extension of valuations to algebraic extensions) and is unique.
(P3) Krasner's lemma (henselian form). Let (K,v) be henselian, let Ω be an algebraic extension field carrying a valuation W extending v (unique by (P2)), let α, β ∈ Ω, and suppose W(β−α) > W(α−α′) for every K-conjugate α′ ≠ α of α. Then α ∈ K(β). Proof: let m ∈ K(β)[T] be the minimal polynomial of α over K(β); its roots are among the K-conjugates of α. Suppose some α′ ≠ α is a root. Then α, α′ are conjugate over K(β), so there is a K(β)-embedding τ: K(β,α) → Ω with τ(α) = α′; extend τ to an automorphism τ̃ of Ω. Since K(β) is henselian by (P2) and W∘τ̃ agrees with W on K(β), uniqueness of the extension of the valuation gives W∘τ̃ = W, i.e. τ̃ is an isometry. As τ̃ fixes β, W(β−α′) = W(τ̃(β−α)) = W(β−α). But then W(α−α′) = W((α−β)+(β−α′)) ≥ min(W(β−α), W(β−α′)) = W(β−α), contradicting the hypothesis. Hence m has the single root α, deg m = 1, α ∈ K(β). ∎
(P4) No proper immediate separable extensions. Let (K,v) be henselian with v(K^x) = Z, and let (F,w) be an immediate separable algebraic extension, i.e. w(F^x) = v(K^x) and k_F = k̄. Then F = K. Proof: first note that immediacy gives the approximation property (∗): for every x ∈ F^x there is c ∈ K with w(x−c) > w(x): indeed w(x) = v(c₀) for some c₀ ∈ K^x, then x/c₀ ∈ O_F has residue equal to c̄₁ for some c₁ ∈ O, and w(x − c₀c₁) = w(c₀) + w(x/c₀ − c₁) > w(c₀) = w(x). Now fix a ∈ F with minimal polynomial f ∈ K[T] of degree d; let α₁ = a, …, α_d be the roots of f in an algebraic closure Ω of K̂, valued by the unique extension W of v̂ (hence of v). If d ≥ 2 set δ := min_{i≥2} W(α₁−α_i) (a well-defined element of the value group, since f is separable so α₁ ≠ α_i). Using (∗) iteratively, choose s₁ = c₁ ∈ K with γ₁ := W(a−s₁) > W(a), then s_{n+1} = s_n + c_{n+1} with γ_{n+1} := W(a − s_{n+1}) > γ_n. All γ_n lie in W(F^x) = v(K^x) = Z, and a strictly increasing sequence of integers is unbounded, so γ_n > δ for n ≫ 0. For such n, W(a − s_n) > W(a − α_i) for all i ≥ 2, so Krasner's lemma (P3) applied in Ω over the henselian field K gives K(a) ⊆ K(s_n) = K, i.e. a ∈ K. Since a was arbitrary, F = K. ∎
(P5) Fundamental inequality. Choose x₁,…,x_e ∈ L^x whose values represent distinct cosets of v(k^x) in w(L^x), and y₁,…,y_f ∈ O_L whose residues form a k̄-basis of k̄_L. Then the ef products z_{ij} = x_i y_j are linearly independent over k. Indeed, if Σ a_{ij} x_i y_j = 0 with a_{ij} ∈ k, put S_i = Σ_j a_{ij} y_j; if S_i ≠ 0, with μ_i := min_j v(a_{ij}) ∈ v(k^x) we have S_i = π^{μ_i}u_i where the residue of u_i is Σ_{j: v(a_{ij})=μ_i} ā_{ij} ȳ_j ≠ 0 (linear independence of the ȳ_j over k̄), so w(S_i) = μ_i ∈ v(k^x); the values w(x_i S_i) then lie in distinct cosets of v(k^x), so their minimum is attained exactly once and Σ_i x_i S_i ≠ 0. Hence ef ≤ [L:k]; in particular e ≤ n and f ≤ n are finite.

(P6) Irreducible polynomials stay irreducible over the completion. Let f ∈ k[T] be monic irreducible separable of degree n. Then f is irreducible in K̂[T]. Proof: suppose f = g·h in K̂[T] with g, h monic of degrees m and n−m, both ≥ 1. The roots of g form a subset of the roots of f, which all lie in the splitting field N of f over k; hence the coefficients of g lie in N, and by assumption they lie in K̂. So F := k(coeffs of g) is a subfield of K̂, finite separable over k (it sits in the Galois extension N/k). With the valuation induced from K̂, (P1) gives v_F(F^x) ⊆ v̂(K̂^x) = v(k^x) and k_F ⊆ k_{K̂} = k̄, while the reverse inclusions are trivial; so F/k is immediate. By (P4), F = k, so g ∈ k[T] — contradicting the irreducibility of f over k. ∎

(P7) Complete DVRs are defectless for separable extensions. Let (F,v) be a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformiser π, ring of integers O, residue field κ, and let E/F be finite separable of degree n, with (unique) extended valuation w, valuation ring O_E, uniformiser Π, e = [w(E^x):v(F^x)], f = [κ_E:κ]. Then n = e·f. Proof. (i) O_E = {x ∈ E : w(x) ≥ 0} is the integral closure of O in E: an element with w ≥ 0 satisfies its monic minimal polynomial, whose coefficients have nonnegative valuation (otherwise, looking at the conjugate of minimal valuation in a normal closure, the lowest term of the polynomial cannot cancel); conversely an element integral over O satisfies a monic polynomial over O, forcing w(x) ≥ 0. (ii) O_E is a finitely generated O-module: E/F separable means the trace pairing (x,y) ↦ Tr_{E/F}(xy) is non-degenerate. Take an F-basis ω₁,…,ω_n of E contained in O_E (multiply any basis by powers of π) and set Δ := det(Tr(ω_iω_j)) ∈ O \ {0}. For x ∈ O_E write x = Σ b_i ω_i with b_i ∈ F; then Σ_i Tr(ω_iω_j)b_i = Tr(xω_j) ∈ O for each j, because xω_j is integral over O and the field trace of an integral element is integral (it is a power of the trace from k(x), i.e. a coefficient of a monic polynomial over O). Cramer's rule gives b_i ∈ (1/Δ)O. Hence O_E ⊆ (1/Δ)Σ O ω_i ≅ O^n; since O is a PID, O_E is free of finite rank over O, and its rank is n because its F-span is E. (iii) Two computations of dim_κ(O_E/πO_E). Because O_E is free of rank n over O, O_E/πO_E ≅ (O/π)^n, so dim_κ(O_E/πO_E) = n. On the other hand w(E^x) ⊇ v(F^x) with finite index e; w(E^x) is a finitely generated torsion-free abelian group of rank 1, hence ≅ Z, so w is discrete on E and O_E is a DVR with uniformiser Π. Since w(π) = e·w(Π), π/Π^e is a unit of O_E, so πO_E = Π^e O_E. The filtration O_E ⊇ ΠO_E ⊇ … ⊇ Π^e O_E = πO_E has successive quotients Π^t O_E/Π^{t+1}O_E ≅ O_E/Π = κ_E (multiplication by Π^t), each of κ-dimension f. Adding dimensions in this exact sequence gives dim_κ(O_E/πO_E) = e·f. Hence n = e·f. ∎

MAIN PROOF. Apply (P1) and (P2) to k: K̂ is a complete discrete valuation ring, henselian, with v̂(K̂^x) = v(k^x) and residue field k_{K̂} = k̄. Let n = [L:k] and let α ∈ L be a primitive element (L/k finite separable, as it is Galois), with minimal polynomial f over k of degree n. By (P6), f is irreducible over K̂, so L̂ := L ⊗_k K̂ ≅ K̂[T]/(f) is a field with [L̂:K̂] = n; it is complete (finite-dimensional over the complete field K̂), separable over K̂, and canonically the compositum L·K̂ inside an algebraic closure K̂^alg, with L embedded by a ↦ a⊗1 and dense in L̂ (K is dense in K̂). The unique valuation Ŵ of K̂^alg restricts to L as an extension of v, hence as w by the uniqueness in (P2); since L is dense in L̂ and L̂ is complete Hausdorff, L̂ is (as a valued field) the completion of (L,w). By (P1) applied to (L,w), completion does not change value group or residue field: Ŵ(L̂^x) = w(L^x) and k_{L̂} = k̄_L. Applying (P7) to the complete DVR K̂ and the finite separable extension L̂/K̂ gives n = ê·f̂ with ê = [Ŵ(L̂^x):v̂(K̂^x)] and f̂ = [k_{L̂}:k_{K̂}]. Substituting Ŵ(L̂^x) = w(L^x), v̂(K̂^x) = v(k^x), k_{L̂} = k̄_L, k_{K̂} = k̄ yields ê = [w(L^x):v(k^x)] =: e and f̂ = [k̄_L:k̄] =: f. Therefore [L:k] = n = e·f = [w(L^x):v(k^x)]·[k̄_L:k̄], which is exactly the statement that the defect d(L/k) := [L:k]/(e·f) equals 1. Finally, e and f are positive integers with product n (and a priori ef ≤ n by (P5), so both are finite), hence each of them divides [L:k]. The trivial case L = k is covered (e = f = 1, n = 1). This completes the proof. (Remark: the argument never used normality of L/k, only separability, so the equality holds for every finite separable extension of a henselian discretely valued field; the Galois hypothesis of the statement is more than enough.)

lemma_95.statement: Let (k,v) be a henselian discretely valued field and let D be a finite-dimensional central division algebra over k, endowed with a valuation w extending v. Then the quotient group w(D^\times)/v(k^\times) is finite and cyclic.
lemma_95.proof:
Let $\Gamma := w(D^{\times})$ be the value group of $w$ and $\Gamma_k := v(k^{\times}) = w(k^{\times}) \subseteq \Gamma$ the value group of $k$. Since $v$ is discrete, $\Gamma_k$ is infinite cyclic; we identify it with $\mathbb{Z} \subset \Gamma$. The group $\Gamma$ is a priori only a totally ordered (not necessarily abelian) group, written additively: $w(xy) = w(x) + w(y)$ and $w(x+y) \ge \min(w(x), w(y))$. The order is characterised by $\gamma \ge 0 \iff \gamma = w(x)$ for some $x \in \mathcal{O}_D := \{x \in D^{\times} : w(x) \ge 0\} \cup \{0\}$. Note $w(1) = 0$ and $w(-y) = w(-1) + w(y) = w(y)$, because $w(-1) + w(-1) = w(1) = 0$ and a totally ordered group has no element of order $2$.

Step 1: $\Gamma_k$ is central in $\Gamma$. For $c \in k^{\times}$ and $x \in D^{\times}$ we have $cx = xc$ since $k$ is the center, hence $w(c) + w(x) = w(x) + w(c)$.

Step 2: $[\Gamma : \Gamma_k] \le [D:k] = n^2 < \infty$. First, an ultrametric lemma: if $y_1,\dots,y_t \in D^{\times}$ and $w(y_1) < w(y_i)$ for all $i \ge 2$, then $w(y_1 + \cdots + y_t) = w(y_1)$. Indeed, $w(y_1 + \cdots + y_t) \ge w(y_1)$ by the ultrametric inequality; writing $y_1 = (y_1 + \cdots + y_t) - (y_2 + \cdots + y_t)$ gives $w(y_1) \ge \min\big(w(\textstyle\sum_i y_i),\, \min_{i\ge2} w(y_i)\big)$, and since $\min_{i\ge2} w(y_i) > w(y_1)$ we get $w(y_1) \ge w(\sum_i y_i)$. Consequently a sum of nonzero elements of $D$ can vanish only if the minimum of the values is attained at least twice. Now pick $x_1,\dots,x_r \in D^{\times}$ whose values lie in pairwise distinct cosets of $\Gamma_k$ in $\Gamma$. If $\sum_i c_i x_i = 0$ with all $c_i \in k^{\times}$, then the values $w(c_i x_i) = v(c_i) + w(x_i)$ are pairwise distinct (equality for $i \neq j$ would force $w(x_i) - w(x_j) = v(c_j) - v(c_i) \in \Gamma_k$), so the minimum is attained exactly once, contradiction. Thus $x_1,\dots,x_r$ are $k$-linearly independent, $r \le \dim_k D = n^2$, and $[\Gamma:\Gamma_k] \le n^2$.

Step 3: the order on $\Gamma$ is bi-invariant. It suffices to show the positive cone $P = \{\gamma \in \Gamma : \gamma \ge 0\}$ is closed under conjugation, equivalently that $\mathcal{O}_D$ is stable under inner automorphisms.
3a. If $x \in \mathcal{O}_D$ then $x$ is integral over $\mathcal{O}_k$. The subalgebra $k(x) \subset D$ is a field (it is a finite-dimensional commutative $k$-domain), so the minimal polynomial $P(T) = T^m + a_{m-1}T^{m-1} + \cdots + a_0 \in k[T]$ of $x$ exists. Since $(k,v)$ is henselian, $v$ has a unique extension $\tilde v$ to every algebraic extension of $k$; fix one on a splitting field $\Omega$ of $P$ (existence of extensions is the Krull-Chevalley extension theorem). Both $\tilde v|_{k(x)}$ and $w|_{k(x)}$ extend $v$ on $k(x)$, so by uniqueness they coincide and $\tilde v(x) = w(x) \ge 0$. Any other root $\alpha$ of $P$ in $\Omega$ is the image of $x$ under a $k$-embedding $k(x) \hookrightarrow \Omega$, which extends to a $k$-automorphism $\sigma$ of $\Omega$ (as $\Omega/k$ is normal); then $\sigma\tilde v$ is an extension of $v$ to $\Omega$, hence equals $\tilde v$, and $\tilde v(\alpha) = \tilde v(\sigma x) = (\sigma\tilde v)(x) = \tilde v(x) \ge 0$. All roots of $P$ thus have nonnegative value, and each coefficient $a_i$, being (up to sign) a sum of products of roots, satisfies $v(a_i) \ge 0$ by the ultrametric inequality. Hence $P$ is monic with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_k$: $x$ is integral over $\mathcal{O}_k$.
3b. If $y \in D$ is integral over $\mathcal{O}_k$ then $y \in \mathcal{O}_D$. Take a monic relation $y^m + c_{m-1}y^{m-1} + \cdots + c_0 = 0$ with $c_i \in \mathcal{O}_k$. The $c_i$ lie in the center $k$, so inside the commutative ring $k[y]$, if $w(y) < 0$ we may multiply by $y^{-m}$ to obtain $1 = -(c_{m-1} y^{-1} + \cdots + c_0 y^{-m})$. For each $j \ge 1$, $w(c_j y^{-j}) \ge v(c_j) - j\, w(y) \ge -j\, w(y) > 0$, so the right-hand side has value $> 0$ by the ultrametric inequality, contradicting $w(1) = 0$. Hence $w(y) \ge 0$.
3c. For $x \in \mathcal{O}_D$ and $g \in D^{\times}$, the element $g x g^{-1}$ satisfies the same polynomial $P(T)$, since the coefficients are central: $P(gxg^{-1}) = g P(x) g^{-1} = 0$. By 3a and 3b, $g x g^{-1} \in \mathcal{O}_D$. Thus $P$ is conjugation-invariant. The induced total order $\gamma \ge \delta \iff \gamma - \delta \in P$ is right-invariant because $(\gamma + \theta) - (\delta + \theta) = \gamma - \delta$, and left-invariant because $\theta + \gamma - (\theta + \delta) = \theta + (\gamma - \delta) + (-\theta) \in P$ by conjugation-invariance of $P$.

Step 4: every element of $\Gamma$ is torsion modulo $\Gamma_k$. Let $a \in D^{\times}$ and $F := k(a)$, a field with $[F:k] = m \le n^2$. The argument of Step 2 applied to the valued field $(F, w|_F)$ gives $[w(F^{\times}) : \Gamma_k] \le m$; the group $w(F^{\times})$ is abelian since $F$ is commutative. Letting $r := [w(F^{\times}) : \Gamma_k]$, the finite abelian group $w(F^{\times})/\Gamma_k$ has exponent dividing $r$, so $r\, w(a) \in \Gamma_k$.

Step 5: $\Gamma$ is abelian. We use a lemma: in a group with a bi-invariant total order, any element with a central positive power is central. Proof: let $g$ satisfy $g^r \in Z(\Gamma)$, $r \ge 1$ (multiplicative notation). If $g > 1$, then for any $h$, $hgh^{-1} > 1$ and comparing $hgh^{-1}$ with $g$: if $hgh^{-1} > g$, then by bi-invariance the power map is strictly increasing on elements $\ge 1$ (induction: $u > v \ge 1 \Rightarrow u^{s+1} = u^{s}u > v^{s}u > v^{s}v = v^{s+1}$), so $g^r = (hgh^{-1})^{r} > g^{r}$, absurd; $hgh^{-1} < g$ is likewise impossible. Hence $hgh^{-1} = g$ for all $h$. If $g < 1$, apply the previous case to $g^{-1} > 1$, whose $r$-th power $(g^r)^{-1}$ is central. If $g = 1$ there is nothing to show.
Now take $a \in D^{\times}$. By Step 4 there is $r \ge 1$ with $w(a)^r \in \Gamma_k$, and by Step 1 $\Gamma_k \subseteq Z(\Gamma)$. By the lemma, $w(a) \in Z(\Gamma)$. As $a$ was arbitrary and $w$ is surjective, $\Gamma$ is abelian.

Step 6: structure of $\Gamma$ and cyclicity of the quotient. $\Gamma$ is abelian and generated by $1 \in \Gamma_k$ together with a set of representatives of the $e := [\Gamma:\Gamma_k] \le n^2$ cosets of $\Gamma_k$, hence is a finitely generated abelian group. It is torsion-free: if $\gamma > 0$ then right invariance gives $s\gamma = (s-1)\gamma + \gamma > (s-1)\gamma \ge \cdots \ge \gamma > 0$ for all $s \ge 1$, so $s\gamma \neq 0$; the case $\gamma < 0$ is analogous. By the structure theorem, $\Gamma \cong \mathbb{Z}^t$. Tensoring $0 \to \Gamma_k \to \Gamma \to \Gamma/\Gamma_k \to 0$ with $\mathbb{Q}$, the finite group $\Gamma/\Gamma_k$ vanishes, so $t = \operatorname{rank}\Gamma = \operatorname{rank}\Gamma_k = 1$. Thus $\Gamma = \mathbb{Z}\gamma_0$ for a generator $\gamma_0 > 0$, and the subgroup $\Gamma_k$ of the infinite cyclic group $\Gamma$ is $\Gamma_k = \mathbb{Z}\,(e\gamma_0)$, where $e = [\Gamma : \Gamma_k] \ge 1$ (so $e = 1$ exactly when $\Gamma = \Gamma_k$, e.g. $D = k$). Therefore
$$ w(D^{\times})/v(k^{\times}) \;=\; \Gamma/\Gamma_k \;=\; \mathbb{Z}\gamma_0 \,/\, \mathbb{Z}(e\gamma_0) \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z},$$
a finite cyclic group (of order $e \le n^2$, the ramification index of $D/k$). This completes the proof.

lemma_98.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$ be the Laurent series field with its $u$-adic valuation. Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $p\nmid m$, let $K=k(z)$ where $z^p-z=s/u^m$, and let $N_{K/k}:K^\times\to k^\times$ be the field norm. Then $t/u^n$ does not belong to $N_{K/k}(K^\times)$.
lemma_98.proof:
Write F_0 = \mathbb{F}_p(s,t), where s,t are algebraically independent over \mathbb{F}_p, so that k = F_0((u)); put c = s/u^m \in k^\times.

STEP 1 (the genuine valuation on k). Every nonzero f \in k is written uniquely as f = \sum_{i\ge i_0} a_i u^i with a_i \in F_0 and a_{i_0} \neq 0; define v(f) = i_0 and v(0) = \infty. This is the u-adic discrete valuation of k, normalised by v(u) = 1. Its valuation ring is O_k = F_0[[u]] with maximal ideal uF_0[[u]], its residue map \sum a_i u^i \mapsto a_0 identifies the residue field k̄ with F_0, v|_{F_0^\times} = 0, and k is complete for v (standard for a Laurent series field).

STEP 2 (K/k is a totally ramified cyclic Galois extension of degree p). We have v(c) = v(s/u^m) = 0 - m = -m < 0 and p \nmid m by hypothesis. By lemma_73 (Spark), an element of a characteristic-p discretely valued field whose value is negative and not divisible by p does not lie in wp(k) = \{x^p - x : x \in k\}; hence c \notin wp(k). Consequently T^p - T - c has no root in k. Let \alpha be a root in a splitting field; its roots are exactly \alpha + i for i \in \mathbb{F}_p (the prime field, since char k = p), so the splitting field is k(\alpha) and Gal(k(\alpha)/k) embeds into the additive group of \mathbb{F}_p by \tau \mapsto \tau(\alpha)-\alpha; hence every root has degree 1 or p over k. Since \alpha \notin k, [k(\alpha):k] = p and k(\alpha)/k is cyclic Galois of degree p, generated by \sigma with \sigma(z) = z+1. Thus K = k(z) is a field with Gal(K/k) = \{\sigma_i := \sigma^i : \sigma_i(z) = z + i,\ i \in \mathbb{F}_p\} \cong \mathbb{F}_p.
