(b) $\bar k(\beta)\subseteq\bar E$ with $[\bar k(\beta):\bar k]=p=[\bar E:\bar k]$, so $\bar E=\bar k(\beta)=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)(\beta)$ with $\beta^{p}=t\,s^{an}$, a purely inseparable extension of $\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$ of degree $p$.
Thus the ramification index and the residue degree of $E/k$ are both $p$ (and the defect is trivial). Note in particular that $e=p<p^{2}=[E:k]$: $E/k$ is NOT totally ramified in the sense $e=[E:k]$ (unlike the subextensions $K/k$ and $L/k$), and no assertion about upper ramification breaks of $E/k$ is made here.

STEP 8. THE INERTIA GROUP IS ALL OF $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$. Let $I=\{\gamma\in\operatorname{Gal}(E/k):\gamma \text{ induces the identity on } \bar E\}$; this is well defined because $v$ is the unique extension of $v$ to $E$, so each $\gamma$ preserves $\mathcal O_E$ and acts on $\bar E$ trivially on $\bar k$. For any $\gamma\in\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$, using that $\gamma$ fixes $\bar k$ elementwise and that $\beta^{p}=t\,s^{an}\in\bar k$:
  $\gamma(\beta)^{p}=\gamma(\beta^{p})=\gamma(t\,s^{an})=t\,s^{an}=\beta^{p}$,
so $(\gamma(\beta)-\beta)^{p}=\gamma(\beta)^{p}-\beta^{p}=0$ in the field $\bar E$, whence $\gamma(\beta)=\beta$. Since $\bar E=\bar k(\beta)$ by Step 7(b), $\gamma$ is the identity on $\bar E$. Thus every element of $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$ lies in $I$, i.e. $I=\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)\cong C_p\times C_p$; equivalently, the residue extension carries no separable part, being purely inseparable.

All the claimed assertions are established: $K$ and $L$ are linearly disjoint over $k$, $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)\cong C_p\times C_p$, $v(E^\times)=\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$, $\bar E/\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$ is purely inseparable of degree $p$, $e=f=p$, and the inertia group of $E/k$ is all of $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$. QED.

lemma_121.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic p>0, and for a field F write wp(F)=\{t^p-t : t\in F\}. Let c\in k\setminus wp(k) and let K=k(z) be the Artin-Schreier extension of k with z^p-z=c. Then wp(K)\cap k = wp(k)+\mathbb{F}_p\cdot c; equivalently, the kernel of the natural homomorphism k/wp(k)\to K/wp(K) is the one-dimensional \mathbb{F}_p-subspace generated by the class of c.
lemma_121.proof:
Throughout, p denotes a prime (the characteristic of a field is a prime), and for a field F of characteristic p we write wp(F) = {t^p - t : t \in F}. We repeatedly use two elementary facts: (a) for i \in \mathbb{F}_p one has i^p = i (true for i = 0, and for i \neq 0 because \mathbb{F}_p^\times has order p-1, so i^{p-1} = 1); (b) the map wp is \mathbb{F}_p-linear: wp(x+y) = (x+y)^p-(x+y) = (x^p-x)+(y^p-y) = wp(x)+wp(y) by the freshman's dream, and wp(\lambda x) = \lambda^p x^p - \lambda x = \lambda(x^p-x) = \lambda\,wp(x) for \lambda \in \mathbb{F}_p. Hence wp(F) is an \mathbb{F}_p-subspace of F (viewed as an \mathbb{F}_p-vector space), and F/wp(F) is an \mathbb{F}_p-vector space.

STEP 1: The polynomial f(T) = T^p - T - c is irreducible over k.
First, f'(T) = -1 \neq 0, so f is separable. Work in an algebraic closure \Omega of k and let \theta be a root of f, so \theta^p - \theta = c. For every i \in \mathbb{F}_p, f(\theta+i) = (\theta+i)^p - (\theta+i) - c = (\theta^p - \theta - c) + (i^p - i) = 0 + 0 = 0. Thus f has the p distinct roots \theta + i (i \in \mathbb{F}_p), all lying in k(\theta); since \deg f = p, f splits in k(\theta), and k(\theta)/k is normal, hence Galois (separability holds because f is separable).
Now let g \in k[T] be any monic irreducible factor of f, of degree m, say f = g\cdot h. The roots of g in \Omega are distinct (g | f and f separable) and are of the form \theta + j with j \in J, for a subset J \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p of size m. Comparing the coefficient of T^{m-1} in g = \prod_{j \in J}(T-(\theta+j)) gives -\sum_{j\in J}(\theta+j) = -(m\theta + s) \in k, where s := \sum_{j\in J} j \in \mathbb{F}_p \subseteq k. Hence m\theta + s \in k. If 1 \le m \le p-1, then m is invertible in k, and so \theta = m^{-1}(m\theta+s) - m^{-1}s \in k. But then c = \theta^p - \theta = wp(\theta) \in wp(k), contradicting the hypothesis c \notin wp(k). Therefore m = p. Since every monic irreducible factor of f has degree p and \deg f = p, f itself is irreducible over k. (Note that the argument also shows: if f has one root in k, i.e. c \in wp(k), then all roots are in k and f splits; irreducibility is equivalent to c \notin wp(k).)

STEP 2: Structure of K = k(z).
Since f is irreducible, K := k[T]/(f) is a field, K = k(z) with z the class of T and z^p - z = c, [K:k] = p, and 1, z, \dots, z^{p-1} is a k-basis of K. For each i \in \mathbb{F}_p, since f(z+i) = 0 (by the computation in Step 1), the assignment z \mapsto z+i defines a k-algebra homomorphism k[T]/(f) = K \to K; it is injective (a nonzero ring map from a field), hence it is an automorphism because K is finite-dimensional over k and the map is k-linear (injective \Rightarrow surjective). Denote it by \sigma_i. The \sigma_i are pairwise distinct since \sigma_i(z) = z+i are distinct. Thus |Gal(K/k)| \ge p = [K:k], so equality holds: K/k is Galois with Gal(K/k) = {\sigma_i : i \in \mathbb{F}_p} \cong \mathbb{Z}/p. Put \sigma := \sigma_1; by induction \sigma^i(z) = z + i, so \sigma^i = \sigma_i and \sigma generates Gal(K/k). Consequently the fixed field of \sigma is the fixed field of the whole Galois group, namely K^{\sigma} = k (Artin's theorem / fundamental theorem of Galois theory: [K : K^{Gal}] = |Gal| = p = [K:k], so K^{Gal} = k).

STEP 3: The p-th-power-fixed elements of K are exactly \mathbb{F}_p.
In the field K, the equation x^p = x says that x is a root of T^p - T, a nonzero polynomial of degree p, so it has at most p roots in K. By fact (a), every i \in \mathbb{F}_p \subset K is such a root. Hence {x \in K : x^p = x} = \mathbb{F}_p.

STEP 4: wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p\cdot c \subseteq wp(K) \cap k.
Since k \subseteq K, evaluating wp on an element of k gives the same result in k and in K, so wp(k) \subseteq wp(K); trivially wp(k) \subseteq k. Also c = z^p - z = wp(z) \in wp(K), and c \in k. Since wp(K) is an additive subgroup of K stable under multiplication by \mathbb{F}_p (Step (b)), the whole line \mathbb{F}_p\cdot c lies in wp(K) \cap k. As wp(K) \cap k is an additive subgroup of K, the sum wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p\cdot c is contained in wp(K) \cap k.

STEP 5: wp(K) \cap k \subseteq wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p\cdot c.
Let a \in wp(K) \cap k; choose y \in K with y^p - y = a. Because a \in k = K^{\sigma}, applying \sigma to the equation and using that \sigma is a field homomorphism (so \sigma(y^p) = \sigma(y)^p) gives \sigma(y)^p - \sigma(y) = \sigma(a) = a. Hence
  (\sigma(y)-y)^p = \sigma(y)^p - y^p = (\sigma(y)+a) - (y+a) = \sigma(y)-y,
where the first equality is the freshman's dream in K. By Step 3, j := \sigma(y) - y belongs to \mathbb{F}_p.
Case j = 0: then \sigma(y) = y, so y \in K^{\sigma} = k, and a = y^p - y = wp(y) \in wp(k) \subseteq wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p c.
Case j \neq 0: set \mu := y - jz. Then \sigma(\mu) = \sigma(y) - j\sigma(z) = (y + j) - j(z+1) = y - jz = \mu, so \mu \in K^{\sigma} = k. Since j \in \mathbb{F}_p we have j^p = j, and using c = z^p - z:
  a = y^p - y = (jz+\mu)^p - (jz+\mu) = j^p z^p + \mu^p - jz - \mu = j(z^p - z) + (\mu^p - \mu) = j\cdot c + wp(\mu).
As j \in \mathbb{F}_p and \mu \in k, this exhibits a \in \mathbb{F}_p\cdot c + wp(k).
The two cases exhaust all possibilities, so wp(K) \cap k \subseteq wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p c. Together with Step 4 this proves
  wp(K) \cap k = wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p\cdot c.

STEP 6: The equivalent cohomological-free formulation.
Because wp(k) \subseteq wp(K) (Step 4), the inclusion k \hookrightarrow K induces a well-defined \mathbb{F}_p-linear homomorphism \varphi : k/wp(k) \to K/wp(K), t + wp(k) \mapsto t + wp(K): if t' - t \in wp(k) \subseteq wp(K) the image coset does not change. The kernel of the composite k \hookrightarrow K \twoheadrightarrow K/wp(K) is k \cap wp(K), and since wp(k) is contained in it, factoring gives ker(\varphi) = (k \cap wp(K))/wp(k). By Step 5 this equals (wp(k) + \mathbb{F}_p c)/wp(k), which is precisely the \mathbb{F}_p-subspace of k/wp(k) generated by the class c + wp(k).
It remains to check that this subspace is one-dimensional over \mathbb{F}_p, i.e. that the classes \lambda c + wp(k) (\lambda \in \mathbb{F}_p) are pairwise distinct. If \lambda c - \lambda' c \in wp(k) with \lambda \neq \lambda', then (\lambda-\lambda')c \in wp(k) with \lambda-\lambda' \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times; letting \nu = (\lambda-\lambda')^{-1} \in \mathbb{F}_p and using that wp(k) is an \mathbb{F}_p-subspace, c = \nu((\lambda-\lambda')c) \in wp(k), contradicting the hypothesis. Hence c + wp(k) \neq 0 and its \mathbb{F}_p-span has exactly p elements, i.e. is one-dimensional.
Thus the kernel of k/wp(k) \to K/wp(K) is exactly the one-dimensional \mathbb{F}_p-subspace generated by the class of c, which is the claimed equivalent form of the equality proved in Step 5. This completes the proof.

lemma_122.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. Then $D$ contains an element $a\notin k$ with $a^p-a\in k$ if and only if $D$ contains a subfield $K$ of degree $p$ over $k$ that is Galois over $k$.
lemma_122.proof:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and $D$ a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. Note first that the prime field $\mathbb F_p$ is contained in $k$, and that $i^p=i$ for every $i\in\mathbb F_p$. We prove the two implications separately; both are elementary Artin--Schreier arguments, and the hypothesis that $\deg D=p^2$ is not used (the hypothesis that $D$ is a division ring is used in Part II).

We record one input from linear algebra, used in Part I.

**Lemma (Artin's independence of automorphisms).** Distinct $k$-automorphisms $\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_{m-1}$ of a field $K$ are linearly independent over $K$ as functions $K\to K$.
*Proof.* Suppose a nontrivial relation $\sum_i \lambda_i\sigma_i=0$ (as functions $K\to K$) exists, and choose one with the minimal number $m\ge 2$ of nonzero coefficients; relabel so that all $\lambda_i\neq 0$. Since $\sigma_0\neq\sigma_1$, there is $x\in K$ with $\sigma_0(x)\neq\sigma_1(x)$. Applying the relation to $xy$, for every $y\in K$: $\sum_i\lambda_i\sigma_i(x)\sigma_i(y)=0$. Multiplying the original relation (evaluated at $y$) by $\sigma_0(x)$ and subtracting gives $\sum_i \lambda_i(\sigma_i(x)-\sigma_0(x))\sigma_i(y)=0$ for all $y$, i.e. a shorter relation, since the $i=0$ term vanishes while the $i=1$ coefficient $\lambda_1(\sigma_1(x)-\sigma_0(x))\neq 0$. This contradicts minimality. $\square$

**Part I ($\Leftarrow$).** Suppose $D$ contains a subfield $K$ with $[K:k]=p$ and $K/k$ Galois. Then $\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)$ is a group of prime order, hence cyclic; fix a generator $\sigma$, so $\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)=\langle\sigma\rangle$ with $\sigma^p=\mathrm{id}$, and the fixed field $K^{\langle\sigma\rangle}$ equals $k$.

Define the $k$-linear maps $\wp,K\to K$, $\wp(x)=\sigma(x)-x$, and $\operatorname{Tr}:K\to k$, $\operatorname{Tr}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}\sigma^j(x)$.

(1) $\operatorname{Tr}\neq 0$ as a map: by Artin's lemma the automorphisms $\mathrm{id},\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{p-1}$ are linearly independent over $K$, so their sum is not the zero function.

(2) $\operatorname{Tr}\circ\wp=0$: $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(x)-x)=\sum_j\sigma^{j+1}(x)-\sum_j\sigma^{j}(x)=0$ (telescoping, using $\sigma^p=\mathrm{id}$).

(3) $\dim_k\operatorname{im}\wp=p-1$: $\ker\wp=\{x:\sigma(x)=x\}=K^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=k$, of $k$-dimension $1$; rank--nullity on the $p$-dimensional $k$-space $K$ gives $\dim_k\operatorname{im}\wp=p-1$.

(4) $\dim_k\ker\operatorname{Tr}=p-1$: by (1), $\operatorname{Tr}$ is a nonzero $k$-linear functional on $K$, so its kernel is a hyperplane.

From (2), (3), (4), $\operatorname{im}\wp=\ker\operatorname{Tr}$. Since $\operatorname{Tr}(1)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}1=p\cdot 1=0$ in characteristic $p$, we have $1\in\ker\operatorname{Tr}=\operatorname{im}\wp$; hence there exists $a\in K$ with
$$\sigma(a)-a=1,\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad \sigma(a)=a+1.$$
Then $a\notin k$, for otherwise $\sigma(a)=a$, contradicting $a+1\neq a$. Moreover, using $(u+v)^p=u^p+v^p$ in characteristic $p$,
$$\sigma(a^p-a)=\sigma(a)^p-\sigma(a)=(a+1)^p-(a+1)=(a^p+1)-(a+1)=a^p-a,$$
so $a^p-a\in K^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=k$. Thus $a\in D\setminus k$ satisfies $a^p-a\in k$, as required.

**Part II ($\Rightarrow$).** Suppose $D$ contains $a\notin k$ with $a^p-a=c\in k$. Put $f(T)=T^p-T-c\in k[T]$; then $f(a)=0$.

(1) $k[a]$ is a field. Indeed $f$ is monic, so $a$ is integral (hence algebraic) over $k$, and $k[a]$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space spanned by $1,a,\dots,a^{p-1}$. It is a subring of the division ring $D$, hence has no zero divisors. For $0\neq x\in k[a]$, the $k$-linear map $m_x:k[a]\to k[a]$, $y\mapsto xy$, is injective because $D$ has no zero divisors, hence surjective by finite-dimensionality; so $xy=1$ for some $y\in k[a]$, i.e. $x^{-1}\in k[a]$. Thus $k[a]=k(a)$ is a subfield of $D$ containing $k$.

(2) $f$ splits into distinct linear factors over $k(a)$. For each $i\in\mathbb F_p\subset k$ we have $a+i\in k(a)$ and, since $i^p=i$ and $c\in k$,
$$f(a+i)=(a+i)^p-(a+i)-c=(a^p+i^p)-a-i-c=(a^p-a-c)+ (i^p-i)=0.$$
The $p$ elements $a+i$ ($i\in\mathbb F_p$) are pairwise distinct ($a+i=a+j\Rightarrow i=j$), and $f'=pT^{p-1}-1=-1\neq 0$, so $f$ is separable and has exactly $p$ distinct roots in any extension field. Hence in $k(a)[T]$,
$$f(T)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p}\bigl(T-(a+i)\bigr).$$

(3) $k(a)/k$ is Galois. Let $\mu\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $a$ over $k$; then $\mu\mid f$, so $\mu$ is separable and every root of $\mu$ is one of the $a+i\in k(a)$, i.e. $\mu$ splits into linear factors over $k(a)$. Since $k(a)$ is generated over $k$ by the root $a$ of $\mu$ and contains all roots of $\mu$, it is the splitting field of the separable polynomial $\mu$; therefore $k(a)/k$ is Galois.

(4) $[k(a):k]=p$. Consider
$$\Phi:\operatorname{Gal}(k(a)/k)\longrightarrow(\mathbb F_p,+),\qquad \Phi(\tau)=\tau(a)-a.$$
This is well defined: $\tau(a)$ is again a root of $\mu$, hence of $f$, so $\tau(a)=a+i$ for a unique $i\in\mathbb F_p$. It is a homomorphism because $\tau(a)-a\in\mathbb F_p\subset k$ is fixed by every $\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(k(a)/k)$:
$$\Phi(\sigma\tau)=\sigma\tau(a)-a=\sigma\bigl(\tau(a)-a\bigr)+\sigma(a)-a=(\tau(a)-a)+(\sigma(a)-a)=\Phi(\tau)+\Phi(\sigma).$$
It is injective because $k(a)=k(a)$ is generated by $a$ over $k$: $\Phi(\sigma)=0$ means $\sigma(a)=a$, hence $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$. Consequently $[k(a):k]=|\operatorname{Gal}(k(a)/k)|$ divides $p$. Since $a\notin k$, the degree is $>1$, so $[k(a):k]=p$ (and $\operatorname{Gal}(k(a)/k)\cong C_p$).

Thus $K:=k(a)$ is a subfield of $D$ of degree $p$ over $k$ which is Galois over $k$.

Combining Parts I and II gives the claimed equivalence. (Remark: the same argument is valid for $p=2$ as well; the division hypothesis is used only in step (1) of Part II, where it guarantees that $k[a]$ has no zero divisors — over a general central simple algebra $k[a]$ need not even be a domain.)

lemma_124.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ equipped with a discrete valuation $v\colon K^{\times}\to\mathbb{Z}$ with residue field $\kappa$. If $c\in K$ satisfies $c=x^p-x$ for some $x\in K$ with $v(c)<0$, then $v(c)$ is divisible by $p$, and for any $\varpi\in K^{\times}$ with $v(\varpi)=1$ the residue of $c\,\varpi^{-v(c)}$ in $\kappa^{\times}$ is a $p$-th power.
lemma_124.proof:
We write the proof from first properties of a discrete valuation; no external result is needed.

**Setup and notation.** Since $p=\operatorname{char}K>0$, $p$ is a prime, so $p\ge 2$. Extend $v$ to all of $K$ by setting $v(0)=\infty$, with the conventions $\infty+a=\infty$ and $\infty\ge a$ for every $a\in\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\}$. Then:
(V1) $v(ab)=v(a)+v(b)$ for all $a,b\in K$ (for $v$: $K^{\times}\to\mathbb Z$ is a group homomorphism, so $v(a^n)=n\,v(a)$ for $a\ne0$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$);
(V2) $v(a-b)\ge\min(v(a),v(b))$ (ultrametric inequality, which for a discrete valuation follows from $v(1)=0$, $v(-a)=v(a)$ and $v(a+b)\ge\min(v(a),v(b))$, the latter since if $v(a)\ne v(b)$ is not the case one factors out the smaller valuation and uses that elements of valuation $\ge0$ form a ring);
(V3) if $v(a)\ne v(b)$ then $v(a-b)=\min(v(a),v(b))$. Indeed, assume $v(a)<v(b)$. By (V2), $v(a-b)\ge v(a)$. If the inequality were strict, then from $a=(a-b)+b$ and (V2) we would get $v(a)\ge\min(v(a-b),v(b))>v(a)$, a contradiction. Hence equality.

Let $\mathcal O=\{a\in K:v(a)\ge0\}$ be the valuation ring, $\mathfrak m=\{a\in K:v(a)>0\}$ its maximal ideal, and let $\operatorname{res}:\mathcal O\to\kappa=\mathcal O/\mathfrak m$ denote the residue homomorphism. The residue map is a surjective ring homomorphism, it sends $\mathcal O^{\times}=\{v=0\}$ onto $\kappa^{\times}$, and it is multiplicative: $\operatorname{res}(ab)=\operatorname{res}(a)\operatorname{res}(b)$.

**Step 1: $c\ne0$.** If $c=0$ then $v(c)=\infty$, contradicting $v(c)<0$. So $c\in K^{\times}$.

**Step 2: $v(x)<0$.** Suppose instead that $v(x)\ge0$. Then $v(x^p)=p\,v(x)\ge0$, and by (V2) $v(c)=v(x^p-x)\ge\min(v(x^p),v(x))=\min(p\,v(x),v(x))\ge0$, contradicting $v(c)<0$. Hence $v(x)<0$. Put $n:=v(x)\in\mathbb Z$, so $n<0$.

**Step 3: $v(c)=p\,n$, so $p\mid v(c)$.** Since $p\ge2$ and $n<0$, we have $p n-n=(p-1)n<0$, i.e. $v(x^p)=pn<n=v(x)$; the two valuations are distinct. Applying (V3) with $a=x^p$, $b=x$ gives
$$v(c)=v(x^p-x)=\min\big(v(x^p),v(x)\big)=\min(pn,n)=pn.$$
Thus $v(c)=p\,v(x)$ is divisible by $p$. (In particular $c\varpi^{-v(c)}=c\varpi^{-pn}$ has valuation $v(c)-pn\,v(\varpi)=pn-pn=0$, so it is a unit of $\mathcal O$ and its residue is an element of $\kappa^{\times}$; this also shows the residue map may legitimately be applied to it.)

**Step 4: the residue is a $p$-th power.** Define $y:=x\varpi^{-n}\in K^{\times}$. Then
$$v(y)=v(x)-n\,v(\varpi)=n-n\cdot 1=0,$$\nso $y\in\mathcal O^{\times}$ and $\bar y:=\operatorname{res}(y)\in\kappa^{\times}$.
We compute in $K$:
$$c\,\varpi^{-pn}=(x^p-x)\varpi^{-pn}=x^p\varpi^{-pn}-x\varpi^{-pn}=(x\varpi^{-n})^{p}-\big(x\varpi^{-n}\big)\varpi^{\,n-pn}=y^{p}-y\,\varpi^{(1-p)n}.$$
Both summands lie in $\mathcal O$: $y^p\in\mathcal O^{\times}$, and
$$v\!\big(y\,\varpi^{(1-p)n}\big)=v(y)+(1-p)n\,v(\varpi)=0+(1-p)n=(1-p)n>0,$$\nthe last inequality because $1-p<0$ and $n<0$. Hence $y\,\varpi^{(1-p)n}\in\mathfrak m$ and $\operatorname{res}\big(y\,\varpi^{(1-p)n}\big)=0$.
Applying the ring homomorphism $\operatorname{res}$ to the displayed identity gives
$$\operatorname{res}\big(c\,\varpi^{-v(c)}\big)=\operatorname{res}\big(c\,\varpi^{-pn}\big)=\operatorname{res}(y^p)-0=\big(\operatorname{res}(y)\big)^{p}=\bar y^{\,p}.$$
Since $\bar y\in\kappa^{\times}$ and $\kappa$ is a field, $\bar y^{\,p}\in\kappa^{\times}$ (consistently with Step 3, where we saw the residue is nonzero). Thus $\operatorname{res}(c\varpi^{-v(c)})$ is the $p$-th power in $\kappa^{\times}$ of $\operatorname{res}(x\varpi^{-v(x)})$.

**Conclusion.** We have shown $v(c)=p\,v(x)$ is divisible by $p$, and that for every $\varpi\in K^{\times}$ with $v(\varpi)=1$ the residue of $c\varpi^{-v(c)}$ in $\kappa^{\times}$ equals $\big(\operatorname{res}(x\varpi^{-v(x)})\big)^p$, a $p$-th power. This proves the lemma.

(Remark, not needed for the statement: the conclusion is independent of the choice of $\varpi$; if $\varpi'=\varepsilon\varpi$ with $v(\varepsilon)=0$, then $c\varpi'^{-v(c)}=c\varpi^{-v(c)}\varepsilon^{-pn}$, whose residue is $\bar y^{\,p}\,(\bar\varepsilon^{-n})^{p}=(\bar y\,\bar\varepsilon^{-n})^{p}$, again a $p$-th power.)

lemma_125.statement: Let $\kappa$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $k=\kappa((u))$ be the Laurent series field over $\kappa$. Then $u$ belongs to $\wp(k)=\{x^p-x : x\in k\}$; explicitly, $u=y^p-y$ where $y=-\sum_{i\geq 0}u^{p^{i}}\in\kappa((u))$.
lemma_125.proof:
We work with $k=\kappa((u))$, the field of formal Laurent series over the field $\kappa$ of characteristic $p>0$. Recall that an element of $k$ is a formal sum $\sum_{n\ge N} a_n u^n$ with $N\in\mathbb Z$, $a_n\in\kappa$, and that $k$ is complete for the $u$-adic valuation $v$ normalised by $v(u)=1$: a sequence $(f_m)$ converges to $f$ if and only if for every $N\ge 1$ there is $M$ such that $f_m-f\in u^{N}\kappa[[u]]$ for all $m\ge M$. In particular a series $\sum_{i\ge 0} g_i$ with $g_i\in k$ is well defined whenever $v(g_i)\to +\infty$, and $\kappa[[u]]\subset k$.

**Step 1: the series $y$ is a well-defined element of $k$.**
For $m\ge 0$ put $s_m=-\sum_{i=0}^{m} u^{p^{i}}\in\kappa[u]$. Since $p\ge 2$, the exponents $1=p^0<p^1<\cdots<p^m<\cdots$ are strictly increasing, so for $m'>m$ we have
$$s_{m'}-s_m=-\sum_{i=m+1}^{m'} u^{p^{i}}\in u^{p^{m+1}}\kappa[[u]],\qquad\text{hence } v(s_{m'}-s_m)\ge p^{m+1}\xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{}\infty .$$
Thus $(s_m)$ is $u$-adically Cauchy, and by completeness it converges to an element $y\in\kappa[[u]\subset k$. Equivalently and concretely, $y$ is the power series
$$y=\sum_{n\ge 1} a_n u^{n},\qquad a_n=\begin{cases}-1_{\kappa} & \text{if } n=p^{i}\text{ for some } i\ge 0,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
which has non-negative exponents only (so $y\in\kappa[[u]$) and whose truncation modulo $u^{N}$ agrees with $s_m$ as soon as $p^{m}>N$; this identifies the limit with the notation $y=-\sum_{i\ge 0}u^{p^{i}}$.

**Step 2: the Frobenius map is $u$-adically continuous.**
For $x,x'\in k$ write $x=x'+\delta$. Then, in characteristic $p$, the binomial theorem gives $x^{p}=(x'+\delta)^{p}=x'^{p}+\delta^{p}$, because $\binom{p}{j}\equiv 0\pmod p$ for $0<j<p$. Hence $v(x^{p}-x'^{p})=v(\delta^{p})=p\,v(\delta)=p\,v(x-x')$. In particular $x\mapsto x^{p}$ is (uniformly) continuous for the $u$-adic topology.

**Step 3: compute $y^{p}$.**
First, for a *finite* sum, iterating the identity $(a+b)^{p}=a^{p}+b^{p}$ gives $(\sum_{i=0}^{m} a_i)^{p}=\sum_{i=0}^{m}a_i^{p}$. Also $(-a)^{p}=-a^{p}$ in any characteristic $p>0$: for $p=2$ one has $-a^{p}=a^{p}=(a)^{2}=(-a)^{p}$, and for $p$ odd, $(-a)^{p}=(-1)^{p}a^{p}=-a^{p}$. Therefore
$$s_m^{\,p}=\Big(-\sum_{i=0}^{m}u^{p^{i}}\Big)^{p}=-\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(u^{p^{i}}\big)^{p}=-\sum_{i=0}^{m}u^{p^{i+1}}.$$
By Step 2 and Step 1,
$$y^{p}=\Big(\lim_{m\to\infty}s_m\Big)^{p}=\lim_{m\to\infty}s_m^{\,p}=\lim_{m\to\infty}\Big(-\sum_{i=0}^{m}u^{p^{i+1}}\Big).$$
The partial sums $t_m=-\sum_{i=0}^{m}u^{p^{i+1}}$ converge, since $t_{m'}-t_m=-\sum_{i=m+1}^{m'}u^{p^{i+1}}\in u^{p^{m+2}}\kappa[[u]]$, to the series $t=-\sum_{i\ge 1}u^{p^{i}}$. Hence
$$y^{p}=-\sum_{i\ge 1}u^{p^{i}}.$$
(One may check this coefficient-wise as well: $y=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nu^n$ with $a_n\in\{0,-1\}$, so $y^{p}=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n^{p}u^{np}=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n u^{np}$, whose non-zero coefficients are exactly at the exponents $np=p^{i+1}$, $i\ge 0$, and equal $-1$.)

**Step 4: the telescoping computation of $y^{p}-y$.**
Using $-y=\sum_{i\ge 0}u^{p^{i}}$ (which holds because negation is a continuous, indeed linear, operation, so it commutes with the limit of the partial sums),
$$y^{p}-y=y^{p}+(-y)=-\sum_{i\ge 1}u^{p^{i}}+\sum_{i\ge 0}u^{p^{i}}.$$
We evaluate the coefficient of each power $u^{n}$ in the right-hand side. Because the sequence $(p^{i})_{i\ge0}$ is strictly increasing, exactly one of the following holds:
- $n=1=p^{0}$: this exponent occurs only in the second sum (the first sum involves only exponents $p^{i}$ with $i\ge1$, all $\ge p\ge 2$), contributing coefficient $+1$;
- $n=p^{j}$ for some $j\ge 1$: the exponent occurs in both sums, contributing coefficient $-1+1=0$;
- $n\ge 1$ is not a power of $p$: the coefficient is $0$.

Since both sums lie in $\kappa[[u]]$, equality of power series is equality of coefficients, and we obtain
$$y^{p}-y=u.$$

**Step 5: conclusion.**
We have exhibited an element $y=-\sum_{i\ge 0}u^{p^{i}}\in\kappa[[u]]\subset\kappa((u))=k$ with $y^{p}-y=u$. By definition of $\wp(k)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in k\}$, this means $u\in\wp(k)$, which is the claim.

(Remark, explaining why such a $y$ must exist and why it is this series: on the complete metric space $u\kappa[[u]]$ the map $T(z)=z^{p}-u$ satisfies $v(T(z)-T(z'))=p\,v(z-z')>v(z-z')$ whenever $v(z-z')\ge1$, so $T$ is a contraction with a unique fixed point, and a fixed point is precisely a solution of $z^{p}-z=u$. Iterating $T$ from $0$ gives $T(0)=-u$, $T^{2}(0)=-u-u^{p}$, $T^{3}(0)=-u-u^{p}-u^{p^{2}}$, and in general $T^{m+1}(0)=-\sum_{i=0}^{m}u^{p^{i}}=s_m$, whose limit is exactly the $y$ above. This also shows $y$ is the unique element of $u\kappa[[u]]$ with $y^{p}-y=u$; the full solution set in $k$ is $y+\mathbb F_{p}$.)

lemma_123.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be field extensions of $k$ that are Galois cyclic of degree $p$, and let $A$ and $B$ be central division $k$-algebras of degree $p$ containing $k$-isomorphic copies of $K_1$ and $K_2$, respectively, as maximal subfields. If the tensor product $A\otimes_k B$ is a division ring, then $A\otimes_k B$ is a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for $G$ isomorphic to $C_p\times C_p$.
lemma_123.proof:
Write $D:=A\otimes_k B$, which is assumed to be a division ring, and fix $k$-algebra embeddings $\iota_1\colon K_1\hookrightarrow A$ and $\iota_2\colon K_2\hookrightarrow B$ whose images are maximal subfields. Write $G_i=\mathrm{Gal}(K_i/k)\cong C_p$ for $i=1,2$.

**Step 1: $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$.**

First we record a linear-algebra fact: if $R$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra and $F/k$ is any field extension, then $Z(R\otimes_k F)=Z(R)\otimes_k F$. Indeed, choose a $k$-basis $\{r_1,\dots,r_s\}$ of $R$ with structure constants $r_ir_j=\sum_\ell \gamma_{ij}^\ell r_\ell$, $\gamma_{ij}^\ell\in k$. An element $x=\sum_i x_i r_i$ lies in the centre if and only if, for every $m$, the $s$ coordinate equations $\sum_i x_i\gamma_{im}^\ell-\sum_i x_i\gamma_{mi}^\ell=0$ ($\ell=1,\dots,s$) hold; these are linear equations in the coordinates with coefficients in $k$. Writing the system as $Mv=0$ with $M$ a matrix over $k$, the solution space over $F$ of the base-changed system $M_Fv=0$ equals $\ker(M)\otimes_k F$: the rank of a matrix is the largest size of a non-vanishing minor, and a minor (a polynomial with integer coefficients in the entries) vanishes over $k$ if and only if it vanishes over $F$; hence $\dim_F\ker M_F=\dim_k\ker M$, and the natural inclusion $\ker M\otimes_k F\hookrightarrow\ker M_F$ is then an equality. Applying this to $R=D$ (with the basis $\{e_i\otimes f_j\}$ coming from $k$-bases of $A$ and $B$) gives $Z(D)\otimes_k F=Z(D\otimes_k F)$ for every extension $F/k$.

Now take $F=k_{\mathrm{sep}}$. Since $A$ and $B$ are central simple of degree $p$, they are split by $k_{\mathrm{sep}}$, and by associativity of base change
$$(A\otimes_k B)\otimes_k k_{\mathrm{sep}}\;\cong\;(A\otimes_k k_{\mathrm{sep}})\otimes_{k_{\mathrm{sep}}}(B\otimes_k k_{\mathrm{sep}})\;\cong\;M_p(k_{\mathrm{sep}})\otimes_{k_{\mathrm{sep}}}M_p(k_{\mathrm{sep}})\;\cong\;M_{p^2}(k_{\mathrm{sep}}),$$
whose centre is $k_{\mathrm{sep}}$ (the centre of a matrix algebra over a field is the scalar matrices). Thus $Z(D)\otimes_k k_{\mathrm{sep}}=k_{\mathrm{sep}}$, so $\dim_k Z(D)=1$. Since $k\subseteq Z(D)$ (the tensor product is over $k$), we get $Z(D)=k$. Being a division ring with centre $k$, $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra, and $\dim_k D=\dim_k A\cdot\dim_k B=p^2\cdot p^2=p^4$, so $\deg D=p^2$.

**Step 2: $K_1\otimes_k K_2$ embeds in $D$.**

Consider the $k$-linear map $\iota_1\otimes\iota_2\colon K_1\otimes_k K_2\to A\otimes_k B=D$. Since $\iota_1,\iota_2$ are injective maps of $k$-vector spaces, they split (every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits); choosing $k$-linear retractions $r_1\colon A\to K_1$, $r_2\colon B\to K_2$, the composite $(r_1\otimes r_2)\circ(\iota_1\otimes\iota_2)=\mathrm{id}$, so $\iota_1\otimes\iota_2$ is injective. It is a ring homomorphism because $\iota_1(x)\cdot(1)=1\cdot\iota_1(x)$ and elements of $A\otimes 1$ commute with elements of $1\otimes B$ in $A\otimes_k B$: $(x\otimes y)(x'\otimes y')=xx'\otimes yy'$. It sends $1\otimes 1$ to $1$. Hence $R:=\mathrm{im}(\iota_1\otimes\iota_2)\cong K_1\otimes_k K_2$ is a commutative $k$-subalgebra of $D$ containing $1$, of $k$-dimension $p^2$.

**Step 3: $R$ is a field (so $K_1,K_2$ are linearly disjoint over $k$).**

$R$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $k$-algebra without zero-divisors, because it is a subring of the division ring $D$. For $0\neq a\in R$, multiplication by $a$ is an injective $k$-linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $R$, hence surjective; so there is $b\in R$ with $ab=1$, and commutativity makes $a$ a unit. Thus $R$ is a field. Identifying it with $K_1\otimes_k K_2$, this says exactly that $K_1$ and $K_2$ are linearly disjoint over $k$, and
$$[R:k]=\dim_k(K_1\otimes_k K_2)=p\cdot p=p^2.$$

**Step 4: $R/k$ is Galois with group $G_1\times G_2\cong C_p\times C_p$.**

For $(\sigma,\tau)\in G_1\times G_2$ define $\sigma\otimes\tau$ on $K_1\otimes_k K_2$ by $(\sigma\otimes\tau)(x\otimes y)=\sigma(x)\otimes\tau(y)$; this is a well-defined $k$-automorphism (its inverse is $\sigma^{-1}\otimes\tau^{-1}$), and it preserves $R$. The action is faithful: if $\sigma\otimes\tau=\mathrm{id}$, then for every $x\in K_1$ we have $\sigma(x)\otimes 1=x\otimes 1$; the map $x\mapsto x\otimes 1$ is injective (it is $\mathrm{id}_{K_1}\otimes\iota$ where $\iota\colon k\hookrightarrow K_2$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda\cdot 1$, is injective, and tensoring an injective map of vector spaces with $K_1$ stays injective), hence $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$; symmetrically $\tau=\mathrm{id}$. Thus $\Gamma:=G_1\times G_2$ is a group of $k$-automorphisms of the field $R$ with $|\Gamma|=p^2$. By Artin's theorem on fixed fields, $R/R^{\Gamma}$ is Galois of degree $|\Gamma|=p^2$. Since $k\subseteq R^{\Gamma}$ and $[R:k]=p^2$, we must have $R^{\Gamma}=k$, and $R/k$ is a Galois field extension with $\mathrm{Gal}(R/k)=\Gamma\cong C_p\times C_p$.

**Step 5: $R$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.**

Apply the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) to the simple $k$-subalgebra $R\subseteq D$: $\dim_k R\cdot\dim_k C_D(R)=\dim_k D$, i.e. $p^2\cdot\dim_k C_D(R)=p^4$, so $\dim_k C_D(R)=p^2$. As $R$ is commutative, $R\subseteq C_D(R)$, and equality of dimensions forces $C_D(R)=R$. By the last clause of ref_1, $R$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ (equivalently, $\dim_k R=p^2=\deg D$).

**Step 6: Conclusion.**

The field $R$ is a commutative étale $k$-algebra (it is a finite separable field extension, being Galois) of dimension $p^2=|\Gamma|$, equipped with an action of $\Gamma$ by $k$-automorphisms with $R^{\Gamma}=k$; that is, $R$ is a $\Gamma$-Galois $k$-algebra in the sense of the definitions, and it sits in $D$ as a maximal subalgebra. Applying lemma_106 to the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $n=p^2$ and the maximal subfield $R$, which is Galois over $k$ with group $\Gamma$, there is a map $c\colon\Gamma\times\Gamma\to R^{\times}$ such that
$$D\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{g\in\Gamma} R\,u_g,\qquad u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)\,u_g,\qquad u_gu_h=c(g,h)\,u_{gh}$$
for all $\lambda\in R$ and $g,h\in\Gamma$. This is exactly the crossed product algebra $(R,\Gamma,c)$ as defined, and $\Gamma\cong C_p\times C_p$. Hence $A\otimes_k B$ is a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_p\times C_p$ (take $L=R=K_1\otimes_k K_2$). $\quad\blacksquare$

(Remark. The argument shows that the division hypothesis forces $K_1$ and $K_2$ to be linearly disjoint over $k$, so that $K_1\otimes_k K_2$ is itself a $C_p\times C_p$-Galois maximal subfield of $A\otimes_k B$; this is the concrete form of the general fact that a tensor product of two cyclic degree-$p$ algebras which is a division algebra has a $C_p\times C_p$-Galois maximal subfield. Note that the hypothesis $p>2$ is not used in an essential way; the argument is valid for every prime $p$.)

lemma_126.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. If $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^2$, then there exist a subfield $K$ of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$, and an element $b\in K$ that is not of the form $x^p-x$ for any $x\in K$, such that for a root $w$ of $T^p-T-b$ the centralizer $C_D(K)$ satisfies $C_D(K)\otimes_K K(w)\cong M_p(K(w))$.
lemma_126.proof:
Let char(k) = p > 2 and let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p^2 which is isomorphic to a crossed product (L, G, c) with |G| = p^2. We construct the required K and b in five steps.

Step 1: D contains a maximal subfield which is Galois over k with group G.
By the definition of a G-crossed product (and by ref_3, which realises (L, G, c) = \bigoplus_{g\in G} L u_g as a central simple k-algebra of degree |G| containing L as a commutative subalgebra), the algebra (L, G, c) contains L as a commutative k-subalgebra; concretely, L identifies with the direct summand L u_1 of the vector-space direct sum \bigoplus_{g\in G} L u_g, so the map x \mapsto x u_1 identifies L with a k-subalgebra of (L,G,c). Fix an isomorphism \varphi : (L, G, c) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } D and put L' := \varphi(L) \subseteq D. Then L' is a commutative k-subalgebra of D with
   dim_k L' = dim_k L = |G| = p^2 = deg(D).
(Here dim_k L = |G| because, by the definition of a Galois G-algebra recalled in the conjecture, L is etale over k of k-dimension |G| with L^G = k.)

The algebra L' is etale over k (etale-ness is preserved by k-algebra isomorphism), it carries an action of G by k-automorphisms, and (L')^G = k. Thus L' is a commutative etale k-algebra of dimension |G| with G-action and fixed algebra k, so ref_2(i) applies: G permutes the primitive idempotents of L' transitively, and if H is the stabilizer of one of them then L' \cong M^{[G:H]} with M a field Galois over k with group H, and L' is a field if and only if H = G, in which case L'/k is Galois with group G.

We claim H = G. Indeed, L' is a k-subalgebra of the division ring D, hence has no zero divisors: if e \in L' is an idempotent then e(e-1) = 0 forces e = 0 or e = 1. Therefore 1 is the only primitive idempotent of L', so m = 1 and [G:H] = m = 1, i.e. H = G. By ref_2(i), L' is a field and L'/k is a Galois field extension with Gal(L'/k) = G. (Equivalently: a finite-dimensional commutative domain over k is a field — for 0 \neq a \in L' the map x \mapsto ax is injective, hence surjective, k-linear on L', so 1 \in aL' — and then Artin's fixed-field theorem gives [L':L'^G] = [L':k] = |G|, so L'/k is Galois with group G.) Since dim_k L' = p^2 = deg D, the field L' is a maximal subfield of D.

Step 2: Choice of the subgroup H and of K.
By lemma_111, a group G of order p^2 is abelian, isomorphic to C_{p^2} or to C_p \times C_p. In either case G contains a subgroup H of order p (take a non-trivial element if exp(G) = p, or the p-th powers if G \cong C_{p^2}; equivalently, Cauchy's theorem gives an element of order p). Since G is abelian, H is normal in G. Define
   K := (L')^H \subseteq L' \subseteq D.
Then K is a subfield of D. By the Galois correspondence applied to the Galois extension L'/k with group G, the extension K/k is Galois with
   Gal(K/k) \cong G/H,
which has order |G|/|H| = p^2/p = p; every group of prime order is cyclic, so Gal(K/k) is cyclic of order p, and [K:k] = p. This is the required subfield K.

Step 3: L'/K is an Artin--Schreier extension with parameter b \notin wp(K).
The extension L'/K is Galois with group Gal(L'/K) = H (again by the Galois correspondence, since H \trianglelefteq G), hence is Galois of degree p over K. By Artin--Schreier theory (ref_14(a)), there exists b \in K \setminus wp(K), where wp(K) = \{x^p - x : x \in K\}, such that L' = K(w) for a root w of T^p - T - b. This b is the required element: it is not of the form x^p - x with x \in K.

For completeness we record two standard facts about this polynomial that we use below. (i) T^p - T - b is irreducible over K: if \alpha is one root in a separable closure K_s, the full root set is \{\alpha + i : i \in \mathbb{F}_p\}, and the Galois group G_K acts on it through a homomorphism G_K \to (\mathbb{F}_p, +) (the image records \gamma(\alpha) - \alpha); the image is a subgroup of the group of prime order p, hence is \{0\} or all of \mathbb{F}_p. If it were \{0\} then \alpha \in K and b = \alpha^p - \alpha \in wp(K), contradiction. So the image is \mathbb{F}_p, the action on the roots is transitive, and the minimal polynomial of \alpha over K has degree p, i.e. equals T^p - T - b. (ii) The field K(w) does not depend on which root w is chosen, since any two roots differ by an element of \mathbb{F}_p \subset K. Hence the statement 'for a root w of T^p - T - b, C_D(K) \otimes_K K(w) \cong M_p(K(w))' is well defined.

Step 4: The centralizer C_D(K).
By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), since K is a subfield of the central simple k-algebra D containing k, the centralizer C_D(K) is a central simple K-algebra of degree
   deg(C_D(K)) = deg(D)/[K:k] = p^2/p = p,
and dim_K C_D(K) = p^2 (equivalently, dim_k K \cdot dim_k C_D(K) = dim_k D, i.e. p \cdot dim_k C_D(K) = p^4).

Step 5: L' is a maximal subfield of C_D(K), hence splits it.
Every element of L' commutes with every element of K, because both lie in the commutative field L'. Therefore L' \subseteq C_D(K). As a K-subalgebra, L' is a field of degree [L':K] = p = deg(C_D(K)). Consequently L' is a maximal subfield of the K-central simple algebra C_D(K): any subfield of C_D(K) containing L' has K-degree at most deg(C_D(K)) = p, so it equals L'. (Ref_1 also gives C_{C_D(K)}(L') = L', confirming maximality.)

Finally we apply the maximal-subfield splitting criterion of ref_5 to the K-central simple algebra C_D(K) of degree n = p and to the field extension L'/K of degree m = p = n: since L' embeds in C_D(K) as a subalgebra (as shown above, as a maximal subfield), L' splits C_D(K), that is
   C_D(K) \otimes_K L' \cong M_p(L') = M_p(C_D(K) \otimes_K K(w) ... )
more precisely, since L' = K(w),
   C_D(K) \otimes_K K(w) \cong M_p(K(w)).

(For readers preferring an explicit argument for this last isomorphism: with B := C_D(K) and P := L', the commuting left and right multiplications give a K-algebra homomorphism B \otimes_K P \to \mathrm{End}_P(B), b \otimes \alpha \mapsto (x \mapsto b x \alpha), well defined because k is central, and P-linear because P is commutative; B is a free right P-module of rank dim_K B / [P:K] = p^2/p = p, so dim_K \mathrm{End}_P(B) = p^2 \cdot p = p^3 = dim_K (B \otimes_K P); the map is injective since B \otimes_K P is a free right P-module and the map is the natural embedding of a dense ring of endomorphisms whose commutant is C_B(P) = P (ref_1), so by the double centralizer theorem it is an isomorphism B \otimes_K P \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{End}_P(B) \cong M_p(P).)

Conclusion. The subfield K = (L')^H of D is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group G/H of order p, the element b \in K \setminus wp(K) satisfies L' = K(w) for a root w of T^p - T - b, and C_D(K) \otimes_K K(w) \cong M_p(K(w)). This is exactly the assertion of the lemma. (The hypothesis p > 2 is not used beyond what is needed for the statement; the argument is valid for every prime p.)

lemma_127.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. Let $K$ be a subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$, let $b\in k$ be an element that is not of the form $x^p-x$ for any $x\in K$, and let $w$ be a root of $T^p-T-b$. If the centralizer $C_D(K)$ satisfies $C_D(K)\otimes_K K(w)\cong M_p(K(w))$, then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for $G$ isomorphic to $C_p\times C_p$.
lemma_127.proof:
Write $\wp(F)=\{x^p-x:x\in F\}$ for a field $F$ of characteristic $p$.

**Step 1: the centralizer $C_D(K)$.** Since $\deg D=p^2$, $\dim_k D=p^4$. The subfield $K\subset D$ has $[K:k]=p$, which divides $\deg D=p^2$. By the double-centralizer theorem (ref_1), $C_D(K)$ is a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[K:k]=p^2/p=p$, Brauer equivalent to $D\otimes_k K$; in particular $\dim_K C_D(K)=p^2$. Since $K$ is commutative, $K\subseteq C_D(K)$.

**Step 2: the Artin--Schreier extension $K(w)/K$ is a field of degree $p$, Galois cyclic.** Fix a separable closure $\Omega$ of $k$ containing $D$, and view $w\in\Omega$ as a root of $f(T)=T^p-T-b\in K[T]$ (note $b\in k\subset K$). For every $i\in\mathbb F_p$ one has $(w+i)^p-(w+i)=w^p-w+i-i=b$, so $w+i$ is a root of $f$. Conversely, if $y$ is any root of $f$ then $y^p-y=w^p-w$, i.e. $(y-w)^p=y-w$, hence $y-w\in\mathbb F_p$. Thus the roots of $f$ are exactly $w+i$, $i\in\mathbb F_p$, all of them lying in $K(w)$; so $K(w)$ is the splitting field over $K$ of the separable polynomial $f$, and $K(w)/K$ is Galois. The map $\operatorname{Gal}(K(w)/K)\to(\mathbb F_p,+)$, $\sigma\mapsto$ the unique $i$ with $\sigma(w)=w+i$, is an injective group homomorphism, so $|\operatorname{Gal}(K(w)/K)|$ divides the prime $p$. By hypothesis $b\notin\wp(K)$, so $f$ has no root in $K$, hence $w\notin K$ and $[K(w):K]>1$. As $K(w)/K$ is Galois, $[K(w):K]=|\operatorname{Gal}(K(w)/K)|=p$. Let $\tau$ denote the generator with $\tau(w)=w+1$; then $\operatorname{Gal}(K(w)/K)=\langle\tau\rangle\cong C_p$. (Equivalently, $T^p-T-b$ is irreducible over $K$.)

**Step 3: $K(w)$ embeds into $C_D(K)$.** Apply the embedding criterion ref_5 with base field $K$, algebra $A=C_D(K)$ (central simple of degree $n=p$), and the field extension $K(w)/K$ of degree $m=p=n$ (so $m\mid n$). The hypothesis $C_D(K)\otimes_K K(w)\cong M_p(K(w))$ says precisely that $K(w)$ splits $C_D(K)$; the "in particular" clause of ref_5 (the case $m=n$) then yields a $K$-embedding $\iota:K(w)\hookrightarrow C_D(K)$. Composing with the inclusion $C_D(K)\hookrightarrow D$ we view $E:=\iota(K(w))$ as a subfield of $D$. Because $\iota$ is a $K$-algebra map, $\iota(c)=c$ for all $c\in K$, so $K\subset E$ and $E=K(\iota(w))$.

**Step 4: $E$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.** Since $\iota$ is an isomorphism $K(w)\xrightarrow{\sim}E$ fixing $K$, $[E:K]=p$ and $[E:k]=[E:K][K:k]=p\cdot p=p^2=\deg D$. Applying ref_1 to the subfield $E\subset D$: $C_D(E)$ is a central simple $E$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[E:k]=p^2/p^2=1$, hence $C_D(E)=E$; by the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1, $E$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

**Step 5: $E/k$ is Galois with group $C_p\times C_p$.**
(a) *Separability.* $E/K$ is Galois, hence separable, and $K/k$ is Galois, hence separable; separability is transitive for finite extensions, so $E/k$ is separable.
(b) *Normality.* Let $\sigma:E\to\Omega$ be a $k$-embedding. Then $\sigma|_K:K\to\Omega$ is a $k$-embedding of the normal extension $K/k$, so $\sigma(K)=K$. Moreover $\sigma(\iota(w))$ is again a root of $T^p-T-b\in K[T]$; by the root computation of Step 2 (applied to the root $\iota(w)$) there is a unique $i\in\mathbb F_p$ with $\sigma(\iota(w))=\iota(w)+i$. Hence $\sigma(E)=\sigma(K(\iota(w)))=\sigma(K)(\iota(w)+i)=K(\iota(w))=E$, so $\sigma$ is an automorphism of $E$. Thus $E/k$ is normal, and with (a), $E/k$ is Galois of degree $p^2$.
(c) *Restriction sequence.* Since $K/k$ is Galois, the restriction map $\operatorname{res}:\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)\to\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)$ is surjective: given $\sigma_0\in\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)\subseteq\operatorname{Hom}_k(K,\Omega)$, the extension theorem for embeddings gives a $k$-embedding $\tilde\sigma:E\to\Omega$ with $\tilde\sigma|_K=\sigma_0$, and normality of $E/k$ makes $\tilde\sigma$ an automorphism of $E$. The kernel is $\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)=\langle\tau_E\rangle$, where $\tau_E$ is the $K$-automorphism of $E$ with $\tau_E(\iota(w))=\iota(w)+1$ (conjugate to $\tau$ by $\iota$); this kernel has order $p$.
(d) *All elements have exponent $p$.* Fix a generator $\sigma_0$ of $\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)$, and let $\rho\in\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$. Write $\rho|_K=\sigma_0^{j}$ with $0\le j\le p-1$, and $\rho(\iota(w))=\iota(w)+i$ with $i\in\mathbb F_p$. Since $i\in\mathbb F_p\subset k$ and $\rho$ is a $k$-automorphism, $\rho(i)=i$; by induction $\rho^{n}(\iota(w))=\iota(w)+n\,i$ for all $n\ge1$, so $\rho^{p}(\iota(w))=\iota(w)+p\,i=\iota(w)$. On the other hand $\rho^{p}|_K=(\rho|_K)^{p}=\sigma_0^{jp}=(\sigma_0^{p})^{j}=\mathrm{id}$ because $\sigma_0$ has order $p$. As $E=K(\iota(w))$, it follows that $\rho^{p}=\mathrm{id}$. Hence $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$ has exponent dividing $p$; in particular it contains no element of order $p^2$ and is not cyclic.
(e) *Conclusion on the group.* By lemma_111, a group of order $p^2$ is abelian and is isomorphic either to $C_{p^2}$ or to $C_p\times C_p$. Since $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$ has order $p^2$ (Step 5(b)) and is not cyclic (Step 5(d)), $\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)\cong C_p\times C_p$.

**Step 6: $D$ is a crossed product.** Apply lemma_106 with $A=D$ (a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $n=p^2$) and $L=E$, which by Step 4 is a maximal subfield of $D$ and by Step 5 is Galois over $k$ with group $G:=\operatorname{Gal}(E/k)$. It provides a map $c:G\times G\to E^\times$ and a $k$-algebra isomorphism
$$D\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{g\in G} E\,u_g,\qquad u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)u_g,\qquad u_gu_h=c(g,h)\,u_{gh}\quad(\lambda\in E,\ g,h\in G),$$
which is exactly a crossed product algebra $(E,G,c)$ in the sense of the definition recalled in the statement, with $G\cong C_p\times C_p$.

If one wants the acting group to be literally $C_p\times C_p$, choose an isomorphism $\varphi:C_p\times C_p\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }G$ and set $c'(x,y)=c(\varphi(x),\varphi(y))$; then $E\,u_x\mapsto E\,u_{\varphi(x)}$ gives $(E,C_p\times C_p,c')\cong(E,G,c)\cong D$, and $E^{C_p\times C_p}=E^{G}=k$, so the Galois-$G$-algebra condition in the definition of crossed product is satisfied.

**Remarks.** (i) The hypothesis $b\notin\wp(K)$ was used exactly to ensure $[K(w):K]=p$, so that $E$ has degree $p^2=\deg D$ and is a maximal subfield. (ii) Note $\wp(k)\subseteq\wp(K)$, so $b\notin\wp(k)$ as well; this is not needed for the argument. (iii) The assumption $p>2$ is not used: the argument works verbatim for $p=2$.

lemma_128.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, write $\wp(F)=\{x^p-x:x\in F\}$ for a field $F$ of characteristic $p$, and let $K/k$ be a Galois extension of degree $p$ with generator $\sigma$, acting on $K/\wp(K)$. Then the homomorphism of $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector spaces $k/\wp(k)\to (K/\wp(K))^{\sigma}$ induced by the inclusion $k\subset K$ has cokernel of dimension one over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
lemma_128.proof:
We prove that coker(k/\wp(k) \to (K/\wp(K))^{\sigma}) is a one-dimensional \mathbb{F}_p-vector space, by constructing an explicit \mathbb{F}_p-linear surjection \delta:(K/\wp(K))^{\sigma}\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{F}_p whose kernel is exactly the image of k/\wp(k).

STEP 0 (Elementary preliminaries). In any field F of characteristic p, \wp(x)=x^p-x is additive (\wp(x+y)=\wp(x)+\wp(y)), hence \wp(F) is an additive subgroup and F/\wp(F) is an \mathbb{F}_p-vector space; moreover \ker(\wp)=\{x\in F:x^p=x\}=\mathbb{F}_p, since T^p-T has at most p roots and contains \mathbb{F}_p. Also, for \lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p and w in a char-p field, \wp(\lambda w)=\lambda^p w^p-\lambda w=\lambda(w^p-w)=\lambda\wp(w), so \wp is \mathbb{F}_p-linear. Finally, for every x in a char-p field and every field automorphism \alpha, \wp(\alpha(x))=\alpha(x)^p-\alpha(x)=\alpha(x^p-x)=\alpha(\wp(x)); i.e. \wp commutes with automorphisms.

STEP 1 (Artin--Schreier normal form). Since K/k is Galois of degree p, by Artin--Schreier theory (ref_14(a)) there are c_0\in k\setminus\wp(k) and z_0\in K with K=k(z_0) and z_0^p-z_0=c_0; the group Gal(K/k) acts by z_0\mapsto z_0+\lambda, \lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p. Since \sigma\neq\mathrm{id}, \sigma(z_0)=z_0+\lambda_0 with \lambda_0\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}. Put z=\lambda_0^{-1}z_0 and c=\lambda_0^{-1}c_0. Then
   z^p-z=\lambda_0^{-1}(z_0^p-z_0)=c\in k,
and c\notin\wp(k): indeed \wp(k) is an \mathbb{F}_p-subspace (Step 0), so c=\wp(w) with w\in k would give c_0=\wp(\lambda_0 w)\in\wp(k), a contradiction. Also \sigma(z)=\lambda_0^{-1}(z_0+\lambda_0)=z+1. Thus, replacing z_0 by z, we have
   K=k(z),\quad z^p-z=c\in k\setminus\wp(k),\quad \sigma(z)=z+1, \quad\text{so}\quad z^p=z+c, \tag{1}
and Gal(K/k)=\{1,\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{p-1}\} with \{1,z,\dots,z^{p-1}\} a k-basis of K. Write \operatorname{Tr}=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\sigma^i (the field trace, since K/k is Galois with this Galois group). Note \operatorname{Tr}\circ\sigma=\operatorname{Tr}, because \sigma permutes the elements \sigma^i.

STEP 2 (A power sum in \mathbb{F}_p). We claim \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} i^{r}=0 in \mathbb{F}_p for 0\le r\le p-2, and \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} i^{p-1}=-1. For r=0 the sum is p=0. For 1\le r\le p-2: the group \mathbb{F}_p^{\times} is cyclic of order p-1, so there is j\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times} with j^r\neq 1; multiplication by j permutes \mathbb{F}_p, hence S:=\sum_i i^r=\sum_i (ji)^r=j^r S, so (1-j^r)S=0 and S=0. For r=p-1: 0^{p-1}=0 and i^{p-1}=1 for i\neq 0, so the sum is p-1=-1.

STEP 3 (The trace on the power basis). For 0\le j\le p-1,
   \operatorname{Tr}(z^j)=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(z+i)^j=\sum_{m=0}^{j}\binom{j}{m}z^{m}\Big(\sum_{i=0}^{p-1} i^{j-m}\Big),
using \sigma^i(z)=z+i, hence \sigma^i(z^j)=(z+i)^j. By Step 2 the inner sum is 0 unless j-m=p-1 (the case j-m=0 gives p=0), in which case it is -1. If j\le p-2 there is no m\ge 0 with j-m=p-1, so \operatorname{Tr}(z^j)=0. If j=p-1 the only surviving term is m=0: \binom{p-1}{0}z^0(-1)=-1. Hence
   \operatorname{Tr}(1)=0,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(z^j)=0\ (1\le j\le p-2),\quad \operatorname{Tr}(z^{p-1})=-1, \tag{2}
and consequently \ker(\operatorname{Tr})=\mathrm{span}_k\{1,z,\dots,z^{p-2}\}.

STEP 4 (Image of \sigma-1; additive Hilbert 90 in this form). For 1\le i\le p-1,
   (\sigma-1)(z^i)=(z+1)^i-z^i=\textstyle\sum_{m=0}^{i-1}\binom{i}{m}z^{m},
which is a polynomial in z of degree exactly i-1 with leading coefficient \binom{i}{i-1}=i\neq 0 in \mathbb{F}_p. Hence (\sigma-1)(z),(\sigma-1)(z^2),\dots,(\sigma-1)(z^{p-1}) form a k-basis of \mathrm{span}_k\{1,z,\dots,z^{p-2}\} (triangular change of basis with non-zero diagonal 1,2,\dots,p-1). Since (\sigma-1)(1)=0, we obtain
   (\sigma-1)K=\mathrm{span}_k\{1,z,\dots,z^{p-2}\}=\ker(\operatorname{Tr}), \tag{3}
i.e. b\in K satisfies \operatorname{Tr}(b)=0 if and only if b=\sigma(x)-x for some x\in K.

STEP 5 (Definition of \delta). Put U:=(K/\wp(K))^{\sigma}=\{\bar a\in K/\wp(K):\sigma(\bar a)=\bar a\}=\{\bar a: (\sigma-1)a\in\wp(K)\}. For \bar a\in U choose y\in K with
   \wp(y)=(\sigma-1)a, \tag{4}
and define \delta(\bar a):=\operatorname{Tr}(y).
(a) \delta(\bar a)\in\mathbb{F}_p: using that \wp commutes with automorphisms (Step 0) and \operatorname{Tr}\circ\sigma=\operatorname{Tr},
   \wp(\operatorname{Tr}(y))=\textstyle\sum_i \sigma^i(y^p-y)=\operatorname{Tr}(\wp(y))=\operatorname{Tr}((\sigma-1)a)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma a)-\operatorname{Tr}(a)=0.
Since \operatorname{Tr}(y)\in k and \ker\wp\cap k=\mathbb{F}_p, we get \operatorname{Tr}(y)\in\mathbb{F}_p.
(b) Independence of y: any two solutions of (4) differ by an element of \ker\wp=\mathbb{F}_p, and \operatorname{Tr}(n)=pn=0 for n\in\mathbb{F}_p.
(c) Independence of the representative a: if a'=a+\wp(a'') with a''\in K, then, using \wp\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ\wp,
   (\sigma-1)a'=(\sigma-1)a+(\sigma-1)\wp(a'')=\wp(y)+\wp((\sigma-1)a'')=\wp(y+(\sigma-1)a''),
so y+(\sigma-1)a'' is an admissible choice for a', and \operatorname{Tr}(y+(\sigma-1)a'')=\operatorname{Tr}(y)+\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma a'')-\operatorname{Tr}(a'')=\operatorname{Tr}(y).
Thus \delta:U\to\mathbb{F}_p is a well-defined map; it is \mathbb{F}_p-linear because for \bar a,\bar b\in U with witnesses y_a,y_b, one has \wp(y_a+y_b)=(\sigma-1)(a+b), so \delta(\bar a+\bar b)=\operatorname{Tr}(y_a+y_b)=\delta(\bar a)+\delta(\bar b), and \delta(\lambda\bar a)=\lambda\delta(\bar a) for \lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p by \mathbb{F}_p-linearity of \wp and of \operatorname{Tr}.

STEP 6 (ker \delta = im(k/\wp(k))).
(\supseteq) Let \bar a be the image of \bar\lambda\in k/\wp(k), so a=\lambda+\wp(b) with \lambda\in k, b\in K. Then (\sigma-1)a=(\sigma-1)\wp(b)=\wp((\sigma-1)b), so y=(\sigma-1)b is admissible, and \delta(\bar a)=\operatorname{Tr}((\sigma-1)b)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma b)-\operatorname{Tr}(b)=0.
(\subseteq) Let \bar a\in U with \delta(\bar a)=0, and choose y with \wp(y)=(\sigma-1)a. Then \operatorname{Tr}(y)=0, so by (3) there is x\in K with y=(\sigma-1)x. Hence (\sigma-1)(\wp(x))=\wp((\sigma-1)x)=\wp(y)=(\sigma-1)a, i.e. \sigma(a-\wp(x))=a-\wp(x). Thus \lambda:=a-\wp(x) is fixed by \sigma, hence lies in k=K^{\sigma} (K/k is Galois with group \langle\sigma\rangle). Therefore \bar a is the image of \bar\lambda\in k/\wp(k).

STEP 7 (\delta is surjective). Take y:=-z^{p-1}. By (2), \operatorname{Tr}(y)=-\operatorname{Tr}(z^{p-1})=1. Compute \wp(y) using z^p=z+c from (1):
   \wp(y)=y^p-y=-(z^{p-1})^p+z^{p-1}=z^{p-1}-(z^p)^{p-1}=z^{p-1}-(z+c)^{p-1}.
The top-degree terms cancel: (z+c)^{p-1}=z^{p-1}+(p-1)c\,z^{p-2}+\cdots, so z^{p-1}-(z+c)^{p-1}=-\sum_{m=0}^{p-2}\binom{p-1}{m}c^{p-1-m}z^{m}\in\mathrm{span}_k\{1,z,\dots,z^{p-2}\}=:W. By (3), W=(\sigma-1)K, so there exists a\in K with (\sigma-1)a=\wp(y). Then \bar a\in U and \delta(\bar a)=\operatorname{Tr}(y)=1. Hence \delta is surjective.

STEP 8 (Conclusion). By Steps 6 and 7, \delta induces an isomorphism of \mathbb{F}_p-vector spaces
   (K/\wp(K))^{\sigma}\big/\mathrm{im}\big(k/\wp(k)\big)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\mathbb{F}_p,
so the cokernel of k/\wp(k)\to (K/\wp(K))^{\sigma} has dimension exactly one over \mathbb{F}_p.

(Remark: the argument never used p>2; it is valid for every prime p. Note also that the map k/\wp(k)\to (K/\wp(K))^{\sigma} need not be injective — its kernel is the one-dimensional space \mathbb{F}_p\cdot\bar c, as in ref_14(b) — which is irrelevant for the cokernel statement proved above.)

lemma_129.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$ and residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ with the valuation $w$ extending $v$ and having residue division ring $\bar k$. Let $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ be the associated graded ring and $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ the graded subring coming from $k$. Suppose that for every $y\in D$ with $w(y)\in \frac{1}{p}\mathbb{Z}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$ and $p\,w(y)<0$, the $p$-th power of the initial form $\mathrm{in}_w(y)$ does not belong to $\mathrm{gr}(k)$. Then $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^p-x\in k$.
lemma_129.proof:
We argue by contradiction: assume there exists $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^p-x\in k$, and derive a violation of the stated hypothesis on $p$-th powers of initial forms.

PRELIMINARIES ON THE GRADED RING. Since $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra, $k=Z(D)$, and since $w$ extends $v$ we have $w(c)=v(c)$ for every $c\in k^{\times}$; in particular $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z\subseteq w(D^{\times})$. For $\gamma\in w(D^{\times})$ put $D_{\ge\gamma}=\{y\in D^{\times}:w(y)\ge\gamma\}\cup\{0\}$ and $D_{>\gamma}=\{y\in D^{\times}:w(y)>\gamma\}\cup\{0\}$, and let $\mathrm{gr}(D)_\gamma=D_{\ge\gamma}/D_{>\gamma}$. For $0\ne y\in D$ write $\mathrm{in}(y)$ for the class of $y$ in $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{w(y)}$; it is a non-zero homogeneous element of degree $w(y)$. Because $w$ is a valuation on a division ring, $w(uv)=w(u)+w(v)$ for all $u,v\in D^{\times}$, and the multiplication $\mathrm{gr}(D)_\gamma\times\mathrm{gr}(D)_\delta\to\mathrm{gr}(D)_{\gamma+\delta}$ given by $(u+D_{>\gamma})(v+D_{>\delta})=uv+D_{>\gamma+\delta}$ is well defined and satisfies
$$\mathrm{in}(uv)=\mathrm{in}(u)\,\mathrm{in}(v)\qquad(u,v\in D^{\times});$$
indeed $w(uv)=\gamma+\delta$, so the coset of $uv$ in $D_{\ge\gamma+\delta}/D_{>\gamma+\delta}$ is precisely $\mathrm{in}(uv)$. In particular $\mathrm{in}(u^p)=\mathrm{in}(u)^p$ for all $u\in D^{\times}$. We shall also use the elementary fact that $\mathrm{in}(u)=\mathrm{in}(u')$ if and only if $w(u)=w(u')$ and $w(u-u')>w(u)$.

Finally, the natural homomorphism $\mathrm{gr}(k)\to\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is injective: for $\gamma\in\mathbb Z$ one has $D_{\ge\gamma}\cap k=k_{\ge\gamma}$ and $D_{>\gamma}\cap k=k_{>\gamma}$, because $w|_{k^{\times}}=v$ and $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$. We thus identify $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ with its (graded) image in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$; for $c\in k^{\times}$ the element $\mathrm{in}(c)$, computed in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$, lies in $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{v(c)}$.

STEP 1 (initial form of an Artin--Schreier element). Let $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^p-x=a\in k$. First, $a\ne 0$: if $a=0$, then $x$ is a root of $T^p-T=\prod_{\lambda\in\mathbb F_p}(T-\lambda)$ in $k[T]$; the factors $x-\lambda$ pairwise commute (the $\lambda$ are central) and $D$ is a division ring, so $\prod_{\lambda}(x-\lambda)=0$ forces $x-\lambda=0$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p\subset k$, contradicting $x\notin k$. Hence $a\in k^{\times}$.

We now apply the proved lemma lemma_109 (user Spark) to the henselian discretely valued field $(k,v)$ of characteristic $p>0$, the central division $k$-algebra $D$ with valuation $w$ extending $v$ and residue division ring $\bar k$, and the element $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^p-x\in k$. Its hypotheses are exactly those of the present lemma, and it yields
$$w(x)<0,\qquad p\,w(x)=v(x^p-x)=v(a),\qquad \mathrm{in}(x)^p=\mathrm{in}(x^p-x)=\mathrm{in}(a)\in\mathrm{gr}(k),$$
with $\mathrm{in}(a)$ homogeneous of strictly negative degree $p\,w(x)$. For completeness we recall the mechanism: $w(x)<0$ and $p>1$ give $p\,w(x)<w(x)$, so $w(x^p-x)=\min\{p\,w(x),w(x)\}=p\,w(x)$ and $\mathrm{in}(x^p-x)=\mathrm{in}(x^p)$; then $\mathrm{in}(x^p)=\mathrm{in}(x)^p$ by multiplicativity, and $\mathrm{in}(x^p-x)=\mathrm{in}(a)$ since $x^p-x=a$. Two consequences are recorded: (i) $w(x)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$ (as $p\,w(x)=v(a)\in\mathbb Z$), and (ii) $\mathrm{in}(x)^p\in\mathrm{gr}(k)$ with $\deg=p\,w(x)<0$.

STEP 2 (shifting by elements of $k$ when the value is integral). Choose a uniformizer $\varpi\in k$ with $v(\varpi)=1$; then $w(\varpi)=1$ and $\varpi$ is central in $D$. Claim: if $y\in D$ satisfies $w(y)=n\in\mathbb Z$, there exists $t\in k$ with $w(y-t)>w(y)$. Indeed, $z:=y\varpi^{-n}$ has $w(z)=0$, so $z\in\mathcal O_D^{\times}$ where $\mathcal O_D=\{u:w(u)\ge0\}$, and it has a residue $\bar z$ in the residue division ring $\bar D=\mathcal O_D/\{u:w(u)>0\}$. By hypothesis the natural map $\bar k\to\bar D$ (induced by $\mathcal O_k\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_D$, which is well defined since $w|_k=v$) is an isomorphism, so $\bar z$ is the residue of some $s\in\mathcal O_k$. Then $w(z-s)>0$, and with $t:=s\varpi^{n}\in k$ we get $y-t=(z-s)\varpi^{n}$, hence $w(y-t)=w(z-s)+n>n=w(y)$. This proves the claim.

STEP 3 (iteration). Define a sequence as follows. Put $x_0=x$. Given $x_i$ with $w(x_i)\in\mathbb Z$, choose $t_i\in k$ as in Step 2 applied to $y=x_i$ and set $x_{i+1}:=x_i-t_i$; stop as soon as some $x_i$ has $w(x_i)\notin\mathbb Z$.

Every $x_i$ that is defined satisfies the hypotheses of Step 1. Namely:
- $x_i\notin k$: otherwise $x=x_i+\sum_{j<i}t_j\in k$, since all $t_j\in k$.
- $x_i^p-x_i\in k$: since $t_j\in k=Z(D)$, the elements $x_j$ and $t_j$ commute, so $x_{j+1}^p=(x_j-t_j)^p=x_j^p-t_j^p$, and by induction $x_i^p-x_i=(x^p-x)-\sum_{j<i}(t_j^p-t_j)=a-\sum_{j<i}(t_j^p-t_j)\in k$.
Hence Step 1 applies to each $x_i$, giving
$$w(x_i)\in\tfrac1p\mathbb Z,\qquad w(x_i)<0,\qquad \mathrm{in}(x_i)^p\in\mathrm{gr}(k)\ \text{ of degree } p\,w(x_i)<0.$$
(Notice in particular that no $x_i$ can have value $\ge 0$, so the iteration never reaches value $0$ or above.)

The iteration must stop with a non-integral value. Indeed, $w(x_0)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z\cap\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$ in the case where no stopping occurs, and $w(x_0)<0$, so $w(x_0)=-m$ for some integer $m\ge1$. As long as the values stay integral they are strictly increasing integers, hence $w(x_{i+1})\ge w(x_i)+1$ and by induction $w(x_i)\ge -m+i$. If the process did not stop, it would be defined for $i=m$ with $w(x_m)$ an integer satisfying $w(x_m)\ge 0$, contradicting $w(x_m)<0$. Therefore there is an index $i\le m$ with $w(x_i)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z\setminus\mathbb Z$.

STEP 4 (contradiction). Set $y:=x_i$ for that index. Then
- $w(y)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z\setminus\mathbb Z$;
- $p\,w(y)=v(y^p-y)<0$, so $p\,w(y)<0$;
- $\mathrm{in}_w(y)^p\in\mathrm{gr}(k)$.
But the hypothesis of the lemma asserts that for every $y\in D$ with $w(y)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z\setminus\mathbb Z$ and $p\,w(y)<0$, the $p$-th power $\mathrm{in}_w(y)^p$ does NOT belong to $\mathrm{gr}(k)$. This is a contradiction.

CONCLUSION. The assumed element $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^p-x\in k$ cannot exist; that is, $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^p-x\in k$. (Note that the argument uses only the henselian discrete valuation, the fact that $w$ extends $v$ and has residue division ring $\bar k$, and the hypothesis on $p$-th powers of initial forms; the degree $p^2$ of $D$ and the inequality $p>2$ are not needed beyond what is stated, and no assertion about the value group $w(D^{\times})$ was made.)

lemma_130.statement: Let $k$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ with valuation $w$ extending $v$, residue division ring $\bar k$, and value group $w(D^\times)=\frac{1}{p^2}\mathbb{Z}$. Suppose that $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^p\in k$ and $w(x)\in\frac{1}{p}\mathbb{Z}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$. Then $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^p\in k$.
lemma_130.proof:
We argue by contradiction. Throughout, $w\colon D\to \mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$ is a valuation of the division ring $D$; by this we mean that $w(0)=\infty$, that $w(ab)=w(a)+w(b)$ for all $a,b\in D$ (valuation axiom, applied in the division ring $D$; multiplicativity is part of the data of $w$, it is not derived from the ultrametric law), that $w(a+b)\geq \min(w(a),w(b))$, that $w|_{k}=v$, that the residue division ring $\bar D$ equals $\bar k$ (so the structural map $\bar k\to \bar D$ is an isomorphism, i.e. every element of $\mathcal O_D$ has the same residue as some element of $\mathcal O_k$), and that $w(D^\times)=\frac{1}{p^{2}}\mathbb{Z}$.

We record two elementary consequences of the axioms. (a) $w(1)=0$, $w(-a)=w(a)$, and $w(a^{-1})=-w(a)$ for $a\neq 0$ (all from $w(ab)=w(a)+w(b)$). (b) (Strictness for unequal values.) If $w(a)\neq w(b)$ then $w(a+b)=\min(w(a),w(b))$: indeed, if $w(a)<w(b)$ and $w(a+b)>w(a)$, then $w(a)=w((a+b)-b)\geq\min(w(a+b),w(b))=w(a+b)>w(a)$, a contradiction.

Claim 1 (approximation of elements of integral value by elements of $k$). Let $z\in D$ and let $n=w(z)\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then there exists $c\in k$ with $w(z-c)>n$.
Proof of Claim 1. Since $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, choose a uniformiser $\varpi\in k^\times$ with $v(\varpi)=1$. Put $u=\varpi^{-n}z\in D^\times$. Then $w(u)=w(\varpi^{-n})+w(z)=-n\cdot v(\varpi)+n=-n+n=0$, so $u\in\mathcal O_D^\times$ and it has a non-zero residue $\bar u\in\bar D$. Because $\bar D=\bar k$ and $\mathcal O_k\twoheadrightarrow\bar k=\mathcal O_k/\mathfrak m_k$ is surjective, there is $c'\in\mathcal O_k$ whose residue in $\bar k=\bar D$ equals $\bar u$; equivalently $w(u-c')>0$. Set $c=\varpi^{n}c'\in k$ (note the exponent $n$, which may be negative, in which case $\varpi^{n}\in k^\times$ is still in $k$). Then $z-c=\varpi^{n}(u-c')$, hence by multiplicativity $w(z-c)=w(\varpi^{n})+w(u-c')=n+w(u-c')>n$. This proves Claim 1. (No perfection of $\bar k$ was used.)

Claim 2 (one reduction step). Let $y\in D\setminus k$ satisfy $y^{p}\in k$ and $w(y)\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then there is $c\in k^\times$ with $v(c)=w(y)$ such that, putting $y'=y-c$, one has $y'^{p}\in k$ and $w(y')\in\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$, and exactly one of the following holds:
(i) $y'=0$;  (ii) $y'\in D\setminus k$ and $w(y')\in\frac1p\mathbb{Z}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$;  (iii) $y'\in D\setminus k$, $w(y')\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $w(y')\geq w(y)+1$.
Proof of Claim 2. Apply Claim 1 with $z=y$, $n=w(y)$ to get $c\in k$ with $w(y-c)>w(y)$, and set $y'=y-c$.
We first show $c\neq 0$ and $v(c)=w(y)$. If $c=0$ then $y'=y$ and $w(y')=w(y)$, contradicting $w(y')>w(y)$. So $c\neq 0$ and $v(c)=w(c)$ is defined. If $v(c)<w(y)$, then $w(c)\neq w(y)$, so by (b) $w(y-c)=\min(w(y),w(c))=v(c)<w(y)$, contradiction. If $v(c)>w(y)$, then similarly $w(y-c)=w(y)$, contradiction. Hence $v(c)=w(y)$.
Next, $y'^{p}\in k$: since $c\in k\subset Z(D)$, the elements $y$ and $c$ commute, so they lie in the commutative $k$-subalgebra $k[y]\subset D$. In this commutative ring of characteristic $p$ the binomial theorem applies, and since $\binom{p}{i}\equiv 0\pmod p$ for $1\leq i\leq p-1$, we get $y'^{p}=(y-c)^{p}=y^{p}-c^{p}$. Now $y^{p}\in k$ by hypothesis and $c^{p}\in k$, so $y'^{p}\in k$. (This is the only place centrality of $c$ is used; additivity of Frobenius in the non-commutative ring $D$ is NOT invoked.)
Since $y\notin k$ and $y^{p}\in k$, we have $y\neq 0$, hence $y^{p}\neq 0$ in the division ring $D$, and therefore $y^{p}\in k^{\times}$ and $p\,w(y)=w(y^{p})=v(y^{p})\in\mathbb Z$. The same reasoning applied to $y'$ gives: if $y'\neq 0$ then $y'^{p}\in k^{\times}$ and $p\,w(y')=v(y'^{p})\in\mathbb Z$, i.e. $w(y')\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$.
It remains to split into the three cases. If $y'=0$ we are in (i). Assume $y'\neq 0$. If $y'\in k$, then $y=y'+c\in k$ (as $c\in k$), contradicting $y\notin k$; hence $y'\notin k$. If moreover $w(y')\notin\mathbb Z$ we are in (ii). If $w(y')\in\mathbb Z$, then $w(y')$ and $w(y)$ are integers with $w(y')>w(y)$, so $w(y')\geq w(y)+1$, and we are in (iii). This proves Claim 2.

Now suppose, towards a contradiction, that there exists $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^{p}\in k$. Then $x\neq0$, so $x^{p}\in k^{\times}$ and $p\,w(x)=v(x^{p})\in\mathbb Z$, i.e. $w(x)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$.
Case A: $w(x)\notin\mathbb Z$. Then $w(x)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z\setminus\mathbb Z$ while $x\notin k$ and $x^{p}\in k$, contradicting the hypothesis of the lemma. So Case A is impossible.
Case B: $w(x)\in\mathbb Z$. We iterate Claim 2. Set $x_{0}=x$. As long as case (iii) of Claim 2 occurs at step $j$, we obtain $c_{j}\in k^{\times}$ and $x_{j+1}=x_{j}-c_{j}$ with
 $v(c_{j})=w(x_{j})$, $\quad x_{j+1}\notin k$, $\quad x_{j+1}^{p}\in k$, $\quad w(x_{j+1})\in\mathbb Z$, $\quad w(x_{j+1})\geq w(x_{j})+1$.
By induction, as long as the iteration continues through step $j$ one has $w(x_{j})\geq w(x)+j$ and $v(c_{j})=w(x_{j})\geq w(x)+j$; in particular $v(c_{0})<v(c_{1})<v(c_{2})<\cdots$ is strictly increasing and tends to $+\infty$.
If at some step $j$ case (i) occurs, i.e. $x_{j+1}=0$, then $x=x_{j+1}+\sum_{i\leq j}c_{i}=\sum_{i\leq j}c_{i}\in k$, contradicting $x\notin k$. If at some step $j$ case (ii) occurs, the element $x_{j+1}$ satisfies $x_{j+1}\notin k$, $x_{j+1}^{p}\in k$ and $w(x_{j+1})\in\frac1p\mathbb Z\setminus\mathbb Z$, contradicting the hypothesis of the lemma. Hence the iteration cannot stop: we obtain infinite sequences $(x_{j})_{j\geq0}$ in $D\setminus k$ and $(c_{j})_{j\geq0}$ in $k^{\times}$ with $x_{j}=x-\sum_{i<j}c_{i}$ and
 $w(x_{j})\in\mathbb Z,\ \ x_{j}^{p}\in k,\ \ w(x_{j})\geq w(x)+j,\ \ v(c_{j})=w(x_{j})\geq w(x)+j.$

Claim 3 (tails). For each $j\geq 0$ the series $s=\sum_{i\geq0}c_{i}$ converges in $k$, and with $s_{j}=\sum_{i<j}c_{i}$ one has $v(s-s_{j})=v(c_{j})$.
Proof of Claim 3. Since $v(c_{i})\to\infty$, the sequence $(s_{j})$ is Cauchy: for $N>M$, $v(s_{N}-s_{M})=v(\sum_{i=M}^{N-1}c_{i})\geq\min_{M\leq i\leq N-1}v(c_{i})=v(c_{M})\to\infty$. As $k$ is complete, $s_{j}\to s$ for some $s\in k$.
Auxiliary observation: if $(t_{i})_{i\geq j}$ is a family in $k$ with $v(t_{i})\to\infty$ and $T=\lim_{N}\sum_{i=j}^{N}t_{i}$, then $v(T)\geq\min_{i\geq j}v(t_{i})$. Indeed, let $\gamma=\min_{i\geq j}v(t_{i})$ (a minimum exists since $v(t_i)\to\infty$, so only finitely many values lie below any bound); the partial sums satisfy $v(\sum_{i=j}^{N}t_{i})\geq\gamma$ by the ultrametric law. If $v(T)<\gamma$, then for every $N$, $v(T-\sum_{i=j}^{N}t_{i})=v(T)$ because $v(\sum_{i=j}^{N}t_{i})\geq\gamma>v(T)$ and (b) applies; then $T-\sum_{i=j}^{N}t_{i}$ would not tend to $0$, contradicting convergence. Hence $v(T)\geq\gamma$.
Applying the observation to $T=\sum_{i>j}c_{i}=s-s_{j}-c_{j}$ gives $v(s-s_{j}-c_{j})\geq\min_{i>j}v(c_{i})=v(c_{j+1})>v(c_{j})$. Since the two values $v(c_{j})$ and $v(s-s_{j}-c_{j})$ are unequal, (b) yields $v(s-s_{j})=v\big(c_{j}+(s-s_{j}-c_{j})\big)=v(c_{j})$. This proves Claim 3.

Conclusion of Case B. For every $j\geq0$, using $x-s=(x-s_{j})-(s-s_{j})=x_{j}-(s-s_{j})$ and $w|_{k}=v$,
 $w(x-s)\ \geq\ \min\big(w(x_{j}),\,w(s-s_{j})\big)=\min\big(w(x_{j}),\,v(s-s_{j})\big)=\min\big(w(x_{j}),\,v(c_{j})\big)=w(x_{j})\ \geq\ w(x)+j,$
where the third equality uses Claim 3 and $v(c_{j})=w(x_{j})$. Thus $w(x-s)$ is greater than or equal to $w(x)+j$ for every integer $j\geq0$. If $x-s\neq0$ then $w(x-s)\in\frac{1}{p^{2}}\mathbb{Z}$ is a fixed rational number, and choosing $j>w(x)-w(x-s)$ gives a contradiction. Hence $x-s=0$, i.e. $x=s\in k$, contradicting $x\notin k$.

Both cases lead to a contradiction, so no element $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^{p}\in k$ exists. This completes the proof.

Remarks on the use of the hypotheses: $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$ and $\bar D=\bar k$ are used exactly in Claim 1 (existence of a uniformiser and lifting of residues from $\bar D$ to $\mathcal O_k$); completeness of $k$ is used in Claim 3; the description $w(D^{\times})=\frac1{p^{2}}\mathbb Z$ is used only to know that $w$ is discrete-valued at the last step (in fact $w(x-s)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$ already follows from $(x-s)^{p}\in k$ once one notes $x - s$ need not be $p$-central, so the given value group is the convenient a priori discreteness). The characteristic assumption $p>2$ is more than needed for the binomial step, which only uses that $p$ is the characteristic. The added arithmetic hypothesis is genuinely needed: without it the conclusion is false (e.g. a totally ramified cyclic algebra $(L/k,\sigma,\varpi)$ of degree $p^{2}$ has $w(D^{\times})=\frac1{p^{2}}\mathbb Z$, residue field $\bar k$, and $x=y^{p}$ for $y^{p^{2}}=\varpi$ is $p$-central with $w(x)=\frac1p$), which is exactly the situation the hypothesis excludes.

lemma_133.statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $n$. Suppose $D$ is isomorphic as a $k$-algebra to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ where $G$ is a group of order $n$ and $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$. Then $L$ is a field, and its image in $D$ under such an isomorphism is a maximal subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$.
lemma_133.proof:
Write $A:=(L,G,c)=\bigoplus_{g\in G}Lu_g$ for the crossed product, and let $\Phi:A\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}D$ be a $k$-algebra isomorphism (unital). Recall from the hypotheses: $L$ is an \'etale (hence commutative) $k$-algebra with an action of $G$ by $k$-automorphisms, $\dim_k L=|G|=n$, and $L^G=k$; also $\dim_k D=n^2$ since $\deg D=n$. (Consistency check: $\dim_k A=[L:k]\cdot|G|=n\cdot n=n^2=\dim_k D$.) The case $n=1$ is trivial ($G=\{1\}$, $L=L^G=k$, $D=k$), so we argue in general; the argument below also covers $n=1$ verbatim.

STEP 1. The algebra $L$ embeds as a unital $k$-subalgebra of $A$.
By definition $A$ is a free left $L$-module with basis $\{u_g\}_{g\in G}$, and multiplication is determined by $(xu_g)(yu_h)=x\,{}^{g}y\;c(g,h)\,u_{gh}$ (this is associative because $c$ is a $2$-cocycle); in particular $u_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}$ and ${}^{1}=\mathrm{id}_L$. Write the unit of $A$ (which exists, $A\cong D$) as $1_A=\sum_{h\in G}x_hu_h$ with uniquely determined $x_h\in L$. For each $g\in G$,
$$u_g=1_Au_g=\sum_h x_hu_hu_g=\sum_h x_h\,c(h,g)\,u_{hg}.$$
Comparing coefficients of the basis element $u_g$ (only $h=1$ contributes) gives $x_1c(1,g)=1$, and comparing coefficients of $u_{hg}\neq u_g$ gives $x_hc(h,g)=0$, whence $x_h=0$ for $h\neq1$ (as $c(h,g)\in L^\times$). Thus $1_A=x_1u_1$ with $x_1\in L^\times$, and $x_1c(1,g)=1$ for all $g\in G$, in particular $x_1c(1,1)=1$. Consider $\lambda:L\to A$, $\lambda(x):=x\cdot 1_A=(xx_1)u_1$. Then:
- $\lambda$ is $k$-linear and $\lambda(1_L)=x_1u_1=1_A$;
- $\lambda$ is injective, since $\lambda(x)=0$ means $(xx_1)u_1=0$, so $xx_1=0$ by freeness of the basis, hence $x=0$ as $x_1\in L^\times$;
- $\lambda$ is multiplicative: $(xu_1)(yu_1)=x\,{}^{1}y\,c(1,1)u_1=xy\,c(1,1)u_1$, so
$$\lambda(x)\lambda(y)=(xx_1u_1)(yx_1u_1)=x\,x_1\,y\,x_1\,c(1,1)\,u_1=xy\,(x_1c(1,1))\,x_1u_1=xy\,x_1u_1=\lambda(xy),$$
using that $L$ is commutative and $x_1c(1,1)=1$.
So $\lambda$ identifies $L$ with the unital $k$-subalgebra $L1_A=Lu_1\subset A$. Set $L':=\Phi(L1_A)\subset D$; it is a commutative unital $k$-subalgebra with $[L':k]=\dim_k L=n$, and $\Phi|_L:L\xrightarrow{\sim}L'$ is an isomorphism of $k$-algebras.

STEP 2. $L$ is a field.
Since $D$ is a division ring, $L'$ has no zero divisors: $ab=0$ with $a,b\in L'$ and $a\neq0$ gives $b=a^{-1}(ab)=0$ in $D$. Let $0\neq a\in L'$. Multiplication by $a$, $m_a:L'\to L'$, $y\mapsto ay$, is $k$-linear (as $L'$ is commutative) and injective by the previous sentence; since $\dim_k L'=n<\infty$, $m_a$ is surjective. Hence there is $y\in L'$ with $ay=1$. Then $a(ya-1)=aya-a=a-a=0$, and again the absence of zero divisors with $a\neq0$ gives $ya=1$. Thus every non-zero element of $L'$ is a unit of $L'$, i.e. $L'$ is a field. Being isomorphic to $L'$, the algebra $L$ is a field as well.
(Equivalently, by the structure theory of Galois $G$-algebras, $L\cong M^m$ with $M/k$ a Galois field extension with group the stabiliser $H\le G$ and $m=[G:H]$; $m\ge2$ would give zero divisors, so $m=1$.)

STEP 3. $L/k$ is a Galois extension with Galois group $G$.
Let $H:=\mathrm{im}\big(G\to\mathrm{Aut}_k(L)\big)$; the fixed field is $L^H=L^G=k$. We use Artin's inequality: if $\mathcal H$ is a finite group of automorphisms of a field $E$ with fixed field $F$, then $[E:F]\le|\mathcal H|$. For completeness here is the proof. Write $\mathcal H=\{\sigma_1=\mathrm{id},\dots,\sigma_t\}$ and suppose $[E:F]\ge t+1$; choose $x_1,\dots,x_{t+1}\in E$ linearly independent over $F$. The homogeneous system $\sum_{j=1}^{t+1}\sigma_i(x_j)Y_j=0$ ($i=1,\dots,t$) has $t$ equations and $t+1$ unknowns over the field $E$, so it has a non-zero solution; pick a solution $a=(a_1,\dots,a_{t+1})$ with support of minimal size $r$, and relabel so that $\mathrm{supp}(a)=\{1,\dots,r\}$. Necessarily $r\ge2$: if $r=1$ then the equation for $\sigma_i$ reads $\sigma_i(x_1)a_1=0$, forcing $x_1=0$, contradicting independence. For any $\tau\in\mathcal H$, the vector $(\tau(a_j))_j$ is again a solution: given $i$, choose $i'$ with $\sigma_{i'}=\tau^{-1}\sigma_i$; then $\sum_j\sigma_{i'}(x_j)a_j=0$, and applying $\tau$ yields $\sum_j\sigma_i(x_j)\tau(a_j)=0$. Hence, for each $\tau$, $b^{(\tau)}_j:=a_j\tau(a_r)-\tau(a_j)a_r$ is a solution (an $E$-linear combination of the two solutions $a$ and $(\tau(a_j))$); its $r$-th coordinate is $a_r\tau(a_r)-\tau(a_r)a_r=0$, so its support is strictly smaller than $\{1,\dots,r\}$, and by minimality $b^{(\tau)}=0$. Thus $a_j\tau(a_r)=\tau(a_j)a_r$ for all $j,\tau$, and $c_j:=a_ja_r^{-1}\in E$ satisfies $\tau(c_j)=c_j$ for all $\tau\in\mathcal H$, i.e. $c_j\in F$. The equation for $\sigma_1=\mathrm{id}$ is $\sum_{j\le r}x_ja_j=0$, i.e. $x_r=-\sum_{j<r}c_jx_j$ with $c_j\in F$, contradicting the $F$-linear independence of $x_1,\dots,x_r$. Hence $[E:F]\le t$.

Applying this to $E=L$, $\mathcal H=H$, $F=k$ gives $n=[L:k]\le|H|\le|G|=n$. Therefore all inequalities are equalities: $|H|=|G|$, so $G\to H$ is an isomorphism (the action is faithful), and $[L:k]=|H|$.
It remains to see that $H$ is the full automorphism group and that $L/k$ is Galois. Fix an algebraic closure $\bar k\supseteq L$. Then $H\subseteq\mathrm{Aut}_k(L)\subseteq\mathrm{Hom}_k(L,\bar k)$, and $|\mathrm{Hom}_k(L,\bar k)|=[L:k]_s\le[L:k]$ (the separable degree is at most the degree; e.g. writing $L=k(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_s)$, a $k$-embedding is determined by the images of the $\alpha_i$, each of which is a root of a minimal polynomial, giving at most $\prod_i[k(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_i):k(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{i-1})]=[L:k]$ choices). Since $|H|=[L:k]$, both inclusions are equalities: $\mathrm{Aut}_k(L)=H$ and $[L:k]_s=[L:k]$. The equality $[L:k]_s=[L:k]$ says $L/k$ is separable; the equality $\mathrm{Aut}_k(L)=\mathrm{Hom}_k(L,\bar k)$ says every $k$-embedding $L\hookrightarrow\bar k$ maps $L$ onto $L$, i.e. $L/k$ is normal. Hence $L/k$ is a Galois extension and $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)=H\cong G$; via the (now faithful) action, we identify $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)=G$.

STEP 4. $L'$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.
Apply the double centraliser theorem for central simple algebras (ref. ref_1) to the subfield $L'\supseteq k$ of the central simple $k$-algebra $D$: $\dim_k L'\cdot\dim_k C_D(L')=\dim_k D$, and $C_D(L')$ is a central simple $L'$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[L':k]=n/n=1$. Thus $\dim_k C_D(L')=n^2/n=n=\dim_k L'$. As $L'$ is commutative, $L'\subseteq C_D(L')$, so $C_D(L')=L'$. If $E$ is any subfield of $D$ with $L'\subseteq E$, then $E$ is commutative, so $E\subseteq C_D(L')=L'$, whence $E=L'$. Hence $L'$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

STEP 5. The Galois structure on the image.
Transport the $G$-action to $L'$ by $g\cdot\Phi(x):=\Phi(gx)$; this is well defined because $\Phi$ is an isomorphism and $G$ acts on $L$, and it makes $\Phi$ $G$-equivariant. Then $(L')^G=\Phi(L^G)=\Phi(k)=k$, and by Step 3 applied to $L'$ (isomorphic to $L$ as a $k$-algebra, with $[L':k]=|G|$ and $G$ acting by $k$-automorphisms with fixed field $k$) the extension $L'/k$ is Galois with $\mathrm{Gal}(L'/k)=G$.

Conclusion: $L$ is a field, and its image $L'=\Phi(L\cdot1_A)$ in $D$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$. (In particular $(L,G,c)$ is a classical crossed product built from a Galois maximal subfield, in agreement with the crossed-product criterion.)

lemma_132.statement: Let $k$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose valuation $w$ satisfies $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$, with residue division ring $\bar D$. Then $D$ contains an element $a\notin k$ with $a^p-a\in k$ if and only if $\bar D$ contains an element $\alpha\notin\bar k$ with $\alpha^p-\alpha\in\bar k$.
lemma_132.proof:
Notation and standing facts. Let $O_k$ be the valuation ring of $k$, $\pi\in O_k$ a uniformizer, so $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z\cdot v(\pi)$; we identify $v(k^\times)$ with $\mathbb Z$ by $v(\pi)=1$. The hypothesis $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ thus says $w(D^\times)=\mathbb Z$: every $x\in D^\times$ can be written $x=\pi^{m}u$ with $m=w(x)\in\mathbb Z$ and $u\in D^\times$ with $w(u)=0$. Put $O_D=\{x:w(x)\ge 0\}$, $M_D=\{x:w(x)>0\}$; $O_D$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $M_D$ (its units are exactly $\{w=0\}$, and $1-xy$ is a unit whenever $w(x)>0,\,w(y)\ge0$), $\bar D=O_D/M_D$ is a division ring of characteristic $p$, and $O_k\hookrightarrow O_D\to\bar D$ identifies $\bar k=O_k/\pi$ with a subfield of $Z(\bar D)$. We write $\bar x$ for the residue of $x\in O_D$. We use three classical facts about complete discretely valued fields, each recalled with its (standard) justification: (H1) $O_k$ is henselian: if $g\in O_k[T]$ and $\bar r$ is a simple root of $\bar g\in\bar k[T]$, then $g$ has a unique root $r\in O_k$ with $\bar r$ equal to $\bar r$ (Newton iteration $r_{n+1}=r_n-g(r_n)/g'(r_n)$, which converges because $v(g'(r_n))=0$).
