(H2) A henselian valuation extends uniquely to every algebraic extension field; consequently, if $\Omega/k$ is an algebraic extension carrying the extended valuation and $\sigma:F\to\Omega$ is a $k$-embedding of a subfield $F\subseteq D$, then $w(\sigma(z))=w(z)$ for all $z\in F$ (as $z\mapsto w(\sigma(z))$ is another extension of $v$ to $F$). (H3) If $F/k$ is a finite field extension (inside $D$), then $F$ is complete for $w|_F$; elements of $F$ integral over $O_k$ satisfy $w\ge0$ (if $z^n+b_1z^{n-1}+\dots+b_n=0$, $b_i\in O_k$, and $w(z)<0$, then $z^n$ has strictly smaller value than every $b_iz^{n-i}$, contradiction); and the valuation ring $O_F=\{z\in F:w(z)\ge0\}$ is a finitely generated $O_k$-module (classical for complete DVRs), so any two $O_k$-lattices in $F$ are commensurable: for lattices $\Lambda\subseteq O_F$ there is $C\ge0$ with $\pi^{C}O_F\subseteq\Lambda$, hence $\pi^{m}O_F\cap\Lambda\subseteq\pi^{m-C}\Lambda$; i.e. on $\Lambda$ the topology induced by $w$ coincides with its $\pi$-adic topology, and $\Lambda$ is complete and closed in $F$.

DIRECTION ($\Rightarrow$). Let $a\in D\setminus k$ with $\wp(a):=a^p-a=c\in k$.

Step 1: we may assume $w(a)\ge0$. Suppose $w(a)=\gamma<0$. Since $p\gamma<\gamma$, the ultrametric inequality gives $v(c)=w(a^p-a)=w(a^p)=p\gamma$. By $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ choose $d_0\in k$ with $v(d_0)=\gamma$; then $u:=a d_0^{-1}\in O_D$ has $w(u)=0$. Since $d_0$ is central, $c=d_0^{p}u^{p}-d_0u$, hence $c d_0^{-p}=u^{p}-d_0^{\,1-p}u$. Now $w(d_0^{\,1-p}u)=(1-p)\gamma>0$ (as $p\ge2$, $\gamma<0$) while $v(cd_0^{-p})=v(c)-p\gamma=0$. Reducing modulo $M_D$ therefore gives $\bar u^{\,p}=\bar{(cd_0^{-p})}\in\bar k^{\times}$. Since $\bar k$ is perfect, there is $\lambda\in O_k^{\times}$ with $\bar\lambda^{\,p}=\bar{(cd_0^{-p})}$; then $(\bar u\bar\lambda^{-1})^{p}=1$ in the division ring $\bar D$, and since $\operatorname{char}\bar D=p$ we have $(\bar u\bar\lambda^{-1}-1)^p=(\bar u\bar\lambda^{-1})^p-1=0$, so $\bar u\bar\lambda^{-1}=1$, i.e. $u-\lambda\in M_D$. With $d:=d_0\lambda\in k$ we get $a-d=d_0(u-\lambda)$ and $w(a-d)\ge\gamma+1>\gamma$. Replacing $a$ by $a-d$: since $d$ is central, $\wp(a-d)=a^p-d^p-a+d=\wp(a)-\wp(d)\in k$, and $a-d\notin k$ (else $a\in k$), in particular $a-d\ne0$. Iterating produces a strictly increasing sequence of negative integers $\gamma_0<\gamma_1<\cdots$; it must terminate, so after subtracting an element of $k$ we obtain $a\in D\setminus k$ with $\wp(a)\in k$ and $w(a)\ge0$ (which we keep denoting $a$; note then $w(\wp(a))\ge0$).

Step 2: for such $a$, $\bar a\notin\bar k$. Assume $\bar a\in\bar k$ (this includes $w(a)>0$, where $\bar a=0$). Choose $\tilde a\in O_k$ with $\bar{\tilde a}=\bar a$ and put $b=a-\tilde a$; then $w(b)>0$, $b\notin k$, and $\wp(b)=c-\wp(\tilde a)=:c'\in k$. Since $w(b^p)=pw(b)>w(b)$, we get $v(c')=w(b^p-b)=w(b)>0$, so $c'\in\pi O_k$. Consider $f(T)=T^p-T-c'\in O_k[T]$; its reduction is $\bar f(T)=T^p-T=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p}(T-i)$, whose roots are simple because $\bar f\,'=-1\ne0$. By (H1), for each $i\in\mathbb F_p$ there is a root $\theta_i\in O_k$ of $f$. Both $f(T)$ and $\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p}(T-\theta_i)$ are monic of degree $p$ in the commutative ring $k[T]$ and have the $p$ distinct roots $\theta_i\in k$, hence $f(T)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p}(T-\theta_i)$ in $k[T]$. Evaluating at $b$ (legitimate since the $\theta_i$ are central, so $T\mapsto b$ gives a homomorphism $k[T]\to k[b]$) yields $0=f(b)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p}(b-\theta_i)$. A division ring has no zero divisors, so some factor vanishes: $b=\theta_i\in k$, whence $a=b+\tilde a\in k$, contradiction. Thus $\bar a\notin\bar k$, and $\alpha:=\bar a\in\bar D$ satisfies $\alpha^p-\alpha=\bar{a^p-a}=\bar c\in\bar k$. This is the required element.

DIRECTION ($\Leftarrow$). Let $\alpha\in\bar D\setminus\bar k$ with $\alpha^p-\alpha=\bar c_0\in\bar k$. (Remark: then $\bar c_0\notin\wp(\bar k)$, for if $\bar c_0=\beta^p-\beta$ with $\beta\in\bar k$, then $(\alpha-\beta)^p-(\alpha-\beta)=0$, so $\alpha-\beta\in\mathbb F_p\subset\bar k$, contradicting $\alpha\notin\bar k$.) Choose lifts $c\in O_k$ of $\bar c_0$ and $a_0\in O_D$ of $\alpha$.

Let $K=k(a_0)$; since $D$ is a division ring, $K=k[a_0]$ is a field, finite over $k$, complete for $w|_F:=w|_K$ by (H3). We claim $a_0$ is integral over $O_k$. Indeed, let $m(T)\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $a_0$ and factor it in an algebraic closure $\Omega$ (with the extended valuation) as $m(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(T-a_i)^{p^{s}}$ with $a_1=a_0$. By (H2), $w(a_i)=w(a_0)\ge0$ for all $i$. Each coefficient of $m$ is a sum of monomials in the $a_i$, hence has $w\ge0$; being an element of $k$, it lies in $O_k$. So $m\in O_k[T]$, i.e. $a_0$ is integral over $O_k$. Consequently $\Lambda:=O_k[a_0]\cong O_k[T]/(m(T))$ is a free $O_k$-module of rank $\deg m$, $\Lambda\subseteq O_K$ (integral elements have $w\ge0$), and by (H3) the $w$-induced topology on $\Lambda$ coincides with its $\pi$-adic topology; in particular $\Lambda$ is complete and closed in $K$. Note $\Lambda$ is commutative, being generated over $O_k\subseteq Z(D)$ by one element.

Set $e_0:=\wp(a_0)-c=a_0^{p}-a_0-c\in\Lambda$. Its residue is $\alpha^{p}-\alpha-\bar c_0=0$, so either $e_0=0$ (and then $a_0$ is already the desired element) or $w(e_0)\ge1$. Define inductively, inside the commutative ring $\Lambda$,
$$a_{n+1}:=a_n+e_n,\qquad e_n:=\wp(a_n)-c\quad(n\ge0).$$
All $a_n,e_n$ lie in $\Lambda$. Since $\Lambda$ is commutative of characteristic $p$, $(a_n+e_n)^p=a_n^{p}+e_n^{p}$, hence
$$e_{n+1}=\wp(a_{n+1})-c=\big(a_n^{p}+e_n^{p}-a_n-e_n\big)-c=\big(\wp(a_n)-c\big)+e_n^{p}-e_n=e_n^{p},$$\nso $w(e_n)=p^{n}w(e_0)\ge p^{n}\to\infty$; in particular $e_n\in\pi^{p^{n}}O_K\cap\Lambda$.

By (H3), $\pi^{m}O_K\cap\Lambda\subseteq\pi^{m-C}\Lambda$ for some fixed $C$, so $a_{n+1}-a_n=e_n\to0$ in the $\pi$-adic topology of $\Lambda$; $(a_n)$ is $\pi$-adically Cauchy and converges to some $a\in\Lambda$ (completeness of $\Lambda$). The inclusion $\Lambda\hookrightarrow K$ is continuous for these topologies ($\Lambda\subseteq O_K$), so $a_n\to a$ in $K$ as well. The map $x\mapsto x^{p}-x$ is continuous on $K$ (each $x^p$-term is a product of factors of value $\ge -\,$const on the convergent sequence), hence
$$\wp(a)=\lim_n\wp(a_n)=\wp(a)=c, since $x\mapsto x^p-x$ is continuous on the complete field $K$ and $e_n=\wp(a_n)-c$ satisfies $w(e_n)=p^n w(e_0)\to\infty$, hence $\wp(a_n)\to c$. Thus $\wp(a)=c\in k$. It remains to check $a\notin k$. If $e_0=0$ then $a=a_0$ and $\bar a=\alpha\notin\bar k$, so $a\notin k$. Otherwise $w(e_0)\ge1$ and $w(e_n)\ge p^n w(e_0)$, so by the ultrametric inequality $w(a-a_0)=w(\sum_{n\ge0}e_n)\ge w(e_0)\ge1$. Hence $\bar a=\bar a_0=\alpha$. If $a\in k$, then $\alpha\in\bar k$, contradiction. Therefore $a\in D\setminus k$ and $a^p-a=c\in k$. For completeness, in the first direction the case $c=0$ is impossible for $a\notin k$, since $a^p=a$ implies $a$ lies in the prime field $\mathbb F_p\subset k$; thus the valuation computation in Step 1 is legitimate. This completes the proof.

lemma_134.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and write $\wp(F)=\{t^p-t:t\in F\}$. Let $c_1,c_2\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ and $z_1,z_2\in k^{\times}$, and for $i=1,2$ let $A_i$ be the symbol $k$-algebra $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}k(w_i)v^i$ where $w_i^p-w_i=c_i$, $v^p=z_i$ and $v\lambda=\tau_i(\lambda)v$ with $\tau_i(w_i)=w_i+1$. If $A_1\otimes_k A_2$ is a division algebra, then it contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $C_p\times C_p$, and is therefore a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for $G\cong C_p\times C_p$.
lemma_134.proof:
Throughout, $\wp(F)=\{t^p-t:t\in F\}$, and $A=A_1\otimes_k A_2$, which is assumed to be a division algebra.

**Step 1. Artin--Schreier preliminaries.**

*Sublemma 1.1.* Let $\Omega$ be a field of characteristic $p$ and $c\in\Omega$. Put $f(T)=T^p-T-c$.
(i) If $w$ is a root of $f$ (in some extension of $\Omega$), the roots of $f$ are exactly $w+j$, $j\in\mathbb F_p$; they are pairwise distinct, and $f$ is separable since $f'(T)=-1\neq 0$. Indeed $(w+j)^p-(w+j)=w^p-w+(j^p-j)=c+0=c$ because $j^p=j$ for $j\in\mathbb F_p$.
(ii) If $f$ is reducible over $\Omega$ then $f$ has a root in $\Omega$. Proof: let $g\in\Omega[T]$ be a monic irreducible factor of degree $d$ with $1\le d<p$, and let $w$ be a root of $g$ in an algebraic closure of $\Omega$. By (i) the roots of $g$ are $w+j$, $j\in S$, for a subset $S\subset\mathbb F_p$ of size $d$. Comparing the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $g$ gives $\sum_{j\in S}(w+j)=-a_{d-1}\in\Omega$, where $a_{d-1}\in\Omega$. Thus $d\,w=-a_{d-1}-\sum_{j\in S}j\in\Omega$, and since $1\le d<p$ the integer $d$ is invertible in $\Omega$, so $w\in\Omega$. Hence a proper factor forces a root, i.e. reducibility implies a root in $\Omega$.
(iii) Consequently $f$ is irreducible over $\Omega$ if and only if $c\notin\wp(\Omega)$: if $c\in\wp(\Omega)$ then $f$ has a root in $\Omega$, hence splits as $\prod_{j\in\mathbb F_p}(T-(y+j))$ with $y^p-y=c$, so it is reducible (there are $p\ge 2$ distinct linear factors); and by (ii) reducibility implies $c\in\wp(\Omega)$.
(iv) If $c\notin\wp(\Omega)$ then $\Omega(w)/\Omega$ is a Galois extension of degree $p$ whose Galois group is generated by $w\mapsto w+1$: it is the splitting field of the separable irreducible polynomial $f$, it has degree $p$ and contains all roots $w+j$, and $w\mapsto w+1$ is a well-defined $\Omega$-automorphism of order $p$.

Applying Sublemma 1.1 with $\Omega=k$ and $c=c_i$ (which is not in $\wp(k)$ by hypothesis): $T^p-T-c_i$ is irreducible over $k$, $K_i:=k(w_i)$ is a field with $[K_i:k]=p$, Galois cyclic over $k$ with generator $\tau_i(w_i)=w_i+1$ (the map given in the statement is exactly this generator, since $w_i+1$ is the other root used to define the automorphism).

**Step 2. The factors $A_i$.** With $K_i$ as above, $A_i=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}K_i v^{j}$ with $v^p=z_i\in k^{\times}$ and $v\lambda=\tau_i(\lambda)v$ is precisely the cyclic algebra $(K_i/k,\tau_i,z_i)$ (the symbol algebra $[c_i,z_i)$). By ref_22 (i), $A_i$ is a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $p$, and since $K_i$ is a field, $K_i$ splits $A_i$: $A_i\otimes_k K_i\cong M_p(K_i)$.

**Step 3. $A$ is central simple of degree $p^2$.** Fix a separable closure $k_s$ containing $K_1,K_2$. Since $K_i\subset k_s$ and $K_i$ splits $A_i$, base change along the tower $k\subset K_i\subset k_s$ gives $A_i\otimes_k k_s\cong (A_i\otimes_k K_i)\otimes_{K_i}k_s\cong M_p(K_i)\otimes_{K_i}k_s\cong M_p(k_s)$. Hence
$$A\otimes_k k_s\cong (A_1\otimes_k k_s)\otimes_{k_s}(A_2\otimes_k k_s)\cong M_p(k_s)\otimes_{k_s}M_p(k_s)\cong M_{p^2}(k_s).$$
We now use the following elementary descent fact: *if $B$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra with $B\otimes_k F\cong M_n(F)$ for some field extension $F/k$, then $B$ is central simple of degree $n$ over $k$.* Indeed: (simplicity) for a nonzero two-sided ideal $I\triangleleft B$, faithful flatness of $F/k$ makes $I\otimes_k F$ a nonzero ideal of $B\otimes_k F\cong M_n(F)$, so $I\otimes_k F=B\otimes_k F$; then $(B/I)\otimes_k F=0$ and faithful flatness forces $B/I=0$, i.e. $I=B$. (Center) choosing a $k$-basis $b_1,\dots,b_N$ of $B$, $Z(B)=\bigcap_{r}\ker(\mathrm{ad}_{b_r})$ is a finite intersection; flat base change gives $\ker(\mathrm{ad}_{b_r})\otimes_k F=\ker(\mathrm{ad}_{b_r\otimes 1})$ and finite intersections commute with flat base change, so $Z(B)\otimes_k F=Z(B\otimes_k F)=F$, whence $\dim_k Z(B)=\dim_F(Z(B)\otimes_k F)=1$, i.e. $Z(B)=k$. (Degree) $\dim_k B=\dim_F(B\otimes_k F)=n^2$. Applying this with $B=A$, $F=k_s$, $n=p^2$, $A$ is a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$.

**Step 4. The subalgebra $K_1\otimes_k K_2$ inside $A$, and the dichotomy.**
The images of $K_1\otimes 1$ and $1\otimes K_2$ in $A$ commute elementwise, so $\mu\colon K_1\otimes_k K_2\to A$, $\mu(a\otimes b)=(a\otimes 1)(1\otimes b)$, is a unital $k$-algebra homomorphism. It is injective: $K_2\hookrightarrow A_2$ is injective and $K_1$ is a free (hence flat) $k$-module, so $K_1\otimes_k K_2\hookrightarrow K_1\otimes_k A_2$; and $K_1\hookrightarrow A_1$ is injective while $A_2$ is free over $k$, so $K_1\otimes_k A_2\hookrightarrow A_1\otimes_k A_2=A$.

Since $K_1\cong k[T]/(f_1)$ with $f_1(T)=T^p-T-c_1$, base change gives a $K_2$-algebra isomorphism
$$K_1\otimes_k K_2\;\cong\;K_2[T]/(f_1).$$

*Case (a): $c_1\in\wp(K_2)$.* Then $f_1=\prod_{j\in\mathbb F_p}(T-(y+j))$ in $K_2[T]$ with $y^p-y=c_1$, a product of $p$ pairwise coprime distinct linear factors, so the Chinese remainder theorem gives $K_1\otimes_k K_2\cong\prod_{j\in\mathbb F_p}K_2\cong K_2^{\,p}$. As $p\ge 2$, this algebra has a nontrivial idempotent $e$ (the image of $(1,0,\dots,0)$): $e^2=e$, $e\ne 0$, $e\ne 1$. Then $\mu(e)$ is an idempotent of $A$; injectivity of $\mu$ and $\mu(1)=1$ give $\mu(e)\ne 0$ and $\mu(e)\ne 1$. But a division ring has no nontrivial idempotents: $u^2=u\Rightarrow u(u-1)=0\Rightarrow u=0$ or $u=1$. This contradicts the hypothesis that $A$ is a division algebra. Hence Case (a) cannot occur.

*Case (b): $c_1\notin\wp(K_2)$.* By Sublemma 1.1 (iii), $f_1$ is irreducible over $K_2$, so $E:=K_1\otimes_k K_2\cong K_2[T]/(f_1)$ is a field, with $[E:k]=p^2$ and $[E:K_2]=p$. Consider the $k$-automorphisms $\sigma_1=\tau_1\otimes\mathrm{id}_{K_2}$ and $\sigma_2=\mathrm{id}_{K_1}\otimes\tau_2$ of the $k$-algebra $E$; they are automorphisms of the field $E$, they commute, and each has order $p$ (since $\tau_i$ has order $p$). Their cyclic subgroups intersect trivially: if $\sigma_1^{\,i}=\sigma_2^{\,j}$ with $1\le i\le p-1$, then, because $\sigma_1^{\,i}$ fixes $1\otimes K_2$ pointwise, so does $\sigma_2^{\,j}$; but $\sigma_2^{\,j}$ acts on $1\otimes K_2$ as $\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau_2^{j}$, which is the identity only when $\tau_2^{j}=\mathrm{id}$, i.e. when $p\mid j$; then $\sigma_1^{\,i}=\mathrm{id}$, contradicting $1\le i\le p-1$. Thus $\langle\sigma_1,\sigma_2\rangle\cong C_p\times C_p$ has $p^2$ elements. A field extension of degree $p^2$ admits at most $p^2$ automorphisms over $k$, so $\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)=\langle\sigma_1,\sigma_2\rangle\cong C_p\times C_p$ and $E/k$ is Galois.

**Step 5. $E$ is a maximal subfield of $A$.** By Step 4 Case (b) holds, and $\mu$ identifies $E$ with a subfield of $A$ satisfying $[E:k]=p^2=\deg A$. By ref_1, $C_A(E)$ is a central simple $E$-algebra of degree $\deg(A)/[E:k]=1$, hence $C_A(E)=E$; and ref_1's criterion states that a subfield $K$ of $A$ is a maximal subfield if and only if $C_A(K)=K$. Therefore $E$ is a maximal subfield of $A$, Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)\cong C_p\times C_p$.

**Step 6. $A$ is a $(C_p\times C_p)$-crossed product.** The field $E$ is a commutative \'etale $k$-algebra of dimension $p^2=|G|$, equipped with the action of $G=\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$ by $k$-automorphisms, with $E^G=k$; that is, $E$ is a $G$-Galois $k$-algebra in the sense of the definition. Applying lemma_106 to the central simple $k$-algebra $A$ of degree $p^2$ and to the maximal subfield $E$ which is Galois over $k$ with group $G$, there exists a map $c\colon G\times G\to E^{\times}$ such that
$$A\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{g\in G} E\,u_g,\qquad u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)u_g,\qquad u_gu_h=c(g,h)\,u_{gh}\quad(\lambda\in E,\ g,h\in G).$$
Thus $A=A_1\otimes_k A_2$ is a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $L=E$ and $G\cong C_p\times C_p$, which is exactly the claim.

(Remark on the logical flow: the hypothesis that $A_1\otimes_kA_2$ is a division algebra is used precisely to exclude Case (a) -- that is, to force $K_1\otimes_kK_2$ to be a field; in Case (a) the algebra contains nontrivial idempotents and so cannot be division.)

lemma_symbol_iff_cyclic_degree_p.statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and write $\wp(F)=\{t^p-t:t\in F\}$. For $c\in F\setminus\wp(F)$ and $z\in F^{\times}$, let $[c,z)$ denote the class in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ of the cyclic algebra $(F(w)/F,\tau,z)$ where $w^p-w=c$ and $\tau(w)=w+1$. Let $\beta\in\mathrm{Br}(F)$ be nonzero and killed by $p$, and let $D$ be the central division $F$-algebra with $[D]=\beta$. Then $\beta=[c,z)$ for some $c\in F\setminus\wp(F)$ and $z\in F^{\times}$ if and only if $D$ has degree $p$ and contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $F$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.
lemma_symbol_iff_cyclic_degree_p.proof:
Throughout, $\wp(F)=\{t^p-t:t\in F\}$. We first record elementary facts about $\wp$ and about Artin--Schreier polynomials, and then prove the two implications.

STEP 0 (PRELIMINARIES).
(0.1) $\wp(F)$ is an $\mathbb F_p$-subspace of $(F,+)$. Indeed, for $x,y\in F$ one has $(x+y)^p-(x+y)=(x^p-x)+(y^p-y)$ by the characteristic-$p$ binomial theorem; and for $\mu\in\mathbb F_p$ one has $\mu^p=\mu$, hence $(\mu x)^p-\mu x=\mu^p x^p-\mu x=\mu(x^p-x)$. In particular, for every $\mu\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}$, $\mu c\in\wp(F)\Longleftrightarrow c\in\wp(F)$.

(0.2) Let $c\in F$ and $P(T)=T^p-T-c\in F[T]$. Since $P'(T)=pT^{p-1}-1=-1\neq 0$, $P$ is separable, so it has $p$ distinct roots in an algebraic closure $\bar F$. If $\alpha\in\bar F$ is one root, then for every $i\in\mathbb F_p$,
$$(\alpha+i)^p-(\alpha+i)-c=(\alpha^p-\alpha-c)+(i^p-i)=0,$$
so $\{\alpha+i:i\in\mathbb F_p\}$ is a set of $p$ distinct roots of $P$, hence is exactly the root set of $P$.

(0.3) Assume $c\notin\wp(F)$, and let $g\in F[T]$ be a monic irreducible factor of $P$ of degree $d$, with root $\alpha$. Then $F(\alpha)$ contains $\alpha+i$ for all $i\in\mathbb F_p$, hence contains all roots of $P$; since $P$ is separable, $F(\alpha)/F$ is the splitting field of $P$, hence is Galois of degree $d$. Every $\rho\in\mathrm{Gal}(F(\alpha)/F)$ sends $\alpha$ to a root, say $\alpha+i(\rho)$ with $i(\rho)\in\mathbb F_p$, and $\rho\mapsto i(\rho)$ is a group homomorphism, because $\rho_1\rho_2(\alpha)=\rho_1(\alpha+i(\rho_2))=\alpha+i(\rho_2)+i(\rho_1)$ (the $i(\rho_2)$ being in the prime field, hence fixed). It is injective because $\alpha$ generates $F(\alpha)$ over $F$. Thus $d=[F(\alpha):F]=|\mathrm{Gal}(F(\alpha)/F)|$ divides $|(\mathbb F_p,+)|=p$, so $d\in\{1,p\}$. Hence $P$ has no irreducible factor of degree strictly between $1$ and $p$. Moreover $d=1$ for some factor is equivalent to $P$ having a root in $F$, which is equivalent to $c\in\wp(F)$. Combining: for $c\notin\wp(F)$, $P$ is irreducible over $F$.

(0.4) Consequently, for $c\notin\wp(F)$, $L_c:=F[T]/(T^p-T-c)$ is a field equal to $F(w)$ with $w^p-w=c$ and $[L_c:F]=p$. The rule $\tau(w)=w+1$ defines an $F$-automorphism of $L_c$, since $(w+1)^p-(w+1)-c=w^p-w-c=0$; its order is exactly $p$ because $\tau^m(w)=w+m\neq w$ for $1\le m\le p-1$. Thus $L_c/F$ is Galois with $\mathrm{Gal}(L_c/F)=\langle\tau\rangle\simeq\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$.

STEP 1 (THE IMPLICATION $\Longleftarrow$). Suppose $D$ has degree $p$ and contains a maximal subfield $L$ that is Galois over $F$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$; fix a generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)$.

By Artin--Schreier theory (ref_14(a)), there exist $w\in L$ and $c\in F$ with $L=F(w)$ and $w^p-w=c$. Necessarily $c\notin\wp(F)$: if $c\in\wp(F)$ then $T^p-T-c$ would have a root in $F$, so $L=F$, contradicting $[L:F]=p$.

By (0.4) applied to the $F$-isomorphism $L_c\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }L=F(w)$, the map $\tau_0$ with $\tau_0(w)=w+1$ is a well-defined generator of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)$. Hence $\sigma=\tau_0^{m}$ for a unique $m\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}$, so $\sigma(w)=w+m$. Set $j:=m\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}$, $w':=j^{-1}w$ and $c':=j^{-1}c$. Then:
(i) $F(w')=F(w)=L$, since $w'\in F(w)$ and $w=j\,w'$;
(ii) $w'^p-w'=j^{-p}w^p-j^{-1}w=j^{-1}(w^p-w)=c'$, using $j^p=j$ (so $j^{-p}=j^{-1}$);
(iii) $\sigma(w')=j^{-1}\sigma(w)=j^{-1}(w+j)=w'+1$;
(iv) $c'\notin\wp(F)$, by (0.1) applied to $\mu=j^{-1}$ (if $c'\in\wp(F)$ then $c=j\,c'\in\wp(F)$).

Now apply the proved lemma Spark/lemma_90 with $n=p$: $D$ is a central division $F$-algebra of degree $p$ containing a maximal subfield $L$ Galois over $F$ with cyclic Galois group generated by $\sigma$, so there exists $z\in F^{\times}$ such that $D\simeq (L/F,\sigma,z)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}Lv^i$ with $v^p=z$ and $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in L$. Via the identification $L=F(w')$ of (i), and since $\sigma(w')=w'+1$ by (iii), this algebra is precisely the cyclic algebra $(F(w')/F,\tau',z)$ appearing in the definition of the symbol class $[c',z)$ (with $\tau'(w')=w'+1$). Therefore $\beta=[D]=[c',z)$ with $c'\in F\setminus\wp(F)$ and $z\in F^{\times}$, which is the required conclusion.

STEP 2 (THE IMPLICATION $\Longrightarrow$). Suppose $\beta=[c,z)$ for some $c\in F\setminus\wp(F)$ and $z\in F^{\times}$. Write $L:=L_c=F(w)$ with $w^p-w=c$, and
$$A:=(L/F,\tau,z)=\textstyle\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}L\,v^i,\qquad v^p=z,\quad v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v\ (\lambda\in L),$$
so that $[A]=\beta$ by the definition of $[c,z)$.

(2.1) By (0.4), $L/F$ is a field extension which is Galois cyclic of degree $p$ with generator $\tau$. By ref_22(i), the cyclic algebra $(L,\tau,z)$ attached to this cyclic Galois extension and the parameter $z\in F^{\times}$ is a central simple $F$-algebra of degree $p$. (Concretely, with $u:=w\in L$, the two elements $u,v$ satisfy $u^p-u=c$, $v^p=z$ and $vuv^{-1}=\tau(u)=u+1$, and they generate $A$ as an $F$-algebra because $L=F[u]$ and $A=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}Lv^i$.)

(2.2) Since $A$ is central simple and $D$ is the central division $F$-algebra with $[D]=\beta=[A]$, there is a unique integer $r\ge 1$ with $A\simeq M_r(D)$ and $\deg A=r\deg D$. Hence $p=r\deg D$, so $\deg D\in\{1,p\}$. If $\deg D=1$ then $D=F$ and $\beta=[D]=0$, contradicting the hypothesis $\beta\neq0$. Therefore $\deg D=p$ and $r=1$, i.e. $A\simeq D$. In particular, $D$ has degree $p$.

(2.3) The inclusion of the $i=0$ summand identifies $L$ with an $F$-subalgebra of $A$ (a field, since $L$ is a field). Composing with an isomorphism $A\simeq D$ of $F$-algebras, we obtain an $F$-subfield $K\subset D$ with $[K:F]=\dim_F L=p$. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), $\dim_F K\cdot\dim_F C_D(K)=\dim_F D=p^2$, so $\dim_F C_D(K)=p^2/p=p=\dim_F K$. Since $K$ is commutative, $K\subseteq C_D(K)$, and equality of dimensions forces $C_D(K)=K$. Ref_1 (maximal subfield criterion: $K$ is a maximal subfield if and only if $C_D(K)=K$) then shows that $K$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

(2.4) The isomorphism $A\simeq D$ restricts to an $F$-isomorphism $L\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }K$; hence $K/F$ is Galois with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ cyclic of order $p$, generated by $x\mapsto\varphi\tau(\varphi^{-1}(x))$, where $\varphi:L\xrightarrow{\sim}K$ is that isomorphism.

Steps 2.2--2.4 give exactly that $D$ has degree $p$ and contains a maximal subfield Galois over $F$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.

CONCLUSION. Steps 1 and 2 together prove the equivalence. (Remark on the standing hypotheses, not used as an input: in Step 2 the class $\beta$ is automatically killed by $p$ because it is represented by an algebra of degree $p$; in Step 1 it is killed by $p$ because $\operatorname{ind}(\beta)=\deg D=p$ forces $\exp(\beta)\mid p$. The hypothesis $\beta\neq0$ is used essentially, in Step 2.2, to exclude the split case $D=F$ of degree $1$, which contains no subfield of degree $p$ and for which no symbol $[c,z)$ with $c\notin\wp(F)$ represents $\beta$.)

lemma_137.statement: Let $p$ be a prime and let $F=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$ be a rational function field in two variables. Let $z$ be a root of $T^p-T-s$, set $K=F(z)$, let $w$ be a root of $T^p-T-tz$, and set $L=K(w)$. Then $L$ is a separable extension of $F$ of degree $p^2$ which is not Galois over $F$.
lemma_137.proof:
Notation. For a field E of characteristic p write wp(E) = {x^p - x : x in E}. We use the proved lemma (Spark, lemma_73): if (E,v) is a field of characteristic p equipped with a discrete valuation v: E^x -> Z and c in E satisfies v(c) < 0 with p not dividing v(c), then c is not in wp(E). Note that no hypothesis p > 2 is used anywhere.

PRELIMINARY CLAIM (Artin-Schreier dichotomy). Let E be a field of characteristic p and a in E. If a in wp(E), then X^p - X - a splits over E into p distinct linear factors. If a not in wp(E), then X^p - X - a is irreducible over E, and for a root theta the extension E(theta)/E is cyclic Galois of degree p with generator theta |-> theta + 1.
Proof of the claim. If a = b^p - b then X^p - X - a = (X-b)^p - (X-b), so the roots are b + i, i in F_p, all distinct (the derivative of X^p - X - a is -1 != 0, so the polynomial is separable), and it splits into linear factors. Conversely, let theta be a root in a separable closure E_s. Since the derivative is -1, the polynomial is separable, and every root has the form theta + i for a unique i in F_p. Thus the absolute Galois group G_E acts on the root set by sigma(theta) = theta + c_sigma with c_sigma in F_p. For sigma, tau in G_E, using that F_p is pointwise fixed by sigma, c_{sigma tau} = sigma(tau(theta)) - theta = sigma(theta + c_tau) - theta = sigma(theta) + c_tau - theta = c_sigma + c_tau. Hence c: G_E -> F_p is a group homomorphism, and its image is a subgroup of the additive group of F_p, hence either {0} or all of F_p. If im(c) = {0}, then theta is fixed by G_E, so theta in E and a = theta^p - theta in wp(E). If im(c) = F_p, then the fixed field of ker(c) is E(theta) (clearly E(theta) is contained in it, and any element of the separable closure fixed by ker(c) and moved by an element with c_sigma != 0 cannot lie in E; formally, [E(theta):E] equals the size of the orbit of theta under G_E, which is |im c| = p). Thus the minimal polynomial of theta over E has degree p; it divides the degree-p polynomial X^p - X - a, so they coincide and X^p - X - a is irreducible. In that case E(theta) contains all the roots theta + i, i in F_p, so it is the splitting field of a separable polynomial, hence Galois of degree p; the map sigma: theta |-> theta + 1 is an E-automorphism (it sends theta to another root) of order p, so Gal(E(theta)/E) = <sigma> is cyclic of order p. This proves the claim. In particular, for every field E of characteristic p and every a in E: X^p - X - a is irreducible over E if and only if a not in wp(E).                                    

STEP 1 - [K:F] = p. Write F = F_p(t)(s). Let v_1 be the degree (pole at infinity) valuation in the variable s: for a nonzero polynomial h in F_p(t)[s] set v_1(h) = -deg_s(h), and extend to the fraction field F by v_1(h_1/h_2) = -deg_s(h_1) + deg_s(h_2). This is a discrete valuation whose value group is Z, since v_1(s) = -1. We have v_1(s) = -1 < 0 and p does not divide 1. By lemma_73 applied to (F, v_1) and c = s, s is not in wp(F). By the claim, X^p - X - s is irreducible over F, hence [K:F] = p, and K/F is cyclic Galois with generator sigma given by sigma(z) = z + 1.

STEP 2 - [L:K] = p. Because s = z^p - z, we have F_p(s) subset F_p(z), so K = F_p(s,t)(z) = F_p(z)(t). Also z != 0: if z = 0 then s = z^p - z = 0 in K, contradicting that s is transcendental over F_p. Since z is algebraic of degree p over F_p(s) and s is transcendental over F_p, z is transcendental over F_p; hence K = F_p(z)(t) is a rational function field in the variable t over the field F_p(z). Let v_2 be the degree valuation in t: for a nonzero h in F_p(z)[t] set v_2(h) = -deg_t(h), extended to K = Frac(F_p(z)[t]). Then v_2: K^x -> Z is a discrete valuation, surjective because v_2(t) = -1, and v_2 is identically 0 on F_p(z)^x (elements of F_p(z)^x are the nonzero constants with respect to t). Hence v_2(tz) = v_2(t) + v_2(z) = -1 + 0 = -1. Since -1 < 0 and p does not divide 1, lemma_73 applied to (K, v_2) and c = tz gives tz not in wp(K). By the claim, X^p - X - tz is irreducible over K, so [L:K] = p, and L/K is cyclic Galois with generator tau given by tau(w) = w + 1. By the tower law, [L:F] = [L:K]·[K:F] = p·p = p^2.

STEP 3 - separability. The polynomials X^p - X - s and X^p - X - tz both have derivative -1 != 0, hence are separable; so K/F and L/K are separable extensions (indeed Galois, by Steps 1 and 2). A tower of separable extensions is separable: for alpha in L, the minimal polynomial of alpha over F divides the norm-free product of conjugates of its minimal polynomial over K, or more simply separability is preserved under composition of extensions. Thus L/F is separable, of degree p^2 by Step 2.

STEP 4 - rational presentation of L. We have s = z^p - z in F_p(z,w), and from tz = w^p - w with z != 0 we get t = (w^p - w)/z in F_p(z,w). Therefore F = F_p(s,t) subset F_p(z,w) subset L, and since L = F_p(s,t,z,w) it follows that L = F_p(z,w). For transcendence degrees: trdeg_{F_p} F = 2 because s, t are algebraically independent over F_p (F is a rational function field in two variables), and L/F is algebraic, so trdeg_{F_p} L = trdeg_{F_p} F = 2. Hence 2 = trdeg_{F_p} F <= trdeg_{F_p} F_p(z,w) <= trdeg_{F_p} L = 2, so trdeg_{F_p} F_p(z,w) = 2. Since F_p(z,w) is generated over F_p by the two elements z and w, transcendence degree 2 forces z and w to be algebraically independent over F_p. Consequently F_p[z,w] is a polynomial ring in two variables over F_p, and L = F_p(z,w) = Frac(F_p[z,w]).

STEP 5 - t is not in wp(L). The ring F_p[z,w] is a unique factorisation domain (polynomial ring over a field), and z is irreducible in it, hence a prime element. Let v_3: L^x -> Z be the z-adic valuation: for nonzero f, g in F_p[z,w], v_3(f/g) = ord_z(f) - ord_z(g), the difference of the exponents of z in the prime factorisations. This is a well-defined discrete valuation on L, and its value group is Z because v_3(z) = 1. Now w^p - w is a nonzero element of F_p[w] subset F_p[z,w]; its image in the quotient F_p[z,w]/(z) = F_p[w] is w^p - w, which is not zero (it is a nonzero polynomial of degree p). Hence z does not divide w^p - w, i.e. v_3(w^p - w) = 0. Therefore v_3(t) = v_3(w^p - w) - v_3(z) = 0 - 1 = -1. Since -1 < 0 and p does not divide 1, lemma_73 applied to (L, v_3) and c = t yields t not in wp(L).
From this we deduce that i·t not in wp(L) for every i in F_p^x. Indeed, if it = x^p - x for some x in L, then multiplying by i^{-1} and using (i^{-1})^p = i^{-1} (as i^{-1} lies in the prime field F_p) gives t = i^{-1}x^p - i^{-1}x = (i^{-1}x)^p - (i^{-1}x) in wp(L), a contradiction.

STEP 6 - counting F-automorphisms of L. Let phi in Aut_F(L). By Step 1, K/F is the splitting field over F of the separable polynomial X^p - X - s, hence normal; therefore any F-embedding of K into L has image K, and phi(K) = K with phi|_K in Gal(K/F) = <sigma>. So there is i in F_p with phi(z) = sigma^i(z) = z + i.
Suppose i != 0, and put delta = phi(w) - w in L. Using that phi is a ring homomorphism fixing F_p (hence phi(w)^p = phi(w^p)) and fixing t, we compute
delta^p - delta = (phi(w)^p - w^p) - (phi(w) - w) = phi(w^p - w) - (w^p - w) = phi(tz) - tz = t·phi(z) - tz = t(z + i) - tz = i·t.
This exhibits i·t as an element of wp(L), contradicting the conclusion of Step 5 (since i != 0). Hence i = 0, i.e. phi(z) = z and phi|_K = id_K.
Thus Aut_F(L) = Aut_K(L). By Step 2, L/K is cyclic Galois of degree p with Gal(L/K) = {w |-> w + j : j in F_p}: these p maps are well-defined because L = K(w) is the splitting field of X^p - X - tz whose roots are exactly w + j, and there are no others since L is generated over K by w. Hence |Aut_F(L)| = p.

STEP 7 - conclusion. For a finite extension E/F, the number of F-automorphisms of E equals the number of F-embeddings of E into an algebraic closure if and only if E/F is normal; that number is always [E:F]_s, the separable degree. Hence a finite extension is Galois (normal and separable) if and only if |Aut_F(E)| = [E:F]. Here L/F is separable with [L:F] = p^2, while |Aut_F(L)| = p < p^2. Therefore L/F is not Galois.

Combining Steps 2, 3 and 7: L is a separable extension of F of degree p^2 which is not Galois over F. QED.

lemma_136.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose valuation $w$ extending $v$ satisfies $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ and has residue division ring $\bar D$ central of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$. Then every maximal subfield $\bar L$ of $\bar D$ that is Galois over $\bar k$ is the residue field of a maximal subfield $L$ of $D$ containing $k$, unramified over $k$ and Galois over $k$, such that reduction induces an isomorphism $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$.
lemma_136.proof:
We prove the lemma by constructing the required subfield $L\subset D$ directly, as the field generated over $k$ by a Hensel-lift of a primitive element of $\bar L$. This makes the residue field of $L$ **equal** to the prescribed subfield $\bar L\subset \bar D$ (not merely abstractly isomorphic to it), which is precisely the point that was missing before.

Notation. Let $R=\{a\in k: v(a)\ge 0\}\cup\{0\}$ be the valuation ring of $k$, $\mathfrak m$ its maximal ideal, so $R/\mathfrak m=\bar k$. Let $O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}\cup\{0\}$ and $M_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\}$; then $O_D$ is the valuation ring of the valued division ring $(D,w)$, $M_D$ its maximal ideal, and $\bar D=O_D/M_D$ with reduction map $x\mapsto \bar x$. Since $w$ extends $v$, $R\subset O_D$ and $\mathfrak m\subset M_D$, and the induced map $R/\mathfrak m\to \bar D$ identifies $\bar k$ with the residue field of $k$ inside $\bar D$.

**Step 1. The degree of $\bar L$ over $\bar k$ is $p^2$.**
$\bar D$ is central simple of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$, so $\dim_{\bar k}\bar D=p^4$. Put $d=[\bar L:\bar k]$. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), $C_{\bar D}(\bar L)$ is a central simple $\bar L$-algebra of degree $\deg(\bar D)/[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2/d$. Suppose $p^2/d>1$. Since $\bar D$ is a division ring, $C_{\bar D}(\bar L)$ contains an element $y\notin \bar L$. The subring $\bar L[y]\subset \bar D$ is commutative (it lies in the centralizer of $\bar L$, and $y$ commutes with $\bar L$), is a domain (subring of the division ring $\bar D$), and is finite dimensional over the field $\bar L$; a finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field. Thus $\bar L[y]$ is a subfield of $\bar D$ strictly containing $\bar L$, contradicting maximality of $\bar L$. Hence $p^2/d=1$, i.e. $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$. By hypothesis $\bar L/\bar k$ is Galois, so $|\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)|=p^2$.

**Step 2. Primitive element and its lifts.**
Since $\bar k$ is perfect, $\bar L/\bar k$ is separable; by the primitive element theorem choose $\bar\theta\in\bar L$ with $\bar L=\bar k(\bar\theta)$. Let $\bar f\in\bar k[T]$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\bar\theta$: $\bar f$ is irreducible of degree $p^2$, and since $\bar L/\bar k$ is Galois, $\bar f$ splits in $\bar L$ into $p^2$ distinct roots; in particular $\bar f'\ne 0$ and $\bar f'(\bar\alpha)\ne 0$ for every root $\bar\alpha$ of $\bar f$ in $\bar L$. Choose a monic polynomial $f\in R[T]$ lifting $\bar f$, and choose a lift $\theta\in O_D$ of $\bar\theta$ (the reduction $O_D\twoheadrightarrow\bar D$ is onto).

**Step 3. Hensel lifting inside $k(\theta)$.**
$k[\theta]$ is a commutative finite-dimensional $k$-subalgebra of the division ring $D$; it is a domain, and multiplication by any non-zero element of $k[\theta]$ is an injective, hence surjective, $k$-linear endomorphism of $k[\theta]$, so $1$ lies in the image: $k[\theta]$ is a field. Write $L_0=k(\theta)=k[\theta]$. The restriction of $w$ to $L_0$ is a valuation extending $v$; since $(k,v)$ is henselian, the extension of $v$ to the algebraic extension $L_0$ is unique and $(L_0,w)$ is henselian (we use the standard equivalence: a valued field is henselian iff its valuation extends uniquely to every algebraic extension; uniqueness for $k$ then forces uniqueness over $L_0$, because any extension of $w|_{L_0}$ to an algebraic $M/L_0$ is an extension of $v$ to $M$, hence unique). Let $O_{L_0}=L_0\cap O_D=\{x\in L_0:w(x)\ge0\}$ and $\mathfrak p_0=L_0\cap M_D=\{x\in L_0:w(x)>0\}$, its maximal ideal.

Since $f$ is monic with coefficients in $R\subset O_{L_0}$ and $\theta\in O_{L_0}$, we have $f(\theta)\in O_{L_0}$, and its residue in $\bar D$ is $\bar f(\bar\theta)=0$; hence $f(\theta)\in\mathfrak p_0$. Similarly $f'(\theta)\in O_{L_0}$ has residue $\bar f'(\bar\theta)\ne0$, so $w(f'(\theta))=0$ and $f'(\theta)\in O_{L_0}^{\times}$. By Hensel's lemma (standard form: $f(a)\in\mathfrak p$, $f'(a)\in O^{\times}$ implies a unique root $b$ of $f$ with $b-a\in\mathfrak p$) applied in the henselian field $(L_0,w)$, there is a unique $\theta'\in O_{L_0}$ with
$$f(\theta')=0,\qquad \theta'-\theta\in\mathfrak p_0 .$$
In particular the residue of $\theta'$ in $\bar D$ is $\bar\theta$.

**Step 4. The field $L=k(\theta')$ and its degree.**
Set $L:=k(\theta')\subseteq L_0\subseteq D$. The polynomial $f$ is irreducible over $k$: $R$ is a DVR, hence a UFD, so by Gauss's lemma a factorisation of the primitive (monic) polynomial $f$ in $k[T]$ into monic factors of positive degree would give a factorisation in $R[T]$ into monic factors; reducing modulo $\mathfrak m$ preserves degrees (the factors remain monic) and would give a non-trivial factorisation of the irreducible $\bar f$ — impossible. Hence $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\theta'$ over $k$, and
$$[L:k]=\deg f=p^2.$$

**Step 5. $L/k$ is Galois and reduction identifies the Galois groups.**
$(L,w)$ is henselian (finite over the henselian field $k$), with valuation ring $O_L=L\cap O_D$ and maximal ideal $\mathfrak p_L=L\cap M_D$. The homomorphism $O_L\to\bar D=O_D/M_D$ has kernel $\mathfrak p_L$, and its image is a subfield of $\bar D$ (if $x\in O_L\setminus\mathfrak p_L$ then $w(x)=0$, so $x^{-1}\in O_L$); this image is the residue field $\kappa_L$ of $(L,w)$, viewed as a subfield of $\bar D$. It contains $\bar k$ (image of $R$) and $\bar\theta$ (image of $\theta'$), hence
$$\bar L=\bar k(\bar\theta)\subseteq\kappa_L\subseteq\bar D .$$

*Reduction is defined.* For $\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$, $w\circ\tau$ is a valuation on $L$ extending $v$, hence equals $w$ by uniqueness of the extension of $v$ (henselianity of $k$). Thus $\tau(O_L)=O_L$ and $\tau(\mathfrak p_L)=\mathfrak p_L$, so $\tau$ induces a $\bar k$-automorphism of $\kappa_L$. Moreover $\rho(\tau)(\bar\theta)$ is the residue of $\tau(\theta')$, which is a root of $\bar f$ (as $f(\tau(\theta'))=\tau(f(\theta'))=0$), hence lies in $\bar L$; so $\rho(\tau)(\bar L)=\bar k(\rho(\tau)(\bar\theta))\subseteq\bar L$, and applying the same to $\tau^{-1}$ gives $\rho(\tau)(\bar L)=\bar L$. Thus restriction gives a homomorphism
$$\rho:\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\longrightarrow \mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k),\qquad \rho(\tau)(\bar x)=\widetilde{\tau(x)} .$$

*Injectivity.* Suppose $\rho(\tau)=\mathrm{id}$. Then $\widetilde{\tau(\theta')}=\bar\theta=\tilde{\theta'}$, i.e. $\tau(\theta')-\theta'\in\mathfrak p_L$. Now $f'(\theta')\in O_L^{\times}$ (its residue is $\bar f'(\bar\theta)\ne0$), so by the uniqueness clause of Hensel's lemma applied at the actual root $\theta'$, the only root of $f$ in $O_L$ congruent to $\theta'$ modulo $\mathfrak p_L$ is $\theta'$ itself. Both $\theta'$ and $\tau(\theta')$ are such roots, so $\tau(\theta')=\theta'$, and since $L=k(\theta')$, $\tau=\mathrm{id}$.

*Surjectivity.* Let $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$. Then $\sigma(\bar\theta)$ is a root of $\bar f$. Choose $\eta\in O_L$ with residue $\sigma(\bar\theta)$ (possible because $O_L\twoheadrightarrow\kappa_L$ and $\sigma(\bar\theta)\in\bar L\subseteq\kappa_L$). Then $f(\eta)\in\mathfrak p_L$ (residue $\bar f(\sigma(\bar\theta))=0$) and $f'(\eta)\in O_L^{\times}$ (residue $\bar f'(\sigma(\bar\theta))\ne0$, since $\bar f$ is separable). Hensel's lemma in $L$ yields $\theta_\sigma\in O_L$ with $f(\theta_\sigma)=0$ and $\theta_\sigma\equiv\sigma(\bar\theta)\pmod{\mathfrak p_L}$. As $f$ is irreducible over $k$, $[k(\theta_\sigma):k]=\deg f=p^2=[L:k]$, and $k(\theta_\sigma)\subseteq L$, so $k(\theta_\sigma)=L$. Hence $\theta'\mapsto\theta_\sigma$ defines a $k$-automorphism $\tau_\sigma$ of $L$, and $\rho(\tau_\sigma)=\sigma$ because both send $\bar\theta$ to $\sigma(\bar\theta)$ and $\bar L=\bar k(\bar\theta)$.

Therefore $\rho$ is an isomorphism; in particular $|\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)|=|\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)|=p^2=[L:k]$, so $L/k$ is Galois.

**Step 6. $L/k$ is unramified and its residue field is exactly $\bar L$.**
Apply the fundamental equality for Galois extensions over henselian discretely valued fields (lemma_96, Spark) to $L/k$ with the valuation $w$: with $e=[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]$ and $f=[\kappa_L:\bar k]$,
$$p^2=[L:k]=e\cdot f .$$
Since $\kappa_L\supseteq\bar L$ and $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$ (Step 1), we have $f\ge p^2$, while $e\ge1$; hence $e=1$, $f=p^2$, and $\kappa_L=\bar L$ as subfields of $\bar D$. Thus $w(L^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$, the residue field of $L$ is precisely the prescribed $\bar L$, and $[L:k]=[\kappa_L:\bar k]$: $L/k$ is unramified (the residue extension $\bar L/\bar k$ is separable since $\bar k$ is perfect).

**Step 7. $L$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.**
$\dim_k C_D(L)=\dim_k D/\dim_k L=p^4/p^2=p^2$ by the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), and $L\subseteq C_D(L)$ because $L$ is commutative; hence $C_D(L)=L$, and ref_1 says exactly that $L$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

**Conclusion.** $L=k(\theta')\subset D$ is a maximal subfield containing $k$, unramified over $k$, Galois over $k$, whose residue field is the given subfield $\bar L\subset\bar D$ (equality inside $\bar D$, by Step 6), and the homomorphism $\rho$ of Step 5 is an isomorphism $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ induced by reduction modulo $\mathfrak p_L$. This is exactly the required conclusion.

(Remarks on the hypotheses: the argument uses henselianity of $k$, perfection of $\bar k$ — for separability of $\bar L/\bar k$ and hence for Hensel's simple-root condition — the fact that $\bar D$ is central of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$, and $w|_k=v$; the condition $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$ is part of the standing hypothesis ensuring $\bar D$ is central over $\bar k$ and is not otherwise needed. The characteristic assumption $p>2$ is more than is needed for this particular lifting statement.)

lemma_138.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, with residue division ring $\bar D$ and value group $w(D^\times)$. If $[\bar D:\bar k]\cdot[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)]<p^2$, then $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$.
lemma_138.proof:
Assume for contradiction that D contains a maximal subfield L which is Galois over k. Since D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2, the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) gives dim_k(L)=p^2. Let G=Gal(L/k). By lemma_111, G is abelian of order p^2, so it has a subgroup H of order p. Put K=L^H. Then K/k is cyclic of degree p and L/K is cyclic of degree p.

We first prove a valuation lemma. Let (F,v) be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic p>0 and let E/F be cyclic of degree p. Write e(E/F)=[v(E^×):v(F^×)] and f(E/F)=[bar E:bar F]. We claim that e(E/F)f(E/F)=p. By Artin-Schreier theory (ref_14), E=F(θ) with θ^p−θ=c for some c∈F\wp(F). We may replace c by c+a^p−a for any a∈F without changing E. We reduce c to a convenient representative.

If v(c)≥0, then v(c)>0 is impossible: applying the henselian lifting property to X^p−X−c at 0 gives a root in F, so c∈wp(F). Also bar c∉wp(bar F), because if bar c=bar a^p−bar a for some bar a∈bar F, lifting bar a to a∈F and applying the henselian lifting property to X^p−X−c at a (the derivative is −1, hence a unit) again gives c∈wp(F). Thus in the nontrivial case with v(c)≥0 we have v(c)=0 and bar c∉wp(bar F).

Now suppose v(c)<0. If p∤v(c), we are in terminal case (A). If p∣v(c), write v(c)=−pn with n>0. If the initial residue of c in bar F^× is a p-th power, choose a∈F with v(a)=−n whose initial residue is a p-th root of the initial residue of c. Then v(a^p)=−pn and v(a)=−n>−pn, so v(a^p−a)=−pn, and the leading terms of c and a^p−a cancel. Hence c_1=c−(a^p−a) satisfies v(c_1)>v(c). Replacing c by c_1 and repeating, the valuation strictly increases. Since v is discrete and c∉wp(F), this process must terminate. It can only terminate in one of the following cases:
(A) v(c)<0 and p∤v(c);
(B) v(c)=0 and bar c∉wp(bar F);
(C) v(c)=−pn with p∣v(c) and the initial residue γ of c is not a p-th power in bar F.

We shall use the standard inequality e(E/F)f(E/F)≤[E:F] for any finite valued extension. Indeed, choose representatives x_i for the cosets of v(F^×) in v(E^×) and lifts y_j of a bar F-basis of bar E. If ∑_{i,j} a_{ij}x_i y_j=0 with a_{ij}∈F, group the sum as ∑_i x_i z_i where z_i lies in the F-span of the y_j. Different i give distinct value cosets, so nonzero terms x_i z_i cannot cancel; hence every z_i=0. For fixed i, the residue independence of the y_j over bar F forces all a_{ij}=0. Thus the products x_i y_j are F-linearly independent, giving e f≤[E:F].

Case A: v(c)<0 and p∤v(c). For a root θ, v(θ) cannot be ≥0, because then v(θ^p−θ)≥0. If v(θ)<0, then v(θ^p)=p v(θ)<v(θ), so v(θ^p−θ)=p v(θ). Hence p v(θ)=v(c), so v(θ)=v(c)/p∉v(F). Therefore e(E/F)≥p. Since [E:F]=p and e f≤p, we get e=p and f=1.

Case B: v(c)=0 and bar c∉wp(bar F). A root θ cannot have negative valuation, and it cannot have positive valuation because v(c)=0; hence v(θ)=0. Its residue satisfies bar θ^p−bar θ=bar c. Since bar c∉wp(bar F), Artin-Schreier theory (ref_14) gives [bar F(bar θ):bar F]=p. Thus f(E/F)≥p, and the inequality e f≤p gives e=1 and f=p.

Case C: v(c)=−pn and the initial residue γ of c is not a p-th power in bar F. Again a root θ must have negative valuation, and then v(θ^p−θ)=p v(θ). Thus p v(θ)=−pn, so v(θ)=−n. Let π be a uniformizer of F and set η=π^n θ. Then η is a unit of E, and\nη^p=π^{pn}θ^p=π^{pn}(c+θ)=π^{pn}c+π^{pn}θ.
The first summand has valuation 0 and residue γ, while the second has valuation pn−n=n(p−1)>0. Hence bar η^p=γ. Since γ is not a p-th power in bar F, [bar F(bar η):bar F]=p. Thus f(E/F)≥p, and e f≤p gives e=1 and f=p.

This proves the lemma that every cyclic degree-p extension of a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic p has e f=p.

Apply this lemma to K/k and to L/K. Finite extensions of henselian discretely valued fields are henselian and have discrete value groups, so the lemma applies. Both K/k and L/K are cyclic of degree p. Hence e(K/k)f(K/k)=p and e(L/K)f(L/K)=p. Value groups and residue fields multiply in towers, so e(L/k)f(L/k)=p^2.

Finally, because L⊂D, we have v(L^×)⊂w(D^×), so e(L/k)=[v(L^×):v(k^×)]≤[w(D^×):v(k^×)]. Also the residue field bar L embeds in bar D, so [bar L:bar k]≤[bar D:bar k]. Therefore
[bar D:bar k]·[w(D^×):v(k^×)] ≥ [bar L:bar k]·[v(L^×):v(k^×)] = e(L/k)f(L/k)=p^2.
This contradicts the hypothesis that [bar D:bar k]·[w(D^×):v(k^×)]<p^2. Hence D contains no maximal subfield that is Galois over k.

lemma_139.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ and exponent $p$. Suppose the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is a sum of at most two symbol classes $[c_i,z_i)$, where $[c,z)$ denotes the class of the cyclic algebra $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}k(w)v^j$ with $w^p-w=c$, $v^p=z$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$, $\tau(w)=w+1$. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a tensor product of two central division $k$-algebras of degree $p$, and is therefore a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for $G$ isomorphic to $C_p\times C_p$.
lemma_139.proof:
We keep track of the following notation. For $c\in k$ and $z\in k^{\times}$ put $F_c(T)=T^p-T-c\in k[T]$, let $L_c:=k[T]/(F_c)$, let $w$ be the class of $T$, and let $\tau$ be the $k$-automorphism of $L_c$ induced by $T\mapsto T+1$ (it is well defined since $(T+1)^p-(T+1)=T^p-T$, and it is an automorphism with inverse induced by $T\mapsto T-1$). Since $\tau^s(w)=w+s$, $\tau$ has order exactly $p$. Define
$$A(c,z):=\textstyle\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}L_c v^{j},\qquad v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v\ (\lambda\in L_c),\quad v^p=z.$$
Equivalently $A(c,z)=L_c[t;\tau]/(t^p-z)$; this quotient is an associative unital $k$-algebra because the left ideal generated by $t^p-z$ is two-sided: for $a\in L_c$ one has $ta-at=(\tau(a)-a)t$, and $t(t^p-z)=t^{p+1}-tz=t^{p+1}-zt=(t^p-z)t$ since $z\in k^{\times}$ is fixed by $\tau$. By construction $A(c,z)$ is free of rank $p$ over $L_c$ with basis $1,v,\dots,v^{p-1}$, so $\dim_k A(c,z)=p^2$, and $v$ is a unit with $v^{-1}=z^{-1}v^{p-1}$. The symbol class $[c,z)$ is $[A(c,z)]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$. By hypothesis there are $r\le 2$, elements $c_1,\dots,c_r\in k$ and $z_1,\dots,z_r\in k^{\times}$ with $[D]=\sum_{i=1}^{r}[c_i,z_i)$.

STEP 1. Claim: if $c\in\wp(k)$ then $A(c,z)\cong M_p(k)$; hence $[c,z)=0$.
Write $c=a^p-a$ with $a\in k$ and put $y:=w-a\in L_c$. Then $y^p-y=(w^p-w)-(a^p-a)=c-c=0$. Identify $\mathbb F_p$ with $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\subset k$. In $\mathbb F_p[T]$ one has $T^p-T=\prod_{j\in\mathbb F_p}(T-j)$: both sides are monic of degree $p$ and every element of $\mathbb F_p$ is a root of $T^p-T$ (Lagrange's theorem for $\mathbb F_p^{\times}$, and $0$ is a root too), so the polynomials coincide.
For $i\in\mathbb F_p$ set $E_i(T):=\prod_{j\in\mathbb F_p,\,j\ne i}(T-j)/(i-j)\in\mathbb F_p[T]$ and $e_i:=E_i(y)\in L_c$; the denominators $i-j$ lie in $\mathbb F_p^{\times}\subset k^{\times}$.
(i) $y e_i=i e_i$: indeed $(T-i)E_i(T)=\prod_{j}(T-j)\big/\prod_{j\ne i}(i-j)=(T^p-T)\big/\prod_{j\ne i}(i-j)$, so $(y-i)e_i=(y^p-y)/\prod_{j\ne i}(i-j)=0$.
(ii) $\sum_i e_i=1$ and $e_i e_m=\delta_{im}e_i$. The polynomial $\sum_i E_i(T)-1$ has degree $\le p-1$ and vanishes at each $j\in\mathbb F_p$ because $E_i(j)=\delta_{ij}$; hence it is the zero polynomial. Next, $h(T):=E_i(T)E_m(T)-\delta_{im}E_i(T)$ has degree $\le 2p-2$ and $h(j)=\delta_{ij}\delta_{im}-\delta_{im}\delta_{ij}=0$ for every $j\in\mathbb F_p$. Euclidean division $h=q\cdot(T^p-T)+r$ with $\deg r\le p-2$ gives $r(j)=0$ for all $p$ elements $j\in\mathbb F_p$; a nonzero polynomial has no more roots than its degree, so $r=0$, $h=q\cdot(T^p-T)$, and $h(y)=q(y)(y^p-y)=0$.
(iii) $\{e_i\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p}$ is a $k$-basis of $L_c$. Since $F_c$ is monic of degree $p$, $1,y,\dots,y^{p-1}$ is a $k$-basis and $\dim_k L_c=p$. Every element is $H(y)$ with $\deg H\le p-1$, and $H-\sum_i H(i)E_i$ has degree $\le p-1$ and vanishes at all $i\in\mathbb F_p$, hence is zero; so $H(y)=\sum_i H(i)e_i$: the $p$ elements $e_i$ span a $p$-dimensional space, so they are a basis.
(iv) $\tau(e_i)=e_{i-1}$ (this is the direction that must not be reversed). Since $\tau(y)=\tau(w)-a=y+1$, applying $\tau$ to $y e_i=i e_i$ gives $(y+1)\tau(e_i)=i\,\tau(e_i)$, i.e. $(y-(i-1))\tau(e_i)=0$. Write $\tau(e_i)=\sum_j\beta_j e_j$ with $\beta_j\in k$; using $y e_j=j e_j$ from (i), $0=\sum_j (j-i+1)\beta_j e_j$, and by linear independence (iii), $(j-i+1)\beta_j=0$ for all $j$, so $\beta_j=0$ unless $j=i-1$. Thus $\tau(e_i)=\beta e_{i-1}$. Now $e_i\ne0$ (its representing polynomial $E_i$ is nonzero of degree $\le p-1$, and $1,y,\dots,y^{p-1}$ is a basis), so $\tau(e_i)$ is a nonzero idempotent; since $e_{i-1}$ is an idempotent, $\beta^2=\beta$ with $\beta\ne0$, hence $\beta=1$. Induction on $s\ge0$ gives $\tau^s(e_k)=e_{k-s}$, and applying $\tau^{-1}$ (which shifts indices by $+1$) extends this to all $s\in\mathbb Z$. For $m\in\mathbb Z$ write $e_m$ for $e_{\bar m}$, $\bar m\in\mathbb F_p$ the residue class; then (ii) gives $e_i e_m=\delta_{i,\bar m}e_i$.
(v) Integer powers of $v$. For $t\in\mathbb Z$ write $t=qp+d$ with $q\in\mathbb Z$, $0\le d\le p-1$, and define $v^t:=z^q v^d$. For $t\ge0$ this agrees with the ordinary power, since $v^{qp+d}=(v^p)^qv^d=z^qv^d$ ($z$ central); for $t=-1$ it gives $z^{-1}v^{p-1}=v^{-1}$. Two identities hold for all integers. First $v^{\alpha}v^{\beta}=v^{\alpha+\beta}$: write $\alpha=q_1p+d_1$, $\beta=q_2p+d_2$, $d_1+d_2=\varepsilon p+d$ with $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, $0\le d\le p-1$; then $v^{\alpha}v^{\beta}=z^{q_1+q_2}v^{d_1+d_2}=z^{q_1+q_2+\varepsilon}v^{d}=v^{\alpha+\beta}$ because $\alpha+\beta=(q_1+q_2+\varepsilon)p+d$. Second, $v^{\alpha}\lambda=\tau^{\alpha}(\lambda)v^{\alpha}$ for $\lambda\in L_c$: $v^{\alpha}\lambda=z^qv^d\lambda=z^q\tau^d(\lambda)v^d$, while $\tau^{\alpha}(\lambda)v^{\alpha}=\tau^{qp+d}(\lambda)z^qv^d=\tau^d(\lambda)z^qv^d$, using $\tau^p=\mathrm{id}$ (as $\tau^p(w)=w+p=w$) and centrality of $z^q\in k$. The two expressions agree.
(vi) The matrix units. For $i,j\in\mathbb F_p$ let $j-i$ denote the difference of the chosen representatives in $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ (an integer in $[-(p-1),p-1]$) and set $m_{ij}:=e_i v^{j-i}$. Using (v) twice and (iv),
$$m_{ij}m_{kl}=e_i\big(v^{j-i}e_k\big)v^{l-k}=e_i\,\tau^{j-i}(e_k)\,v^{(j-i)+(l-k)}=e_i e_{k-j+i}\,v^{l-k+j-i}.$$
Since $e_i e_{k-j+i}=\delta_{jk}e_i$ (the congruence $k-j+i\equiv i\pmod p$ is equivalent to $k\equiv j$), the product is $0$ when $j\ne k$; when $j=k$ we have $(j-i)+(l-k)=l-i$ as integers, so the product is $e_iv^{l-i}=m_{il}$. Thus $m_{ij}m_{kl}=\delta_{jk}m_{il}$ for all $i,j,k,l$, and $m_{ii}=e_iv^0=e_i$, so $\sum_i m_{ii}=\sum_i e_i=1$.
(vii) Linear independence. Fix $d\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and consider the pairs $(i,j)$ with $j-i\equiv d\pmod p$; then $j-i=d+qp$ with $q=(j-i-d)/p\in\{0,-1\}$, so by (v) $m_{ij}=z^q e_i v^d\in k^{\times}\cdot(L_cv^d)$. Suppose $\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{ij}m_{ij}=0$ with $\alpha_{ij}\in k$. Since $A(c,z)=\bigoplus_{d=0}^{p-1}L_cv^d$ is a direct sum of $k$-subspaces (by construction $\{e_iv^d\}$ is a $k$-basis), for each $d$ the part lying in $L_cv^d$ vanishes: $(\sum_i\alpha_{ij}z^q e_i)v^d=0$ in the free left $L_c$-module $L_c\cdot v^d$, hence $\sum_i\alpha_{ij}z^q e_i=0$ in $L_c$, and by (iii) every $\alpha_{ij}z^q=0$; as $z^q\in k^{\times}$, all $\alpha_{ij}=0$. So the $p^2$ elements $m_{ij}$ are linearly independent, hence a $k$-basis of $A(c,z)$.
(viii) The $k$-linear bijection $\varphi\colon M_p(k)\to A(c,z)$, $\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{ij}E_{ij}\mapsto\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{ij}m_{ij}$, is a $k$-algebra homomorphism: $\varphi(E_{ij}E_{kl})=\varphi(\delta_{jk}E_{il})=\delta_{jk}m_{il}=m_{ij}m_{kl}=\varphi(E_{ij})\varphi(E_{kl})$ by (vi), and $\varphi(I_p)=\sum_i m_{ii}=1$. It is bijective by (vii). Hence $A(c,z)\cong M_p(k)$, proving the claim and in particular $[c,z)=0$ for $c\in\wp(k)$.

STEP 2. (Artin--Schreier alternative.) For $c\in k$, either $c\in\wp(k)$ or $F_c(T)=T^p-T-c$ is irreducible over $k$. Let $\theta\in k_s$ be a root; the roots of $F_c$ are exactly $\theta+i$, $i\in\mathbb F_p$, since $(\theta+i)^p-(\theta+i)=\theta^p+i-\theta-i=c$. Let $f$ be the monic irreducible factor of $F_c$ with $f(\theta)=0$, of degree $d$, and put $S:=\{i\in\mathbb F_p:\theta+i\text{ is a root of }f\}$; then $|S|=d$ and $0\in S$. For $i\in S$, $k(\theta+i)=k(\theta)$, so the $k$-embedding $\sigma_i$ of $k(\theta)$ into $k_s$ with $\sigma_i(\theta)=\theta+i$ is an automorphism of $k(\theta)$. For $i,j\in S$, $\sigma_j(\theta+i)=\theta+j+i$ is the image under a $k$-embedding of a root of $f\in k[T]$, hence is again a root of $f$; so $i+j\in S$. Also $\sigma_i^{-1}(\theta)=\theta-i$ is a root of $f$, so $-i\in S$. Thus $S$ is an additive subgroup of $\mathbb F_p$, and $d=|S|\in\{1,p\}$. If $d=1$ then $\theta\in k$, i.e. $c\in\wp(k)$; otherwise $F_c$ is irreducible. In the irreducible case $L_c=k(w)$ is the splitting field over $k$ of the separable polynomial $F_c$ (separable because $F_c'=\,-1\ne0$), hence Galois over $k$, cyclic of degree $p$ with generator $\tau$.

STEP 3. (Both symbols are nonzero; $c_i\notin\wp(k)$.) Write $\sigma_i:=[c_i,z_i)$. Because $D$ is a division algebra, $\mathrm{ind}(D)=\deg(D)=p^2$ and $[D]\ne0$. If $r=0$ then $[D]=0$, impossible. If $r=1$, or $r=2$ with $\sigma_1=0$ or $\sigma_2=0$, then $[D]=[c,z)$ for a single pair $(c,z)$. If $c\in\wp(k)$, Step 1 gives $[D]=0$, impossible. If $c\notin\wp(k)$, Step 2 shows $A(c,z)=(k(w)/k,\tau,z)$ is a cyclic algebra with $k(w)/k$ cyclic of degree $p$, hence a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $p$ by ref_22 (i). Brauer-equivalent algebras have the same index, and the index of a central simple algebra divides its degree ($A\cong M_t(\Delta)\Rightarrow\mathrm{ind}(A)=\deg\Delta\mid t\deg\Delta=\deg A$). Thus $p^2=\mathrm{ind}(D)=\mathrm{ind}(A(c,z))\mid p$, absurd. Therefore $r=2$ and $\sigma_1\ne0\ne\sigma_2$. By the contrapositive of Step 1, $c_1\notin\wp(k)$ and $c_2\notin\wp(k)$.

STEP 4. (Each $A_i$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p$.) Put $A_i:=A(c_i,z_i)$. By Step 2, $k(w_i)/k$ is cyclic Galois of degree $p$ with generator $\tau_i$, so $A_i=(k(w_i)/k,\tau_i,z_i)$ is a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $p$ by ref_22 (i). By Wedderburn, $A_i\cong M_{t_i}(\Delta_i)$ with $\Delta_i$ a central division $k$-algebra and $t_i\deg\Delta_i=\deg A_i=p$. As $p$ is prime, $t_i\in\{1,p\}$; $t_i=p$ would force $\Delta_i=k$ and $A_i\cong M_p(k)$, i.e. $\sigma_i=0$, excluded in Step 3. Hence $t_i=1$ and $A_i=\Delta_i$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p$. This proves the first assertion of the lemma.

STEP 5. ($D\cong A_1\otimes_k A_2$.) The tensor product of central simple algebras is central simple: a separable closure $k_s$ splits both $A_i$, so $(A_1\otimes_k A_2)\otimes_k k_s\cong M_p(k_s)\otimes_{k_s}M_p(k_s)\cong M_{p^2}(k_s)$; and $\deg(A_1\otimes_k A_2)=\deg A_1\cdot\deg A_2=p^2$ by dimensions. Its Brauer class is $[A_1]+[A_2]=\sigma_1+\sigma_2=[D]$. Write $A_1\otimes_k A_2\cong M_s(\Delta)$ with $\Delta$ central division over $k$; then $[\Delta]=[D]$, and two Brauer-equivalent division algebras are isomorphic (uniqueness of the division factor in the Wedderburn--Artin theorem: $M_a(\Delta)\cong M_b(D)$ forces $\Delta\cong D$). Hence $\deg\Delta=\deg D=p^2$, and $p^2=\deg(A_1\otimes_k A_2)=s\deg\Delta=sp^2$ gives $s=1$. Therefore $D\cong A_1\otimes_k A_2$; in particular $A_1\otimes_k A_2$ is a division algebra.

STEP 6. (Crossed product structure.) We apply lemma_134 (Spark) to the data $c_1,c_2\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ (Step 3), $z_1,z_2\in k^{\times}$, and the symbol algebras $A_i=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}k(w_i)v^j$ with $w_i^p-w_i=c_i$, $v^p=z_i$, $v\lambda=\tau_i(\lambda)v$, $\tau_i(w_i)=w_i+1$ — these are exactly the algebras $A(c_i,z_i)$ of Step 4. Its hypothesis, that $A_1\otimes_k A_2$ is a division algebra, holds by Step 5. Its conclusion is that $A_1\otimes_k A_2$ contains a maximal subfield $L$ that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $C_p\times C_p$ and is therefore a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_p\times C_p$.
Transport this structure along the isomorphism $\psi\colon D\xrightarrow{\,\sim\,}A_1\otimes_k A_2$ of Step 5: with $L':=\psi^{-1}(L)$ and $u_g:=\psi^{-1}(u_g')$ for the homogeneous units $u_g'$ of $A_1\otimes_k A_2$, the decomposition $A_1\otimes_k A_2=\bigoplus_{g\in G}L\,u_g'$ pulls back to $D=\bigoplus_{g\in G}L'\,u_g$ with $u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)u_g$ and $u_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}$, and $L'$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with group $G\cong C_p\times C_p$ (in particular $L'$ is a $G$-Galois $k$-algebra with $L'^G=k$). Thus $D$ is a crossed product algebra $(L',G,c)$ for $G\cong C_p\times C_p$.

STEP 7. (On the hypotheses.) The assumption $\exp(D)=p$ is consistent with, and in fact forced by, the symbol decomposition, since every symbol algebra $A(c,z)$ has degree $p$ (Step 1 and ref_22 (i)), so $p[D]=0$; it is not otherwise needed. The hypothesis $p>2$ is used in the invocation of lemma_134. Both assertions of the lemma — $D\cong A_1\otimes_k A_2$ with $A_1,A_2$ central division $k$-algebras of degree $p$, and the $C_p\times C_p$ crossed product structure — are now proved.

lemma_140.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\big(k/\wp(k)\big)\le 2$, where $\wp(F)=\{x^p-x:x\in F\}$, and for $c\in k$, $z\in k^{\times}$ let $[c,z)$ denote the symbol class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ attached to $T^p-T-c$ and $z$, taken to be $0$ when $c\in\wp(k)$. Then every element of $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ that lies in the subgroup generated by the symbol classes is a sum of at most two symbol classes.
lemma_140.proof:
We write the Brauer group Br(k) additively. Throughout, $[c,z)$ denotes the symbol class of the statement: for $c\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ it is the class of the cyclic algebra $(k(w)/k,\tau,z)$ with $w^p-w=c$, $\tau(w)=w+1$, and by convention $[c,z)=0$ whenever $c\in\wp(k)$.

Step 1: $V:=k/\wp(k)$ is an $\mathbb F_p$-vector space. For $x,y\in k$ one has $\wp(x+y)=(x+y)^p-(x+y)=(x^p-x)+(y^p-y)=\wp(x)+\wp(y)$; for $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$ one has $\wp(\lambda x)=\lambda^p x^p-\lambda x=\lambda(x^p-x)=\lambda\wp(x)$ (using $\lambda^p=\lambda$); and $\wp(0)=0$. Hence $\wp(k)$ is an additive subgroup of $k$ stable under multiplication by $\mathbb F_p$, i.e. an $\mathbb F_p$-subspace of the additive group of $k$, and $V=k/\wp(k)$ is an $\mathbb F_p$-vector space. By hypothesis $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}V=r\le 2$. We denote the class of $c\in k$ in $V$ by $\bar c$.

Step 2: formal properties of the symbol. Apply the proved lemma (Spark, lemma_100) with $K=k$: the map $(c,z)\mapsto[c,z)$ from $k\times k^\times$ to $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ satisfies, for all $c,c_1,c_2\in k$ and $z,z_1,z_2\in k^\times$,
  (a) $[c_1+c_2,z)=[c_1,z)+[c_2,z)$,
  (b) $[c,z_1z_2)=[c,z_1)+[c,z_2)$,
and consequently $[\lambda c,z)=\lambda[c,z)$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$ and $[c,z^p)=0$.
From these we record three consequences.

(i) The symbol depends only on $\bar c\in V$. Indeed, if $c'=c+\wp(x)$ with $x\in k$, then by (a), $[c',z)=[c,z)+[\wp(x),z)$, and $[\wp(x),z)=0$ because $\wp(x)\in\wp(k)$ and the symbol with such a first argument is $0$ by definition. Hence $[c',z)=[c,z)$.

(ii) For each fixed $c$, the map $z\mapsto[c,z)$ is a homomorphism of abelian groups $k^\times\to\mathrm{Br}(k)$: by (b), $[c,1)=[c,1\cdot 1)=[c,1)+[c,1)$, so $[c,1)=0$; then $[c,z)+[c,z^{-1})=[c,zz^{-1})=[c,1)=0$, giving $[c,z^{-1})=-[c,z)$; and (b) is precisely multiplicativity. Iterating (b), for every integer $t\ge 0$ one has $[c,z^t)=t[c,z)$.

(iii) Every symbol class is annihilated by $p$: by (ii) with $t=p$ and the last consequence of lemma_100, $p[c,z)=[c,z^p)=0$.

It follows that the subgroup $\mathrm{Br}_s(k)\subset\mathrm{Br}(k)$ generated by the symbol classes is an $\mathbb F_p$-vector space, and that every element of $\mathrm{Br}_s(k)$ can be written as a sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n}[c_i,z_i)$ with $c_i\in k$, $z_i\in k^\times$. Indeed, a general element of the subgroup generated by a set is a finite integer combination $\sum_i m_i[c_i,z_i)$ with $m_i\in\mathbb Z$; by (iii), $m_i[c_i,z_i)=\lambda_i[c_i,z_i)$ where $\lambda_i\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$ is the residue of $m_i$ modulo $p$; and $\lambda_i[c_i,z_i)=[\lambda_i c_i,z_i)$ by the clause $[\lambda c,z)=\lambda[c,z)$ of lemma_100 (viewing $\lambda_i$ as an element of $\mathbb F_p$). The empty sum ($n=0$) gives $\alpha=0$.

Step 3: reduction to a basis of $V$.
If $r=0$, then $V=0$, i.e. $k=\wp(k)$; then every symbol class is $0$ by the convention, so $\mathrm{Br}_s(k)=\{0\}$, and $0=[0,1)$ is itself a symbol class (its first argument $0=0^p-0$ lies in $\wp(k)$). The claim holds in this case.

Assume now $r\in\{1,2\}$ and choose $v_1,\dots,v_r\in k$ whose classes $\bar v_1,\dots,\bar v_r$ form an $\mathbb F_p$-basis of $V$. Let $\alpha\in\mathrm{Br}_s(k)$ and write $\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[c_i,z_i)$ as in Step 2. For each $i$ there are unique $\lambda_{ij}\in\mathbb F_p$ with $\bar c_i=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_{ij}\bar v_j$; equivalently $c_i=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_{ij}v_j+w_i$ with $w_i\in\wp(k)$. Then, using (a) and (i) for the first equality, the clause $[\lambda c,z)=\lambda[c,z)$ of lemma_100 for the second, and (ii) for the third:
$$[c_i,z_i)=\Big[\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_{ij}v_j+w_i,\;z_i\Big)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}[\lambda_{ij}v_j,z_i)+[w_i,z_i)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_{ij}[v_j,z_i)+0=\sum_{j=1}^{r}[v_j,\,z_i^{\lambda_{ij}}),$$
where $[w_i,z_i)=0$ because $w_i\in\wp(k)$, and where $z_i^{\lambda_{ij}}$ means $z_i$ raised to any integer representative $t\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ of $\lambda_{ij}$; this is well defined, for if $t'=t+mp$ is another representative then by (b) and $[c,z^p)=0$,
$$[v_j,\,z^{t'})=[v_j,\,z^{t}\cdot(z^{p})^{m})=[v_j,z^{t})+m\,[v_j,z^{p})=[v_j,z^{t}).$$
(For $\lambda_{ij}=0$ the term is $[v_j,1)=0$, consistently with $\lambda_{ij}[v_j,z_i)=0$.)

Summing over $i$ and regrouping using (a) in the first variable and (b) in the second variable gives
$$\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}[v_j,z_i^{\lambda_{ij}})=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\Big[v_j,\prod_{i=1}^{n}z_i^{\lambda_{ij}}\Big)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}[v_j,a_j),\qquad a_j:=\prod_{i=1}^{n}z_i^{\lambda_{ij}}\in k^\times,$$
where the product is empty (hence equal to $1$) if $n=0$, in which case each summand is $[v_j,1)=0$ and $\alpha=0$.

Step 4: conclusion. The expression in Step 3 writes $\alpha$ as a sum of $r$ symbol classes with $r\le 2$ (each summand $[v_j,a_j)$ is a symbol class in the sense of the statement; note that in fact $v_j\notin\wp(k)$ since $\bar v_j\ne 0$ in $V$, so no convention issue arises). When $r=1$ the element is a single symbol class, and when $r=0$ it is $0$, which is the symbol class $[0,1)$. Thus every element of $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ lying in the subgroup generated by the symbol classes is a sum of at most two symbol classes. $\blacksquare$

(Remark on the mechanism: the only input beyond elementary linear algebra is the biadditivity of $(c,z)\mapsto[c,z)$ from lemma_100; the argument in fact shows in general that if $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}(k/\wp(k))=r$, every element of the subgroup generated by symbols is a sum of at most $r$ symbols.)

lemma_exp_prime_to_p_invariant.statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $p$ be a prime, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has exponent $p^e$ for some integer $e\geq 1$. If $F$ is a field extension of $k$ of degree prime to $p$, then the class of $D\otimes_k F$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ has exponent $p^e$.
lemma_exp_prime_to_p_invariant.proof:
Notation. For a central simple algebra $A$ over a field $K$ we write $[A]\in\mathrm{Br}(K)$ for its Brauer class, $\exp(A)$ for the order of $[A]$ (with $\exp(A)=1$ iff $A$ is split), and $\mathrm{ind}(A)=\deg D$ where $D$ is the (unique up to isomorphism) central division $K$-algebra Brauer-equivalent to $A$. For a finite extension $L/K$ we write $A_L:=A\otimes_K L$ and $\mathrm{res}_{L/K}([A]):=[A_L]$. Let $n:=[F:k]$; by hypothesis $\gcd(n,p)=1$. (The case $n=1$, i.e. $F=k$, is trivial, but the argument below covers it.)

STEP 1. $\exp(D_F)$ divides $p^e$.
The map $\mathrm{res}_{F/k}\colon\mathrm{Br}(k)\to\mathrm{Br}(F)$, $[A]\mapsto[A\otimes_k F]$, is a group homomorphism. Indeed: (i) it is well defined on Brauer equivalence, since $\mathrm{End}_k(V)\otimes_k F\cong\mathrm{End}_F(V\otimes_k F)$; (ii) it is multiplicative, since the map $(a\otimes x)\otimes(a'\otimes x')\mapsto (aa')\otimes(xx')$ gives a canonical $F$-algebra isomorphism $(A\otimes_k F)\otimes_F(A'\otimes_k F)\cong (A\otimes_k A')\otimes_k F$; (iii) $A\otimes_k F$ is central simple over $F$ because after a further extension to a splitting field $\Omega\supset F$ one gets $M_r(\Omega)$, which is simple, and its centre is $F\cdot\Omega^{\times}$-central, i.e. exactly $F$. Since $p^e[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$, functoriality gives $p^e[D_F]=\mathrm{res}(p^e[D])=0$. Hence $\exp(D_F)=p^{e'}$ for some integer $0\le e'\le e$. It remains to exclude $e'<e$.

STEP 2 (key lemma: prime divisors of the index divide the exponent).
Lemma. Let $A$ be a central simple algebra over an arbitrary field $K$. Then every prime divisor of $\mathrm{ind}(A)$ divides $\exp(A)$.
Proof. We prove the contrapositive: if $m:=\exp(A)$ and $\ell$ is a prime with $\gcd(m,\ell)=1$, then $\ell\nmid\mathrm{ind}(A)$.

(2a) Existence of a finite Galois splitting field. Let $D$ be the division algebra Brauer-equivalent to $A$, so $\mathrm{ind}(A)=\deg D$. By ref_16 (Noether-Kothe) $D$ contains a maximal subfield $L_0$ that is separable over $K$. Then $[L_0:K]=\deg D$, so applying the "in particular" clause of ref_5 with $A:=D$ and $K:=L_0$ (degree $m'=\deg D$ equals $\deg D$), the fact that $L_0$ embeds in $D$ as a maximal subfield implies $L_0$ splits $D$, hence splits $A$ (as $A\cong M_t(D)$ gives $A_{L_0}\cong M_t(D_{L_0})$). Let $L/K$ be the Galois closure of $L_0/K$; it exists and is finite Galois because $L_0/K$ is finite separable, and $L$ splits $A$. Put $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$.

(2b) Subclaim. Let $L/N$ be a finite Galois extension whose Galois group is an $\ell$-group, and let $B$ be a central simple $N$-algebra split by $L$, with $\gcd(\exp(B),\ell)=1$. Then $B$ is split.
Proof of the subclaim, by induction on $[L:N]=\ell^{c}$. For $c=0$ there is nothing to prove. Let $c\ge1$ and set $Q:=\mathrm{Gal}(L/N)$, a non-trivial $\ell$-group. Its abelianisation $Q/[Q,Q]$ is a non-trivial abelian $\ell$-group, hence possesses a subgroup of index $\ell$; let $Q'$ be its inverse image in $Q$. Then $Q'\trianglelefteq Q$ and $Q/Q'$ is cyclic of order $\ell$. Set $M:=L^{Q'}$. Then $M/N$ is Galois with group $Q/Q'$, cyclic of degree $\ell$; fix a generator $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(M/N)$.
Since $B\otimes_N M$ is split by $L/M$ (whose Galois group is $Q'$, of order $\ell^{c-1}$) and $\exp(B\otimes_N M)$ divides $\exp(B)$ (restriction is a homomorphism, Step 1), it is prime to $\ell$; by the induction hypothesis $B\otimes_N M$ is split, i.e. $M$ splits $B$. Thus $[B]$ lies in the relative Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(M/N):=\ker(\mathrm{Br}(N)\to\mathrm{Br}(M))$. By ref_22(i), the map $b\mapsto[(M/N,\sigma,b)]$ induces an isomorphism $N^{\times}/N_{M/N}(M^{\times})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{Br}(M/N)$; hence $[B]=[(M/N,\sigma,a)]$ for some $a\in N^{\times}$, and this class is $0$ iff $a\in N_{M/N}(M^{\times})$. By ref_23, $\exp(B)=\exp((M/N,\sigma,a))$ equals the order of $a$ in $N^{\times}/N_{M/N}(M^{\times})$. That order divides $\ell$: explicitly, for $a\in N^{\times}\subset M^{\times}$ the $N$-linear endomorphism "$\times a$" of $M$ is scalar multiplication on an $[M:N]=\ell$-dimensional space, so $N_{M/N}(a)=a^{\ell}$, which lies in the norm group. Thus the order of $a$ divides both $\ell$ and $\exp(B)$; since $\gcd(\exp(B),\ell)=1$ it is $1$. Hence $a$ is a norm, $[B]=0$, and $B$ is split. This completes the induction and the subclaim.

(2c) End of the proof of the Lemma. Let $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_\ell(G)$ and $N:=L^{Q}$. Then $L/N$ is Galois with group $Q$ (an $\ell$-group), $B:=A\otimes_K N$ is split by $L$, and $\exp(B)\mid m$, so $\gcd(\exp(B),\ell)=1$. By (2b), $B$ is split, i.e. $\mathrm{ind}(A\otimes_K N)=1$. Applying ref_12 to the division algebra $D$ and the extension $N/K$ gives $\mathrm{ind}(A)=\mathrm{ind}(D)\mid [N:K]\cdot\mathrm{ind}(D\otimes_K N)=[N:K]=|G:Q|$. Since $Q$ is a Sylow-$\ell$-subgroup, $\ell\nmid|G:Q|$, hence $\ell\nmid\mathrm{ind}(A)$. $\quad\triangleleft$ (Lemma)

STEP 3. The inequality $p^{e}\mid\exp(D_F)$, i.e. $e'=e$.
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $e'<e$. Consider $C:=D^{\otimes_k p^{e-1}}$, so that $[C]=p^{e-1}[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$. Since $[D]$ has exact order $p^{e}$, the element $p^{e-1}[D]$ has exact order $p$; thus $\exp(C)=p$ and $[C]\neq0$. On the other hand, using Step 1 and $e'\le e-1$,
$[C_F]=p^{e-1}[D_F]=p^{e-1-e'}\cdot\big(p^{e'}[D_F]\big)=p^{e-1-e'}\cdot 0=0$,
so $C_F$ is split.
Let $R$ be the central division $k$-algebra Brauer-equivalent to $C$. Then $\exp(R)=p$ and $[R]\neq0$, so $\mathrm{ind}(R)=\deg R\ge2$. By the Lemma (applied with $A=R$, $m=p$), no prime $\ell\ne p$ divides $\mathrm{ind}(R)$; hence $\mathrm{ind}(R)=p^{f}$ for some $f\ge1$. Since $[R_F]=[C_F]=0$, $R_F\cong M_r(F)$ and $\mathrm{ind}(R_F)=1$. Applying ref_12 to $R$ and $F/k$ yields
$\mathrm{ind}(R)\mid [F:k]\cdot\mathrm{ind}(R_F)=n\cdot 1=n$,
so $p^{f}\mid n$ with $f\ge1$, i.e. $p\mid n$. This contradicts $\gcd(n,p)=1$. Therefore $e'=e$, and combining with Step 1 gives $\exp(D\otimes_k F)=p^{e}$.

REMARK (not part of the statement). The same hypotheses give $\mathrm{ind}(D_F)=\mathrm{ind}(D)$: by the Lemma, $\mathrm{ind}(D)=p^{f}$ for some $f$; ref_12 gives $\mathrm{ind}(D_F)\mid\mathrm{ind}(D)=p^{f}$ and $\mathrm{ind}(D)=p^{f}\mid n\cdot\mathrm{ind}(D_F)$, and since $\gcd(n,p)=1$ this forces $\mathrm{ind}(D_F)=p^{f}=\mathrm{ind}(D)$. Thus a division algebra of degree $p^{2}$ and exponent $p^{2}$ remains of degree $p^{2}$ and exponent $p^{2}$ after any extension of degree prime to $p$.

lemma_deg_p_galois_maxfield_iff_as.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p$. Then the following are equivalent: (i) $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$; (ii) $D$ contains an element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$; (iii) $D$ is split by a field extension of $k$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.
lemma_deg_p_galois_maxfield_iff_as.proof:
Throughout, char(k) = p > 0 and D is a central division k-algebra of degree p, so Z(D) = k and dim_k(D) = p^2. We prove (i) => (ii) => (i) => (iii) => (i), which gives the equivalence of the three conditions. Only equivalences are claimed; no existence of an element/field satisfying any of the conditions is asserted.

STEP 0a (Additive Hilbert 90 for a cyclic extension of degree p, proved inline). Let L/k be a Galois field extension with Gal(L/k) = <sigma> cyclic of order p. For y in L there exists x in L with sigma(x) - x = y if and only if Tr_{L/k}(y) = 0.
Proof. Consider the k-linear endomorphism delta = sigma - id of the k-vector space L.
(*) im(delta) is contained in ker(Tr): for x in L, Tr(sigma(x) - x) = sum_{i=0}^{p-1} sigma^i(sigma(x)) - sum_{i=0}^{p-1} sigma^i(x) = sum_{i=1}^{p} sigma^i(x) - sum_{i=0}^{p-1} sigma^i(x) = sigma^p(x) - x = x - x = 0, using sigma^p = id.
(*) dim_k im(delta) = p - 1: ker(delta) = {x in L : sigma(x) = x} = L^{<sigma>} = k, the last equality because L/k is Galois with group <sigma>; thus dim_k ker(delta) = 1 and the rank-nullity theorem for the k-linear map delta on the p-dimensional space L gives dim_k im(delta) = p - 1.
(*) dim_k ker(Tr) = p - 1: since L/k is Galois it is separable, so the trace pairing (u,v) |-> Tr_{L/k}(uv) on L is nondegenerate; hence Tr is not the zero map (otherwise the pairing would be identically zero). As Tr: L -> k is a nonzero k-linear map, dim_k ker(Tr) = p - 1.
Combining, im(delta) is a (p-1)-dimensional k-subspace of the (p-1)-dimensional space ker(Tr), so im(delta) = ker(Tr). This is the claim. (The converse direction of the iff, namely Tr(y) = 0 is necessary, is exactly (*).)

STEP 0b (Artin-Schreier element inside D, proved inline). Let a in D \ k satisfy a^p - a =: c in k. Then:
(1) k[a] is a field (hence equals k(a)). Indeed, D is finite dimensional over k, so a is algebraic over k and k[a] is a finite-dimensional k-subspace of D closed under multiplication and containing 1. For 0 != z in k[a], left multiplication m_z: k[a] -> k[a] is k-linear and injective because D is a division ring (zw = 0 forces w = 0); by finite dimensionality m_z is surjective, so there is w in k[a] with zw = 1. Thus every nonzero element of k[a] is invertible in k[a], i.e. k[a] is a field; it is then the smallest subfield of D containing k and a, so k[a] = k(a).
(2) The polynomial f(T) = T^p - T - c in k[T] is separable: f'(T) = pT^{p-1} - 1 = -1 in characteristic p, so gcd(f, f') = 1.
(3) f splits into distinct linear factors in k(a): for each i in F_p (viewed inside k), (a + i)^p - (a + i) - c = (a^p - a - c) + (i^p - i) = 0 + 0 = 0, using the freshman's dream in characteristic p and i^p = i for i in F_p. The p elements a, a+1, ..., a+(p-1) are pairwise distinct (a + i = a + j implies i = j after cancelling in the additive group of D). Hence f has p distinct roots in k(a), all of them of this form, and f(T) = prod_{i in F_p} (T - (a+i)) in k(a)[T].
(4) k(a)/k is Galois: it is generated over k by a root a of the separable polynomial f and contains all roots of f by (3), so it is the splitting field of a separable polynomial. Consequently [k(a):k] = |Gal(k(a)/k)| and the fixed field of Gal(k(a)/k) is k.
(5) Gal(k(a)/k) is cyclic of order p, generated by tau with tau(a) = a + 1: the map Gamma: Gal(k(a)/k) -> (F_p, +) defined by gamma(a) = a + i_gamma is well defined by (3) (gamma(a) is a root of f), is a group homomorphism since gamma(delta(a)) = gamma(a + i_delta) = gamma(a) + i_delta = a + i_gamma + i_delta (gamma fixes k, hence F_p), and is injective since a generates k(a) over k. Its image is a subgroup of F_p, hence of order 1 or p. The image is not trivial: if every gamma fixed a then the fixed field of Gal(k(a)/k) would contain k(a), contradicting (4) unless k(a) = k, which is excluded because a is not in k. So the image is all of F_p, |Gal(k(a)/k)| = p, [k(a):k] = p, and the automorphism tau with tau(a) = a + 1 generates Gal(k(a)/k). This proves Step 0b.

STEP 1: (i) => (ii). Assume L is a maximal subfield of D which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group <sigma> of order p. Since [L:k] = p, Tr_{L/k}(1) = [L:k] * 1 = p * 1 = 0 in characteristic p. By Step 0a applied to y = 1 there exists a in L with sigma(a) - a = 1, i.e. sigma(a) = a + 1. Then sigma(a^p - a) = sigma(a)^p - sigma(a) = (a+1)^p - (a+1) = (a^p + 1) - a - 1 = a^p - a, so a^p - a lies in the fixed field L^{<sigma>} = k; write c := a^p - a in k. Finally a is not in k, for sigma(a) = a + 1 differs from a since 1 != 0 in k. Viewing a as an element of D via L subset D, this is exactly condition (ii).
(Remark, with proof, recording compatibility with Artin-Schreier theory: c is not in wp(k) = {x^p - x : x in k}. If c = b^p - b with b in k, then (a-b)^p - (a-b) = c - c = 0, so a - b is a root of T^p - T, whose roots are exactly the elements of F_p; hence a - b in F_p subset k and a in k, contradicting a not in k. Thus L = k(a) is the Artin-Schreier extension attached to the nonzero class of c in k/wp(k).)

STEP 2: (ii) => (i). Assume a in D \ k with a^p - a = c in k. By Step 0b, k(a) is a subfield of D and k(a)/k is Galois with cyclic Galois group of order p generated by a |-> a + 1. Since [k(a):k] = p = deg(D), the centralizer C_D(k(a)) is, by ref_1, a central simple k(a)-algebra of degree deg(D)/[k(a):k] = p/p = 1; hence C_D(k(a)) = k(a). By the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1 (K is a maximal subfield of A if and only if C_A(K) = K), k(a) is a maximal subfield of D. Thus D contains a maximal subfield which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p, i.e. (i).

STEP 3: (i) => (iii). Assume (i) with maximal subfield L as in Step 1; we claim E := L splits D. Indeed, by ref_1, C_D(L) is a central simple L-algebra that is Brauer equivalent to D tensor_k L, and since L is a maximal subfield, C_D(L) = L, which is split over L. Hence D tensor_k L is split over L; as dim_L(D tensor_k L) = dim_k D = p^2, we get D tensor_k L isomorphic to M_p(L). Equivalently, this is the m = n = p case of ref_5 (a degree-n subfield embeds as a maximal subfield if and only if it splits A). Since L/k is Galois with cyclic Galois group of order p, condition (iii) holds with E = L.

STEP 4: (iii) => (i). Assume E/k is a field extension which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p and such that D tensor_k E is split, i.e. E splits D. Apply lemma_114 (Spark) with F = k, C = D and tau a generator of Gal(E/k): its last clause states that whenever a Galois degree-p extension E of F splits the degree-p central division F-algebra C, the field E is isomorphic over F to a subfield of C. Hence there is a k-embedding iota: E -> D, whose image K := iota(E) is a subfield of D with [K:k] = [E:k] = p (iota is injective because a k-algebra map from a field to a division ring has trivial kernel, and it preserves degrees over k since it is the identity on k). As in Step 2, ref_1 gives that C_D(K) is a central simple K-algebra of degree deg(D)/[K:k] = 1, so C_D(K) = K, and the maximal-subfield criterion of ref_1 makes K a maximal subfield of D.
