(This embedding is also the direct content of ref_5 with n = m = p: E embeds in D as a maximal subfield if and only if ind(D tensor_k E) divides deg(D)/p = 1, which holds because E splits D.) Finally, K/k is Galois with cyclic Galois group of order p: being Galois is invariant under k-isomorphism of field extensions — separability is transported by iota, and |Aut_k(K)| = |Aut_k(E)| = [E:k] = [K:k] because conjugation by iota gives a group isomorphism Aut_k(E) -> Aut_k(K) (every k-automorphism of K corresponds to one of E, and E/k being Galois gives |Aut_k(E)| = [E:k]). Thus K is a maximal subfield of D that is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p, which is (i).

CONCLUSION. Steps 1-4 give (i) <=> (ii) <=> (iii), establishing the equivalence of the three stated conditions. Note explicitly that the argument proves only the equivalence: it shows that having a cyclic Galois maximal subfield, having an Artin-Schreier element a not in k with a^p - a in k, and being split by a cyclic Galois degree-p extension are the same property of D; it does not assert that any degree-p division algebra has this property (that would be the cyclicity/symbol question, which is not used or needed here).

lemma_143.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation. Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $p\nmid m$ and $p\nmid n$, and let $K=k(z)$ where $z^p-z=s\,u^{-m}$. Then for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and every $\mu\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$, the element $\mu\, t\, u^{-n}+\lambda\, s\, u^{-m}$ does not belong to $\wp(K)=\{x^p-x:x\in K\}$.
lemma_143.proof:
Throughout, for a field $F$ of characteristic $p$ we write $\wp(F)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in F\}\subseteq F$.

**Preliminary: $\wp(F)$ is an $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector subspace of $F$.** The map $\wp\colon F\to F$, $x\mapsto x^{p}-x$, is additive, since for $x,y\in F$
$$(x+y)^{p}-(x+y)=(x^{p}+y^{p})-x-y=(x^{p}-x)+(y^{p}-y),$$
using that the characteristic is $p$, so that all intermediate binomial coefficients $\binom{p}{i}$, $0<i<p$, vanish. It is $\mathbb{F}_p$-homogeneous, since for $a\in\mathbb{F}_p$ one has $a^{p}=a$ and hence
$$(ax)^{p}-ax=a^{p}x^{p}-ax=a(x^{p}-x).$$
Thus $\wp(F)$ is an $\mathbb{F}_p$-subspace of $F$ (it contains $0=0^{p}-0$, and is closed under addition and under multiplication by scalars of $\mathbb{F}_p$). Consequently, for any $c\in F$, the sum $\wp(F)+\mathbb{F}_p\cdot c$ is again an $\mathbb{F}_p$-subspace of $F$. This is the only linearity fact used below; in particular we only ever add to or subtract from an element of $\wp(k)$ an element of the summand $\mathbb{F}_p\cdot c$ that appears in the description of $\wp(K)\cap k$ supplied by lemma_121.

**Step 1: the element $c:=s\,u^{-m}$ does not belong to $\wp(k)$.** Take the coefficients $\lambda_{0}=1\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mu_{0}=0\in\mathbb{F}_p$; the pair $(\lambda_0,\mu_0)=(1,0)$ is not $(0,0)$. The hypotheses of lemma_104 are satisfied by the present field $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$ and the given positive integers $m,n$ with $p\nmid m$, $p\nmid n$. Lemma_104 therefore asserts that $\lambda_0\,s\,u^{-m}+\mu_0\,t\,u^{-n}=s\,u^{-m}$ does not belong to $\wp(k)$. So $c\in k\setminus\wp(k)$.

**Step 2: description of $\wp(K)\cap k$.** By hypothesis $K=k(z)$ with $z^{p}-z=s\,u^{-m}=c$, i.e. $K/k$ is the Artin--Schreier extension attached to $c$. Since $c\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ by Step 1, lemma_121 applies (with the field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$) and gives
$$\wp(K)\cap k=\wp(k)+\mathbb{F}_p\cdot c=\{\,(x^{p}-x)+a\,s\,u^{-m}\;:\;x\in k,\ a\in\mathbb{F}_p\,\}.$$

**Step 3: reduction to a nonzero $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear combination, and contradiction.** Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mu\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$, and put
$$\beta:=\mu\,t\,u^{-n}+\lambda\,s\,u^{-m}.$$
Since $m,n\ge 1$, both terms of $\beta$ have a pole at $u=0$; in particular $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)[u^{-1}]\subset\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))=k$. Thus $\beta\in k$, which is the only property of $\beta$ that will be used.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that $\beta\in\wp(K)$. As just noted $\beta\in k$, so $\beta\in\wp(K)\cap k$, and by the description in Step 2 there exist $x\in k$ and $a\in\mathbb{F}_p$ with
$$\beta=(x^{p}-x)+a\,s\,u^{-m}.$$
Rearranging in the field $k$ (subtracting $a\,s\,u^{-m}$, which is legitimate inside the $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space $k$) gives
$$x^{p}-x=\beta-a\,s\,u^{-m}=\mu\,t\,u^{-n}+\lambda\,s\,u^{-m}-a\,s\,u^{-m}=\mu\,t\,u^{-n}+(\lambda-a)\,s\,u^{-m}.$$
Since the left-hand side is $\wp(x)$ with $x\in k$, the right-hand side belongs to $\wp(k)$. Writing $\lambda'=\lambda-a\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mu'=\mu\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and using commutativity of addition in $k$, we have shown
$$\lambda'\,s\,u^{-m}+\mu'\,t\,u^{-n}\in\wp(k).$$
The pair $(\lambda',\mu')$ is nonzero, because $\mu'=\mu\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$, so $\mu'\neq 0$. But lemma_104, applied to the same field $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$ and the same integers $m,n$ (still satisfying $p\nmid m$, $p\nmid n$), asserts precisely that for every pair $(\lambda',\mu')\in\mathbb{F}_p^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ one has $\lambda'\,s\,u^{-m}+\mu'\,t\,u^{-n}\notin\wp(k)$. This is a contradiction.

Hence the assumption $\beta\in\wp(K)$ is false, and
$$\mu\,t\,u^{-n}+\lambda\,s\,u^{-m}\notin\wp(K)$$
for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and every $\mu\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$, as claimed.

**Remark on the hypotheses.** The assumption $p>2$ is used only to satisfy the hypotheses of lemma_104; the assumptions $p\nmid m$ and $p\nmid n$ likewise. No hypothesis that $m$ and $n$ be distinct is needed here, since lemma_104 holds for all positive $m,n$ with $p\nmid m$ and $p\nmid n$, and lemma_121 involves only $m$ (through $c=s\,u^{-m}$).

lemma_144.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a discretely valued field with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$ and residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra endowed with a valuation $w$ extending $v$, and suppose the residue division ring of $D$ is $\bar k$. Write $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ and $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ for the associated graded rings, with $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ viewed as a graded subring of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ via $k\subset D$. Then for every integer $m$ the homogeneous component $\mathrm{gr}(D)_m$ coincides with $\mathrm{gr}(k)_m$.
lemma_144.proof:
We prove that for every $m\in\mathbb Z$ the canonical homomorphism $\varphi_m\colon \mathrm{gr}(k)_m\longrightarrow \mathrm{gr}(D)_m$ induced by the inclusion $k\subset D$ is an isomorphism; this is exactly the assertion that the degree-$m$ homogeneous component of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ coincides with that of $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ (under the standard model $\mathrm{gr}(\,\cdot\,)_\gamma=A^{\geq\gamma}/A^{>\gamma}$, the map $\varphi_m$ is literally the inclusion of a subgroup, so "is an isomorphism" reads as "coincide").

STEP 0 (Notation and the graded components). Write $\Gamma_k=v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$ and $\Gamma=w(D^\times)$. Since $k^\times\subset D^\times$ and $w|_{k^\times}=v$, we have the inclusions of ordered groups
$$\mathbb Z=v(k^\times)\ \subset\ w(D^\times)=\Gamma .\qquad(\ast)$$
In particular every $m\in\mathbb Z$ lies in $\Gamma$, so both $\mathrm{gr}(k)_m$ and $\mathrm{gr}(D)_m$ are among the components that are actually indexed. For a valued division ring/field $(A,\omega)$ and $\gamma\in\omega(A^\times)$ we set
$$A^{\geq\gamma}=\{x\in A:\omega(x)\geq\gamma\}\cup\{0\},\qquad A^{>\gamma}=\{x\in A:\omega(x)>\gamma\}\cup\{0\},$$
which are additive subgroups of $(A,+)$ with $A^{>\gamma}\subset A^{\geq\gamma}$, and $\mathrm{gr}(A)_\gamma:=A^{\geq\gamma}/A^{>\gamma}$. For $x\in A^{\geq\gamma}$ we denote by $\mathrm{in}_\omega(x)$ its class in $\mathrm{gr}(A)_\gamma$; if $\omega(x)=\gamma$ this class is nonzero (it is the initial form of $x$). Every element of $\mathrm{gr}(A)_\gamma$ is $0$ or of the form $\mathrm{in}_\omega(x)$ with $\omega(x)=\gamma$: indeed a class in $A^{\geq\gamma}/A^{>\gamma}$ is represented by some $x$ with $\omega(x)\geq\gamma$, and if $\omega(x)>\gamma$ the class is $0$.

STEP 1 (Elementary properties of the valuation $w$ on the division ring $D$). For $x,y\in D^\times$ one has $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$, $w(1)=0$, hence $w(-1)=0$, $w(x^{-1})=-w(x)$, and $w(x-y)=w(x)+w(1-x^{-1}y)\geq\min(w(x),w(y))$. Consequently:
(i) $V_D:=D^{\geq 0}$ is a subring of $D$: for $x,y\in V_D$ we have $w(x-y)\geq\min(w(x),w(y))\geq 0$ and, if $x,y\neq0$, $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)\geq0$.
(ii) $M_D:=D^{>0}$ is a two-sided ideal of $V_D$: for $a\in M_D$, $d\in V_D$, $w(ad)=w(a)+w(d)>0+0=0$, and similarly $da\in M_D$; additivity is clear.
(iii) $\overline D:=V_D/M_D$ is a division ring: if $\overline u\neq0$ with $u\in V_D$, then $u\notin M_D$, so $w(u)=0$, whence $w(u^{-1})=0$ and $u^{-1}\in V_D$, giving $\overline u^{-1}=\overline{u^{-1}}$.
(iv) The residue map $\rho_D\colon V_D\twoheadrightarrow\overline D$ is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $M_D$; in particular $\rho_D(u)\neq0$ for every $u\in V_D$ with $w(u)=0$, and $\rho_D(x)=\rho_D(y)$ iff $w(x-y)>0$ (with the convention $w(0)=+\infty$).
All these are the standard axioms-and-consequences for valuations on (possibly noncommutative) division rings; note that commutativity of $D$ was never used.

STEP 2 (Compatibility with $k$, and the meaning of the hypothesis). Put $V_k=k^{\geq0}$, $M_k=k^{>0}$, $\rho_k\colon V_k\twoheadrightarrow\bar k$. Because $w|_k=v$, we have $V_k=k\cap V_D$ and $M_k=k\cap M_D$; hence $k\cap M_D=M_k$ and the inclusion $\iota\colon k\hookrightarrow D$ restricts to a ring map $V_k\to V_D$ carrying $M_k$ into $M_D$, and therefore induces an injective homomorphism of residue division rings
$$\bar\iota\colon\bar k=V_k/M_k\hookrightarrow V_D/M_D=\overline D,\qquad \rho_k(c)\longmapsto\rho_D(c),$$
injective because it is a unital homomorphism out of a field. The hypothesis "the residue division ring of $D$ is $\bar k$" means precisely that $\bar\iota$ is an isomorphism. We shall use the following consequence, which we record explicitly: 
$$\text{for every }u\in V_D\text{ there exists }c\in V_k\text{ with }\rho_D(u)=\rho_D(c).\qquad(\dagger)$$
Proof of $(\dagger)$: $\rho_D(u)\in\overline D=\bar\iota(\bar k)$, so $\rho_D(u)=\bar\iota(\rho_k(c))=\rho_D(c)$ for some $c\in V_k$.

STEP 3 ($\varphi_m$ is well defined and injective). Fix $m\in\mathbb Z$. Since $w|_k=v$, for $x\in k$ we have $v(x)\geq m\iff w(x)\geq m$ and $v(x)>m\iff w(x)>m$; that is,
$$k^{\geq m}=k\cap D^{\geq m},\qquad k^{>m}=k\cap D^{>m}.$$
Hence the assignment $c+k^{>m}\longmapsto c+D^{>m}$ defines a group homomorphism $\varphi_m\colon\mathrm{gr}(k)_m\to\mathrm{gr}(D)_m$, and it is injective: if $c\in k^{\geq m}$ maps to $0$, then $c\in D^{>m}=k\cap D^{>m}=k^{>m}$, so $c+k^{>m}=0$.

STEP 4 ($\varphi_m$ is surjective). Let $\xi\in\mathrm{gr}(D)_m= D^{\geq m}/D^{>m}$. If $\xi=0$ then $\xi=\varphi_m(0)$. Otherwise $\xi=\mathrm{in}_w(a)$ for some $a\in D$ with $w(a)=m$. Choose a uniformiser $\pi\in k$ with $v(\pi)=1$ (exists because $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$); then $\pi^m\in k^\times$ and $v(\pi^m)=w(\pi^m)=m$. Set
$$b:=a\,\pi^{-m}\in D^\times .$$
By multiplicativity of $w$, $w(b)=w(a)-w(\pi^m)=m-m=0$. Thus $b\in V_D$ with $w(b)=0$, so $\rho_D(b)\neq0$. By $(\dagger)$ choose $c\in V_k$ with $\rho_D(c)=\rho_D(b)$; then $\rho_D(c)=\rho_D(b)\neq0$, so $c\notin M_D\cap k=M_k$, i.e. $v(c)=0$ (as $c\in V_k$ gives $v(c)\geq0$). Moreover $\rho_D(b-c)=\rho_D(b)-\rho_D(c)=0$, hence $w(b-c)>0$.
Now consider $d:=\pi^m c\in k$. We have $v(d)=v(\pi^m)+v(c)=m+0=m$, so $d\in k^{\geq m}$ with $v(d)=m$, and $\mathrm{in}_v(d)$ is a well-defined nonzero element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)_m$ with $\varphi_m(\mathrm{in}_v(d))=\mathrm{in}_w(d)$. Finally,
$$a-d=\pi^m b-\pi^m c=\pi^m(b-c),$$
so by multiplicativity $w(a-d)=w(\pi^m)+w(b-c)=m+w(b-c)>m$. Therefore $a$ and $d$ have the same class in $D^{\geq m}/D^{>m}$, i.e.
$$\xi=\mathrm{in}_w(a)=\mathrm{in}_w(d)=\varphi_m(\mathrm{in}_v(d)).$$
This proves surjectivity of $\varphi_m$.
(Equivalently, in terms of initial forms: $\mathrm{in}_w(a)=\mathrm{in}_w(\pi^m)\,\mathrm{in}_w(b)=\mathrm{in}_w(\pi^m)\,\mathrm{in}_w(c)=\mathrm{in}_w(\pi^mc)$, using $w(\pi^m)=m$, $w(b)=0$ and $\mathrm{in}_w(b)=\mathrm{in}_w(c)$, which holds because $w(b-c)>0$.)

STEP 5 (Conclusion and structural form). Steps 3 and 4 show that $\varphi_m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\in\mathbb Z$, i.e. $\mathrm{gr}(D)_m=\mathrm{gr}(k)_m$. Concretely, since $\rho_k\colon\{c\in k:v(c)=0\}\xrightarrow{\sim}\bar k^\times$ and multiplication by $\pi^m$ identifies $\{c:v(c)=0\}$ with $\{d\in k:v(d)=m\}$, one has $\mathrm{gr}(k)_m=\bar k\cdot\mathrm{in}_v(\pi^m)$; via $\varphi_m$ this reads
$$\mathrm{gr}(D)_m=\bar k\cdot \mathrm{in}_w(\pi^m)=\{\mathrm{in}_w(d):d\in k,\ v(d)=m\}\cup\{0\}.$$
For $m=0$ this recovers $\mathrm{gr}(D)_0=\overline D=\bar k=\mathrm{gr}(k)_0$, and the isomorphisms are compatible with multiplication: $\varphi_{m+m'}(xy)=\varphi_m(x)\varphi_{m'}(y)$ whenever $v(x)=m$, $v(y)=m'$, since both sides equal $\mathrm{in}_w(xy)$ with $w(xy)=m+m'$. Thus the sub-$\mathbb Z$-graded ring $\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}\mathrm{gr}(D)_m$ of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is exactly $\mathrm{gr}(k)$; the only components of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ that can be "new" are those of degree $\gamma\in w(D^\times)\setminus\mathbb Z$.

(Remark on the hypotheses used: the argument used only that $w$ is a valuation on the division ring $D$ whose restriction to $k$ is $v$, that $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$ so that a uniformiser power $\pi^m\in k^\times$ of value $m$ exists, and that $\bar k\xrightarrow{\sim}\overline D$. Centrality and finite-dimensionality of $D$, completeness or henselianity of $k$, and the characteristic were not needed.)

lemma_145.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$. Suppose that (i) every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose Brauer class is killed by $p$ is a crossed product algebra for $C_p\times C_p$, (ii) every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p$ over $k$ is a crossed product algebra for a group of order $p$, and (iii) every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose Brauer class is not killed by $p$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$. Then every central simple $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ over $k$ is a crossed product algebra for some group of order $p^2$.
lemma_145.proof:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ satisfying (i), (ii), (iii), and let $A$ be a central simple $k$-algebra with $\deg A=p^2$. We prove $A$ is a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^2$.

**Step 1: Wedderburn reduction to the division algebra.** By the Wedderburn structure theorem for central simple algebras there are a central division $k$-algebra $D$, unique up to $k$-isomorphism, and an integer $m\ge 1$ with
$$A \simeq M_m(D)=D\otimes_k M_m(k).$$
Taking degrees, $p^2=\deg A=m\cdot \deg D$; hence $\deg D=p^e$ for some $e\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $m=p^{2-e}$. The case $e=0$ means $\deg D=1$, i.e. $D=k$. Since $[M_m(k)]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$, $D$ is Brauer equivalent to $A$: $[A]=[D]$.

**Step 2: $D$ is a crossed product for a group of order $\deg D$.** We claim there are a group $H$ with $|H|=\deg D$ and an $H$-Galois $k$-algebra $L$ with $D\simeq (L,H,c)$. (When $D=k$ we take $H=\{1\}$.) We argue by cases on $e$.

*Case $e=0$.* Then $D=k$. Take $H=\{1\}$, $L=k$, $c\equiv 1$. Then $L$ is etale over $k$ of $k$-dimension $1=|H|$, and $L^H=L=k$, so $L$ is an $H$-Galois algebra, and $(L,H,1)=L\,u_1=k\simeq D$. (Here $\deg D=1=|H|$.)

*Case $e=1$.* Then $\deg D=p$, and hypothesis (ii) applied to the central division $k$-algebra $D$ yields $D\simeq (L,H,c)$ with $|H|=p=\deg D$.

*Case $e=2$ and $p[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$.* Hypothesis (i) applied to $D$ (a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose Brauer class is killed by $p$) yields $D\simeq (L,H,c)$ with $H\cong C_p\times C_p$; in particular $|H|=p^2=\deg D$.

*Case $e=2$ and $p[D]\neq 0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$.* Hypothesis (iii) applied to $D$ yields a maximal subfield $L\subset D$ which is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group $H:=\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ of order $p^2$. We now invoke lemma_106 with $n=\deg D=p^2$ and this maximal subfield $L$: it gives a map $c:H\times H\to L^\times$ and a $k$-algebra isomorphism
$$D\;\simeq\;\bigoplus_{\sigma\in H} L\,u_\sigma,\qquad u_\sigma\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)u_\sigma,\quad u_\sigma u_\tau=c(\sigma,\tau)u_{\sigma\tau}.$$
It remains to check that this is a crossed product in the sense of the stated definition: $L$ is a field, separable over $k$ (it is Galois), hence etale; $\dim_k L=[L:k]=|H|=p^2$ because $L/k$ is Galois; $H$ acts on $L$ by $k$-automorphisms; and $L^H=k$ by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory (equivalently, Artin's theorem on the fixed field of a finite automorphism group, using $[L:k]=|H|$). Thus $L$ is an $H$-Galois $k$-algebra and $D\simeq (L,H,c)$ with $|H|=p^2=\deg D$.

These four cases are exhaustive (the dichotomy $p[D]=0$ versus $p[D]\neq0$ in the case $e=2$ is a literal law of logic, so no information about the exponent of $D$ is needed), which proves the claim.

**Step 3: Lifting the crossed product from $D$ to $A$.** We apply lemma_reduce_p2_from_div to $A$ and its Brauer-equivalent division algebra $D$: its hypotheses are exactly that $A\simeq D\otimes_k M_m(k)$ with $\deg D=p^e$, $e\in\{0,1,2\}$, and that $D$ is a crossed product for a group $H$ of order $\deg D$, with the trivial group allowed when $D=k$; this is precisely what Step 1 and Step 2 provide. The lemma concludes that $A$ is a crossed product algebra $(L',G,c')$ for some group $G$ of order $p^2$, which is the desired statement.

For completeness we spell out the mechanism behind Step 3, which also verifies it directly. Put $K=C_p^{\,2-e}$, so $|K|=p^{2-e}=m$ and $G:=H\times K$ has order $|H|\,|K|=p^e\cdot p^{2-e}=p^2$. By lemma_split_regular_crossed, the algebra $k^{K}$ of $|K|$ copies of $k$ with $K$ acting by translation is a $K$-Galois $k$-algebra and $(k^{K},K,1)\simeq M_{|K|}(k)=M_m(k)$. Taking $L_1=L$ (the $H$-Galois algebra realising $D$) and $L_2=k^{K}$, reference ref_10 says that $L_1\otimes_k L_2$, contained in $D\otimes_k M_m(k)$, is a $(H\times K)$-Galois $k$-algebra and that $D\otimes_k M_m(k)$ is an $(H\times K)$-crossed product. Since $D\otimes_k M_m(k)\simeq M_m(D)\simeq A$, this exhibits $A$ as a $(L_1\otimes_k L_2,\,H\times K,\,c'')$ crossed product with $|H\times K|=p^2=\deg A$, in accordance with the definition (the algebra $L_1\otimes_k L_2$ is etale of dimension $|H||K|=p^2$ with fixed ring $L_1^H\otimes_k L_2^K=k\otimes_k k=k$). In the case $e=2$ this degenerates to $K=\{1\}$ and $A\simeq D$, already handled in Step 2.

Thus in every case $A$ is a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^2$. This completes the proof.

lemma_146.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and write $\wp(F)=\{x^p-x:x\in F\}$. Let $C$ be a central division $K$-algebra of degree $p$, and let $b\in K\setminus\wp(K)$, with $K(b)$ the field obtained by adjoining to $K$ a root of $T^p-T-b$ and $\tau$ the $K$-automorphism sending that root to itself plus $1$. Then $C\otimes_K K(b)\cong M_p(K(b))$ if and only if there exists $z\in K^{\times}$ such that the Brauer class of $C$ equals the class of the cyclic algebra $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}K(b)v^i$ with $v^p=z$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in K(b)$.
lemma_146.proof:
Throughout, write $\wp(F)=\{x^p-x:x\in F\}$ for a field $F$ of characteristic $p>0$, and write $[X]$ for the Brauer class of a central simple algebra $X$.

STEP 1. The Artin--Schreier extension is cyclic Galois of degree $p$.  Fix an algebraic closure $K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ and choose $\theta\in K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ with $\theta^p-\theta=b$; the field denoted $K(b)$ in the statement is $E:=K(\theta)$, and $\tau$ is the $K$-automorphism with $\tau(\theta)=\theta+1$.  Let $f(T)=T^p-T-b\in K[T]$.
(a) $f$ is separable: $f'(T)=pT^{p-1}-1=-1\neq 0$, so $\gcd(f,f')=1$.
(b) The roots of $f$ in $K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ are exactly $\theta+i$, $i\in\mathbb F_p$, because $(\theta+i)^p-(\theta+i)-b=(\theta^p-\theta-b)+(i^p-i)=0$, and they are $p$ distinct elements (as $\theta+i=\theta+j\Rightarrow i=j$); since $\deg f=p$, these are all the roots.
(c) $f$ is irreducible over $K$.  If not, let $g$ be a monic irreducible factor of degree $d<p$, $1\le d\le p-1$, with roots $\theta+i_1,\dots,\theta+i_d$, $i_j\in\mathbb F_p$.  The coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $g$ is $-(d\theta+i_1+\cdots+i_d)\in K$.  Since $d\not\equiv 0\pmod p$, $d$ is invertible in $K$, so $\theta\in K$, whence $b=\theta^p-\theta\in\wp(K)$, contradicting the hypothesis $b\notin\wp(K)$.
(d) From (c), $[E:K]=p$.  All roots of $f$ lie in $E$, so $E/K$ is normal, and it is separable by (a); hence $E/K$ is Galois of degree $p$.  The map $\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)\to(\mathbb F_p,+)$, $\sigma\mapsto i$ where $\sigma(\theta)=\theta+i$, is injective (a $K$-automorphism of $E=K(\theta)$ is determined by $\sigma(\theta)$) and both groups have order $p$, so it is an isomorphism.  Consequently $\tau$ (the element corresponding to $1$) has order $p$ and generates $\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)=\{1,\tau,\dots,\tau^{p-1}\}$.

STEP 2. The cyclic algebras $A_z$.  For $z\in K^{\times}$ put $A_z:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}E v^{i}$ with $v^p=z$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in E$.  By reference ref_22(i), applied to the cyclic Galois *field* extension $E/K$ with generator $\tau$ and parameter $z\in K^{\times}$: (i) $A_z$ is a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $p$, so its class $[A_z]\in\operatorname{Br}(K)$ is defined; and (ii) $E$ splits $A_z$, i.e. $A_z\otimes_K E\cong M_p(E)$.

STEP 3. Proof of ($\Leftarrow$).  Assume $[C]=[A_z]$ in $\operatorname{Br}(K)$ for some $z\in K^{\times}$.  The restriction map $\operatorname{res}\colon\operatorname{Br}(K)\to\operatorname{Br}(E)$, $[X]\mapsto[X\otimes_K E]$, is a group homomorphism, so
$[C\otimes_K E]=\operatorname{res}([C])=\operatorname{res}([A_z])=[A_z\otimes_K E]=0$ by Step 2(ii).
Now $C\otimes_K E$ is a central simple $E$-algebra of degree $\deg C=p$ (base change of a central simple algebra by a field extension is central simple of the same degree).  Hence $C\otimes_K E\cong M_r(\Delta)$ for a central division $E$-algebra $\Delta$ with $r\cdot\deg\Delta=p$.  Its Brauer class is $[\Delta]$, which is trivial, so $\Delta\cong E$ and therefore $r=p$.  Thus $C\otimes_K E\cong M_p(E)$, i.e. $C\otimes_K K(b)\cong M_p(K(b))$.

STEP 4. Proof of ($\Rightarrow$).  Assume $C\otimes_K E\cong M_p(E)$.
(a) Embedding of $E$ in $C$.  Apply ref_5 with $A=C$ (a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $n=\deg C=p$) and the field extension $E/K$ of degree $m=p$, which divides $n$.  Our hypothesis says exactly that $C\otimes_K E\cong M_m(B)$ with $B=E$, which is the first (equivalently, $\operatorname{ind}(C\otimes_K E)=1$ divides $n/m=1$), so ref_5 yields a $K$-algebra embedding $\iota\colon E\hookrightarrow C$.  Set $L:=\iota(E)\subset C$; then $L$ is a subfield of $C$ containing $K$ with $\dim_K L=[E:K]=p$.
(b) $L$ is a maximal subfield of $C$.  Since $L$ is commutative, $L\subseteq C_C(L)$.  By ref_1 (double centralizer theorem), $\dim_K L\cdot\dim_K C_C(L)=\dim_K C=p^2$, so $\dim_K C_C(L)=p^2/p=p$, and the inclusion $L\subseteq C_C(L)$ of $K$-spaces of equal dimension gives $C_C(L)=L$.  The "in particular" clause of ref_1 then says precisely that $L$ is a maximal subfield of $C$.
(c) $L/K$ is cyclic Galois.  Because $\iota\colon E\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }L$ is a $K$-algebra isomorphism, conjugation by $\iota$ is a group isomorphism $\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$: for each $j$ the map $\sigma_j:=\iota\tau^{j}\iota^{-1}$ is a $K$-automorphism of $L$, and every $K$-automorphism of $L$ is of this form (transporting along $\iota$).  Thus $L/K$ is Galois with cyclic Galois group generated by $\sigma:=\iota\tau\iota^{-1}$.
(d) Cyclic presentation of $C$.  Apply lemma_90 (Spark) with $k=K$, $D=C$, $n=p$, the maximal subfield $L$ and its generator $\sigma$: there exists $z\in K^{\times}$ such that $C$ is $K$-isomorphic to the cyclic algebra $(L/K,\sigma,z)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}L u^{i}$ with $u^p=z$ and $u\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)u$ for all $\lambda\in L$.
(e) Transport of scalars along $\iota$.  Define a $K$-linear map $\chi\colon A_z=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}E v^{i}\to\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}L u^{i}$ by $\chi\big(\sum_i\lambda_i v^{i}\big)=\sum_i\iota(\lambda_i)u^{i}$.  Since $\iota$ is a $K$-vector-space isomorphism $E\simeq L$ and both sums are direct, $\chi$ is a $K$-linear bijection.  It is multiplicative: $A_z$ is, by definition, the quotient of the free associative $K$-algebra on the symbols $\{\lambda:\lambda\in E\}\cup\{V\}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the relations expressing that $E\ni\lambda\mapsto\lambda$ is $K$-linear and multiplicative, together with $V^p-z$ and $V\lambda-\tau(\lambda)V$.  In $\bigoplus_i L u^i$ the corresponding relations hold: $\iota$ is a $K$-algebra map on $E$; $u^p=z$; and $u\,\iota(\lambda)=\sigma(\lambda)u=\iota\tau(\lambda)u=\iota(\tau(\lambda))\,u$.  Hence the assignment $V\mapsto u$, $\lambda\mapsto\iota(\lambda)$ induces a $K$-algebra homomorphism $A_z\to\bigoplus_iLu^i$, which is $\chi$, and being bijective it is a $K$-algebra isomorphism.  Composing with the isomorphism of (d) gives $C\cong A_z$ as $K$-algebras, whence $[C]=[A_z]$ in $\operatorname{Br}(K)$; that is, the Brauer class of $C$ equals the class of the cyclic algebra $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}K(b)v^{i}$ with $v^p=z$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$.

STEP 5. Steps 3 and 4 together give $C\otimes_K K(b)\cong M_p(K(b))$ if and only if there exists $z\in K^{\times}$ with $[C]=[A_z]$, which is the desired equivalence.  (Note that only $p>0$ was used; the argument does not require $p>2$.)

Remark on the structure of the argument: ref_22(i) also asserts that $z\bmod N_{E/K}(E^{\times})\mapsto[A_z]$ identifies $K^{\times}/N_{E/K}(E^{\times})$ with the relative Brauer group $\operatorname{Br}(E/K)=\ker(\operatorname{Br}(K)\to\operatorname{Br}(E))$; the two directions proved above are the surjectivity and the vanishing halves of that identification, spelled out here in the Artin--Schreier situation with the embedding criterion (ref_5) and the cyclic presentation (lemma_90) in place of cohomological machinery.

lemma_147.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$, and let $w$ be the valuation of $D$ extending $v$, with residue division ring $\bar D$ and value group $w(D^\times)$. If $[\bar D:\bar k]\cdot[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)]<p^2$, then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^2$.
lemma_147.proof:
We write $V_k=\{a\in k: v(a)\ge 0\}\cup\{0\}$, $\mathfrak m_k=\{a\in k: v(a)>0\}\cup\{0\}$, $\bar k=V_k/\mathfrak m_k$, and likewise $V_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}\cup\{0\}$, $\mathfrak m_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\}\cup\{0\}$, $\bar D=V_D/\mathfrak m_D$. Because $w$ extends $v$ we have $V_k=V_D\cap k$ and $\mathfrak m_k=\mathfrak m_D\cap k$; hence the inclusion $V_k\hookrightarrow V_D$ descends to an injective homomorphism $\bar k\hookrightarrow\bar D$, so we view $\bar k$ as a (central) subfield of the division ring $\bar D$. Put
$$E:=[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)],\qquad F:=[\bar D:\bar k].$$
The hypothesis $E\cdot F<p^2$ (a product of cardinals) forces both $E$ and $F$ to be finite integers with $1\le E\cdot F\le p^2-1$.

The proof has two steps: first we show $D$ has no maximal subfield which is Galois over $k$; then we use the fact that a crossed-product division algebra always has one.

**Step 1. $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$.**

Suppose, for a contradiction, that $M\subset D$ is a subfield, maximal among subfields of $D$, with $M/k$ Galois.

(1a) *Degree of $M$.* Since $M$ is maximal by inclusion, its centralizer satisfies $C_D(M)=M$: indeed $C_D(M)$ is a division $k$-subalgebra of $D$; if $x\in C_D(M)\setminus M$, then the $k$-subalgebra $M(x)$ generated by $M$ and $x$ lies in $C_D(M)$, is commutative (as $x$ commutes with $M$ and with itself) and is a finite-dimensional commutative domain over $k$, hence a field properly containing $M$, contradicting the maximality of $M$. (If instead one takes "maximal subfield" to mean a subalgebra that is a field of $k$-dimension $\deg D$, then the conclusion of (1a) is immediate and this paragraph may be skipped.) By the double centralizer theorem for central simple algebras (ref_ 1), $\dim_k M\cdot\dim_k C_D(M)=\dim_k D$. With $C_D(M)=M$ and $\dim_k D=(\deg D)^2=p^4$ this gives $[M:k]^2=p^4$, hence
$$[M:k]=p^2.$$

(1b) *Fundamental equality on $M$.* Restrict $w$ to $M$; write $w_M:=w|_M$. This is a valuation of $M$ extending $v$. Since $(k,v)$ is henselian and $M/k$ is algebraic, $w_M$ is the unique extension of $v$ to $M$; let $\bar M$ denote its residue field. Applying the fundamental equality for finite Galois extensions over a henselian discretely valued field (lemma_96) to $M/k$ with the valuation $w_M$ gives
$$[M:k]=[w(M^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar M:\bar k].\tag{1}$$
In particular both factors on the right are finite; set $e:=[w(M^\times):v(k^\times)]$ and $f:=[\bar M:\bar k]$, so $e\cdot f=[M:k]=p^2$ by (1a).

(1c) *Comparison of value groups.* Since $M^\times\subset D^\times$ and $w$ restricts to $w_M$, we have $v(k^\times)\subseteq w(M^\times)\subseteq w(D^\times)$ as abelian groups. By the tower formula for group indices,
$$E=[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)]=[w(D^\times):w(M^\times)]\cdot[w(M^\times):v(k^\times)]=[w(D^\times):w(M^\times)]\cdot e,$$
so $e\le E$.

(1d) *Comparison of residue fields.* Consider the composite ring homomorphism
$$V_M:=\{x\in M: w(x)\ge0\}=M\cap V_D\;\hookrightarrow\; V_D\twoheadrightarrow \bar D.$$
Its kernel is $M\cap\mathfrak m_D=\{x\in M: w(x)>0\}$. This is precisely the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_M$ of the valuation ring $V_M$: every element of $V_M$ with $w(x)>0$ is a non-unit of $V_M$ (its inverse lies in $M$ and has negative value), while every $x\in V_M$ with $w(x)=0$ has $x^{-1}\in M\cap V_D=V_M$ and hence is a unit. Thus the composite induces an injective homomorphism of fields
$$\iota:\bar M=V_M/\mathfrak m_M\hookrightarrow \bar D.$$
The map is $\bar k$-linear, because $w$ extends $v$, so its image is a subfield of the division ring $\bar D$ containing $\bar k$. Viewing $\bar D$ as a right vector space over the fields $\bar k\subseteq\iota(\bar M)$, the tower law gives
$$F=[\bar D:\bar k]=[\bar D:\iota(\bar M)]\cdot[\iota(\bar M):\bar k]=[\bar D:\iota(\bar M)]\cdot f,$$
and since $F$ is finite, $f\le F$.

(1e) *Contradiction.* Combining (1a), (1c) and (1d),
$$p^2=[M:k]=e\cdot f\le E\cdot F<p^2,$$
which is impossible. Hence no such $M$ exists: $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$. (This is exactly the content of lemma_138; we reproduced the argument above rather than quoting it, and the only input used was the fundamental equality lemma_96 together with elementary properties of the restriction of $w$.)

**Step 2. A crossed product would supply such a maximal subfield.**

Assume, for a contradiction, that $D\simeq (L,G,c)$ as $k$-algebras for some group $G$ of order $p^2$ and some Galois $G$-algebra $L$ over $k$ (so $L$ is etale commutative of $k$-dimension $|G|=p^2$ with $L^G=k$, and $c:G\times G\to L^\times$ is a $2$-cocycle). Take $n=p^2=\deg D$ in lemma_133: since $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $n$ isomorphic to the crossed product $(L,G,c)$ with $|G|=n$, lemma_133 asserts that $L$ is a field and that its image $M\subset D$ under such an isomorphism is a maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$.

But such an $M$ does not exist by Step 1. This contradiction shows that no isomorphism $D\simeq (L,G,c)$ can exist for any group $G$ of order $p^2$.

Conclusion: under the hypothesis $[\bar D:\bar k]\cdot[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)]<p^2$, the division algebra $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^2$. $\blacksquare$

(Remarks on the hypotheses: henselianity of $v$ is used exactly twice — to ensure the restriction of $w$ to $M$ is the unique extension of $v$ and hence that the fundamental equality (1) applies, and, implicitly, in the existence/uniqueness of the extension $w$ of $v$ to $D$, which is part of the statement. The assumption $p>2$ is not used beyond matching the hypotheses of lemma_96/lemma_138; the argument is valid verbatim for $p=2$.)

lemma_148.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p$. Let $c\in k$ and let $K$ be the Artin-Schreier etale $k$-algebra $k[T]/(T^p-T-c)$, with $\tau$ the $k$-automorphism induced by $T\mapsto T+1$. For all $a,\lambda\in k$, the norm $N_{K/k}(a+\lambda T)$ equals $a^p-a\lambda^{p-1}+c\lambda^p$.
lemma_148.proof:
Notation: write wp(k) = {t^p - t : t \in k}, let f(T) = T^p - T - c \in k[T], and denote by T also the residue class of the indeterminate in K = k[T]/(f).

STEP 0 (the automorphism \tau, and freeness). In characteristic p one has (T+1)^p = T^p + 1, since the intermediate binomial coefficients \binom{p}{j}, 0 < j < p, are divisible by p. Hence the k-endomorphism of k[T] sending T to T+1 maps f(T) to (T+1)^p - (T+1) - c = T^p + 1 - T - 1 - c = f(T), so it descends to a k-algebra endomorphism \tau of K; likewise T \mapsto T-1 gives an endomorphism \tau', and \tau\tau' = \tau'\tau = id since they compose to the identity on the generator T. Thus \tau \in Aut_k(K)^{\times}, and by induction \tau^i(T) = T + i for all i \in \mathbb{Z}; consequently \tau^i = id iff p \mid i, so \tau has order p and \tau^0 = 1, \tau, \dots, \tau^{p-1} are pairwise distinct.
Because f is monic of degree p, K is a free k-module with basis 1, T, \dots, T^{p-1}; in particular K \neq 0 and the structure map k \to K, s \mapsto s\cdot 1_K, is injective (s\cdot 1_K = 0 forces s = 0 by the basis).

STEP 1 (norm). For x \in K define N_{K/k}(x) := \det_k(m_x), where m_x : K \to K, y \mapsto xy, is the k-linear multiplication map (the norm of the finite locally free, in fact finite free, algebra K/k).

STEP 2 (Lemma: the norm is the product of the \tau-conjugates). For every x \in K,
  \prod_{i=0}^{p-1} \tau^i(x) = N_{K/k}(x)\cdot 1_K.   (\ast)
Proof of the lemma. First, f'(T) = pT^{p-1} - 1 = -1 \neq 0, so \gcd(f, f') = 1 and f is separable: it has p distinct roots in any splitting field.

Case A: c \notin wp(k). Then f has no root in k. Let \Omega/k be an algebraic closure and t \in \Omega a root of f. For each i \in \mathbb{F}_p \subset k, Fermat's little theorem gives i^p = i, hence (t+i)^p - (t+i) = t^p + i^p - t - i = t^p - t = c, so every t+i is a root of f; these p elements are distinct, hence they are all the roots of f. Thus f splits in k(t), so k(t)/k is normal, and it is separable since f is; hence k(t)/k is Galois. Every \sigma \in Gal(k(t)/k) satisfies \sigma(t) = t + i(\sigma) for a unique i(\sigma) \in \mathbb{F}_p, and \sigma \mapsto i(\sigma) is an injective homomorphism Gal(k(t)/k) \hookrightarrow (\mathbb{F}_p,+) (a k-automorphism of k(t) is determined by the image of t). Therefore |Gal(k(t)/k)| divides p. It is not 1, for t \notin k (else c = t^p - t \in wp(k)). Hence |Gal(k(t)/k)| = p = [k(t):k], so the minimal polynomial \mu_t of t over k has degree p; being a monic divisor of the monic degree-p polynomial f having t as a root, it equals f. Thus f is irreducible and K \simeq k(t) is a Galois field extension of k of degree p; its Galois group has order p and contains the p distinct automorphisms \tau^0,\dots,\tau^{p-1}, so Gal(K/k) = \{\tau^0,\dots,\tau^{p-1}\}.

We now prove the standard fact used here: if E/k is a finite Galois field extension, then N_{E/k}(z) = \prod_{\sigma \in Gal(E/k)} \sigma(z) for all z \in E. Let d = [k(z):k], r = [E:k(z)], n = [E:k] = rd, and let \mu_z \in k[X] be the minimal polynomial of z. Since E is a free k(z)-module of rank r and m_z is k(z)-linear, \chi_{E/k}(m_z) = (\chi_{k(z)/k}(m_z|_{k(z)}))^r; and \chi_{k(z)/k}(m_z|_{k(z)}) = \mu_z because both are monic of degree d and \mu_z divides the characteristic polynomial. So \chi_{E/k}(m_z) = \mu_z^{\,r}. The d distinct roots of \mu_z in \Omega are the values \rho(z), \rho ranging over the d distinct k-embeddings \rho: k(z) \to \Omega (k(z)/k is separable as a subextension of the separable extension E/k). Fix one extension \tilde\rho: E \to \Omega of \rho; since E/k is normal, the image of every k-embedding E \to \Omega is E, so the extensions of \rho to E are exactly \tilde\rho \circ \gamma, \gamma \in Gal(E/k(z)), and there are r of them (E/k(z) is Galois because E/k is). Therefore
  \prod_{\sigma \in Gal(E/k)} \sigma(z) = \prod_{\rho} \prod_{\gamma \in Gal(E/k(z))} \tilde\rho(\gamma(z)) = \prod_{\rho} \rho(z)^{r} = \big((-1)^d \mu_z(0)\big)^{r},
using \mu_z(X) = \prod_\rho (X - \rho(z)), i.e. \prod_\rho \rho(z) = (-1)^d \mu_z(0). On the other hand, \det(m_z) = (-1)^n \chi_{E/k}(m_z)(0) = (-1)^{rd} \mu_z(0)^r = \big((-1)^d \mu_z(0)\big)^r. Hence N_{E/k}(z) = \prod_\sigma \sigma(z), as claimed. Applying this with E = K, z = x and Gal(K/k) = \{\tau^i\} gives (\ast) in Case A.

Case B: c = t^p - t for some t \in k. Then the p distinct elements t + i (i \in \mathbb{F}_p) are roots of f, hence f(T) = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} (T - (t+i)) in k[T] (both sides monic of degree p with the same p distinct roots). The ideals (T - (t+i)) are pairwise comaximal since the t+i are distinct, so the Chinese remainder theorem yields a k-algebra isomorphism
  \varphi : K \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} k = k^{p}, \qquad x \longmapsto \big(x(t+i)\big)_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p},
where x(t+i) is the evaluation at t+i of any polynomial representative of x (well defined, because f(t+i) = 0). Under \varphi, \tau acts as the cyclic shift: \varphi(\tau x)_i = (\tau x)(t+i) = x(t+i+1) = \varphi(x)_{i+1}, where i \mapsto i+1 is a p-cycle on \mathbb{F}_p.
Write y = \varphi(x) = (y_i)_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p}. Since \varphi conjugates m_x to multiplication by y on k^p, and the latter is diagonal in the basis of primitive idempotents, N_{K/k}(x) = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} y_i. The j-th coordinate of \varphi\big(\prod_{i} \tau^i x\big) equals \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} (\tau^i x)(t+j) = \prod_{i} y_{j+i} = \prod_{m} y_m, because i \mapsto j+i is a bijection of \mathbb{F}_p. Hence \varphi\big(\prod_i \tau^i x\big) = (\textstyle\prod_m y_m)_{j \in \mathbb{F}_p} = \varphi\big((\prod_m y_m)\cdot 1_K\big), and since \varphi is injective, \prod_i \tau^i(x) = N_{K/k}(x)\cdot 1_K. This proves (\ast) in Case B.

Since exactly one of the two cases holds (c \in wp(k) or not), the lemma is proved.

STEP 3 (explicit computation of the product). Since \tau^i fixes k pointwise and \tau^i(T) = T + i, for each i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\} we have \tau^i(a + \lambda T) = a + \lambda(T+i). Hence
  P := \prod_{i=0}^{p-1} \tau^i(a + \lambda T) = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} (a + \lambda T + \lambda i).

Subcase \lambda = 0: then P = a^p, and the claimed formula gives a^p - a\cdot 0^{p-1} + c\cdot 0^{p} = a^p (valid since p > 2 ensures p-1 \ge 1), so the formula holds.

Subcase \lambda \neq 0: set Y = T + a/\lambda \in K; then a + \lambda T + \lambda i = \lambda(Y + i), so
  P = \lambda^{p} \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} (Y + i).
We use the polynomial identity over \mathbb{F}_p:
  \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} (X + i) = X^p - X.
Indeed, X^p - X is monic of degree p and every element of \mathbb{F}_p is a root (Fermat), and since its derivative pX^{p-1} - 1 = -1 is nonzero the p roots are simple, so X^p - X = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p}(X - i) in \mathbb{F}_p[X]; as i \mapsto -i permutes \mathbb{F}_p, \prod_i (X-i) = \prod_i (X+i). Substituting X = Y, valid in any commutative \mathbb{F}_p-algebra, and using (u+v)^p = u^p + v^p together with T^p - T = c in K:
  \prod_{i \in \mathbb{F}_p} (Y+i) = Y^p - Y = \big(T + \tfrac{a}{\lambda}\big)^{p} - \big(T + \tfrac{a}{\lambda}\big) = \big(T^p - T\big) + \big(\tfrac{a}{\lambda}\big)^{p} - \tfrac{a}{\lambda} = c + \tfrac{a^p}{\lambda^p} - \tfrac{a}{\lambda}.
Multiplying by \lambda^p and using \lambda^p \cdot a^p/\lambda^p = a^p and \lambda^p \cdot a/\lambda = a\lambda^{p-1}:
  P = c\lambda^{p} + a^{p} - a\lambda^{p-1} = \big(a^{p} - a\lambda^{p-1} + c\lambda^{p}\big)\cdot 1_K.

STEP 4 (conclusion). By the lemma of Step 2, P = N_{K/k}(a + \lambda T)\cdot 1_K, and by Step 3, P = (a^{p} - a\lambda^{p-1} + c\lambda^{p})\cdot 1_K. Since k \to K, s \mapsto s\cdot 1_K, is injective (Step 0), it follows that
  N_{K/k}(a + \lambda T) = a^{p} - a\lambda^{p-1} + c\lambda^{p}
for all a, \lambda \in k. \hfill \blacksquare

lemma_149.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$ be the Laurent series field with its $u$-adic valuation. Let $K=k(z)$ where $z^p-z=s\,u^{-(p-1)}$. Then $1+t\,u$ does not belong to the norm group $N_{K/k}(K^\times)$.
lemma_149.proof:
Let $v$ be the $u$-adic valuation of $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)((u))$, normalized by $v(u)=1$, with valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)[[u]]$ and residue field $\kappa=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$. The field $k$ is complete for $v$, and $\kappa$ embeds into $\mathcal{O}_k$ as the constant series, with $\kappa\cap u\mathcal{O}_k=\{0\}$.

**Step 1: The extension $K/k$.** Put $\Pi:=uz\in K$. Using $z^p-z=s\,u^{-(p-1)}$ we get
$$\Pi^p=u^pz^p=u^p\bigl(z+s\,u^{-(p-1)}\bigr)=u^{p-1}\Pi+s\,u,$$
so $\Pi$ is a root of $f(T)=T^p-u^{p-1}T-su\in\mathcal{O}_k[T]$. This polynomial is Eisenstein at $u$: the non-leading coefficients are $-u^{p-1}$ (valuation $p-1\ge 1$) and $-su$ (valuation $1$), and the constant term $-su\notin u^2\mathcal{O}_k$. Indeed Eisenstein's criterion holds here: if $f=gh$ with $g,h\in\mathcal{O}_k[T]$ monic of positive degrees $r,s$, then reducing mod $u$ gives $\bar g\,\bar h=\bar T^{\,p}$ in $\kappa[\bar T]$, hence $\bar g=\bar T^{\,r}$, $\bar h=\bar T^{\,s}$ with $r,s\ge1$, so both constant terms of $g,h$ lie in $u\mathcal{O}_k$ and the constant term of $f$ would lie in $u^2\mathcal{O}_k$, contradiction. Since $f$ is monic (hence primitive), Gauss's lemma gives irreducibility in $k[T]$. As $z=\Pi/u$ and $\Pi=uz$, we have $K=k(z)=k(\Pi)$, $[K:k]=p$, and $\{1,\Pi,\dots,\Pi^{p-1}\}$ is a $k$-basis of $K$.

The extension is Galois: for each $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$,
$$(\Pi+u\lambda)^p-u^{p-1}(\Pi+u\lambda)-su=\bigl(\Pi^p-u^{p-1}\Pi-su\bigr)+u^p(\lambda^p-\lambda)=0,$$
so all $p$ roots $\Pi+u\lambda$ of $f$ lie in $K$; they are distinct, giving $p$ distinct $k$-automorphisms $\sigma_\lambda$ with $\sigma_\lambda(\Pi)=\Pi+u\lambda$ (equivalently $\sigma_\lambda(z)=z+\lambda$). Thus $K/k$ is cyclic of degree $p$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)=\{\sigma_\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p\}$.

**Step 2: The valuation $w$ and the basis formula.** Since $k$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$, the classical theorem on extensions of valuations to complete discretely valued fields gives a unique valuation $w$ on $K$ extending $v$, given explicitly by $w(x)=v\bigl(N_{K/k}(x)\bigr)/p$. In particular $w|_k=v$ and $w$ is $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$-invariant. The characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $\Pi$ is $f$, so $N_{K/k}(\Pi)=(-1)^p\cdot(-su)=su$ (as $p$ is odd), hence $w(\Pi)=v(su)/p=1/p$.

*Claim.* For $0\ne x=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}a_j\Pi^j$ with $a_j\in k$, one has $w(x)=\min_{0\le j\le p-1}\bigl(v(a_j)+j/p\bigr)$.
*Proof.* Since $w$ is a valuation with $w|_k=v$ and $w(\Pi)=1/p$, $w(a_j\Pi^j)=v(a_j)+j/p$. The numbers $v(a_j)+j/p$ for which $a_j\ne0$ are pairwise distinct modulo $\mathbb{Z}$ (equality would force $(j-i)/p\in\mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $j=i$), hence pairwise distinct as real numbers; the non-archimedean axiom iterated ($w(A+B)=\min(wA,wB)$ when $wA\ne wB$) gives the formula. $\square$

Consequences we use: (i) $\mathcal{O}_K=\{w\ge0\}=\bigoplus_{j}\mathcal{O}_k\Pi^j$; (ii) $J:=\{y\in\mathcal{O}_K:w(y)\ge2\}$ is an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$ (product of elements of values $\ge0$ and $\ge2$ has value $\ge2$), and $J\cap k=\{y\in k:v(y)\ge2\}=u^2\mathcal{O}_k$.

**Step 3: Reduction to $x=a_0(1+\beta)$.** Suppose, for a contradiction, that $1+tu=N_{K/k}(x)$ for some $x\in K^\times$. Since $1+tu\in\mathcal{O}_k^\times$, $v(1+tu)=0$, so $w(x)=v(N_{K/k}(x))/p=0$. Write $x=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}a_j\Pi^j$, $a_j\in k$. By the Claim, $\min_j\bigl(v(a_j)+j/p\bigr)=0$; the minimum is attained at a unique index $j_0$, and $v(a_{j_0})=-j_0/p\in\mathbb{Z}$ forces $j_0=0$ (as $0\le j_0/p<1$). Thus $v(a_0)=0$, i.e. $a_0\in\mathcal{O}_k^\times$, and for $j\ge1$, $v(a_j)\ge -j/p>-1$, so $v(a_j)\ge0$ and $a_j\in\mathcal{O}_k$. Hence
$$x=a_0\,(1+\beta),\qquad \beta=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}b_j\Pi^j,\quad b_j:=a_j/a_0\in\mathcal{O}_k,$$
with $w(\beta)=\min_{j\ge1}\bigl(v(b_j)+j/p\bigr)\ge 1/p>0$, so $w(1+\beta)=0$. Since $a_0\in k^\times$ and $[K:k]=p$, $N_{K/k}(a_0)=a_0^{\,p}$, so
$$1+tu=a_0^{\,p}\,N_{K/k}(1+\beta).\tag{3.1}$$

**Step 4: The congruence $N_{K/k}(1+\beta)\equiv 1+s\,u\,b_1^{\,p}\pmod{J}$.** Set $X:=1+\beta$ and $Y:=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1} j\,b_j\Pi^{j-1}\in\mathcal{O}_K$ (so $w(Y)\ge0$), and $Z:=uY$ (so $w(Z)\ge1$).

(4a) *Congruence of the conjugates.* For each $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and each $j$, the binomial expansion gives $(\Pi+u\lambda)^j=\Pi^j+j\Pi^{j-1}u\lambda+\sum_{i=2}^{j}\binom{j}{i}\Pi^{j-i}(u\lambda)^i$, and for $i\ge2$ (necessarily $i\le j$) each term has $w$-value $\ge (j-i)/p+i\ge 2$, i.e. lies in $J$. Multiplying by $b_j\in\mathcal{O}_k$ (which preserves $J$) and summing over $j$ yields $\sigma_\lambda(\beta)\equiv\beta+u\lambda Y\pmod J$, hence
$$\sigma_\lambda(X)\equiv X+\lambda Z\pmod J\qquad\text{for all }\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p.$$

(4b) *Multiplying.* By the telescoping identity $\prod_i x_i-\prod_i y_i=\sum_i (x_i-y_i)(\prod_{j<i}x_j)(\prod_{j>i}y_j)$ and the fact that $J$ is an ideal, the congruences of (4a) multiply: $N_{K/k}(X)=\prod_{\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p}\sigma_\lambda(X)\equiv\prod_{\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p}(X+\lambda Z)\pmod J$. In any commutative $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra the identity $\prod_{\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p}(A+\lambda B)=A^p-AB^{p-1}$ holds (it follows from $\prod_{\lambda}(T-\lambda)=T^p-T$, which gives $\prod_\lambda(1+\lambda C)=1-C^{p-1}$, applied with $C=B/A$ and cleared of denominators, hence universally). Thus
$$N_{K/k}(X)\equiv X^p-XZ^{p-1}\pmod J.$$
Since $w(X)=0$ and $w(Z)\ge1$, we get $w(XZ^{p-1})=(p-1)w(Z)\ge p-1\ge2$ (using $p\ge3$), so $XZ^{p-1}\in J$ and $N_{K/k}(X)\equiv X^p\pmod J$.

(4c) *The $p$-th power.* In characteristic $p$, $X^p=(1+\beta)^p=1+\beta^p$. Moreover $\beta^p=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}b_j^{\,p}\Pi^{jp}$, and for $j\ge2$, $w(b_j^{\,p}\Pi^{jp})=p\,v(b_j)+j\ge j\ge2$, so $\beta^p\equiv b_1^{\,p}\Pi^p\pmod J$. Finally, using $\Pi^p=u^{p-1}\Pi+su$, we have $b_1^{\,p}\Pi^p=b_1^{\,p}u^{p-1}\Pi+s\,u\,b_1^{\,p}$ with $w(b_1^{\,p}u^{p-1}\Pi)=p\,v(b_1)+p-1+1/p\ge p-1+1/p\ge2$ (as $p\ge3$). Hence
$$N_{K/k}(1+\beta)\equiv 1+s\,u\,b_1^{\,p}\pmod J.$$
Both $N_{K/k}(1+\beta)$ and $1+s\,u\,b_1^{\,p}$ lie in $k$, so their difference lies in $J\cap k=u^2\mathcal{O}_k$: there exists $\gamma\in\mathcal{O}_k$ with
$$N_{K/k}(1+\beta)=1+s\,u\,b_1^{\,p}+u^2\gamma.\tag{4.1}$$

**Step 5: Comparing residues (corrected final deduction).** Write $\bar a_0:=a_0\bmod u\in\kappa^\times$ (so $a_0=\bar a_0+u\alpha$ with $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_k$) and $\bar b_1:=b_1\bmod u\in\kappa$ (so $b_1=\bar b_1+u\alpha'$, $\alpha'\in\mathcal{O}_k$). Then
$$a_0^{\,p}=\bar a_0^{\,p}+u^{p}\alpha^{p}\equiv\bar a_0^{\,p}\pmod{u^2\mathcal{O}_k}\quad(\text{since }p\ge2),$$
$$s\,u\,b_1^{\,p}=s\,u\,\bar b_1^{\,p}+s\,u^{p+1}\alpha'^{\,p}\equiv s\,u\,\bar b_1^{\,p}\pmod{u^2\mathcal{O}_k}\quad(\text{since }p+1\ge4\ge2),$$
and $a_0^{\,p}u^2\gamma\in u^2\mathcal{O}_k$. Substituting (4.1) into (3.1) and reducing modulo $u^2\mathcal{O}_k$ gives the congruence in $\mathcal{O}_k=\kappa[[u]]$
$$1+t\,u\equiv \bar a_0^{\,p}\bigl(1+s\,u\,\bar b_1^{\,p}\bigr)\pmod{u^2\mathcal{O}_k},\tag{5.1}$$
with $\bar a_0,\bar b_1\in\kappa$ (note: $b_1$ itself need not lie in $\kappa$; only its residue $\bar b_1$ does).

Comparing the constant terms of (5.1) via the residue map $\mathcal{O}_k\twoheadrightarrow\kappa$ yields $1=\bar a_0^{\,p}$ in the field $\kappa$; since the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$ is injective on $\kappa$ and $1^p=1$, we get $\bar a_0=1$. Substituting into (5.1): $t\,u-s\,u\,\bar b_1^{\,p}\in u^2\mathcal{O}_k$, i.e. $t-s\,\bar b_1^{\,p}\in u\mathcal{O}_k$. But $t-s\,\bar b_1^{\,p}\in\kappa$, and $\kappa\cap u\mathcal{O}_k=\{0\}$ (a constant power series with zero constant term is zero). Therefore
$$t=s\,\bar b_1^{\,p}\quad\text{in }\kappa=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t).$$
If $\bar b_1=0$ this reads $t=0$, impossible in $\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)$. Otherwise $\bar b_1^{\,p}=t/s\in\kappa^\times$. We show this is impossible. Let $v_t$ be the $t$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{F}_p(s,t)=\mathrm{Frac}(\mathbb{F}_p(s)[t])$ attached to the prime element $t$ of the UFD $\mathbb{F}_p(s)[t]$, normalized by $v_t(t)=1$; then $v_t$ is trivial on $\mathbb{F}_p(s)^\times$, so $v_t(s)=0$ and $v_t(t/s)=1$. For any $y\in\kappa^\times$, $v_t(y^p)=p\,v_t(y)\in p\mathbb{Z}$. Since $p>2$, $1\notin p\mathbb{Z}$, so $t/s$ cannot be a $p$-th power in $\kappa^\times$ — contradiction. (Equivalently: $\{1,t,\dots,t^{p-1}\}$ is a basis of $\kappa$ over $\kappa^p\supseteq\mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p)$, and $t/s$ has $t$-degree $1$.)

Thus no $x\in K^\times$ satisfies $N_{K/k}(x)=1+tu$, i.e. $1+tu\notin N_{K/k}(K^\times)$. $\blacksquare$

lemma_151.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$. Let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ with canonical valuation $w$ extending $v$, with $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ and residue division ring $\bar D$ central of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$. If $\bar D$ is a crossed product algebra $(\bar L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^2$, then $D$ is a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c')$ for some maximal subfield $L$ of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$.
lemma_151.proof:
We argue in four steps: (1) the residue ring $\bar D$ is a division ring of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$; (2) from the hypothesis that $\bar D$ is a $G$-crossed product we extract a maximal subfield of $\bar D$ which is Galois over $\bar k$ with group $G$; (3) we lift that subfield to a maximal subfield $L\subset D$ which is unramified and Galois over $k$, with the same Galois group; (4) we turn $L\subset D$ into the required crossed product decomposition.

Step 0. Preliminaries on the characteristics. Since $\mathrm{char}(k)=p$, the element $p\cdot 1_k=0$, and the residue map $\mathcal O_D\to\bar D$ sends $1$ to $1$, so $\mathrm{char}(\bar k)=p>2$ as well; in particular $\bar k$ is a field of characteristic $p>2$, as required to apply the cited lemmas with base field $\bar k$.

Step 1. $\bar D$ is a division ring. Let $\mathcal O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}$ and $\mathfrak m_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\}$, so $\bar D=\mathcal O_D/\mathfrak m_D$. Take a non-zero residue class $\bar a\in\bar D$, represented by $a\in\mathcal O_D$ with $w(a)=0$ (non-zero in the residue ring means exactly $w(a)=0$, since $w(a)\ge0$ for $a\in\mathcal O_D$). As $a\neq0$ in the division algebra $D$, $a^{-1}\in D$ exists and $w(a^{-1})=-w(a)=0$, so $a^{-1}\in\mathcal O_D$. Its residue $\overline{a^{-1}}$ satisfies $\bar a\,\overline{a^{-1}}=\overline{aa^{-1}}=\bar 1=\overline{a^{-1}a}$, so $\bar a$ is a unit. Hence $\bar D$ is a division ring; by hypothesis it is central over $\bar k$ and of degree $p^2$, i.e. $[\bar D:\bar k]=(\deg\bar D)^2=p^4$.

Step 2. A Galois maximal subfield of $\bar D$ with group $G$. By hypothesis there is a $\bar k$-algebra isomorphism $\bar D\simeq(\bar L,G,c)$, where $G$ is a group of order $p^2$ and $\bar L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $\bar k$ (commutative etale $\bar k$-algebra of dimension $|G|=p^2$ with $\bar L^G=\bar k$). We apply lemma_133 with base field $\bar k$, $n=p^2$, and the central division $\bar k$-algebra $\bar D$ of degree $n=p^2$ (just established in Step 1). Its hypotheses are satisfied verbatim: $\bar D$ is isomorphic as a $\bar k$-algebra to the crossed product $(\bar L,G,c)$ with $|G|=p^2=n$ and $\bar L$ a Galois $G$-algebra over $\bar k$. The conclusion is that $\bar L$ is a field and its image in $\bar D$ under the given isomorphism is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$ which is Galois over $\bar k$ with Galois group $G$. Identifying $\bar L$ with that image, we have:
\[\text{$\bar L\subset\bar D$ a maximal subfield, } \bar L/\bar k \text{ Galois with } \mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)=G,\ [\bar L:\bar k]=|G|=p^2.\]

Step 3. Lifting $\bar L$ to a Galois maximal subfield of $D$. We apply lemma_136. Its hypotheses are exactly the hypotheses of the present lemma: $(k,v)$ is henselian discretely valued of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$; $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$; $w$ is the valuation of $D$ extending $v$ with $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$; and the residue division ring $\bar D$ is central of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$. Since $\bar L$ is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$ which is Galois over $\bar k$ (Step 2), lemma_136 yields a maximal subfield $L\subset D$ containing $k$, unramified over $k$ and Galois over $k$, whose residue field is $\bar L$, and such that reduction induces an isomorphism
\[\rho:\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k).\]
In particular $[L:k]=p^2=\deg D$, so $L$ is a maximal subfield, and composing $\rho$ with the equality $\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)=G$ from Step 2 gives a group isomorphism
\[\varphi:G=\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)\ \xrightarrow{\ \rho^{-1}\ }\ \mathrm{Gal}(L/k).\]
Via $\varphi$, the group $G$ acts on $L$ by $k$-automorphisms: $g\cdot x=\varphi(g)(x)$. We record that $L$ is then a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ in the sense of the definitions: $L$ is a field, hence a commutative etale $k$-algebra of dimension $[L:k]=p^2=|G|$; the action is by $k$-algebra automorphisms through $\varphi$; and $L^G=L^{\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)}=k$ by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory (because $\varphi$ is surjective onto $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$).

Step 4. The crossed product decomposition. We apply lemma_106 with $A=D$, $n=p^2$, and $L$ the maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ (identified with $G$ through $\varphi$). It provides elements $u_\sigma\in D^\times$ for $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ such that
\[D=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)} L\,u_\sigma,\qquad u_\sigma\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)u_\sigma\ \ (\lambda\in L),\qquad u_\sigma u_\tau=c_0(\sigma,\tau)\,u_{\sigma\tau}\]
for a map $c_0:\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\times\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\to L^\times$.
Now define, for each $g\in G$, the unit $v_g:=u_{\varphi(g)}\in D^\times$, and define $c':G\times G\to L^\times$ by $c'(g,h):=c_0(\varphi(g),\varphi(h))$. Then, since $\varphi$ is a group isomorphism, $\{v_g:g\in G\}=\{u_\sigma:\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\}$, so
\[D=\bigoplus_{g\in G} L\,v_g,\]
and for $\lambda\in L$ and $g,h\in G$:
\[v_g\lambda=u_{\varphi(g)}\lambda=\varphi(g)(\lambda)\,u_{\varphi(g)}=g(\lambda)v_g,\]
\[v_gv_h=u_{\varphi(g)}u_{\varphi(h)}=c_0(\varphi(g),\varphi(h))\,u_{\varphi(g)\varphi(h)}=c'(g,h)\,u_{\varphi(gh)}=c'(g,h)\,v_{gh}.\]
Thus $D$ is exactly the crossed product algebra $(L,G,c')$ as defined in the statement, where $L$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\simeq G$ (indeed equal to $G$ through $\varphi$).

This completes the proof: starting from the crossed product structure $(\bar L,G,c)$ on $\bar D$, lemma_133 produced a $G$-Galois maximal subfield $\bar L$ of $\bar D$, lemma_136 lifted it to a maximal subfield $L$ of $D$ Galois over $k$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\simeq G$, and lemma_106 converted that Galois maximal subfield into the required crossed product decomposition $D=(L,G,c')$.

lemma_152.statement: Let $p>2$ be a prime and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)((u))$ be the Laurent series field in $u$ over $\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)$, with its $u$-adic valuation. The images of $s$, $t$, $r$, and $u$ in $k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^p$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
lemma_152.proof:
Write K := \mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r) and k := K((u)). We prove that the classes of s, t, r, u in the \mathbb{F}_p-vector space k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{p} are linearly independent.

STEP 0 (Linear independence criterion in k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{p}). Since k^{\times} is abelian, the quotient k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{p} is an \mathbb{F}_p-vector space: for \lambda \in \mathbb{F}_p, represented by an integer a with 0 \le a \le p-1, set \lambda\cdot[\xi] := [\xi^{a}]. This is well defined: if \xi = \xi'\eta^{p} then \xi^{a} = (\xi')^{a}(\eta^{a})^{p}, so [\xi^{a}] = [(\xi')^{a}]; and p\cdot[\xi] = [\xi^{p}] = 0. Consequently, elements x_1,\dots,x_n are linearly independent if and only if a relation x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n} \in (k^{\times})^{p} with each a_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\} forces a_1 = \cdots = a_n = 0. We verify this for (x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) = (s,t,r,u).

STEP 1 (The u-adic valuation kills the exponent of u). Every nonzero element \xi \in k = K((u)) has a unique expansion \xi = \sum_{i \ge i_0} a_i u^{i} with a_i \in K and a_{i_0} \ne 0; the u-adic valuation is v(\xi) := i_0. It is a surjective homomorphism v : k^{\times} \to \mathbb{Z} with v(u) = 1. Moreover, for c \in K^{\times}, viewed as a constant Laurent series, v(c) = 0, because the lowest exponent occurring is 0. In particular v(s) = v(t) = v(r) = 0.

Assume now that
  s^{a} t^{b} r^{c} u^{d} = y^{p}      (1)
for some y \in k^{\times} and integers a,b,c,d with 0 \le a,b,c,d \le p-1. Applying v and using that v is a homomorphism,
  d = a v(s) + b v(t) + c v(r) + d v(u) = v(y^{p}) = p\,v(y).
Hence p divides d; since 0 \le d \le p-1, we obtain d = 0.

STEP 2 (A p-th root of an element of K lies in K). Write y = \sum_{i \ge i_0} y_i u^{i} with y_i \in K and y_{i_0} \ne 0. Because k is commutative of characteristic p, the Frobenius is a ring homomorphism, so
  y^{p} = \sum_{i \ge i_0} y_i^{p} u^{p i}.
By Step 1, (1) reads y^{p} = s^{a} t^{b} r^{c} \in K^{\times}, and the Laurent expansion of this constant series has exactly one nonzero coefficient, namely the coefficient of u^{0}. By uniqueness of the Laurent expansion in K((u)), y_i^{p} = 0 for every i \ne 0; since K is a field (in particular reduced), y_i = 0 for i \ne 0. Thus y = y_0 \in K^{\times}, and (1) becomes
  y^{p} = s^{a} t^{b} r^{c} \quad \text{in } K.      (2)

STEP 3 (The s-adic valuation kills a). View K as the rational function field K_s(s) in one variable over K_s := \mathbb{F}_p(t,r). The polynomial ring K_s[s] is a unique factorization domain in which s is a prime element. Hence each h \in K^{\times} can be written uniquely as h = s^{n} f/g with n \in \mathbb{Z} and f,g \in K_s[s] satisfying f(0)g(0) \ne 0 (take a coprime representation h = f_0/g_0 and let n be the exponent of s in the factorization of f_0/g_0; uniqueness follows from uniqueness of factorization). Defining v_s(h) := n gives a well-defined discrete valuation: for h = s^{n}f/g and h' = s^{n'}f'/g' one has hh' = s^{n+n'}(ff')/(gg') with (ff')(0)(gg')(0) = f(0)g(0)f'(0)g'(0) \ne 0, so v_s(hh') = v_s(h) + v_s(h'); and v_s(h+h') \ge \min(v_s(h),v_s(h')) follows by putting over a common denominator not divisible by s. By construction v_s(s) = 1, and since t, r \in K_s^{\times} = \mathbb{F}_p(t,r)^{\times} are nonzero constants with respect to the variable s, v_s(t) = v_s(r) = 0.
Applying v_s to (2) and using additivity,
  p\,v_s(y) = v_s(y^{p}) = a\,v_s(s) + b\,v_s(t) + c\,v_s(r) = a.
Thus a \in p\mathbb{Z}; together with 0 \le a \le p-1 this gives a = 0.

STEP 4 (The t- and r-adic valuations kill b and c). Exactly the same construction applies after permuting the variables. Viewing K as \mathbb{F}_p(s,r)(t), the prime element t of \mathbb{F}_p(s,r)[t] defines the t-adic valuation v_t : K^{\times} \to \mathbb{Z} with v_t(t) = 1 and, because s, r \in \mathbb{F}_p(s,r)^{\times}, with v_t(s) = v_t(r) = 0. Applying v_t to (2) yields p\,v_t(y) = a\cdot 0 + b\cdot 1 + c\cdot 0 = b, hence b \in p\mathbb{Z} and therefore b = 0. Likewise, viewing K as \mathbb{F}_p(s,t)(r), the r-adic valuation v_r satisfies v_r(r) = 1 and v_r(s) = v_r(t) = 0, and applying it to (2) gives p\,v_r(y) = c, whence c = 0.

STEP 5 (Conclusion). We have shown a = b = c = d = 0, so the assumed relation among the classes of s, t, r, u in k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{p} was trivial. By the criterion of Step 0, the images of s, t, r and u in k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{p} are linearly independent over \mathbb{F}_p.

(Remark: the argument uses only that p is prime; the hypothesis p > 2 is more than needed, so it is certainly satisfied.)

lemma_154.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation. Let $n$ and $q$ be positive integers with $p\nmid n$, and let $K=k(w)$ where $w^p-w=t\,u^{-n}$. Then $u(1+r u^q)\notin N_{K/k}(K^{\times})$.
lemma_154.proof:
Write $F=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)$, so $k=F((u))$, and let $v=v_u$ be the normalized $u$-adic valuation ($v(u)=1$, $v(F^\times)=0$). The field $k$ is complete, hence henselian, with residue field $F$. Put $c=t\,u^{-n}$ and $a=u(1+ru^q)=u+ru^{q+1}$; then $v(c)=-n$ and $v(a)=1$ (since $q\ge 1$ gives $v(ru^{q+1})=q+1>1=v(u)$).

**Step 1: $K/k$ is cyclic of degree $p$.** Since $v(c)=-n<0$ and $p\nmid n=v(c)$ (up to sign), lemma 73 (Spark) gives $c\notin\wp(k)=\{x^p-x:x\in k\}$. In characteristic $p$ the roots of $T^p-T-c$ are $w,w+1,\dots,w+(p-1)$ for any root $w$; hence for any root $w$ the field $k(w)$ contains all roots, so $k(w)/k$ is Galois with group a subgroup of $(\mathbb{F}_p,+)$. If $T^p-T-c$ had a proper irreducible factor of degree $d$, then for a root $w$ of that factor we would have $d=[k(w):k]=|{\rm Gal}(k(w)/k)|$, a divisor of $p$; since $w\notin k$ we get $d>1$, hence $d=p$, a contradiction. So $T^p-T-c$ is irreducible, $K=k(w)$ is a field, $[K:k]=p$, and $\tau\colon w\mapsto w+1$ generates $G={\rm Gal}(K/k)\simeq C_p$.

**Step 2: The valuation of $K$.** As $k$ is henselian, $v$ extends uniquely to a valuation $v_K$ on $K$. Since $v_K(c)=-n<0$, we cannot have $v_K(w)\ge0$ (else $v_K(w^p-w)\ge0$). Thus $v_K(w)<0$, so $p\,v_K(w)<v_K(w)$ and $v_K(w^p-w)=p\,v_K(w)$. Hence $p\,v_K(w)=v_K(c)=-n$, i.e. $v_K(w)=-n/p$. Consequently $\frac1p\mathbb{Z}\subseteq v_K(K^\times)$. By lemma 96 (Spark), applied to the Galois extension $K/k$ over the henselian field $(k,v)$, $p=[K:k]=[v_K(K^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar K:F]$. Since the first factor is at least $p$ and divides $p$, it equals $p$: $v_K(K^\times)=\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$ and the residue field of $K$ is $F$ (the extension is totally ramified, defectless).

**Step 3: Reduction to a Brauer-group statement.** Consider the cyclic algebra $D=(K/k,\tau,a)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}Kv^i$ with $v^p=a$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$ for $\lambda\in K$; this is exactly the symbol algebra $[c,a)$. By ref. 22 (i), $D$ is a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $p$, and $b\mapsto[(K/k,\tau,b)]$ induces an isomorphism $k^\times/N_{K/k}(K^\times)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }{\rm Br}(K/k)\subseteq {\rm Br}(k)$. Therefore $a\in N_{K/k}(K^\times)$ if and only if $D\cong M_p(k)$. We prove $a\notin N_{K/k}(K^\times)$ by showing that $D$ is a division algebra; for this we construct a valuation on $D$.

**Step 4: The graded ring of $K$.** The associated graded ring of $k$ is $\mathrm{gr}(k)=F[u,u^{-1}]$ with $\deg u=1$. For $x=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}b_jw^j\in K$ ($b_j\in k$) the values $v_K(b_jw^j)=v(b_j)-jn/p$ are pairwise distinct modulo $\mathbb{Z}$ for distinct $j$ (as $p\nmid n$), hence $v_K(x)=\min_j\,(v(b_j)-jn/p)$ (terms whose values differ by a non-integer cannot cancel in the ultrametric inequality). Thus $\{1,w,\dots,w^{p-1}\}$ is an orthogonal basis and $\mathrm{gr}(K)=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}\mathrm{gr}(k)\,\theta^j$ with $\theta={\rm in}(w)$, $\deg\theta=-n/p$, uniquely. Since $v(c)=-n<-n/p=v(w)$, we get $\theta^p={\rm in}(w^p)={\rm in}(c+w)={\rm in}(c)=t\,u^{-n}$. Hence as graded rings
$$\mathrm{gr}(K)\;\cong\;F[u,u^{-1}][\theta]/(\theta^p-t\,u^{-n}).$$

**Step 5: The automorphism $\tau$ is trivial on $\mathrm{gr}(K)$.** For $x=\sum_j b_jw^j\in K$, $\tau(x)-x=\sum_{j\ge1}b_j\big((w+1)^j-w^j\big)$, and $(w+1)^j-w^j=\sum_{l=0}^{j-1}\binom{j}{l}w^l$ has value $(j-1)v_K(w)=-jn/p+n/p$ (the coefficient $j\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}$ is nonzero in $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the values $l\,v_K(w)$ are strictly decreasing in $l$). Therefore $v_K\big(b_j((w+1)^j-w^j)\big)=(v(b_j)-jn/p)+n/p\ge v_K(x)+n/p>v_K(x)$ for every $j$, whence $v_K(\tau(x)-x)>v_K(x)$. So ${\rm in}(\tau(x))={\rm in}(x)$ for all $x$, i.e. the induced automorphism $\bar\tau$ of $\mathrm{gr}(K)$ is the identity.

**Step 6: The graded ring of $D$.** Define, for $x=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}x_iv^i\in D$ with $x_i\in K$, $w_D(x)=\min_i\big(v_K(x_i)+i/p\big)$ and $w_D(0)=\infty$. Note first that $v_K\circ\tau^i=v_K$ (an automorphism over $k$ preserves the unique extension of $v$), and that $v(a)=1=p\cdot(1/p)$, so on monomials
$$w_D\big(x_iv^i\cdot y_jv^j\big)=w_D\big(x_i\tau^i(y_j)v^{i+j}\big)=v_K(x_i)+v_K(y_j)+\tfrac{i+j}{p}=w_D(x_iv^i)+w_D(y_jv^j),$$
using $v^{i+j}=a\,v^{i+j-p}$ with $v(a)=1$ when $i+j\ge p$. Hence $D_{\ge\alpha}D_{\ge\beta}\subseteq D_{\ge\alpha+\beta}$, where $D_{\ge\gamma}=\{x:w_D(x)\ge\gamma\}$, and $\mathrm{gr}(D)=\bigoplus_\gamma D_{\ge\gamma}/D_{>\gamma}$ is a graded ring. Since $D_{\ge\gamma}=\bigoplus_i K_{\ge\gamma-i/p}v^i$ and $D_{>\gamma}=\bigoplus_i K_{>\gamma-i/p}v^i$ hold by the very definition of $w_D$, we get, with $V={\rm in}(v)$ of degree $1/p$,
$$\mathrm{gr}(D)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}\mathrm{gr}(K)\,V^i ,$$
a direct sum of $\mathrm{gr}(k)$-modules, with $V\cdot{\rm in}(\xi)={\rm in}(v\xi)={\rm in}(\xi v)={\rm in}(\tau(\xi))V={\rm in}(\xi)V$ by Step 5 (so $V$ is central) and $V^p={\rm in}(v^p)={\rm in}(a)=u$ (as $a=u+ru^{q+1}$ with $v(u)=1<q+1$). Therefore
$$\mathrm{gr}(D)\;\cong\;F[u,u^{-1}][\theta,V]\big/(\theta^p-t\,u^{-n},\;V^p-u).$$

**Step 7: $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is a domain.** Substituting $u=V^p$: the maps $u\mapsto V^p,\theta\mapsto\theta,V\mapsto V$ and $V\mapsto V,\theta\mapsto\theta,V^{-1}\mapsto V^{p-1}u^{-1}$ (valid since $V^p=u\in D^\times$) are mutually inverse ring isomorphisms
$$\mathrm{gr}(D)\;\cong\;F[V,V^{-1}][\theta]\big/(\theta^p-t\,V^{-pn}).$$
We use the elementary fact: if $A$ is a UFD of characteristic $p$ with fraction field $E$ and $f\in A$ is nonzero, then $X^p-f$ is irreducible in $A[X]$ iff $f\notin A^p$. Indeed, over a closure, $X^p-f=(X-\alpha)^p$ with $\alpha^p=f$; if $\alpha\notin E$, then $E(\alpha)/E$ is purely inseparable of degree $p$ and the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ is $(X-\alpha)^p=X^p-f$, irreducible in $E[X]$ and hence in $A[X]$ by Gauss; if $\alpha\in E$ then $f=\alpha^p\in E^p$, and for $f\in A$ with $A$ a UFD, $f\in E^p$ forces $f\in A^p$ (writing $f=(a/b)^p$ with $a,b\in A$ coprime gives $fb^p=a^p$, so $b^p\mid a^p$, $b\mid a$, $b$ a unit). Here $A=F[V,V^{-1}]$ is a PID, hence a UFD, and $A^p=F^p[V^p,V^{-p}]$. The element $f=t\,V^{-pn}$ is a single Laurent monomial with coefficient $t$; it lies in $A^p$ only if $t\in F^p$. But $t\notin F^p=\mathbb{F}_p(s^p,t^p,r^p)$: if $t=(P/Q)^p$ with $P,Q\in\mathbb{F}_p[s,t,r]$ coprime, then $tQ^p=P^p$, and comparing the $t$-adic valuation of both sides gives $1+p\,v_t(Q)\equiv 0\pmod p$, impossible. Hence $f\notin A^p$, so $\theta^p-tV^{-pn}$ is irreducible in the UFD $A[\theta]$, hence prime, and the quotient $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is a domain.

**Step 8: $w_D$ is a valuation and $D$ is a division ring.** We already have $w_D(x+y)\ge\min(w_D(x),w_D(y))$, $w_D(x)=\infty\Leftrightarrow x=0$, and $w_D(xy)\ge w_D(x)+w_D(y)$. For $x,y\ne0$, the product of initial forms in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ satisfies ${\rm in}(x){\rm in}(y)={\rm in}(xy)$ by definition of the graded product (well defined because of the multiplicativity of the filtration). Since $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is a domain and ${\rm in}(x),{\rm in}(y)\ne0$, we get ${\rm in}(xy)\ne0$, i.e. $w_D(xy)=w_D(x)+w_D(y)$. Thus $w_D$ is a valuation on $D$; in particular $D$ has no zero divisors. A finite-dimensional $k$-algebra without zero divisors is a division ring (left multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective, hence surjective, $k$-linear map). So $D$ is a division algebra of degree $p>1$.

**Step 9: Conclusion.** Since $D$ is a division algebra, $D\not\cong M_p(k)$ (the latter has zero divisors for $p\ge2$), so $[D]\ne0$ in ${\rm Br}(k)$. By the criterion of Step 3, $a\notin N_{K/k}(K^\times)$, i.e.
$$u(1+ru^q)\notin N_{K/k}(K^\times),$$
which is the claim. (Note that the argument uses only $q\ge1$ and $p\nmid n$; the role of $r$ is precisely that $t\notin\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)^p$, and the extra variables $s,r$ enter only through the irreducibility in Step 7.)

lemma_153.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation. Let $m$ be a positive integer with $p\nmid m$, and let $K=k(z)$ where $z^p-z=s\,u^{-m}$. Then $u\notin N_{K/k}(K^{\times})$.
lemma_153.proof:
Let $v$be the $u$-adic valuation on $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)((u))$, normalized by $v(u)=1$, and let $\kappa=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)$ be its residue field. Put $a=s u^{-m}$. Since $v(a)=-m<0$ and $p
mid m$, Lemma lemma_73 gives $a
otin \wp(k)=\{x^p-x:x\in k\}$. Hence $f(T)=T^p-T-a$ has no root in $k$. It is irreducible over $k$: if it had an irreducible factor $g$ of degree $d$ with $1\le d<p$, then for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$ the polynomial $g(T+\lambda)$ is again an irreducible factor of $f$, because $f(T+\lambda)=f(T)$. No nonconstant polynomial of degree $<p$ can be invariant under $T\mapsto T+\lambda$ for $\lambda
e0$ in characteristic $p$, so the $p$ polynomials $g(T+\lambda)$ are distinct; their total degree $pd$ exceeds $p$, impossible. Thus $K=k(z)=k[T]/(f)$ is a field, cyclic of degree $p$ over $k$, with generator $\sigma(z)=z+1$. Claim 1. The formula $w(\sum_{i=0}^{p-1} b_i z^i)=\min_i (v(b_i)-mi/p)$ defines a valuation $w$ on $K$ extending $v$. Proof of Claim 1. On $R=k[T]$ define $
u(\sum b_i T^i)=\min_i(v(b_i)-mi/p)$. This is a Gauss valuation with weight $-m/p$; its associated graded ring is $\mathrm{gr}(k)[Z]$ with $\deg Z=-m/p$, hence a domain. The element $f=T^p-T-a$ has $
u(f)=-m$ and initial form $F=Z^p-sU^{-m}$ in $\mathrm{gr}(k)[Z]$, where $U=\mathrm{in}(u)$ has degree $1$. In the fraction field $\kappa(U)$, $sU^{-m}$ is not a $p$th power, since the $U$-adic valuation is $-m$, not divisible by $p$. Therefore $F$ is irreducible over $\kappa(U)$, hence prime in $\mathrm{gr}(k)[Z]$. Division by $f$ gives a unique remainder of ordinary degree $<p$. Because the images of $1,Z,\ldots,Z^{p-1}$ form a $\mathrm{gr}(k)$-basis of $\mathrm{gr}(k)[Z]/(F)$, the initial form of a nonzero class in $R/(f)$ is represented by the initial form of its remainder. Thus the remainder formula defines a valuation on $K$, and the associated graded ring is $\mathrm{gr}(K)\simeq \kappa[Z,U^{\pm1}]/(Z^p-sU^{-m})$, with $\deg Z=-m/p$, $\deg U=1$. This proves Claim 1. Claim 2. The automorphism $\sigma$ is an isometry of $w$ and acts trivially on $\mathrm{gr}(K)$. Proof of Claim 2. Write $x=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1} b_l z^l$. The numbers $\lambda_l=v(b_l)-ml/p$ are pairwise distinct: if $\lambda_l=\lambda_{l'}$ with $l
e l'$, then $v(b_l)-v(b_{l'})=m(l-l')/p$, an integer equal to a non-integral rational number, impossible because $p
mid m$ and $|l-l'|<p$. Let $l_0$ be the unique index with $\lambda_{l_0}=\min_l\lambda_l$. Expanding $\sigma(x)=\sum_l b_l(z+1)^l=\sum_j c_j z^j$, with $c_j=\sum_{l\ge j} inom{l}{j}b_l$, we have $c_{l_0}=b_{l_0}$ modulo terms of strictly larger $v$-valuation, because for $l>l_0$ the inequality $\lambda_l>\lambda_{l_0}$ implies $v(b_l)>v(b_{l_0})$. For $j
e l_0$, every term in $c_j$ has shifted valuation $v(b_l)-mj/p=(v(b_l)-ml/p)+m(l-j)/p>\lambda_{l_0}$. Hence the minimum defining $w(\sigma(x))$ is again $\lambda_{l_0}$, and the initial form is the same as that of $b_{l_0}z^{l_0}$. Thus $w(\sigma(x))=w(x)$ and $\mathrm{in}(\sigma(x))=\mathrm{in}(x)$. lemma_155.statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, and let $a_1,\dots,a_n\in F^{\times}$ be such that the $p^n$ monomials $\prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i^{e_i}$, with $0\le e_i\le p-1$ for each $i$, are linearly independent over the subfield $F^p$. Then the $F$-algebra $F[X_1,\dots,X_n]/(X_1^p-a_1,\dots,X_n^p-a_n)$ is a field, purely inseparable of degree $p^n$ over $F$.
lemma_155.proof:
We prove the statement exactly as filed, whose hypothesis is **p-independence over F^p** (an ADDITIVE condition), which is strictly stronger than F_p-independence of the classes in F^×/(F^×)^p (a MULTIPLICATIVE condition).

**Remark 0 (relation to the earlier counterexample).** The hypothesis here is genuinely stronger than independence modulo p-th powers, and the previously exhibited example F = F_p(s,t), a_1 = s, a_2 = 1+s does **not** satisfy it: (1+s) - s - 1 = 0 is a non-trivial F^p-linear relation among the monomials {1, s, 1+s, s(1+s)} (the constant 1 lies in F_p ⊂ F^p), i.e. 1+s ∈ F^p(s) = F^p(a_1). Everything below uses only p-independence over F^p, and no claim that A is a domain or reduced is made before the final dimension count.

Notation. char(F) = p > 0; for e = (e_1,...,e_n) ∈ Z_{\ge 0}^n write a^e := ∏_{i=1}^n a_i^{e_i} and, in an extension, x^e := ∏ x_i^{e_i}. Hypothesis (H): the p^n elements a^e, 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1, are linearly independent over F^p. Note that (H) passes to subfamilies; in particular, for each m ≤ n the p^m monomials in a_1,...,a_m with exponents in [0,p-1] are linearly independent over F^p (take those with e_i = 0 for i > m).

=====================================================================
PART I. p-independent families and the fields F^p(a_1,...,a_m).

Lemma 1.1. For each m = 0,1,...,n the ring F^p[a_1,...,a_m] is a field, equal to F^p(a_1,...,a_m), and is spanned over F^p by the p^m monomials a^e with 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1 for i ≤ m. Consequently (H) is equivalent to [F^p(a_1,...,a_m):F^p] = p^m (and these monomials then form an F^p-basis).

Proof. Each a_i ∈ F^× satisfies T^p - a_i^p ∈ F^p[T], since a_i^p ∈ F^p; hence a_i is integral (purely inseparable of exponent ≤ 1) over F^p. Inducting on m: if R_{m-1} := F^p[a_1,...,a_{m-1}] is a field, then R_m = R_{m-1}[a_m] = R_{m-1}(a_m) is a field because a_m is algebraic over R_{m-1}. So F^p[a_1,...,a_m] is a field containing F^p and all a_i, hence equal to F^p(a_1,...,a_m). For the spanning claim: every element is a polynomial in a_1,...,a_m with coefficients in F^p, and any monomial with exponent e_i ≥ p factors as a_i^{e_i} = (a_i^p)·a_i^{e_i-p} with a_i^p ∈ F^p; iterating reduces all exponents to [0,p-1]. Thus the p^m monomials span F^p(a_1,...,a_m) over F^p, so [F^p(a_1,...,a_m):F^p] ≤ p^m, with equality iff the spanning set is linearly independent. Under (H) the relevant subfamily is independent, giving [F^p(a_1,...,a_m):F^p] = p^m; the converse is immediate since a spanning set of cardinality equal to the degree is a basis. ∎

=====================================================================
PART II. The purely inseparable tower has degree p^n.

Fix an algebraic closure Ω ⊇ F. For each i choose x_i ∈ Ω with x_i^p = a_i (there is exactly one such root in Ω, since T^p - a_i = (T - x_i)^p). Put K_0 := F and K_m := F(x_1,...,x_m) ⊂ Ω for m ≥ 1.

Claim. For every m = 0,...,n: [K_m : F] = p^m, and the set B_m := {x^e : 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1 for i ≤ m, e_i = 0 for i > m} is an F-basis of K_m.

Proof by induction on m. m = 0: K_0 = F and B_0 = {1}. Inductive step: assume the claim for m-1 (m ≥ 1).

(a) K_{m-1}^p = F^p(a_1,...,a_{m-1}). Indeed, every element of K_{m-1} = F(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) has the form h(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) with h ∈ F(T_1,...,T_{m-1}) a rational function; writing h = P/Q with P,Q ∈ F[T_1,...,T_{m-1}], raising to the p-th power gives (P/Q)^p(x) = P^{(p)}(a_1,...,a_{m-1})/Q^{(p)}(a_1,...,a_{m-1}), where P^{(p)} is obtained by raising the coefficients of P to the p-th power (they land in F^p) and using x_i^{p·α_i} = a_i^{α_i}. Thus K_{m-1}^p ⊆ F^p(a_1,...,a_{m-1}). Conversely F^p ⊆ K_{m-1}^p because every c ∈ F^p is d^p with d ∈ F ⊆ K_{m-1}, and a_i = x_i^p ∈ K_{m-1}^p for i ≤ m-1; hence F^p(a_1,...,a_{m-1}) ⊆ K_{m-1}^p.

(b) x_m ∉ K_{m-1}. Suppose x_m ∈ K_{m-1}. Then a_m = x_m^p ∈ K_{m-1}^p = F^p(a_1,...,a_{m-1}). By Lemma 1.1 (applied to m-1), F^p(a_1,...,a_{m-1}) is the F^p-span of the monomials a_1^{e_1}···a_{m-1}^{e_{m-1}} with 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1, so a_m = Σ_{e'} c_{e'} a_1^{e_1}···a_{m-1}^{e_{m-1}} with c_{e'} ∈ F^p. Hence 1·a_m - Σ_{e'} c_{e'} a_1^{e_1}···a_{m-1}^{e_{m-1}}·a_m^0 = 0 is a non-trivial F^p-linear relation among the monomials a_1^{e_1}···a_m^{e_m} with 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1 (the coefficient of a_m = a_m^1 is 1 ≠ 0, and no other monomial occurring equals a_m). This contradicts (H) restricted to that subfamily. Hence x_m ∉ K_{m-1}.

(c) [K_m : K_{m-1}] = p. Over Ω we have T^p - a_m = T^p - x_m^p = (T - x_m)^p, so the minimal polynomial μ ∈ K_{m-1}[T] of x_m satisfies μ = (T - x_m)^d for some integer d with 1 ≤ d ≤ p. By (b), d ≥ 2. If d ≤ p-1, then the coefficient of T^{d-1} in μ is -d·x_m ∈ K_{m-1}; but d is an integer with 1 ≤ d ≤ p-1, so d ∈ F_p^× ⊂ F^× ⊂ K_{m-1}^×, and therefore x_m = -(coefficient)/d ∈ K_{m-1}, contradicting (b). Thus d = p, μ = T^p - a_m, and [K_m : K_{m-1}] = p with basis {1, x_m, ..., x_m^{p-1}}.

(d) Conclusion of the induction. [K_m:F] = [K_m:K_{m-1}]·[K_{m-1}:F] = p·p^{m-1} = p^m. Since K_m = K_{m-1}(x_m), every element is Σ_{e_m=0}^{p-1} b_{e_m} x_m^{e_m} with b_{e_m} ∈ K_{m-1}, and expanding each b_{e_m} in the inductive basis B_{m-1} shows B_m spans K_m over F. Linear independence is the standard tower-basis fact: if Σ_{e_m} (Σ_{e'} λ_{e',e_m} b_{e'}) x_m^{e_m} = 0 with b_{e'} ∈ B_{m-1}, then Σ_{e'} λ_{e',e_m} b_{e'} = 0 for each e_m by independence of {1,...,x_m^{p-1}} over K_{m-1}, and then all λ_{e',e_m} = 0 by independence of B_{m-1} over F. ∎

Taking m = n: [K_n : F] = p^n, with F-basis B_n = {x^e : 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1}.

=====================================================================
PART III. Identification of A with K_n.

Let R = F[X_1,...,X_n], f_i = X_i^p - a_i, I = (f_1,...,f_n), A = R/I; write x̄_i for the class of X_i.

(1) dim_F A ≤ p^n. We show R = I + span_F{X^e : 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1}, by induction on n. For n = 1 this is the division algorithm by the monic polynomial f_1: P = Q f_1 + r with deg r < p. For the step, view R = F[X_1][X_2,...,X_n]; since f_1 is monic in X_1, dividing P ∈ R by f_1 as a polynomial in X_1 with coefficients in F[X_2,...,X_n] gives P = Q f_1 + Σ_{e_1=0}^{p-1} X_1^{e_1} P_{e_1} with P_{e_1} ∈ F[X_2,...,X_n]. By the induction hypothesis applied to F[X_2,...,X_n]/(f_2,...,f_n), each P_{e_1} is congruent modulo (f_2,...,X_n-relations) to an F-linear combination of X_2^{e_2}···X_n^{e_n}, 0 ≤ e_i ≤ p-1. Hence P ≡ Σ_e c_e X^e mod I, proving the claim and dim_F A ≤ p^n.

(2) The evaluation map. Define Φ: R → K_n by X_i ↦ x_i (an F-algebra homomorphism). It is surjective because K_n = F(x_1,...,x_n). Moreover Φ(f_i) = x_i^p - a_i = 0 for all i, so I ⊆ ker Φ and Φ descends to a surjective F-algebra homomorphism φ: A ↠ K_n with φ(x̄_i) = x_i.

(3) φ is an isomorphism. φ is a surjective F-linear map, so dim_F A ≥ dim_F K_n = p^n by Part II. Combined with (1), dim_F A = p^n = dim_F K_n, and a surjective linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces of equal dimension is bijective. Hence φ is a bijective ring homomorphism: A ≅ K_n as F-algebras. In particular A is a field (and I is a maximal ideal of R); the nonzero nilpotents that occur when (H) fails cannot occur here because the dimension count forces φ to be injective.

=====================================================================
PART IV. Purely inseparability and degree.

Each x_i ∈ Ω satisfies x_i^p = a_i ∈ F, so x_i is purely inseparable over F (its minimal polynomial divides T^p - a_i = (T-x_i)^p, hence equals T^{p^r} - c for some r ≤ 1 and has the single root x_i).
