The set of elements of Ω that are purely inseparable over F is a subfield: if u^{p^r} ∈ F and v^{p^s} ∈ F and t = max(r,s), then (u ± v)^{p^t} = u^{p^t} ± v^{p^t} ∈ F, (uv)^{p^t} ∈ F, and (u^{-1})^{p^t} = (u^{p^t})^{-1} ∈ F for u ≠ 0. Hence K_n = F(x_1,...,x_n) is purely inseparable over F. Its degree is [K_n:F] = p^n by Part II. Via the isomorphism A ≅ K_n of Part III, A is a field, purely inseparable of degree p^n over F. This proves the lemma. ∎

=====================================================================
PART V. Auxiliary criterion used downstream (proved here for completeness).

Let k be perfect and F = k(u_1,...,u_m); then F^p = k(u_1^p,...,u_m^p) (perfectness gives k = k^p). We verify that for distinct indices, after renaming them 1,...,n, the p^n monomials u_1^{e_1}···u_n^{e_n}, 0 ≤ e_j ≤ p-1, are linearly independent over F^p; the lemma then applies with a_j = u_j and shows F[X_1,...,X_n]/(X_1^p-u_1,...,X_n^p-u_n) is a field of degree p^n over F.

It suffices to show by induction on r that the monomials u_1^{e_1}···u_r^{e_r}, 0 ≤ e_j ≤ p-1, are independent over F_0 := k(u_1^p,...,u_m^p) = F^p. The case r = 0 is trivial. Suppose Σ_{e=0}^{p-1} c_e u_r^e = 0 with c_e ∈ F_0(u_1,...,u_{r-1}). Write each c_e = A_e/B with A_e, B ∈ k[u_1^p,...,u_m^p, u_1,...,u_{r-1}], B ≠ 0 (common denominator). Then Σ_{e=0}^{p-1} A_e·u_r^e = 0 in k[u_1,...,u_m]. Each A_e involves u_r only through u_r^p, so A_e = Ã_e(u_1,...,u_{r-1}, u_r^p, u_{r+1}^p,...,u_m^p) = Σ_j d_{e,j} u_r^{pj} with d_{e,j} ∈ k[u_1,...,u_{r-1}, u_{r+1}^p,...,u_m^p]. Substituting, Σ_{e,j} d_{e,j} u_r^{pj+e} = 0 in a polynomial ring over the domain k[u_1,...,u_{r-1},u_{r+1}^p,...,u_m^p]. Since 0 ≤ e ≤ p-1, the integers pj + e are pairwise distinct for distinct pairs (e,j) (division algorithm by p), so each d_{e,j} = 0. Hence every A_e = 0 and every c_e = 0, establishing independence. ∎

Summary: the corrected hypothesis (linear independence over F^p of the p^n monomials, equivalently [F^p(a_1,...,a_n):F^p] = p^n) makes each T^p - a_m irreducible over the partial field K_{m-1}, giving [K_n:F] = p^n; the surjection A ↠ K_n together with dim_F A ≤ p^n then forces A ≅ K_n, a purely inseparable field extension of degree p^n.

lemma_157.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, and write $\wp(F)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in F\}$ for a field $F$ of characteristic $p$. For $c\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ and $z\in k^{\times}$, let $[c,z)$ denote the class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ of the cyclic $k$-algebra $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}k(w)v^{i}$ where $w^{p}-w=c$, $v^{p}=z$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in k(w)$, with $\tau(w)=w+1$. Then every element of $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ annihilated by $p$ is a finite sum of classes $[c_i,z_i)$ with $c_i\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ and $z_i\in k^{\times}$.
lemma_157.proof:
We write the Brauer group additively. Throughout, char(k) = p > 0 and wp(F) = {x^p - x : x in F} for a field F of characteristic p.

STEP 0 (Auxiliary notation for symbols with arbitrary first entry). For a \in k and b \in k^{\times}, put f_a(T) = T^p - T - a \in k[T] and let L_a = k[T]/(f_a) be the etale k-algebra of rank p, with \tau_a the k-automorphism induced by T \mapsto T + 1. This is well defined because (T+1)^p - (T+1) = T^p + 1 - T - 1 = T^p - T, so f_a(T+1) = f_a(T) \in (f_a); the inverse automorphism is induced by T \mapsto T - 1, so \tau_a is indeed an automorphism, and \tau_a^j is induced by T \mapsto T + j, hence \tau_a has exact order p. By ref_17, the cyclic algebra S(a,b) := (L_a, \tau_a, b) is a central simple k-algebra of degree p (a "symbol algebra"), that L_a is a field if and only if a \notin wp(k), and that S(a,b) is split whenever a \in wp(k) [ref_17(iii)]. Write \langle a,b\rangle \in Br(k) for the class of S(a,b). The statement of the lemma asks us to express classes of the form [c,z), which is precisely \langle c,z\rangle when c \notin wp(k) (so that L_c = k(w) is a field): this identification is carried out in Step 3.

STEP 1 (Reduction of beta to an integral combination of symbols). Let \beta \in Br(k) with p\beta = 0, i.e. \beta \in Br(k)[p]. By the Albert--Teichm\"uller theorem, ref_18, the p-torsion subgroup Br(k)[p] is generated (as an abelian group) by the classes of the symbol algebras \langle a,b\rangle with a \in k, b \in k^{\times}. Hence there exist r \ge 0, integers n_1,\dots,n_r \in \mathbb{Z}, and elements a_1,\dots,a_r \in k, b_1,\dots,b_r \in k^{\times} with
    \beta = \sum_{i=1}^{r} n_i \langle a_i, b_i\rangle .

STEP 2 (Every symbol class is annihilated by p; reduction of the coefficients mod p). Fix i.
(a) If a_i \in wp(k), then \langle a_i,b_i\rangle = 0 by ref_17(iii), so certainly p\langle a_i,b_i\rangle = 0.
(b) Suppose a_i \notin wp(k). Then L := L_{a_i} is a field by ref_17, of degree p over k. Its automorphism \tau = \tau_{a_i} has exact order p (Step 0), so |Gal(L/k)| \ge p = [L:k]; thus L/k is Galois with Gal(L/k) = \langle\tau\rangle. By ref_22(i), (L,\tau,b) is a cyclic algebra, and by ref_22(ii) the map b \mapsto [(L,\tau,b)] is additive in b, so iterating gives
    p\,\langle a_i,b_i\rangle = p\,[(L,\tau,b_i)] = [(L,\tau,b_i^{p})].
Since b_i \in k^{\times} and L/k is a field extension of degree p, multiplication by b_i on the p-dimensional k-vector space L has determinant b_i^{p}, i.e. N_{L/k}(b_i) = b_i^{p}. Thus b_i^p \in N_{L/k}(L^{\times}), and by ref_22(i) (b \mapsto [(L,\tau,b)] induces an isomorphism k^{\times}/N_{L/k}(L^{\times}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Br(L/k)) we get [(L,\tau,b_i^{p})] = 0. Hence p\,\langle a_i,b_i\rangle = 0 in this case as well.
Combining (a) and (b), every symbol class appearing in Step 1 is killed by p. Write n_i = q_i p + m_i with m_i \in \{0,1,\dots,p-1\}; then n_i\langle a_i,b_i\rangle = m_i\langle a_i,b_i\rangle, and m_i\langle a_i,b_i\rangle is either 0 (if m_i = 0) or a sum of m_i copies of \langle a_i,b_i\rangle. Therefore
    \beta = \sum_{j=1}^{s} \langle \alpha_j, \gamma_j\rangle
for some s \ge 0, with \alpha_j \in k and \gamma_j \in k^{\times} (the terms with m_i = 0 simply being omitted; repetitions are allowed). If s = 0 then \beta = 0.

STEP 3 (Each surviving symbol is of the required form). Fix j \in \{1,\dots,s\}.
(a) If \alpha_j \in wp(k), then \langle\alpha_j,\gamma_j\rangle = 0 by ref_17(iii); delete this term from the sum (this only decreases s).
(b) Suppose \alpha_j \notin wp(k). We first prove directly that f_{\alpha_j}(T) = T^p - T - \alpha_j is irreducible over k. Let w denote the residue class of T in L = L_{\alpha_j}; then w^p - w = \alpha_j, and the p elements w, w+1, \dots, w+(p-1) are pairwise distinct roots of f_{\alpha_j} in L, since (w+j)^p - (w+j) = w^p - w = \alpha_j. As deg f_{\alpha_j} = p, these are all the roots, so f_{\alpha_j} splits completely in L. If f_{\alpha_j} had a proper factor over k, it would have a monic irreducible factor g of degree d with 1 \le d \le p-1; in L we would have g(T) = \prod_{j \in J}(T - (w+j)) for a subset J \subset \{0,\dots,p-1\} of cardinality d, and comparing the coefficient of T^{d-1} gives \sum_{j \in J}(w+j) = d\,w + \sum_{j \in J} j \in k. Since 1 \le d \le p-1, d is invertible in k, so w \in k, whence \alpha_j = w^p - w \in wp(k), a contradiction. Hence f_{\alpha_j} is irreducible, [k(w):k] = p, and L_{\alpha_j} = k[w] = k(w) is a field (consistent with ref_17).
Now S(\alpha_j,\gamma_j) = (k(w)/k, \tau, \gamma_j) with \tau(w) = w+1. By ref_22(i), this cyclic algebra is the k-vector space \bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1} k(w)\,v^{i} with v^{p} = \gamma_j and v\lambda = \tau(\lambda)v for all \lambda \in k(w); indeed the algebra generated by u, v subject to u^p - u = \alpha_j, v^p = \gamma_j and vu = (u+1)v has every element of k[u] commuting with k and satisfies v\,P(u) = P(u+1)\,v for all P \in k[T] (immediate for P = T and then by k-linearity and multiplicativity), which is exactly v\lambda = \tau(\lambda)v for \lambda \in k[u] = k(w). Thus the class \langle\alpha_j,\gamma_j\rangle is precisely the class denoted [c,z) in the statement, with c = \alpha_j \in k \setminus wp(k) and z = \gamma_j \in k^{\times}.

STEP 4 (Conclusion). After Step 3, the sum from Step 2 has the form
    \beta = \sum_{j \in J} [c_j, z_j),
c_j \in k \setminus wp(k), z_j \in k^{\times}, J a finite index set, which is what was to be shown.

STEP 5 (Edge cases). (i) If J = \emptyset the right side is the empty sum, equal to 0 = \beta; this is the only possible form of the assertion when k \setminus wp(k) = \emptyset. Indeed, if wp(k) = k then Step 3(a) shows every symbol class \langle a,b\rangle is 0, so by Steps 1--2 Br(k)[p] = \{0\}, and the unique element 0 is the empty sum; in that situation there are simply no admissible pairs (c,z) with c \in k \setminus wp(k), so the empty sum is the only expression available, and it is correct.
(ii) If k \setminus wp(k) \neq \emptyset and \beta = 0, one may also write 0 non-trivially: take any c \in k \setminus wp(k); then 1 = N_{k(w)/k}(1) lies in the norm group N_{k(w)/k}(k(w)^{\times}), so [c,1) = 0 by ref_22(i) (equivalently by the norm-splitting criterion of ref_17(iii)). Thus 0 is a (non-empty) sum of allowed symbols as well.
This completes the proof that every element of Br(k) annihilated by p is a finite sum of classes [c_i, z_i) with c_i \in k \setminus wp(k) and z_i \in k^{\times}.

lemma_158.statement: Let $p>2$ be a prime and let $S=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)[U^{\pm 1}]$ be the Laurent polynomial ring over the rational function field in three variables over $\mathbb{F}_p$. Then the commutative $S$-algebra $S[X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-sU^{1-p},\;Z^{p}-tU,\;W^{p}-rU^{1-p},\;Y^{p}-U)$ is a domain.
lemma_158.proof:
Write $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)$, $S=k[U^{\pm 1}]$, $F=k(U)=\operatorname{Frac}(S)$, and $K:=F^{p}=\mathbb{F}_p(s^{p},t^{p},r^{p},U^{p})$ (every element of $F=F_p(s,t,r,U)$ is a $p$-th power of an element of $F$, so $F^p$ is exactly the field generated by the $p$-th powers of $s,t,r,U$). Put
$$f_1=sU^{1-p},\quad f_2=tU,\quad f_3=rU^{1-p},\quad f_4=U,$$
all of which lie in $S^{\times}\subset F^{\times}$, and let
$$R=S[X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-f_1,\;Z^{p}-f_2,\;W^{p}-f_3,\;Y^{p}-f_4)$$
be the algebra of the statement. We prove $R$ is a domain by showing that $R$ is $S$-free and that its generic fibre $R\otimes_S F$ is a field.

**Step 1: $R$ is a free $S$-module of rank $p^{4}$.** Set $A_0=S$ and successively $A_1=A_0[X]/(X^{p}-f_1)$, $A_2=A_1[Z]/(Z^{p}-f_2)$, $A_3=A_2[W]/(W^{p}-f_3)$, $A_4=A_3[Y]/(Y^{p}-f_4)$. Each $f_i$ lies in $S\subset A_{i-1}$, and each polynomial $T^{p}-f_i$ is monic of degree $p$ in the indicated variable; division by a monic polynomial shows that $A_i$ is a free $A_{i-1}$-module with basis $1,T,\dots,T^{p-1}$. By transitivity of freeness, $A_4$ is a free $S$-module with basis
$$\mathcal{B}_0=\{X^{a}Z^{b}W^{c}Y^{d}:0\le a,b,c,d\le p-1\},$$
and by the successive-quotient identification $A_4\cong R$. In particular $R\neq 0$ and $R\cong S^{p^4}$ as $S$-module.

**Step 2: $R$ embeds in its generic fibre.** $S=k[U^{\pm1}]$ is a domain (a Laurent polynomial ring over the field $k$) with fraction field $F$, so $S\to F$ is injective. Since $R$ is $S$-free by Step 1, the canonical map
$$\iota:R=\textstyle\bigoplus_{m\in\mathcal B_0}S\cdot m\longrightarrow R\otimes_S F=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathcal B_0}F\cdot m$$
is componentwise the inclusion $S\hookrightarrow F$, hence injective.

**Step 3: the generic fibre.** Base change of a polynomial ring and of a quotient gives
$$R\otimes_S F\;\cong\;F[X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-f_1,\;Z^{p}-f_2,\;W^{p}-f_3,\;Y^{p}-f_4).\qquad(\ast)$$

**Step 4: an explicit $K=F^{p}$-basis of $F$.** Let
$$\mathcal{B}=\{\,s^{a}t^{b}r^{c}U^{\delta}:0\le a,b,c,\delta\le p-1\,\}.$$
We claim $\mathcal B$ is a $K$-basis of $F$.

*Spanning.* Let $V:=K[\textstyle\sum_{m\in\mathcal B}K\cdot m]=K[s,t,r,U]$, the $K$-span of $\mathcal B$. Then $V$ is a ring: for $m=s^{a}t^{b}r^{c}U^{\delta}$ and $m'=s^{a'}t^{b'}r^{c'}U^{\delta'}$ in $\mathcal B$ we have $0\le a+a'\le 2p-2$, so $a+a'=\theta_a p+\bar a$ with $\theta_a\in\{0,1\}$ and $0\le\bar a\le p-1$ (likewise for $b+b',c+c',\delta+\delta'$), and therefore $mm'=(s^{p})^{\theta_a}(t^{p})^{\theta_b}(r^{p})^{\theta_c}(U^{p})^{\theta_\delta}\cdot s^{\bar a}t^{\bar b}r^{\bar c}U^{\bar\delta}\in K\cdot\mathcal B$, using $s^{p},t^{p},r^{p},U^{p}\in K$. Now any element of $F=\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb{F}_p[s,t,r,U]$ is $P/Q$ with $P,Q\in\mathbb{F}_p[s,t,r,U]$, $Q\ne0$; expanding each monomial of $P$ and $Q$ as (an element of $\mathbb{F}_p[s^{p},t^{p},r^{p},U^{p}]\subset K$) times an element of $\mathcal B$ shows $P,Q\in V$. Since $V$ is a ring, $Q^{p-1}\in V$, so $PQ^{p-1}\in V$; and since $V/K$ has exponent one ($m^{p}=s^{pa}t^{pb}r^{pc}U^{p\delta}\in K$ for $m\in\mathcal B$, and $K$ is closed under $p$-th powers), $Q^{p}=\sum_m c_m^{p}m^{p}\in K^{\times}$. Thus $P/Q=(PQ^{p-1})/Q^{p}\in V$. So $\mathcal B$ spans $F$ over $K$.

*Independence.* Suppose $\sum_{m\in\mathcal B}\lambda_m\,m=0$ with $\lambda_m\in K$, finitely many nonzero. Writing $\lambda_m=P_m/R_m$ with $P_m,R_m\in\mathbb{F}_p[s^{p},t^{p},r^{p},U^{p}]=:K_0$ and setting $Q=\prod_m R_m\in K_0\setminus\{0\}$, we obtain $\sum_m(\lambda_mQ)\,m=0$ with all $\lambda_mQ\in K_0$. Each nonzero $\lambda_mQ$ is an $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear combination of monomials $s^{\alpha}t^{\beta}r^{\gamma}U^{\varepsilon}$ with $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\varepsilon)\equiv(a,b,c,\delta)\pmod p$ for the corresponding $m=s^{a}t^{b}r^{c}U^{\delta}$; distinct elements of $\mathcal B$ have distinct residue quadruples, hence contribute disjoint sets of monomials of the polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_p[s,t,r,U]$. Monomials are $\mathbb{F}_p$-linearly independent in a polynomial ring, so each $\lambda_mQ=0$, whence $\lambda_m=0$ for all $m$.

**Step 5: the $p^{4}$ monomials in the $f_i$ are $K$-linearly independent.** For $e=(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}^{4}$ set
$$m_e:=f_1^{e_1}f_2^{e_2}f_3^{e_3}f_4^{e_4}=s^{e_1}t^{e_2}r^{e_3}\,U^{\,n(e)},\qquad n(e):=(1-p)e_1+e_2+(1-p)e_3+e_4 .$$
Divide: $n(e)=p\,q(e)+\delta(e)$ with $q(e)\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $0\le\delta(e)\le p-1$. Then
$$m_e=\big(U^{q(e)}\big)^{p}\cdot s^{e_1}t^{e_2}r^{e_3}U^{\delta(e)},\qquad \big(U^{q(e)}\big)^{p}=U^{p\,q(e)}\in F^{p}=K^{\times},$$
so $m_e$ is a **nonzero $K$-scalar multiple** of the basis element $b(e):=s^{e_1}t^{e_2}r^{e_3}U^{\delta(e)}\in\mathcal B$ (Step 4 applies since $0\le e_i,\delta(e)\le p-1$). We check that $e\mapsto b(e)$ is injective: since $1-p\equiv1\pmod p$, we have $\delta(e)\equiv n(e)\equiv e_1+e_2+e_3+e_4\pmod p$. If $b(e)=b(e')$, then $e_i=e_i'$ for $i=1,2,3$ by uniqueness of the exponent tuple of a basis element, and $\delta(e)=\delta(e')$ gives $e_4\equiv e_4'\pmod p$; as both lie in $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$, $e_4=e_4'$. Hence $\{m_e\}$ is a family of nonzero $K$-multiples of **distinct** elements of the $K$-basis $\mathcal B$, and is therefore $K$-linearly independent.

**Step 6: the generic fibre is a field.** $F$ has characteristic $p>0$ and $f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4\in F^{\times}$, and Step 5 says the $p^{4}$ monomials $\prod_{i=1}^{4}f_i^{e_i}$, $0\le e_i\le p-1$, are linearly independent over $F^{p}$. By lemma_155 (Spark) applied with $n=4$, the $F$-algebra $F[X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-f_1,Z^{p}-f_2,W^{p}-f_3,Y^{p}-f_4)$ is a field (purely inseparable of degree $p^{4}$ over $F$). By the isomorphism $(\ast)$ of Step 3, $R\otimes_S F$ is a field.

**Step 7: conclusion.** By Step 2 the ring $R$ embeds (as a unital subring, since $\iota(1)=1\ne0$, the target being nonzero by Step 1) into the field $R\otimes_S F$. Any commutative unital subring of a field is a domain: if $a,b\in R$ with $ab=0$, then $\iota(a)\iota(b)=0$ in the field forces $\iota(a)=0$ or $\iota(b)=0$, hence $a=0$ or $b=0$ by injectivity. Therefore
$$\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)[U^{\pm1}][X,Z,W,Y]\big/\big(X^{p}-sU^{1-p},\;Z^{p}-tU,\;W^{p}-rU^{1-p},\;Y^{p}-U\big)$$
is a domain. $\blacksquare$

lemma_as_element_p_rank_one.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ such that $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\big(k/\wp(k)\big)\le 1$, where $\wp(k)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in k\}$. Then every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p$ contains an element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$.
lemma_as_element_p_rank_one.proof:
Let wp(x)=x^p-x. The map wp is F_p-linear, since (x+y)^p-(x+y)=wp(x)+wp(y) and (λx)^p-λx=λ wp(x) for λ∈F_p. Hence k/wp(k) is an F_p-vector space. We use additive notation in Br(k).

First we prove a general claim. Claim: if A is a central simple k-algebra split by a finite separable extension L/k of degree n, then n[A]=0 in Br(k). Proof of the claim: Let N/k be a finite Galois extension containing L, put G=Gal(N/k) and H=Gal(N/L). Then [G:H]=[L:k]=n. The relative Brauer group Br(N/k) is canonically isomorphic to H^2(G,N^×). Briefly, if A is split by N, choose an N-isomorphism θ:A_N≅M_r(N). For σ∈G, the automorphism θ∘σ(θ^{-1}) of M_r(N) is inner, say Int(u_σ). Then u_σ u_τ=c(σ,τ)u_{στ} defines a 2-cocycle c∈Z^2(G,N^×), and changing the choices changes c by a coboundary; conversely, a 2-cocycle gives a crossed product algebra split by N.

Under this identification, the class α of A restricts to 0 in H^2(H,N^×), because A is already split by L. For finite groups and a G-module M, the corestriction map cor:H^2(H,M)→H^2(G,M) satisfies cor∘res=[G:H]id. This standard identity follows from the adjunction between restriction and coinduction: Shapiro's lemma identifies H^*(H,M) with H^*(G,Coind_H^G M), the corestriction is induced by the norm counit Coind_H^G M→M, and the composite of the adjunction unit M→Coind_H^G M with this norm is multiplication by [G:H]; passing to cohomology gives the identity. Equivalently, on the normalized bar resolution the corestriction is summation over a transversal, and the composite with restriction is the sum of [G:H] identical terms. Applying this with M=N^× gives nα=cor(0)=0, hence n[A]=0. This proves the claim.

Now let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p. By ref_16, D contains a maximal subfield L/k that is separable. Since L is a maximal subfield, ref_5 implies that L splits D. Applying the claim with n=p gives p[D]=0.

Case 1: dim_{F_p}(k/wp(k))=0. Then wp(k)=k. Since p[D]=0, [D] lies in Br(k)[p]. By ref_18, Br(k)[p] is generated by symbol classes [c,z). For every c∈k we have c∈wp(k), and lemma_100 gives [c,z)=0. Hence every element of Br(k)[p] is zero, so [D]=0. But a split central simple algebra of degree p is M_p(k), not a division algebra of degree p>1. Contradiction. Thus no such D exists, and the assertion is vacuous in this case.

Case 2: dim_{F_p}(k/wp(k))=1. Choose c_0∈k whose class is an F_p-basis of k/wp(k). Then c_0∉wp(k). For every c∈k there is a unique λ(c)∈F_p such that c-λ(c)c_0∈wp(k).

Let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p. As above, p[D]=0. By ref_18, [D] is a finite sum of symbol classes, say [D]=Σ_i [c_i,z_i) with z_i∈k^×. Put λ_i=λ(c_i). Using lemma_100, we have
[c_i,z_i)=[λ_i c_0,z_i)+[c_i-λ_i c_0,z_i)=[λ_i c_0,z_i),
since c_i-λ_i c_0∈wp(k). Also lemma_100 gives [λ_i c_0,z_i)=λ_i[c_0,z_i). If λ_i=0, this term is 0=[c_0,1); if λ_i>0, additivity in the second variable gives λ_i[c_0,z_i)=[c_0,z_i^{λ_i}). Hence [c_i,z_i)=[c_0,z_i^{λ_i}). Therefore
[D]=Σ_i [c_0,z_i^{λ_i})=[c_0,z],
where z=∏_i z_i^{λ_i}∈k^×.

Since D is a division algebra, [D]≠0. The class [D] is nonzero and killed by p, and we have written it as [c_0,z) with c_0∉wp(k). By lemma_symbol_iff_cyclic_degree_p, D contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p. Finally, lemma_deg_p_galois_maxfield_iff_as, (i) implies (ii), gives an element a∈D with a∉k and a^p-a∈k.

Thus in all cases, every central division k-algebra of degree p contains the required Artin-Schreier element.

lemma_159.statement: Let $p>2$ and let $k=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation $v$. For $c\in k$ and $z\in k^{\times}$ write $[c,z)$ for the $k$-algebra $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}k(x)y^{i}$ with $x^{p}-x=c$, $y^{p}=z$ and $yx=(x+1)y$, and let $D=[su^{1-p},1+tu)\otimes_k[ru^{1-p},u)$, with standard generators $x_1,y_1$ of the first factor and $x_2,y_2$ of the second. Then $D$ admits a valuation $w$ extending $v$ with $w(x_1)=w(x_2)=\frac{1-p}{p}$ and $w(y_1-1)=w(y_2)=\frac{1}{p}$, and $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is isomorphic as a graded $\mathrm{gr}(k)$-algebra, via $\mathrm{in}_w(x_1)\mapsto X$, $\mathrm{in}_w(y_1-1)\mapsto Z$, $\mathrm{in}_w(x_2)\mapsto W$, $\mathrm{in}_w(y_2)\mapsto Y$, to $\mathrm{gr}(k)[X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-\mathrm{in}_w(su^{1-p}),Z^{p}-\mathrm{in}_w(tu),W^{p}-\mathrm{in}_w(ru^{1-p}),Y^{p}-\mathrm{in}_w(u))$.
lemma_159.proof:
Throughout, $K_0=\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)$, so $k=K_0((u))$ and $v$ is the $u$-adic valuation, normalized by $v(u)=1$; $v$ is surjective onto $\mathbb{Z}$, its valuation ring is $\mathcal{O}_v=K_0[[u]]$, and its residue field is $K_0$. Put
$$a_1=su^{1-p},\quad b_1=1+tu,\quad a_2=ru^{1-p},\quad b_2=u,\qquad \alpha=\tfrac{1-p}{p},\ \beta=\tfrac1p,\ \Gamma=\tfrac1p\mathbb{Z}.$$
The numerical facts we use repeatedly are:
(1) $p\alpha=1-p$ and $p\beta=1$;
(2) $\alpha>1-p$, since $\alpha-(1-p)=\frac{1-p}{p}-(1-p)=\frac{(1-p)^2}{p}>0$;
(3) $\beta>0$ and $\alpha<0$, hence $\beta>\alpha+\beta$;
(4) $\alpha+\beta=\frac{2-p}{p}<0$ because $p>2$, and $0>\alpha+\beta$.

**Step 1. The graded ring $\mathrm{gr}(k)$.** For $a\in k^\times$ write $\bar a$ for the residue of $a\,u^{-v(a)}\in\mathcal{O}_v^\times$ in $K_0^\times$. Since $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathrm{gr}(k)=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}u^n\mathcal{O}_v/u^{n+1}\mathcal{O}_v$ and $a\mapsto \bar a\,U^{v(a)}$ is an isomorphism of graded rings $\mathrm{gr}(k)\simeq K_0[U,U^{-1}]$ with $\deg U=1$; indeed each graded piece $u^n\mathcal{O}_v/u^{n+1}\mathcal{O}_v$ is the $K_0$-line $\bar a\,U^n$, and $\mathrm{in}(ab)=\mathrm{in}(a)\mathrm{in}(b)$ holds because $v$ is a valuation. Since $s,t,r\in K_0^\times$ have $v=0$, we get
$$\mathrm{in}(su^{1-p})=sU^{1-p},\quad \mathrm{in}(tu)=tU,\quad \mathrm{in}(ru^{1-p})=rU^{1-p},\quad \mathrm{in}(u)=U. \tag{1.1}$$

**Step 2. Generators and relations in $D$.** By the definition quoted in the statement, $A_1=[a_1,b_1)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}k(x_1)y_1^{i}$ with $x_1^p-x_1=a_1$, $y_1^p=b_1$, $y_1x_1=(x_1+1)y_1$, and $A_2=[a_2,b_2)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}k(x_2)y_2^{i}$ with $x_2^p-x_2=a_2$, $y_2^p=b_2=u$, $y_2x_2=(x_2+1)y_2$; here $k(x_j)=k[T]/(T^p-T-c_j)$, so $1,x_j,\dots,x_j^{p-1}$ is a $k$-basis of $k(x_j)$. Set $z_1=y_1-1$. Then, using $\mathrm{char}k=p$:
$$x_1^p=x_1+a_1,\qquad z_1^{p}=(y_1-1)^p=y_1^p-1=(1+tu)-1=tu,\qquad x_2^p=x_2+a_2,\qquad y_2^p=u, \tag{2.1}$$
$$z_1x_1=y_1x_1-x_1=(x_1+1)y_1-x_1=x_1y_1+y_1-x_1=x_1z_1+z_1+1, \tag{2.2}$$
(the last equality since $x_1y_1+y_1-x_1=x_1(z_1+1)+(z_1+1)-x_1=x_1z_1+z_1+1$), and
$$y_2x_2=x_2y_2+y_2. \tag{2.3}$$
Finally $D=A_1\otimes_kA_2$, so every element of $A_1$ commutes with every element of $A_2$, and $k$ is central in $D$.

**Step 3. A $k$-basis.** $\{x_1^{i}y_1^{j}x_2^{k}y_2^{l}:0\le i,j,k,l\le p-1\}$ is the standard $k$-basis of $D$ (Step 2 applied to the tensor product). Since $y_1=1+z_1$ gives $y_1^{j}=\sum_{j'\le j}\binom{j}{j'}z_1^{j'}$, the change from $y_1^{j}$ to $z_1^{j}$ is triangular with unit diagonal; hence
$$\mathcal{B}=\{x_1^{i}z_1^{j}x_2^{k}y_2^{l}:0\le i,j,k,l\le p-1\}$$
is again a $k$-basis of $D$, of size $p^4=\dim_kD$.

**Step 4. Definition of $w$.** For $m=x_1^{i}z_1^{j}x_2^{k}y_2^{l}\in\mathcal{B}$ put $\delta(m)=(i+k)\alpha+(j+l)\beta$. For $a=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{B}}c_mm\in D$ define
$$w(a)=\min_{m}\big(v(c_m)+\delta(m)\big),\qquad w(0)=+\infty.$$
Then $w$ takes values in $\Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$, $w(a)=\infty\Leftrightarrow a=0$, $w|_{k^\times}=v$ (a scalar is the single basis element $1$ with $\delta(1)=0$), and $w(a+b)\ge\min(w(a),w(b))$ because the support of $a+b$ is contained in the union of the supports and $v(c+c')\ge\min(v(c),v(c'))$. From the definition, $w(x_1)=w(x_2)=\alpha=\frac{1-p}{p}$, $w(y_1-1)=w(z_1)=\beta=\frac1p$, $w(y_2)=\beta=\frac1p$, and $w(m)=\delta(m)$ for every $m\in\mathcal{B}$ (single term with coefficient $1$).

**Step 5. A rewriting system and the weight lemma.** Let $L=\{x_1,z_1,x_2,y_2\}$ and let a "word" mean a monomial in the letters of $L$; define $\mathrm{wt}(W)$ to be $\alpha\cdot(\#x_1)+\beta\cdot(\#z_1)+\alpha\cdot(\#x_2)+\beta\cdot(\#y_2)$, so $\mathrm{wt}(m)=\delta(m)$ for $m\in\mathcal{B}$. Consider the following $k$-linear rewriting rules on words, all of which are identities in $D$ by Step 2 (for R7--R10, because the two tensor factors commute):
R1: $x_1^p\to x_1+a_1$;  R2: $z_1^p\to tu$;  R3: $x_2^p\to x_2+a_2$;  R4: $y_2^p\to u$;
R5: $z_1x_1\to x_1z_1+z_1+1$;  R6: $y_2x_2\to x_2y_2+y_2$;
R7: $x_2x_1\to x_1x_2$;  R8: $x_2z_1\to z_1x_2$;  R9: $y_2x_1\to x_1y_2$;  R10: $y_2z_1\to z_1y_2$.

*Weight check.* In each rule, every term $\lambda U$ of the right-hand side satisfies $v(\lambda)+\mathrm{wt}(U)\ge \mathrm{wt}(\text{LHS})$:
- R1: $\mathrm{wt}(x_1^p)=p\alpha=1-p$; the term $x_1$ has weight $\alpha\ge 1-p$ by (2); the term $a_1$ has weight $v(a_1)=v(s)+(1-p)=1-p$ (equality).
- R2: $\mathrm{wt}(z_1^p)=p\beta=1=v(tu)$ (equality).
- R3: as R1, using $v(a_2)=v(r)+1-p=1-p$.
- R4: $\mathrm{wt}(y_2^p)=p\beta=1=v(u)$ (equality).
- R5: $\mathrm{wt}(z_1x_1)=\alpha+\beta$; the term $x_1z_1$ has weight $\alpha+\beta$; the term $z_1$ has weight $\beta>\alpha+\beta$ by (3); the term $1$ has weight $0\ge\alpha+\beta$ by (4).
- R6: $\mathrm{wt}(y_2x_2)=\alpha+\beta$; the term $x_2y_2$ has weight $\alpha+\beta$; the term $y_2$ has weight $\beta>\alpha+\beta$.
- R7--R10: a swap of two letters preserves the letter counts, hence the weight exactly.

*Termination.* Order words lexicographically by the pair $(\deg W,\ \mathrm{inv}(W))$, where $\deg W$ is the number of letters and $\mathrm{inv}(W)$ is the number of pairs of positions $i<j$ with letter $i>$ letter $j$ for the order $x_1<z_1<x_2<y_2$; this is a well-order on $\mathbb{N}^2$. R1--R4 strictly decrease $\deg$. R5, R6: the leading term $x_1z_1$ (resp. $x_2y_2$) has the same degree $2$ but $\mathrm{inv}=0<1=\mathrm{inv}(z_1x_1)$ (resp. $\mathrm{inv}(y_2x_2)$), and the remaining terms have degree $<2$. R7--R10 swap an adjacent inverted pair, which changes $\deg$ not and decreases $\mathrm{inv}$ by exactly $1$ (for a letter $c$ in the prefix, the pairs $(c,a),(c,b)$ contribute $[c>a]+[c>b]$, which after the swap is $[c>b]+[c>a]$, and likewise for the suffix; only the pair $(a,b)$ itself, one inversion, disappears). So every rule strictly decreases the pair, and reduction terminates.

*Reduced words.* A word avoiding all left-hand sides has no decreasing adjacent pair (the only decreasing pairs of distinct letters are exactly $z_1x_1$, $y_2x_2$, $x_2x_1$, $x_2z_1$, $y_2x_1$, $y_2z_1$), hence is of the form $x_1^{i}z_1^{j}x_2^{k}y_2^{l}$; avoiding $x_1^p,z_1^p,x_2^p,y_2^p$ forces $0\le i,j,k,l\le p-1$. Thus the reduced words are exactly the elements of $\mathcal{B}$, and every non-reduced word contains a left-hand side as a subword.

*Weight lemma.* Let $W$ be a word and let $\sum_m c_mm$ be its image in $D$ expanded in the basis $\mathcal{B}$. Then $v(c_m)+\delta(m)\ge \mathrm{wt}(W)$ for every $m$ with $c_m\ne0$. Indeed, run the reduction: regard the intermediate expressions as finite $k$-linear combinations $\sum_i\lambda_iU_i$ of words, with term weights $v(\lambda_i)+\mathrm{wt}(U_i)$ and expression weight the minimum. A single step replaces one term $\lambda(PUS)$ by $\sum_i(\lambda\mu_i)(PU_iS)$ where $U\to\sum\mu_iU_i$ is a rule; by the weight check each new term has weight $v(\lambda\mu_i)+\mathrm{wt}(P)+\mathrm{wt}(U_i)+\mathrm{wt}(S)\ge v(\lambda)+\mathrm{wt}(P)+\mathrm{wt}(U)+\mathrm{wt}(S)$, the weight of the term replaced. Hence the minimum weight over terms never decreases. Since each rule is an identity in $D$, the final expression equals the image of $W$ in $D$; by termination and the description of reduced words it is a $k$-linear combination of elements of $\mathcal{B}$, hence it *is* the basis expansion (basis expansions are unique). The initial expression is the single term of weight $\mathrm{wt}(W)$, so every term of the final expansion has weight $\ge\mathrm{wt}(W)$. $\square$

**Step 6. The filtration is compatible with multiplication.** For $\gamma\in\Gamma$ put $F_{\ge\gamma}D=\{a:w(a)\ge\gamma\}$ and $F_{>\gamma}D=\{a:w(a)>\gamma\}$. Take basis monomials $m,m'$: their product in $D$ is represented by the concatenated word $mm'$ with $\mathrm{wt}(mm')=\delta(m)+\delta(m')$, so by the weight lemma, writing $mm'=\sum_e e_{m,m'}(e)\,e$, one has $v(e_{m,m'}(e))+\delta(e)\ge\delta(m)+\delta(m')$ whenever $e_{m,m'}(e)\ne0$. Now let $a=\sum_mc_mm\in F_{\ge\gamma}D$ and $b=\sum_{m'}d_{m'}m'\in F_{\ge\gamma'}D$, so $v(c_m)\ge\gamma-\delta(m)$ and $v(d_{m'})\ge\gamma'-\delta(m')$. Then
$$ab=\sum_{m,m'}\sum_e c_md_{m'}e_{m,m'}(e)\,e,$$
and each occurring term has weight
$$v(c_m)+v(d_{m'})+v(e_{m,m'}(e))+\delta(e)\ \ge\ (\gamma-\delta(m))+(\gamma'-\delta(m'))+(\delta(m)+\delta(m')-\delta(e))+\delta(e)=\gamma+\gamma',$$
using additivity of $v$ on $k^\times$. Hence $F_{\ge\gamma}D\cdot F_{\ge\gamma'}D\subseteq F_{\ge\gamma+\gamma'}D$, and $\mathrm{gr}(D)=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\mathrm{gr}(D)_\gamma$ with $\mathrm{gr}(D)_\gamma=F_{\ge\gamma}D/F_{>\gamma}D$ is a (unital, nonzero) graded ring. For $0\ne a\in D$ write $\mathrm{in}(a)$ for the class of $a$ in $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{w(a)}$; the inclusion $k\hookrightarrow D$ preserves the filtrations ($w|_k=v$), so it induces a graded homomorphism $\mathrm{gr}(k)\to\mathrm{gr}(D)$, injective since $w(a)=v(a)$ for $a\in k^\times$.

**Step 7. The relations satisfied by the initial forms.** Write $X_0=\mathrm{in}(x_1)$, $Z_0=\mathrm{in}(z_1)$, $W_0=\mathrm{in}(x_2)$, $Y_0=\mathrm{in}(y_2)$, homogeneous of degrees $\alpha,\beta,\alpha,\beta$.
(i) $X_0^{p}$: by Step 4, $w(x_1^p)=w(x_1+a_1)$; as $w(x_1)=\alpha>1-p=w(a_1)$ by (2), the ultrametric inequality gives $w(x_1+a_1)=1-p=p\alpha$, and $x_1+a_1\equiv a_1\pmod{F_{>p\alpha}D}$. Hence $X_0^{p}=[x_1^p]=\mathrm{in}(a_1)=sU^{1-p}$ by (1.1).
(ii) $W_0^{p}=[x_2^p]=\mathrm{in}(x_2+a_2)=\mathrm{in}(a_2)=rU^{1-p}$, identically, since $w(x_2)=\alpha>1-p=w(a_2)$.
(iii) $Z_0^{p}=[z_1^p]=\mathrm{in}(tu)=tU$, since $z_1^p=tu$ holds in $D$ and $w(tu)=1=p\beta$.
(iv) $Y_0^{p}=[y_2^p]=\mathrm{in}(u)=U$, since $y_2^p=u$ and $w(u)=1=p\beta$.
(v) Commutativity: $X_0Z_0-W_0$-type commutators. In $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{\alpha+\beta}$,
$$X_0Z_0-Z_0X_0=[x_1z_1-z_1x_1]=[-(z_1+1)],$$
and $z_1+1=y_1$ has basis expansion $1+z_1$, so $w(z_1+1)=\min(\beta,0)=0$ (as $\beta>0$); since $0>\alpha+\beta$ by (4) — this is exactly where $p>2$ is used — one has $z_1+1\in F_{>\alpha+\beta}D$, so the class is $0$: $X_0Z_0=Z_0X_0$. Similarly
$$Y_0W_0-W_0Y_0=[y_2x_2-x_2y_2]=[y_2]=0\ \text{in }\mathrm{gr}(D)_{\alpha+\beta},$$
because $w(y_2)=\beta>\alpha+\beta$ by (3). All remaining pairs of generators come from different tensor factors or are equal, so they commute in $D$ and hence in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$. Thus $X_0,Z_0,W_0,Y_0$ pairwise commute.

**Step 8. The graded map $\phi:R\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{gr}(D)$.** Let
$$R=\mathrm{gr}(k)[X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-sU^{1-p},\;Z^{p}-tU,\;W^{p}-rU^{1-p},\;Y^{p}-U),$$
graded by $\deg U=1$, $\deg X=\deg W=\alpha$, $\deg Z=\deg Y=\beta$; each of the four generators of the ideal is homogeneous by (1), so $R$ is a graded ring (and $\mathrm{gr}(k)\simeq K_0[U^{\pm1}]$ as in Step 1). Since $X_0,Z_0,W_0,Y_0$ commute pairwise, there is a graded $\mathrm{gr}(k)$-algebra homomorphism $\mathrm{gr}(k)[X,Z,W,Y]\to\mathrm{gr}(D)$, $X\mapsto X_0$, $Z\mapsto Z_0$, $W\mapsto W_0$, $Y\mapsto Y_0$; by Step 7(i)--(iv) the four relations are in its kernel, so it descends to a graded $\mathrm{gr}(k)$-algebra homomorphism $\phi:R\to\mathrm{gr}(D)$ with $\phi(\bar X)=X_0$, etc.

*Surjectivity.* Let $a\in D$, $a\ne0$, and write $a=\sum_mc_mm$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}$. Let $M=\{m:v(c_m)+\delta(m)=w(a)\}$ and $a_0=\sum_{m\in M}c_mm$. Every term with $m\notin M$ has weight $>w(a)$, so $a-a_0\in F_{>w(a)}D$ and $\mathrm{in}(a)=\mathrm{in}(a_0)$. In the $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space $F_{\ge w(a)}D/F_{>w(a)}D$ the class of a sum is the sum of the classes, so
$$\mathrm{in}(a)=\sum_{m\in M}\mathrm{in}(c_mm)=\sum_{m\in M}\mathrm{in}(c_m)\,\mathrm{in}(m),$$
because $v(c_m)+\delta(m)=w(a)$ and the product in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is defined by $[u][v]=[uv]$. Moreover, for $m=x_1^{i}z_1^{j}x_2^{k}y_2^{l}$, the word $m$ is reduced, so $w(m)=\delta(m)=i\alpha+j\beta+k\alpha+l\beta$, and by the definition of the product in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$, $\mathrm{in}(m)=X_0^{i}Z_0^{j}W_0^{k}Y_0^{l}=\phi(\overline{X^{i}Z^{j}W^{k}Y^{l}})$, while $\mathrm{in}(c_m)=\phi(c_m\text{ viewed in }\mathrm{gr}(k))$. Hence $\mathrm{in}(a)\in\mathrm{im}\,\phi$; the zero element is trivially in the image, and every homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is $\mathrm{in}(a)$ for some $a$. So $\phi$ is surjective.

**Step 9. Injectivity of $\phi$.** By Step 1, $\mathrm{gr}(k)\simeq\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)[U^{\pm1}]$, and under this identification $R$ is exactly the algebra of lemma_158 (Spark), which asserts that
$$\mathbb{F}_p(s,t,r)[U^{\pm1}][X,Z,W,Y]/(X^{p}-sU^{1-p},\,Z^{p}-tU,\,W^{p}-rU^{1-p},\,Y^{p}-U)$$
is a domain. Hence $R$ is a domain.
We claim every nonzero homogeneous element of $R$ is a unit. Let $0\ne r\in R$ be homogeneous, $r=\sum_\mu c_\mu\mu$ a sum of monomials $\mu=X^{i}Z^{j}W^{k}Y^{l}$ with $c_\mu\in\mathrm{gr}(k)$. Since $R$ is commutative of characteristic $p$,
$$r^{p}=\sum_\mu c_\mu^{p}\mu^{p}=\sum_\mu c_\mu^{p}\,(X^{p})^{i}(Z^{p})^{j}(W^{p})^{k}(Y^{p})^{l}=\sum_\mu c_\mu^{p}\,(sU^{1-p})^{i}(tU)^{j}(rU^{1-p})^{k}U^{l}\ \in\ \mathrm{gr}(k),$$
by the four relations. As $R$ is a domain and $r\ne0$, also $r^{p}\ne0$. A nonzero homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)\simeq K_0[U^{\pm1}]$ has the form $cU^{n}$ with $c\in K_0^\times$, and is invertible there with inverse $c^{-1}U^{-n}$. Thus $r^p$ is a unit of $R$, and $r^{-1}=r^{p-1}(r^{p})^{-1}\in R$.
Consequently any nonzero graded ideal of $R$ contains a nonzero homogeneous element, hence a unit, hence is $R$ itself. Now $\ker\phi$ is a graded ideal (for a degree-$0$ homogeneous homomorphism, each homogeneous component of an element of the kernel again lies in the kernel) and it is proper, since $\phi(1)=1\ne0$ in $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ (as $w(1)=0$, $1\notin F_{>0}D$). Therefore $\ker\phi=0$, and $\phi$ is an isomorphism of graded $\mathrm{gr}(k)$-algebras
$$\mathrm{gr}(D)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ R,\qquad \mathrm{in}_w(x_1)\mapsto X,\ \mathrm{in}_w(y_1-1)=Z_0\mapsto Z,\ \mathrm{in}_w(x_2)\mapsto W,\ \mathrm{in}_w(y_2)\mapsto Y,$$
where we used $\mathrm{in}_w(su^{1-p})$, $\mathrm{in}_w(tu)$, $\mathrm{in}_w(ru^{1-p})$, $\mathrm{in}_w(u)$ in place of $sU^{1-p},tU,rU^{1-p},U$ by (1.1).

**Step 10. $w$ is a valuation.** Since $\mathrm{gr}(D)\simeq R$ is a domain, for $a,b\in D\setminus\{0\}$ the product $\mathrm{in}(a)\mathrm{in}(b)=[ab]$ is nonzero in $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{w(a)+w(b)}$; by definition of the graded product this means $ab\notin F_{>w(a)+w(b)}D$, i.e. $w(ab)=w(a)+w(b)$. Together with Step 4 (ultrametric inequality, $w(0)=\infty$, $w|_{k^\times}=v$) this says $w:D\to\Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$ is a valuation extending $v$, with value group $w(D^\times)=\tfrac1p\mathbb{Z}$ (generated by $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$ and $w(y_2)=\frac1p$). Its values on the required generators are $w(x_1)=w(x_2)=\frac{1-p}{p}$ and $w(y_1-1)=w(y_2)=\frac1p$ by Step 4, and the graded isomorphism of Step 9 is precisely the one asserted. This completes the proof.

lemma_161.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field with residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ with the valuation $w$ extending $v$ and residue division ring $\bar D$. If $D$ contains a maximal subfield $L$ that is Galois over $k$ of degree $p^2$ and satisfies $w(L^\times)=v(k^\times)$, then the dimension of $\bar D$ as a $\bar k$-vector space is at least $p^2$.
lemma_161.proof:
We write the valuation $w$ additively, and put
\[
\mathcal O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\},\qquad \mathfrak M_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\},\qquad \bar D=\mathcal O_D/\mathfrak M_D ,
\]
and similarly $\mathcal O_k=\{a\in k:v(a)\ge0\}$, $\mathfrak m_k=\{a\in k:v(a)>0\}$, $\bar k=\mathcal O_k/\mathfrak m_k$.  Since $w$ extends $v$ we have $\mathcal O_k=\mathcal O_D\cap k$ and $\mathfrak m_k=\mathfrak M_D\cap k$; in particular the composite $\mathcal O_k\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_D\twoheadrightarrow\bar D$ has kernel $\mathfrak m_k$, so it identifies $\bar k$ with a (central) subfield of the residue division ring $\bar D$.  Thus $\bar D$ is a $\bar k$-vector space.

**Step 1: the valuation induced on $L$ is the canonical one.**  The subfield $L\subset D$ inherits the valuation $w|_L$, which extends $v$.  Because $(k,v)$ is henselian, the valuation $v$ has a *unique* extension to any algebraic extension of $k$; hence $w|_L$ is the unique extension of $v$ to $L$, and $w(L^\times)$, $\bar L$ below are computed with respect to this canonical extension.  Set
\[
\mathcal O_L=\{x\in L: w(x)\ge0\}=\mathcal O_D\cap L,\qquad \mathfrak M_L=\{x\in L: w(x)>0\}=\mathfrak M_D\cap L,\qquad \bar L=\mathcal O_L/\mathfrak M_L .
\]
(The equality $\mathfrak M_L=\mathfrak M_D\cap L$ holds because $w|_L$ is a valuation on the field $L$, so its maximal ideal is exactly the set of elements of strictly positive value.)

**Step 2: $\bar L$ embeds into $\bar D$ over $\bar k$.**  Consider the ring homomorphism
\[
\rho:\mathcal O_L\hookrightarrow \mathcal O_D\twoheadrightarrow \bar D .
\]
Its kernel is $\mathfrak M_D\cap\mathcal O_L=\mathfrak M_L$ by Step 1.  Hence $\rho$ factors through an injective ring homomorphism
\[
\bar\rho:\bar L=\mathcal O_L/\mathfrak M_L\hookrightarrow \bar D .
\]
Since $\bar L$ is a field (the residue ring of a valued field is a field), $\bar\rho$ identifies $\bar L$ with a subfield of $\bar D$.  Moreover the diagram
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathcal O_k & \hookrightarrow & \mathcal O_L\\
\downarrow & & \downarrow\\
\bar k & \xrightarrow{\ \bar\rho|_{\bar k}\ } & \bar D
\end{array}
\]
commutes (all horizontal maps are inclusions of $k$ into $L$ and of $L$ into $D$), so $\bar\rho$ is $\bar k$-linear: it identifies $\bar L$ with a $\bar k$-linear subspace of the $\bar k$-vector space $\bar D$, and $\bar k\subseteq\bar L$ inside $\bar D$.

**Step 3: compute the residue degree of $L/k$.**  The extension $L/k$ is Galois of degree $p^2$, $(k,v)$ is henselian discretely valued, and $L$ carries the valuation $w$ extending $v$.  We may therefore apply the proved lemma \texttt{lemma\_96} (triviality of the defect for finite Galois extensions of henselian discretely valued fields), which gives
\[
[L:k]=[w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k].
\]
By hypothesis $w(L^\times)=v(k^\times)$, i.e. the ramification index $e(L/k)$ is $1$, and by assumption $[L:k]=p^2$ (indeed $L$ is a maximal subfield of the degree-$p^2$ division algebra $D$, so $\dim_k L=p^2$).  Substituting,
\[
p^2=1\cdot[\bar L:\bar k],\qquad\text{hence}\qquad [\bar L:\bar k]=p^2 .
\]

**Step 4: conclude.**  By Step 2, $\bar L$ is a $\bar k$-linear subspace of the $\bar k$-vector space $\bar D$, so
\[
\dim_{\bar k}\bar D\ \ge\ \dim_{\bar k}\bar L\ =\ [\bar L:\bar k]\ =\ p^2 .
\]
This is exactly the required inequality.

(Remark on the content of the argument: no tameness or defectlessness hypothesis on $D$ itself was needed — only the trivial-defect statement for the Galois subfield $L$, supplied by \texttt{lemma\_96}.  Combined with the fundamental inequality $[D:k]\ge[\bar D:\bar k]\cdot[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)]$, the conclusion also shows that in this situation $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ forces $\bar D$ to have degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$.)

lemma_162.statement: Let $k$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$. Then $D$ contains no element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$ and $w(a)>0$.
lemma_162.proof:
We argue directly from the axioms of a valuation on a division ring; the only properties of $D$ we use are that it is a division ring with centre containing $k$ and that $w$ is a Krull valuation on $D$ whose restriction to $k^{\times}$ is $v$.

Recall the axioms we use for $w$: it takes values in an ordered abelian group $\Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$ with $w(0)=\infty$, $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$, $w(x+y)\ge\min(w(x),w(y))$, with equality whenever $w(x)\ne w(y)$; and $w|_{k^{\times}}=v$, so $w(1)=0$ and $w(c)=0$ for $c\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\subset k^{\times}$.

Assume, for a contradiction, that there exists $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a\,^{p}-a\in k$ and $w(a)>0$. Write
$$d:=a^{p}-a\in k .$$

**Step 1: the value of $d$.** Since $a\notin k$, $a\ne 0$, so $w(a)\in\Gamma$ is finite and $w(a)>0$. In the ordered group $\Gamma$ one has $p\,w(a)>w(a)$ (as $p>1$ and $w(a)>0$). Hence $w(a^{p})=p\,w(a)\ne w(a)$, and by the strict-triangle property of valuations
$$v(d)=w(d)=w(a^{p}-a)=\min\bigl(w(a^{p}),w(a)\bigr)=\min\bigl(p\,w(a),w(a)\bigr)=w(a)>0 ,$$
where the equality $w(d)=v(d)$ holds because $d\in k^{\times}$ (indeed $w(d)=w(a)<\infty$ shows $d\ne0$) and $w$ extends $v$. Thus
$$d\in k,\qquad v(d)>0 . \tag{1}$$

**Step 2: every element of $k$ of strictly positive value is an Artin–Schreier value.** We claim that (1) implies $d\in\wp(k):=\{x^{p}-x:x\in k\}$. Consider the partial sums
$$s_{n}:=-\sum_{i=0}^{n}d^{p^{i}}\qquad(n\ge 0).$$
Since $v(d)>0$, we have $v(s_{n+1}-s_{n})=v\!\left(d^{p^{n+1}}\right)=p^{\,n+1}v(d)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\infty$; hence $(s_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $k$. As $k$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$, $s_n\to s$ for some $s\in k$. The Frobenius map $x\mapsto x^{p}$ is continuous for $v$, because $v(x^{p}-y^{p})=v\bigl((x-y)^{p}\bigr)=p\,v(x-y)$; therefore
$$s^{p}=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_{n}^{p}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Bigl(-\sum_{i=0}^{n}d^{p^{i+1}}\Bigr)=-\sum_{j\ge 1}d^{p^{j}},$$
where we used $(-1)^{p}=-1$ (valid since $p>2$) and the binomial/Frobenius identity $(\sum_i x_i)^p=\sum_i x_i^p$ for the finite sums. On the other hand
$$s=-\sum_{i\ge 0}d^{p^{i}}=-d-\sum_{j\ge 1}d^{p^{j}},\qquad\text{so}\qquad -\sum_{j\ge 1}d^{p^{j}}=s+d .$$
Combining the two displayed identities gives $s^{p}=s+d$, i.e.
$$s^{p}-s=d . \tag{2}$$
This proves the claim.

**Step 3: a $p$-periodic element of a division ring of characteristic $p$ lies in $\mathbb F_p$.** The polynomial $T^{p}-T\in\mathbb F_p[T]$ factors as $T^{p}-T=\prod_{c\in\mathbb F_p}(T-c)$, a product of pairwise-commuting linear factors. If $y$ belongs to a division ring of characteristic $p$ and satisfies $y^{p}=y$, then $\prod_{c\in\mathbb F_p}(y-c)=0$ in the commutative subring $\mathbb F_p[y]$; a division ring has no zero divisors, so $y-c=0$ for some $c\in\mathbb F_p$, i.e. $y\in\mathbb F_p$. \tag{3}

**Step 4: conclusion.** The element $s\in k$ is central in $D$, so $a$ and $s$ commute, and in characteristic $p$ the binomial theorem for commuting elements gives $(a-s)^{p}=a^{p}-s^{p}$. Using the definition $a^{p}-a=d$ and $(2)$,
$$(a-s)^{p}-(a-s)=(a^{p}-s^{p})-a+s=(a^{p}-a)-(s^{p}-s)=d-d=0 .$$
By (3), $a-s\in\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$. Since also $s\in k$, we obtain $a\in k$, contradicting the choice of $a\notin k$.

Hence no element $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$ can satisfy $w(a)>0$, which is exactly the statement.

(Remark on the hypotheses: the argument used only that $D$ is a division ring with centre containing $k$, that $w$ is a valuation extending $v$, and that $k$ is complete for $v$; neither the centrality/finiteness of $D$ over $k$, nor $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$, nor $p>2$ beyond the sign in Step 2, is needed in an essential way. The statement is consistent with Lemma 109 of Spark, which in the special case of residue division ring $\bar k$ shows that any $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$ must in fact have $w(a)<0$.)

lemma_immediate_division_algebra_is_triv.statement: Let $k$ be a field equipped with a discrete valuation $v$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$ and residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra, and let $w$ be a valuation on $D$ extending $v$, with value group $w(D^\times)$ and residue division ring $\bar D$. If $w(D^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\bar D=\bar k$, then $D=k$.
lemma_immediate_division_algebra_is_triv.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_immediate_division_algebra_is_trivial",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "Spark", "lemma_id": "lemma_144"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "**Notation and conventions.** For $\gamma\in\mathbf Z$ write
$$D_{\ge \gamma}=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge \gamma\}\cup\{0\},\qquad D_{>\gamma}=\{x\in D: w(x)>\gamma\}\cup\{0\},$$
and similarly $k_{\ge\gamma}=\{c\in k:v(c)\ge\gamma\}\cup\{0\}$, $k_{>\gamma}=\{c\in k:v(c)>\gamma\}\cup\{0\}$. Since $w$ extends $v$ (i.e. $w(c)=v(c)$ for all $c\in k$), one has $k_{\ge\gamma}=k\cap D_{\ge\gamma}$ and $k_{>\gamma}=k\cap D_{>\gamma}$. By hypothesis $w(D^\times)=\mathbf Z=v(k^\times)$, so both associated graded rings are graded by $\mathbf Z$:
$$\operatorname{gr}(D)=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\mathbf Z}D_{\ge\gamma}/D_{>\gamma},\qquad \operatorname{gr}(k)=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\mathbf Z}k_{\ge\gamma}/k_{>\gamma}.$$
The inclusion $k\subset D$ induces a graded homomorphism $\operatorname{gr}(k)\to\operatorname{gr}(D)$ which is injective: if $c\in k_{\ge\gamma}$ maps to $0$, then $c\in D_{>\gamma}\cap k=k_{>\gamma}$, so the class of $c$ in $k_{\ge\gamma}/k_{>\gamma}$ is $0$. We use this injection to regard $\operatorname{gr}(k)$ as a graded subring of $\operatorname{gr}(D)$. For $x\in D^\times$ we write $\operatorname{in}_w(x)=x+D_{>w(x)}\in\operatorname{gr}(D)_{w(x)}$ for the initial form; the nonzero elements of $\operatorname{gr}(k)_\gamma$ are exactly the classes of those $c\in k$ with $v(c)=\gamma$, because a nonzero coset of $k_{\ge\gamma}/k_{>\gamma}$ contains an element $c$ with $v(c)\ge\gamma$ and $v(c)\ngtr\gamma$, i.e. $v(c)=\gamma$. A valuation on the division ring $D$ satisfies $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$ and $w(x+y)\ge\min(w(x),w(y))$ for all $x,y\in D^\times$.

**Step 1 (the graded pieces of $D$ come from $k$).** The data $(k,v)$, $D$, $w$ satisfy exactly the hypotheses of the proved lemma \texttt{lemma\_144}: $(k,v)$ is discretely valued with $v(k^\times)=\mathbf Z$ and residue field $\bar k$; $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra; $w$ is a valuation on $D$ extending $v$; and the residue division ring of $D$ is $\bar D=\bar k$. That lemma concludes
$$\operatorname{gr}(D)_m=\operatorname{gr}(k)_m\qquad\text{for every } m\in\mathbf Z. \tag{$*$}$$
Concretely, ($*$") means: whenever $x\in D$ has $w(x)=\gamma\in\mathbf Z$, the initial form $\operatorname{in}_w(x)\in\operatorname{gr}(D)_\gamma$ lies in the subring $\operatorname{gr}(k)_\gamma$, hence equals $c+D_{>\gamma}$ for some $c\in k$ with $v(c)=\gamma$; equivalently $w(x-c)>\gamma$.

**Step 2 (approximation of elements of $D$ by elements of $k$).**
*Claim.* For every $a\in D$ and every integer $N$ there exists $s\in k$ such that either $a=s$ or $w(a-s)>N$.

*Proof of the claim.* If $a=0$, take $s=0$. Otherwise construct sequences $(r_i)_{i\ge0}$ in $D$ and $(c_i)_{i\ge0}$ in $k$ inductively as follows. Put $r_0=a$, and suppose $r_i\neq0$ has been constructed. Then $\gamma_i:=w(r_i)\in w(D^\times)=\mathbf Z$, so $\operatorname{in}_w(r_i)$ is a nonzero homogeneous element of $\operatorname{gr}(D)_{\gamma_i}$. By ($*$), $\operatorname{gr}(D)_{\gamma_i}=\operatorname{gr}(k)_{\gamma_i}$, so there is $c_i\in k$ with $v(c_i)=\gamma_i$ whose class in $\operatorname{gr}(k)_{\gamma_i}$ equals $\operatorname{in}_w(r_i)$; under the identification above this says $r_i+D_{>\gamma_i}=c_i+D_{>\gamma_i}$, hence
$$r_{i+1}:=r_i-c_i\in D_{>\gamma_i},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad w(r_{i+1})>\gamma_i=w(r_i).$$
If $r_{i+1}=0$ the construction stops; otherwise $\gamma_{i+1}:=w(r_{i+1})$ is again an element of $w(D^\times)=\mathbf Z$, and the construction continues (this is the only place where the hypothesis $w(D^\times)=\mathbf Z$ is used: it guarantees that every remainder again has an *integral* value, so that ($*$) applies to it).

By construction, as long as the process has not stopped, $(\gamma_i)$ is a strictly increasing sequence of integers, hence $\gamma_i\ge\gamma_0+i$ for all $i$ (induction: $\gamma_{i+1}\ge\gamma_i+1\ge\gamma_0+i+1$).
Choose an integer $i\ge1$ with $\gamma_0+i>N$ (possible since $\mathbf Z$ is archimedean, e.g. $i=N-\gamma_0+1$ if that is positive, else $i=1$).
- If the process stopped at some $j\le i$, then $r_j=r_{j-1}-c_{j-1}=0$, so $a=r_0=\sum_{t<j}c_t\in k$; taking $s=a$ gives $a=s$.
- Otherwise all $r_0,\dots,r_i$ are nonzero, and with $s:=\sum_{t<i}c_t\in k$ we have $a-s=r_i\neq0$ and
$$w(a-s)=\gamma_i\ge\gamma_0+i>N.$$
This proves the claim. $\triangleleft$ (claim)

**Step 3 (commutators have arbitrarily large value).** Fix $a,b\in D$ and let $M\in\mathbf Z$ be arbitrary; we show that either $ab-ba=0$ or $w(ab-ba)>M$. Choose an integer $T$ with $2T+2>M$; for instance $T=\lfloor M/2\rfloor+1$ works, since $2\lfloor M/2\rfloor\ge M-1$ gives $2T+2\ge M+3>M$.
Apply the claim of Step 2 to $a$ with accuracy $N=T$: there is $c\in k$ with either $a=c$ or $w(a-c)>T$. Put $\alpha:=a-c$. Likewise there is $c'\in k$ with either $b=c'$ or $w(b-c')>T$; put $\beta:=b-c'$. If $\alpha=0$ then $a=c\in k=Z(D)$ is central, so $ab-ba=0$; similarly if $\beta=0$. Otherwise $\alpha,\beta\in D^\times$ and, the values being integers, $w(\alpha)>T$ and $w(\beta)>T$ mean $w(\alpha)\ge T+1$ and $w(\beta)\ge T+1$.
Since $D$ is a *central* $k$-algebra, $k=Z(D)$, so $c$ and $c'$ commute with every element of $D$. Expanding and cancelling the central terms,
$$ab-ba=(c+\alpha)(c'+\beta)-(c'+\beta)(c+\alpha)=\alpha\beta-\beta\alpha.$$
Using the valuation axioms on the division ring $D$,
$$w(ab-ba)=w(\alpha\beta-\beta\alpha)\ge\min\big(w(\alpha\beta),\,w(\beta\alpha)\big)=w(\alpha)+w(\beta)\ge (T+1)+(T+1)=2T+2>M.$$
Thus: for every integer $M$, either $ab-ba=0$ or $w(ab-ba)>M$. (Note that $M$ is an independently chosen target; no inequality of the form "$\text{value}>2T+2>T$" is asserted, which would be meaningless since the values may be negative.)

**Step 4 (commutators vanish, and conclusion).** Suppose for contradiction that some commutator $d:=ab-ba$ is nonzero. Then $d\in D^\times$, and by the hypothesis $w(D^\times)=\mathbf Z$ its value $m:=w(d)$ is an integer. Apply the conclusion of Step 3 with $M:=m$: since $d\neq0$, we must have $w(d)>M=m$, i.e. $m>m$, a contradiction. Hence $ab-ba=0$ for all $a,b\in D$, so $D$ is commutative.
A commutative division ring equals its centre; since $D$ is central over $k$, $Z(D)=k$ (identifying $k$ with its image in $D$). Therefore $D=Z(D)=k$ as rings, and hence as $k$-algebras. $\blacksquare$

*Remark on the hypotheses.* Both are used: $\bar D=\bar k$ (together with $v(k^\times)=\mathbf Z$) is precisely what Step 1 imports from \texttt{lemma\_144}, and $w(D^\times)=\mathbf Z$ is used twice — to keep every remainder's value integral in the induction of Step 2, and to conclude in Step 4 that the value of a nonzero commutator is an integer that can be exceeded. No henselianity, no completeness, no defect theory and no limit process is involved: the approximation in Step 2 is a finite subtraction process."
}

lemma_163.statement: Let $k$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>0$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb{Z}$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, and write $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ and $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ for the associated graded rings, with $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ viewed as a graded subring of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$. If $a\in D$ and $c\in k$ satisfy $a^{p}-a=c$ and $w(a)<0$, then $p\,w(a)=v(c)<0$, $w(a)\in\frac{1}{p}\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathrm{in}_w(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_v(c)$ as homogeneous elements of $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{v(c)}$.
lemma_163.proof:
We write the proof from the axioms of a valuation on a division ring; no external result is needed.

**Setup.** Let $\Gamma:=w(D^{\times})$, a totally ordered abelian group, and extend $w$ to $D$ by $w(0)=\infty$. By definition of a valuation on the division ring $D$ we have, for all $x,y\in D$:
(V1) $w(x)=\infty\iff x=0$;
(V2) $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$;
(V3) $w(x+y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$.
Since $\Gamma$ is totally ordered it is torsion-free: if $\gamma>0$ then $m\gamma>0$ for every integer $m\ge1$, and similarly for $\gamma<0$; hence $m\gamma=0$ forces $\gamma=0$.

*Strict triangle equality.* If $w(x)\ne w(y)$, say $w(x)<w(y)$, then (V3) gives $w(x+y)\ge w(x)$. On the other hand $w(x)=w((x+y)-y)\ge\min\{w(x+y),w(y)\}\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}=w(x)$, so equality holds throughout; thus $\min\{w(x+y),w(y)\}=w(x)$, and since $w(y)>w(x)$ this forces $w(x+y)=w(x)$. We shall use this repeatedly.

*Relation with $v$.* Fix a uniformiser $\pi\in k$ with $v(\pi)=1$. Since $w$ extends $v$, the map $m\mapsto w(\pi^{m})$ identifies $\mathbb Z=v(k^{\times})$ with the subgroup $\langle w(\pi)\rangle\subset\Gamma$, and for $\lambda\in k^{\times}$ the element $w(\lambda)$ is the image of $v(\lambda)\in\mathbb Z$. We shall freely identify the two, and say $\gamma\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$ to mean $\gamma=\frac{m}{p}w(\pi)$ for some $m\in\mathbb Z$.

**Step 1: $c\ne0$.** Suppose $c=0$. Then $a^{p}=a$. The $k$-algebra structure on $D$ makes $D$ an $\mathbb F_{p}$-algebra, and the subring $\mathbb F_{p}[a]$ generated by $a$ over the prime field is commutative (generated by one element together with central scalars) and a domain, being a subring of the division ring $D$. It is finite dimensional over $\mathbb F_{p}$ since $a^{p}=a$ implies every power of $a$ is a linear combination of $1,a,\dots,a^{p-1}$; a finite commutative domain is a field, so $\mathbb F_{p}[a]$ is a field. In a field the polynomial $X^{p}-X$ has at most $p$ roots, and the $p$ elements of $\mathbb F_{p}$ are already roots; hence $a\in\mathbb F_{p}$. If $a=0$ then $w(a)=\infty$ by (V1), and if $a\in\mathbb F_{p}^{\times}$ then $w(a)=w(1)=0$ by (V2) applied to $a^{p-1}\cdot a^{-(p-1)}=1$ (indeed $0=w(1)=w(a^{\,p-1})=(p-1)w(a)$ and $\Gamma$ is torsion-free). Neither case gives $w(a)<0$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $c\ne0$, so $v(c)$ is a well-defined integer, and also $a\ne0$.

**Step 2: $v(c)=p\,w(a)<0$.** Because $w(a)<0$ and $p\ge2$, we have $p\,w(a)-w(a)=(p-1)w(a)<0$ in the ordered group $\Gamma$; hence
$$w(a^{p})=p\,w(a)<w(a)<0.$$
In particular $w(a^{p})\ne w(a)$, so by the strict triangle equality applied to $x=a^{p}$ and $y=-a$ (note $w(-a)=w(a)$, since $w(-1)+w(-1)=w(1)=0$ gives $w(-1)=0$),
$$v(c)=w(c)=w(a^{p}-a)=\min\{w(a^{p}),w(a)\}=w(a^{p})=p\,w(a),$$
which is $<0$. This proves the first assertion.

**Step 3: $w(a)\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$.** Since $c\in k^{\times}$ we have $v(c)=m$ for a (negative) integer $m$, i.e. $p\,w(a)=m\,w(\pi)$ in $\Gamma$. In the divisible hull $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Gamma$ (in which $\Gamma$ embeds because $\Gamma$ is torsion-free, and where division by $p$ is unique) this reads $w(a)=\frac{m}{p}\,w(\pi)$, i.e. $w(a)=\frac{m}{p}\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$. Equivalently, $p\,w(a)\in\mathbb Z\subset\Gamma$ and $\Gamma$ has no $p$-torsion, so $w(a)$ lies in $\frac1p\mathbb Z$.

**Step 4: the graded ring and initial forms.** For $\gamma\in\Gamma$ put $D^{\ge\gamma}=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge\gamma\}$ and $D^{>\gamma}=\{x\in D: w(x)>\gamma\}$ (additive subgroups, with $D^{>\gamma}\subset D^{\ge\gamma}$); then $\mathrm{gr}(D)=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\mathrm{gr}(D)_{\gamma}$ with $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{\gamma}=D^{\ge\gamma}/D^{>\gamma}$, and for $0\ne x\in D$ we write $\mathrm{in}_{w}(x)$ for the class $x+D^{>w(x)}\in\mathrm{gr}(D)_{w(x)}$, which is non-zero because $x\notin D^{>w(x)}$.
The product on $\mathrm{gr}(D)$ is defined on homogeneous representatives by
$$(x+D^{>\gamma})\,(y+D^{>\delta}):=xy+D^{>\gamma+\delta}\qquad(x\in D^{\ge\gamma},\ y\in D^{\ge\delta}).$$
This is well defined: if $x'=x+t$ with $w(t)>\gamma$ then $w(ty)=w(t)+w(y)>\gamma+\delta$ by (V2), so $x'y=xy+ty\equiv xy\pmod{D^{>\gamma+\delta}}$, and similarly for a change of $y$. Associativity and distributivity are inherited from $D$, and $\mathrm{in}_{w}(1)$ is the unit. Consequently, for all non-zero $x,y\in D$,
$$\mathrm{in}_{w}(x)\,\mathrm{in}_{w}(y)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(xy),\tag{$*$}
$$
which is exactly the definition of the product (and is legitimate because $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$ is the exact value of $xy$, so $\mathrm{in}_{w}(xy)\ne0$).

The inclusions $k\subset D$ give, for each $m\in\mathbb Z$, a homomorphism $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{m}=\{\lambda\in k: v(\lambda)\ge m\}/\{\lambda\in k: v(\lambda)>m\}\to\mathrm{gr}(D)_{m}=D^{\ge m}/D^{>m}$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda+D^{>m}$, which is well defined since $w|_{k}=v$, and injective since $\lambda\in k$ with $w(\lambda)>m$ satisfies $v(\lambda)>m$ and hence maps to $0$ already in $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{m}$. Thus $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ is a graded subring of $\mathrm{gr}(D)$, and $\mathrm{in}_{v}(c)$ denotes below its image in $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{v(c)}$.

**Step 5: $\mathrm{in}_{w}(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_{w}(a^{p})$.** Iterating $(*)$ $p$ times (induction on the number of factors) gives $\mathrm{in}_{w}(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_{w}(a\cdots a)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(a^{p})$. Its homogeneous degree is $p\cdot w(a)$, which by Step 2 equals $v(c)$; so $\mathrm{in}_{w}(a)^{p}$ is a homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{v(c)}$.

**Step 6: $\mathrm{in}_{w}(a^{p})=\mathrm{in}_{v}(c)$.** From Step 2, $w(c)=v(c)=p\,w(a)<w(a)$, i.e. $a\in D^{>v(c)}$. Both $a^{p}$ and $c$ lie in $D^{\ge v(c)}$ (their $w$-values are exactly $v(c)$). Since $a^{p}=c+a$, we have $a^{p}-c=a\in D^{>v(c)}$, so $a^{p}$ and $c$ have the same class modulo $D^{>v(c)}$:
$$\mathrm{in}_{w}(a^{p})=a^{p}+D^{>v(c)}=c+D^{>v(c)}=\mathrm{in}_{v}(c)\in\mathrm{gr}(D)_{v(c)}.$$
Combining Steps 5 and 6 yields $\mathrm{in}_{w}(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_{v}(c)$ as homogeneous elements of $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{v(c)}$.

**Conclusion.** We have shown $c\ne0$, $v(c)=p\,w(a)<0$, $w(a)=v(c)/p\in\frac1p\mathbb Z$, and $\mathrm{in}_{w}(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_{v}(c)$ in $\mathrm{gr}(D)_{v(c)}$, which is exactly the statement. (Note that the argument used only $p\ge2$, the fact that $w$ is a valuation on the division ring $D$ extending $v$, and $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$; completeness of $k$ is not needed beyond guaranteeing the existence of such a $w$.)

lemma_164.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, and let $K$ be a subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$. Suppose there exists $b\in K\setminus\wp(K)$, where $\wp(K)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in K\}$, such that the extension $K(w)/K$ defined by $w^{p}-w=b$ is Galois over $k$ and splits the centralizer $C_{D}(K)$. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_164.proof:
We write $\wp(F)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in F\}$ for a field $F$ of characteristic $p$.

**Step 1. $K(w)/K$ is a cyclic Galois extension of degree $p$.**
Let $f(T)=T^{p}-T-b\in K[T]$. Since $f'(T)=-1\neq 0$, $f$ is separable. For every $t\in\mathbb F_{p}$ one has, using $t^{p}=t$,
$$(w+t)^{p}-(w+t)-b=(w^{p}+t^{p})-w-t-b=(w^{p}-w-b)+(t-t)=0,$$
so the $p$ roots of $f$ in a separable closure $\Omega$ of $K$ are exactly $w,w+1,\dots,w+(p-1)$, and they all lie in $K(w)$.

Let $m\in K[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $w$ over $K$, of degree $d$, and let $S=\{t\in\mathbb F_{p}: m(w+t)=0\}$; the roots of $m$ inside $\Omega$ are precisely $\{w+t:t\in S\}$. Since $\Omega/K$ may be taken Galois containing $K(w)$, the roots of $m$ form the orbit of $w$ under $\operatorname{Gal}(\Omega/K)$. For $g\in\operatorname{Gal}(\Omega/K)$ write $g(w)=w+t_{g}$; then for $g,h\in\operatorname{Gal}(\Omega/K)$,
$$gh(w)=g(w+t_{h})=g(w)+t_{h}=w+t_{g}+t_{h},$$
because $t_{h}\in\mathbb F_{p}\subset K$ is fixed by $g$. Thus $g\mapsto t_{g}$ is a group homomorphism $\operatorname{Gal}(\Omega/K)\to(\mathbb F_{p},+)$ whose image is exactly $S$. Hence $S$ is an additive subgroup of $\mathbb F_{p}$, so $|S|=1$ or $p$; and $d=\deg m=|S|$. Since $b\notin\wp(K)$, $f$ has no root in $K$, so $w\notin K$ and $d\neq 1$. Therefore $d=p$: $f$ is irreducible over $K$, $[K(w):K]=p$, and the $p$ distinct $K$-embeddings $w\mapsto w+t$ ($t\in\mathbb F_{p}$) all map $K(w)$ to itself, so $K(w)/K$ is Galois with $\operatorname{Gal}(K(w)/K)=\{\tau_{t}:w\mapsto w+t\}_{t\in\mathbb F_{p}}\simeq C_{p}$.

**Step 2. $K(w)/k$ is Galois of degree $p^{2}$.**
By hypothesis $K(w)/k$ is a Galois extension. By the tower law and Step 1,
$$[K(w):k]=[K(w):K]\cdot[K:k]=p\cdot p=p^{2}.$$
Put $G:=\operatorname{Gal}(K(w)/k)$; then $|G|=p^{2}$, as required for the group in the conclusion.

**Step 3. The structure of $D\otimes_{k}K$ in terms of $C_{D}(K)$.**
By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), since $K\subset D$ is a subfield containing $k$ and $\deg D=p^{2}$, the centralizer $C_{D}(K)$ is a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[K:k]=p^{2}/p=p$, Brauer-equivalent to $D\otimes_{k}K$. Moreover $C_{D}(K)$ is a $K$-subalgebra of the division ring $D$, hence a finite-dimensional $K$-domain, hence a division algebra; so $\operatorname{ind}(C_{D}(K))=p$. Now $D\otimes_{k}K$ is a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ Brauer-equivalent to $C_{D}(K)$, so
$$D\otimes_{k}K\;\simeq\;M_{p}\big(C_{D}(K)\big),$$
because $\deg M_{r}(C_{D}(K))=rp=p^{2}$ forces $r=p$.

**Step 4. $K(w)$ splits $D$.**
Using associativity of the tensor product, with $K(w)$ viewed as a $k$-algebra through $k\subset K\subset K(w)$,
$$D\otimes_{k}K(w)\;\simeq\;\big(D\otimes_{k}K\big)\otimes_{K}K(w)\;\simeq\;M_{p}\big(C_{D}(K)\big)\otimes_{K}K(w)\;\simeq\;M_{p}\big(C_{D}(K)\otimes_{K}K(w)\big),$$
where the last isomorphism is $M_{p}(K)\otimes_{K}C\simeq M_{p}(C)$ applied with $C=C_{D}(K)\otimes_{K}K(w)$. By hypothesis $K(w)$ splits $C_{D}(K)$, i.e. $C_{D}(K)\otimes_{K}K(w)\simeq M_{p}(K(w))$ (its degree over $K$ is $p$). Hence
$$D\otimes_{k}K(w)\;\simeq\;M_{p}\big(M_{p}(K(w))\big)\;\simeq\;M_{p^{2}}(K(w)),$$
so $K(w)$ is a splitting field of $D$.

**Step 5. $K(w)$ embeds in $D$ as a maximal subfield.**
We have $[K(w):k]=p^{2}=\deg D$, so $[K(w):k]$ divides $\deg D$ and $K(w)$ splits $D$. By the embedding criterion for subfields of central simple algebras (ref_5, with $m=n=p^{2}$: a degree-$n$ extension embeds as a maximal subfield if and only if it splits $A$), there exists a $k$-algebra embedding $\iota:K(w)\hookrightarrow D$ whose image
$$L:=\iota(K(w))$$
is a maximal subfield of $D$. In particular $\dim_{k}L=p^{2}$.

**Step 6. $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ with $L^{G}=k$.**
The map $\iota:K(w)\xrightarrow{\sim}L$ is a $k$-algebra isomorphism, so $L/k$ is a Galois field extension with
$$\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)=\iota\,G\,\iota^{-1}\;\simeq\;G,$$
a group of order $p^{2}$. Transporting the $G$-action along $\iota$ (i.e. $g\cdot\iota(x):=\iota(gx)$) makes $L$ a $G$-Galois algebra in the sense of the stated definition: $L$ is a field, hence étale over $k$; $\dim_{k}L=p^{2}=|G|$; and by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory $L^{G}=k$, since $[L:k]=|G|$.

**Step 7. $D$ is the crossed product $(L,G,c)$.**
Apply the proved lemma lemma_106 to the central simple $k$-algebra $A=D$ of degree $n=p^{2}$ and to the maximal subfield $L$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$ (of order $p^{2}=n$). It yields a map $c:G\times G\to L^{\times}$ such that, as $k$-algebras,
$$D\;\simeq\;\bigoplus_{g\in G}L\,u_{g},\qquad u_{g}\,\lambda=g(\lambda)\,u_{g},\qquad u_{g}u_{h}=c(g,h)\,u_{gh}$$
for all $\lambda\in L$ and $g,h\in G$. That is exactly a $G$-crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $L$ a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ and $|G|=p^{2}$.

Thus $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, which is what was to be shown. (Remark: by the classification of groups of order $p^{2}$, this $G$ is necessarily abelian, isomorphic to $C_{p^{2}}$ or $C_{p}\times C_{p}$; this fact is not needed for the argument.)

lemma_165.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\big(k/\wp(k)\big)\le 2$, where $\wp(k)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in k\}$. Then every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is killed by $p$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.
lemma_165.proof:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ with $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}(k/\wp(k))\le 2$, where $\wp(k)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in k\}$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class satisfies $p\,[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$. We prove $D\cong (L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.

Step 1: $[D]\neq 0$ and $\exp(D)=p$.  If $[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$, then $D$ is Brauer-equivalent to $k$, i.e. $D\cong M_{n}(k)$ for some $n\ge 1$. Since $D$ is a division algebra and $M_{n}(k)$ has zero divisors for every $n\ge 2$ (e.g. a matrix unit $e_{11}$ is a nontrivial idempotent), we must have $n=1$, so $D=k$ and $\deg D=1$, contradicting $\deg D=p^{2}\ge 9$ (as $p>2$). Hence $[D]\neq 0$. The order of $[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ divides $p$ by hypothesis and is strictly larger than $1$; being a divisor of the prime $p$, it equals $p$. Thus $D$ has exponent exactly $p$.

Step 2: $[D]$ is a finite sum of symbol classes.  First note that $\wp\colon k\to k$, $x\mapsto x^{p}-x$, is a homomorphism of additive groups, since $(x+y)^{p}-(x+y)=(x^{p}-x)+(y^{p}-y)$ in characteristic $p$; hence $\wp(k)$ is an additive subgroup of $k$. Moreover $\wp(\lambda x)=\lambda^{p}x-\lambda x=\lambda(x^{p}-x)=\lambda\,\wp(x)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb F_{p}$, so $\wp(k)$ is stable under the $\mathbb F_{p}$-scalar multiplication and $k/\wp(k)$ is an $\mathbb F_{p}$-vector space; the hypothesis $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}(k/\wp(k))\le 2$ is therefore well defined. Since $\mathrm{char}(k)=p>0$, lemma_157 applies to $k$: every element of $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ annihilated by $p$ is a finite sum of classes $[c_{i},z_{i})$ with $c_{i}\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ and $z_{i}\in k^{\times}$, where $[c,z)$ denotes the class of the cyclic algebra $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}k(w)v^{j}$ with $w^{p}-w=c$, $v^{p}=z$ and $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in k(w)$, $\tau(w)=w+1$. Applying this to our class $[D]$, which is annihilated by $p$ by hypothesis, we obtain an integer $r\ge 1$ with
$$[D]=\sum_{i=1}^{r}[c_{i},z_{i}),\qquad c_{i}\in k\setminus\wp(k),\ z_{i}\in k^{\times}.$$
In particular, $[D]$ lies in the subgroup of $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ generated by the symbol classes (with the convention of lemma_140 that $[c,z)=0$ when $c\in\wp(k)$, a convention compatible with the notation just used, since here no $c_i$ lies in $\wp(k)$).

Step 3: the symbol length of $[D]$ is at most two.  Because $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}(k/\wp(k))\le 2$, lemma_140 applies to $k$: every element of $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ belonging to the subgroup generated by the symbol classes is a sum of at most two symbol classes. Applied to $[D]$ (Step 2), it yields elements $a_{1},a_{2}\in k$ and $b_{1},b_{2}\in k^{\times}$ such that
$$[D]=[a_{1},b_{1})+[a_{2},b_{2}).$$
(Consistency check, not needed later: neither $a_i$ can lie in $\wp(k)$, for then the corresponding symbol class is $0$ and $[D]$ would be a single symbol class, hence of index dividing $p$; but $D$ is division, so $\mathrm{ind}(D)=\deg D=p^{2}$, a contradiction. Thus both symbols are nontrivial.)

Step 4: apply lemma_139.  We verify each hypothesis of lemma_139 for the algebra $D$:
(i) $\mathrm{char}(k)=p>2$ — given in the statement;
(ii) $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ — given;
(iii) $D$ has exponent $p$ — Step 1;
(iv) the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is a sum of at most two symbol classes $[c_{i},z_{i})$, where $[c,z)$ is the class of the cyclic algebra $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}k(w)v^{j}$ with $w^{p}-w=c$, $v^{p}=z$, $v\lambda=\tau(\lambda)v$, $\tau(w)=w+1$ — this is exactly Step 3, with the identical notation for symbols.
Lemma_139 then concludes that $D\cong D_{1}\otimes_{k}D_{2}$ with $D_{1},D_{2}$ central division $k$-algebras of degree $p$, and that $D$ is therefore a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.

Step 5: conclusion.  The algebra produced in Step 4 has precisely the form demanded by the statement: $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$ is a group of order $p^{2}$, $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ (i.e. an étale $k$-algebra of $k$-dimension $|G|=p^{2}$ equipped with an action of $G$ by $k$-automorphisms satisfying $L^{G}=k$), $c\colon G\times G\to L^{\times}$ is a $2$-cocycle, and $D\cong\bigoplus_{g\in G}Lu_{g}$ with $u_{g}x=g(x)u_{g}$ and $u_{g}u_{h}=c(g,h)u_{gh}$ for all $x\in L$ and $g,h\in G$. Since $D$ was an arbitrary central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class is killed by $p$, the lemma is proved.

Remark (not used in the argument above). The mechanism inside lemma_139 is the standard one: each degree-$p$ factor is a cyclic (Artin–Schreier) algebra, and the tensor product of the two corresponding degree-$p$ cyclic Galois subalgebras is a $C_{p}\times C_{p}$-Galois algebra of dimension $p^{2}$ inside $D_{1}\otimes_{k}D_{2}$, which then yields the crossed product decomposition.

lemma_167.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and write $\wp(F)=\{x^p-x:x\in F\}$. Let $c_1,c_2\in k\setminus\wp(k)$ and $z_1,z_2\in k^{\times}$, and for $i=1,2$ let $A_i$ be the symbol algebra $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}k(x_i)y_i^{j}$ with $x_i^{p}-x_i=c_i$, $y_i^{p}=z_i$ and $y_i\lambda=\tau_i(\lambda)y_i$ for $\lambda\in k(x_i)$, where $\tau_i(x_i)=x_i+1$. Then $K_1\otimes_k K_2$, with $K_i=k(x_i)$, is a Galois $(C_p\times C_p)$-algebra over $k$, and $A_1\otimes_k A_2$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(K_1\otimes_k K_2,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_p\times C_p$.
lemma_167.proof:
We write \(\wp(F)=\{t^{p}-t:t\in F\}\), \(K_i=k(x_i)\) with \(x_i^{p}-x_i=c_i\), and \(A_i=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}K_i y_i^{j}\) with \(y_i^{p}=z_i\in k^{\times}\), \(y_i\lambda=\tau_i(\lambda)y_i\), \(\tau_i(x_i)=x_i+1\).

STEP 1. The factor algebras and the fields \(K_i\). Fix \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The polynomial \(f_i(T)=T^{p}-T-c_i\in k[T]\) has no root in \(k\) because \(c_i\notin\wp(k)\). Suppose \(f_i\) were reducible over \(k\) and let \(\alpha\) be a root in an extension. The roots of \(f_i\) are exactly \(\alpha,\alpha+1,\dots,\alpha+(p-1)\), all of which lie in \(k(\alpha)\); hence \(k(\alpha)/k\) is Galois with Galois group a subgroup of \((\mathbb F_p,+)\), so \([k(\alpha):k]\in\{1,p\}\). Since \(\alpha\notin k\), \([k(\alpha):k]=p\), contradicting reducibility of a degree-\(p\) polynomial having a proper factor. Thus \(f_i\) is irreducible, \(K_i=k(x_i)\) is a field of degree \(p\) over \(k\); \(f_i'=-1\neq0\) gives separability, and every \(k\)-embedding of \(K_i\) sends \(x_i\mapsto x_i+j\) with \(j\in\mathbb F_p\in K_i\), so \(K_i/k\) is Galois with group \(\langle\tau_i\rangle\cong C_p\). In particular \(K_i\) is an étale \(k\)-algebra of dimension \(p=|C_p|\) with \(K_i^{\langle\tau_i\rangle}=k\), i.e. a Galois \(C_p\)-algebra. By ref_17, \(A_i\) is the symbol algebra \([c_i,z_i)\), a central simple \(k\)-algebra of degree \(p\) which is a cyclic crossed product whose structure Galois algebra is exactly \(K_i=k[x_i]\).

STEP 2. \(L:=K_1\otimes_k K_2\) is étale of dimension \(p^2\). Put \(x=x_1\otimes1\), \(x'=1\otimes x_2\); then \(L=k[x,x']\) with \(x^{p}-x=c_1\), \(x'^{p}-x'=c_2\), \(xx'=x'x\), and the natural map \(K_1[T]/(T^{p}-T-c_2)\to L\), \(T\mapsto 1\otimes x_2\), is an isomorphism. The polynomial \(T^{p}-T-c_2\in K_1[T]\) still has derivative \(-1\neq0\), hence no repeated roots in an algebraic closure, so the quotient is a product of finite separable field extensions of \(K_1\); thus \(L\) is étale over \(K_1\), hence étale over \(k\). Also \(\dim_k L=\dim_k K_1\cdot\dim_k K_2=p^{2}\). (Note that \(L\) need not be a field — e.g. it splits if the two Artin--Schreier extensions coincide — which is harmless, since the definition only asks for an étale algebra.)

STEP 3. The \(G\)-action and the invariants. Define \(\sigma=\tau_1\otimes\mathrm{id}_{K_2}\) and \(\tau=\mathrm{id}_{K_1}\otimes\tau_2\); on generators, \(\sigma(x)=x+1,\ \sigma(x')=x'\), \(\tau(x)=x,\ \tau(x')=x'+1\). These are well-defined \(k\)-automorphisms: for \(a\in\mathbb F_p\), \((x+a)^{p}-(x+a)-c_1=(x^{p}-x-c_1)+(a^{p}-a)=0\) and similarly for \(x'\), and the assignment with parameter \(a\) has inverse the assignment with parameter \(-a\). The maps \(\sigma,\tau\) commute (they act on different tensor factors), and each has exact order \(p\): \(\sigma^{a}(x)=x+a\neq x\) for \(0<a<p\) since \(a\neq0\) in \(k\), and likewise for \(\tau\). Moreover \(\langle\sigma\rangle\cap\langle\tau\rangle=\{1\}\): if \(\sigma^{a}=\tau^{b}\) with \(0\le a,b\le p-1\), evaluating at \(x\) gives \(x+a=x\), so \(a\equiv0\pmod p\), and then \(\tau^{b}=\mathrm{id}\) forces \(b\equiv0\pmod p\) (evaluate at \(x'\)). Hence \(G:=\langle\sigma\rangle\times\langle\tau\rangle\cong C_p\times C_p\) has order \(p^{2}=\dim_k L\).

Invariants. By the normal basis theorem applied to the Galois extension \(K_1/k\), choose \(\theta\in K_1\) with \(\{\tau_1^{i}\theta\}_{i=0}^{p-1}\) a \(k\)-basis of \(K_1\), and let \(\{b_\mu\}\) be a \(k\)-basis of \(K_2\). Then \(\{\tau_1^{i}\theta\otimes b_\mu\}_{i,\mu}\) is a \(k\)-basis of \(L\), and \(\sigma(\tau_1^{i}\theta\otimes b_\mu)=\tau_1^{i+1}\theta\otimes b_\mu\) (index \(i\) mod \(p\)). Writing \(w=\sum_{i,\mu}a_{i\mu}(\tau_1^{i}\theta\otimes b_\mu)\) with \(a_{i\mu}\in k\), the equality \(\sigma(w)=w\) is equivalent to \(a_{i\mu}=a_{i+1,\mu}\) for all \(i,\mu\), i.e. to \(w=N\otimes\beta\) where \(N=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\tau_1^{i}\theta=\operatorname{Tr}_{K_1/k}(\theta)\in k\) and \(\beta=\sum_{\mu}a_{0\mu}b_{\mu}\in K_2\). Here \(N\neq0\) since it is a \(k\)-linear combination with all coefficients \(1\) of distinct members of a \(k\)-basis. Thus \(N\in k^{\times}\) and \(L^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=\{N\otimes\beta:\beta\in K_2\}=1\otimes_k K_2\cong K_2\) (equality as subsets of \(L\), because \(N\in k^{\times}\)). Since the two actions commute, \(L^{G}=(L^{\langle\sigma\rangle})^{\langle\tau\rangle}=(1\otimes K_2)^{\langle\tau\rangle}=1\otimes K_2^{\langle\tau_2\rangle}=1\otimes k=k\).

(This is precisely the \(G_1\times G_2\)-Galois-algebra conclusion of ref_10 applied to the cyclic crossed products \(A_i\) of ref_17; the computation above is the direct verification.) Combining Steps 2 and 3: \(L=K_1\otimes_k K_2\) is an étale \(k\)-algebra of dimension \(p^2=|G|\), \(G\cong C_p\times C_p\) acts on it by \(k\)-automorphisms, and \(L^{G}=k\). That is the first claim: \(L\) is a Galois \((C_p\times C_p)\)-algebra over \(k\).

STEP 4. An \(L\)-basis of \(A_1\otimes_k A_2\). Write \(y=y_1\otimes1\), \(y'=1\otimes y_2\). These are units in \(A_1\otimes_k A_2\) (\(y^{-1}=z_1^{-1}y^{p-1}\), \((y')^{-1}=z_2^{-1}(y')^{p-1}\)), they commute with each other, \(y^{p}=z_1\in k^{\times}\), \((y')^{p}=z_2\in k^{\times}\), and \(yx=(x+1)y\), \(y'x'=(x'+1)y'\), while \(y\) commutes with \(x'\) and \(y'\) commutes with \(x\) (different tensor factors). For \(g=(a,b)\in G\) with \(0\le a,b\le p-1\) set \(u_g=y^{a}(y')^{b}\). Since \(A_i=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}K_i y_i^{j}\) as \(K_i\)-vector space and \(K_i=\bigoplus_{r=0}^{p-1}k\,x_i^{r}\), the monomials \(\{x^{r}x'^{s}y^{i}(y')^{j}:0\le r,s,i,j\le p-1\}\) form a \(k\)-basis of \(A_1\otimes_k A_2\), while \(\{x^{r}x'^{s}\}\) is a \(k\)-basis of \(L\). Hence \(A_1\otimes_k A_2=\bigoplus_{g\in G}L\,u_g\) is free of rank \(|G|=p^{2}\) over \(L\).

STEP 5. The crossed-product relations and the cocycle. For \(g=(a,b)\), conjugation \(\psi_g(\lambda)=u_g\lambda u_g^{-1}\) is a \(k\)-algebra endomorphism of \(A_1\otimes_k A_2\). Using \(yxy^{-1}=x+1\) and that \(y'\) commutes with \(x\), an easy induction gives \(\psi_g(x)=y^{a}xy^{-a}=x+a\in L\), and similarly \(\psi_g(x')=x'+b\in L\); hence \(\psi_g(L)\subseteq L\). Since \(\psi_g\circ\psi_{g'}=\psi_{gg'}\) (the scalar factors \(u_gu_{g'}u_{gg'}^{-1}\in k^{\times}\) are central and cancel), \(\psi_g\) is invertible on \(L\) with inverse \(\psi_{g^{-1}}\), so \(\psi_g|_L\in\mathrm{Aut}_k(L)\); it agrees with the action of \(g\) on the generators \(x,x'\), hence on all of \(L\). Thus
  \[u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)\,u_g\qquad(\lambda\in L,\ g\in G).\]
For the products, with \(g=(a,b)\), \(h=(a',b')\) and \(\varepsilon(r,s)=0\) if \(r+s<p\) and \(\varepsilon(r,s)=1\) if \(r+s\ge p\), we have \(y^{a}y^{a'}=z_1^{\varepsilon(a,a')}y^{a+a'-\varepsilon(a,a')p}\) and likewise for \(y'\), so
  \[u_gu_h=z_1^{\varepsilon(a,a')}z_2^{\varepsilon(b,b')}\,u_{gh},\qquad c(g,h):=z_1^{\varepsilon(a,a')}z_2^{\varepsilon(b,b')}\in k^{\times}\subset L^{\times}.\]
Clearly \(c(1,g)=c(g,1)=1\). For the cocycle identity, use associativity in \(A_1\otimes_k A_2\) and Step 4: for \(g,h,k\in G\),
  \[(u_gu_h)u_k=c(g,h)c(gh,k)\,u_{ghk},\qquad u_g(u_hu_k)=u_gc(h,k)u_{hk}=g(c(h,k))c(g,hk)u_{ghk}=c(h,k)c(g,hk)u_{ghk},\]
where \(g(c(h,k))=c(h,k)\) because \(c(h,k)\in k\) is fixed by \(G\). Comparing the coefficient of the basis element \(u_{ghk}\) over \(L\) yields \(c(g,h)c(gh,k)=c(h,k)c(g,hk)\). So \(c:G\times G\to L^{\times}\) is a normalized \(2\)-cocycle, and \((L,G,c)\) is a well-defined \(G\)-crossed product algebra in the sense of the definition.

STEP 6. The isomorphism. Define \(\Phi:(L,G,c)\to A_1\otimes_k A_2\) on the free \(L\)-module with basis \(\{u_g\}_{g\in G}\) by \(\Phi(\sum_g\lambda_gu_g)=\sum_g\lambda_gu_g\) (right side computed in \(A_1\otimes_kA_2\)). By Step 4, \(\Phi\) is a \(k\)-linear bijection, with \(\Phi|_L=\mathrm{id}_L\) and \(\Phi(1)=1\). For basis elements, using Step 5,
  \[\Phi((\lambda u_g)(\mu u_h))=\Phi(\lambda\,g(\mu)\,u_gu_h)=\lambda\,g(\mu)\,c(g,h)\,u_{gh},\]
  \[\Phi(\lambda u_g)\,\Phi(\mu u_h)=\lambda u_g\mu u_h=\lambda\,(u_g\mu u_g^{-1})\,u_gu_h=\lambda\,g(\mu)\,c(g,h)\,u_{gh}.\]
The two expressions coincide, so \(\Phi\) preserves products of \(L\)-basis elements and is therefore a \(k\)-algebra isomorphism.

CONCLUSION. \(K_1\otimes_kK_2\) is a Galois \((C_p\times C_p)\)-algebra over \(k\) (Step 3) and \(A_1\otimes_kA_2\cong(K_1\otimes_kK_2,\,G,\,c)\) with \(G\cong C_p\times C_p\) (Step 6), which is the claim. As a consistency check, since \(L\) is a \(G\)-Galois algebra and \(c\) a normalized \(2\)-cocycle, ref_3 (converse direction) gives that \((L,G,c)\), hence \(A_1\otimes_kA_2\), is central simple of degree \(p^2\) with \(L\) a maximal commutative subalgebra; this matches ref_10, which in the present situation already predicts that the tensor product of the two cyclic degree-\(p\) crossed products \(A_i\) is a \(C_p\times C_p\)-crossed product built from \(K_1\otimes_kK_2\).

lemma_166.statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $p$ be a prime, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. If $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group isomorphic to $C_p\times C_p$, then the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is annihilated by $p$.
lemma_166.proof:
The statement of lemma_166 is FALSE as written, so no proof exists; below is a counterexample, valid for every prime p, in which D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2 containing a maximal subfield Galois over k with group C_p x C_p, while exp(D) = p^2, so that p[D] \neq 0 in Br(k).

STEP 0. The field. Let k = \mathbb{F}_p((t)), complete for the t-adic valuation v with v(k^\times) = \mathbb{Z}, valuation ring \mathbb{F}_p[[t]] and residue field \mathbb{F}_p.

STEP 1. Norms in unramified extensions. Claim: if M/L is unramified of degree m of complete discretely valued fields with finite residue fields, then N_{M/L}(M^\times) = { y \in L^\times : m divides v_L(y) }.
Proof. A uniformizer \pi of L is also a uniformizer of M and is fixed by every L-embedding of M, so N(\pi) = \pi^m; writing x = \pi^i \varepsilon gives v_L(N(x)) = mi + v_L(N(\varepsilon)) with N(\varepsilon) integral and invertible (N(\varepsilon)^{-1} = N(\varepsilon^{-1})), hence v_L(N(\varepsilon)) = 0. This proves \subseteq. For \supseteq it suffices that N : \mathcal{O}_M^\times \to \mathcal{O}_L^\times is onto. Write U_L^{(i)} = 1 + \pi^i \mathcal{O}_L.
