(b) For $m\in\mathbb Z$, every non-zero element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)_m$ is of the form $\mathrm{in}_v(x)$ with $x\in k^\times$, $v(x)=m$; and then necessarily $w(x-m\text{ term})$... precisely, if $\mathrm{in}_w(y)=\mathrm{in}_v(x)$ for $y\in D$, $x\in k$, then $y-x\in I_{>w(y)}$, i.e. $w(y-x)>w(y)$.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose there exists $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^p-a=c\in k$.

**Step 1: $c\ne 0$.** If $c=0$ then $a^p=a$, so $a$ is algebraic over $\mathbb F_p$. The subring $\mathbb F_p[a]$ is commutative (it is generated by one element over the central field $\mathbb F_p$), and since $a^p=a$ every power of $a$ is a linear combination of $1,a,\dots,a^{p-1}$, so $\mathbb F_p[a]$ is a finite-dimensional, hence finite, commutative integral domain (a subring of the division ring $D$). A finite domain is a field; inside the field $\mathbb F_p[a]$ the polynomial $T^p-T$ has at most $p$ roots, and the $p$ elements of $\mathbb F_p$ are already roots, so $a\in\mathbb F_p\subset k$, contradicting $a\notin k$. Hence $c\ne0$; in particular $a\ne0$.

**Step 2: reduction to an element of non-negative value.** We claim there exist $x_1,\dots,x_r\in k$ such that, with $a_0:=a$, $c_0:=c$ and
$$a_{i+1}:=a_i-x_{i+1},\qquad c_{i+1}:=c_i-(x_{i+1}^{\,p}-x_{i+1})\in k,$$\nfor $i=0,\dots,r-1$, one has $w(a_r)\ge 0$.

We construct these inductively. Suppose $a_i$ has been produced with
$$(\ast_i)\qquad a_i\notin k,\quad a_i^{p}-a_i=c_i\in k,\quad w(a_i)<0 .$$
(The case $i=0$ is exactly our assumption, since $a_0=a\notin k$; note that if $w(a)\ge0$ we may stop immediately with $r=0$.) Because $a_i\notin k$ we have $a_i\ne0$, so $\mathrm{in}_w(a_i)$ is a well-defined non-zero homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ of degree $w(a_i)<0$. Applying **lemma_163** to $a_i$ and $c_i$ (its hypotheses are satisfied: $k$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>0$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, $a_i^p-a_i=c_i\in k$, $w(a_i)<0$) we obtain
$$p\,w(a_i)=v(c_i)<0,\qquad w(a_i)\in\tfrac1p\mathbb Z,\qquad \mathrm{in}_w(a_i)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_v(c_i)\in\mathrm{gr}(k)_{v(c_i)}\subset\mathrm{gr}(k).$$
Thus the homogeneous element $\mathrm{in}_w(a_i)$ of negative degree has its $p$-th power in $\mathrm{gr}(k)$. By hypothesis (2) of the lemma, $\mathrm{in}_w(a_i)$ must belong to $\mathrm{gr}(k)$. Since $\mathrm{in}_w(a_i)\ne0$ and, by (a), $\mathrm{gr}(k)_\gamma=0$ for $\gamma\notin\mathbb Z$, its degree $w(a_i)$ lies in $\mathbb Z$; by (b) there is $x_{i+1}\in k^\times$ with $v(x_{i+1})=w(a_i)$ and $\mathrm{in}_v(x_{i+1})=\mathrm{in}_w(a_i)$. Then $w(a_i-x_{i+1})>w(a_i)$ by (b). Moreover, since $x_{i+1}\in k$ is central in $D$ and $\mathrm{char}\,D=p$,
$$a_{i+1}^{p}-a_{i+1}=(a_i-x_{i+1})^{p}-(a_i-x_{i+1})=(a_i^{p}-a_i)-(x_{i+1}^{p}-x_{i+1})=c_{i+1}\in k .$$
Also $a_{i+1}\notin k$: otherwise $a=a_{i+1}+(x_1+\cdots+x_{i+1})\in k$, contradiction. Hence $(\ast_{i+1})$ holds whenever $w(a_{i+1})<0$, and the construction continues.

This construction cannot continue indefinitely. Indeed, all the values $w(a_i)$ that are $<0$ lie in $\tfrac1p\mathbb Z$ (by lemma_163, applied at each such step) and satisfy $w(a_i)\ge w(a_0)$, so they belong to the finite set $S=(\tfrac1p\mathbb Z)\cap[w(a_0),0)$, which has at most $p|w(a_0)|+1$ elements. Since the values strictly increase at each step, at most $|S|$ steps occur. Therefore there is an index $r\ge0$ with $w(a_r)\ge0$. Set $b:=a_r$ and $c':=c_r$. We have
$$b\notin k,\qquad b^{p}-b=c'\in k,\qquad w(b)\ge0.$$

**Step 3: producing an element of strictly positive value.** Since $w(b)\ge0$, also $w(b^p)=p\,w(b)\ge0$, hence $v(c')=w(c')=w(b^p-b)\ge\min(pw(b),w(b))\ge0$. Thus $b\in\mathcal O_w$, $c'\in\mathcal O_k$, and taking residues in $\bar D$ (a ring homomorphism on $\mathcal O_w$) gives
$$\bar b^{\,p}-\bar b=\overline{b^p-b}=\bar c'\in\bar k .$$
(If $w(b)>0$ this reads $0-0=0$.) By hypothesis (1) of the lemma, $\bar D$ contains no element outside $\bar k$ whose Artin--Schreier value lies in $\bar k$; hence $\bar b\in\bar k$. Choose $\lambda\in\mathcal O_k\subset k$ with $\bar\lambda=\bar b$. Then $b-\lambda\in I_{>0}$, i.e.
$$d:=b-\lambda\ \ \text{satisfies}\ \ w(d)>0 .$$
Furthermore $d\notin k$ (otherwise $b=d+\lambda\in k$), and as $\lambda$ is central and $\mathrm{char}\,D=p$,
$$d^{p}-d=(b-\lambda)^p-(b-\lambda)=(b^p-b)-(\lambda^p-\lambda)=c'-(\lambda^p-\lambda)\in k .$$

**Step 4: contradiction.** We have produced an element $d\in D$ with $d\notin k$, $d^p-d\in k$ and $w(d)>0$. This contradicts **lemma_162**, which states that over a field $k$ complete for a discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, a central division $k$-algebra $D$ with the valuation $w$ extending $v$ contains no element $a\notin k$ with $a^p-a\in k$ and $w(a)>0$.

The contradiction shows that no such $a$ exists, i.e. $D$ contains no element $a\notin k$ with $a^p-a\in k$. $\blacksquare$

lemma_180.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, write $\wp(F)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in F\}$, let $c\in k\setminus\wp(k)$, let $K=k(z)$ with $z^{p}-z=c$, and let $\sigma$ be the $k$-automorphism of $K$ with $\sigma(z)=z+1$. Then the homomorphism of $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector spaces $k/(\wp(k)+\mathbb{F}_p\cdot c)\to (K/\wp(K))^{\sigma}$ induced by the inclusion $k\hookrightarrow K$ is injective, and its cokernel is one-dimensional over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
lemma_180.proof:
We write wp(u) = u^p - u, Δ = σ - 1 (so Δ(u) = σ(u) - u), and Tr = Tr_{K/k} = Σ_{i=0}^{p-1} σ^i.

**Step 1: K/k is Galois of degree p with group <σ>.** The polynomial f(T) = T^p - T - c has derivative -1, hence is separable, and it has no root in k because c ∉ wp(k). If α is a root (in an algebraic closure), the full root set is {α + i : i ∈ F_p}, all contained in k(α); thus the splitting field is k(α), and Gal(k(α)/k) embeds in the translation group {α ↦ α + i} ≅ Z/p, acting transitively on the roots (there is no root in k). Hence f is irreducible, K = k(z) is a field, [K:k] = p, Gal(K/k) = {1, σ, …, σ^{p-1}} with σ^i(z) = z + i, and K^σ = k.

**Step 2: The spaces involved.** wp is additive ((u+v)^p - (u+v) = wp(u) + wp(v)) and wp(tu) = t·wp(u) for t ∈ F_p, so wp(K) is an F_p-subspace of K; it is σ-stable since σ(wp(u)) = wp(σ(u)). Hence K/wp(K) is an F_p-vector space with F_p-linear σ-action, and
  (K/wp(K))^σ = { x̄ : x ∈ K, Δx ∈ wp(K) },  x̄ := class of x in K/wp(K).
Both Δ and Tr are k-linear endomorphisms of K (Tr lands in k).

**Step 3: im(Δ) = ker(Tr).** (i) im(Δ) ⊆ ker(Tr): Tr(Δw) = Σ_{i=0}^{p-1} σ^{i+1}(w) - Σ_{i=0}^{p-1} σ^i(w) = 0 by reindexing and σ^p = 1. (ii) ker(Δ) = K^σ = k, so by rank–nullity over k, dim_k im(Δ) = [K:k] - 1 = p - 1. (iii) Tr ≠ 0: expanding, Tr(z^{p-1}) = Σ_{i∈F_p}(z+i)^{p-1} = Σ_{j=0}^{p-1} C(p-1,j) z^{p-1-j} (Σ_{i∈F_p} i^j). For 0 ≤ j ≤ p-2 one has Σ_{i∈F_p} i^j = 0: for j = 0 it equals p = 0, and for 1 ≤ j ≤ p-2, choosing a ∈ F_p^× with a^j ≠ 1 gives Σ_i i^j = Σ_i (ai)^j = a^j Σ_i i^j, so the sum vanishes. For j = p-1, Σ_{i∈F_p} i^{p-1} = Σ_{i≠0} 1 = p - 1 = -1. Hence Tr(z^{p-1}) = -1 ≠ 0 (this also holds for p = 2, where Tr(z) = z + (z+1) = 1 = -1). Thus Tr: K → k is a nonzero k-linear map onto k, so dim_k ker(Tr) = p - 1. Combining (i)–(iii), im(Δ) = ker(Tr).

**Step 4: Injectivity.** The inclusion k → K sends a ∈ k to a σ-invariant class (Δa = 0). Its kernel is {a ∈ k : a ∈ wp(K)} = wp(K) ∩ k = wp(k) + F_p·c, by lemma_121 (Spark). Hence k/(wp(k) + F_p·c) ↪ (K/wp(K))^σ injectively.

**Step 5: An F_p-linear functional Ψ: (K/wp(K))^σ → F_p.** Let V = (K/wp(K))^σ and x̄ ∈ V; choose y ∈ K with wp(y) = Δx (exists since x̄ ∈ V) and set Ψ(x̄) = Tr(y). We check this is well defined.
(a) Tr(y) ∈ F_p: using that Frobenius commutes with each σ^i, wp(Tr y) = Σ_i σ^i(y)^p - Σ_i σ^i(y) = Σ_i σ^i(wp y) = Tr(Δx) = 0 by Step 3(i). The elements of the field k with wp = 0 are exactly F_p (T^p - T has at most p roots, and all of F_p are roots).
(b) Independence of y: if wp(y') = wp(y) then (y'-y)^p = y'-y, so y' - y ∈ F_p, and Tr(y') = Tr(y) + Tr(t) = Tr(y) + p·t = Tr(y) for t = y'-y.
(c) Independence of the representative x: replacing x by x + wp(w) gives Δ(x + wp(w)) = Δx + Δ(wp w) = wp(y) + wp(Δw) = wp(y + Δw), where we used Δ∘wp = wp∘Δ, verified directly: (σu - u)^p - (σu - u) = σ(u)^p - u^p - σ(u) + u = σ(wp u) - wp(u). The new trace is Tr(y + Δw) = Tr(y) + 0 = Tr(y).
Additivity: for x̄₁, x̄₂ ∈ V with wp(y_m) = Δx_m, wp(y₁+y₂) = Δ(x₁+x₂), so Ψ(x̄₁+x̄₂) = Tr(y₁+y₂) = Ψ(x̄₁)+Ψ(x̄₂); similarly Δ(t x) = wp(t y) gives Ψ(t x̄) = t Ψ(x̄) for t ∈ F_p. So Ψ is F_p-linear.

**Step 6: ker Ψ = image of k.** If x̄ is the image of a ∈ k, then Δa = 0 = wp(0), so Ψ(x̄) = Tr(0) = 0. Conversely, suppose Ψ(x̄) = 0 with wp(y) = Δx. Then Tr(y) = 0, so by Step 3, y = Δu for some u ∈ K. Then Δx = wp(y) = wp(Δu) = Δ(wp u), hence Δ(x - wp u) = 0, so a := x - wp u ∈ ker(Δ) = k, and x̄ equals the image of a.

**Step 7: Ψ is surjective.** Take y₀ = -z^{p-1}; by Step 3(iii), Tr(y₀) = 1. Then Tr(wp y₀) = wp(Tr y₀) = wp(1) = 1^p - 1 = 0, so wp(y₀) ∈ ker(Tr) = im(Δ), and there exists x ∈ K with Δx = wp(y₀). Then x̄ ∈ V and Ψ(x̄) = Tr(y₀) = 1 ≠ 0.

**Step 8: Conclusion.** By Steps 4 and 6, the image of k/(wp(k) + F_p·c) in V is exactly ker Ψ, and the induced map k/(wp(k)+F_p·c) → V is injective (Step 4). By Step 7, Ψ induces an F_p-linear isomorphism V / im(k) ≅ V/ker Ψ ≅ F_p. Therefore the cokernel of k/(wp(k) + F_p·c) → (K/wp(K))^σ is a one-dimensional F_p-vector space. ∎

lemma_174.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation with perfect residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra with the valuation $w$ extending $v$ and residue division ring $\bar D$, and suppose that $\bar D$ is a field which is purely inseparable over $\bar k$. Then every subfield $K$ of $D$ that is finite separable over $k$ has residue field $\bar k$, and consequently $[K:k]=[w(K^\times):v(k^\times)]$, i.e. $K/k$ is totally ramified.
lemma_174.proof:
PROOF.

=== Notation and general facts ===
Since $v$ is a discrete valuation we normalise it so that $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$, and we fix a uniformiser $\pi\in k$ with $v(\pi)=1$. Write $\mathcal O_v=\{c\in k:v(c)\ge 0\}$, $\mathfrak m_v=\{c:v(c)>0\}$, so $\bar k=\mathcal O_v/\mathfrak m_v$, which is perfect by hypothesis; $k$ is complete for $v$.

The valuation $w$ on the division ring $D$ has value group $\Gamma:=w(D^{\times})$ (an ordered abelian group), and $\mathcal O_w=\{\alpha\in D:w(\alpha)\ge 0\}$, $\mathfrak m_w=\{\alpha:w(\alpha)>0\}$. Because $w(\alpha\beta)=w(\alpha)+w(\beta)$ and $w(\alpha^{-1})=-w(\alpha)$, $\mathcal O_w$ is a subring of $D$ whose units are exactly $\{\alpha:w(\alpha)=0\}=\mathcal O_w\setminus\mathfrak m_w$; hence $\mathfrak m_w$ is the unique maximal two-sided ideal of $\mathcal O_w$, $\bar D:=\mathcal O_w/\mathfrak m_w$ is a division ring, and the reduction map $\mathrm{red}\colon\mathcal O_w\twoheadrightarrow\bar D$ is a surjective ring homomorphism.

The field $\bar k$ lies in the centre of $\bar D$: for $c\in\mathcal O_v$ and $\alpha\in\mathcal O_w$ one has $c\alpha=\alpha c$ since $c\in k=Z(D)$, and applying $\mathrm{red}$ gives $\mathrm{red}(c)\mathrm{red}(\alpha)=\mathrm{red}(\alpha)\mathrm{red}(c)$; every element of $\bar D$ is a reduced value, so $\mathrm{red}(c)\in Z(\bar D)$. Consequently $\mathrm{char}\,\bar D=\mathrm{char}\,\bar k$ (both equal the additive order of $1$, and $\bar D\ne 0$). Thus the only relevant characteristic is the residue characteristic; we never split on $\mathrm{char}\,k$, which may be $0$ with $\mathrm{char}\,\bar k=p>0$.

For a subfield $F\subseteq D$ we write $\Gamma_F:=w(F^{\times})$, $\mathcal O_F:=\mathcal O_w\cap F=\{a\in F:w(a)\ge0\}$, $\mathfrak m_F:=\mathfrak m_w\cap F$, $\bar F:=\mathcal O_F/\mathfrak m_F$. Note $\Gamma_k=v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z\subseteq\Gamma_F$.

=== Claim 1. $\dim_{\bar k}\bar D\le [D:k]$. ===
Let $\bar\alpha_1,\dots,\bar\alpha_r\in\bar D$ be $\bar k$-linearly independent, with $\alpha_i\in\mathcal O_w$ (possible by surjectivity of reduction). We show $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ are $k$-linearly independent. Suppose $\sum_i a_i\alpha_i=0$ with $a_i\in k$; if some $a_i\ne0$, let $\mu=\min_i v(a_i)$ over the non-zero $a_i$ and put $b_i=\pi^{-\mu}a_i\in\mathcal O_v$. Then $\sum_i b_i\alpha_i=0$, every $b_i$ has $v(b_i)\ge0$ (so $b_i\alpha_i\in\mathcal O_w$, as $w(b_i\alpha_i)=v(b_i)+w(\alpha_i)\ge0$), and at least one $b_i$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_v$, i.e. $v(b_i)=0$. Reducing gives $\sum_i\mathrm{red}(b_i)\bar\alpha_i=0$ in $\bar D$ with some $\mathrm{red}(b_i)\ne0$: a non-trivial $\bar k$-linear relation, contradiction. Hence $r\le\dim_k D=[D:k]$, and since the independent set was arbitrary, $\dim_{\bar k}\bar D\le[D:k]<\infty$. In particular $\bar D/\bar k$ is a finite (hence algebraic) field extension, $\bar D$ being a field by hypothesis.

=== Claim 2. $\bar D=\bar k$. ===
We split on the residue characteristic.
(a) $\mathrm{char}\,\bar k=0$. Then $\mathrm{char}\,\bar D=0$. Let $\xi\in\bar D$. By Claim 1, $\xi$ is algebraic over $\bar k$; the subring $\bar k[\xi]$ is a commutative domain (it is a subring of the division ring $\bar D$, and $\xi$ commutes with $\bar k\subseteq Z(\bar D)$) which is finite dimensional over $\bar k$ (a $\bar k$-subspace of $\bar D$), and a finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field; so $\bar k(\xi)$ is a field, finite over $\bar k$. Being a subextension of the purely inseparable extension $\bar D/\bar k$, the extension $\bar k(\xi)/\bar k$ is purely inseparable; being of characteristic $0$ it is separable. Let $\Omega$ be an algebraic closure of $\bar k(\xi)$. Separability gives $[\bar k(\xi):\bar k]=|\mathrm{Hom}_{\bar k}(\bar k(\xi),\Omega)|$, while pure inseparability says the minimal polynomial of $\xi$ over $\bar k$ has exactly one root in $\Omega$, so every $\bar k$-embedding fixes $\xi$ and hence $|\mathrm{Hom}_{\bar k}(\bar k(\xi),\Omega)|=1$; thus $[\bar k(\xi):\bar k]=1$ and $\xi\in\bar k$.
(b) $\mathrm{char}\,\bar k=p>0$. Let $\xi\in\bar D$. Since $\bar D$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$ there is $m\ge0$ with $\xi^{p^{m}}\in\bar k$. Since $\bar k$ is perfect, the $p^{m}$-power map on $\bar k$ is bijective, so there is $\eta\in\bar k$ with $\eta^{p^{m}}=\xi^{p^{m}}$. The subring $\bar k[\xi]$ is commutative ($\bar k$ is central in $\bar D$), and in a commutative ring of characteristic $p$ the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^{p^{m}}$ is additive; hence $(\xi-\eta)^{p^{m}}=\xi^{p^{m}}-\eta^{p^{m}}=0$. A division ring has no non-zero nilpotent elements, so $\xi=\eta\in\bar k$.
In both cases $\bar D=\bar k$.

=== Claim 3. The residue field of $K$ is $\bar k$. ===
$\mathcal O_K=\mathcal O_w\cap K$ is the valuation ring of the valued field $(K,w|_K)$ and $\mathfrak m_K=\mathfrak m_w\cap K$ is its maximal ideal: indeed for $a\in\mathcal O_K^{\times}$ one has $a^{-1}\in\mathcal O_K$ iff $w(a)=0$, so $\mathcal O_K\setminus\mathfrak m_K=\mathcal O_K^{\times}$ is the unit group. Restricting $\mathrm{red}$ to $\mathcal O_K$ gives a ring homomorphism $\mathcal O_K\to\bar D$ with kernel $\mathfrak m_K$, hence an injective homomorphism of fields $\bar K=\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak m_K\hookrightarrow\bar D$. Its image contains $\mathrm{red}(\mathcal O_v)=\bar k$. By Claim 2, $\bar D=\bar k$, so the inclusion is an equality: $\bar K=\bar k$, i.e. $f(K/k):=[\bar K:\bar k]=1$. This is the first assertion of the lemma.

=== Claim 4 (strict triangle inequality; independence across distinct value cosets). ===
(a) If $w(a)\ne w(b)$ then $w(a+b)=\min(w(a),w(b))$; by induction, if $w(a_1),\dots,a_n$ have pairwise distinct values then $w(\sum_i a_i)=\min_i w(a_i)$ (so such a sum is non-zero).
Proof of (a): assume $w(a)<w(b)$. Subadditivity gives $w(a+b)\ge w(a)$. If $w(a+b)>w(a)$ then $w(a)=w((a+b)-b)\ge\min(w(a+b),w(b))>w(a)$, absurd. Hence $w(a+b)=w(a)$. The induction step uses that $w(\sum_{i<n}a_i)=\min_{i<n}w(a_i)$ is distinct from $w(a_n)$, so the two-term case applies.
(b) Let $x_1,\dots,x_r\in K^{\times}$ have $w(x_i)$ in pairwise distinct cosets of $\mathbb Z=v(k^{\times})$ in $\Gamma_K$. Then $x_1,\dots,x_r$ are $k$-linearly independent.
Proof: if $\sum_i c_i x_i=0$ with $c_i\in k$ and $I=\{i:c_i\ne0\}\ne\emptyset$, then for $i\in I$ the values $w(c_ix_i)=v(c_i)+w(x_i)$ lie in pairwise distinct cosets of $\mathbb Z$, hence are pairwise distinct; by (a) the sum has value $\min_{i\in I}(v(c_i)+w(x_i))\in\Gamma_K$, so it is non-zero, contradiction. Thus all $c_i=0$. Note that no finiteness of $\Gamma_K/\mathbb Z$ is used.

=== Claim 5. $e:=[\Gamma_K:\mathbb Z]$ is finite, $e\le[K:k]$, and every positive element of $\Gamma_K$ is $\ge 1/e$. ===
If $\Gamma_K/\mathbb Z$ were infinite we could choose $[K:k]+1$ elements of $K^{\times}$ whose values lie in pairwise distinct cosets; Claim 4(b) would then exhibit $[K:k]+1$ $k$-linearly independent elements of $K$, impossible. So $e<\infty$, and taking a maximal family as in Claim 4(b) gives $e\le[K:k]$. Finally, for $\delta\in\Gamma_K$ the image of $\delta$ in the group $\Gamma_K/\mathbb Z$ of order $e$ satisfies $e\delta\in\mathbb Z$; if $\delta>0$ then $e\delta\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, so $\delta\ge1/e$. In particular $\Gamma_K\subseteq\frac1e\mathbb Z$, so no element of $\Gamma_K$ dominates all integers.

=== Claim 6 (coset representatives with a Gauss property). ===
There are $t_1,\dots,t_e\in K^{\times}$ whose values form a set of representatives of $\Gamma_K/\mathbb Z$ with $0\le w(t_j)<1$ for all $j$, and for all $c_1,\dots,c_e\in k$,
$\qquad w\big(\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{e}c_jt_j\big)=\min_j\big(v(c_j)+w(t_j)\big)\qquad(*)$
(non-zero coefficients only; the empty minimum corresponds to the sum $0$).
Proof: given a coset $C\in\Gamma_K/\mathbb Z$ pick $\gamma\in C$; then $e\gamma=m\in\mathbb Z$, and $\gamma':=\gamma-\lfloor m/e\rfloor$ still lies in $C$ (as $\lfloor m/e\rfloor\in\mathbb Z$) and satisfies $0\le\gamma'=m/e-\lfloor m/e\rfloor<1$; choose $t$ with $w(t)=\gamma'$. Doing this for each of the $e$ cosets gives the $t_j$. For $(*)$: if $c_i,c_j\ne0$ with $i\ne j$ and $v(c_i)+w(t_i)=v(c_j)+w(t_j)$, then $w(t_i)-w(t_j)=v(c_j)-v(c_i)\in\mathbb Z$, contradicting that the $w(t_j)$ lie in distinct cosets. So the values of the non-zero terms $c_jt_j$ are pairwise distinct, and $(*)$ follows from Claim 4(a). Taking all $c_j=1$ shows the $t_j$ are $k$-linearly independent, so $\dim_k M=e$ where $M:=\sum_j k t_j$.

=== Claim 7. $M$ is complete for the metric induced by $w$. ===
By the previous claim $\Phi\colon k^{e}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }M$, $(c_j)\mapsto\sum_j c_jt_j$ is a $k$-linear isomorphism. Let $(x_\nu)$ be $w$-Cauchy in $M$, $x_\nu=\sum_j c_j^{(\nu)}t_j$. Given an integer $B$, for $\nu,\mu$ large, $w(x_\nu-x_\mu)\ge B$; by $(*)$, for every $j$ we have $v(c_j^{(\nu)}-c_j^{(\mu)})+w(t_j)\ge B$, hence $v(c_j^{(\nu)}-c_j^{(\mu)})\ge B-w(t_j)\ge B-1$ (as $w(t_j)<1$). Thus each $(c_j^{(\nu)})$ is $v$-Cauchy in $k$ and converges, since $k$ is complete, to some $c_j\in k$. Then $x:=\sum_j c_jt_j\in M$ and $w(x_\nu-x)\ge\min_j\big(v(c_j^{(\nu)}-c_j)+w(t_j)\big)$, which exceeds every integer for $\nu$ large; so $x_\nu\to x$ in $M$.

=== Claim 8. $\mathcal O_K\subseteq M$; consequently $K=M$ and $[K:k]=e$. ===
Let $y\in\mathcal O_K$, $y\ne0$. We construct, as long as the remainders are non-zero, sequences $(i_m)_{m\ge0}$ in $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, $(j_m)$ in $\{1,\dots,e\}$, $(\lambda_m)$ in $\mathcal O_v$, and remainders $r_m\in K$ with $r_0=y$ and
$\qquad r_m=\pi^{i_m}t_{j_m}\lambda_m+r_{m+1},\qquad w(r_m)\ge w(y)+m/e.\qquad(\dagger)$
Suppose $r_m\ne0$ and $w(r_m)\ge w(y)+m/e\ge0$. Since $\Gamma_K=\bigsqcup_j\,(w(t_j)+\mathbb Z)$ there are unique $i\in\mathbb Z$, $j\in\{1,\dots,e\}$ with $w(r_m)=i+w(t_j)$. As $w(r_m)\ge0$ and $w(t_j)<1$, we get $i=w(r_m)-w(t_j)>-1$, hence $i\ge0$. Put $u:=\pi^{-i}t_j^{-1}r_m\in K^{\times}$; then $w(u)=w(r_m)-i-w(t_j)=0$, so $u\in\mathcal O_K^{\times}$. By Claim 3, $\mathrm{red}(u)\in\bar K=\bar k=\mathrm{red}(\mathcal O_v)$; choose $\lambda\in\mathcal O_v$ with $\mathrm{red}(\lambda)=\mathrm{red}(u)$, i.e. $w(u-\lambda)>0$. By Claim 5, $w(u-\lambda)\ge1/e$. Define $r_{m+1}:=\pi^{i}t_j(u-\lambda)$ and $(i_m,j_m,\lambda_m):=(i,j,\lambda)$. Then $r_m=\pi^{i_m}t_{j_m}\lambda_m+r_{m+1}$ and $w(r_{m+1})=i+w(t_j)+w(u-\lambda)\ge w(r_m)+1/e\ge w(y)+(m+1)/e$, which is $(\dagger)$. (If some $r_m=0$ the construction stops and the argument below is simpler.)

Let $s_N:=\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\pi^{i_m}t_{j_m}\lambda_m\in M$ (each term lies in $M$ since $\pi^{i_m}\lambda_m\in k$). Then $y-s_N=r_N$, so by $(\dagger)$ the values $w(y-s_N)\ge w(y)+N/e$ exceed every integer as $N\to\infty$. Moreover $(s_N)$ is $w$-Cauchy in $M$, since for $M>N$, $w(s_M-s_N)=w(r_N-r_M)\ge\min(w(r_N),w(r_M))\to\infty$. By Claim 7 there is $z\in M$ with $s_N\to z$, i.e. $w(s_N-z)$ exceeds every integer. Then $w(y-z)\ge\min(w(y-s_N),w(s_N-z))$ exceeds every integer. By Claim 5, $\Gamma_K\subseteq\frac1e\mathbb Z$, so no element of $\Gamma_K$ is larger than all integers; therefore $y-z=0$ and $y=z\in M$. Hence $\mathcal O_K\subseteq M$.

Now let $a\in K^{\times}$; write $w(a)=i+w(t_j)$ with $i\in\mathbb Z$ (possibly negative) and set $u:=\pi^{-i}t_j^{-1}a$, which has value $0$, so $u\in\mathcal O_K\subseteq M$. Since $M$ is a $k$-vector space and $\pi^{i}\in k^{\times}$, $a=\pi^{i}u\in M$. Thus $K=M$, and $[K:k]=\dim_k M=e$ by the independence of the $t_j$ noted in Claim 6.

=== Conclusion ===
Claim 3 gives $\bar K=\bar k$: every subfield $K\subseteq D$ finite separable over $k$ has residue field $\bar k$ (the separability hypothesis is in fact not needed for the argument). Claim 8 gives
$\qquad [K:k]=e=[\Gamma_K:\mathbb Z]=[w(K^{\times}):v(k^{\times})],$
which is exactly the assertion that $K/k$ is totally ramified. $\blacksquare$

(Consistency remark: combined with the general fundamental inequality $[K:k]\ge [w(K^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\,[\bar K:\bar k]$, the equality $\bar K=\bar k$ forces $[K:k]\ge e$, and Claim 8 gives the reverse inequality; equivalently, a finite subextension of $D$ over a complete discretely valued field with perfect residue field has no defect and, its residue degree being $1$, is totally ramified.)

lemma_182.statement: Let $k$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation $v$ of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ and residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra with the valuation $w$ extending $v$ and residue division ring $\bar D$, and let $a\in D\setminus k$ satisfy $a^{p}-a\in k$. Then either $w(a)<0$ and $p\,w(a)=v(a^{p}-a)<0$, or $w(a)=0$, $v(a^{p}-a)=0$, and the residue $\bar a\in\bar D$ satisfies $\bar a^{p}-\bar a\in\bar k$ with $\bar a\notin\bar k$.
lemma_182.proof:
We write the valuation as w: D -> Γ ∪ {∞}, a Krull valuation of the division ring D (so w(xy)=w(x)+w(y), w(x+y) ≥ min{w(x),w(y)}, w(0)=∞, w(1)=0) whose restriction to k is v; Γ = w(D^×) is a totally ordered abelian group containing v(k^×)=ℤ. Since D ⊃ k, D has characteristic p. The argument uses only p ≥ 2; the hypothesis p>2 is stronger than needed.

PART 0. Formal facts about the value group. Since (-1)^2 = 1 we have 2w(-1) = w(1) = 0 in the ordered (hence torsion-free) group Γ, so w(-1)=0 and therefore w(-x) = w(x) for every x ∈ D^× (and trivially for x=0). Also, in any ordered abelian group, nγ < 0 whenever γ<0 and n≥1, and nγ > 0 whenever γ>0 and n≥1.

PART 1. Strict triangle inequality. If u,v ∈ D with w(u) < w(v), then w(u+v) = w(u). Indeed the ultrametric inequality gives w(u+v) ≥ min{w(u),w(v)} = w(u). If instead w(u+v) > w(u), apply the ultrametric inequality to the identity u = (u+v) - v: w(u) ≥ min{w(u+v), w(-v)} = min{w(u+v), w(v)}, where w(-v)=w(v) by Part 0. By assumption w(u+v) > w(u), and by hypothesis w(v) > w(u); hence min{w(u+v), w(v)} > w(u), giving w(u) > w(u), a contradiction. (The subtraction must be applied to u = (u+v) - v; applying it to v = (u+v) - u would only give min{w(u+v),w(u)} = w(u) and no contradiction.)

PART 2. The valuation ring of D. Put O_D = {x ∈ D : w(x) ≥ 0} and M_D = {x ∈ D : w(x) > 0}.
(a) O_D is a subring of D containing 1: w(0)=∞ ≥ 0, w(1)=0; for x,y ∈ O_D one has w(x-y) ≥ min{w(x),w(y)} ≥ 0 and w(xy) = w(x)+w(y) ≥ 0.
(b) M_D is a two-sided ideal of O_D: for r,s ∈ M_D, w(r-s) ≥ min{w(r),w(s)} > 0; and for r ∈ M_D, s ∈ O_D, w(rs) = w(r)+w(s) = w(sr) > 0 since w(s) ≥ 0.
(c) The units of O_D are exactly the elements of value 0: if w(x)=0 then w(x^{-1}) = -w(x) = 0, so x^{-1} ∈ O_D; conversely if x ∈ O_D is a unit of O_D with w(x) > 0, then x^{-1} ∈ O_D and 0 = w(1) = w(x)+w(x^{-1}) ≥ w(x) > 0, a contradiction. Thus M_D = O_D \ O_D^× is the set of non-units, hence the unique maximal two-sided ideal, and D̄ := O_D/M_D is a division ring. The reduction map ρ: O_D → D̄, ρ(x) = x̄ := x + M_D, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel M_D. (We do not claim O_D is a subdivision ring: that is false, e.g. w(x)=0, w(y)>0 gives w(xy^{-1})<0.)
(d) Since w|_k = v, with O_k = {α ∈ k : v(α) ≥ 0} and m_k = {α ∈ k : v(α) > 0}, we have O_k ⊂ O_D and m_k ⊂ M_D; the induced map k̄ = O_k/m_k → D̄ is injective (its kernel is O_k ∩ M_D = m_k), so k̄ is a subdivision ring of D̄, and for α ∈ O_k the image ρ(α) in D̄ is exactly the residue ᾱ ∈ k̄ ⊂ D̄.

PART 3. Roots of T^p - T. If x ∈ D satisfies x^p = x, then x ∈ 𝔽_p. Indeed, if x = 0 there is nothing to prove; otherwise x·x^{p-1} = x·1 and cancellation in the division ring D gives x^{p-1} = 1. The subring 𝔽_p[x] ⊂ D is then a commutative integral domain spanned over 𝔽_p by 1, x, …, x^{p-2}, hence finite, hence a field. In that field the polynomial T^p - T has at most p roots, and the p elements of 𝔽_p are all roots; since x is a root, x ∈ 𝔽_p.

PART 4. A Hensel-type lifting (proved from scratch, using only completeness of k). Let γ ∈ k with v(γ) > 0. Define b_0 = 0 and b_{n+1} = b_n^p - γ, and set δ_n := b_n^p - b_n - γ. Then δ_0 = -γ and v(δ_0) = v(γ) > 0. Inductively,
  δ_{n+1} = b_{n+1}^p - b_{n+1} - γ = (b_n^p - γ)^p - (b_n^p - γ) - γ = b_n^{p^2} - γ^p - b_n^p = (b_n^p - b_n)^p - γ^p,
using (X-Y)^p = X^p - Y^p in characteristic p. Since b_n^p - b_n = δ_n + γ, this equals (δ_n+γ)^p - γ^p = δ_n^p + γ^p - γ^p = δ_n^p. Hence v(δ_n) = p^n v(γ) → ∞. Moreover b_{n+1} - b_n = b_n^p - γ - b_n = δ_n, so v(b_{n+1}-b_n) = p^n v(γ) → ∞: (b_n) is Cauchy for the v-adic topology, and by completeness b_n → β ∈ k. Also v(b_n) > 0 for all n (v(b_0)=∞, and v(b_{n+1}) ≥ min{p·v(b_n), v(γ)} > 0), so passing to the limit, v(β) ≥ v(γ) > 0, i.e. β ∈ m_k. Finally we show β^p - β - γ = 0. Note f(β) - δ_n := (β^p - β - γ) - (b_n^p - b_n - γ) = (β - b_n)^p - (β - b_n). For m > n we have b_m - b_n = Σ_{i=n}^{m-1} δ_i, whose terms have strictly increasing valuations, so p-1 successive applications of Part 1 give v(b_m - b_n) = v(δ_n). Since the closed ball {x : v(x - b_n) ≥ v(δ_n)} contains all b_m (m>n), it contains β; thus v(β - b_n) ≥ v(δ_n), and therefore v(f(β) - δ_n) ≥ min{v((β-b_n)^p), v(β-b_n)} ≥ v(β-b_n) ≥ v(δ_n). If f(β) ≠ 0, choose n with v(δ_n) > v(f(β)); then v(f(β)-δ_n) ≥ v(δ_n) > v(f(β)), and Part 1 applied to u = δ_n, v' = f(β) - δ_n gives v(f(β)) = v(δ_n + (f(β)-δ_n)) = min{v(δ_n), v(f(β)-δ_n)} ≥ v(δ_n) > v(f(β)), a contradiction. Hence β^p - β = γ, with β ∈ m_k.

PART 5. Positive value is impossible for elements outside k. Let x ∈ D \ k with x^p - x ∈ k. Then w(x) > 0 cannot occur. Suppose w(x) > 0. Then w(x^p) = p·w(x) and w(-x) = w(x); as (p-1)w(x) > 0, we get w(x^p) > w(-x). Part 1 with u = -x and v = x^p gives w(x^p - x) = w(-x + x^p) = w(-x) = w(x) > 0. Put γ := x^p - x ∈ k; then v(γ) = w(γ) > 0, so by Part 4 there is β ∈ k with β^p - β = γ. Because β ∈ k = Z(D), β commutes with x, so the binomial theorem in characteristic p gives (x-β)^p = x^p - β^p, hence (x-β)^p - (x-β) = (x^p - x) - (β^p - β) = γ - γ = 0. By Part 3, x - β ∈ 𝔽_p ⊂ k, whence x ∈ k, contradiction.

MAIN PROOF. Set c := a^p - a ∈ k. First, c ≠ 0: if c = 0 then a^p = a and Part 3 gives a ∈ 𝔽_p ⊂ k, contradicting a ∉ k. Since a ≠ 0, exactly one of w(a) < 0, w(a) = 0, w(a) > 0 holds.

Case 1: w(a) < 0. Then w(a^p) = p·w(a) and w(-a) = w(a). Since (p-1)w(a) < 0, we have p·w(a) < w(a), i.e. w(a^p) < w(-a). By Part 1 with u = a^p and v = -a,
  v(c) = w(c) = w(a^p - a) = w(a^p + (-a)) = w(a^p) = p·w(a) < 0.
This is the first alternative.

Case 2: w(a) > 0. Excluded by Part 5 (applied to x = a).

Case 3: w(a) = 0. Then w(a^p) = p·0 = 0 and w(-a) = 0, so w(c) ≥ min{w(a^p), w(-a)} = 0; as c ∈ k^×, v(c) = w(c) ≥ 0, i.e. c ∈ O_k. We claim v(c) = 0. If v(c) > 0, Part 4 yields β ∈ k with β^p - β = c; as β ∈ Z(D), (a-β)^p = a^p - β^p, so (a-β)^p - (a-β) = c - c = 0, and Part 3 gives a - β ∈ 𝔽_p ⊂ k, hence a ∈ k, contradiction. Thus v(c) = 0 and the residue c̄ ∈ k̄^× is nonzero.

Since w(a) = 0, a ∈ O_D and ā := ρ(a) ∈ D̄ is defined. As ρ: O_D → D̄ is a ring homomorphism (Part 2),
  ā^p - ā = ρ(a)^p - ρ(a) = ρ(a^p - a) = ρ(c),
and because c ∈ O_k, ρ(c) is the image of c̄ ∈ k̄ under the embedding k̄ ↪ D̄ of Part 2(d). Hence ā^p - ā = c̄ ∈ k̄.

Finally ā ∉ k̄. Suppose ā ∈ k̄; then ā = ρ(λ) for some λ ∈ O_k, so w(a - λ) > 0, i.e. x := a - λ ∈ M_D. Since λ ∈ k = Z(D), (a-λ)^p = a^p - λ^p, so
  x^p - x = (a^p - a) - (λ^p - λ) = c - (λ^p - λ) ∈ k.
If x ∉ k, this contradicts Part 5; if x ∈ k, then a = x + λ ∈ k, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence ā ∉ k̄. This is the second alternative.

The three cases exhaust all possibilities, so exactly one of the two stated alternatives holds: either w(a) < 0 with p·w(a) = v(a^p-a) < 0, or w(a) = 0, v(a^p-a) = 0, and ā ∈ D̄ \ k̄ satisfies ā^p - ā = (a^p-a)̄ ∈ k̄. ∎

lemma_as_residue_cyclic.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a valued field of characteristic $p>0$ with valuation ring $\mathcal O_k$ and residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra endowed with a valuation $w$ extending $v$ and residue division ring $\bar D$. Let $z\in D$ satisfy $z^{p}-z=c$ for some $c\in\mathcal O_k$ whose residue does not lie in $\wp(\bar k)=\{y^{p}-y:y\in\bar k\}$. Then the subfield $\bar k(\bar z)$ of $\bar D$ generated by the residue of $z$ is Galois over $\bar k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.
lemma_as_residue_cyclic.proof:
We prove the statement from the axioms of a valuation on a division ring; note that the argument uses only that $\bar D$ is a division ring containing $\bar k$ in its centre and that $w|_k=v$ (centrality of $D$ over $k$ is used only to place $\bar k$ in $Z(\bar D)$; no discreteness, henselianity, or degree bound is needed).

STEP 0 (Standing facts about $w$). By definition $w\colon D\to \Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$ is a map to an ordered abelian group $\Gamma$ (written additively, with $\infty$ larger than all elements) such that $w(x)=\infty\iff x=0$, $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$, $w(x+y)\ge\min(w(x),w(y))$, $w(1)=0$. Set $\mathcal O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}$ and $M_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\}$.
(a) $\mathcal O_D$ is a subring: $w(x-y)\ge\min(w(x),w(y))\ge 0$ and $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)\ge 0$, and $w(1)=0$.
(b) $M_D$ is a two-sided ideal of $\mathcal O_D$: for $a\in\mathcal O_D$, $x\in M_D$ one has $w(ax)=w(a)+w(x)\ge 0+w(x)>0$, and similarly $w(xa)>0$.
(c) Every element of $\mathcal O_D\setminus M_D$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_D$: $w(x)=0\Rightarrow w(x^{-1})=-w(x)=0$, so $x^{-1}\in\mathcal O_D$. Hence $M_D=\operatorname{Jac}(\mathcal O_D)$ and $\bar D=\mathcal O_D/M_D$ is a division ring; the quotient map $x\mapsto\bar x$ is a surjective ring homomorphism $\mathcal O_D\twoheadrightarrow\bar D$.
(d) Since $w$ extends $v$, $\mathcal O_D\cap k=\mathcal O_k$ and $M_D\cap k=\{a\in k: v(a)>0\}$. Thus the composite $\mathcal O_k\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_D\twoheadrightarrow\bar D$ is a ring homomorphism with kernel the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_k$, so it induces an injective homomorphism $\iota\colon\bar k=\mathcal O_k/\{v>0\}\hookrightarrow\bar D$, $\bar a\mapsto\bar a$; we identify $\bar k$ with its image.
(e) $\bar k\subseteq Z(\bar D)$: for $a\in\mathcal O_k$, $b\in\mathcal O_D$ we have $ab=ba$ in $D$ because $k\subseteq Z(D)$, hence $\bar a\,\bar b=\bar b\,\bar a$ in $\bar D$; a general element of $\bar k$ is $\bar a\,\bar b^{-1}$ with $b\ne0$, and it commutes with every $\bar c\in\bar D$ since $\bar b^{-1}$ does. Also $\operatorname{char}\bar k=p$, because $\operatorname{char}k=p$, so $\mathbb F_p\subseteq\bar k$.

STEP 1 ($c\ne0$ and $v(c)\ge0$). As $c\in\mathcal O_k$, either $c=0$ or $v(c)\ge0$. If $c=0$ then its residue is $\bar c=0=0^p-0\in\wp(\bar k)$, against the hypothesis. Hence $c\ne0$ and $v(c)\ge0$.

STEP 2 ($w(z)\ge0$). First $z\ne0$, for $z=0$ would give $c=0$, excluded in Step 1. Suppose for contradiction that $w(z)<0$. Since $p\ge2$ and $\Gamma$ is an ordered abelian group, $(p-1)w(z)<0$, so $w(z^p)=p\,w(z)<w(z)$. We use the strict ultrametric equality: if $w(x)\ne w(y)$ then $w(x+y)=\min(w(x),w(y))$; indeed, assuming $w(x)<w(y)$, one has $w(x+y)\ge w(x)$, and if $w(x+y)>w(x)$ then $w(x)=w((x+y)-y)\ge\min(w(x+y),w(y))=w(x+y)>w(x)$, absurd. Applying this with $x=z^p$ and $y=-z$ (note $w(-z)=w(z)$, because $2w(-1)=w(1)=0$ and $\Gamma$ is torsion-free, so $w(-1)=0$) gives
$$v(c)=w(c)=w(z^p-z)=\min\bigl(w(z^p),w(z)\bigr)=w(z^p)=p\,w(z)<0,$$
contradicting Step 1. Therefore $w(z)\ge0$, i.e. $z\in\mathcal O_D$, and its residue $\bar z\in\bar D$ is defined.

STEP 3 (residue equation). Since $x\mapsto\bar x$ is a ring homomorphism on $\mathcal O_D$, and it restricts to the map defining the embedding $\bar k\hookrightarrow\bar D$ of Step 0(d),
$$\bar z^{\,p}-\bar z=\overline{z^p-z}=\bar c\in\bar k .
$$

STEP 4 ($\bar z\notin\bar k$). If $\bar z\in\bar k$, then Step 3 gives $\bar c=\bar z^{\,p}-\bar z\in\wp(\bar k)$, contradicting the hypothesis on $c$.

STEP 5 (irreducibility of $f(T)=T^p-T-\bar c$ over $\bar k$). Work first inside a commutative splitting field $\Omega$ of $f$ over $\bar k$, and let $\alpha\in\Omega$ be a root.
(i) $f$ has no root in $\bar k$: a root $\beta$ would give $\bar c=\beta^p-\beta\in\wp(\bar k)$.
(ii) For every $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$ one has $\lambda^p=\lambda$, hence $(\alpha+\lambda)^p-(\alpha+\lambda)=\alpha^p-\alpha+(\lambda^p-\lambda)=\alpha^p-\alpha=\bar c$. Thus the $p$ elements $\alpha+\lambda$ ($\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$) are pairwise distinct roots of $f$ in $\Omega$; as $\deg f=p$, they are all the roots and $f=\prod_{\lambda\in\mathbb F_p}\bigl(T-(\alpha+\lambda)\bigr)$ in $\Omega[T]$, with all roots simple (equivalently, $f'=pT^{p-1}-1=-1\ne0$, so $\gcd(f,f')=1$ and $f$ is separable).
(iii) Let $g\in\bar k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $\bar k$, of degree $d\ge1$. Since $f(\alpha)=0$, $g\mid f$ in $\bar k[T]$, so in $\Omega[T]$ the multiset of roots of $g$ is $\{\alpha+\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda\}$ for a subset $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb F_p$ with $0\in\Lambda$ and $|\Lambda|=d$ (the roots of $f$ are simple, so $g$ is a product of distinct linear factors of $f$). The coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $g$ equals $-\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\alpha+\lambda)=-(d\alpha+s)$ with $s=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\lambda\in\mathbb F_p\subseteq\bar k$. Since $g\in\bar k[T]$, this coefficient, say $\gamma$, lies in $\bar k$, so $d\alpha=-\gamma-s\in\bar k$. If $d<p$, then $d$ is a positive integer prime to $p=\operatorname{char}\bar k$, hence invertible in $\bar k$, and $\alpha\in\bar k$, contradicting (i). Therefore $d=p$, and since $g$ is monic of degree $p$ and divides the monic polynomial $f$ of degree $p$, $g=f$. So $f$ is irreducible over $\bar k$ and $[\bar k(\alpha):\bar k]=p$.

STEP 6 ($\bar k(\bar z)/\bar k$ is a field extension of degree $p$). Because $\bar k\subseteq Z(\bar D)$ (Step 0(e)), the substitution map $\mathrm{ev}\colon\bar k[T]\to\bar D$, $T\mapsto\bar z$, is a well-defined ring homomorphism. Its kernel contains $f$ by Step 3; since $f$ is irreducible (Step 5) and nonzero, and $\bar z\notin\bar k$ (Step 4) shows the kernel is not $(0)$, the kernel is exactly $(f)$. Hence $\bar k[\bar z]\cong\bar k[T]/(f)$ is a field of dimension $p$ over $\bar k$; in particular $\bar k[\bar z]=\bar k(\bar z)$ and $[\bar k(\bar z):\bar k]=p$. (Equivalently: $\bar k[\bar z]$ is a commutative domain finite-dimensional over $\bar k$, hence a field.)

STEP 7 (the automorphisms). For each $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p$, the substitution $T\mapsto\bar z+\lambda$ defines a ring homomorphism $\bar k[T]\to\bar k(\bar z)$ (all involved elements commute, as $\bar z$ commutes with $\bar k$ and with $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p\subseteq\bar k$). Its kernel contains $f$, because
$$f(\bar z+\lambda)=(\bar z+\lambda)^p-(\bar z+\lambda)-\bar c=(\bar z^{\,p}-\bar z-\bar c)+(\lambda^p-\lambda)=0+0=0 .
$$
By Step 6 the kernel is $(f)$, so it induces a $\bar k$-algebra homomorphism $\varphi_\lambda\colon\bar k(\bar z)\to\bar k(\bar z)$ with $\varphi_\lambda(\bar z)=\bar z+\lambda$. The image of $\varphi_\lambda$ contains $\bar k$ and $\bar z+\lambda$, hence also $\bar z=(\bar z+\lambda)-\lambda$; so $\varphi_\lambda$ is surjective, hence a field automorphism of $\bar k(\bar z)$ fixing $\bar k$. Distinct $\lambda$ give distinct automorphisms (they differ on $\bar z$), and $\varphi_\lambda\circ\varphi_\mu=\varphi_{\lambda+\mu}$ since $\varphi_\lambda(\varphi_\mu(\bar z))=\varphi_\lambda(\bar z+\mu)=\bar z+\lambda+\mu$ and both maps are the identity on $\bar k$. Thus $\lambda\mapsto\varphi_\lambda$ is an injective group homomorphism $(\mathbb F_p,+)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(\bar k(\bar z)/\bar k)$, whose image $G=\{\varphi_\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb F_p\}$ has order $p$.

STEP 8 (Galois and cyclic). A finite extension of degree $n$ admits at most $n$ automorphisms over the base field, so $|\operatorname{Aut}(\bar k(\bar z)/\bar k)|\le[\bar k(\bar z):\bar k]=p$; by Step 7 equality holds. Hence $\bar k(\bar z)/\bar k$ is Galois (it is separable, since having $[L:k]$ base-embeddings into an algebraic closure forces every element's minimal polynomial to be separable, and it is normal: in the commutative polynomial ring $\bar k(\bar z)[T]$ the two degree-$p$ polynomials $f(T)$ and $\prod_{\lambda\in\mathbb F_p}\bigl(T-(\bar z+\lambda)\bigr)$ have cancelling leading terms, so their difference has degree $\le p-1$ and vanishes at the $p$ distinct points $\bar z+\lambda$ of the field $\bar k(\bar z)$, whence it is zero: $f$ splits completely in $\bar k(\bar z)$, which is therefore the splitting field of the separable polynomial $f$). Finally Step 7 identifies
$$\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k(\bar z)/\bar k)=\{\varphi_\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb F_p\}\cong(\mathbb F_p,+),$$
and because $p$ is prime, $(\mathbb F_p,+)$ is cyclic of order $p$, generated by $\varphi_1\colon\bar z\mapsto\bar z+1$. This is exactly the required conclusion: $\bar k(\bar z)$ is Galois over $\bar k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.

lemma_184.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, value group $w(D^\times)$ and residue division ring $\bar D$. Suppose $[w(D^\times):v(k^\times)]=p^2$ and that every element of $\bar D$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$. Then every maximal subfield $L$ of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ has residue field $\bar L=\bar k$ and value group $w(L^\times)=w(D^\times)$, that is, $L/k$ is totally ramified.
lemma_184.proof:
We prove the statement in several steps. Throughout, $\mathcal O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_D=\{x:w(x)>0\}$ and residue division ring $\bar D=\mathcal O_D/\mathfrak m_D$; $\bar k$ is the residue field of $\mathcal O_{k,v}$, which we identify with its image in $\bar D$.

Step 1: The residue division ring is $\bar D=\bar k$.
Because $k=Z(D)$, the residue field $\bar k$ lies in the centre of $\bar D$: indeed for $c\in\mathcal O_k$ and $a\in\mathcal O_D$ we have $ca=ac$, hence $\bar c\,\bar a=\bar a\,\bar c$. Let $\alpha\in\bar D$. By hypothesis $\alpha$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$, so there is an integer $n\ge 0$ with $\alpha^{p^{n}}\in\bar k$. Since $\bar k$ is perfect, the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^{p^{n}}$ is a bijection of $\bar k$; choose the unique $\beta\in\bar k$ with $\beta^{p^{n}}=\alpha^{p^{n}}$. As $\beta\in Z(\bar D)$ it commutes with $\alpha$, so in characteristic $p$ we get $(\alpha-\beta)^{p^{n}}=\alpha^{p^{n}}-\beta^{p^{n}}=0$. A division ring has no non-zero nilpotent elements, hence $\alpha=\beta\in\bar k$. Thus $\bar D\subseteq\bar k$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate, so
$$\bar D=\bar k .$$
(In particular $[\bar D:\bar k]=1$.)

Step 2: The degree of $L$ over $k$.
Let $L\subset D$ be a maximal subfield which is Galois over $k$. Apply the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) to the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ and the simple $k$-subalgebra $L$: since $L$ is a maximal subfield we have $C_D(L)=L$, and $\dim_k L\cdot\dim_k C_D(L)=\dim_k D$. Hence $[L:k]^{2}=[D:k]=p^{4}$, so
$$[L:k]=p^{2}.$$

Step 3: The residue field of $L$ is $\bar k$.
Restrict $w$ to $L$; write $w_L=w|_L$. Since $v$ is henselian, $v$ has a unique extension to the algebraic extension $L/k$ (a standard equivalent form of Hensel's axiom: the extensions of $v$ to an algebraic extension are in bijection with the extensions to the henselization, and henselianity means there is exactly one), so $w_L$ is that unique extension, and $\mathcal O_L=\{x\in L: w_L(x)\ge0\}=L\cap\mathcal O_D$, $\mathfrak m_L=L\cap\mathfrak m_D$. The residue homomorphism $\mathcal O_D\to\bar D$ therefore restricts to a ring homomorphism $\mathcal O_L\to\bar D$ whose kernel is $\mathfrak m_L$; its image is thus a subring of $\bar D$ isomorphic to the field $\bar L=\mathcal O_L/\mathfrak m_L$, hence a subfield of $\bar D$. This exhibits $\bar L$ as a subfield of $\bar D$ containing $\bar k$ (the map $\bar k\to\bar L$ induced by $\mathcal O_k\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_L$ is injective, so $\bar k\subseteq\bar L$). By Step 1, $\bar D=\bar k$, so
$$\bar k\subseteq\bar L\subseteq\bar D=\bar k,\qquad\text{hence }\ \bar L=\bar k,\ \ [\bar L:\bar k]=1.$$

Step 4: The value group of $L$ has index $p^{2}$ over $v(k^{\times})$.
The field $L/k$ is a finite Galois extension, and $(k,v)$ is a henselian discretely valued field. We may therefore apply lemma_96 (Spark), which gives, for the valuation $w_L$ extending $v$,
$$[L:k]=[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k].$$
Substituting $[L:k]=p^{2}$ (Step 2) and $[\bar L:\bar k]=1$ (Step 3) yields
$$[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]=p^{2}.$$

Step 5: $w(L^{\times})=w(D^{\times})$.
Clearly $v(k^{\times})\subseteq w(L^{\times})\subseteq w(D^{\times})$, since $k^{\times}\subseteq L^{\times}\subseteq D^{\times}$. Moreover $v(k^{\times})$ is central in $w(D^{\times})$: for $\gamma=w(d)$ with $d\in D^{\times}$ and $\delta=v(c)$ with $c\in k^{\times}$, one has $\gamma+\delta=w(dc)=w(cd)=\delta+\gamma$ because $c$ is central in $D$. Hence $v(k^{\times})$ is a normal subgroup of $w(D^{\times})$, the quotient $w(D^{\times})/v(k^{\times})$ is a group of order $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]=p^{2}$ by hypothesis, and $w(L^{\times})/v(k^{\times})$ is a subgroup of it. By Step 4 this subgroup has order $p^{2}$, so by Lagrange's theorem it is the whole quotient:
$$w(L^{\times})=w(D^{\times}).$$

Step 6: Conclusion.
Steps 3 and 5 say exactly that $\bar L=\bar k$ and $w(L^{\times})=w(D^{\times})$, i.e. that $L/k$ is totally ramified. Since $L$ was an arbitrary maximal subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$, the lemma is proved.

Remark on the use of the hypotheses (not needed for the argument above): the proof shows that the conclusion already follows from the two facts (i) $\bar k$ perfect together with "every element of $\bar D$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$" — which force $\bar D=\bar k$ — and (ii) $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]=p^{2}$. The assumption $\deg D=p^{2}$ is used only through $[L:k]=p^{2}$, and the hypothesis $p>2$ is not used at all. Note also that $\bar D=\bar k$ is what the phrase "every element of $\bar D$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$" amounts to over a perfect residue field; no defect computation for $D$ itself is required.

lemma_183.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field with perfect residue field $\bar k$, let $L/k$ be a finite Galois extension, and let $w$ be the valuation of $L$ extending $v$, with residue field $\bar L$. Then $\bar L/\bar k$ is a finite Galois extension; in particular, if $\bar L$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$, then $\bar L=\bar k$.
lemma_183.proof:
**Notation.** Let $R=\mathcal O_v=\{x\in k: v(x)\ge 0\}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_v$ and residue field $\bar k=R/\mathfrak m$, which is perfect by hypothesis; fix a uniformiser $\pi\in R$ with $v(\pi)=1$. Let $n=[L:k]$, $G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$, and let $V'$ denote the integral closure of $R$ in $L$. Write $\mathcal O_w=\{y\in L: w(y)\ge 0\}$, $\mathfrak m_w$ for its maximal ideal, $\bar L=\mathcal O_w/\mathfrak m_w$, and denote the residue of $y\in\mathcal O_w$ by $\bar y$.

**Step 1. The integral closure $V'$ is a DVR, is the unique valuation ring of $L$ lying over $R$, and is $G$-stable.**

(1a) *$V'$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.* Choose any $k$-basis $z_1,\dots,z_n$ of $L$. For each $i$, let $T^{m_i}+c^{(i)}_{m_i-1}T^{m_i-1}+\cdots+c^{(i)}_0\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $z_i$ over $k$. Pick $b\in k^{\times}$ with $v(b)\ge\max\big(0,\ \max_{i,j}\{-v(c^{(i)}_{m_i-j})\}\big)$. Then $v(b)\ge 0$, and for $1\le j\le m_i$ we have $v(b^{j}c^{(i)}_{m_i-j})=j\,v(b)+v(c^{(i)}_{m_i-j})\ge v(b)+v(c^{(i)}_{m_i-j})\ge 0$. Substituting $T=y/b$ into the minimal polynomial of $z_i$ and multiplying by $b^{m_i}$ shows that $e_i:=bz_i$ satisfies the monic polynomial $T^{m_i}+b\,c^{(i)}_{m_i-1}T^{m_i-1}+\cdots+b^{m_i}c^{(i)}_0\in R[T]$. Hence $e_i\in V'$, and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is a $k$-basis of $L$ contained in $V'$.

Because $L/k$ is Galois it is separable, so the trace pairing $(x,y)\mapsto\mathrm{Tr}_{L/k}(xy)$ on $L$ is non-degenerate; let $e_1^*,\dots,e_n^*$ be the dual basis, so that $y=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Tr}_{L/k}(y e_i)\,e_i^*$ for every $y\in L$. Take $y\in V'$. Then $y e_i\in V'$, i.e. $y e_i$ is integral over $R$. The element $\mathrm{Tr}_{L/k}(y e_i)$ lies in $k$ and is the sum of the $n$ distinct $k$-embeddings $L\hookrightarrow k_s$ applied to $y e_i$; each such image is a root of the same monic polynomial over $R$ satisfied by $y e_i$, hence is integral over $R$, and the sum of elements integral over $R$ is integral over $R$. Since a valuation ring is integrally closed in its fraction field, $\mathrm{Tr}_{L/k}(y e_i)\in R$. Therefore $V'\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^n R e_i^*$, a free $R$-module of rank $n$. As $R$ is a DVR, it is a PID, hence Noetherian, so every submodule of a finitely generated module is finitely generated; thus $V'$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.

(1b) *Every nonzero prime of $V'$ is maximal and contracts to $\mathfrak m$; $\dim V'=1$.* Let $\mathfrak p\ne(0)$ be a prime of $V'$ and choose $0\ne p\in\mathfrak p$. Let $T^m+c_{m-1}T^{m-1}+\cdots+c_0\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $p$ over $k$; $c_0\ne0$ because $p\ne0$ and $L$ is a field. Each $c_j$ is, up to sign, an elementary symmetric function in the $k$-conjugates of $p$; each conjugate satisfies the same monic equation over $R$ as $p$, hence is integral over $R$, so $c_j$ is integral over $R$ and lies in $k$, whence $c_j\in R$. From $c_0=-p\,(p^{m-1}+c_{m-1}p^{m-2}+\cdots+c_1)$ we obtain $c_0\in pV'\subseteq\mathfrak p$. Thus $\mathfrak p\cap R$ is a nonzero prime of the DVR $R$, hence $\mathfrak p\cap R=\mathfrak m$. Then $V'/\mathfrak p$ is integral over $R/\mathfrak m=\bar k$, which is a field; an integral extension of a field is a field, so $V'/\mathfrak p$ is a field and $\mathfrak p$ is maximal. Nonzero primes exist: $V'$ is not a field, since $\pi\in\mathfrak m\subseteq V'$ is a non-unit of $V'$ (otherwise $1/\pi\in V'\cap k$, and $V'\cap k$ consists of the elements of $k$ integral over $R$, which is $R$ itself, contradicting $v(1/\pi)=-1$); the lying-over theorem applied to the integral extension $R\subseteq V'$ then yields primes of $V'$ contracting to $\mathfrak m$, which are nonzero and maximal. Consequently the longest chains of primes of $V'$ are $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak p$, i.e. $\dim V'=1$.

(1c) *$V'$ is local.* Suppose $\mathfrak m_1\ne\mathfrak m_2$ are maximal ideals of $V'$. Since $V'$ is not a field, $(0)$ is not maximal, so both $\mathfrak m_i$ are nonzero, and by (1b) $\mathfrak m_i\cap R=\mathfrak m$. Distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, so by the Chinese remainder theorem there is $x\in V'$ with $x\equiv1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak m_1)$ and $x\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak m_2)$. Let $P(T)=T^d+a_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $k$. Since $x$ is integral over $R$, some monic $F\in R[T]$ satisfies $F(x)=0$; then $P\mid F$ in $k[T]$ with $P$ monic, and Gauss's lemma ($R$ is a UFD) gives $P\in R[T]$. Because $P$ is monic, its reduction $\bar P\in\bar k[T]$ is monic of degree exactly $d$ (no degree drop). Reducing the identity $P(x)=0$ in $V'/\mathfrak m_1\cong$ a field, where the coefficients of $P$ reduce modulo $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_1\cap R$ and $x$ maps to $1$, gives $\bar P(1)=0$; reducing in $V'/\mathfrak m_2$, where $x$ maps to $0$, gives $\bar P(0)=0$. Write $\bar P=T^{a}\bar H$ with $a\ge1$ and $\bar H(0)\ne0$. Then $0=\bar P(1)=1^{a}\bar H(1)$ gives $\bar H(1)=0$, so $\bar H$ is non-constant of degree $d-a\ge1$. Thus $\bar P=\bar g_0\bar h_0$ with $\bar g_0=T^{a}$ and $\bar h_0=\bar H$, both monic of positive degree and coprime (the only irreducible factor of $T^{a}$ is $T$, which does not divide $\bar H$). We apply Hensel's lemma for the henselian local ring $R$ **in its monic form**: if $F\in R[T]$ is monic and $\bar F=\bar g_0\bar h_0$ in $\bar k[T]$ with $\bar g_0,\bar h_0$ monic and coprime, then $F=gh$ with $g,h\in R[T]$ monic, $\bar g=\bar g_0$, $\bar h=\bar h_0$. (Monicity of $F$ guarantees $\deg\bar F=\deg F$, and monicity of $g,h$ then forces $\deg g=\deg\bar g_0$, $\deg h=\deg\bar h_0$.) Since $P$ is monic, it applies and yields $P=gh$ in $R[T]$ with $g,h$ monic of degrees $a\ge1$ and $d-a\ge1$; this is a non-trivial factorisation of $P$ in $k[T]$, contradicting the irreducibility of $P$. Hence $V'$ has a unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m'$.

(1d) *$V'$ is a DVR, hence a valuation ring of $L$, and $V'\cap k=R$.* The ring $V'$ is a domain, Noetherian by (1a), local by (1c), of dimension one by (1b), and integrally closed in $L$ by transitivity of integrality (an element of $L$ integral over $V'$ is integral over $R$, hence lies in $V'$). By the standard characterisation of discrete valuation rings — a Noetherian local integrally closed domain of dimension one is a DVR — with all hypotheses verified in (1a)-(1d), $V'$ is a DVR. In particular $V'$ is a valuation ring of $L$. Finally $V'\cap k=R$, since the elements of $k$ integral over $R$ are exactly the elements of $R$ ($R$ integrally closed in $k$).

(1e) *Uniqueness of the valuation ring over $R$.* Let $A$ be any valuation ring of $L$ with $A\cap k=R$. First, $V'\subseteq A$: for $y\in V'$, $y$ is integral over $R\subseteq A$, hence integral over $A$, and $A$ is integrally closed in its fraction field $L$. Next we use the following elementary fact: if $V\subseteq A$ are valuation rings of a field $F$, then $A=V_{\mathfrak p}$ with $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak m_A\cap V$. Proof: $\mathfrak m_A\subseteq V$, for if $t\in\mathfrak m_A$ and $t\notin V$ then $t^{-1}\in\mathfrak m_V\subseteq V\subseteq A$, so $t\in A^{\times}$, impossible; and an element of $V\cap\mathfrak m_A$ cannot be a unit of $V$, else it would be a unit of $A$. Hence $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak m_A$. For $x\in A$: if $x\in V$ then $x\in V_{\mathfrak p}$; if $x\notin V$ then $x^{-1}\in\mathfrak m_V\subseteq V$, and $x^{-1}\in A^{\times}$ (both $x$ and $x^{-1}$ are in $A$), so $x^{-1}\in V\setminus\mathfrak p$ and $x=(x^{-1})^{-1}\in V_{\mathfrak p}$. Conversely $a/s$ with $a\in V\subseteq A$ and $s\in V\setminus\mathfrak p\subseteq A\setminus\mathfrak m_A=A^{\times}$ lies in $A$. Applying this with $V=V'$, whose only prime ideals are $(0)$ and $\mathfrak m'$, we get $A\in\{V'_{(0)},\,V'_{\mathfrak m'}\}=\{L,\,V'\}$. Since $A\cap k=R\ne k$, $A\ne L$, so $A=V'$.

(1f) *Identification of $\mathcal O_w$, and $G$-invariance.* Because $w|_k=v$, we have $\mathcal O_w\cap k=R$, so (1e) gives $\mathcal O_w=V'$ and $\mathfrak m_w=\mathfrak m'$. For $\sigma\in G$, $\sigma(R)=R$ (as $\sigma$ fixes $k$ pointwise), and $\sigma$ carries elements integral over $R$ to elements integral over $R$, so $\sigma(V')\subseteq V'$; applying the same to $\sigma^{-1}$ gives $\sigma(V')=V'$. Hence $\sigma(\mathcal O_w)=\mathcal O_w$ and $\sigma(\mathfrak m_w)=\mathfrak m_w$. Moreover $w\circ\sigma$ is a valuation of $L$ whose restriction to $k$ is $v$. To see that $w$ is the *unique* such valuation, note that $w(L^{\times})$ is an ordered abelian group containing $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$ with finite index $e=[w(L^{\times}):\mathbb Z]$ (finiteness: $y^n\in k$ up to... precisely, for $y\in L^{\times}$, $y$ is algebraic of degree $\le n$ over $k$, so $n\,w(y)\in\mathbb Z$), hence $w(L^{\times})$ is archimedean and, under the unique normalisation sending $1=v(\pi)$ to $1$, sits inside $\frac1e\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb R$; and for $y\in L^{\times}$ and $m\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ge1$, $$w(y)\ge m/n\iff w(y^{n}\pi^{-m})\ge0\iff y^{n}\pi^{-m}\in\mathcal O_w,$$ so $w$ is completely determined by its valuation ring together with the normalisation $w|_k=v$. Since $\mathcal O_{w\circ\sigma}=\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal O_w)=\mathcal O_w$ and $(w\circ\sigma)|_k=v$, it follows that $w\circ\sigma=w$.

**Step 2. Induced automorphisms of the residue field.** For $\sigma\in G$, Step 1f gives $\sigma(\mathcal O_w)=\mathcal O_w$ and $\sigma(\mathfrak m_w)=\mathfrak m_w$, so $\sigma$ induces a map $\bar\sigma:\bar L\to\bar L$, $\bar y\mapsto\overline{\sigma(y)}$. This is well defined (if $\bar y=\bar z$ then $y-z\in\mathfrak m_w$, so $\sigma(y)-\sigma(z)=\sigma(y-z)\in\mathfrak m_w$), is a field automorphism (it is a homomorphism because $\sigma$ is, and bijective with inverse $\overline{\sigma^{-1}}$), and fixes $\bar k$: for $a\in R$, $\bar\sigma(\bar a)=\overline{\sigma(a)}=\bar a$. Thus each $\sigma$ yields an element of $\mathrm{Aut}(\bar L/\bar k)$. (We do not claim, and do not need, that $G\to\mathrm{Aut}(\bar L/\bar k)$ is surjective.)

**Step 3. Finiteness: $[\bar L:\bar k]\le [L:k]$.** Let $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_m\in\bar L$ be $\bar k$-linearly independent and choose lifts $r_1,\dots,r_m\in\mathcal O_w$. Suppose $\sum_i\lambda_i r_i=0$ is a non-trivial $k$-linear relation. Choose $c\in k^{\times}$ with $c\lambda_i\in R$ for all $i$ and $\min_i v(c\lambda_i)=0$, so that some $c\lambda_i$ is a unit of $R$. Then $\sum_i(c\lambda_i)r_i=0$ with all coefficients in $R$; reducing modulo $\mathfrak m_w$ gives $\sum_i\overline{c\lambda_i}\,\xi_i=0$ in $\bar L$. By $\bar k$-linear independence, $\overline{c\lambda_i}=0$ for all $i$, i.e. $c\lambda_i\in\mathfrak m_w\cap k=\mathfrak m$ for all $i$, contradicting that some $c\lambda_i$ is a unit. Hence $r_1,\dots,r_m$ are $k$-linearly independent, so $m\le n=[L:k]$. Therefore $\dim_{\bar k}\bar L\le n<\infty$: $\bar L/\bar k$ is a finite (hence algebraic) extension.

**Step 4. Normality of $\bar L/\bar k$.** Let $\xi\in\bar L$ and choose $\alpha\in\mathcal O_w$ lifting it. Let $P(T)=T^d+a_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $k$. As in (1c), Gauss's lemma applied to any monic equation over $R$ satisfied by $\alpha$ gives $P\in R[T]$, and $P$ is monic of degree $d$, so $\bar P\in\bar k[T]$ is monic of degree $d$. Since $L/k$ is Galois, all $k$-conjugates of $\alpha$ lie in $L$: writing the distinct conjugates as $\alpha_1=\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_r$, each $\alpha_j=\sigma_j(\alpha)$ for some $\sigma_j\in G$, and by Step 1f each $\alpha_j\in\sigma_j(\mathcal O_w)=\mathcal O_w$. Hence in $L[T]$, $P(T)=\prod_{j=1}^{r}(T-\alpha_j)$, and reducing coefficients modulo $\mathfrak m$ (a ring homomorphism $R[T]\to\bar k[T]\hookrightarrow\bar L[T]$, valid because $P$ is monic so $\deg\bar P=d=r$-counted with multiplicity) gives $$\bar P(T)=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\bigl(T-\bar\alpha_j\bigr)\in\bar L[T],$$ i.e. $\bar P$ splits completely into linear factors over $\bar L$. Now $\bar P(\xi)=\overline{P(\alpha)}=\bar 0$, so the minimal polynomial $Q\in\bar k[T]$ of $\xi$ over $\bar k$ divides $\bar P$ in $\bar k[T]$; consequently $Q$ also splits completely into linear factors in $\bar L[T]$. We have shown that every irreducible polynomial over $\bar k$ having one root in $\bar L$ splits completely in $\bar L$; together with the finiteness from Step 3 this means $\bar L/\bar k$ is a normal extension.

**Step 5. Separability and conclusion.** The residue field $\bar k$ is perfect by hypothesis, so every algebraic extension of $\bar k$ is separable; in particular $\bar L/\bar k$ is separable. A finite extension which is both normal and separable is Galois. Hence $\bar L/\bar k$ is a finite Galois extension, which is the first claim.

**Step 6. The purely inseparable clause.** Assume moreover that $\bar L$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$. For any $\bar y\in\bar L$, its minimal polynomial over $\bar k$ is separable by Step 5, while pure inseparability forces it to be a power of $T-\bar y$; the only polynomial with both properties is $T-\bar y$. Hence $\bar y\in\bar k$, so $\bar L=\bar k$. (Equivalently: perfectness of $\bar k$ means the Frobenius $\bar k\to\bar k$, $t\mapsto t^p$, is surjective, so no element of any extension field of $\bar k$ outside $\bar k$ can be purely inseparable over $\bar k$.) This proves the asserted consequence, and the lemma is proved in full.

lemma_185.statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, let $k=F((u))$ be the Laurent series field with its $u$-adic valuation $v$, let $A$ be a central division $F$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, and let $D=A\otimes_{F}k$, written as $A((u))$. Then $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$; the map $w\big(\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^{i}\big)=\min\{i:\alpha_i\neq 0\}$ is a valuation on $D$ extending $v$, its value group is $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$, its residue division ring is isomorphic to $A$, and for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ the map $A\to \mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n$ sending $\alpha$ to the initial form $\mathrm{in}_w(\alpha u^{n})$ is an isomorphism of $F$-vector spaces.
lemma_185.proof:
We prove the statement in seven steps. (The hypotheses $p>2$ and $\deg A=p^{2}$ are used only to fix the numerical value $\dim_F A=p^{4}$; every step below is valid for an arbitrary central division $F$-algebra $A$ and the Laurent series field $k=F((u))$.)

Notation and conventions. A *valuation on a (possibly noncommutative) division ring* $R$ means a map $w:R\to \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$ such that (V1) $w(x)=\infty\iff x=0$; (V2) $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$ for all $x,y$; (V3) $w(x+y)\ge\min(w(x),w(y))$ (with $\infty$ largest). Its valuation ring is $\mathcal{O}_w=\{x:w(x)\ge 0\}$ and its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak{m}_w=\{x:w(x)>0\}$: $\mathcal{O}_w$ is a subring by (V2),(V3), $\mathfrak{m}_w$ is a two-sided ideal since for $a\in\mathfrak{m}_w$, $r\in\mathcal{O}_w$ one has $w(ra)=w(r)+w(a)=w(ar)\ge 0+w(a)>0$, and $\mathcal{O}_w\setminus\mathfrak{m}_w=\{x:w(x)=0\}=\mathcal{O}_w^{\times}$ (if $w(x)=0$ then $w(x^{-1})=-w(x)=0$, so $x^{-1}\in\mathcal{O}_w$); hence $\mathfrak{m}_w$ is the unique maximal ideal and $\overline{R}=\mathcal{O}_w/\mathfrak{m}_w$ is a division ring. The associated graded ring is $\mathrm{gr}_w(R)=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} I_n/I_{n+1}$ where $I_n=\{x\in R:w(x)\ge n\}$: each $I_n$ is an additive subgroup by (V3) (and contains $0$ since $\infty\ge n$), $I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n$, and $I_nI_m\subseteq I_{n+m}$ because $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)\ge n+m$. We write $[x]_n$ for the class of $x\in I_n$ in $I_n/I_{n+1}=\mathrm{gr}_w(R)_n$, and for $x\ne 0$ the initial form is $\mathrm{in}_w(x)=[x]_{w(x)}$. Finally, $\mathrm{gr}_w(R)_0=\overline{R}$ is a division ring, so each homogeneous piece $\mathrm{gr}_w(R)_n$ is a left $\overline{R}$-vector space by multiplication in the graded ring; via the residue map this makes $\mathrm{gr}_w(R)_n$ an $F$-vector space, explicitly $c\cdot[x]_n=[cx]_n$ for $c\in F\subseteq \mathcal{O}_w$ (and $0\cdot[x]_n=0$).

Step 1: the identification $D=A\otimes_F k\cong A((u))$ as $k$-algebras.
Let $S$ be the set of formal sums $\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^i$ with $N\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\alpha_i\in A$, equipped with the Cauchy product $(\sum_i\alpha_i u^i)(\sum_j\beta_j u^j)=\sum_n(\sum_{i+j=n}\alpha_i\beta_j)u^n$ (the inner sum is finite, since only $i\ge r$, $j\ge s$ occur). This is an associative unital ring: for $x=\sum_{i\ge r}\alpha_iu^i$, $y=\sum_{j\ge s}\beta_ju^j$, $z=\sum_{k\ge t}\gamma_ku^k$, the coefficient of $u^n$ in both $(xy)z$ and $x(yz)$ is $\sum_{i+j+k=n}\alpha_i(\beta_j\gamma_k)=\sum_{i+j+k=n}(\alpha_i\beta_j)\gamma_k$, a finite sum. The element $1_Au^0$ is the identity, and the central element $u:=1_Au^1$ is invertible with inverse $1_Au^{-1}$; the subring $\{\sum c_i u^i\cdot 1_A\}$ is canonically $F((u))=k$, and it commutes with everything because $F=Z(A)$. Thus $S$ is a $k$-algebra, denoted $A((u))$.
Define $\Phi:A\times F((u))\to S$ by $\Phi(a,f)=\sum_i (c_i a)u^i$ where $f=\sum_i c_i u^i\in F((u))$. This map is $F$-bilinear: $\Phi(a,f+g)=\Phi(a,f)+\Phi(a,g)$ and $\Phi(a,\lambda f)=\sum_i(\lambda c_i a)u^i=\sum_i(c_i(\lambda a))u^i=\Phi(\lambda a,f)$, and similarly in the first variable. Hence $\Phi$ induces an $F$-linear map $\widetilde\Phi:A\otimes_F F((u))\to S$ with $\widetilde\Phi(a\otimes f)=\sum_i(c_ia)u^i$. On elementary tensors,
$\widetilde\Phi(a\otimes f)\,\widetilde\Phi(b\otimes g)=\big(\sum_i(c_ia)u^i\big)\big(\sum_j(d_jb)u^j\big)=\sum_n\big(\sum_{i+j=n}c_id_j\,ab\big)u^n=\widetilde\Phi(ab,fg)=\widetilde\Phi\big((a\otimes f)(b\otimes g)\big)$,
using that the scalars $c_i,d_j\in F$ commute with $a,b$. Since elementary tensors span $A\otimes_Fk$ over $F$, $\widetilde\Phi$ is a ring homomorphism, and it is $k$-linear because $\widetilde\Phi((a\otimes 1)(1\otimes h))=\widetilde\Phi(a\otimes h)=h\cdot\widetilde\Phi(a\otimes 1)$ for $h\in k$.
Bijectivity: let $e_1,\dots,e_m$ be an $F$-basis of $A$ ($m=\dim_F A=p^4$). Given $x=\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^i\in S$, write $\alpha_i=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_{j,i}e_j$ with $\lambda_{j,i}\in F$ uniquely; since $\alpha_i=0$ for $i<N$, each $f_j:=\sum_i\lambda_{j,i}u^i$ is a legitimate element of $F((u))$ (finitely many negative-degree terms), and $x=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j e_j=\widetilde\Phi\big(\sum_j e_j\otimes f_j\big)$. Uniqueness of this preimage follows because $\widetilde\Phi(\sum_j e_j\otimes g_j)=0$ means $\sum_j g_{j,i}e_j=0$ in $A$ for every $i$, hence all $g_{j,i}=0$. So $\widetilde\Phi$ is a $k$-algebra isomorphism; we identify $D=A\otimes_Fk$ with $A((u))$. In particular $\dim_k D=\dim_F A=p^4$, with $k$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_m$.

Step 2: $D=A((u))$ is a division ring.
Let $0\ne x=\sum_{i\ge r}\alpha_i u^i$ with $\alpha_r\ne 0$. Then $x=u^r\big(\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha_{r+i}u^i\big)=u^r\alpha_r(1+y)$, where $y=\sum_{i\ge1}\delta_i u^i$ with $\delta_i=\alpha_r^{-1}\alpha_{r+i}\in A$ (invertibility of $\alpha_r$ uses that $A$ is a division ring), and $u$ is central so the rearrangement is legitimate. Since $y\in uA[[u]]$ and $u$ is central, $y^{t}\in u^{t}A[[u]]$ for all $t\ge1$ (the coefficient of $u^{n}$ in $y^{t}$ is a sum of products $\delta_{i_1}\cdots\delta_{i_t}$ with $i_1+\cdots+i_t=n$, hence vanishes when $n<t$). Therefore $z:=\sum_{t\ge0}(-y)^{t}\in A[[u]]\subset S$ is well defined: the coefficient of $u^n$ in $z$ is the finite sum of the coefficients of $u^n$ in $(-y)^t$, $0\le t\le n$. For each $M\ge0$, $(1+y)\sum_{t=0}^{M}(-y)^t=\sum_{t=0}^{M}(-y)^t-\sum_{t=1}^{M+1}(-y)^t=1-(-y)^{M+1}$, because $y(-y)^{t-1}=-(-y)^t$. Comparing the coefficient of each fixed $u^n$ and taking $M\ge n$ (so that $(-y)^{M+1}\in u^{M+1}A[[u]]$ has vanishing $u^n$-coefficient) gives $(1+y)z=1$. The same computation on the other side gives $z(1+y)=1$. Hence $1+y$ is a unit, and $x^{-1}=(1+y)^{-1}\alpha_r^{-1}u^{-r}\in S$: indeed $x\,(1+y)^{-1}\alpha_r^{-1}u^{-r}=u^r\alpha_r(1+y)(1+y)^{-1}\alpha_r^{-1}u^{-r}=u^r\alpha_r\alpha_r^{-1}u^{-r}=1$. So every nonzero element of $D$ is invertible: $D$ is a division ring.

Step 3: $D$ is central over $k$, of degree $p^2$.
If $x=\sum_{i\ge r}\alpha_i u^i$ is central in $D$, then for every $\beta\in A\subset D$ the equality $x\beta=\beta x$ reads $\sum_i(\alpha_i\beta-\beta\alpha_i)u^i=0$, whence $\alpha_i\beta=\beta\alpha_i$ for all $i$, i.e. $\alpha_i\in Z(A)=F$ (as $A$ is central over $F$). Thus $x\in F((u))=k$. Conversely every element of $k$ is central, because $F=Z(A)$ and $u$ commutes with $A$. Hence $Z(D)=k$. Being a division ring finite-dimensional ($\dim_k D=p^4$ by Step 1) over its center $k$, $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $\sqrt{p^4}=p^2$.

Step 4: $w$ is a valuation on $D$ extending $v$.
Define $w(0)=\infty$ and, for $x=\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^i\ne0$, $w(x)=\min\{i:\alpha_i\ne0\}$ (the minimum exists because the set $\{i\ge N:\alpha_i\ne0\}$ is nonempty and bounded below). Then:
(V1) holds by definition: $w(x)=\infty$ exactly when $x=0$, and otherwise $w(x)\in\mathbb{Z}$.
(V3): write $x=\sum\alpha_iu^i$, $y=\sum\beta_iu^i$ and put $\mu=\min(w(x),w(y))$ (if one of $x,y$ is $0$ the inequality is trivial). For $i<\mu$ both $\alpha_i=0$ and $\beta_i=0$, so the $u^i$-coefficient of $x+y$ is $0$, whence $w(x+y)\ge\mu$.
(V2): let $w(x)=r$, $w(y)=s$, so $\alpha_r\ne0$, $\beta_s\ne0$. The product $xy=\sum_{n\ge r+s}\gamma_nu^n$ has $\gamma_n=\sum_{i+j=n}\alpha_i\beta_j$, and for $n=r+s$ the only surviving term is $\gamma_{r+s}=\alpha_r\beta_s\ne0$, because $A$ is a division ring and hence has no zero divisors. Thus $w(xy)=r+s=w(x)+w(y)$; in particular $w(1)=0$ since $w(1)^2$-type check: $w(1)=w(1\cdot1)=2w(1)$ forces $w(1)=0$.
Extension of $v$: for $c=\sum_i c_i u^i\in k^{\times}$, viewed inside $D$ as $\sum_i (c_i1_A)u^i$, the coefficient $c_i1_A$ is $0$ in $A$ if and only if $c_i=0$ (as $A$ is a nonzero $F$-vector space and $1_A\ne0$); hence $w(c)=\min\{i:c_i\ne0\}=v(c)$, and $w(0)=\infty=v(0)$. So $w|_k=v$.

Step 5: the value group is $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$.
By construction $w(D^{\times})\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$. For any $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ the element $u^{n}\in k^{\times}\subseteq D^{\times}$ satisfies $w(u^{n})=v(u^{n})=n$, so $\mathbb{Z}\subseteq w(D^{\times})$. (Equivalently, $w$ is surjective onto $\mathbb{Z}$, and $w(D^{\times})$ is a subgroup since $w(xy^{-1})=w(x)-w(y)$.) Hence $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$.

Step 6: the residue division ring is isomorphic to $A$.
By definition $\mathcal{O}_w=\{x\in D:w(x)\ge0\}=\{\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha_i u^i\}=A[[u]]$ and $\mathfrak{m}_w=\{x\in D:w(x)>0\}=uA[[u]]$. Consider $\rho:\mathcal{O}_w\to A$, $\rho(\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha_iu^i)=\alpha_0$. It is additive, and multiplicative because the constant term of a Cauchy product is $\alpha_0\beta_0$; it maps $1$ to $1_A$. It is surjective, since $\rho(\alpha u^0)=\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in A$, and its kernel is exactly $\{\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha_i u^i:\alpha_0=0\}=uA[[u]]=\mathfrak{m}_w$. By the first isomorphism theorem $\mathcal{O}_w/\mathfrak{m}_w\cong A$ as rings (indeed as $F$-algebras: $\rho$ restricts to the identity on $F\subseteq\mathcal{O}_w$). Thus the residue division ring $\overline{D}$ is isomorphic to $A$; in particular it is a central division $F$-algebra of degree $p^2$, and its center is $\bar k=F$ (the residue field of $k$).

Step 7: the maps $\varphi_n:A\to\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n$, $\alpha\mapsto[\alpha u^{n}]_n$ (which equals $\mathrm{in}_w(\alpha u^{n})$ for $\alpha\ne0$) are $F$-vector space isomorphisms.
First, for $\alpha\in A^{\times}$ the element $\alpha u^{n}$ has lowest nonzero index $n$, so $w(\alpha u^{n})=n$; hence $\alpha u^{n}\in I_n$ and $\varphi_n$ is well defined for all $\alpha$ (with $\varphi_n(0)=0$).
Additivity: for $\alpha,\beta\in A$ both $\alpha u^{n},\beta u^{n}\in I_n$, so in the quotient group $I_n/I_{n+1}$ we have $\varphi_n(\alpha+\beta)=[(\alpha+\beta)u^{n}]_n=[\alpha u^{n}]_n+[\beta u^{n}]_n=\varphi_n(\alpha)+\varphi_n(\beta)$.
$F$-linearity: for $c\in F$, using the $F$-module structure on $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n$ described in the conventions, $c\cdot\varphi_n(\alpha)=[c\,\alpha u^{n}]_n=\varphi_n(c\alpha)$ (here $c\alpha$ is the product in $A$, and the product of homogeneous elements in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ is $[x]_r[y]_s=[xy]_{r+s}$, which is well defined because $w$ is multiplicative: if $x'=x+m$ with $w(m)>r$ then $w(x'y-xy)=w(my)=w(m)+w(y)>r+s$).
Surjectivity: let $\xi\in\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n=I_n/I_{n+1}$, say $\xi=[x]_n$ with $x=\sum_{i\ge n}\alpha_i u^i$. If $w(x)>n$ then $\xi=0=\varphi_n(0)$. Otherwise $w(x)=n$, so $\alpha_n\ne0$, and $x-\alpha_nu^{n}=\sum_{i\ge n+1}\alpha_iu^i\in I_{n+1}$, whence $\xi=[\alpha_nu^{n}]_n=\varphi_n(\alpha_n)$.
Injectivity: if $\varphi_n(\alpha)=0$ then $\alpha u^{n}\in I_{n+1}$, i.e. $w(\alpha u^{n})\ge n+1>n$. If $\alpha\ne0$ we showed $w(\alpha u^{n})=n$, a contradiction; hence $\alpha=0$.
Thus each $\varphi_n$ is an isomorphism of $F$-vector spaces.

Conclusion. $D=A\otimes_Fk\cong A((u))$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ (Steps 1--3); $w$ is a valuation on $D$ extending $v$ (Step 4) with $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ (Step 5); its residue division ring is $\mathcal{O}_w/\mathfrak{m}_w\cong A$ (Step 6); and for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ the map $\alpha\mapsto\mathrm{in}_w(\alpha u^{n})$ is an $F$-vector space isomorphism $A\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n$ (Step 7). (As a by-product, the maps $\varphi_n$ assemble into a graded $F$-algebra isomorphism $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)\cong A[U^{\pm1}]$ with $U$ a central indeterminate of degree $1$, since $\mathrm{in}_w(x)\mathrm{in}_w(y)=\mathrm{in}_w(xy)$ holds for all $x,y\ne0$ by multiplicativity of $w$.)

lemma_187.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^2$ if and only if at least one of the following holds: $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$; or $D$ contains two distinct subfields $K_1$ and $K_2$, each Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$, such that every element of $K_1$ commutes with every element of $K_2$.
lemma_187.proof:
Throughout we use the definitions of the conjecture: a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) is built from a Galois G-algebra L over k, i.e. a commutative etale k-algebra with dim_k(L)=|G|, equipped with an action of G by k-automorphisms, such that L^G=k.

STEP 0 (group theory: the groups of order p^2). Let G be any group of order p^2. The class equation gives |G| = |Z(G)| + sum_i [G:C_G(x_i)], where the x_i run over representatives of the non-central conjugacy classes; each index [G:C_G(x_i)] is >1 and divides |G|=p^2, hence is divisible by p. Reducing modulo p yields |Z(G)| ≡ |G| ≡ 0 (mod p), and by Lagrange |Z(G)| ∈ {p, p^2}. If |Z(G)| = p, then G/Z(G) has order p and is therefore cyclic; but if G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is abelian (choosing g with G = <g>·Z(G), any two elements g^i z and g^j z' commute because powers of g commute among themselves and with central elements), contradicting |Z(G)| = p < p^2. Hence |Z(G)| = p^2, i.e. G = Z(G) is abelian. If G contains an element σ of order p^2 then G = <σ> ≅ C_{p^2}. Otherwise every non-identity element has order p; pick 1 ≠ σ ∈ G and τ ∈ G \ <σ>. Since G is abelian, <σ,τ> is a subgroup strictly containing <σ>, so its order is p^2 and G = <σ><τ> with <σ> ∩ <τ> = {1} (the intersection is a proper subgroup of the order-p group <σ>), whence G ≅ C_p × C_p. Consequently, in the case G ≅ C_p × C_p there exist two distinct subgroups H_1 = <σ> and H_2 = <τ> of G, both of order p.

STEP 1 (converse direction, first alternative). Assume D contains a maximal subfield L which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group G of order p^2. Then: L is etale over k (it is a finite separable field extension); dim_k(L) = [L:k] = |Gal(L/k)| = p^2 = |G| (Galois theory); and L^G = k (again Galois theory, the fixed field of the full Galois group of a Galois extension is the base field). Thus L is a Galois G-algebra over k in the sense of the conjecture. Since D is central simple of degree n = p^2 and L ⊂ D is a maximal subfield Galois over k with group G, lemma_106 applies and yields a map c: G × G → L^× such that D ≅ ⊕_{σ∈G} L u_σ as k-algebras, with u_σ λ u_σ^{-1} = σ(λ) for all λ ∈ L and u_σ u_τ = c(σ,τ) u_{στ}. (Mechanism, as proved in lemma_106: Skolem–Noether realises each σ by a unit u_σ; the u_σ are L-linearly independent by Dedekind's lemma on independence of automorphisms and dim_L D = p^2 = |G|; and u_σ u_τ u_{στ}^{-1} centralises L, hence lies in L^× because a maximal subfield is self-centralising, C_D(L) = L, by the double centralizer theorem (ref_1).) So D is the crossed product (L,G,c) with |G| = p^2.

STEP 2 (converse direction, second alternative). Assume D contains two distinct subfields K_1, K_2, each Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p, such that every element of K_1 commutes with every element of K_2. By lemma_177 the compositum L := K_1 K_2 is a maximal subfield of D which is Galois over k with Gal(L/k) ≅ C_p × C_p. For completeness we recall the explicit verification, which is the content of lemma_177: (i) K_1 ∩ K_2 is an intermediate field of the extension K_1/k of prime degree p, so K_1 ∩ K_2 = k or K_1; the second possibility would give K_1 ⊆ K_2 and then equality by comparing degrees, contradicting K_1 ≠ K_2; hence K_1 ∩ K_2 = k. (ii) Since K_2/k is Galois, K_1 and K_2 are linearly disjoint over k: indeed, in the ambient (division) algebra D, the F-algebra L = K_1 K_2 is a field finite over k, K_2 ⊗_k K_1 → L has kernel a prime ideal, and because K_2/k is Galois with K_1 ∩ K_2 = k the tensor product K_2 ⊗_k K_1 is a field (K_2 and K_1 are linearly disjoint), so the map is an isomorphism and [L:k] = p·p = p^2. (iii) Thus [L:k] = p^2 = deg(D), so C_D(L) = L and L is a maximal subfield by the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1. (iv) Restriction to K_1 and K_2 gives an injective homomorphism Gal(L/k) → Gal(K_1/k) × Gal(K_2/k) (injective because L is generated over k by K_1 ∪ K_2), and both sides have order p^2, so it is an isomorphism Gal(L/k) ≅ C_p × C_p.
Now apply Step 1 to this maximal Galois subfield L, with G := Gal(L/k) ≅ C_p × C_p, which has order p^2: as in Step 1, L is etale of dimension p^2 = |G| with L^G = k, and lemma_106 exhibits D as the crossed product (L,G,c). Hence D is a crossed product for a group of order p^2.

STEP 3 (forward direction). Assume D is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) for some group G of order p^2; here L is a Galois G-algebra over k by definition. Apply lemma_133 with n = p^2: L is a field, and its image in D under the given isomorphism is a maximal subfield of D which is Galois over k with Galois group G. Identifying L with that image, we may write L ⊂ D. By Step 0, G is abelian and is either cyclic of order p^2 or isomorphic to C_p × C_p.

Case 3a: G ≅ C_{p^2}. Then L is a maximal subfield of D which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p^2; the first alternative holds.

Case 3b: G ≅ C_p × C_p. By Step 0 choose two distinct subgroups H_1, H_2 ⊂ G of order p, and set K_i := L^{H_i} ⊂ L ⊂ D, the fixed field of H_i. By the fundamental theorem of Galois theory applied to the finite Galois field extension L/k with group G:
 • [K_i : k] = [L^{H_i} : k] = [G : H_i] = p^2/p = p;
 • H_i is normal in G because G is abelian, hence K_i/k is Galois with Gal(K_i/k) ≅ G/H_i; this quotient has order p, hence is cyclic of order p;
 • K_1 ≠ K_2, because H ↦ L^H is an inclusion-reversing bijection between subgroups of G and intermediate fields of L/k, so distinct subgroups have distinct fixed fields;
 • every element of K_1 commutes with every element of K_2, since both K_1 and K_2 are contained in the commutative field L ⊂ D.
Thus the second alternative holds.

CONCLUSION. Steps 1 and 2 give the implication "(first alternative) or (second alternative) ⇒ D is a crossed product (L,G,c) with |G| = p^2"; Step 3 gives the converse. This establishes the claimed equivalence. (Remark: the argument never uses p > 2; the hypothesis is inherited from the surrounding context and only makes the statement stronger.)

lemma_188.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, write $\wp(F)=\{t^{p}-t:t\in F\}$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, and let $K$ be a subfield of $D$ that is Galois cyclic of degree $p$ over $k$ with generator $\sigma$. Suppose there exist $b\in K\setminus\wp(K)$ and $y\in K$ such that $\sigma(b)-b=y^{p}-y$, such that $\mathrm{Tr}_{K/k}(y)=0$, and such that the Artin-Schreier extension $K(w)/K$ defined by $w^{p}-w=b$ splits the centralizer $C_{D}(K)$. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.
lemma_188.proof:
Write $\wp(t)=t^{p}-t$. We are given: $D$ a central division $k$-algebra with $\deg D=p^{2}$; $K\subset D$ a subfield, Galois cyclic of degree $p$ over $k$ with generator $\sigma$; elements $b\in K\setminus\wp(K)$ and $y\in K$ with $\sigma(b)-b=\wp(y)$, $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(y)=0$; and the hypothesis that the Artin--Schreier extension $K(w)/K$, $\wp(w)=b$, splits $C_D(K)$.

Step 1: The centralizer $C_D(K)$. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), applied to the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ and the subfield $K$, $C_D(K)$ is a central simple $K$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[K:k]=p^{2}/p=p$; in particular $\dim_K C_D(K)=p^{2}$. It is a division ring: it is a $K$-subalgebra of the division ring $D$, and if $0\neq z\in C_D(K)$ then $z^{-1}\in D$ satisfies $z^{-1}x=xz^{-1}$ for all $x\in K$, so $z^{-1}\in C_D(K)$.

Step 2: $T^{p}-T-b$ is irreducible over $K$. Since $b\notin\wp(K)$ it has no root in $K$. Suppose it factored as $f=gh$ over $K$ with $1\le d:=\deg g\le p-1$. In a splitting field, if $u$ is one root then the $p$ roots of $f(T)=T^{p}-T-b$ are exactly $u+i$, $i\in\mathbb F_{p}$ (because $\wp(u+i)=\wp(u)+i^{p}-i=\wp(u)$). The roots of $g$ are then $u+i$ for $i$ in a subset $S\subset\mathbb F_{p}$ of size $d$, so the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $g$ is $-\sum_{i\in S}(u+i)=-d\,u-\sum_{i\in S}i\in K$. As $1\le d\le p-1$, $d$ is invertible in $K$, whence $u\in K$, contradiction. Thus $K(w)$ is a field with $[K(w):K]=p$, Galois cyclic over $K$ with generator $w\mapsto w+1$.

Step 3: Realising $w$ inside $C_D(K)$. By hypothesis $K(w)$ splits $C_D(K)$, and $[K(w):K]=p=\deg_K C_D(K)$. By the embedding criterion (ref_5, maximal case: a degree-$n$ field extension embeds as a maximal subfield of a degree-$n$ central simple algebra iff it splits it), there is a $K$-embedding $\iota:K(w)\hookrightarrow C_D(K)$ whose image is a maximal subfield. Put $u=\iota(w)$. Then $u^{p}-u=\iota(w^{p}-w)=\iota(b)=b$ (as $\iota$ is $K$-linear and $b\in K$), $K(u)=\iota(K(w))$ is a field with $[K(u):K]=p$, and $u$ commutes with every element of $K$.

Step 4: $E:=K(u)$ is a maximal subfield of $D$. We have $[E:k]=[E:K][K:k]=p\cdot p=p^{2}=\deg D$. Since $E$ is commutative, $E\subseteq C_D(E)$; by the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), $\dim_k C_D(E)=\dim_k D/\dim_k E=p^{4}/p^{2}=p^{2}=\dim_k E$, so $C_D(E)=E$, and ref_1's criterion ("$K$ maximal subfield iff $C_A(K)=K$") shows $E$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

Step 5: The iterates of $\sigma$ on $b$. Claim: for every $j\ge 0$, $\sigma^{j}(b)-b=\wp(z_j)$ with $z_j:=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\sigma^{i}(y)\in K$ (so $z_0=0$). Induction on $j$: for $j=0$ it is trivial. Given it for $j$,
$\sigma^{j+1}(b)-b=\sigma(\sigma^{j}(b)-b)+(\sigma(b)-b)=\sigma(\wp(z_j))+\wp(y)=\wp(\sigma(z_j))+\wp(y)=\wp(\sigma(z_j)+y)=\wp(z_{j+1}),$
using that $\sigma$ commutes with the Frobenius.
