Consistency check: $z_p=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\sigma^{i}(y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(y)=0$, and the formula then gives $\sigma^{p}(b)-b=0$, as it must since $\sigma^{p}=\mathrm{id}$. Moreover each $\sigma^{j}(b)\notin\wp(K)$: if $\sigma^{j}(b)=t^{p}-t$ then $b=\sigma^{j}(b)-\wp(z_j)=\wp(t-z_j)$, contradiction.

Step 6: $E/k$ is Galois. Let $k_s$ be a separable closure of $k$ containing $E$, and $\iota:E\to k_s$ a $k$-embedding. Since $K/k$ is Galois, $\iota(K)=K$ and $\iota|_K=\sigma^{j}$ for a unique $j\bmod p$. Then $\iota(u)^{p}-\iota(u)=\iota(u^{p}-u)=\iota(b)=\sigma^{j}(b)$, while by Step 5 $(u+z_j)^{p}-(u+z_j)=b+\wp(z_j)=\sigma^{j}(b)$. Hence $\delta:=\iota(u)-u-z_j$ satisfies $\delta^{p}=\delta$, so $\delta\in\mathbb F_{p}\subseteq K\subseteq E$, and $\iota(u)=u+z_j+\delta\in E$. Therefore $\iota(E)=\iota(K)(\iota(u))=K(\iota(u))=E$: every $k$-embedding of $E$ into $k_s$ is an automorphism, i.e. $E/k$ is normal. It is separable because $K/k$ is (Galois) and $u$ is separable over $K$ (its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides $T^{p}-T-b$, whose derivative is $-1\neq0$, so that polynomial is separable). Hence $E/k$ is Galois with group $\Gamma:=\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$ of order $[E:k]=p^{2}$; in particular $E^{\Gamma}=k$.

Step 7: The restriction sequence. $E=K(u)$ is the splitting field over $K$ of $T^{p}-T-b$ (all roots $u+i$, $i\in\mathbb F_{p}$, lie in $E$), so $\mathrm{Gal}(E/K)=\langle\tau\rangle\cong C_{p}$ with $\tau(u)=u+1$, $\tau|_K=\mathrm{id}$. The restriction map $\mathrm{res}:\Gamma\to\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ is surjective: any $k$-embedding $\tilde\sigma:K\hookrightarrow k_s$ extends to a $k$-embedding $\tilde\sigma:E\hookrightarrow k_s$ (standard extension of embeddings into an algebraic closure), and normality of $E/k$ forces $\tilde\sigma(E)=E$. Thus $\mathrm{res}$ is onto with kernel $\langle\tau\rangle$, consistently with $|\Gamma|=p^{2}$.

Step 8: A lift of $\sigma$ acting by $u\mapsto u+y$. Choose $\tilde\sigma\in\Gamma$ with $\tilde\sigma|_K=\sigma$. Then $\tilde\sigma(u)^{p}-\tilde\sigma(u)=\sigma(b)=b+\wp(y)=(u+y)^{p}-(u+y)$, so $\tilde\sigma(u)-(u+y)$ is a root of $T^{p}-T$, i.e. equals some $i\in\mathbb F_{p}$. Define $\varphi:=\tau^{-i}\tilde\sigma\in\Gamma$. Since $\tau^{-i}$ is the identity on $K$ and sends $u$ to $u-i$, we get $\varphi|_K=\sigma$ and $\varphi(u)=\tau^{-i}(u+y+i)=(u-i)+y+i=u+y$.

Step 9: $\varphi$ has order $p$. Inductively, $\varphi^{m}(u)=u+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\sigma^{j}(y)$ for $m\ge1$: indeed $\varphi^{m+1}(u)=\varphi(u)+\varphi(y)=u+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\sigma^{j}(y)+\sigma^{m}(y)$, using $\varphi|_K=\sigma$; and $\varphi^{m}|_K=\sigma^{m}$. For $m=p$ the sum is $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(y)=0$, so $\varphi^{p}(u)=u$ and $\varphi^{p}|_K=\mathrm{id}$; as $E=K(u)$ this gives $\varphi^{p}=\mathrm{id}_E$. Since $\varphi|_K=\sigma$ has order $p$, $\varphi$ has order exactly $p$.

Step 10: $\Gamma\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$. We check $\varphi$ and $\tau$ commute on the generators of $E=K(u)$: on $K$, $\varphi\tau=\sigma\circ\mathrm{id}=\sigma=\mathrm{id}\circ\sigma=\tau\varphi$; on $u$, $\varphi\tau(u)=\varphi(u+1)=u+y+1=\tau(u+y)=\tau\varphi(u)$. Hence $\varphi\tau=\tau\varphi$, so $\langle\varphi,\tau\rangle=\{\varphi^{a}\tau^{b}:0\le a,b\le p-1\}$. Its order is $p^{2}/|\langle\varphi\rangle\cap\langle\tau\rangle|$, and the intersection is trivial: every element of $\langle\tau\rangle$ fixes $K$ pointwise, whereas $\varphi^{a}|_K=\sigma^{a}\ne\mathrm{id}$ for $a\not\equiv0$. Thus $|\langle\varphi,\tau\rangle|=p^{2}=|\Gamma|$, so $\Gamma=\langle\varphi\rangle\times\langle\tau\rangle\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.

Step 11: Crossed product structure. The field $E$ is finite separable over $k$, hence an etale $k$-algebra; $\dim_k E=p^{2}=|\Gamma|$; $\Gamma$ acts on $E$ by $k$-automorphisms; and $E^{\Gamma}=k$ because $E/k$ is a Galois field extension with full automorphism group $\Gamma$. So $E$ is a $\Gamma$-Galois algebra over $k$ in the sense of the definition. Applying lemma_106 with $A=D$, $n=p^{2}$, $L=E$ (a maximal subfield of $D$, Step 4) and $G=\Gamma$, we obtain a map $c:\Gamma\times\Gamma\to E^{\times}$ such that $D\cong\bigoplus_{g\in\Gamma}E\,u_{g}$ with $u_{g}\lambda=g(\lambda)u_{g}$ and $u_{g}u_{h}=c(g,h)u_{gh}$. Therefore $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$, as claimed.

(Remark on the role of the hypotheses: $b\notin\wp(K)$ makes $K(w)/K$ a genuine degree-$p$ field extension, the splitting hypothesis plus the embedding criterion puts $u$ with $\wp(u)=b$ inside $C_D(K)$, the condition $\sigma(b)-b=\wp(y)$ makes $E=K(u)$ normal over $k$ and gives a lift $\varphi$ of $\sigma$ with $\varphi(u)=u+y$, and the trace-zero condition $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(y)=0$ is exactly what forces $\varphi^{p}=1$, excluding the cyclic group $C_{p^{2}}$.)

lemma_189.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, write $\wp(F)=\{x^{p}-x:x\in F\}$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ if and only if there exist a subfield $K$ of $D$ that is Galois cyclic of degree $p$ over $k$ with generator $\sigma$, an element $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}$, and an element $b\in K\setminus\wp(K)$ with $\sigma(b)-\lambda b\in\wp(K)$, such that the Artin-Schreier extension $K(w)/K$ defined by $w^{p}-w=b$ splits the centralizer $C_{D}(K)$.
lemma_189.proof:
Throughout, char(k)=p>2 and D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2.

ELEMENTARY FACTS (proved once and used below).
(a) For any field F of characteristic p, wp(F)={x^p-x} is an F_p-subspace of (F,+): (x^p-x)+(y^p-y)=(x+y)^p-(x+y), and a(x^p-x)=(ax)^p-(ax) for a in F_p. Moreover every field automorphism alpha of F satisfies alpha(wp(F))=wp(F), since alpha(x^p-x)=alpha(x)^p-alpha(x).
(b) Artin-Schreier basics (cf. ref_14). For a in F, if w is one root of f_a(T)=T^p-T-a in an extension, the full root set is {w+j : j in F_p} (because (w+j)^p-(w+j)=w^p-w). Hence f_a has a root in F iff a in wp(F), and then it splits completely in F; if a not in wp(F) then f_a is irreducible (any proper factor would contain one of its roots), it is separable since f_a'(T)=-1, and F(w)/F is Galois cyclic of degree p with Galois group {w |-> w+j : j in F_p}. Conversely every Galois extension of F of degree p has this form (ref_14(a)). Also (ref_14(b)): for a,a' not in wp(F), the fields K(wp^{-1}a) and K(wp^{-1}a') inside a separable closure coincide iff a' is in F_p^x a + wp(K).
(c) Every group of order p^2 is abelian: Z(G) is nontrivial (G a p-group); if |Z(G)|=p then G/Z(G) is cyclic of order p, and a group whose quotient by its centre is cyclic is abelian, contradiction. So Z(G)=G. In particular every subgroup is normal. Also G has an element of order p: for 1\neq g in G, ord(g) is p or p^2, and in the latter case g^p has order p.

(=>) Assume D is isomorphic to a crossed product (L,G,c) with |G|=p^2.

Step 1. Apply lemma_133 with n=p^2=deg D (note dim_k L=|G|=p^2): the image M of L in D is a maximal subfield of D, Galois over k with Gal(M/k) isomorphic to G. Thus [M:k]=p^2, and by (c) Gal(M/k) is abelian.

Step 2. Pick rho in Gal(M/k) of order p (exists by (c)) and set H=<rho>, K=M^H. Since Gal(M/k) is abelian, H is normal, so by the fundamental theorem K/k is Galois with Gal(K/k) ~ Gal(M/k)/H of order p, hence cyclic; also [K:k]=p and [M:K]=p. The restriction map Gal(M/k) -> Gal(K/k) is surjective with kernel Gal(M/K)=H (fundamental theorem, using that K/k is Galois); choose tau in Gal(M/k) mapping to a generator and put sigma:=tau|_K.

Step 3. M/K is Galois with group H=<rho> of order p. By (b) (ref_14(a)), M=K(u) with u^p-u=b, b in K\wp(K). Since b in K is fixed by rho, rho(u) is again a root of T^p-T-b, so rho(u)=u+j_0 with j_0 in F_p; j_0\neq 0, for otherwise rho would fix both K and u, i.e. rho=id on M=K(u). Replacing u by j_0^{-1}u (which still generates M over K) replaces b by j_0^{-p}b=j_0^{-1}b (as j_0^p=j_0); this is still outside wp(K) because wp(K) is an F_p-subspace (a). Hence we may assume rho(u)=u+1, and we rename j_0^{-1}b as b.

Step 4. Set y:=tau(u)-u. Using that Gal(M/k) is abelian, rho(y)=rho(tau(u))-rho(u)=tau(rho(u))-(u+1)=tau(u+1)-u-1=tau(u)-u=y, so y in M^H=K. Now, computing inside the field M (u and y commute):
sigma(b)=tau(b)=tau(u^p-u)=tau(u)^p-tau(u)=(u+y)^p-(u+y)=(u^p-u)+(y^p-y)=b+(y^p-y).
Thus sigma(b)-lambda b in wp(K) holds with lambda:=1 in F_p^x (p>2 guarantees 1\neq0 in F_p).

Step 5. It remains to see that the Artin-Schreier extension K(w)/K, w^p-w=b, splits C_D(K). Since M is commutative and contains K, M is contained in C_D(K). By ref_1 (double centralizer theorem), C_D(K) is a central simple K-algebra of degree deg(D)/[K:k]=p^2/p=p, so dim_K C_D(K)=p^2. Since b\notin\wp(K), K(w)=K[T]/(T^p-T-b) is a field by (b), so the K-algebra homomorphism K(w) -> C_D(K) sending w to u is injective (its kernel is a proper ideal of a field). Its image is K(u)=M, of K-dimension p=deg C_D(K); this image is a maximal subfield of C_D(K), since any subfield F of C_D(K) containing K satisfies [F:K]^2 <= dim_K C_D(K)=p^2, by ref_1 (dim_K F * dim_K C_{C_D(K)}(F)=dim_K C_D(K) together with C_{C_D(K)}(F) \supseteq F). Ref_5, applied over the base field K to the central simple K-algebra C_D(K) of degree n=p and the extension K(w)/K of degree m=p=n, then says that an embedding of K(w) as a maximal subfield is equivalent to K(w) splitting C_D(K). Hence K(w) splits C_D(K).

Collecting: K is a subfield of D Galois cyclic of degree p over k with generator sigma, lambda=1 in F_p^x, b in K\wp(K) with sigma(b)-lambda b in wp(K), and K(w)/K splits C_D(K).

(<=) Conversely, suppose there exist K subset D Galois cyclic of degree p over k with generator sigma, lambda in F_p^x, and b in K\wp(K) with sigma(b)-lambda b in wp(K), such that K(w)/K defined by w^p-w=b splits C_D(K).

Step 1. Because b\notin\wp(K), (b) implies K(w)=K[T]/(T^p-T-b) is a field, Galois cyclic of degree p over K. The extension K(w)/k is finite separable: K/k is separable (it is Galois) and K(w)/K is separable since (T^p-T-b)'=-1.

Step 2. Claim: K(w)/k is Galois. By Step 1 it suffices to prove normality. Fix a separable closure k_s/k containing K; since K(w)/K is finite separable, the inclusion K -> k_s extends to a K-embedding K(w) -> k_s; identify K(w) with its image, so w in k_s with w^p-w=b. (k_s is also a separable closure of K, as K/k is finite separable.)

Write sigma(b)=lambda b+(t^p-t) with t in K. We show by induction on i>=1 that sigma^i(b)-lambda^i b in wp(K). For i=1 this is the hypothesis. For the induction step, using sigma(wp(K))=wp(K) (fact (a)) and lambda in F_p subset k fixed by sigma:
sigma^{i+1}(b)-lambda^{i+1}b = sigma(sigma^i(b)-lambda^i b) + lambda^i (sigma(b)-lambda b),
which is a sum of two elements of the additive group wp(K). Hence sigma^i(b) in lambda^i b + wp(K) with lambda^i in F_p^x. In particular sigma^i(b)\notin\wp(K): if sigma^i(b) were in wp(K), then lambda^i b = (sigma^i(b)) - (sigma^i(b)-lambda^i b) would lie in wp(K), forcing b in wp(K), contradiction.

Now take any gamma in Gal(k_s/k). Since K/k is Galois, gamma(K)=K and gamma|_K=sigma^i for a unique i in {0,...,p-1}. As K(w) is generated over K by w,
gamma(K(w)) = gamma(K)(gamma(w)) = K(gamma(w)),   and   gamma(w)^p-gamma(w)=gamma(b)=sigma^i(b).
Thus gamma(K(w))=K(wp^{-1}sigma^i(b)) (the field generated over K by a root of T^p-T-sigma^i(b); this is independent of the chosen root, since roots differ by elements of F_p). Both b and sigma^i(b) avoid wp(K) and sigma^i(b) lies in F_p^x b + wp(K), so ref_14(b) gives K(wp^{-1}sigma^i(b)) = K(wp^{-1}b) = K(w) inside k_s. Therefore gamma(K(w))=K(w) for every gamma in Gal(k_s/k), i.e. K(w)/k is normal; with separability, K(w)/k is Galois (of degree [K(w):K][K:k]=p*p=p^2).

Step 3. We apply lemma_164 to D, to the subfield K of D, which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p, and to the element b in K\wp(K): Step 2 shows that the extension K(w)/K defined by w^p-w=b is Galois over k, and by hypothesis this extension splits the centralizer C_D(K). Lemma_164 concludes that D is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L,G,c) for some group G of order p^2.

Both implications are established, which proves the lemma.

(Remarks. (i) In the forward direction the element lambda can always be taken equal to 1. (ii) The splitting hypothesis in the converse is equivalent, by ref_5, to C_D(K) containing an element u with u^p-u=b: such a u gives an embedding of the field K(w) into C_D(K), and conversely an embedding of K(w) into the degree-p K-algebra C_D(K) exists whenever K(w) splits it, since then ind(C_D(K)\otimes_K K(w))=1 divides p/p=1; the field K(w)/K has degree p=deg C_D(K), so the embedding criterion of ref_5 applies.)

lemma_as_laurent_dichotomy.statement:
Let $p>2$ be a prime and let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p$. Let $A$ be a central division $F$-algebra, let $k=F((u))$ and $D=A((u))$, both endowed with their $u$-adic valuations. If $D$ contains an element $a
otin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$, then either $A$ contains an element $\alpha
otin F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha\in F$, or $A$ contains an element $	heta
otin F$ with $	heta^{p}\in F$.
lemma_as_laurent_dichotomy.proof:
Throughout, $p>2$ is a prime, $F$ has characteristic $p$, and $A$ is a central division $F$-algebra ($Z(A)=F$, every non-zero element of $A$ is invertible). We write $k=F((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation $v$, and $D=A((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation $w$.

PART I. STRUCTURE OF $D=A((u))$ AND OF $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$.

Elements of $D$ are formal series $x=\sum_{i\ge N(x)}x_i u^i$ with $N(x)\in\mathbb Z$, $x_i\in A$, and $x_{N(x)}\ne 0$ (for $x\ne0$); i.e. $D=A[[u]][u^{-1}]$, the localisation of the series ring in the *central* indeterminate $u$. Since $u$ is central, multiplication is $xy=\sum_s\big(\sum_{i+j=s}x_iy_j\big)u^s$, where the inner sum is finite (non-zero terms require $i\ge N(x)$, $j\ge N(y)$, $i+j=s$). Define $w(x)=N(x)$ for $x\ne0$ and $w(0)=\infty$.

(1) $w$ is a valuation on the ring $D$ with $w(D^\times)=\mathbb Z$. Indeed, for $x,y\ne0$ the coefficient of $u^{N(x)+N(y)}$ in $xy$ is $x_{N(x)}y_{N(y)}$, which is non-zero because $A$ is a division ring (hence has no zero divisors); so $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$. Also $w(x+y)\ge\min(w(x),w(y))$: if $w(x)<w(y)$ the coefficient of $u^{w(x)}$ in $x+y$ is $x_{w(x)}\ne0$, so equality holds, and if $w(x)=w(y)$ the leading coefficient is a sum, so $w(x+y)\ge w(x)$. Taking $x=u$ shows $w(D^\times)=\mathbb Z$.

(2) $D$ is a division ring. Let $x\ne0$, $N=N(x)$, $x_N\in A^\times$. Since $u$ is central, $x=u^{N}x'$ with $x'=x_N+x_{N+1}u+x_{N+2}u^2+\cdots\in A[[u]]$. Write $x'=x_N(1-z)$ with $z=-\sum_{i\ge1}x_N^{-1}x_{N+i}u^{i}\in uA[[u]]$. Then $\sum_{j\ge0}z^{j}\in A[[u]]$ is well defined (as $z^{j}\in u^{j}A[[u]]$, the coefficient of each fixed power $u^{s}$ in the sum involves only $j\le s$), and $(1-z)\sum_{j=0}^{J}z^{j}=1-z^{J+1}$ with $z^{J+1}\in u^{J+1}A[[u]]$ shows $(1-z)^{-1}=\sum_{j\ge0}z^{j}$ in $A[[u]]$; the same identity on the other side gives $x'^{-1}=(\sum_{j\ge0}z^{j})x_N^{-1}\in A[[u]]$. Hence $x^{-1}=x'^{-1}u^{-N}\in D$.

(3) $Z(D)=k$. If $z=\sum_i z_i u^i\in D$ commutes with every element of $A^\times\subset D^\times$, then for each $\alpha\in A^\times$, comparing coefficients in $\alpha z=\sum_i(\alpha z_i)u^i=\sum_i(z_i\alpha)u^i=z\alpha$ gives $\alpha z_i=z_i\alpha$ for all $i$, so $z_i\in Z(A)=F$. Thus $z\in F((u))=k$. Conversely $k\subset Z(D)$ because $F=Z(A)$ and $u$ is central. So $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra and $w$ restricts to $v$ on $k$ (both are the $u$-adic valuation).

(4) Valuation ring and residue ring. $\mathcal O_D:=\{x:w(x)\ge0\}=A[[u]]$, and by the invertibility argument of (2) with $N=0$ an element $\sum_{i\ge0}x_iu^i\in A[[u]]$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_D$ iff $x_0\ne0$. Hence $\mathfrak m:=uA[[u]]=\{w\ge1\}$ is exactly the set of non-units of $\mathcal O_D$, so it is the (two-sided, in fact central, generated by the central element $u$) maximal ideal, and the constant-term map
$$\rho:\mathcal O_D=A[[u]]\longrightarrow A,\qquad \textstyle\sum_{i\ge0}x_iu^i\longmapsto x_0,$$
which is a ring homomorphism because $u$ is central (the constant term of a product is the product of the constant terms), is surjective with kernel $\mathfrak m$. Thus the residue division ring of $D$ is $A$. Moreover $\mathcal O_D\cap k=F[[u]]$, and $\rho$ restricts to the usual residue map $F[[u]]\twoheadrightarrow F$; in particular $\rho\big(\mathcal O_D\cap Z(D)\big)=F$.

(5) The graded ring. For each $n\in\mathbb Z$, $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n=\{w\ge n\}/\{w>n\}=u^{n}A[[u]]/u^{n+1}A[[u]]$, and $\alpha\mapsto$ (class of $\alpha u^{n}$) is an isomorphism of abelian groups $A\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n$. Under these identifications the product is $(\alpha u^{n})(\beta u^{n'})=\alpha\beta\,u^{n+n'}$, so
$$\mathrm{gr}_w(D)\cong A[u^{\pm1}],$$
the Laurent polynomial ring in a central indeterminate $u$ of degree $1$ over $A$. This graded ring is a domain: the leading coefficient of a product of two non-zero homogeneous-type elements is a product of non-zero elements of $A$, hence non-zero.

Finally, $k=F((u))$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, and $\mathrm{char}(k)=p>2$. Thus $k$ and $D$ satisfy the hypotheses of lemma_162 and lemma_163.

PART II. THE ELEMENT $a$.

Let $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^{p}-a=c\in k$. Since $w(D^\times)=\mathbb Z$, exactly one of $w(a)>0$, $w(a)=0$, $w(a)<0$ holds.

Case 1: $w(a)>0$. Impossible by lemma_162 applied to the complete discretely valued field $(k,v)$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, $\mathrm{char}(k)=p>2$, and the central division $k$-algebra $D$ with the extending valuation $w$: it asserts that no $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$ can have $w(a)>0$.

Case 2: $w(a)=0$. Write $a=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i u^{i}$ with $a_0\ne0$. Then $a\in\mathcal O_D$, so $c=a^{p}-a\in\mathcal O_D\cap k=F[[u]]$. Applying the homomorphism $\rho$ gives
$$\bar a^{\,p}-\bar a=\rho(c)\in F,\qquad \bar a:=\rho(a)=a_0\in A.$$
If $\bar a\notin F$, then $\alpha:=\bar a$ is the required Artin--Schreier element of $A$. Suppose instead $\bar a\in F$. Put $b:=a-\bar a$; since $\bar a\in F\subset Z(D)$, the binomial expansion has no cross terms, so
$$b^{p}-b=(a^{p}-a)-(\bar a^{\,p}-\bar a)=c-(\bar a^{\,p}-\bar a)\in k.$$
Moreover $w(b)>0$, because subtracting the constant term $\bar a=a_0$ cancels the degree-$0$ part of $a$, and $b\notin k$, for otherwise $a=b+\bar a\in k$. This contradicts lemma_162 (Case 1). Hence $\bar a\notin F$, and Case 2 always yields $\alpha=\bar a\in A\setminus F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha=\rho(c)\in F$.

Case 3: $w(a)=-m<0$ with $m\ge1$. Write $a=\sum_{i\ge -m}a_i u^{i}$ with $a_{-m}=:\theta\ne0$ (so $\theta\in A^\times$, $A$ being a division ring). By lemma_163 (applicable by Part I: $k$ complete discretely valued of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, $D$ a central division $k$-algebra with extending valuation $w$, $a^{p}-a=c\in k$, $w(a)<0$) we have $p\,w(a)=v(c)=-pm<0$ and, in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$,
$$\mathrm{in}_w(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_v(c).$$
Under $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)\cong A[u^{\pm1}]$ we have $\mathrm{in}_w(a)=\theta\,u^{-m}$ and $\mathrm{in}_v(c)=t\,u^{-pm}$ for some $t\in F^\times$. As $u$ is central of degree $1$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$,
$$\theta^{p}u^{-pm}=(\theta u^{-m})^{p}=\mathrm{in}_w(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_v(c)=t\,u^{-pm},$$
hence $\theta^{p}=t\in F^\times$.

For completeness we spell out the same identity by direct coefficient comparison, which uses only the formulas of Part I. In $a^{p}=\prod_{r=1}^{p}\big(\sum_{i\ge-m}a_iu^{i}\big)=\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_p\ge -m}a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_p}u^{i_1+\cdots+i_p}$, the exponent sum $i_1+\cdots+i_p$ equals $-pm$ only when all $i_r=-m$; hence the coefficient of $u^{-pm}$ in $a^{p}$ is $\theta^{p}\ne0$, so $w(a^{p})=-pm$ with leading coefficient $\theta^{p}$. Since $pm>m$ (as $p\ge2$, $m\ge1$), the exponents occurring in $-a$ are $\ge -m>-pm$, so $-a$ contributes nothing in degree $-pm$. Thus $c=a^{p}-a$ has valuation $-pm$ and leading coefficient $\theta^{p}$. As $c\in k=F((u))$, that leading coefficient lies in $F$, i.e. $\theta^{p}\in F^\times$ (and $v(c)=-pm$), as claimed.

If $\theta\notin F$, then $\theta$ is the required $p$-central element of $A$: $\theta\in A\setminus F$ and $\theta^{p}=t\in F$.

If $\theta\in F$, set $a_1:=a-\theta u^{-m}$. Here $\theta u^{-m}\in F((u))=k=Z(D)$ by (3), so again there are no cross terms:
$$a_1^{p}-a_1=(a^{p}-a)-\big((\theta u^{-m})^{p}-\theta u^{-m}\big)=c-\big(\theta^{p}u^{-pm}-\theta u^{-m}\big)\in k.$$
Furthermore $w(a_1)>-m$, because the leading terms $\theta u^{-m}$ cancel, so $a_1=\sum_{i>-m}a_i u^{i}$; and $a_1\notin k$, for otherwise $a=a_1+\theta u^{-m}\in k$.

PART III. ITERATION AND TERMINATION.

We construct a sequence $a^{(0)},a^{(1)},\dots$ with $a^{(0)}=a$, each $a^{(j)}\in D\setminus k$ satisfying $(a^{(j)})^{p}-a^{(j)}\in k$, as follows. Given $a^{(j)}$:
- $w(a^{(j)})>0$ cannot occur, by lemma_162;
- if $w(a^{(j)})=0$, Case 2 produces $\alpha\in A\setminus F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha\in F$, and we stop (first alternative of the conclusion);
- if $w(a^{(j)})=-m_j<0$, Case 3 produces the leading coefficient $\theta_j\in A^\times$ with $\theta_j^{p}\in F$. If $\theta_j\notin F$ we stop with $\theta:=\theta_j$ (second alternative). If $\theta_j\in F$ we set $a^{(j+1)}:=a^{(j)}-\theta_j u^{-m_j}$, which by the computation in Case 3 again lies in $D\setminus k$, satisfies $(a^{(j+1)})^{p}-a^{(j+1)}\in k$, and has $w(a^{(j+1)})>w(a^{(j)})$.

Thus, as long as the procedure has not terminated, the integers $w(a^{(j)})$ form a strictly increasing sequence which is $\le -1$ for every negative-valuation step and which can never be positive (lemma_162). Since $w(a^{(0)})=-m$, all these values lie in the finite set $\{-m,-m+1,\dots,-1\}$, so there are at most $m$ indices $j$ with $w(a^{(j)})<0$. Consequently the procedure must terminate: either at some step it yields $\theta_j\in A\setminus F$ with $\theta_j^{p}\in F$, or at some index $j$ one reaches $w(a^{(j)})=0$, in which case Case 2 yields $\alpha\in A\setminus F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha\in F$.

In every possible case, $A$ contains either an Artin--Schreier element over $F$ (an $\alpha\notin F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha\in F$) or a $p$-central element over $F$ (a $\theta\notin F$ with $\theta^{p}\in F$). This is exactly the stated dichotomy. $\qquad\blacksquare$

(Remarks on the use of hypotheses: $p>2$ is used only through the hypotheses of lemma_162 and lemma_163; the elimination of the sub-case $\bar a\in F$ in Case 2 and of the positive-valuation case relies on the completeness of $k=F((u))$ and $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$ as required there; centrality of $u$ and $Z(D)=k$ are what make the subtractions $a-\theta_j u^{-m_j}$ preserve the condition $x^{p}-x\in k$, since only then does $(x-z)^{p}=x^{p}-z^{p}$ hold.)

lemma_190.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ such that every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$. Then every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ if and only if every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is annihilated by $p$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_190.proof:
We fix a field $k$ of characteristic $p>2$ and we assume throughout the standing hypothesis

(H) every central division $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class $[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$.

We must prove the equivalence of the two assertions

(A) every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ is isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$;
(B) every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is annihilated by $p$ is isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.

We first record a consequence of (H) that will be used repeatedly.

Claim. Under (H), every central division $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$ with $p[D]\neq 0$ is isomorphic to a crossed product $(M,G,c)$ with $G$ cyclic of order $p^{2}$.

Proof of the claim. Let $D$ be such a division algebra. By (H) there is a subfield $M\subseteq D$ which is a maximal subfield of $D$ and is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(M/k)$ of order $p^{2}$. We check that $M$, with this $G$-action, satisfies the definition of a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ recalled in the statement of the conjecture:
- $M$ is an etale $k$-algebra: a finite separable field extension is etale, and a Galois extension is in particular separable;
- $\dim_k M=[M:k]=|G|=p^{2}$, since $M/k$ is Galois with group $G$, so the dimension equals the order of the group;
- $M^{G}=k$, by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory.
Thus $M$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$, and $|G|=p^{2}=\deg D$. Applying the proved lemma lemma_106 (the crossed-product criterion from a Galois maximal subfield) to the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$ and to its maximal subfield $M$ which is Galois over $k$ with group $G$, we obtain a map $c:G\times G\to M^{\times}$ such that $D\simeq\bigoplus_{g\in G}M u_{g}$ with $u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)u_g$ and $u_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}$ for all $\lambda\in M$, $g,h\in G$. That is exactly a crossed product algebra $(M,G,c)$ with $|G|=p^{2}$ (indeed $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$). This proves the claim.

We now prove the two implications of the equivalence.

(1) (A) $\Rightarrow$ (B). Assume (A), and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ with $p[D]=0$. Since (A) applies to every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, without any restriction on its Brauer class, it applies in particular to this $D$; hence $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$. As $D$ was arbitrary in the subclass $\{D:\;p[D]=0\}$, (B) holds. (This direction is just the restriction of a universally quantified statement to a subclass; it needs no hypothesis on $k$.)

(2) (B) $\Rightarrow$ (A). Assume (B). Let $D$ be an arbitrary central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$; we must show $D$ is a crossed product for some group of order $p^{2}$. The class $[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$ either satisfies $p[D]=0$ or it does not; these two cases are exhaustive and we treat them separately.

Case 1: $p[D]=0$. Then $D$ belongs to the class of division algebras considered in (B), so by (B) there exist a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, a Galois $G$-algebra $L$ over $k$ and a $2$-cocycle $c:G\times G\to L^{\times}$ with $D\simeq(L,G,c)$. Done.

Case 2: $p[D]\neq 0$. Then the claim proved above applies to $D$: using the hypothesis (H) we obtain a maximal subfield $M\subseteq D$ which is Galois over $k$ with cyclic group $G=\mathrm{Gal}(M/k)$ of order $p^{2}$, and lemma_106 then exhibits $D$ as a crossed product $(M,G,c)$ with $|G|=p^{2}$. Done.

Since in both cases $D$ is a crossed product for a group of order $p^{2}$, and $D$ was an arbitrary central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, assertion (A) holds.

Combining (1) and (2) gives the claimed equivalence, which completes the proof of the lemma. (No edge case is missed: the dichotomy $p[D]=0$ versus $p[D]\neq 0$ is exhaustive for every $D$, and in Case 2 the group produced, being cyclic of order $p^{2}$, has order $p^{2}$ as required, while the algebra $(M,G,c)$ satisfies the definition of a $G$-crossed product because $M$ is a Galois $G$-algebra, as verified in the claim.)

lemma_191.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$. Then $D$ contains an element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$ if and only if $D$ contains a subfield $K$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.
lemma_191.proof:
Write $\wp(F)=\{t^{p}-t:t\in F\}$ for a field $F$ of characteristic $p$. We prove both implications; note that the hypothesis "$\deg D=p^{2}$" is only part of the ambient context and is not used in the argument (the only property of $D$ used is that it is a division ring, so that $k[a]$ is a domain).

=====================================================================
Part I: ($\Leftarrow$) A cyclic Galois subfield of degree $p$ yields an Artin--Schreier element.
=====================================================================

Assume $K\subset D$ is a subfield which is Galois over $k$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)=\langle\sigma\rangle$ cyclic of order $p$. Since $K/k$ is Galois, the fixed field is $K^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=K^{\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)}=k$.

Step 1 (additive Hilbert 90 in the cyclic case, proved here in full). View $K$ as a $k$-vector space of dimension $p$, and consider the $k$-linear endomorphisms $\sigma-1$ and $\mathrm{Tr}=\mathrm{Tr}_{K/k}=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\sigma^{i}$ of $K$ (the latter identity holds because $K/k$ is Galois with group $\{1,\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{p-1}\}$).

(a) $\mathrm{Tr}\circ(\sigma-1)=\sigma^{p}-1=0$ as an operator, since $\sigma^{p}=1$; hence $\mathrm{im}(\sigma-1)\subseteq\ker(\mathrm{Tr})$.

(b) $\dim_k\mathrm{im}(\sigma-1)=p-\dim_k\ker(\sigma-1)=p-\dim_k K^{\sigma}=p-1$, because $\ker(\sigma-1)=\{x\in K:\sigma(x)=x\}=K^{\sigma}=k$.

(c) $\mathrm{Tr}\neq 0$ as a $k$-linear map. Indeed, by Dedekind's lemma on the linear independence of distinct automorphisms, the $p$ distinct automorphisms $1,\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{p-1}$ of the field $K$ are linearly independent over $K$, hence in particular they are not the zero endomorphism of the additive group of $K$; thus $\mathrm{Tr}=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\sigma^{i}$ is a nonzero $k$-linear functional $K\to k\subset K$. Therefore $\ker(\mathrm{Tr})$ is a hyperplane: $\dim_k\ker(\mathrm{Tr})=p-1$.

(d) From (a), (b), (c): two $k$-subspaces with $\mathrm{im}(\sigma-1)\subseteq\ker(\mathrm{Tr})$ and equal finite dimension $p-1$, so
$$\mathrm{im}(\sigma-1)=\ker(\mathrm{Tr}).$$
This is the additive Hilbert 90 statement we need.

Step 2 (apply Step 1 to $x=1$). Since $\mathrm{char}(k)=p$, $\mathrm{Tr}_{K/k}(1)=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\sigma^{i}(1)=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}1=p\cdot 1=0$. Hence $1\in\ker(\mathrm{Tr})=\mathrm{im}(\sigma-1)$, so there exists $a\in K$ with
$$\sigma(a)-a=1,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sigma(a)=a+1.$$
Then $a\notin k$, for $a\in k=K^{\sigma}$ would give $\sigma(a)=a$, contradicting $\sigma(a)=a+1\neq a$ (as $1\neq0$ in a field).

Now compute, using that $\sigma$ is a field automorphism of characteristic $p$ (so $(u+v)^{p}=u^{p}+v^{p}$):
$$\sigma(a^{p}-a)=\sigma(a)^{p}-\sigma(a)=(a+1)^{p}-(a+1)=(a^{p}+1)-(a+1)=a^{p}-a.$$
Thus $a^{p}-a$ is fixed by $\sigma$, hence fixed by all of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$, so $a^{p}-a\in K^{\sigma}=k$. Since $K\subset D$, the element $a$ lies in $D$. We have produced $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$.

=====================================================================
Part II: ($\Rightarrow$) An Artin--Schreier element generates a cyclic Galois subfield of degree $p$.
=====================================================================

Assume $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^{p}-a=c\in k$.

Step 1 ($k(a)$ is a subfield of $D$). Since $a\in D$, the $k$-subalgebra $k[a]\subseteq D$ generated by $a$ is a commutative ring without zero divisors (it is a subring of the division ring $D$) and is finite dimensional over $k$, because $a$ satisfies the monic polynomial $f(T):=T^{p}-T-c\in k[T]$ (indeed $f(a)=a^{p}-a-c=0$), so $k[a]$ is spanned by $1,a,\dots,a^{p-1}$. A finite-dimensional commutative $k$-domain is a field (for $0\neq x\in k[a]$, multiplication by $x$ is an injective, hence surjective, $k$-linear map of $k[a]$, so $x^{-1}\in k[a]$). Hence $k[a]=k(a)$ is a subfield of $D$.

Step 2 (the minimal polynomial of $a$ over $k$ is $f(T)=T^{p}-T-c$, so $[k(a):k]=p$). Let $m(T)\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $a$ over $k$, of degree $d$, $1\le d\le p$; then $m\mid f$ in $k[T]$. Note $f'(T)=-1\neq0$, so $f$ is separable, hence so is $m$; in a splitting field $\Omega$ of $f$ over $k$, the $p$ roots of $f$ are exactly $a+i$ for $i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}=\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\subset k$ (since $(a+i)^{p}-(a+i)=a^{p}+i^{p}-a-i=a^{p}-a=c$), and they are distinct. The roots of $m$ in $\Omega$ therefore form a subset $S=\{a+i:j\in J\}$ with $J\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}$, $|J|=d$, and $a\in S$ (as $m(a)=0$, so $a=a+0$). Comparing the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $m(T)=\prod_{s\in S}(T-s)$, we get
$$-\,(\text{coeff.~of }T^{d-1}\text{ in }m)=\sum_{s\in S}s=\sum_{j\in J}(a+j)=d\cdot a+\Big(\sum_{j\in J}j\Big).$$
The left-hand side lies in $k$, and $\sum_{j\in J}j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\subset k$; hence $d\cdot a\in k$. Since $1\le d\le p$ and $m$ has degree $d$, if $d=p$ we are done. Suppose $d<p$; then $d\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}$, so $a=(d\cdot a)/d\in k$, contradicting $a\notin k$. (The case $d=1$ is exactly the excluded assertion $a\in k$.) Hence $d=p$ and $[k(a):k]=p$.

Step 3 ($k(a)/k$ is Galois with cyclic Galois group of order $p$). The polynomial $f(T)=T^{p}-T-c$ splits completely over $k(a)$ as $f(T)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}(T-(a+i))$, and each $a+i\in k(a)$; so $k(a)$ is a splitting field over $k$ of the separable polynomial $f$, hence $k(a)/k$ is normal and separable, i.e. Galois. Every $k$-embedding $\iota:k(a)\hookrightarrow\overline{k}$ sends $a$ to a root of $m=f$, so $\iota(a)=a+i$ for a unique $i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$, and each $i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ does occur (as $a+i\in k(a)$, the assignment $a\mapsto a+i$ defines a $k$-endomorphism of $k(a)$, which is an automorphism since it is injective and $k(a)$ is finite dimensional over $k$). Thus
$$\mathrm{Gal}(k(a)/k)=\{\tau_{i}:a\mapsto a+i\mid i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\},\qquad \tau_{i}\circ\tau_{j}=\tau_{i+j},$$
so $\mathrm{Gal}(k(a)/k)\cong(\mathbb{F}_{p},+)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, cyclic of order $p$; explicitly $\tau_{1}$ generates it, and $|\mathrm{Gal}(k(a)/k)|=p=[k(a):k]$, consistent with the Galois property.

Taking $K:=k(a)$ we obtain a subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.

=====================================================================
Conclusion
=====================================================================
Parts I and II together give: $D$ contains $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$ if and only if $D$ contains a subfield $K$ Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$. $\blacksquare$

(Remark on the hypotheses: the argument uses only that $D$ is a division ring containing $k$ in its centre; the degree $p^{2}$ assumption, and the assumption $p>2$ that appears elsewhere in the development, play no role here. The two constructions are inverse in spirit: $K\mapsto a$ with $\sigma(a)=a+1$ (additive Hilbert 90, Step 1 of Part I), and $a\mapsto k(a)$ (Part II).)

lemma_192.statement: Let $F$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p>2$, let $D$ be a central division $F$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, and let $u$ be an indeterminate. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ over $F$ if and only if $D\otimes_{F}F((u))$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L',G,c')$ for some group of order $p^{2}$ over $F((u))$.
lemma_192.proof:
Write $K:=F((u))$, let $v$ be the $u$-adic valuation of $K$, with valuation ring $\mathcal O_K=F[[u]]$, uniformiser $u$, value group $v(K^{\times})=\mathbb Z$ and residue field $\bar K=F$. Since $K$ is complete for $v$, it is henselian. Throughout, $D((u))$ denotes $D\otimes_F K$ via $\alpha\otimes\sum f_i u^i\mapsto\sum \alpha f_i u^i$ (this is a ring isomorphism: an element of $D\otimes_F K$ is a finite sum $\sum_j d_j\otimes g_j(u)$, i.e. a series whose coefficients lie in the finite-dimensional $F$-span of the $d_j$, and conversely such a series is obtained by expanding the coefficients in that span).

DIRECTION ($\Rightarrow$). Suppose $D\simeq (L,G,c)$ with $|G|=p^{2}$ and $L$ a $G$-Galois $F$-algebra: $L$ is etale over $F$, $\dim_F L=|G|$, $G$ acts by $F$-algebra automorphisms, and $L^G=F$.

Claim 1: $L_K:=L\otimes_F K$ is a $G$-Galois $K$-algebra.
(a) Etaleness: $L\simeq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\ell_i$ with each $\ell_i/F$ finite separable, say $\ell_i=F(\alpha_i)$ with minimal polynomial $f_i$. Then $\ell_i\otimes_F K\simeq K[T]/(f_i)$, and $f_i'=0$ would contradict separability of $\ell_i/F$, so $f_i'\neq 0$ in $K[T]$ as well; hence $K[T]/(f_i)$ is a product of finite separable field extensions of $K$, i.e. etale over $K$. Thus $L_K$ is etale over $K$.
(b) Dimension: $\dim_K L_K=\dim_F L=p^{2}=|G|$.
(c) Action: $g\cdot(x\otimes\lambda):=(gx)\otimes\lambda$ is a well defined $K$-algebra automorphism of $L_K$ (on simple tensors $g$ is an $F$-algebra automorphism and $K$ is fixed), and $g\mapsto(g\otimes\mathrm{id})$ is a group action.
(d) Invariants: the sequence of $F$-vector spaces $0\to L^G\to L\xrightarrow{\varphi}\prod_{g\in G}L$, $\varphi(x)=(gx-x)_{g\in G}$, is exact. Tensoring with $K$, which is free and hence flat over $F$, keeps it exact; the kernel of $\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_K$ is exactly $(L\otimes_F K)^G$. Hence $(L\otimes_F K)^G=L^G\otimes_F K=F\otimes_F K=K$.
This proves Claim 1.

Claim 2: $D\otimes_F K\simeq (L_K,G,c_K)$ as $K$-algebras, where $c_K(g,h):=c(g,h)\otimes 1\in L_K^{\times}$.
Indeed, as $K$-vector spaces $(L,G,c)\otimes_F K=\bigoplus_{g\in G}(L\otimes_F K)u_g$, and on homogeneous elements the product in the tensor product is
$((x\otimes\lambda)u_g)\cdot((y\otimes\mu)u_h)=(x\,u_g y\,u_h)\otimes\lambda\mu=(x\,g(y)\,c(g,h)\,u_{gh})\otimes\lambda\mu=(x\otimes\lambda)\,(g(y)\otimes\mu)\,(c(g,h)\otimes 1)\,u_{gh}=(x\otimes\lambda)\,g(y\otimes\mu)\,c_K(g,h)\,u_{gh},$
using that $G$ acts trivially on $K$, so $(g(y)\otimes\mu)=g(y\otimes\mu)$. Thus the relations $u_g\,z=g(z)u_g$ and $u_gu_h=c_K(g,h)u_{gh}$ hold, giving the isomorphism $D\otimes_F K\simeq(L_K,G,c_K)$. Finally $c_K$ is a $2$-cocycle: from $c(g,h)c(gh,k)=g(c(h,k))c(g,hk)$ in $L^{\times}$ we get $c_K(g,h)c_K(gh,k)=c(g,h)c(gh,k)\otimes1=(g(c(h,k))\otimes1)(c(g,hk)\otimes1)=g(c_K(h,k))c_K(g,hk)$.
Since $L_K$ is a $G$-Galois $K$-algebra and $|G|=p^2$, this exhibits $D\otimes_F F((u))$ as a crossed product algebra $(L_K,G,c_K)$ over $K=F((u))$ for the group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.

DIRECTION ($\Leftarrow$). Assume $D\otimes_F K\simeusime (L',G,c')$ with $|G|=p^{2}$ and $L'$ a $G$-Galois $K$-algebra; put $\mathcal D:=D\otimes_F K=D((u))$.

Step 1 (the $u$-adic valuation on $\mathcal D$). Apply lemma_185 with the roles $F\mapsto F$, $A\mapsto D$, $k\mapsto K$: $\mathcal D$ is a central division $K$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, the map $w\big(\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^{i}\big)=\min\{i:\alpha_i\neq0\}$ is a valuation on $\mathcal D$ extending $v$, its value group is $w(\mathcal D^{\times})=v(K^{\times})=\mathbb Z$, and its residue division ring is isomorphic to $D$. Concretely, $\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}=\{x:w(x)\ge0\}=D[[u]]$ and $\mathfrak p_{\mathcal D}=\{x:w(x)>0\}=uD[[u]]$, which is a two-sided ideal because $w(ax),w(xa)\ge w(x)$; the constant-term map $\mathrm{res}:D[[u]]\twoheadrightarrow D$, $\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha_i u^i\mapsto\alpha_0$, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $uD[[u]]$ (the constant term of a product is the product of constant terms), so $\bar{\mathcal D}:=\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}/\mathfrak p_{\mathcal D}\simeq D$, in agreement with lemma_185.

Step 2 (a Galois maximal subfield of $\mathcal D$). By lemma_133 applied to the central division $K$-algebra $\mathcal D$ of degree $p^2=|G|$ and the crossed product structure $\mathcal D\simeusime (L',G,c')$, the algebra $L'$ is a field and its image $M\subset\mathcal D$ is a maximal subfield of $\mathcal D$ which is Galois over $K$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(M/K)\simeq G$. In particular $[M:K]=p^{2}$.

Step 3 (ramification computation). Because $K$ is henselian, $v$ has a unique extension to the algebraic extension $M/K$; the restriction $w|_M$ is such an extension, hence it is that unique extension. Its valuation ring is $\mathcal O_M=\{x\in M:w(x)\ge0\}=M\cap D[[u]]$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p_M=M\cap uD[[u]]$, and its residue field is $\bar M$. Applying lemma_96 to the henselian discretely valued field $K$ and the finite Galois extension $M/K$ gives
$[M:K]=[w(M^{\times}):v(K^{\times})]\cdot[\bar M:F].$
Since $M^{\times}\subset\mathcal D^{\times}$ we have $w(M^{\times})\subset w(\mathcal D^{\times})=\mathbb Z=v(K^{\times})$ (and $v(K^{\times})\subset w(M^{\times})$ as $w$ extends $v$), so $[w(M^{\times}):v(K^{\times})]=1$. As $[M:K]=p^{2}$, it follows that $[\bar M:F]=p^{2}$.

Step 4 (the residue field is a subfield of $D$). Restricting $\mathrm{res}:D[[u]]\to D$ to $\mathcal O_M$ gives a ring homomorphism with kernel $\mathcal O_M\cap uD[[u]]=\mathfrak p_M$; hence it induces an injective homomorphism $\imath:\bar M=\mathcal O_M/\mathfrak p_M\hookrightarrow D$. Its image $N:=\imath(\bar M)$ is a subfield of $D$. The map $\mathrm{res}$ is $F$-linear and $F^{\times}\subset\mathcal O_M^{\times}$ with $\mathrm{res}(a)=a$ for $a\in F^{\times}$, so $F\subset N$, and $[N:F]=[\bar M:F]=p^{2}$.

Step 5 ($N$ is a maximal subfield of $D$). Apply the double centralizer theorem, ref_1, to the subfield $N\subset D$: $C_D(N)$ is a central simple $N$-algebra with $[C_D(N):F]=[D:F]/[N:F]=p^{4}/p^{2}=p^{2}$, and $C_D(C_D(N))=N$. Since $N$ is commutative, $N\subseteq C_D(N)$, and equality of $F$-dimensions forces $C_D(N)=N$; by the maximal subfield criterion in ref_1, $N$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

Step 6 ($N/F$ is Galois). Apply lemma_183 to the henselian discretely valued field $K=F((u))$ with perfect residue field $F$ and the finite Galois extension $M/K$: the residue extension $\bar M/F$ is finite Galois. Since $\imath:\bar M\xrightarrow{\sim}N$ is an $F$-algebra isomorphism, $N/F$ is Galois, with group $\Gamma:=\mathrm{Gal}(N/F)$ of order $[N:F]=p^{2}$ (necessarily $\Gamma\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(M/K)\simeq G$).

Step 7 (conclusion). Apply lemma_106 to the central simple $F$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$ and the maximal subfield $N$ which is Galois over $F$ with group $\Gamma$: there exists a map $c:\Gamma\times\Gamma\to N^{\times}$ such that $D\simeq\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma}N u_{\gamma}$ with $u_{\gamma}\lambda=\gamma(\lambda)u_{\gamma}$ and $u_{\gamma}u_{\delta}=c(\gamma,\delta)u_{\gamma\delta}$ for all $\lambda\in N$ and $\gamma,\delta\in\Gamma$. That is, $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(N,\Gamma,c)$ over $F$ for the group $\Gamma$ of order $p^{2}$.

Both implications are established, which completes the proof of the equivalence. (Remark: the forward implication used neither $p>2$ nor the perfectness of $F$; the reverse implication uses perfectness of $F$ exactly in the hypotheses of lemma_185 and lemma_183, and $p>2$ likewise.)

lemma_194.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$. If $D$ contains no element $x$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$, then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_194.proof:
Write $[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$ for the Brauer class of $D$; by hypothesis $p[D]\neq 0$, and $D$ is a division algebra, so $\dim_k D=(\deg D)^2=p^4$ and every maximal subfield of $D$ has degree $p^2$ over $k$. We must show that under the extra hypothesis

$(\ast)$\quad there is no $x\in D$ with $x^{p^2}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$,

$D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^2$. We argue by contradiction, in five steps.

**Step 1 (groups of order $p^{2}$).\** Let $G$ be any group with $|G|=p^{2}$. Then $G$ is abelian: $G$ acts on itself by conjugation, and the class equation gives
$$|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i [G:C_G(x_i)],$$
where the $x_i$ range over representatives of the non-central conjugacy classes. Each index $[G:C_G(x_i)]$ is an integer $>1$ dividing $|G|=p^{2}$, hence is divisible by $p$; since $p$ divides $|G|$, the equation forces $p$ to divide $|Z(G)|$, so $Z(G)\neq 1$. If $G$ were non-abelian we would have $|Z(G)|=p$, so $G/Z(G)$ would have order $p$ and hence be cyclic, generated by some $gZ(G)$. Every element of $G$ would then be of the form $g^{a}z$ with $z\in Z(G)$, and any two such elements commute (since $g$ commutes with itself and with every central element), contradicting non-abelianness. Thus $Z(G)=G$: $G$ is abelian. By the structure theorem for finite abelian groups, $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$ or $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.

**Step 2 (a crossed-product structure forces a cyclic Galois maximal subfield).\** Suppose, towards a contradiction, that $D\cong (L,G,c)$ as $k$-algebras for some group $G$ with $|G|=p^{2}=\deg D$, where $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ (so $L$ is etale of $k$-dimension $|G|$ with $L^{G}=k$, by the definition recalled in the conjecture). All hypotheses of lemma_133 (Spark) are satisfied with $n=p^{2}$: $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $n$ isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ with $|G|=n$ and $L$ a Galois $G$-algebra. That lemma yields that $L$ is a field and that its image $M\subset D$ under the isomorphism is a maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(M/k)\cong G$. In particular $[M:k]=|G|=p^{2}$, consistent with $M$ being a maximal subfield.

By Step 1, $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$ or $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$. If $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$, then $D$ would contain a maximal subfield Galois over $k$ with Galois group $C_{p}\times C_{p}$, and lemma_166 (Spark) applied to $D$ and $M$ would give $p[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$, contradicting the hypothesis $p[D]\neq0$. Hence $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$, and
$$(\dagger)\qquad D\ \text{contains a maximal subfield } M \text{ that is Galois over } k \text{ with cyclic Galois group of order } p^{2}.$$
(In the standard terminology of the theory of $p$-algebras, $(\dagger)$ says precisely that $D$ is a *cyclic* division algebra of degree $p^{2}$; this is the formulation of Albert's criterion used in the next step.)

**Step 3 (Albert's cyclicity criterion gives a purely inseparable maximal subfield).\** We apply the reference ref_19 (Albert's cyclicity criterion) with $n=2$: $\mathrm{char}(k)=p$ and $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ which is cyclic by $(\dagger)$. The criterion states that a cyclic $p$-algebra of degree $p^{n}$ contains a simple purely inseparable maximal subfield, that is, a subfield of the form $k(x)$ with $[k(x):k]=p^{n}$ and $x^{p^{n}}\in k$. With $n=2$ we obtain an element $x\in D$ such that
$$x^{p^{2}}\in k\qquad\text{and}\qquad [k(x):k]=p^{2}.$$
(For orientation only, not used below: the hypotheses also force $\exp(D)=p^{2}$, since $\exp(D)\mid \mathrm{ind}(D)=\deg D=p^{2}$, $\exp(D)\neq1$ as $D$ is a non-split division algebra, and $\exp(D)\neq p$ because $p[D]\neq0$; so we are exactly in the exponent-$p^{2}$ situation of the classical statement of the criterion.)

**Step 4 (the element $x$ satisfies $x^{p}\notin k$).\** Assume for a contradiction that $x^{p}\in k$. Then $x$ is a root of the polynomial $f(T)=T^{p}-x^{p}\in k[T]$, which has degree $p$; consequently the $k$-subalgebra $k[x]=k(x)$ generated by $x$ has $k$-dimension at most $p$. This contradicts $[k(x):k]=p^{2}>p$ obtained in Step 3. Hence $x^{p}\notin k$. (This is exactly the equivalence $[k(x):k]=p^{n}\Longleftrightarrow x^{p^{n-1}}\notin k$, valid for $x$ with $x^{p^{n}}\in k$, recorded in ref_19; we have spelled out the computation.

**Step 5 (contradiction).\** The element $x\in D$ constructed in Steps 3 and 4 satisfies $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$, contradicting the hypothesis $(\ast)$ on $D$. Therefore the supposition in Step 2 is impossible: there is no group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ and no $2$-cocycle $c:G\times G\to L^{\times}$ with $D\cong (L,G,c)$.

This completes the proof.

*Remark.* Combined with the forward implication proved in Step 2, the argument shows that for a central division $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$ with $p[D]\neq0$, the following are equivalent: $D$ is a crossed product for some group of order $p^{2}$; $D$ is cyclic (contains a Galois maximal subfield with group $C_{p^{2}}$); $D$ contains an element $x$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$ (equivalently, a simple purely inseparable maximal subfield). The lemma is the contrapositive of the last implication.

lemma_193.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$. If $D$ contains a maximal subfield $E$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$, then $D$ contains an element $x$ with $x^{p^2}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$; in particular $k(x)$ is a purely inseparable maximal subfield of $D$.
lemma_193.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_193.

Setup and notation. Write G := Gal(E/k); by hypothesis G is cyclic of order p^2, and we fix a generator sigma, so G = <sigma>. Then dim_k E = p^2 = deg D and dim_k D = p^4. (The extra hypotheses p > 2 and [D] not in Br(k)[p] are not needed below; the argument works for every prime p, and we do not try to manufacture a use for them.)

Step 1. C_D(E) = E.
The subalgebra E of D is a field, hence a simple k-subalgebra. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) applied to B = E inside the central simple k-algebra D, we have dim_k(E) * dim_k(C_D(E)) = dim_k(D), hence dim_k C_D(E) = p^4 / p^2 = p^2. Since E is commutative, E is contained in C_D(E); equality of finite k-dimensions forces C_D(E) = E. (Consistently, ref_1 then also says E is a maximal subfield of D, which we already know.)

Step 2. Units of D implementing the elements of G.
The field E is a commutative etale k-algebra (finite separable over k) with dim_k E = p^2 = |G| =: n, the group G acts on E by k-algebra automorphisms, and E^G = k because E/k is Galois with group G. Thus E subset D is a commutative subalgebra of dimension n = deg D which is a G-Galois algebra, so ref_3 applies to A = D: there are units u_tau in D^x (tau in G), with u_1 = 1, such that
  (i)  u_tau * l * u_tau^{-1} = tau(l)  for all l in E,
  (ii) D = direct sum over tau in G of E u_tau,
  (iii) u_tau u_eta = f(tau,eta) u_{tau eta} for a normalized 2-cocycle f : G x G -> E^x.
Equivalently, u_tau * l = tau(l) * u_tau for all l in E. Put u := u_sigma.

Step 3. A unit implementing tau also has inverse implementing tau^{-1}.
Let v in D^x satisfy v l v^{-1} = tau(l) on E for some tau in G. First, v^{-1} preserves E: given l in E, surjectivity of tau on E gives l = tau(l') for some l' in E, and then v^{-1} l v = v^{-1} (tau(l')) v = v^{-1} (v l' v^{-1}) v = l' in E. Second, for m in E, conjugating v^{-1} m v by v gives back m, i.e. m = tau(v^{-1} m v); since tau is a bijection of E, v^{-1} m v = tau^{-1}(m). Applying this to v = u^i (i >= 0), which implements sigma^i on E by induction from Step 2(i), we obtain for all i >= 0 and all l in E:
  u^i l u^{-i} = sigma^i(l)   and   u^{-i} l u^{i} = sigma^{-i}(l),
together with the equivalent forms u^i l = sigma^i(l) u^i and u_{tau} l = tau(l) u_{tau}.

Step 4. For 0 <= i <= p^2 - 1 one has E u^i = E u_{sigma^i}, and D = direct sum_{i=0}^{p^2-1} E u^i.
Fix i with 0 <= i <= p^2 - 1 and l in E. Using Step 2(i) for tau = sigma^i and Step 3 for v = u^i,
  (u^{-i} u_{sigma^i}) l (u^{-i} u_{sigma^i})^{-1} = u^{-i} ( u_{sigma^i} l u_{sigma^i}^{-1} ) u^{i} = u^{-i} sigma^i(l) u^{i} = sigma^{-i}( sigma^i(l) ) = l.
Thus u^{-i} u_{sigma^i} centralizes E, i.e. u^{-i} u_{sigma^i} =: e_i lies in C_D(E) = E (Step 1), and e_i is a unit of E since it is a product of units. Then
  u_{sigma^i} = u^i e_i = sigma^i(e_i) u^i  in E u^i      (using u^i m = sigma^i(m) u^i),
  u^i = u_{sigma^i} e_i^{-1} = sigma^i(e_i^{-1}) u_{sigma^i}  in E u_{sigma^i}   (using u_{sigma^i} m = sigma^i(m) u_{sigma^i}),
so E u^i = E u_{sigma^i} as k-subspaces of D. Since {sigma^i : 0 <= i <= p^2-1} = G, the subspaces E u^i are exactly the summands appearing in the direct-sum decomposition (ii) of Step 2; therefore D = sum_{i=0}^{p^2-1} E u^i and the sum is direct. (This is the corrected replacement for the false assertion that the powers of u are literally the basis units u_tau.)

Step 5. u^{p^2} lies in k^x.
By Step 3, conjugation by u^{p^2} on E is sigma^{p^2} = id_E, so u^{p^2} centralizes E; hence u^{p^2} in C_D(E) = E by Step 1. Furthermore u^{p^2} commutes with u, so sigma(u^{p^2}) = u u^{p^2} u^{-1} = u^{p^2}; that is, u^{p^2} belongs to the fixed field E^{<sigma>} = E^G = k. Since D is a division ring and u != 0, b := u^{p^2} is nonzero; hence b in k^x. (Steps 4 and 5 together say exactly that D is the cyclic algebra (E/k, sigma, b); we use no further properties of the cocycle f.)

Step 6. The element x := u satisfies x^{p^2} in k and x^p not in k.
First, x^{p^2} = u^{p^2} = b in k^x by Step 5. Next, sigma has order p^2, so sigma^p has order p and in particular sigma^p != id_E; choose l in E with sigma^p(l) != l. Then u^p l = sigma^p(l) u^p != l u^p, so u^p does not commute with the element l of D. Every element of k = Z(D) commutes with l. Hence u^p not in k, i.e. x^p not in k. In particular x not in k as well, and x != 0 because D is a division ring.

Step 7. k(x)/k is purely inseparable.
Because x^{p^2} = b in k, every element of k(x) can be written z = sum_{i=0}^{p^2-1} a_i x^i with a_i in k, and then z^{p^2} = sum_i a_i^{p^2} x^{i p^2} = sum_i a_i^{p^2} b^i in k (Frobenius is additive and multiplicative, and x^{i p^2} = b^i). Thus every element of k(x) satisfies a polynomial T^{p^2} - c with c in k, i.e. is purely inseparable over k of exponent at most 2; so k(x)/k is a purely inseparable extension.

Step 8. [k(x):k] = p^2.
Let m(T) in k[T] be the minimal polynomial of x over k and d := deg m = [k(x):k]. Since x^{p^2} - b = 0, the polynomial m divides T^{p^2} - b in k[T] (division algorithm in k[T] applied to T^{p^2} - b by m). Fix an algebraic closure Omega of k(x). In Omega[T] we have T^{p^2} - b = (T - x)^{p^2} (characteristic p), so
  m(T) = (T - x)^d in Omega[T], with 1 <= d <= p^2,          (8.1)
and x is the only root of m in Omega.

Claim A. If z in D satisfies z^p in k and z not in k, then [k(z):k] = p.
Proof of Claim A. Let h in k[T] be the minimal polynomial of z and let Omega' be an algebraic closure of k(z). Since z is a root of T^p - z^p in k[T], h divides T^p - z^p = (T - z)^p in Omega'[T]; the monic divisors of (T - z)^p are the powers (T - z)^t, so h = (T - z)^{deg h} in Omega'[T] with 1 <= deg h <= p, and z is the unique root of h. Since z not in k, deg h >= 2. Suppose p does not divide deg h. Then h'(T) = deg h * (T - z)^{deg h - 1} is a NONZERO polynomial in Omega'[T] of degree deg h - 1 < deg h; because h is irreducible in k[T] it cannot divide h', so gcd(h, h') = 1 in k[T]. Hence h is separable, so h has deg h distinct roots in Omega', contradicting h = (T - z)^{deg h} with deg h >= 2. Therefore p | deg h, and with 2 <= deg h <= p this forces deg h = p, i.e. [k(z):k] = p. This proves Claim A.

End of Step 8. By Step 6, x not in k, so d >= 2. If p did not divide d, then by (8.1) m'(T) = d (T - x)^{d-1} would be a nonzero polynomial of degree d - 1 < d = deg m; irreducibility of m gives gcd(m, m') = 1, so m is separable and has d distinct roots in Omega, contradicting (8.1). Thus p | d. Writing m(T) = sum_j a_j T^j with a_j in k, the identity m' = 0 reads j * a_j = 0 in k for every j, so a_j = 0 whenever p does not divide j. Hence m(T) = g(T^p) for some g in k[T], necessarily of degree d/p. Evaluating at T = x gives g(x^p) = m(x) = 0, so the minimal polynomial h of y := x^p over k divides g in k[T]. Apply Claim A to z = y: y^p = x^{p^2} = b in k and y = x^p not in k by Step 6, so deg h = p. Consequently p = deg h <= deg g = d/p, i.e. d >= p^2. Combined with d <= p^2 from (8.1), this yields d = p^2. (In particular m(T) = T^{p^2} - b, the least e with x^{p^e} in k is e = 2, and this is the justification, previously missing, that the minimal polynomial is a pure p-power binomial rather than an arbitrary divisor of (T - x)^{p^2}.)

Step 9. k(x) is a maximal subfield of D.
We have dim_k k(x) = [k(x):k] = p^2 = deg D. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) applied to the simple k-subalgebra k(x) of D, dim_k C_D(k(x)) = dim_k D / dim_k k(x) = p^4 / p^2 = p^2 = dim_k k(x). Since k(x) is commutative, k(x) subset C_D(k(x)), hence C_D(k(x)) = k(x); by the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1 this says exactly that k(x) is a maximal subfield of D. By Step 7 this maximal subfield is purely inseparable over k.

Conclusion. The element x = u_sigma constructed in Step 2 satisfies x^{p^2} = b in k^x (Step 5), x^p not in k (Step 6), and k(x) is a purely inseparable maximal subfield of D (Steps 7-9). This is precisely the statement of the lemma. QED

lemma_195.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$. Let $K$ be a subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$ and generator $\sigma$. Then there exists $a\in k^{\times}$ such that $p[D]=[(K/k,\sigma,a)]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$, where $[(K/k,\sigma,a)]$ denotes the Brauer class of the cyclic algebra $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}Kv^{i}$ with $v^{p}=a$ and $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in K$.
lemma_195.proof:
We write Br(F) for the Brauer group of a field F, and for a field extension E/F we write res_{E/F}: Br(F) -> Br(E), [A] |-> [A \otimes_F E], for the restriction (scalar extension) homomorphism; this is a group homomorphism because tensor product distributes over tensor product of algebras.

Step 1: The centralizer of K in D.
Apply the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) to A = D (a central simple k-algebra, since D is a central division k-algebra) and to the simple k-subalgebra B = K. It gives:
  (a) C := C_D(K) is a central simple K-algebra;
  (b) deg_K(C) = deg(D)/[K:k] = p^2/p = p (equivalently dim_K C = p^2, and indeed dim_k C = dim_k D / dim_k K = p^4/p = p^3 = p \cdot p^2, consistent);
  (c) C is Brauer equivalent to D \otimes_k K, i.e. in Br(K) one has
        res_{K/k}([D]) = [C].

Step 2: The class [C] is killed by p.
Write C \cong M_r(\Delta) with \Delta a central division K-algebra. Then ind(C) = deg(\Delta) divides deg(C) = p, so ind(C) \in \{1, p\}. The exponent of a central simple algebra divides its index (exp(M_r(\Delta)) = exp(\Delta), and exp(\Delta) | deg(\Delta) for a division algebra), hence exp(C) | p. Therefore
        p \cdot [C] = 0 \quad \text{in } Br(K).

Step 3: p[D] is split by K.
Since res is a group homomorphism and using Step 1(c) and Step 2,
        res_{K/k}(p[D]) = p \cdot res_{K/k}([D]) = p \cdot [C] = 0.
Thus p[D] lies in the kernel of res_{K/k}, that is, in the relative Brauer group
        Br(K/k) := ker(Br(k) \to Br(K)) = { \alpha \in Br(k) : K splits a representative of \alpha }.

Step 4: Identification of Br(K/k) with cyclic algebras over K/k.
The extension K/k is a cyclic Galois *field* extension of degree p with Galois group generated by \sigma. We now apply ref_22(i) with L = K, \sigma as above, and n = p: for a cyclic Galois field extension L/k with generator \sigma, the assignment b \mapsto [(L,\sigma,b)] (the class of the cyclic algebra \bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1} L v^i with v^n = b and v\lambda v^{-1} = \sigma(\lambda)) induces a group isomorphism
        k^{\times}/N_{L/k}(L^{\times}) \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\; Br(L/k).
In particular this map is surjective onto Br(K/k). (Note that the relations v\lambda v^{-1} = \sigma(\lambda) and v\lambda = \sigma(\lambda)v used in ref_22 and in the statement of the present lemma are equivalent, since v is a unit.)

Step 5: Conclusion.
By Step 3, p[D] \in Br(K/k); by the surjectivity in Step 4 there exists a \in k^{\times} with
        p[D] = [(K/k,\sigma,a)] \quad \text{in } Br(k),
which is exactly the required assertion. The element a is well defined modulo the norm group N_{K/k}(K^{\times}) by the injectivity part of the isomorphism in Step 4.

Edge case (p[D] = 0): if p[D] happens to be the trivial class (this is the case exactly when exp(D) = p), the above still applies: the trivial class of Br(K/k) corresponds under the isomorphism of Step 4 to the coset of 1 \in k^{\times}, and indeed 1 = N_{K/k}(1) is a norm, so the cyclic algebra (K/k,\sigma,1) is split; thus one may take a = 1 \in k^{\times}. No separate argument is needed, but this shows the statement is non-vacuous in that case.

Remarks on the consistency of the result: since D has degree p^2, exp(D) divides p^2, so p[D] \in Br(k)[p]; correspondingly each cyclic algebra (K/k,\sigma,a) has degree p and hence exponent dividing p, so both sides are p-torsion classes. Also, the hypothesis that D is a division algebra is used only to guarantee [K:k] = p \mid deg(D) so that C_D(K) has degree p (Step 1); the argument works verbatim for any central simple k-algebra of degree divisible by p containing K as a subfield.

This completes the proof.

lemma_196.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$. If $D$ contains a subfield $K$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$, then the class $p[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has index at most $p$.
lemma_196.proof:
We write [X] for the Brauer class of a central simple algebra X, and for a field extension F/k we write res_{F/k}: Br(k) -> Br(F), [X] |-> [X \otimes_k F], for the restriction (scalar extension) homomorphism. All arguments take place over the arbitrary given field k of characteristic p>2; no valuation theory is used.

Hypotheses. D is a central division k-algebra with deg D = p^2, hence dim_k D = (deg D)^2 = p^4. K \subset D is a subfield with K/k Galois cyclic of degree p; in particular K/k is finite separable of degree p, and dim_k K = p.

Step 1: the centralizer C := C_D(K) is a central division K-algebra of degree p. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), applied to the k-subalgebra K \subset D, C is a central simple K-algebra of degree deg(D)/[K:k] = p^2/p = p. For completeness we spell out the dimension count that ref_1 gives: dim_k(K) \cdot dim_k(C) = dim_k(D), so p \cdot dim_k(C) = p^4, hence dim_k(C) = p^3 and therefore dim_K(C) = p^3/p = p^2 = (deg_K C)^2, i.e. deg_K C = p. Also C is a division ring, because C is a unital K-subalgebra of the division ring D, so it has no zero divisors. (This is exactly the content of the proved lemma lemma_71, which additionally records that [C] = res_{K/k}[D] in Br(K); that Brauer-class identity is not needed below.)

Step 2: there is a field E with K \subset E \subset C, E/K separable of degree p. By the Noether--Koethe theorem (ref_16) applied to the central division K-algebra C, C contains a maximal subfield E that is separable over K. Its degree over K is computed inside C with ref_1: since E is a subfield of the central simple K-algebra C, dim_K(E) \cdot dim_K(C_C(E)) = dim_K(C) = p^2; and since E is a maximal subfield of C, the maximal-subfield criterion of ref_1 gives C_C(E) = E, so dim_K(C_C(E)) = dim_K(E). Hence (dim_K E)^2 = p^2, i.e. [E:K] = dim_K E = p. Thus E/K is a separable extension of degree p. Moreover E \subset C_D(K) \subset D, so E is a subfield of D, and by the tower law [E:k] = [E:K]\cdot[K:k] = p \cdot p = p^2.

Step 3: E splits D. Since E \subset D is a subfield, ref_1 gives dim_k(E) \cdot dim_k(C_D(E)) = dim_k(D) = p^4, so dim_k(C_D(E)) = p^4/p^2 = p^2 = dim_k(E). As E is commutative we have E \subseteq C_D(E), and the two k-dimensions are equal, so C_D(E) = E. By the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1, E is a maximal subfield of D. By the maximal-subfield/splitting equivalence in ref_5 ("when m = n, K embeds in A as a maximal subfield if and only if K splits A"), E splits D, i.e.
   res_{E/k}[D] = [D \otimes_k E] = 0 in Br(E).      (3.1)

Step 4: p \cdot res_{K/k}[D] = 0 in Br(K). Because E/K is finite separable (Step 2), the corestriction homomorphism cor_{E/K}: Br(E) -> Br(K) is defined. Two standard properties are used:
 (i) Transitivity of restriction: res_{E/K} \circ res_{K/k} = res_{E/k}, which holds because there is a canonical K-algebra isomorphism (D \otimes_k K) \otimes_K E \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } D \otimes_k E, (x \otimes a) \otimes b \mapsto x \otimes ab, so scalar extension from k to K and then from K to E equals scalar extension from k to E.
 (ii) The fundamental identity cor_{E/K} \circ res_{E/K} = [E:K] \cdot \mathrm{id}_{Br(K)}. Indeed, identifying Br(F) with the Galois cohomology group H^2(G_F, F_s^{\times}) for a separable closure F_s, res_{E/K} is the usual restriction of cocycles along the inclusion of closed subgroups G_E \subset G_K (of index [E:K], since E/K is finite separable), and cor_{E/K} is the group-cohomology corestriction (transfer); for a subgroup H of finite index in a group G one has cor_H^G \circ res_H^G = [G:H]\cdot\mathrm{id} on H^{\bullet}(G,-) (Mackey's formula for the double cosets H\backslash G/H: the double coset H\cdot 1 \cdot H contributes the identity endomorphism and the other double cosets contribute zero to the composite res\circ cor; equivalently this is the standard "cor\circ res = index" theorem). Applying (ii) with [E:K] = p and then (i) and (3.1):
   p \cdot res_{K/k}[D] = cor_{E/K}(res_{E/K}(res_{K/k}[D])) = cor_{E/K}(res_{E/k}[D]) = cor_{E/K}(0) = 0,
the last equality because cor_{E/K} is a group homomorphism and therefore sends 0 to 0.

Step 5: the degree-p extension K/k splits the class p[D]. Since res_{K/k} is a group homomorphism, res_{K/k}(p[D]) = p \cdot res_{K/k}[D] = 0 by Step 4. Thus (p[D]) \otimes_k K = 0 in Br(K); equivalently, K is a splitting field of the Brauer class p[D], and [K:k] = p.

Step 6: the index bound. Let \Delta be the central division k-algebra representing p[D], so ind(p[D]) := deg \Delta. Because K splits p[D], the algebra \Delta \otimes_k K is split: ind(\Delta \otimes_k K) = 1. Applying ref_12 to \Delta and the finite extension K/k gives the divisibility ind(\Delta) \mid [K:k] \cdot ind(\Delta \otimes_k K) = p \cdot 1 = p. (In ref_12's notation: ind(D \otimes_k K) \mid ind(D) and ind(D) \mid [K:k]\,ind(D \otimes_k K); we use the second divisibility.) Hence ind(p[D]) divides p, so ind(p[D]) \in \{1, p\} and in particular ind(p[D]) \le p. This is precisely the claim.

Edge cases and hypothesis check. If p[D] = 0 in Br(k), then \Delta = k, ind(p[D]) = 1 \le p, and the argument above still applies verbatim (ind(\Delta \otimes_k K) = ind(k \otimes_k K) = 1). All hypotheses used are satisfied: K/k is separable of degree p (it is Galois, indeed cyclic, of degree p), which is exactly what is needed for the corestriction cor_{K/k}-type machinery in Step 4 to be available over an arbitrary field; no henselian, valued-field, or Laurent-series assumption is required, and no crossed-product or Galois-maximal-subfield construction is used. Notice that only [K:k] = p and separability of K/k enter the proof; the assumptions p > 2 and that Gal(K/k) is cyclic are stronger than needed, so they are simply not exploited. (Equivalently, Step 4 says that the exponent of [D \otimes_k K] = [C_D(K)] divides p, which is consistent with the degree-p computation in Step 1; the corestriction computation is what converts that exponent statement over K into the index statement over k.)

lemma_197.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, with residue division ring $\bar D$ and with $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$; suppose $\bar D$ is central of degree $p^{2}$ over $\bar k$. Let $\bar L$ be a maximal subfield of $\bar D$ that is Galois over $\bar k$ with Galois group $G$. Then there exists a subfield $L$ of $D$ that is a maximal subfield, is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$, and has residue field $\bar L$.
lemma_197.proof:
PROOF OF THE REVISED STATEMENT (maximality of L̄ is now a hypothesis).

Notation. Let O_k be the valuation ring of v with uniformizer π, so v(k×) = Z and k̄ = O_k/πO_k. Let O_D = {x ∈ D : w(x) ≥ 0} and M_D = {x ∈ D : w(x) > 0}, so D̄ = O_D/M_D. Since w(D×) = v(k×) = Z: if x ∈ M_D then w(x) = n ≥ 1 = v(πⁿ), so x = πⁿ·(π^{-n}x) with π^{-n}x ∈ O_D, and the reverse inclusion πO_D ⊆ M_D is immediate. Hence
(1)  M_D = πO_D and D̄ = O_D/πO_D.
The residue map ρ_D : O_D → D̄ is thus reduction modulo πO_D; it restricts to the residue map O_k → k̄, and O_k ⊆ O_D because v(c) ≥ 0 ⇒ w(c) ≥ 0.

STEP 1. O_D is a free O_k-module of rank p⁴ with basis lifting a k̄-basis of D̄.
Choose e₁,…,e_{p⁴} ∈ O_D whose residues ē₁,…,ē_{p⁴} form a k̄-basis of D̄; this is possible because ρ_D is surjective and dim_{k̄} D̄ = (deg D̄)² = p⁴ (D̄ is central division of degree p² over k̄).
(i) k-linear independence: suppose Σ c_i e_i = 0 with c_i ∈ k not all zero, and let m = min_i v(c_i). Write c_i = π^m c′_i with c′_i ∈ O_k and at least one c′_i a unit. Then Σ c′_i e_i = 0, every term c′_i e_i lies in O_D, and reducing modulo πO_D by (1) gives Σ c̄′_i ē_i = 0 in D̄ with some c̄′_i ≠ 0, contradicting the k̄-linear independence of the ē_i. Hence all c_i = 0. Since dim_k D = (deg D)² = p⁴, the e_i form a k-basis of D.
(ii) Coefficients of integral elements lie in O_k: let x = Σ c_i e_i ∈ O_D and m = min_i v(c_i). If m < 0, write c_i = π^m c′_i as above; then π^{-m}x = Σ c′_i e_i has residue Σ c̄′_i ē_i ≠ 0 in D̄. But w(π^{-m}x) = w(x) − m ≥ −m > 0, so π^{-m}x ∈ M_D = πO_D by (1), i.e. its residue is 0 — contradiction. Hence m ≥ 0 and all c_i ∈ O_k. Thus O_D = ⊕_{i=1}^{p⁴} O_k e_i; the same computation with arbitrary c_i ∈ k shows moreover w(Σ c_i e_i) = min_i v(c_i), since π^{-m}x has non-zero residue, so w(π^{-m}x) = 0.

STEP 2. The polynomial data. Since L̄ is a maximal subfield of the central division k̄-algebra D̄ of degree p², [L̄ : k̄] = p²; put n = p² = |G|. L̄/k̄ is Galois, hence finite separable, so by the primitive element theorem there is ᾱ ∈ L̄ with L̄ = k̄(ᾱ). Let f̄ ∈ k̄[T] be the minimal polynomial of ᾱ: monic, irreducible, of degree n, and separable, so disc(f̄) ≠ 0 in k̄. Let f ∈ O_k[T] be the monic polynomial obtained by lifting each coefficient of f̄. The discriminant of a monic polynomial is a polynomial in its coefficients, so disc(f) reduces to disc(f̄) ≠ 0; hence
(2)  disc(f) ∈ O_k×.
Choose a ∈ O_D with ρ_D(a) = ᾱ.

STEP 3. Existence of a root b ∈ O_D of f with residue ᾱ. Put R = O_k[a] ⊂ O_D. Then R is commutative (generated over the commutative ring O_k by one element), is a domain (it is a subring of the division ring D), and is a finite O_k-module (an O_k-submodule of O_D, which is finite free over the noetherian ring O_k).
We use the standard structure theorem for finite algebras over a henselian local ring, without reproving it: if (A, m) is henselian local and B is a finite commutative A-algebra, then B ≅ ∏_{i=1}^{r} B_i with each B_i a henselian local A-algebra. (Ingredients: B/mB is artinian, hence a product of local artinian rings; every maximal ideal of B lies over m by lying-over for the integral extension A ⊆ B, so mB ⊆ Jac(B); idempotents lift modulo mB because (A, m) is a henselian pair and B is finite over A; the factors attached to primitive idempotents are local — their maximal ideal is the inverse image of the maximal ideal of the corresponding local artinian factor, namely mB_i — and are henselian.) Applying this to (A, m) = (O_k, πO_k) and B = R, and using that a domain has no idempotents other than 0 and 1, we get r = 1, i.e.
(3)  R is a henselian local ring.
Let m_R denote its maximal ideal. Consider ρ := ρ_D|_R : R → D̄. Its image is k̄[ᾱ], which equals the field k̄(ᾱ) = L̄ because ᾱ is algebraic over k̄. Hence ker ρ = R ∩ M_D is a maximal ideal of R, and since R is local by (3) it is the maximal ideal:
(4)  m_R = R ∩ M_D = R ∩ πO_D.
Now f(a) ∈ R and ρ(f(a)) = f̄(ρ(a)) = f̄(ᾱ) = 0, so f(a) ∈ m_R. Also f′(a) ∈ R and ρ(f′(a)) = f̄′(ᾱ) ≠ 0 because f̄ is separable; hence f′(a) ∉ m_R, i.e. f′(a) ∈ R×. Hensel's lemma in the henselian local ring R, in its simple-root form (if g ∈ R[T], c ∈ R satisfy ḡ(c̄) = 0 and ḡ′(c̄) ≠ 0 in R/m_R, there is a unique b ∈ R with g(b) = 0 and b − c ∈ m_R), applied with g = f and c = a, yields
(5)  b ∈ R ⊆ O_D with f(b) = 0 and b − a ∈ m_R ⊆ M_D; consequently ρ_D(b) = ᾱ.
Note that the whole argument takes place inside the single ring R; no product decomposition and no lifting in a factor is involved.

STEP 4. The model extension E = k[T]/(f).
(a) f is irreducible over k. If f = gh in O_k[T] with deg g, deg h ≥ 1, then the leading coefficients of g and h multiply to 1, so after multiplying g by a unit of O_k and h by its inverse we may take g, h monic; reducing gives f̄ = ḡ·h̄ in k̄[T] with deg ḡ = deg g ≥ 1 and deg h̄ = deg h ≥ 1, contradicting the irreducibility of f̄. Thus f is irreducible in O_k[T], and since O_k is a UFD and f is monic (hence primitive), Gauss's lemma gives irreducibility in k[T]. So E := k[T]/(f) is a field with [E : k] = n, generated by α := T mod f, and O_E := O_k[T]/(f) = O_k[α] is free of rank n over O_k.
(b) O_E is finite étale over O_k: this is the standard discriminant criterion, since f is monic with disc(f) ∈ O_k×. An étale algebra over a normal domain is normal, and O_k is a DVR, hence normal; so O_E is a normal domain, finite over O_k, with fraction field E. Therefore O_E is the integral closure of O_k in E.
(c) Applying the structure theorem quoted in Step 3 to the finite O_k-algebra O_E: O_E ≅ ∏_j O_{E,j}, the factors indexed by the primes of O_E above πO_k. But O_E/πO_E ≅ k̄[T]/(f̄), which is a field (k̄[T]/(f̄) ≅ k̄(ᾱ) = L̄) since f̄ is irreducible; hence πO_E is the unique prime of O_E above πO_k. Therefore
(6)  O_E is a henselian local ring with maximal ideal πO_E and residue field L̄; in particular E/k is unramified of degree n and v(E×) = v(k×).
(d) f splits completely in O_E, and distinct roots have distinct residues. Since L̄/k̄ is Galois of degree n = deg f̄ with L̄ = k̄(ᾱ) and f̄ the minimal polynomial of ᾱ, f̄ splits in L̄ into the n distinct roots σ̄(ᾱ), σ̄ ∈ Gal(L̄/k̄). Fix such a root β̄ and take any lift c ∈ O_E; then f(c) ∈ πO_E (residue f̄(β̄) = 0) and f′(c) ∈ O_E× (residue f̄′(β̄) ≠ 0), so Hensel's lemma in the henselian local ring O_E gives a root β ∈ O_E of f with β ≡ c (mod πO_E), i.e. with residue β̄. Distinctness: if β, β′ ∈ O_E are roots of f with β − β′ ∈ πO_E, write Q(X,Y) = (f(X) − f(Y))/(X − Y) ∈ O_k[X,Y]; then 0 = f(β) − f(β′) = (β − β′)Q(β,β′), and Q(β,β′) ≡ f′(β) (mod πO_E) is a unit of O_E, so β = β′. Hence f has n distinct roots in E and E is the splitting field over k of the separable polynomial f, i.e.
(7)  E/k is Galois of degree n.
(e) The residue-restriction map res : Gal(E/k) → Gal(L̄/k̄) is an isomorphism. Every τ ∈ Gal(E/k) preserves the integral closure O_E of O_k in E, hence preserves πO_E, and induces an automorphism τ̄ of the residue field O_E/πO_E = L̄ fixing k̄. Injectivity: if τ̄ = id, then τ(α) is a root of f in O_E with residue ᾱ = ᾱ, so τ(α) = α by the uniqueness just proved in (d), and E = k(α) forces τ = id. Surjectivity: given σ̄ ∈ Gal(L̄/k̄), σ̄(ᾱ) is a root of f̄ in L̄, so by (d) there is a root β ∈ O_E of f with residue σ̄(ᾱ); the k-homomorphism E = k(α) → E, α ↦ β is then a k-automorphism τ of E, and τ̄(ᾱ) = σ̄(ᾱ); since L̄ = k̄(ᾱ), τ̄ = σ̄. Thus res is an isomorphism Gal(E/k) ≅→ Gal(L̄/k̄) = G.

STEP 5. L := k(b) ⊂ D is Galois over k with group G and residue field L̄. By (5), b ∈ O_D ⊂ D satisfies f(b) = 0. Since f is irreducible over k of degree n = p², [L : k] = n and the k-algebra homomorphism E = k[T]/(f) → L, T ↦ b, is an isomorphism. Transporting (7) and Step 4(e) along this isomorphism, L/k is Galois of degree p² with Gal(L/k) ≅ Gal(E/k) ≅ G. (Equivalently and concretely: f splits in E into n distinct linear factors, so f splits in L into n distinct linear factors, hence L/k is separable and normal of degree n = p².)
Residue field: the valued field (L, w|_L) has valuation ring O_L = L ∩ O_D and maximal ideal M_L = L ∩ M_D; its residue field L̄₁ contains k̄ and ρ_D(b) = ᾱ, hence contains k̄(ᾱ) = L̄. Since L/k is a finite Galois extension of the henselian discretely valued field (k, v), lemma_96 applies:
[L : k] = [w(L×) : v(k×)] · [L̄₁ : k̄].
Therefore [L̄₁ : k̄] ≤ [L : k] = p² = [L̄ : k̄]; combined with the inclusion L̄ ⊆ L̄₁ this forces L̄₁ = L̄ (and also w(L×) = v(k×)). So L has residue field exactly L̄.

STEP 6. L is a maximal subfield of D. By the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), for a subfield K of a central simple k-algebra A one has dim_k K · dim_k C_A(K) = dim_k A, and K is a maximal subfield if and only if C_A(K) = K. Taking A = D, with dim_k D = (deg D)² = p⁴, and K = L, with dim_k L = [L : k] = p², gives dim_k C_D(L) = p². Since L is commutative, L ⊆ C_D(L), and equality of dimensions forces C_D(L) = L. Hence L is a maximal subfield of D.

Steps 5 and 6 together give a subfield L ⊂ D which is a maximal subfield, is Galois over k with Galois group G, and has residue field L̄. This proves the lemma. (The hypothesis char k = p > 2 is not used beyond what is stated; the argument is the standard inertial lifting of a Galois maximal subfield, made explicit via Hensel's lemma.)

lemma_198.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, with residue division ring $\bar D$ and with $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$; suppose $\bar D$ is central of degree $p^{2}$ over $\bar k$. If $L$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$, then the residue field $\bar L$ of $L$ is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$ that is Galois over $\bar k$ with Galois group $G$.
lemma_198.proof:
Notation. Write $\mathcal O_k,v$ for the valuation ring of $(k,v)$, $\mathcal O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}$, $M_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\}$, so $\bar D=\mathcal O_D/M_D$, and $\mathcal O_L=\{x\in L: w(x)\ge 0\}=L\cap\mathcal O_D$, $M_L=L\cap M_D$, so $\bar L=\mathcal O_L/M_L$. Here $w|_{L}$ is the restriction of the given valuation of $D$, which is a valuation on $L$ extending $v$ (its restriction to $k^\times$ is $v$). Since $\deg D=p^2$ we have $\dim_k D=p^4$, and since $\bar D$ is central of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$ we have $\dim_{\bar k}\bar D=p^4$. Throughout, $L/k$ is a finite Galois extension with group $G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$.

Step 1. The centralizer of $L$ in $D$ is $L$ itself, and $[L:k]=p^2$.
First, $C_D(L)=L$. Indeed, $L$ is maximal among the subfields of $D$: if $C_D(L)$ properly contained $L$, choose $y\in C_D(L)\setminus L$. The $k$-subalgebra $L(y)\subset D$ generated by $L$ and $y$ is commutative (as $y$ commutes with $L$ and with itself), is a domain (it lies in the division ring $D$), and is finite-dimensional over $k$. For any nonzero $z\in L(y)$, multiplication by $z$ is an injective $k$-linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $L(y)$, hence surjective, so $1\in z\,L[y]\subset z\,L(y)$: every nonzero element is invertible and $L(y)$ is a field strictly containing $L$, contradicting maximality of $L$. Thus $C_D(L)=L$.
Now apply the double-centralizer dimension identity of ref_1 to the simple $k$-subalgebra $L$ of the central simple $k$-algebra $D$:
$$\dim_k D=[L:k]\cdot \dim_k C_D(L).$$
Substituting $\dim_k D=p^4$ and $\dim_k C_D(L)=\dim_k L=[L:k]$ (the latter because $C_D(L)=L$) gives $[L:k]^2=p^4$, hence $[L:k]=p^2$. Nothing circular is used: the identity $\dim_k C_D(L)=[L:k]$ is a consequence of $C_D(L)=L$, not of the value of $[L:k]$.

Step 2. The value group of $L$ equals $v(k^\times)$, and $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$.
