Because $k$ is henselian for the discrete valuation $v$ and $L/k$ is finite Galois, lemma_96 applies to $L/k$ (with the valuation $w|_L$) and gives the fundamental equality with trivial defect:
$$[L:k]=[w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k].$$
We prove $[w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]=1$ by checking both inclusions explicitly. (i) $v(k^\times)\subseteq w(L^\times)$, since $k^\times\subseteq L^\times$ and $w$ extends $v$. (ii) $w(L^\times)\subseteq w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$, by the hypothesis $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ on $D$ together with $L^\times\subset D^\times$. Hence $w(L^\times)=v(k^\times)$ and the index is $1$. Therefore
$$[\bar L:\bar k]=[L:k]=p^2.$$

Step 3. $\bar L$ is a subfield of $\bar D$ containing $\bar k$.
The natural map $\mathcal O_L=L\cap\mathcal O_D\to \mathcal O_D/M_D=\bar D$ has kernel $L\cap M_D=M_L$, hence induces an injective homomorphism $\bar L\hookrightarrow\bar D$; its image contains the image of $\mathcal O_k$, i.e. contains $\bar k$. So $\bar L$ may (and will) be regarded as a commutative subfield of $\bar D$ containing $\bar k$, and by Step 2, $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$.

Step 4. $\bar L/\bar k$ is a finite Galois extension of degree $p^2$.
This is exactly the content of lemma_183 applied to the henselian discretely valued field $(k,v)$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$ and to the finite Galois extension $L/k$: the residue extension $\bar L/\bar k$ is finite Galois. Combined with Step 2, $|\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)|=[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$.

Step 5. Every $g\in G$ preserves $\mathcal O_L$ and $M_L$, so induces a $\bar k$-automorphism $\rho(g)$ of $\bar L$; thus $\rho\colon G\to\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ is a well-defined group homomorphism.
By Step 1, $\dim_k L=p^2=\deg D$, and $L$ is a commutative etale $k$-subalgebra of $D$ (a field finite separable, indeed Galois, over $k$). Hence ref_2(iv) applies: for each $g\in G$ there is a unit $u_g\in D^\times$ with $g(x)=u_g\,x\,u_g^{-1}$ for all $x\in L$. Since $w$ is a (Krull) valuation on the division ring $D$, it is a homomorphism $D^\times\to\Gamma$ to an ordered group, so for $x\ne0$,
$$w(g(x))=w(u_g)+w(x)-w(u_g)=w(x).$$
Thus $g$ is an isometry of $(L,w)$: $g(\mathcal O_L)=\mathcal O_L$ and $g(M_L)=M_L$. Consequently $g$ induces a well-defined automorphism $\rho(g)$ of $\bar L=\mathcal O_L/M_L$; as $g$ is a $k$-automorphism, $\rho(g)$ fixes $\bar k$ elementwise, so $\rho(g)\in\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ by Step 4. Clearly $\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)$, so $\rho$ is a group homomorphism.
(Remark: the same isometry statement also follows from the general theorem that a henselian valuation extends uniquely to any algebraic extension; the argument above via ref_2(iv) is used instead, since it needs no extra input.)

Step 6. $\rho$ is surjective.
Since $\bar L/\bar k$ is finite separable (Step 4), the primitive element theorem gives $\bar L=\bar k(\bar x_0)$ for some $\bar x_0\in\bar L$; the reduction map $\mathcal O_L\twoheadrightarrow\bar L$ is onto, so choose $x\in\mathcal O_L$ with residue $\bar x=\bar x_0$, and then $\bar L=\bar k(\bar x)$.
Let $m=[k(x):k]$ and let $P(T)=T^m+a_{m-1}T^{m-1}+\cdots+a_0\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $k$ (so $m\ge 1$; in fact $m\ge2$ since $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2>1$ forces $x\notin k$, but nothing depends on this).
We first justify $P\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ directly. Because $L/k$ is normal, every root of $P$ lies in $L$, and each such root equals $g(x)$ for some $g\in G$; write the distinct conjugates as $x_1,\dots,x_m$, each $x_i=g_i(x)$. Each coefficient of $P$ is, up to sign, an elementary symmetric polynomial in $x_1,\dots,x_m$. By Step 5, $w(x_i)=w(x)\ge0$ (as $x\in\mathcal O_L$); using $w(ab)=w(a)+w(b)$ and $w(a+b)\ge\min\{w(a),w(b)\}$, every such symmetric polynomial has $w$-value $\ge0$. The coefficients lie in $k$, where $w=v$, so $v(a_j)\ge0$, i.e. $a_j\in\mathcal O_k$. Hence $P\in\mathcal O_k[T]$.
Since $L/k$ is Galois, $\prod_{g\in G}(T-g(x))$ is fixed by $G$ (it is permuted by the action on the index), hence lies in $k[T]$; it is monic, its distinct roots are exactly $x_1,\dots,x_m$, each occurring with multiplicity $|G|/m=[L:k(x)]$. Therefore in $L[T]$,
$$\prod_{g\in G}(T-g(x))=P(T)^{[L:k(x)]}.$$
All $g(x)$ lie in $\mathcal O_L$, so this is an identity in $\mathcal O_L[T]$. Applying the surjective reduction homomorphism $\mathcal O_L[T]\twoheadrightarrow\bar L[T]$ gives
$$\prod_{g\in G}\bigl(T-\overline{g(x)}\bigr)=\bar P(T)^{[L:k(x)]}\quad\text{in }\bar L[T],$$
where $\bar P\in\bar k[T]$ is monic of degree $m\ge1$, hence nonzero (its leading coefficient reduces to $1\ne0$). Note also $\bar P(\bar x)=0$, since $P(x)=0$ in $\mathcal O_L$.
Now take any $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$. As $\bar P$ has coefficients in $\bar k$,
$$0=\sigma(\bar P(\bar x))=\bar P(\sigma(\bar x)),$$
so $\sigma(\bar x)$ is a root of $\bar P$ in $\bar L$, hence a root of $\prod_{g\in G}(T-\overline{g(x)})$, so $\sigma(\bar x)=\overline{g(x)}=\rho(g)(\bar x)$ for some $g\in G$. Since $\bar L=\bar k(\bar x)$, the two $\bar k$-automorphisms $\sigma$ and $\rho(g)$ of $\bar L$ agree on the generator $\bar x$, hence $\sigma=\rho(g)$. Thus $\rho$ is surjective.

Step 7. $\rho$ is an isomorphism $G\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$.
By Steps 1, 4 and 6, $\rho$ is a surjective homomorphism between finite groups of the same order: $|G|=[L:k]=p^2=[\bar L:\bar k]=|\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)|$. Hence $\rho$ is bijective, i.e. an isomorphism. In particular $\bar L/\bar k$ is Galois with Galois group isomorphic to $G$.

Step 8. $\bar L$ is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$.
Apply ref_1 to the central simple $\bar k$-algebra $\bar D$ (central of degree $p^2$, so $\dim_{\bar k}\bar D=p^4$) and to its simple $\bar k$-subalgebra $\bar L$ (a field, with $\dim_{\bar k}\bar L=[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$ from Step 2/3). The dimension identity gives
$$\dim_{\bar k} C_{\bar D}(\bar L)=\frac{\dim_{\bar k}\bar D}{\dim_{\bar k}\bar L}=\frac{p^4}{p^2}=p^2=\dim_{\bar k}\bar L.$$
Since $\bar L$ is commutative, $\bar L\subseteq C_{\bar D}(\bar L)$; the two $\bar k$-vector spaces have the same finite dimension, so $C_{\bar D}(\bar L)=\bar L$. By the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1 ($K$ is a maximal subfield of a central simple algebra if and only if $C(K)=K$), $\bar L$ is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$.

Conclusion. Steps 7 and 8 together say exactly that $\bar L$ is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$ which is Galois over $\bar k$ with Galois group $G$. This completes the proof. (The hypotheses that $k$ has characteristic $p>2$ and perfect residue field are used to meet the assumptions of lemma_96 and lemma_183; the value-group hypothesis $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ is used in Step 2.)

lemma_199.statement:
Let $p>2$ be a prime, let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p$, and let $A$ be a central division $F$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ that contains no element $\alpha
otin F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha\in F$ and no element $	heta
otin F$ with $	heta^{p}\in F$. Then $D=A\otimes_{F}F((u))$ is a central division $F((u))$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ containing no element $a
otin F((u))$ with $a^{p}-a\in F((u))$; in particular $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_199.proof:
Write $k:=F((u))$, let $v$ be the $u$-adic valuation normalized by $v(u)=1$, so that $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$, $\mathcal O_v=F[[u]]$, and $k$ is complete for $v$; $\operatorname{char} k=p>2$. Write $D:=A\otimes_F k=A((u))=\{\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^{i}: N\in\mathbb Z,\ \alpha_i\in A\}$; the indeterminate $u$ is central in $D$, and every element of $D$ has a UNIQUE expansion $\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^i$ with $\alpha_i\in A$ (i.e. $D=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z} A u^{i}$ as an $F$-vector space).

STEP 1. Structural facts, and calculus of initial forms.
By lemma_185 applied to $F$, $A$ and $u$: $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$; the map $w\big(\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^{i}\big)=\min\{i:\alpha_i\ne 0\}$ is a (Krull) valuation on the division ring $D$ extending $v$; $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$; the residue division ring of $w$ is isomorphic to $A$; and for every $n\in\mathbb Z$ the map $\iota_n:A\to \mathrm{gr}_w(D)_n$, $\alpha\mapsto \operatorname{in}_w(\alpha u^{n})$, is an isomorphism of $F$-vector spaces. We record the consequences we need.

(1a) Since $w$ is a Krull valuation on the division ring $D$, $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$ for all nonzero $x,y\in D$; taking $x=y$ repeatedly gives $w(x^{p})=p\,w(x)$ for all $x\ne0$.

(1b) The associated graded ring $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z} I_n/I_{>n}$, where $I_n=\{x:w(x)\ge n\}$ and $I_{>n}=\{x:w(x)>n\}$, is a graded division ring: for nonzero $x,y$ the product $\operatorname{in}_w(x)\operatorname{in}_w(y):=\operatorname{in}_w(xy)$ is well defined (if $a\in I_{>w(x)}$ then $w(ay)=w(a)+w(y)>w(x)+w(y)=w(xy)$ by (1a), and similarly on the left) and is nonzero because $xy\ne0$. Hence $\operatorname{in}_w(x^{p})=\operatorname{in}_w(x)^{p}$ for every $x\ne0$, by induction on $p$ using multiplicativity of initial forms.

(1c) Because $u$ is central, for $\alpha,\beta\in A^{\times}$ and $n,m\in\mathbb Z$ we have $(\alpha u^{n})(\beta u^{m})=\alpha\beta\,u^{n+m}$, and $w(\alpha\beta u^{n+m})=n+m$ since $A$ is a division ring; therefore
$\qquad\iota_n(\alpha)\,\iota_m(\beta)=\iota_{n+m}(\alpha\beta)$
inside $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{n+m}$. Combining (1b) and (1c): for $\theta\in A^{\times}$ and $N\in\mathbb Z$, putting $x=\theta u^{N}$ gives $\operatorname{in}_w(x^{p})=\iota_N(\theta)^{p}=\iota_{pN}(\theta^{p})$, i.e.
$\qquad\qquad (\ast)\qquad (\theta u^{N})^{p}=\theta^{p}u^{pN}\ \text{ and more generally, if } x=\theta u^{N}+(\text{terms of } w>N),\ \text{ then }\ x^{p}=\theta^{p}u^{pN}+(\text{terms of } w>pN).$
Indeed $\operatorname{in}_w(x)=\iota_N(\theta)$ (as $x-\theta u^{N}\in I_{>N}$), so $\operatorname{in}_w(x^{p})=\operatorname{in}_w(x)^{p}=\iota_N(\theta)^{p}=\iota_{pN}(\theta^{p})=\operatorname{in}_w(\theta^{p}u^{pN})$, which is exactly the assertion $x^{p}-\theta^{p}u^{pN}\in I_{>pN}$. Note that $(\ast)$ is a statement only about the lowest-degree (leading) term; nothing is claimed about the higher coefficients, and no noncommutative reordering of factors is used.

(1d) The valuation ring and its maximal ideal are $\mathcal O_w=\{x:w(x)\ge0\}=A[[u]]$ and $\mathfrak m_w=\{x:w(x)\ge1\}=uA[[u]]$ (the latter is a two-sided ideal because $u$ is central: $w(\sum_{i\ge1}\alpha_i u^{i}\cdot\sum_{j\ge0}\beta_j u^{j})\ge1$). The map $A[[u]]\to A$, $\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha_i u^{i}\mapsto\alpha_0$, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $uA[[u]]$, so the residue division ring is $A$; this identifies $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_0=A$ and $\iota_0$ with the identity $A\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_0$, in agreement with lemma_185.

STEP 2. $D$ contains no element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$.
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $a\in D\setminus k$ satisfies $a^{p}-a=c\in k$. Put $N:=w(a)\in\mathbb Z$; note $a\ne0$ since $a\notin k$.

(2a) Descent of the valuation by subtracting central elements. We claim: for every integer $t$ with $0\le t\le -N$ (if $N\ge0$ there is nothing to prove and we skip to (2b)) there exist $\lambda_t\in k$ and $b_t\in D\setminus k$ such that
$\qquad b_t=a-\lambda_t,\qquad b_t^{p}-b_t\in k,\qquad w(b_t)\ge N+t.$
Proof by induction on $t$. For $t=0$ take $\lambda_0=0$, $b_0=a$.
Inductive step: suppose $b_t$ is constructed with $N_t:=w(b_t)<0$ (if $w(b_t)\ge0$ and $t<-N$ we simply take $\lambda_{t+1}=\lambda_t$, $b_{t+1}=b_t$ and the inequality $w(b_{t+1})\ge N+t+1$ may fail; so instead, in that case we stop the induction and go directly to (2b) with $b:=b_t$, $\lambda:=\lambda_t$, which is all we need). Write the unique expansion of $b_t$ as
$\qquad b_t=\theta_t u^{N_t}+\sum_{i\ge N_t+1}\alpha_i u^{i},\qquad \theta_t\in A^{\times}.$
Then $\operatorname{in}_w(b_t)=\iota_{N_t}(\theta_t)$, and by $(\ast)$,
$\qquad b_t^{p}=\theta_t^{p}u^{pN_t}+(\text{terms of } w>pN_t).$
Since $N_t<0$ and $p\ge3$, we have $(p-1)N_t<0$, i.e. $pN_t<N_t=w(b_t)$. Hence by the ultrametric inequality and (1a),
$\qquad w(c)=w(b_t^{p}-b_t)=\min\{w(b_t^{p}),\,w(b_t)\}=\min\{pN_t,\,N_t\}=pN_t,$
the minimum being attained at the single term $b_t^{p}$, so $\operatorname{in}_w(c)=\operatorname{in}_w(b_t^{p})=\iota_{pN_t}(\theta_t^{p})$. On the other hand $c\in k$, so $c=\sum_{i\ge v(c)}c_i u^{i}$ with $c_i\in F$ and $c_{pN_t}\ne0$ (as $w(c)=pN_t$), whence $\operatorname{in}_w(c)=\iota_{pN_t}(c_{pN_t})$. Since $\iota_{pN_t}$ is injective (it is an isomorphism by lemma_185), we obtain
$\qquad\theta_t^{p}=c_{pN_t}\in F.$
By the hypothesis on $A$ (no element $\theta\notin F$ with $\theta^{p}\in F$), it follows that $\theta_t\in F$. Define $\lambda_{t+1}:=\lambda_t+\theta_t u^{N_t}\in k$ and $b_{t+1}:=b_t-\theta_t u^{N_t}=a-\lambda_{t+1}$. Then:
\ - $b_{t+1}\ne0$: otherwise $a=\lambda_{t+1}\in k$, contradicting $a\notin k$; consequently $b_{t+1}\notin k$ as well (as $b_{t+1}\in k$ would likewise give $a\in k$);
\ - $w(b_{t+1})\ge N_t+1$: the two series $b_t$ and $\theta_t u^{N_t}$ have the same coefficient $\theta_t$ of $u^{N_t}$, so all coefficients of $u^{i}$ with $i\le N_t$ in $b_{t+1}$ vanish;
\ - $b_{t+1}^{p}-b_{t+1}\in k$: the element $\theta_t u^{N_t}$ is central in $D$, hence commutes with $b_t$, so the binomial theorem for commuting elements in characteristic $p$ gives $(b_t-\theta_t u^{N_t})^{p}=b_t^{p}-(\theta_t u^{N_t})^{p}=b_t^{p}-\theta_t^{p}u^{pN_t}$ (all intermediate binomial coefficients $\binom{p}{i}$, $0<i<p$, are $0$ in $F$). Therefore $b_{t+1}^{p}-b_{t+1}=(b_t^{p}-b_t)-\theta_t^{p}u^{pN_t}+\theta_t u^{N_t}\in k$, since $b_t^{p}-b_t=c\in k$ and $\theta_t,\theta_t^{p}\in F$.
This completes the induction, and yields $w(b_{t+1})\ge N+(t+1)$.

(2b) The terminal element. After at most $-N$ steps (and immediately if $N\ge0$) we obtain $\lambda\in k$ and $b:=a-\lambda\in D\setminus k$ with
$\qquad b^{p}-b=c':=c-\lambda^{p}+\lambda\in k\ \quad(\text{again because }\lambda\text{ is central, so }(a-\lambda)^{p}=a^{p}-\lambda^{p}),\qquad w(b)\ge0.$
We distinguish two cases.

Case I: $w(b)>0$. The field $k=F((u))$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>2$; $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$ (Step 1). Thus all hypotheses of lemma_162 hold, and lemma_162 asserts that $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^{p}-x\in k$ and $w(x)>0$. But $b$ is such an element. Contradiction.

Case II: $w(b)=0$. Write $b=\theta+z$ with $\theta=b_0\in A^{\times}$ the constant coefficient and $z=\sum_{i\ge1}b_i u^{i}\in uA[[u]]=\mathfrak m_w$. Then $\operatorname{in}_w(b)=\iota_0(\theta)=\theta$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_0=A$, so by (1b) and (1c) with $N=0$, $\operatorname{in}_w(b^{p})=\theta^{p}$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_0$; equivalently
$\qquad b^{p}=\theta^{p}+y\quad\text{for some }y\in\mathfrak m_w=uA[[u].$]
Hence $c'=b^{p}-b=(\theta^{p}-\theta)+(y-z)$. By (1a), $w(b^{p})=p\,w(b)=0$, so $w(c')\ge\min\{0,0\}=0$; as $c'\in k$ this means $c'\in\mathcal O_v=F[[u]]$, say $c'=\sum_{i\ge0}c'_i u^{i}$ with $c'_i\in F$. Therefore
$\qquad \theta^{p}-\theta-c'_0=\sum_{i\ge1}c'_i u^{i}-y+z.$
The left-hand side lies in $A$ (it is a constant series), while the right-hand side lies in $uA[[u]]$ (each $c'_i\in F\subset A$), whose constant coefficient is $0$. By uniqueness of the expansion in $\bigoplus_{i\ge0}A u^{i}$, both sides are $0$. Thus
$\qquad\qquad \theta^{p}-\theta=c'_0\in F.$
If $\theta\notin F$, this contradicts the hypothesis that $A$ contains no $\alpha\notin F$ with $\alpha^{p}-\alpha\in F$. If $\theta\in F$, put $b':=b-\theta=a-(\lambda+\theta)$. Then $b'\notin k$ (else $a\in k$), $b'^{p}-b'=c'-\theta^{p}+\theta\in k$ (as $\theta$ is central), and $w(b')\ge1>0$ because $b-\theta=z\in uA[[u]]\subset\{x:w(x)\ge1\}$. This again contradicts lemma_162.

Both cases are impossible, so the supposition was false: $D$ contains no element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$. Together with Step 1 this proves the first assertion: $D=A\otimes_F F((u))$ is a central division $F((u))$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ with no Artin--Schreier element over $F((u))$.

STEP 3. $D$ is not a crossed product for any group of order $p^{2}$.
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $D\cong(L,G,c)$ as $k$-algebras for some group $G$ with $|G|=p^{2}$. The field $k=F((u))$ has characteristic $p>2$ and $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, so lemma_176 applies and yields a subfield $K\subset D$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$. Now lemma_191 (applied to $k$ and $D$) states that a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ contains a subfield Galois over $k$ with cyclic group of order $p$ if and only if it contains an element $a\notin k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$; the direction we need gives such an element $a\in D\setminus k$ with $a^{p}-a\in k$. This contradicts Step 2. Hence no such crossed product structure exists on $D$.

Combining Steps 1, 2 and 3 gives the lemma. (Remark on the edge cases: the possibility $b_t=0$ during the induction, the case $N\ge0$ where no descent step is needed, the case $w(b)=0$ with $\theta\in F$, and the case $w(b)>0$ were each treated explicitly above; the only properties of $w$ used beyond lemma_185 are the valuation axioms $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$, $w(x+y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$ and the multiplicativity of initial forms, all justified in (1a)--(1c).)

lemma_200.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ and perfect residue field, and let $K/k$ be a totally ramified Galois extension with cyclic Galois group of order $p$. Then $K=k(z)$ for some $z\in K$ satisfying $z^{p}-z=c$ for an element $c\in k$ with $v(c)<0$ and $p\nmid v(c)$.
lemma_200.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_200",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "Spark", "lemma_id": "lemma_96"}
  ],
  "cited_references": ["ref_14"],
  "proof": "Notation. Write $\mathcal O_k$ for the valuation ring of $v$, $\mathfrak m_k$ for its maximal ideal, $\pi\in\mathcal O_k$ for a uniformizer (exists since $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$), and $\bar k=\mathcal O_k/\mathfrak m_k$ for the residue field, which is perfect of characteristic $p$. For a field $F$ of characteristic $p$ write $\wp(t)=t^{p}-t$; $\wp$ is an additive homomorphism (since $(s+t)^p=s^p+t^p$), and $\wp(-t)=-\wp(t)$. Since $v$ is henselian, $v$ extends uniquely to $K$; denote this extension by $w$, its valuation ring by $\mathcal O_K$, its maximal ideal by $\mathfrak m_K$, and the residue field $\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak m_K$ by $\bar K$; the inclusion $\mathcal O_k\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_K$ induces an inclusion $\bar k\hookrightarrow\bar K$, and the residue map $\mathcal O_K\to\bar K$ is a ring homomorphism restricting to the residue map on $\mathcal O_k$.

Preliminaries on the two standard ingredients.

(H) Hensel's lemma in the form we use. Because $(k,v)$ is a henselian valued field, its valuation ring $\mathcal O_k$ has the factorization-lifting property (this is the standard form of Hensel's lemma, one of the equivalent definitions of henselianity, and it holds in particular for complete discretely valued fields): if $f\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ is monic and $\bar f=\bar f_1\bar f_2$ in $\bar k[T]$ with $\bar f_1,\bar f_2$ monic and coprime, then $f=gh$ with $g,h\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ monic, $\bar g=\bar f_1$, $\bar h=\bar f_2$.

(R) Total ramification. Since $(k,v)$ is henselian discretely valued and $K/k$ is finite Galois, lemma_96 gives $[K:k]=[w(K^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar K:\bar k]$ (trivial defect). Saying that $K/k$ is totally ramified means $[K:k]=[w(K^\times):v(k^\times)]$; by the displayed equality (which applies because $K/k$ is Galois over the henselian field $k$) this is equivalent to $[\bar K:\bar k]=1$, i.e.
$\qquad \bar K=\bar k.$
We use this equivalence in Step 4.

Step 1 (Artin--Schreier generator). The extension $K/k$ is Galois with cyclic group of order $p=\operatorname{char}k$. By Artin--Schreier theory, ref_14 (part (a): every Galois extension of degree $p$ in characteristic $p$ is of the form $k(\wp^{-1}a)$), there are $a\in k$ and $\theta\in K$ with
$\qquad K=k(\theta),\qquad \theta^{p}-\theta=a.$
Moreover $a\notin\wp(k)$: if $a=\wp(t)$ for some $t\in k$, then $\theta-t\in k$, whence $K=k(\theta)=k$, contradicting $[K:k]=p$.

Step 2 (normalising the valuation of the parameter). We prove:

Claim. Let $a\in k$. There exist $Y\in k$ and $c\in k$ with $a=c+\wp(Y)$ such that either $v(c)\ge 0$, or $v(c)<0$ and $p\nmid v(c)$.

Proof of the claim. If $v(a)\ge0$, or if $v(a)<0$ and $p\nmid v(a)$, take $Y=0$, $c=a$. Otherwise $v(a)=-N_0$ with $N_0\ge1$ and $p\mid N_0$; then $N_0\ge p$.

Single reduction step. Suppose $a'\in k$ satisfies $v(a')=-N<0$ with $p\mid N$, and write $a'=u\pi^{-N}$ with $u\in\mathcal O_k^{\times}$. Since $\bar k$ is perfect, $\bar u$ has a $p$-th root $\bar s\in\bar k$; lift $\bar s$ to $s\in\mathcal O_k^{\times}$. Then $v(u-s^{p})\ge1$. Put $y=s\pi^{-N/p}\in k^{\times}$ (note $N/p\ge1$ is an integer). Then $y^{p}=s^{p}\pi^{-N}$, so
$\qquad a'-\wp(y)=u\pi^{-N}-s^{p}\pi^{-N}+s\pi^{-N/p}=(u-s^{p})\pi^{-N}+s\pi^{-N/p}.$
We compute the valuations of the two summands:
$\qquad v\big((u-s^{p})\pi^{-N}\big)=v(u-s^{p})-N\ \ge\ 1-N\ >\ -N,$
since $v(u-s^p)\ge 1$; and, because $N\ge p\ge2$ implies $N/p<N$,
$\qquad v\big(s\pi^{-N/p}\big)=-N/p\ >\ -N.$
Both summands have valuation strictly greater than $-N$, so by the ultrametric inequality
$\qquad v\big(a'-\wp(y)\big)\ \ge\ \min\big(v((u-s^p)\pi^{-N}),\,-N/p\big)\ >\ -N=v(a').$
Thus subtracting $\wp$ of a suitable element raises the valuation strictly.

Iteration. Set $a_0=a$. Having constructed $a_j$ with $v(a_j)=-N_j<0$ and $p\mid N_j$, apply the single step to $a'=a_j$ to get $y_{j+1}\in k$ with $a_{j+1}:=a_j-\wp(y_{j+1})$ satisfying $v(a_{j+1})>v(a_j)$. As long as the process continues, the integers $v(a_0)<v(a_1)<v(a_2)<\cdots\le -1$ form a strictly increasing sequence bounded above by $-1$; hence it must stop after finitely many steps, indeed after at most $N_0$ steps. Say it stops at index $\ell$: then $v(a_\ell)\ge0$, or $v(a_\ell)<0$ with $p\nmid v(a_\ell)$. Define $Y=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}y_j$ and $c=a_\ell$. Since $\wp$ is additive, $\wp(Y)=\sum_j\wp(y_j)$, so
$\qquad c=a_\ell=a-\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\wp(y_j)=a-\wp(Y),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad a=c+\wp(Y),$
and $c$ has the required valuation behaviour. This proves the claim. $\triangleleft$ (claim)

Apply the claim to the $a$ of Step 1, obtaining $Y\in k$ and $c\in k$ with $a=c+\wp(Y)$ and ($v(c)\ge0$, or $v(c)<0$ with $p\nmid v(c)$).

Step 3 (change of generator). Put $z=\theta-Y$. Then
$\qquad z^{p}-z=\theta^{p}-\theta-(Y^{p}-Y)=a-\wp(Y)=c.$
Since $Y\in k$, $k(z)\subseteq k(\theta)=K$ and $\theta=z+Y\in k(z)$, so $k(z)=K$; in particular $z\notin k$. Also $c\notin\wp(k)$: if $c=\wp(t)$ with $t\in k$, then $a=c+\wp(Y)=\wp(t+Y)\in\wp(k)$, contradicting Step 1.

Step 4 (the case $v(c)\ge0$ is impossible). Suppose for a contradiction that $v(c)\ge0$, i.e. $c\in\mathcal O_k$. Then $z$ is a root of the monic polynomial $T^{p}-T-c\in\mathcal O_k[T]$, so $z$ is integral over $\mathcal O_k$. The unique extension $w$ of $v$ to $K$ has valuation ring $\mathcal O_K$, which is integrally closed in $K$ and contains $\mathcal O_k$; hence it contains every element integral over $\mathcal O_k$, so $z\in\mathcal O_K$. Passing to residues in $z^{p}-z=c$ (legitimate since $c=z^p-z\in\mathcal O_K\cap k=\mathcal O_k$) gives, in $\bar K$,
$\qquad \bar z^{\,p}-\bar z=\bar c.$
By (R), total ramification gives $\bar K=\bar k$; hence $\bar z\in\bar k$, and therefore $\bar c\in\wp(\bar k)$. Choose $\bar w\in\bar k$ with $\bar w^{p}-\bar w=\bar c$, and lift $\bar w$ to $b\in\mathcal O_k$. Then
$\qquad x:=c-\wp(b)=c-(b^{p}-b)$
satisfies $\bar x=\bar c-\bar w^{\,p}+\bar w=0$, so $x\in\mathfrak m_k$, i.e. $v(x)\ge1$.

We now show $x\in\wp(k)$, using (H). Consider $f(T)=T^{p}-T-x\in\mathcal O_k[T]$, monic of degree $p$. Its reduction is $\bar f(T)=T^{p}-T\in\bar k[T]$. The prime field $\mathbb F_p\subset\bar k$ consists exactly of the $p$ roots of $T^{p}-T$, so in $\bar k[T]$ we have $T^{p}-T=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p}(T-i)$. Set
$\qquad \bar f_1(T)=T,\qquad \bar f_2(T)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}}(T-i)=(T^{p}-T)/T,$
both monic, with $\bar f=\bar f_1\bar f_2$. They are coprime: $\bar f_2(0)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}}(-i)=(-1)^{p-1}(p-1)!$, a product of non-zero elements of $\bar k$, hence non-zero, so $T\nmid\bar f_2$ and $\gcd(\bar f_1,\bar f_2)=1$. By the henselian factorization-lifting property (H), $f=gh$ with $g,h\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ monic, $\bar g=\bar f_1=T$, $\bar h=\bar f_2$. Since $g$ is monic of degree $1$ with $\bar g=T$, we have $g(T)=T+a_0$ with $a_0\in\mathfrak m_k$. As $g\mid f$ in $k[T]$ and $\deg g=1$, the root $-a_0\in k$ of $g$ is a root of $f$:
$\qquad 0=f(-a_0)=(-a_0)^{p}-(-a_0)-x=-a_0^{p}+a_0-x=-\wp(a_0)-x,$
so $x=-\wp(a_0)=\wp(-a_0)\in\wp(k)$. Consequently
$\qquad c=x+\wp(b)=\wp(-a_0)+\wp(b)=\wp(b-a_0)\in\wp(k),$
contradicting $c\notin\wp(k)$ from Step 3. Hence $v(c)\ge0$ is impossible.

Conclusion. By Step 2, $c$ satisfies either $v(c)\ge0$ or ($v(c)<0$ and $p\nmid v(c)$); Step 4 excludes the first alternative. Therefore $v(c)<0$ and $p\nmid v(c)$, and by Step 3, $K=k(z)$ with $z^{p}-z=c\in k$. This is exactly the required conclusion.

(Remarks on the use of the hypotheses: $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$ supplies the uniformizer $\pi$ and makes the value group $\mathbb Z$, so that divisibility by $p$ of $v(c)$ is meaningful; perfectness of $\bar k$ is used in the single reduction step to extract $p$-th roots of residues; henselianity is used in Step 4 through Hensel's lemma and in the uniqueness of the extension of $v$ to $K$; and $p>2$ (in particular $p\ge2$) is used in the inequality $-N/p>-N$, valid because $N\ge p$, together with $\bar f_2(0)\ne0$, which needs $p-1\ge1$.)
}

lemma_202.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$. If $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, then the class $p[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is represented by a cyclic $k$-algebra of degree $p$; in particular the index of $p[D]$ is at most $p$, so a division algebra of degree $p^{2}$ for which $p[D]$ has index $p^{2}$ is not a crossed product for any group of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_202.proof:
Throughout, char(k) = p > 2, D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2, and we assume D ≅ (L, G, c) as k-algebras for some group G with |G| = p^2 and some 2-cocycle c : G × G → L^×, where L is a Galois G-algebra over k (étale of k-dimension |G| = p^2, with L^G = k).

Step 1: From the crossed product to a Galois maximal subfield of D. We apply lemma_133 (Spark) with n = p^2. Its hypotheses are exactly our situation: D is central division of degree n = p^2 and is isomorphic to a crossed product (L, G, c) with |G| = n. The conclusion is that L is a field and that its image E ⊂ D under such an isomorphism is a maximal subfield of D which is Galois over k with Galois group G. (Concretely, the image of the étale algebra L inside the division algebra D contains no non-trivial idempotent, so L is a product of a single field, i.e. a field; then [E : k] = dim_k L = p^2 = deg(D), so E is maximal, and E^G = L^G = k together with |G| = [E : k] says E/k is Galois with group G.) Thus:
    D contains a maximal subfield E, Galois over k, with Gal(E/k) ≅ G.

Step 2: Every group of order p^2 is abelian (proved here, since we need it). Let G be a group of order p^2. Its centre Z(G) is non-trivial (class equation for a p-group), so |Z(G)| ∈ {p, p^2}. If |Z(G)| = p, then G/Z(G) has order p and is therefore cyclic; but a group whose quotient by its centre is cyclic is abelian — indeed, if G/Z(G) = ⟨gZ(G)⟩, every element of G is of the form g^i z with z ∈ Z(G), and any two such elements g^i z, g^{i'} z' commute because powers of g commute and central elements commute with everything. This contradicts |Z(G)| = p. Hence Z(G) = G, i.e. G is abelian. (So G ≅ C_{p^2} or G ≅ C_p × C_p; we do not need to distinguish them.)

Step 3: D contains a subfield which is Galois cyclic of degree p over k. Since p divides |G| = p^2, Cauchy's theorem gives a subgroup H ≤ G of order p. Because G is abelian (Step 2), H is normal in G. The quotient G/H is a group of order p, hence cyclic; choose σ ∈ G \ H and let σ̄ denote its image in G/H, which then generates G/H. By the Galois correspondence for the Galois extension E/k: the fixed field K := E^H satisfies [K : k] = [G : H] = p, and since H is normal, K/k is Galois with Gal(K/k) = G/H = ⟨σ̄⟩ ≅ C_p. Thus K is a subfield of D (as K ⊂ E ⊂ D) which is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p, generated by σ̄. This step is uniform in the isomorphism type of G: if G ≅ C_{p^2}, K is the unique intermediate field of degree p; if G ≅ C_p × C_p, K is the fixed field of any order-p subgroup (there are p+1 such choices).

Step 4: p[D] is represented by a cyclic algebra of degree p. We apply lemma_195 (Spark) to the division algebra D and the subfield K/k with generator σ̄ of Gal(K/k). It yields an element a ∈ k^× such that, in Br(k),
    p[D] = [(K/k, σ̄, a)],
where (K/k, σ̄, a) is the algebra A := ⊕_{i=0}^{p-1} K v^i with v^p = a and vλ = σ̄(λ)v for all λ ∈ K. By ref_22(i) (cyclic algebra attached to a cyclic Galois algebra of degree n with parameter b ∈ k^× is a central simple k-algebra of degree n), applied with L = K, n = p, b = a, A is a central simple k-algebra of degree p. Hence the class p[D] is represented by a cyclic k-algebra of degree p, which is the first claim.

Step 5: The index of p[D] is at most p. Write A ≅ M_r(Δ) with r ≥ 1 and Δ a central division k-algebra (Wedderburn). Then deg(A) = r · deg(Δ), so ind(p[D]) := deg(Δ) divides deg(A) = p. Therefore ind(p[D]) ∈ {1, p}, and in particular ind(p[D]) ≤ p. (The case ind = 1 is p[D] = 0, which is allowed and harmless.)

Step 6: The contrapositive statement. Let D_0 be a central division k-algebra of degree p^2 with ind(p[D_0]) = p^2. If D_0 were isomorphic to a crossed product (L, G, c) for some group G of order p^2, then Steps 1–5 (applied to D_0) would give ind(p[D_0]) ≤ p. Since p > 2 we have p ≥ 3 and hence p < p^2, contradicting ind(p[D_0]) = p^2. Therefore such a D_0 is not a crossed product for any group of order p^2.

This completes the proof: being a crossed product of degree p^2 forces p[D] to be the class of a cyclic algebra of degree p, hence of index at most p; equivalently, ind(p[D]) = p^2 obstructs D from being a crossed product for any group of order p^2.

lemma_201.statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $A$ be a central simple $k$-algebra of degree $n$ which is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ with $G$ a group of order $n$. For every field extension $F/k$, the base change $L\otimes_k F$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $F$, and $A\otimes_k F$ is isomorphic as an $F$-algebra to the crossed product algebra $(L\otimes_k F,G,c_F)$, where $c_F$ is $c$ composed with $L^\times\to(L\otimes_k F)^\times$. In particular, if for some field extension $F/k$ the algebra $A\otimes_k F$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L',G',c')$ for any group $G'$ of order $n$ over $F$, then $A$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra for any group of order $n$ over $k$.
lemma_201.proof:
Let $\varphi:A\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}B:=(L,G,c)=\bigoplus_{g\in G}Lu_g$ be a $k$-algebra isomorphism, where $|G|=n=\deg A$, $u_gx=g(x)u_g$ and $u_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}$ for all $x\in L$, $g,h\in G$. Fix a field extension $F/k$ and write $L_F:=L\otimes_kF$; let $\iota:L\to L_F$, $x\mapsto x\otimes 1$. We prove the four steps.

STEP 0 (normalisation of $c$). We first put the presentation in normalised form; this is only a change of the chosen basis $\{u_g\}$ and does not change $A$.
Write $1_B=\sum_{g\in G}a_gu_g$ with $a_g\in L$ (the sum is a left $L$-module decomposition). For $h\in G$,
$u_h=1_Bu_h=\sum_g a_gu_gu_h=\sum_g a_gc(g,h)u_{gh}$, and since $G\ni g\mapsto gh$ is a bijection and the sum $\bigoplus_gLu_g$ is direct, comparison of the coefficient of $u_{h'}$ gives $a_{h'h^{-1}}c(h'h^{-1},h)=\delta_{h',h}$. As each $c(g,h)\in L^\times$, we get $a_g=0$ for $g\neq1$ and $a_1c(1,h)=1$ for every $h$. Put $m:=a_1\in L^\times$; then $c(1,h)=m^{-1}$ for all $h$, and $1_B=mu_1$.
Next use the right unit: $u_h=u_h1_B=\sum_g u_ha_gu_g=\sum_gh(a_g)c(h,g)u_{hg}=h(m)c(h,1)u_h$, whence $c(h,1)=h(m)^{-1}$ for all $h$.
Define $v_g:=mu_g$. Since $m\in L^\times$, $Lv_g=Lu_g$ for each $g$, so $B=\bigoplus_gLv_g$ as left $L$-module, and $v_1=mu_1=1_B$. For $x\in L$, $v_gx=mu_gx=mg(x)u_g=g(x)v_g$. Finally
$v_gv_h=(mu_g)(mu_h)=m\,(u_gm)\,u_h=m\,g(m)\,u_gu_h=m\,g(m)c(g,h)u_{gh}=g(m)c(g,h)v_{gh}$,\nwhere the last step uses $u_{gh}=m^{-1}v_{gh}$ and commutativity of $L$. Setting $c'(g,h):=g(m)c(g,h)$ we have $B=\bigoplus_gLv_g$ with $v_gx=g(x)v_g$, $v_gv_h=c'(g,h)v_{gh}$, and $c'(1,g)=m\,c(1,g)=1$, $c'(g,1)=g(m)c(g,1)=g(m)g(m)^{-1}=1$: i.e. $c'$ is normalised and $v_1=1_B$. Since $A\cong B=(L,G,c')$, replacing $c$ by $c'$ we may (and do) assume from now on that
$u_1=1_B\quad$ and $\quad c(1,g)=c(g,1)=1\ \ \forall g\in G.$

STEP 1 ($L_F$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $F$).
(a) *\'etale.* Since $L$ is \'etale over $k$, $L\simeq\prod_{i=1}^rK_i$ with each $K_i/k$ finite separable; write $K_i\simeq k[t]/(f_i)$ with $f_i$ separable irreducible. Then $L_F\simeq\prod_iF[t]/(f_i)$. Because $f_i'\neq0$ and $\gcd(f_i,f_i')=1$ in $k[t]$, the Bezout relation $\alpha_if_i+\beta_if_i'=1$ also holds in $F[t]$, so $f_i$ has no repeated root over $F$; hence $F[t]/(f_i)$ is a product of finite separable field extensions of $F$. Thus $L_F$ is a finite \'etale $F$-algebra.
(b) *Dimension.* A $k$-basis of $L$ is an $F$-basis of $L_F$, so $\dim_FL_F=\dim_kL=|G|$.
(c) *Action.* For $g\in G$ define $g\cdot(x\otimes\lambda):=g(x)\otimes\lambda$. The map $L\times F\to L_F$, $(x,\lambda)\mapsto g(x)\otimes\lambda$, is $k$-bilinear, so this gives a well-defined $F$-linear endomorphism $g\otimes\mathrm{id}$ of $L_F$; it is a ring homomorphism since $(g\otimes\mathrm{id})((x\otimes\lambda)(y\otimes\mu))=g(xy)\otimes\lambda\mu=g(x)g(y)\otimes\lambda\mu=((g\otimes\mathrm{id})(x\otimes\lambda))((g\otimes\mathrm{id})(y\otimes\mu))$, with inverse $g^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}$, and $(gh)\otimes\mathrm{id}=(g\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(h\otimes\mathrm{id})$. Hence $G$ acts on $L_F$ by $F$-algebra automorphisms.
(d) *Invariants.* Let $P:=\mathrm{Map}(G,L)=\bigoplus_{g\in G}L$ and let $\delta:L\to P$ be the $k$-linear map $\delta(x)(g)=g(x)-x$; then $\ker\delta=L^G=k$. Since $G$ is finite, $P\otimes_kF\simeq\bigoplus_g(L\otimes_kF)=\mathrm{Map}(G,L_F)$, and under this identification $\delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_F$ is $y\mapsto\big(g\mapsto(g\cdot y)-y\big)$: indeed for $y=x\otimes\lambda$ one has $(\delta(x)\otimes\lambda)(g)=(g(x)-x)\lambda=(g\cdot y)-y$, and both sides are $k$-linear in $y$. Let $I:=\mathrm{im}\,\delta$. The sequences $0\to L^G\to L\to I\to0$ and $0\to I\to P$ are exact. Every $F$ that is a $k$-vector space is free, hence flat, so tensoring with $F$ keeps both exact: $0\to L^G\otimes_kF\to L\otimes_kF\to I\otimes_kF$ is exact and $0\to I\otimes_kF\to P\otimes_kF$ is exact. Therefore $\ker(\delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_F)=\mathrm{im}(L^G\otimes_kF\to L\otimes_kF)\simeq L^G\otimes_kF=k\otimes_kF\simeq F$. But $\ker(\delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_F)$ is exactly $(L_F)^G$. Hence $(L_F)^G=F\cdot1_{L_F}$.
By (a)--(d), $L_F$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $F$.

STEP 2 (the cocycle $c_F$).
(2a) *The identity satisfied by $c$.* Associativity of $B$ applied to $(u_g,u_h,u_k)$ gives
$(u_gu_h)u_k=c(g,h)u_{gh}u_k=c(g,h)c(gh,k)u_{ghk}$, and
$u_g(u_hu_k)=u_gc(h,k)u_{hk}=g(c(h,k))\,u_gu_{hk}=g(c(h,k))\,c(g,hk)\,u_{ghk}$,\nusing $u_gc(h,k)=g(c(h,k))u_g$. Since $\bigoplus_gLu_g$ is a direct sum, the coefficients of $u_{ghk}$ coincide:
$\qquad c(g,h)\,c(gh,k)=g\big(c(h,k)\big)\,c(g,hk)\qquad(*)$
(the $G$-action on the factor $c(h,k)$ is essential and is part of the identity).
(2b) *Definition and cocycle condition for $c_F$.* The map $\iota$ is a ring homomorphism with $\iota(1)=1$, hence sends units to units (the inverse of $x\otimes1$ is $x^{-1}\otimes1$), and $\iota(ab)=\iota(a)\iota(b)$. Define $c_F(g,h):=\iota(c(g,h))=c(g,h)\otimes1\in(L_F)^\times$. The map $\iota$ is $G$-equivariant for the action of Step 1(c): $\iota(g(x))=g(x)\otimes1=(g\otimes\mathrm{id})(x\otimes1)=g\cdot\iota(x)$. Tensoring $(*)$ with $1$ and factoring,
$c_F(g,h)c_F(gh,k)=(c(g,h)c(gh,k))\otimes1=\big(g(c(h,k))\,c(g,hk)\big)\otimes1=(g(c(h,k))\otimes1)\,(c(g,hk)\otimes1)$
$=(g\otimes\mathrm{id})\big(c(h,k)\otimes1\big)\,c_F(g,hk)=(g\cdot c_F(h,k))\,c_F(g,hk)$,\nwhich is exactly the $2$-cocycle condition for $c_F$ with respect to the $G$-action on $L_F$. Moreover $c_F(1,g)=1\otimes1=c_F(g,1)$ by Step 0, so $c_F$ is normalised.

STEP 3 ($B\otimes_kF\simeq(L_F,G,c_F)$ as $F$-algebras).
Form the $F$-module $C:=\bigoplus_{g\in G}L_F\tilde u_g$ (free with basis $\{\tilde u_g\}$) with multiplication defined on basis elements by $(\alpha\tilde u_g)(\beta\tilde u_h):=\alpha\,(g\cdot\beta)\,c_F(g,h)\,\tilde u_{gh}$ and extended $F$-bilinearly. Note $L_F$ is commutative (base change of the commutative ring $L$).
(i) *Associativity.* For basis elements,
$((\alpha\tilde u_g)(\beta\tilde u_h))(\gamma\tilde u_k)=\big(\alpha(g\cdot\beta)c_F(g,h)(gh\cdot\gamma)c_F(gh,k)\big)\tilde u_{ghk}$,
$(\alpha\tilde u_g)((\beta\tilde u_h)(\gamma\tilde u_k))=\alpha\,g\big(\beta(h\cdot\gamma)c_F(h,k)\big)c_F(g,hk)\tilde u_{ghk}=\big(\alpha(g\cdot\beta)(gh\cdot\gamma)\,(g\cdot c_F(h,k))\,c_F(g,hk)\big)\tilde u_{ghk}$,\nusing that $g\cdot-$ is a ring automorphism; the two coefficients are equal by the cocycle identity of Step 2b and commutativity of $L_F$. Hence $C$ is associative, and by $F$-bilinearity associativity holds for all elements.
(ii) *Unit.* $\tilde u_1$ is a two-sided identity: $(1_{L_F}\tilde u_1)(\alpha\tilde u_g)=1\cdot(1\cdot\alpha)\cdot c_F(1,g)\,\tilde u_g=\alpha\tilde u_g$ and $(\alpha\tilde u_g)(1_{L_F}\tilde u_1)=\alpha\,(g\cdot1_{L_F})\,c_F(g,1)\,\tilde u_g=\alpha\tilde u_g$, using $c_F(1,g)=c_F(g,1)=1$; $F$-bilinearity extends this to all of $C$. Thus $C$ is a unital $F$-algebra, canonically containing $L_F$ via $\alpha\mapsto\alpha\tilde u_1$ (injective because $\{\tilde u_g\}$ is a basis), and by construction $C$ is the crossed product algebra $(L_F,G,c_F)$: its decomposition is $\bigoplus_gL_F\tilde u_g$, $\tilde u_g\alpha=(g\cdot\alpha)\tilde u_g$ and $\tilde u_g\tilde u_h=c_F(g,h)\tilde u_{gh}$.
(iii) *The isomorphism.* Choose a $k$-basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $L$. Then $\{e_iu_g\}_{i,g}$ is a $k$-basis of $B$, $\{e_i\otimes1\}_i$ is an $F$-basis of $L_F$, and $\{(e_i\otimes1)\tilde u_g\}_{i,g}$ is an $F$-basis of $C$, while $\{(e_iu_g)\otimes1\}_{i,g}$ is an $F$-basis of $B\otimes_kF$. Define $\Psi:C\to B\otimes_kF$ by $F$-linear extension of $\Psi\big((e_i\otimes\lambda)\tilde u_g\big):=(e_iu_g)\otimes\lambda$. This is an $F$-linear bijection (basis to basis).
(iv) *Multiplicativity.* From the relations in $B$ one has the product formula $(au_g)(bu_h)=a\,g(b)\,c(g,h)\,u_{gh}$ for $a,b\in L$; in $C$ the product formula is $(\alpha\tilde u_g)(\beta\tilde u_h)=\alpha(g\cdot\beta)c_F(g,h)\tilde u_{gh}$. Take basis elements $\alpha=e_i\otimes\lambda$, $\beta=e_j\otimes\mu$. Then $\alpha(g\cdot\beta)=(e_i\otimes\lambda)(g(e_j)\otimes\mu)=e_ig(e_j)\otimes\lambda\mu$, and multiplying by $c_F(g,h)=c(g,h)\otimes1$ gives $(e_ig(e_j)c(g,h))\otimes\lambda\mu$. Hence
$\Psi\big((\alpha\tilde u_g)(\beta\tilde u_h)\big)=\Psi\big((e_ig(e_j)c(g,h)\otimes\lambda\mu)\tilde u_{gh}\big)=\big(e_ig(e_j)c(g,h)u_{gh}\big)\otimes\lambda\mu$,\nwhile
$\Psi(\alpha\tilde u_g)\,\Psi(\beta\tilde u_h)=\big((e_iu_g)\otimes\lambda\big)\big((e_ju_h)\otimes\mu\big)=\big(e_iu_ge_ju_h\big)\otimes\lambda\mu=\big(e_ig(e_j)u_gu_h\big)\otimes\lambda\mu=\big(e_ig(e_j)c(g,h)u_{gh}\big)\otimes\lambda\mu$.
They agree, so $\Psi$ is multiplicative on basis elements and hence, by $F$-bilinearity, everywhere.
(v) *Unit.* $\Psi(1_C)=\Psi\big((1_L\otimes1)\tilde u_1\big)=(1_Lu_1)\otimes1=1_B\otimes1=1_{B\otimes_kF}$, using $u_1=1_B$ from Step 0.
Thus $\Psi$ is an $F$-algebra isomorphism $C=(L_F,G,c_F)\xrightarrow{\sim}(B\otimes_kF)$, and composing with $\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_F:A\otimes_kF\xrightarrow{\sim}B\otimes_kF$ gives
$A\otimes_kF\;\cong\;(L\otimes_kF,\,G,\,c_F)$\nas $F$-algebras, where $L\otimes_kF$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $F$ (Step 1) and $c_F$ is a normalised $2$-cocycle (Step 2). This proves the first claim.

STEP 4 (the "in particular"). Assume there is a field extension $F/k$ such that $A\otimes_kF$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product $(L',G',c')$ for any group $G'$ of order $n$ over $F$. We argue by contraposition of Steps 1--3: if $A$ were isomorphic over $k$ to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $n$, then Steps 1--3 applied to this $G$ would exhibit $A\otimes_kF\cong(L\otimes_kF,G,c_F)$, where $L\otimes_kF$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $F$, $|G|=n$, and $c_F:G\times G\to(L\otimes_kF)^\times$ is the composed cocycle — i.e. $A\otimes_kF$ would be a crossed product for a group of order $n$ over $F$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $A$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $n$ over $k$. $\blacksquare$

lemma_203.statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $A$ be a central division $F$-algebra containing no element $\alpha\notin F$ with $\alpha^{p^{2}}\in F$. Then $A\otimes_{F}F((u))$ contains no element $x\notin F((u))$ satisfying $x^{p^{2}}\in F((u))$.
lemma_203.proof:
Write $k=F((u))$ and $D=A\otimes_F F((u))$. We prove the contrapositive statement

 $(*)$ for every $x\in D$, $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ implies $x\in k$;

from which the lemma follows immediately (there is then no $x\notin k=F((u))$ with $x^{p^2}\in k$). The argument uses only the $u$-adic valuation and the stated hypothesis on $A$; no external result is needed.

STEP 1 (Model of $D$ as $A((u))$). Let $A((u))$ be the ring of formal Laurent series $\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^{i}$ ($N\in\mathbb Z$, $\alpha_i\in A$) with $u$ a *central* indeterminate, i.e. $(\alpha u^i)(\beta u^j)=(\alpha\beta)u^{i+j}$; two series are equal iff all coefficients agree, and each nonzero series has only finitely many nonzero coefficients below any given degree. Since $A$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ (it is a central division algebra), the natural map $\varphi:A\otimes_F F((u))\to A((u))$, $a\otimes(\sum_i c_i u^i)\mapsto\sum_i (c_i a)u^i$, is a ring isomorphism: it is a homomorphism because $F$ is commutative and central in $A$; taking an $F$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $A$, every element of $A\otimes_F F((u))$ is uniquely $\sum_{j=1}^d e_j\otimes f_j$ with $f_j\in F((u))$ (finitely many nonzero $f_j$), and $\varphi(\sum_j e_j\otimes f_j)=\sum_j e_j f_j=\sum_i(\sum_j c_{j,i}e_j)u^i$; $F$-linear independence of the $e_j$ gives injectivity, and given $\sum_i\alpha_i u^i\in A((u))$ with $\alpha_i=\sum_j c_{j,i}e_j$ the element $\sum_j e_j\otimes(\sum_i c_{j,i}u^i)$ (each $\sum_i c_{j,i}u^i\in F((u))$ because the series is bounded below) maps onto it. We henceforth identify $D=A((u))$. Every element of $k=F((u))$ is central in $D$: $u$ is central by construction and $F\subseteq Z(A)$.

STEP 2 (The valuation). For $y=\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^i\in D$, $y\neq0$, set $w(y)=\min\{i:\alpha_i\neq0\}$, and $w(0)=\infty$. Then:
(a) $w(y+z)\ge\min(w(y),w(z))$ (immediate from the definition).
(b) $w(yz)=w(y)+w(z)$ for $y,z\neq0$. Indeed, with $m=w(y)$, $n=w(z)$, the coefficient of $u^{m+n}$ in $yz$ is $\alpha_m\beta_n$, where $\alpha_m,\beta_n\neq0$; since $A$ is a division ring it has no zero divisors, so $\alpha_m\beta_n\neq0$, and no coefficient of $yz$ of degree $<m+n$ can be nonzero (each product $\alpha_i\beta_j$ with $i+j<m+n$ has $i<m$ or $j<n$, and grouping $yz=\sum_{t\ge m+n}\big(\sum_{i+j=t}\alpha_i\beta_j\big)u^t$ shows the coefficients below $m+n$ vanish). This is exactly where the hypothesis that $A$ is a *division* algebra is used.
(c) $w|_k=v$, the $u$-adic valuation of $k$, and $w(c)=0$ for $c\in k^\times$ iff $v(c)=0$.

STEP 3 (KEY STEP: only the leading coefficient is seen). Let $y\in D$ with $w(y)=0$ and $y^{p^{2}}\in k$. Write $y=\alpha_0+z$, where $\alpha_0\in A$ is the $u^0$-coefficient of $y$ (so $w(y)=0$ gives $\alpha_0\ne0$) and $z=\sum_{i\ge1}\alpha_i u^i$ satisfies $w(z)\ge1$. By distributivity in the (noncommutative) ring $D$,
$$y^{p^{2}}=\sum_{(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_{p^{2}})\in\{0,1\}^{p^{2}}} t_1t_2\cdots t_{p^{2}},\qquad t_r=\begin{cases}\alpha_0,&\varepsilon_r=0,\\ z,&\varepsilon_r=1,\end{cases}$$
a sum of $2^{p^{2}}$ words; no commutativity is used. The word with $\varepsilon_1=\cdots=\varepsilon_{p^2}=0$ equals $\alpha_0^{p^{2}}$. For every other word, by Step 2(b) applied repeatedly, its $w$-value is $\sum_r w(t_r)=\#\{r:\varepsilon_r=1\}\cdot w(z)+\#\{r:\varepsilon_r=0\}\cdot 0\ge1$, since $w(\alpha_0)=0$ (as $\alpha_0\in A^{\times}$, viewed as a degree-$0$ series) and $w(z)\ge1$. By Step 2(a), the sum $R$ of all these other words satisfies $w(R)\ge1$, so
$$y^{p^{2}}=\alpha_0^{p^{2}}+R,\qquad w(R)\ge1 .$$
By hypothesis $y^{p^{2}}=\sum_{i\ge M}\kappa_i u^{i}\in k$ with all $\kappa_i\in F$; since $w(R)\ge1$, $R=\sum_{i\ge1}\rho_i u^{i}$ has zero $u^0$-coefficient. Comparing $u^0$-coefficients (unique by Step 1) yields $\kappa_0=\alpha_0^{p^{2}}\in F$. Thus:

 KEY STEP: $w(y)=0$ and $y^{p^{2}}\in k\ \Longrightarrow\$ the $u^0$-coefficient $\alpha_0$ of $y$ satisfies $\alpha_0^{p^{2}}\in F$.

No assertion is made here about any other coefficient of $y$.

STEP 4 (Peeling off a central leading term). Let $z\in D$ with $z^{p^{2}}\in k$, and let $c\in k$. Since $c$ is central in $D$ it commutes with $z$, so the binomial theorem applies: $(z-c)^{p^{2}}=\sum_{j=0}^{p^{2}}(-1)^{j}\binom{p^{2}}{j}z^{p^{2}-j}c^{j}$. For $0<j<p^{2}$ one has $p\mid\binom{p^{2}}{j}$ (from $j\binom{p^{2}}{j}=p^{2}\binom{p^{2}-1}{j-1}$ and $v_p(j)\le1$ because $0<j<p^{2}$), hence in characteristic $p$ this reduces to $(z-c)^{p^{2}}=z^{p^{2}}-c^{p^{2}}$. As both terms lie in $k$ (and $k$ is a ring, $c^{p^2}\in k$), we get $(z-c)^{p^{2}}\in k$. Moreover, if $c=\beta u^{m}$ is exactly the leading term of $z$ (so $\beta\ne0$), then $z-c=\sum_{i>m}\alpha_i u^{i}$ and hence either $z=c$ or $w(z-c)>m$.

STEP 5 (Induction over the nonzero coefficients). Let $x\in D$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$; if $x=0$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $x\ne0$ and write $x=\sum_{i\ge N}\alpha_i u^{i}$ with $\alpha_N\ne0$. Let $I=\{i\ge N:\alpha_i\ne0\}$; being a subset of $\mathbb Z$ bounded below, $I$ is finite or countably infinite and can be listed strictly increasingly as $i_1<i_2<\cdots$ (i.e. $i_1=\min I$, $i_{n+1}=\min(I\setminus\{i_1,\dots,i_n\})$ whenever the set is nonempty; if $I=\{i_1,\dots,i_M\}$ the list stops at $M$). Define
$$r_1=x,\qquad r_{n+1}=r_n-\alpha_{i_n}u^{i_n}\quad(\text{for each }n\text{ with }i_n\in I).$$
By a straightforward induction on $n$ (no limits), for every index $n$ occurring in the list:
 (i) $r_n=\sum_{i\in I,\,i\ge i_n}\alpha_i u^{i}$, hence $r_n\ne0$ (its leading coefficient is $\alpha_{i_n}\ne0$) and $w(r_n)=i_n$;
 (ii) $r_n^{p^{2}}\in k$;
 (iii) $\alpha_{i_n}^{p^{2}}\in F$, and consequently $\alpha_{i_n}\in F$.
Base $n=1$: (i) is the definition of $I$; (ii) is the hypothesis on $x$.
Inductive step: assume (i),(ii) for $n$. Since $r_n\ne0$, Step 2(b) gives $w(r_nu^{-i_n})=w(r_n)-i_n=0$. Since $u$ is central, $(r_nu^{-i_n})^{p^{2}}=r_n^{p^{2}}u^{-i_np^{2}}\in k$ by (ii). Applying the KEY STEP to $y=r_nu^{-i_n}=\sum_{i\in I,\,i\ge i_n}\alpha_i u^{\,i-i_n}$, whose $u^0$-coefficient is $\alpha_{i_n}$, gives $\alpha_{i_n}^{p^{2}}\in F$ — this proves the first half of (iii). By the hypothesis on $A$ (no element of $A\setminus F$ has its $p^{2}$-power in $F$), $\alpha_{i_n}\in F$. Then $c:=\alpha_{i_n}u^{i_n}\in k$, and Step 4 applied to $z=r_n$ gives $r_{n+1}^{p^{2}}=(r_n-c)^{p^{2}}=r_n^{p^{2}}-\alpha_{i_n}^{p^{2}}u^{i_np^{2}}\in k$, proving (ii) for $n+1$; and (i) for $n+1$ follows from $r_{n+1}=r_n-\alpha_{i_n}u^{i_n}=\sum_{i\in I,\,i>i_n}\alpha_i u^{i}$, whose leading index is $i_{n+1}$ by construction. This completes the induction.

STEP 6 (Conclusion). Every nonzero coefficient of $x$ is one of the $\alpha_{i_n}$, and Step 5(iii) shows each $\alpha_{i_n}\in F$; the vanishing coefficients are in $F$ as well. Hence
$$x=\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_{i_n}u^{i_n}$$
is a Laurent series in $u$ with coefficients in $F$, bounded below by $N$, i.e. $x\in F((u))=k$. (If $I$ is finite this is a polynomial identity, $x=\sum_{n=1}^{M}\alpha_{i_n}u^{i_n}$; if $I$ is infinite it is a genuine element of $F((u))$ — in both cases $x\in k$.) Note that the conclusion is drawn coefficient-by-coefficient, not from any limiting statement about the remainders $r_n$.

Thus $(*)$ holds: every $x\in A\otimes_F F((u))$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in F((u))$ already lies in $F((u))$. Therefore $A\otimes_F F((u))$ contains no element $x\notin F((u))$ satisfying $x^{p^{2}}\in F((u))$, which is the claim. (The same proof works verbatim with $p^{2}$ replaced by any $p^{e}$, $e\ge1$, using the corresponding hypothesis on $A$; only the case $e=2$ is needed and proved here.)

lemma_205.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$. If $D$ contains no element $x$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^{p}\in k$, then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_205.proof:
We argue by reducing the hypothesis of the lemma to the hypothesis of the already proved lemma_194 (Spark), and then applying it.

Setup and notation. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 2 and let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p^2. Recall (from the statement of the conjecture's definitions) that an element x \in D is called p-central if x \notin k and x^p \in k. The hypotheses we assume throughout are:
  (H1) p[D] \neq 0 in Br(k), i.e. the Brauer class of D is not annihilated by p;
  (H2) D contains no p-central element, i.e. for every x \in D, x^p \in k implies x \in k.
We must show that D is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L, G, c) for any group G of order p^2.

Step 1. D contains no element x with x^{p^2} \in k and x^p \notin k.

Proof of Step 1. Suppose, towards a contradiction, that there exists x \in D with x^{p^2} \in k and x^p \notin k. Set y := x^p \in D. Since D is an associative k-algebra, powers of a single element commute with each other and obey the usual laws, so
      y^p = (x^p)^p = x^{p \cdot p} = x^{p^2} \in k.
Moreover y = x^p \notin k by the assumed property of x. Thus y is an element of D with y \notin k and y^p \in k, that is, y is p-central. This contradicts hypothesis (H2). Hence no such x exists: for every x \in D,
      x^{p^2} \in k  \Longrightarrow  x^p \in k.
(In that case (H2) further forces x \in k, so in fact every element of D whose p^2-th power lies in k already lies in k; only the first implication is needed below.)

Step 2. Application of lemma_194.

We check that lemma_194 (Spark) applies verbatim to the pair (k, D):
  - k has characteristic p > 2: this is part of the statement of the present lemma.
  - D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2: this is part of the statement of the present lemma.
  - the class [D] \in Br(k) is not annihilated by p: this is hypothesis (H1).
  - D contains no element x with x^{p^2} \in k and x^p \notin k: this is exactly the conclusion of Step 1.
All hypotheses of lemma_194 are therefore satisfied, and its conclusion is that D is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra (L, G, c) for any group G of order p^2.

Step 3. Conclusion. The conclusion of Step 2 is precisely the statement to be proved. For completeness, phrased as a contradiction: if one assumed D \cong (L, G, c) for some group G of order p^2 and some 2-cocycle c : G \times G \to L^\times with L a G-Galois k-algebra, then Steps 1 and 2 would still apply (they use only (H1) and (H2)), and lemma_194 would assert that D is not such a crossed product — a contradiction. Hence no such G, L, c exist.

Remarks on the logical structure (not used in the deduction). The only point where the hypothesis p[D] \neq 0 is used is in the invocation of lemma_194; the passage from "no p-central element" to "no element x with x^{p^2} \in k, x^p \notin k" in Step 1 is purely formal and holds in any characteristic and any degree. Intuitively, Step 1 says that a p-central element is exactly the p-th power that an element of the forbidden kind would produce: an element x with x^{p^2} \in k but x^p \notin k yields, by taking p-th powers, a purely inseparable element of degree p over k inside D. Thus the absence of p-central elements is a strictly stronger exclusion than the absence of elements generating simple purely inseparable extensions of degree p^2, and lemma_194 turns that exclusion (together with p[D] \neq 0) into the non-existence of Galois maximal subfields, hence of crossed product structures.

lemma_cyclic_p2_has_pcentral.statement: Let $p$ be a prime and let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p$. Let $M/k$ be a cyclic Galois extension of degree $p^{2}$ with generator $\sigma$, let $b\in k^{\times}$, and let $D=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}Mv^{i}$ be the $k$-algebra defined by $v^{p^{2}}=b$ and $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in M$. Then $v^{p}\notin k$ and $(v^{p})^{p}\in k$.
lemma_cyclic_p2_has_pcentral.proof:
We prove the two assertions (v^p)^p \in k and v^p \notin k directly from the defining relations of the cyclic algebra; no hypothesis that D is a division algebra is used.

STEP 0 (What D is). By definition D = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^2-1} M v^i is the cyclic algebra (M/k,\sigma,b): as a left M-module it is free with basis 1, v, v^2, \dots, v^{p^2-1}, and its multiplication is the associative k-bilinear extension of the two rules
  (R1)  v\lambda = \sigma(\lambda) v for all \lambda \in M,      (R2)  v^{p^2} = b .
Equivalently D \cong M[t;\sigma]/(t^{p^2}-b); the polynomial t^{p^2}-b generates a two-sided ideal of the skew polynomial ring because for \lambda \in M one has (t^{p^2}-b)\lambda = t^{p^2}\lambda - b\lambda = \sigma^{p^2}(\lambda)t^{p^2} - b\lambda = \lambda t^{p^2} - b\lambda = \lambda(t^{p^2}-b) (using \sigma^{p^2} = \mathrm{id}_M and b \in k), and t commutes with t^{p^2}-b. Left division by the monic polynomial t^{p^2}-b then identifies the quotient with the free M-module with basis 1,\dots,t^{p^2-1}, which is the direct-sum description above.

STEP 1 (Scalars of k are central in D). Let c \in k. Since M is a k-algebra, c commutes with every \lambda \in M. Since \sigma is a k-automorphism of M, \sigma(c) = c, so vc = \sigma(c)v = cv. As D is generated as a k-algebra by M and v, c lies in the center Z(D). In particular every element of k commutes with v^p.

STEP 2 (v is a unit of D). Using (R2), v \cdot (b^{-1}v^{p^2-1}) = b^{-1}v^{p^2} = b^{-1}b = 1 and (b^{-1}v^{p^2-1})\cdot v = b^{-1}v^{p^2} = 1, so v \in D^\times with v^{-1} = b^{-1}v^{p^2-1}. Hence every power v^i (i \ge 0) is invertible; in particular v^p \in D^\times and v^p \neq 0.

STEP 3 (Commutation formula). Claim: for every integer i \ge 0 and every \lambda \in M, one has v^i \lambda = \sigma^i(\lambda) v^i. Proof by induction on i. For i = 0 the statement is \lambda = \lambda. For i = 1 it is the relation (R1). For the inductive step, using (R1) with \mu := \sigma^i(\lambda) \in M and then the induction hypothesis,
  v^{i+1}\lambda = v\,(v^i\lambda) = v\,(\sigma^i(\lambda)v^i) = (v\,\sigma^i(\lambda))\,v^i = \sigma(\sigma^i(\lambda))\,v\,v^i = \sigma^{i+1}(\lambda)\,v^{i+1}.
This proves the claim. (Here we used only associativity of D and that M is \sigma-stable, which holds since \sigma is an automorphism of M.)

STEP 4 (The p-th power of v^p lies in k). Since v^p is a power of the single element v, the usual laws of exponents hold in the associative ring D (no commutativity is needed): (v^p)^p = v^{p\cdot p} = v^{p^2} = b by (R2). As b \in k^\times \subset k, we obtain (v^p)^p \in k.

STEP 5 (v^p does not lie in k). Suppose for a contradiction that v^p \in k. By Step 1, v^p is then central in D, so for every \lambda \in M,
  v^p \lambda = \lambda v^p .
On the other hand, Step 3 with i = p gives v^p\lambda = \sigma^p(\lambda)v^p. Hence \sigma^p(\lambda)v^p = \lambda v^p for all \lambda \in M. Since v^p is invertible by Step 2, right multiplication by (v^p)^{-1} yields \sigma^p(\lambda) = \lambda for all \lambda \in M, i.e. \sigma^p = \mathrm{id}_M.
But M/k is a cyclic Galois extension of degree p^2 with generator \sigma, i.e. Gal(M/k) = \langle\sigma\rangle is cyclic of order exactly p^2. Thus the order of \sigma is p^2, whereas \sigma^p = \mathrm{id}_M would force the order of \sigma to divide p. This is impossible because p is prime, hence p \ge 2 and 1 \le p \le p^2 - 1 (indeed p^2 - p = p(p-1) \ge 2 > 0), so \sigma^p is a non-identity element of the cyclic group \langle\sigma\rangle of order p^2 (explicitly, \sigma^p has order p). Contradiction. Therefore v^p \notin k.

STEP 6 (Independent check of Step 5 via the direct-sum decomposition). One can also see v^p \notin k from the freeness in Step 0: k \subseteq M = M v^0, and the sum D = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^2-1} M v^i is direct, so M v^0 \cap M v^p = 0 for 1 \le p \le p^2-1. If v^p were in k \subseteq M v^0, then v^p would lie in M v^0 \cap M v^p = 0, contradicting v^p \in D^\times from Step 2. (This uses 1 \le p \le p^2-1, which holds since p \ge 2.)

CONCLUSION. Steps 4 and 5 give exactly the two required assertions: (v^p)^p = b \in k and v^p \notin k. Equivalently, v^p is a p-central element of D in the sense of the definition quoted in the conjecture (an element x with x \notin k and x^p \in k). Note that the argument needed only that p is prime (so that p < p^2 and hence \sigma^p \neq \mathrm{id}), that \sigma has exact order p^2, and that b \in k^\times; in particular it does not require D to be a division algebra, nor p > 2.

lemma_207.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$. Then $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ if and only if $D$ contains an element $x$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$.
lemma_207.proof:
Throughout, $k$ is a field of characteristic $p>2$ and $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class satisfies $p[D]\neq 0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$.

We prove the two implications separately.

**Part I (only if: crossed product $\Rightarrow$ existence of $x$).**
Assume $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$. We argue by contraposition using lemma_194 (Spark). That lemma states: for a field of characteristic $p>2$ and a central division algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$, if $D$ contains no element $x$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$, then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
All the hypotheses of lemma_194 are satisfied by our $k$ and $D$ (characteristic $p>2$; central division of degree $p^{2}$; $p[D]\neq 0$). If $D$ contained no element $x$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$, the lemma would conclude that $D$ is not a crossed product for any group of order $p^{2}$, contradicting our assumption. Hence $D$ does contain an element $x$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$.

**Part II (if: existence of $x$ $\Rightarrow$ crossed product).**
Assume there is $x\in D$ with $a:=x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$.

*Step 1: the degree of $k(x)$ over $k$ is $p^{2}$.* First, $x\notin k$, for otherwise $x^{p}\in k$. Since $x^{p^{2}}=a\in k$, the element $x$ is algebraic over $k$ and its minimal polynomial $\mu\in k[T]$ divides $T^{p^{2}}-a$. In $k(x)[T]$ we have $T^{p^{2}}-a=T^{p^{2}}-x^{p^{2}}=(T-x)^{p^{2}}$ (freshman's dream in characteristic $p$), so $\mu=(T-x)^{p^{i}}$ for some integer $0\le i\le 2$; expanding, $\mu=T^{p^{i}}-x^{p^{i}}$, and since $\mu\in k[T]$ we get $x^{p^{i}}\in k$. The least such $i$ cannot be $0$ (that would give $x\in k$) and cannot be $1$ (that would give $x^{p}\in k$). Hence $i=2$, $\mu=T^{p^{2}}-a$, and $[k(x):k]=p^{2}$; the extension $k(x)/k$ is purely inseparable. Since $D$ is a division ring and $x$ is algebraic over $k$, the $k$-subalgebra $k(x)$ generated by $x$ is indeed a field.

*Step 2: $k(x)$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.* By the subfield part of the double centralizer theorem (ref_1), applied to the central simple $k$-algebra $A=D$ of degree $p^{2}$ and the subfield $K=k(x)$, the centralizer $C_{D}(k(x))$ is a central simple $k(x)$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[k(x):k]=p^{2}/p^{2}=1$. Thus $C_{D}(k(x))=k(x)$, and the final clause of ref_1 ("$K$ is a maximal subfield of $A$ if and only if $C_{A}(K)=K$") shows that $k(x)$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

*Step 3: $k(x)/k$ is normal.* Let $\bar k$ be an algebraic closure of $k$ containing $D$'s centre, and let $\sigma:k(x)\hookrightarrow \bar k$ be any $k$-embedding. Then $\sigma(x)^{p^{2}}=\sigma(x^{p^{2}})=\sigma(a)=a=x^{p^{2}}$, so $(\sigma(x)-x)^{p^{2}}=\sigma(x)^{p^{2}}-x^{p^{2}}=0$ in the field $\bar k$, whence $\sigma(x)=x$ and therefore $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ on $k(x)$. In particular $\sigma(k(x))\subseteq k(x)$, which is precisely normality of $k(x)/k$. (This is the usual fact that purely inseparable extensions are normal, spelled out here.)

*Step 4: $D$ contains a Galois maximal subfield.* By ref_32 (Saltman's normal maximal subfield lemma): if a central division $k$-algebra contains a maximal subfield that is normal over $k$, then it contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$. Applying this to $D$ and the maximal subfield $k(x)$ of Steps 2--3, we obtain a maximal subfield $E\subset D$ that is Galois over $k$. Put $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$. Since $E$ is a maximal subfield of the degree-$p^{2}$ algebra $D$, $[E:k]=\deg(D)=p^{2}$, and since $E/k$ is Galois, $|G|=[E:k]=p^{2}$.

*Step 5: $D$ is the $(E,G,c)$ crossed product.* The field $E$ is a commutative etale $k$-algebra of dimension $p^{2}=|G|$, the action of $G=\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$ is by $k$-automorphisms, and $E^{G}=k$ by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory; so $E$ is a $G$-Galois $k$-algebra in the sense of the definition. Applying lemma_106 (Spark) to the central simple $k$-algebra $A=D$ of degree $n=p^{2}$ and the maximal subfield $E$ Galois over $k$ with group $G$, there exists a map $c:G\times G\to E^{\times}$ such that, as $k$-algebras,
$$D\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{g\in G}E\,u_{g},\qquad u_{g}\lambda=g(\lambda)u_{g},\qquad u_{g}u_{h}=c(g,h)\,u_{gh}\quad(\lambda\in E,\ g,h\in G),$$
which is exactly a crossed product algebra $(E,G,c)$ with $|G|=p^{2}$.

Combining Parts I and II gives the claimed equivalence. (Note that the hypothesis $p[D]\neq 0$ is used only in Part I, via lemma_194; the implication in Part II holds for every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$.)

lemma_204.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ and residue field $\bar k$, let $c\in k$ with $v(c)<0$ and $p\nmid v(c)$, and let $z\in k^{\times}$ with $v(z)=0$ whose residue $\bar z$ lies outside $\bar k^{p}$. Then the symbol algebra $[c,z)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p-1}k(x)y^{i}$ with $x^{p}-x=c$, $y^{p}=z$, $yx=(x+1)y$ is a division algebra of degree $p$, and for the valuation $w$ extending $v$ one has $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]=p$ and residue division ring $\bar D=\bar k(\bar z^{1/p})$, purely inseparable of degree $p$ over $\bar k$.
lemma_204.proof:
Proof.
Let n=v(c). Then n<0 and p does not divide n. Choose pi in k with v(pi)=1. Put K=k(x) where x^p-x=c.

1. Irreducibility and Galois group. Suppose f(T)=T^p-T-c is reducible. Let d be the degree of a proper irreducible factor, 1<=d<p, and let alpha be a root of that factor. Then alpha^p-alpha=c. Taking trace from k(alpha) to k gives Tr(alpha^p)-Tr(alpha)=d c. Since f'=-1, the extension is separable, and Tr(alpha^p)=Tr(alpha)^p. Hence d c=Tr(alpha)^p-Tr(alpha). Since d is nonzero in F_p, c lies in wp(k), where wp(k)={a^p-a | a in k}. But if a in k and v(a)<0, then v(a^p-a)=p v(a)<0 and is divisible by p; if v(a)>=0, then v(a^p-a)>=0. This contradicts n<0 and p not dividing n. Thus f is irreducible. Its roots are x+i, i in F_p, so K/k is cyclic Galois of degree p with generator sigma(x)=x+1.

2. Valuation on K. By the henselian property (unique extension of the valuation to algebraic extensions), v has a unique extension w_K to K. If w_K(x)>=0, then v(c)=w_K(x^p-x)>=0, contradiction. Hence w_K(x)<0. Since p w_K(x)<w_K(x), w_K(x^p-x)=p w_K(x), so p w_K(x)=n and w_K(x)=n/p.
Since gcd(p,n)=1, choose integers r,s with r n + s p =1. Let t=x^r pi^s. Then w_K(t)=r n/p+s=1/p. Thus e_K=[w_K(K^*):v(k^*)]>=p. Lemma_96 applied to the finite Galois extension K/k gives [K:k]=e_K f_K, where f_K is the residue degree. Since [K:k]=p and e_K>=p, we get e_K=p and f_K=1. Also k(t) is a subfield of K whose value group contains 1/p, so its ramification index is at least p; the ramification index of a finite valued extension is at most its degree (choose representatives of distinct value cosets and use the minimal valuation argument), hence [k(t):k]>=p. Therefore K=k(t). Consequently each element of K has a unique expression sum_{i=0}^{p-1} a_i t^i with a_i in k, and w_K(sum a_i t^i)=min_i(v(a_i)+i/p), because the numbers i/p have distinct residues modulo Z. The residue field of K is kbar.

3. The automorphism sigma on the graded ring of K. Let gr_K be the associated graded ring for w_K. Since K is totally ramified with uniformizer t of value 1/p and residue field kbar, gr_K is the graded field kbar[U,U^{-1}] with deg U=1/p. We claim sigma acts trivially on gr_K. Indeed, sigma(t)=(x+1)^r pi^s=t(1+1/x)^r. Since w_K(1/x)>0, sigma(t)/t=1+epsilon with w_K(epsilon)>0. For any homogeneous element of gr_K, represented by a t^m with a in k, sigma(a t^m)=a t^m(1+epsilon)^m, and (1+epsilon)^m is congruent to 1 modulo the maximal ideal. Hence the initial form is unchanged. Thus the induced automorphism on gr_K is the identity.

4. A valuation on D. Write D=K y^0 direct sum ... direct sum K y^{p-1}. Define W(0)=infinity and for d=sum_{i=0}^{p-1} a_i y^i set W(d)=min_i w_K(a_i). Let Gamma=(1/p)Z. For gamma in Gamma put F_gamma D={d in D | W(d)>=gamma}. Then F_gamma D=direct sum F_gamma K y^i, where F_gamma K={a in K | w_K(a)>=gamma}. This is a multiplicative filtration because w_K is a valuation, sigma preserves w_K, and z in k^* has value 0.
Let Y be the initial form of y. Since W(y)=0 and y^p=z, Y^p=zbar. Because sigma acts trivially on gr_K, Y commutes with gr_K. The direct-sum description of the filtration gives gr_F(D)=direct sum_{gamma} (gr_gamma K) Y^i, i=0,...,p-1, as a gr_K-module. Therefore gr_F(D) is isomorphic to gr_K[T]/(T^p-zbar), with T in degree 0.
Now gr_K has fraction field kbar(U). The element zbar is not a p-th power in kbar, hence not a p-th power in kbar(U): p-th powers in kbar(U) lie in kbar^p(U^p). In characteristic p, T^p-zbar is irreducible over kbar(U) because it has no root there. The quotient gr_K[T]/(T^p-zbar) is a free gr_K-module of rank p, hence torsion-free; after inverting nonzero elements of gr_K it becomes the field kbar(U)[T]/(T^p-zbar). Therefore gr_F(D) is a domain.
For nonzero d,d' in D, the initial forms of d and d' are nonzero homogeneous elements of gr_F(D); their product is nonzero because gr_F(D) is a domain. Hence W(dd')=W(d)+W(d'). Also W(d+d')>=min(W(d),W(d')) by the definition. Thus W is a valuation on D extending v.

5. D is a central division algebra. A valuation has no zero divisors: if d,d' are nonzero then W(dd')=W(d)+W(d')<infinity, so dd' is nonzero. D is finite-dimensional over k, so a finite-dimensional domain over a field is a division ring: for 0!=d, left multiplication by d is injective, hence surjective, giving a right inverse; no zero divisors then gives a two-sided inverse.
We compute the center. Let d=sum_{i=0}^{p-1} a_i y^i be central. Commuting with x gives 0=x d-d x=sum_i (x a_i-a_i(x+i)) y^i = -sum_i i a_i y^i, because y^i x=sigma^i(x)y^i=(x+i)y^i and K is commutative. The y^i are linearly independent over K, so i a_i=0 for all i. For i=1,...,p-1, i is a nonzero element of k, hence invertible, so a_i=0. Thus d=a_0 in K. Commuting with y gives a_0 y=y a_0=sigma(a_0)y, so a_0=sigma(a_0). Since K^sigma=k, d lies in k. Therefore Z(D)=k. As dim_k D=p^2, D is a central division algebra of degree p.

6. Value group and residue division ring for W. Since W(D^*)=Gamma=(1/p)Z and v(k^*)=Z, [W(D^*):v(k^*)]=p. The residue division ring is gr_0(D). From the graded ring description, gr_0(D) is isomorphic to kbar[Y]/(Y^p-zbar). Because zbar is not a p-th power in kbar, this quotient is a field, purely inseparable of degree p over kbar. It is kbar(zbar^{1/p}).

7. Uniqueness of the extension of v to D. Let w' be any valuation on the division ring D extending v. Its restriction to K is w_K by uniqueness of the extension to the algebraic extension K/k. Let O_k={a in k | v(a)>=0} union {0}, O_W={d | W(d)>=0}, and O'={d | w'(d)>=0}. We show O_W subset O'.
First O_K is integral over O_k: if a in O_K, then all conjugates sigma^j(a) have the same w_K-value (sigma preserves w_K by uniqueness), so the coefficients of the minimal polynomial of a over k have nonnegative v. Now take d in O_W, so d=sum a_i y^i with a_i in O_K. Let B be the O_k-subalgebra of K generated by all sigma^j(a_i), 0<=j<p. B is a finite O_k-module because it is generated by finitely many integral elements, and sigma(B)=B. Then C=direct sum_{i=0}^{p-1} B y^i is a ring: y^p=z in O_k and y B y^{-1}=sigma(B)=B. It is finite as O_k-module and contains d. Hence d is integral over O_k. A valuation ring in a division ring is integrally closed: if x is not in O', then w'(x)<0, and in a monic polynomial equation over O' the term x^m has strictly smaller valuation than all other terms, impossible. Thus d in O'.
Now define phi:Gamma_W -> Gamma_{w'} by phi(W(d))=w'(d) for d nonzero. This is well defined: if W(d)=W(e), then e^{-1}d and d^{-1}e have W-value 0, hence lie in O_W subset O', so w'(e^{-1}d)=0. It is a group homomorphism and surjective because every value of w' is w'(d)=phi(W(d)). Its kernel is zero: let delta=W(t)=1/p generate Gamma_W. If the kernel contained a nonzero m delta, then m phi(delta)=0; value groups are torsion-free, so phi(delta)=0. Then phi(1)=p phi(delta)=0, but phi(1)=w'(pi)=1, contradiction. Therefore phi is an isomorphism and w'(d)=phi(W(d)) for all d, i.e. w'=W.

Thus the valuation w extending v is unique, and the computed value group and residue division ring are as stated. QED.

lemma_208.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be complete for a discrete valuation of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ and perfect residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, residue division ring $\bar D$ and associated graded ring $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$, and suppose every element of $\bar D$ is purely inseparable over $\bar k$. If $D$ contains a subfield $K$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$, then $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ contains a homogeneous element $y$ of degree $\delta\in\frac{1}{p}\,v(k^{\times})\setminus v(k^{\times})$ such that $y^{p}$ is a nonzero element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{p\delta}$.
lemma_208.proof:
**Setup and notation for the graded ring.** Since $k$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$, it is henselian; hence $v$ has a unique extension to every algebraic extension of $k$, and in particular the given valuation $w$ on $D$ restricts to the unique extension of $v$ to $K$. Write, for $\alpha$ in the value group $w(D^\times)$ (an ordered abelian group containing $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$), $D_{\geq\alpha}=\{x\in D^\times: w(x)\geq \alpha\}\cup\{0\}$ and $D_{>\alpha}=\{x\in D^\times: w(x)>\alpha\}\cup\{0\}$, and $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_\alpha=D_{\geq\alpha}/D_{>\alpha}$. For $0\neq x\in D$ write $\mathrm{in}_w(x)$ for the class of $x$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{w(x)}$. The multiplication $\mathrm{gr}_\alpha\times\mathrm{gr}_\beta\to\mathrm{gr}_{\alpha+\beta}$ is induced by $(x\bmod D_{>\alpha})(y\bmod D_{>\beta})=xy\bmod D_{>\alpha+\beta}$; from the definition one reads off the two elementary facts we shall use: (a) $\mathrm{in}_w(xy)=\mathrm{in}_w(x)\,\mathrm{in}_w(y)$ for all nonzero $x,y\in D$ (so $\mathrm{in}_w(x^m)=\mathrm{in}_w(x)^m$), and (b) if $w(x)<w(y)$ then $x+y\in D_{\geq w(x)}\setminus D_{>w(x)}$, hence $\mathrm{in}_w(x+y)=\mathrm{in}_w(x)$. Because $w|_k=v$, the ring $\mathrm{gr}(k)=\bigoplus_\alpha k_{\geq\alpha}/k_{>\alpha}$ is a graded subring of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$, and for $0\neq c\in k$ the initial form $\mathrm{in}_v(c)$ is a nonzero homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{v(c)}$.

**Step 1: the residue field of $K$ is $k\!\bar{}$.** Put $\mathcal O_K=\mathcal O_D\cap K$ and $\mathcal M_K=\mathcal M_D\cap\mathcal O_K$; indeed for $x\in K$ one has $x\in\mathcal O_K\iff w(x)\ge 0\iff x\in\mathcal O_D$, and similarly $x\in\mathcal M_K\iff w(x)>0\iff x\in\mathcal M_D$. Hence the residue map $\mathcal O_D\twoheadrightarrow \bar D$ induces an injective homomorphism of fields $\bar K=\mathcal O_K/\mathcal M_K\hookrightarrow \bar D$. By hypothesis every element of $\bar D$ is purely inseparable over $k\!\bar{}$, so the same holds for every element of the subfield $\bar K$. Since $k\!\bar{}$ is perfect, this forces $\bar K=k\!\bar{}$: given $\xi\in\bar K$, pure inseparability gives $m\ge 0$ with $\xi^{p^m}=a\in k\!\bar{}$; perfectness of $k\!\bar{}$ gives $\eta\in k\!\bar{}$ with $\eta^{p^m}=a$; then $(\xi-\eta)^{p^m}=\xi^{p^m}-\eta^{p^m}=0$ in the division ring $\bar D$, so $\xi=\eta\in k\!\bar{}$. (This is precisely the \"in particular\" clause of lemma_183, whose standing hypotheses — henselian discretely valued base with perfect residue field, $K/k$ finite Galois — are satisfied; lemma_183 also asserts $\bar K/k\!\bar{}$ is Galois, which is consistent with, and here subsumed by, $\bar K=k\!\bar{}$.)

**Step 2: $K/k$ is totally ramified.** Apply lemma_96 to the finite Galois extension $K/k$ (applicable because $k$ is henselian discretely valued): $[K:k]=[w(K^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar K:k\!\bar{}]$. By Step 1 the second factor is $1$, and $[K:k]=p$, so the ramification index is $e=[w(K^\times):v(k^\times)]=p$ while the residue degree is $f=1$. Thus $K/k$ is totally ramified (residue field unchanged and ramification index equal to the degree), with cyclic Galois group of order $p$.

**Step 3: Artin--Schreier generator of $K$.** We now invoke lemma_200 with the extension $K/k$: the field $(k,v)$ is henselian (being complete) discretely valued of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$ and perfect residue field, and $K/k$ is totally ramified Galois with cyclic group of order $p$. Lemma_200 yields an element $z\in K$ with $K=k(z)$ and
\[
z^p-z=c\qquad\text{for some }c\in k\text{ with }v(c)<0\text{ and }p\nmid v(c).
\]
(The valuation on $K$ occurring there is the unique extension of $v$ to $K$, which coincides with $w|_K$ by henselianity, so values computed in $K$ agree with values computed in $D$.) In particular $c\in k^\times$ and $v(c)=w(c)$.

**Step 4: $w(z)<0$.** If $w(z)\ge 0$, then $w(c)=w(z^p-z)\ge\min\{w(z^p),w(z)\}=\min\{p\,w(z),w(z)\}\ge 0$, contradicting $v(c)<0$. Hence $w(z)<0$; also $z\neq 0$ (indeed $z\notin k$, as $K=k(z)\supsetneq k$).

**Step 5: the graded computation.** We apply lemma_163 to $a=z$ and the equation $z^p-z=c\in k$, whose hypotheses are met: $k$ is complete for a discrete valuation of characteristic $p>0$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, and $w(z)<0$. Its conclusion is
\[
p\,w(z)=v(c)<0,\qquad w(z)\in\tfrac1p\mathbb Z,\qquad \mathrm{in}_w(z)^p=\mathrm{in}_v(c)\ \text{ in }\ \mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}.
\]
For completeness we spell out the argument, which is exactly the one in lemma_163: since $w(z)<0$ and $p>1$, one has $(p-1)w(z)<0$, hence $w(z^p)=p\,w(z)<w(z)$. Therefore in the difference $z^p-z=c$ the strictly minimal value is attained by the single term $z^p$, so by the elementary facts (a),(b) above,
\[
w(c)=w(z^p-z)=\min\{w(z^p),w(z)\}=p\,w(z),\qquad
\mathrm{in}_v(c)=\mathrm{in}_w(c)=\mathrm{in}_w(z^p-z)=\mathrm{in}_w(z^p)=\mathrm{in}_w(z)^p.
\]
Since $c\in k^\times$, the element $\mathrm{in}_v(c)$ is a nonzero homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{v(c)}\subseteq\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}$.

**Step 6: verification of the required properties.** Write $v(c)=-n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and $p\nmid n$ (possible by Step 3). Set
\[
y:=\mathrm{in}_w(z)\in \mathrm{gr}_w(D)_\delta,\qquad \delta:=w(z).
\]
Then:
\begin{itemize}
\item $y$ is a well-defined nonzero homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$, because $z\in D^\times$.
\item By Step 5, $p\delta=p\,w(z)=v(c)=-n$, so $\delta=-n/p\in\tfrac1p\mathbb Z=\tfrac1p v(k^\times)$. Since $p\nmid n$, $n/p\notin\mathbb Z$, hence $\delta\notin\mathbb Z=v(k^\times)$. Thus $\delta\in \tfrac1p v(k^\times)\setminus v(k^\times)$, as required.
\item By Step 5, $y^p=\mathrm{in}_w(z)^p=\mathrm{in}_v(c)$, which is a nonzero element of $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{v(c)}=\mathrm{gr}(k)_{p\delta}$.
\end{itemize}
This is exactly the conclusion of the lemma. (The restriction $p>2$ is used only through the hypotheses of lemma_200 and lemma_163, both of which are satisfied.)

lemma_209.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. If $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^2$, then either $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$, or the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is annihilated by $p$.
lemma_209.proof:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, and suppose we are given a $k$-algebra isomorphism $\varphi:(L,G,c)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }D$, where $G$ is a group of order $p^{2}$ and $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ (i.e. $L$ is etale over $k$ with $\dim_k L=|G|=p^{2}$ and $L^{G}=k$, by the definitions recalled in the conjecture). We must show that either $D$ contains a maximal subfield Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$, or $p[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$.

Step 1: Classification of the groups of order $p^{2}$.
Since $G$ is a finite $p$-group, its centre $Z(G)$ is nontrivial: indeed, by the class equation $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i [G:C_G(x_i)]$, where the sum runs over representatives of the non-central conjugacy classes, and each index $[G:C_G(x_i)]$ is divisible by $p$ (because $C_G(x_i)$ properly contains $Z(G)$-central elements, so $C_G(x_i)\neq G$ and $[G:C_G(x_i)]>1$ divides $|G|=p^{2}$). Hence $p$ divides $|G|-|Z(G)|$, so $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$; in particular $|Z(G)|\in\{p,p^{2}\}$.
If $|Z(G)|=p$, then $G/Z(G)$ has order $p$ and is therefore cyclic, say $G/Z(G)=\langle gZ(G)\rangle$. Then every element of $G$ is of the form $g^{i}z$ with $z\in Z(G)$, and for two such elements $g^{i}z$, $g^{j}z'$ we have $g^{i}z\,g^{j}z'=g^{i+j}zz'=g^{j}z'\,g^{i}z$, so $G$ is abelian, contradicting $Z(G)\neq G$. Thus $|Z(G)|=p^{2}$, i.e. $G$ is abelian.
Now, by Lagrange's theorem every element of $G$ has order $1$, $p$ or $p^{2}$. Exactly one of the following holds:
(a) $G$ contains an element of order $p^{2}$; then $G$ is cyclic, $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$;
(b) every element of $G$ has order dividing $p$.
