By lemma_96 applied to the henselian discretely valued field $(k,v)$ and the finite Galois extension $L/k$, $[L:k]=[w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]\,[\bar L:\bar k]$, hence $p^2=1\cdot[\bar L:\bar k]$, so $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2=\deg\bar D$. By (F4), $\bar L$ is a maximal subfield of $\bar D$.

Galois property of the residue. By lemma_183 (henselian discretely valued base with perfect residue field, $L/k$ finite Galois), $\bar L/\bar k$ is a finite Galois extension. Since $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$, the group $\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ is a group of order $p^2$.

Conclusion of the direction. Apply lemma_106 to the central simple $\bar k$-algebra $\bar D$ of degree $p^2$ and the maximal subfield $\bar L$ which is Galois over $\bar k$: there is a map $\bar c:\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)\times\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)\to\bar L^{\times}$ such that $\bar D\cong\bigoplus_{\bar g}\bar L\,u_{\bar g}$ with $u_{\bar g}\lambda=\bar g(\lambda)u_{\bar g}$ and $u_{\bar g}u_{\bar h}=\bar c(\bar g,\bar h)u_{\bar g\bar h}$. Thus $\bar D$ is a crossed product over $\bar k$ for the group $\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ of order $p^2$.

(In fact the group can be taken to be $G$ itself: the reduction map $\rho:\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\to\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ is defined because $w\circ\sigma=w$ for every $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ (uniqueness of the extension of $v$ to $L$, by (F1)); it is injective — choose $\alpha\in\mathcal O_L$ with $\bar\alpha$ generating $\bar L/\bar k$, then $k(\alpha)$ has residue field containing $\bar k(\bar\alpha)=\bar L$, so by (F3) $[k(\alpha):k]\ge p^2=[L:k]$, i.e.\ $L=k(\alpha)$; $\alpha$ is integral over $\mathcal O_k$ (as $\mathcal O_D$ is contained in a finitely generated $\mathcal O_k$-module and $\mathcal O_k$ is noetherian), so its minimal polynomial $g\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ satisfies $\bar g(\bar\alpha)=0$, whence $\bar g=\bar f$ with $\bar f$ the minimal polynomial of $\bar\alpha$, of degree $p^2$; $\bar f$ is separable, so by (F2) applied in the henselian field $L$ every root of $\bar f$ is the residue of a root of $g$ in $L$, and since $g$ has exactly $p^2$ roots in $L$ (Galois, $L=k(\alpha)$) and $\bar f$ exactly $p^2$ distinct roots, distinct roots of $g$ have distinct residues; thus $\rho(\sigma)=\mathrm{id}$ forces $\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha$, $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$) and both groups have order $p^2$, so $\rho$ is an isomorphism.)

=== Direction ($\Leftarrow$) ===
Assume $\bar D\cong(\bar L_0,G',\bar c)$ is a crossed product over $\bar k$ for a group $G'$ of order $p^2$. By lemma_133 applied over $\bar k$ (with $\bar D$ a central division $\bar k$-algebra of degree $p^2$), $\bar L_0$ is a field and its image $\bar L\subset\bar D$ is a maximal subfield which is Galois over $\bar k$ with group $G'$; so $[\bar L:\bar k]=p^2$ and $\bar L/\bar k$ is Galois of degree $p^2$.

Step 1: a monic polynomial with the right reduction. Since $\bar k$ is perfect, $\bar L/\bar k$ is separable; choose a primitive element $\bar\alpha\in\bar L$ with $\bar L=\bar k(\bar\alpha)$, and let $\bar f\in\bar k[T]$ be its minimal polynomial: $\bar f$ is monic, irreducible, separable, of degree $p^2$, and it splits completely in $\bar L$ (because $\bar L/\bar k$ is Galois, hence is the splitting field of $\bar f$), with $p^2$ distinct roots. Lift $\bar f$ to a monic polynomial $f\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ of degree $p^2$.

Step 2: $f$ has a root in $D$. Choose $b\in\mathcal O_D$ lifting $\bar\alpha$ (possible by surjectivity of $\mathcal O_D\twoheadrightarrow\bar D$). Since the residue map is a ring homomorphism and $f$ lifts $\bar f$, $\overline{f(b)}=\bar f(\bar\alpha)=0$, so $w(f(b))>0$ (or $f(b)=0$, in which case $b$ is already a root and we put $a=b$ below). Also $\overline{f'(b)}=\bar f'(\bar\alpha)\ne0$, because $\bar f$ is separable so $\bar f\nmid\bar f'$ and $\bar\alpha$ is a simple root; hence $w(f'(b))=0$. Thus $w(f(b))>0=2w(f'(b))$. Let $R=k[b]$: this is a subring of the division ring $D$ generated over the centre $k$ by one algebraic element, hence a commutative finite-dimensional domain over $k$, i.e.\ a field. By (F1), $(R,w|_R)$ is henselian, and $f\in\mathcal O_k[T]\subseteq\mathcal O_R[T]$. By (F2) there is a root $a\in\mathcal O_R\subseteq\mathcal O_D$ of $f$ with $w(a-b)>0$, so $\bar a=\bar b=\bar\alpha$.

Step 3: $f$ is irreducible and $k(a)$ is a maximal subfield. If $f=gh$ with $g,h\in k[T]$ monic of positive degree, then the roots of $g$ are roots of $f$, which are integral over $\mathcal O_k$ (as $f$ is monic in $\mathcal O_k[T]$ and $\mathcal O_k$ is a DVR, hence integrally closed); the coefficients of $g$ are symmetric polynomials in some of these roots, hence integral over $\mathcal O_k$ and contained in $k$, so in $\mathcal O_k$; thus $g,h\in\mathcal O_k[T]$ and $\bar f=\bar g\bar h$ is a factorisation into monic polynomials of positive degree, contradicting the irreducibility of $\bar f$. Hence $f$ is irreducible and $[k(a):k]=\deg f=p^2=\deg D$. By (F4), $k(a)$ is a maximal subfield of $D$.

Step 4: the residue field of $k(a)$ is $\bar L$. Put $E=k(a)$, with valuation $w|_E$, henselian by (F1). Since $\bar a=\bar\alpha$, the residue field $\bar E$ contains $\bar k(\bar\alpha)=\bar L$, so by (F3) $p^2=[\bar L:\bar k]\le[\bar E:\bar k]\le[E:k]=p^2$; hence $\bar E=\bar L$ and $[\bar E:\bar k]=[E:k]=p^2$.

Step 5: $E/k$ is Galois. First, $f$ is separable: $f'\ne0$ because $\overline{f'}=\bar f'\ne0$, and $f$ irreducible of degree $>1$ gives $\gcd(f,f')=1$. Next, let $\bar\beta$ be any of the $p^2$ distinct roots of $\bar f$ in $\bar L=\bar E$. Choose $c\in\mathcal O_E$ with $\bar c=\bar\beta$; then $\overline{f(c)}=\bar f(\bar\beta)=0$ gives $w(f(c))>0$, and $\overline{f'(c)}=\bar f'(\bar\beta)\ne0$ gives $w(f'(c))=0$. By (F2) applied in the henselian field $E$, $f$ has a root $\beta\in\mathcal O_E$ with $w(\beta-c)>0$, i.e.\ $\bar\beta=\beta$'s residue. Distinct $\bar\beta$'s therefore give distinct roots $\beta\in E$, so $f$ has at least $p^2$ distinct roots in $E$; as $\deg f=p^2$, $f$ splits in $E$ into $p^2$ distinct linear factors. Thus $E=k(a)$ is the splitting field over $k$ of the separable polynomial $f$, so $E/k$ is Galois with $|\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)|=[E:k]=p^2$.

(Moreover $\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)\xrightarrow{\ \rho\ }\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$ is an isomorphism: the argument of Step 5 shows the $p^2$ roots of $f$ in $E$ have the $p^2$ distinct residues which are the roots of $\bar f$, so distinct roots have distinct residues; if $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$ reduces to the identity then $\sigma(a)$ is a root of $f$ with residue $\bar\alpha=\bar a$, whence $\sigma(a)=a$ and $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$; both groups have order $p^2$.)

Step 6: conclusion. Apply lemma_106 to the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^2$ and the maximal subfield $E=k(a)$, which is Galois over $k$ with group $\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$ of order $p^2$: there exists $c:\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)\times\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)\to E^{\times}$ with $D\cong\bigoplus_{g}E\,u_g$, $u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)u_g$, $u_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}$. Hence $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(E,\mathrm{Gal}(E/k),c)$ for the group $\mathrm{Gal}(E/k)$ of order $p^2$.

Combining the two directions gives the claimed equivalence. (The proof in fact shows the stronger statement that the group of order $p^2$ may be taken the same on both sides, via the reduction isomorphism $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(\bar L/\bar k)$.)

lemma_223.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ and perfect residue field $\bar k$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ with valuation $w$ extending $v$, and suppose $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$ and that the residue division ring of $D$ is $\bar k$. Then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_223.proof:
We argue by contradiction. Suppose $D\cong (L,G,c)$ as $k$-algebras for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, where $L$ is a $G$-Galois $k$-algebra (i.e. $\dim_k L=|G|=p^{2}$, $L$ is etale over $k$, with $G$ acting by $k$-automorphisms and $L^{G}=k$).

Step 1: $D$ contains a maximal subfield Galois over $k$ with group $G$.
Since $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $n=p^{2}$ and is isomorphic to the crossed product $(L,G,c)$ with $|G|=n$, Spark's lemma_133 applies: $L$ is a field, and its image (which we also denote by $L$) is a maximal subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\cong G$. In particular $[L:k]=|G|=p^{2}>1$.

Step 2: $k$ is henselian.
The field $k$ is complete for the discrete valuation $v$; a complete valued field satisfies Hensel's lemma (given monic $f\in\mathcal O_{k}[T]$ and a simple root $\bar a$ of $\bar f\in\bar k[T]$, the Newton iteration $a_{n+1}=a_{n}-f(a_{n})/f'(a_{n})$, starting at any lift $a_{0}$ of $\bar a$, is defined because $v(f'(a_{0}))=v(f'(a_{n}))$ stays $0$ while $v(f(a_{n+1}))\ge 2v(f(a_{n}))\to\infty$, so $(a_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to a root of $f$ lifting $\bar a$). Hence $(k,v)$ is henselian, as required for the application of lemma_96 below.

Step 3: the residue field of $L$ equals $\bar k$.
Let $\mathcal O_{D}=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}\cup\{0\}$ and $\mathfrak M_{D}=\{x\in D:w(x)>0\}\cup\{0\}$. Since $w$ is a valuation on the division ring $D$ (so $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$ and $w(x+y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$), $\mathfrak M_{D}$ is a two-sided ideal of $\mathcal O_{D}$ and is exactly the set of non-units of $\mathcal O_{D}$ (an element $x\neq 0$ of $\mathcal O_{D}$ is a unit iff $w(x)=0$, because $w(x^{-1})=-w(x)$); thus $\bar D=\mathcal O_{D}/\mathfrak M_{D}$ is the residue division ring.
Set $\mathcal O_{L}:=\mathcal O_{D}\cap L$ and $\mathfrak M_{L}:=\mathfrak M_{D}\cap L$. For every $x\in L^{\times}$ either $w(x)\ge 0$ or $w(x^{-1})\ge 0$, so $\mathcal O_{L}$ is a valuation ring of $L$; it is the valuation ring of the restricted valuation $w|_{L}$, and its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak M_{L}$. Hence the residue field of $L$ is $\bar L=\mathcal O_{L}/\mathfrak M_{L}$.
The natural map $\iota:\bar L\to\bar D$, $x\bmod\mathfrak M_{L}\mapsto x\bmod\mathfrak M_{D}$, is a well-defined ring homomorphism, and it is injective: if $x\in\mathcal O_{L}$ maps to $0$ in $\bar D$, then $x\in\mathfrak M_{D}\cap\mathcal O_{L}=\mathfrak M_{L}$, so $x$ is $0$ in $\bar L$. Thus $\bar L$ embeds as a sub-division ring of $\bar D$.
Because $k\subseteq L\subseteq D$ and $w$ extends $v$, we have $\mathcal O_{k}=\mathcal O_{D}\cap k$ and $\mathfrak M_{k}=\mathfrak M_{D}\cap k$, so the residue inclusions give $\bar k\subseteq\bar L\subseteq\bar D$. By hypothesis the residue division ring of $D$ is $\bar D=\bar k$ (the natural map $\bar k\to\bar D$ is an isomorphism). Therefore $\bar L=\bar k$, and consequently $[\bar L:\bar k]=1$.

Step 4: the value group of $L$ equals $v(k^{\times})$.
Since $k\subseteq L$, $v(k^{\times})=w(k^{\times})\subseteq w(L^{\times})$; since $L\subseteq D$, $w(L^{\times})\subseteq w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$ by hypothesis. Hence $w(L^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$ and $[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]=1$.

Step 5: contradiction via the fundamental (defect-free) equality.
$(k,v)$ is henselian discretely valued with residue field $\bar k$, and $L/k$ is a finite Galois extension endowed with the valuation $w|_{L}$ extending $v$ and residue field $\bar L$. Spark's lemma_96 therefore gives
$$[L:k]=[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times)}]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k].$$
Substituting the values from Steps 3 and 4 yields $[L:k]=1\cdot 1=1$, i.e. $L=k$. This contradicts Step 1, which gave $[L:k]=p^{2}\ge 9>1$.

The contradiction shows that no such crossed product structure exists: $D$ is not isomorphic to $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.

(Remark on what was used: the only properties of the valuation needed are $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$ and $\bar D=\bar k$, which force every subfield of $D$ to have trivial ramification and trivial residue extension; since finite Galois extensions of the henselian field $k$ are defectless, $D$ contains no non-trivial finite Galois subextension at all, whereas a $G$-crossed product structure on a division algebra of degree $|G|$ would supply one. The hypotheses $p>2$ and $\deg D=p^{2}$ enter only through $|G|=p^{2}>1$.)

lemma_225.statement: Let $p>2$ be a prime and let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p$. Fix an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $k$ and let $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subset\Omega$ denote the subfield with $p^{2}$ elements. For $c\in k$, let $K\subset\Omega$ be the splitting field of $T^{p^{2}}-T-c$ and let $k_{0}=k\cap\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$. Then for any root $z$ the roots of $T^{p^{2}}-T-c$ are exactly the elements $z+a$ with $a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and the map $\sigma\mapsto(\sigma(z)-z,\,\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}})$ embeds $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ into the semidirect product $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\rtimes\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$, where $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$ acts on the additive group of $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$. In particular, if an element $z$ satisfies $z^{p^{2}}-z\in k$, then $k(z)/k$ is not a Galois extension with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_225.proof:
We work entirely inside the fixed algebraic closure $\Omega$, and we write $\wp(T)=T^{p^{2}}-T$ and $f(T)=T^{p^{2}}-T-c$.

**Step 1. $\wp$ is an additive separable polynomial whose zero set is $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$**

(a) *Additivity.* In characteristic $p$ one has $(x+y)^{p}=x^{p}+y^{p}$ (all intermediate binomial coefficients $\binom{p}{i}$, $0<i<p$, are divisible by $p$); applying this twice gives $(x+y)^{p^{2}}=x^{p^{2}}+y^{p^{2}}$ for all $x,y\in\Omega$. Hence $\wp(x+y)=\wp(x)+\wp(y)$; in particular $\wp(-y)=-\wp(y)$ and $\wp(0)=0$.

(b) *Separability.* $\wp'(T)=p^{2}T^{p^{2}-1}-1=-1\neq 0$, so $\wp$ has no repeated root in $\Omega$; since $\Omega$ is algebraically closed, $\wp$ has exactly $p^{2}$ distinct roots in $\Omega$.

(c) *The roots form a subfield.* Let $Z=\{x\in\Omega:\wp(x)=0\}$. By (a), $Z$ is closed under subtraction, so it is an additive subgroup. If $x,y\in Z$ then $x^{p^{2}}=x$ and $y^{p^{2}}=y$, so $(xy)^{p^{2}}=x^{p^{2}}y^{p^{2}}=xy$, i.e. $xy\in Z$; also $1\in Z$, and for $x\in Z$, $x\neq0$, $(x^{-1})^{p^{2}}=(x^{p^{2}})^{-1}=x^{-1}$, so $x^{-1}\in Z$. Thus $Z$ is a subfield of $\Omega$, and by (b) it has exactly $p^{2}$ elements.

(d) *Uniqueness.* Any subfield of $\Omega$ with $p^{2}$ elements has multiplicative group of order $p^{2}-1$, so every one of its non-zero elements satisfies $T^{p^{2}-1}-1=0$, and $0$ satisfies it trivially; hence such a subfield is contained in $Z$, and by cardinality it equals $Z$. So $Z=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ is the unique subfield of $\Omega$ with $p^{2}$ elements. As an $\mathbb{F}_{p}$-vector space it has dimension $2$, and its additive group is elementarily abelian of exponent $p$: $p\cdot a=0$ for all $a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{2}$.

**Step 2. The roots of $f$ and the description $K=k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$**

Let $z\in\Omega$ with $\wp(z)=c$, i.e. $f(z)=0$. For $a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, additivity (Step 1a) and $\wp(a)=0$ (Step 1d) give $\wp(z+a)=\wp(z)+\wp(a)=c$, so every $z+a$ is a root of $f$. The $p^{2}$ elements $z+a$ ($a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$) are pairwise distinct ($z+a=z+b\Rightarrow a=b$), and $\deg f=p^{2}$, so
$$\{\text{roots of }f\}=z+\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=\{z+a:a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\}.$$
This proves the first assertion of the lemma.

The splitting field is $K=k(\{z+a:a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\})$. Since $z=z+0$ is among the generators, $k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})\supseteq K$ is immediate in one direction: $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq K$ because $a=(z+a)-z\in K$ for every $a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and $z\in K$, so $k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})\subseteq K$; conversely every $z+a$ lies in $k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$, so $K\subseteq k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$. Hence
$$K=k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})=k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}(z).$$
Since $f'=\,-1\neq0$, $f$ is separable, so $K/k$ is a Galois extension (splitting field of a separable polynomial).

**Step 3. Automorphisms preserve $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and $k_{0}$**

Let $k_{0}=k\cap\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$. This is a subfield of $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ containing the prime field $\mathbb{F}_{p}$; because $[\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:\mathbb{F}_{p}]=2$ is prime, $k_{0}$ is either $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ or $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$. In either case $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0}$ is a finite Galois (indeed cyclic, generated by the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^{p}$) extension of degree $[\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k_{0}]\in\{1,2\}$: this is the standard structure theorem for finite fields (finite extensions of finite fields are Galois and cyclic, generated by a power of the Frobenius).

Let $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$. The field $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ is characterized intrinsically inside $\Omega$ as $\{x\in\Omega:x^{p^{2}}=x\}$ (Step 1d), so $\sigma(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and since $\sigma$ fixes $k$ pointwise it fixes $k_{0}=k\cap\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ pointwise. Thus restriction gives a well-defined homomorphism
$$\mathrm{res}:\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)\longrightarrow \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0}),\qquad \sigma\longmapsto\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}.$$
Moreover, since $\sigma$ fixes the coefficients of $f$, $\sigma(z)$ is again a root of $f$; by Step 2 there is a unique element $a_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ with $\sigma(z)=z+a_{\sigma}$.

**Step 4. $\Phi$ is a well-defined injective homomorphism into the semidirect product**

Let $G=\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$, which acts on the additive group of $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ by field automorphisms (each $\varepsilon\in G$ satisfies $\varepsilon(a+b)=\varepsilon(a)+\varepsilon(b)$, so the action is by group automorphisms of $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)$). Form the semidirect product $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\rtimes G$ with multiplication
$$(a,\varepsilon)\,(b,\delta)=(a+\varepsilon(b),\ \varepsilon\delta);$$
this is a group: the multiplication is associative because $\varepsilon(\delta(c))=(\varepsilon\delta)(c)$, the identity is $(0,\mathrm{id})$, and the inverse of $(a,\varepsilon)$ is $(-\varepsilon^{-1}(a),\varepsilon^{-1})$.

Define
$$\Phi:\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)\longrightarrow (\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\rtimes G,\qquad \Phi(\sigma)=(a_{\sigma},\ \sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}),\quad a_{\sigma}=\sigma(z)-z.$$
*Well-defined:* by Step 3, $a_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ and $\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}\in G$.

*Homomorphism:* for $\sigma,\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$,
$$a_{\sigma\tau}=\sigma\tau(z)-z=\sigma(z+a_{\tau})-z=\sigma(z)-z+\sigma(a_{\tau})=a_{\sigma}+\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}(a_{\tau}),$$
where the key point is that $a_{\tau}\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, so $\sigma(a_{\tau})$ means the action of $\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}\in G$ on $a_{\tau}$. Hence
$$\Phi(\sigma\tau)=\big(a_{\sigma}+\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}(a_{\tau}),\ \sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}\circ\tau|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}\big)=\Phi(\sigma)\,\Phi(\tau).$$

*Injectivity:* if $\Phi(\sigma)=(0,\mathrm{id})$, then $\sigma(z)=z$ and $\sigma$ restricts to the identity on $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$; since $K=k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$ (Step 2) and $\sigma$ already fixes $k$, $\sigma$ is the identity on $K$. So $\ker\Phi=\{\mathrm{id}\}$, and $\Phi$ embeds $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ into $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\rtimes\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$. This proves the embedding assertion of the lemma.

**Step 5. Auxiliary structure: the subextension $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k$, surjectivity of $\mathrm{res}$, and the kernel**

*Claim 5.1.* $[k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k]=[\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k_{0}]\in\{1,2\}$, and restriction induces an isomorphism $\mathrm{Gal}(k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$.

*Proof.* If $k_{0}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, then $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k$, so $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=k$ and both sides are $1$; both Galois groups are trivial and the claim holds. Suppose $k_{0}=\mathbb{F}_{p}$, so $[\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k_{0}]=2$. Choose $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ with $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=k_{0}(\omega)$ (a generator of the cyclic group $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}^{\times}$, which generates $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}=k_{0}$), and let $g\in k_{0}[T]$ be its minimal polynomial, $\deg g=2$. Then $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=k(\omega)$. If $g$ were reducible over $k$, then, being quadratic and separable ($g\mid\wp$, whose derivative is $-1$), it would split as $(T-\alpha)(T-\beta)$ over $k$, and $\omega\in\{\alpha,\beta\}\subseteq k$; then $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=k_{0}(\omega)\subseteq k$, forcing $k_{0}=k\cap\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, a contradiction. So $g$ is irreducible over $k$, giving $[k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k]=[k(\omega):k]=2=[\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k_{0}]$. Its roots are $\omega$ and $\omega^{p}$, both lying in $k(\omega)$, so $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k$ is the splitting field of the separable polynomial $g$, hence Galois of degree $2$. Restriction $\mathrm{Gal}(k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k)\to\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$ is well defined by Step 3 (applied inside $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq\Omega$); it is injective because $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=k(\omega)$ is generated over $k$ by $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and both groups have order $2$, so it is an isomorphism. $\square_{5.1}$

*Claim 5.2.* $\mathrm{res}:\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$ is surjective, with kernel $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$; moreover $\Phi$ maps $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$ injectively as a group into $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\times\{\mathrm{id}\}$, so $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$ is an elementary abelian $p$-group of rank at most $2$.

*Proof.* Let $\varepsilon\in\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$. By Claim 5.1 there is $\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k)$ with $\tau|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}=\varepsilon$. Now $K=k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}(z)$ is the splitting field over $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ of $f$, and $\tau$ fixes $k$, hence $\tau(f)=f$. Let $m\in k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $z$ over $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$; then $m\mid f$, so applying $\tau$ to the coefficients gives $\tau(m)\mid\tau(f)=f$. Choose a root $z'$ of $\tau(m)$ in $K$ (it exists because $f$ splits in $K$). The map $\sum_{i}c_{i}z^{i}\mapsto\sum_{i}\tau(c_{i})(z')^{i}$ is a well-defined field isomorphism $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}(z)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}(z')$, because $m$ is the minimal polynomial of $z$ over $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ and $\tau(m)$ is the minimal polynomial of $z'$ over $\tau(k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})=k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$. Its image has degree $\deg\tau(m)=\deg m=[K:k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}]$ over $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, hence equals $K$. Thus we obtain $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ with $\sigma|_{k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}=\tau$, and $\mathrm{res}(\sigma)=\varepsilon$: surjectivity.

For the kernel: $\sigma\in\ker(\mathrm{res})$ iff $\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}=\mathrm{id}$; since $\sigma$ already fixes $k$, this is equivalent to $\sigma$ fixing $k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ pointwise, i.e. $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$. Finally, if $\sigma,\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$ then $\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}=\mathrm{id}$, so the formula of Step 4 reduces to $a_{\sigma\tau}=a_{\sigma}+a_{\tau}$; hence $\sigma\mapsto a_{\sigma}$ is a group homomorphism $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})\to(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)$, injective by the injectivity of $\Phi$. Since $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/p)^{2}$ by Step 1d, the kernel is an elementary abelian $p$-group of rank $\le2$. $\square_{5.2}$

(Notice that the additive cocycle formula only becomes a genuine homomorphism on $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})$ because there $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ pointwise; in general the twisting by $\sigma|_{\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}}$ is exactly what the semidirect product encodes. Also, since $\Phi(\mathrm{Gal}(K/k))$ projects onto $G$ by Claim 5.2, $\Phi(\mathrm{Gal}(K/k))$ is a subgroup of the semidirect product mapping onto the second factor.)

**Step 6. Proof of the "in particular" for $p>2$**

Let $z\in\Omega$ satisfy $z^{p^{2}}-z=c\in k$, and put $c=\wp(z)$. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $k(z)/k$ is a Galois extension with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$. Then $[k(z):k]=p^{2}$, and $k(z)/k$ is normal.

(6a) *$\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k(z)$ and $K=k(z)$.* The polynomial $f\in k[T]$ is separable and has the root $z\in k(z)$; since $k(z)/k$ is normal and algebraic, every irreducible factor of $f$ over $k$ that has a root in $k(z)$ splits completely in $k(z)$; hence $f$ splits completely in $k(z)$. By Step 2 all elements $z+a$, $a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, are roots of $f$, so $z+a\in k(z)$ for all $a$, and therefore $a=(z+a)-z\in k(z)$ for all $a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, i.e. $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k(z)$. Then $K=k(z,\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}})=k(z)$.

(6b) *$\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k$.* From $k\subseteq k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k(z)$ the tower law gives $[k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k]\mid[k(z):k]=p^{2}$. By Claim 5.1, $[k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k]=[\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k_{0}]\in\{1,2\}$. Since $p>2$ is odd, $p^{2}$ is odd, so the only divisor of $p^{2}$ belonging to $\{1,2\}$ is $1$. Hence $[k\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}:k]=1$, i.e. $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k$ (equivalently $k_{0}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, and $G=\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}/k_{0})$ is trivial).

(6c) *Contradiction.* With $G$ trivial, the embedding of Step 4 reads
$$\mathrm{Gal}(k(z)/k)=\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)\hookrightarrow(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\rtimes\{\mathrm{id}\}\simeq(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{2}.$$
Every element of $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)$ satisfies $p\cdot a=0$, so every element of the target has order dividing $p$. But a cyclic group of order $p^{2}$ contains an element of order $p^{2}>p$, and injective homomorphisms preserve orders. Contradiction. Therefore $k(z)/k$ is not a Galois extension with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$.

**Step 7. Remarks clarifying the two hypotheses (not needed above, but recording the exact scope)**

(a) *Why the semidirect product rather than the additive group.* Without the assumption $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k$ the additive statement is false: take $k=\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with $p$ odd and $c=0$. Then $f=\wp$ splits over $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, so $K=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$ and $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)=\langle x\mapsto x^{p}\rangle\simeq\mathbb{Z}/2$, which cannot embed into the additive group $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)$ of exponent $p$ (odd). The semidirect product of the lemma handles this correctly: here $k_{0}=\mathbb{F}_{p}$, $G\simeq\mathbb{Z}/2$, and $\Phi$ is the inclusion onto the second factor. Under the extra hypothesis $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\subseteq k$ one has $k_{0}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$, $G$ trivial, and the embedding degenerates to $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)\hookrightarrow(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)$, which is the form used in applications.

(b) *Uniform exponent bound, and why $p>2$ is required.* In $(\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}},+)\rtimes G$ every element $\varepsilon\in G$ has order dividing $2$ (as $|G|\le2$), and a direct computation gives, for $(a,\varepsilon)$ in the semidirect product,
$$(a,\varepsilon)^{n}=\Big(\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon^{i}(a),\ \varepsilon^{n}\Big),$$
so for $n=2p$: $\varepsilon^{2p}=\mathrm{id}$, and $\sum_{i=0}^{2p-1}\varepsilon^{i}(a)=2p\cdot a=0$ if $\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}$, while if $\varepsilon$ has order $2$ the sum equals $p\,(a+\varepsilon(a))=0$; both vanish because the characteristic is $p$. Hence the whole semidirect product has exponent dividing $2p$. Since $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ embeds into it, $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ has exponent dividing $2p$, and for odd $p$ one has $p^{2}\nmid 2p$, so $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$ can never be cyclic of order $p^{2}$ (combined with (6a), this gives an alternative proof of Step 6 that does not need the count in (6b)). For $p=2$ this bound is $2p=4=p^{2}$ and the argument breaks down, and indeed the assertion is then false: over $k=\mathbb{F}_{2}$, $T^{4}+T+1$ is irreducible (no root in $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ and not divisible by $T^{2}+T+1$, since $(T^{2}+T+1)(T^{2}+T)=T^{4}+T$), so for a root $z$ one has $z^{4}-z=z^{4}+z=1\in k$ and $k(z)=\mathbb{F}_{16}$ is the splitting field with Galois group $\langle\mathrm{Frob}_{2}\rangle\simeq\mathbb{Z}/4$; note that the generator there is the Frobenius $z\mapsto z^{2}=z+\omega$ (with $\omega=z^{2}-z$ a primitive third root of unity in $\mathbb{F}_{4}$), which has order $4$ precisely because it also acts non-trivially on $\mathbb{F}_{4}$, i.e. because of the semidirect factor, not because of a translation. This is exactly why the hypothesis $p>2$ is imposed.

This completes the proof of all assertions of the lemma. ∎

lemma_226.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ having no Galois extension whose Galois group is cyclic of order $p^{2}$. Then every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ that is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ has its class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ annihilated by $p$; equivalently, a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class has order $p^{2}$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra for any group of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_226.proof:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ with no Galois extension whose Galois group is cyclic of order $p^{2}$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ which is isomorphic as a $k$-algebra to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$, where $G$ is a group of order $p^{2}$ and $L$ is a Galois $G$-algebra over $k$ (so $L$ is \'etale commutative of $k$-dimension $|G|=p^{2}$ with $L^{G}=k$).

We write $[D]\in \mathrm{Br}(k)$ for the Brauer class of $D$, and we prove successively the two assertions in the statement.

**Step 1: $L$ is a field, and its image in $D$ is a maximal subfield Galois over $k$ with group $G$.**
This is exactly the content of the proved lemma \textsf{lemma\_133} (Spark), applied with $n=p^{2}$: since $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $n$ isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ with $|G|=n$ and $L$ a Galois $G$-algebra, $L$ is a field and its image $M\subset D$ under such an isomorphism is a maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$; in particular $\mathrm{Gal}(M/k)\simeq G$ and $[M:k]=|G|=p^{2}=\deg D$. (For orientation, the reason is the following. The structure map $\lambda\mapsto \lambda\cdot 1$ identifies $L$ with a $k$-subalgebra of $(L,G,c)$, because $(L,G,c)=\bigoplus_{g\in G}Lu_{g}$ is a free left $L$-module with basis $\{u_{g}\}$; hence $L$ embeds in the division ring $D$, so $L$ is a domain, and a finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field. Artin's fixed-field theorem then says that a field $L$ with a group $G$ of $k$-automorphisms satisfying $L^{G}=k$ is Galois over $k$ with group $G$ and $[L:k]=|G|$; and $\dim_{k}L=p^{2}=\deg D$ forces maximality.)

**Step 2: group-theoretic classification of $G$.**
We show that every group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ is abelian and isomorphic to $C_{p^{2}}$ or to $C_{p}\times C_{p}$.
(a) $Z(G)\neq 1$: the class equation for the conjugation action of $G$ on itself gives $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_{i}[G:C_{G}(x_{i})]$, where the sum runs over the non-central conjugacy classes and each index $[G:C_{G}(x_{i})]$ is $p$ or $p^{2}$, hence divisible by $p$. Since $|G|=p^{2}$, we get $|Z(G)|\equiv p^{2}\equiv 0 \pmod p$; as $1\in Z(G)$, $|Z(G)|\in\{p,p^{2}\}$.
(b) $Z(G)=G$: if $|Z(G)|=p$, then $G/Z(G)$ has order $p$ and is therefore cyclic, say $G/Z(G)=\langle gZ(G)\rangle$. Every element of $G$ then has the form $g^{i}z$ with $z\in Z(G)$, and for two such elements $g^{i}z_{1},g^{j}z_{2}$ one computes $g^{i}z_{1}\,g^{j}z_{2}=g^{i+j}z_{1}z_{2}=g^{j+i}z_{2}z_{1}=g^{j}z_{2}\,g^{i}z_{1}$, so $G$ is abelian, contradicting $Z(G)\neq G$. Hence $G$ is abelian.
(c) Let $m$ be the maximal order of an element of $G$; $m\mid p^{2}$, so $m\in\{p,p^{2}\}$. If $m=p^{2}$, then $G\simeq C_{p^{2}}$. If $m=p$, every non-identity element has order $p$; choose $b\notin\langle a\rangle$ for an element $a$ of order $p$ (possible since $|\langle a\rangle|=p<p^{2}$). Then $\langle a\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle=1$, $\langle a,b\rangle$ has order $p^{2}$ so equals $G$, and $a,b$ commute because $G$ is abelian; thus $G\simeq C_{p}\times C_{p}$.

**Step 3: case analysis, concluding $p[D]=0$.**
By Step 1, $\mathrm{Gal}(M/k)\simeq G$, so by Step 2 exactly one of the following holds.
*Case 1: $G\simeq C_{p^{2}}$.* Then $M/k$ is a Galois field extension whose Galois group is cyclic of order $p^{2}$, contradicting the hypothesis on $k$. This case therefore cannot occur.
*Case 2: $G\simeq C_{p}\times C_{p}$.* Then $D$ contains a maximal subfield ($M$) that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group isomorphic to $C_{p}\times C_{p}$. By the proved lemma \textsf{lemma\_166} (Spark), applied to the central division $k$-algebra $D$ of degree $p^{2}$, the class $[D]$ is annihilated by $p$; that is, $p[D]=0$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$.
Since Case 1 is excluded by hypothesis and Case 2 gives $p[D]=0$, every central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ that is a crossed product for some group of order $p^{2}$ has its Brauer class annihilated by $p$. This is the first assertion of the lemma.

**Step 4: the second formulation.**
Let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class has order exactly $p^{2}$; in particular $p[D]\neq 0$. If $D$ were isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, Step 3 would give $p[D]=0$, a contradiction. Hence such a $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra for any group of order $p^{2}$.

**Step 5: the two formulations are equivalent.**
Step 3 $\Rightarrow$ Step 4 is the argument just given (a class of order $p^{2}$ is not annihilated by $p$). Conversely, assume the second formulation and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ that is a crossed product for some group of order $p^{2}$. Since $D$ is division, $\mathrm{ind}(D)=\deg(D)=p^{2}$, and the exponent of a central simple algebra always divides its index, so $\mathrm{ord}([D])=\exp(D)$ divides $p^{2}$; thus $\mathrm{ord}([D])\in\{1,p,p^{2}\}$. If $p[D]\neq 0$, then $\mathrm{ord}([D])=p^{2}$, and the second formulation says $D$ is not a crossed product, contradicting the choice of $D$. Therefore $p[D]=0$, which is the first formulation. (This last step uses only the standard formal property $\exp\mid\mathrm{ind}$ of the Brauer group and plays no role in the substantive argument of Steps 1--4, which already establishes the first formulation unconditionally under the hypothesis on $k$.)

Combining Steps 3, 4 and 5, the lemma is proved: under the hypothesis that $k$ has no cyclic Galois extension of degree $p^{2}$, every crossed product division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ has Brauer class of exponent dividing $p$, and equivalently a division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class has order $p^{2}$ is a non-crossed product for every group of order $p^{2}$.

lemma_227.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a valued field of characteristic $p>0$, let $D$ be a division ring containing $k$ and endowed with a valuation $w$ extending $v$, and let $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ be the associated graded ring with $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ viewed as a graded subring. Let $a\in D$ and $c\in k$ satisfy $a^{p}-a=c$. Then either $w(a)\ge 0$, in which case $v(c)\ge 0$ and the residue $\bar a$ of $a$ in the residue division ring satisfies $\bar a^{p}-\bar a=\bar c$, or $w(a)<0$, in which case $v(c)=p\,w(a)<0$ and $\mathrm{in}_w(a)^{p}=\mathrm{in}_v(c)$ as homogeneous elements of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}$.
lemma_227.proof:
We set up notation and prove the required properties of the valuation from the axioms, then treat the two alternatives.

STEP 0 (Conventions). A valuation on a division ring $D$ is a map $w\colon D\to \Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\Gamma$ is a linearly ordered abelian group written additively, such that for all $x,y\in D$: (a) $w(x)=\infty$ iff $x=0$; (b) $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)$; (c) $w(x+y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$; with the conventions $\gamma<\infty$ and $\gamma+\infty=\infty$ for all $\gamma$. "W extends $v$" means $w|_{k}=v$. For $\gamma\in\Gamma$ put $D^{\ge\gamma}=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge\gamma\}$ and $D^{>\gamma}=\{x\in D: w(x)>\gamma\}$ (note $0$ belongs to both), and similarly $k^{\ge\delta},k^{>\delta}$ for $\delta\in v(k^{\times})$, using $v(0)=\infty$. We write $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)=\bigoplus_{\gamma}D^{\ge\gamma}/D^{>\gamma}$ and $\mathrm{gr}(k)=\bigoplus_{\delta}k^{\ge\delta}/k^{>\delta}$, and for $0\ne x\in D$, $\mathrm{in}_w(x)$ denotes the class $x+D^{>w(x)}\in \mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{w(x)}$, and likewise $\mathrm{in}_v$.

STEP 1 (Elementary properties of $w$).
(i) $w(1)=0$: indeed $w(1)=w(1\cdot 1)=w(1)+w(1)$ by (b), and $w(1)\ne\infty$ since $1\ne 0$, so cancellation in $\Gamma$ gives $w(1)=0$. Also $w(x^{-1})=-w(x)$ for $x\ne0$, since $0=w(1)=w(x)+w(x^{-1})$.
(ii) $w(-1)=0$: $2w(-1)=w((-1)^2)=w(1)=0$, and a linearly ordered abelian group is torsion-free (if $\gamma>0$ then $n\gamma>0$ for all $n\ge1$), so $w(-1)=0$. Hence $w(-x)=w((-1)x)=w(-1)+w(x)=w(x)$ for all $x$.
(iii) Strict ultrametric inequality: if $w(x)\ne w(y)$ then $w(x+y)=\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$. Assume $w(x)<w(y)$. From (c) applied to $x=(x+y)-y$ we get $w(x)\ge\min\{w(x+y),w(y)\}$; since $w(y)>w(x)$, this forces $w(x+y)\le w(x)$. Combined with $w(x+y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}=w(x)$ we obtain equality.
(iv) If $\gamma<0$ and $n\ge2$ is an integer then $n\gamma<\gamma$: indeed $(n-1)\gamma<0$ (a positive multiple of a negative element is negative), so $n\gamma=\gamma+(n-1)\gamma<\gamma$. Since $p$ is a prime, $p\ge2$, so $\alpha<0\Rightarrow p\alpha<\alpha$.
(v) The valuation ring and the residue division ring. Set $\mathcal O_w:=D^{\ge0}$ and $M_w:=D^{>0}$.
  ($\alpha$) $\mathcal O_w$ is a subring of $D$: $1\in\mathcal O_w$ because $w(1)=0$; if $x,y\in\mathcal O_w$ then $w(x-y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}\ge0$ by (c), so $x-y\in\mathcal O_w$; and $w(xy)=w(x)+w(y)\ge0$ by (b), so $xy\in\mathcal O_w$.
  ($\beta$) $M_w$ is a two-sided ideal of $\mathcal O_w$. Additivity: if $m,m'\in M_w$ then $w(m-m')\ge\min\{w(m),w(m')\}>0$, so $m-m'\in M_w$; also $0\in M_w$. Absorption: take $o\in\mathcal O_w$ and $m\in M_w$. By (b), $w(om)=w(o)+w(m)$; since $w(o)\ge0$ and $w(m)>0$, their sum is $>0$ in the ordered group $\Gamma$, hence $om\in M_w$. Symmetrically $w(mo)=w(m)+w(o)>0$, so $mo\in M_w$. (This is the direct two-sided verification; no statement of the form $D\cdot M_w\cap\mathcal O_w\subseteq M_w$ is used, and indeed such a statement is false, e.g. $m^{-1}\cdot m=1$ for $m\in M_w$.)
  ($\gamma$) $M_w$ is proper: $1\in\mathcal O_w$ has $w(1)=0$, so $1\notin M_w$.
  ($\delta$) The units of $\mathcal O_w$ are exactly the elements of value $0$. If $w(x)=0$ then $x^{-1}\in D$ has $w(x^{-1})=-w(x)=0$ by (i), so $x^{-1}\in\mathcal O_w$ and $x$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_w$. Conversely, if $x\in\mathcal O_w$ has $w(x)>0$ and were a unit of $\mathcal O_w$ with inverse $y\in\mathcal O_w$, then $0=w(1)=w(x)+w(y)\ge w(x)>0$, a contradiction.
  ($\epsilon$) Consequently every element of $\mathcal O_w\setminus M_w$ is a unit, so $M_w$ is the unique maximal two-sided ideal of $\mathcal O_w$, and the quotient $\overline D:=\mathcal O_w/M_w$ is a division ring: a nonzero element of $\overline D$ has the form $x+M_w$ with $x\in\mathcal O_w\setminus M_w$, which is a unit of $\mathcal O_w$ by ($\delta$), and then $(x+M_w)(x^{-1}+M_w)=1+M_w$ (with $x^{-1}\in\mathcal O_w$ since $w(x^{-1})=0$). The residue map $\rho\colon\mathcal O_w\twoheadrightarrow\overline D$, $x\mapsto\bar x:=x+M_w$, is a surjective ring homomorphism.
  ($\zeta$) Since $k\subset D$ with the same $1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p$, we have $p\cdot 1_D=0$, hence $p\cdot 1_{\overline D}=\rho(p\cdot1_D)=0$; so $\overline D$ has characteristic $p$ as well.
  ($\eta$) Because $w|_k=v$, we have $\mathcal O_w\cap k=k^{\ge0}$ and $M_w\cap k=k^{>0}=\ker(v\text{-residue})$, so $\rho|_{k^{\ge0}}$ factors through the residue field $\bar k=k^{\ge0}/k^{>0}$ and the induced map $\bar k\to\overline D$ is injective: if $x\in k^{\ge0}$ maps to $0$ in $\overline D$ then $v(x)=w(x)>0$, i.e. $x=0$ in $\bar k$. Thus for $c\in k$ with $v(c)\ge0$ the symbol $\bar c$ computed in $\bar k$ is identified with $\rho(c)\in\overline D$; we use this identification below.
  ($\theta$) The graded multiplication is well defined: for $x\in D^{\ge\gamma}$, $y\in D^{\ge\delta}$ one has $xy\in D^{\ge\gamma+\delta}$ by (b); if $x'=x+m$ with $m\in D^{>\gamma}$ and $y'=y+n$ with $n\in D^{>\delta}$, then $x'y'=xy+xn+my+mn$ with $w(xn)\ge\gamma+w(n)>\gamma+\delta$, $w(my)\ge w(m)+\delta>\gamma+\delta$ and $w(mn)>\gamma+\delta$, so $x'y'-xy\in D^{>\gamma+\delta}$. Likewise the inclusion $k\hookrightarrow D$ induces an injective graded ring homomorphism $\mathrm{gr}(k)\to\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$: in degree $\delta$, its kernel is $\{x\in k^{\ge\delta}: w(x)>\delta\}=\{x\in k: v(x)>\delta\}$, which is $0$ in $\mathrm{gr}(k)_\delta$. Hence writing $\mathrm{in}_v(c)$ for an element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}$ is legitimate.

STEP 2 (The dichotomy). The value $w(a)$ lies in $\Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$, which is linearly ordered with $\gamma<\infty$ for all $\gamma$. Hence exactly one of $w(a)\ge0$ (this includes $a=0$, where $w(a)=\infty\ge0$) and $w(a)<0$ holds. We treat both.

STEP 3 (Case $w(a)\ge0$). Then $a\in\mathcal O_w$ and $a^p\in\mathcal O_w$. Since $c=a^p-a$ and $w(a^p)=p\,w(a)\ge0$ by (b), the ultrametric inequality (c) gives $w(c)\ge\min\{w(a^p),w(a)\}\ge0$. As $c\in k$, $v(c)=w(c)\ge0$ (if $c=0$ then $v(c)=\infty\ge0$, which is permitted). Thus $\bar a=\rho(a)$ and $\bar c=\rho(c)$ are defined, and because $\rho$ is a ring homomorphism,
$$\bar a^{\,p}-\bar a=\rho(a)^p-\rho(a)=\rho(a^p-a)=\rho(c)=\bar c,$$
where the identification of $\rho(c)$ with the residue of $c$ in $\bar k$ is that of Step 1(v,$\zeta$). This is the first alternative.

STEP 4 (Case $w(a)<0$). Put $\alpha:=w(a)<0$; then $a\ne0$.
(a) By multiplicativity (b), $w(a^p)=p\,\alpha$, and by Step 1(iv) one has $p\alpha<\alpha$.
(b) $w(-a)=w(-1)+w(a)=v(-1)+\alpha=0+\alpha=\alpha$, using $w|_k=v$ and Step 1(ii) (which gives $v(-1)=0$ because $(-1)^2=1$ and $\Gamma$ is torsion-free).
(c) Write $c=a^p-a=a^p+(-a)$. The two summands have distinct values $p\alpha\ne\alpha$ by (a) and (b), so the strict ultrametric identity of Step 1(iii) applies and yields $w(c)=\min\{p\alpha,\alpha\}=p\alpha$. In particular $w(c)\ne\infty$, so $c\ne0$, and since $c\in k^{\times}$ we get $v(c)=w(c)=p\,w(a)<0$.
(d) Identity of initial forms. Both $a^p$ and $c$ are nonzero and satisfy $w(a^p)=p\alpha=v(c)=w(c)$, so both define nonzero homogeneous elements in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{p\alpha}=D^{\ge p\alpha}/D^{>p\alpha}$. By the definition of the graded product in Step 1(v,$\theta$), multiplying $\mathrm{in}_w(a)=a+D^{>\alpha}$ by itself $p$ times gives
$$\mathrm{in}_w(a)^p=\underbrace{(a+D^{>\alpha})\cdots(a+D^{>\alpha})}_{p}=a^p+D^{>p\alpha}.$$
On the other hand $\mathrm{in}_v(c)=c+k^{>v(c)}\in\mathrm{gr}(k)_{v(c)}$, and its image in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}=D^{\ge v(c)}/D^{>v(c)}$ under the injective map of Step 1(v,$\theta$) is $c+D^{>v(c)}=c+D^{>p\alpha}$, because $v(c)=p\alpha$.
Finally, from $a^p-a=c$ we have $a^p-c=a$, and $w(a^p-c)=w(a)=\alpha>p\alpha$ by (a). Hence $a^p-c\in D^{>p\alpha}$, so the two classes coincide in $D^{\ge p\alpha}/D^{>p\alpha}$:
$$\mathrm{in}_w(a)^p=a^p+D^{>p\alpha}=c+D^{>p\alpha}=\mathrm{in}_v(c)$$
as homogeneous elements of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{p\alpha}=\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}$. This is the second alternative.

STEP 5 (Conclusion). Steps 3 and 4 cover both possible signs of $w(a)$ (Step 2), and establish in the first case that $v(c)\ge0$ and $\bar a^{\,p}-\bar a=\bar c$ in $\overline D$, and in the second case that $v(c)=p\,w(a)<0$ and $\mathrm{in}_w(a)^p=\mathrm{in}_v(c)$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{v(c)}$. This completes the proof.

lemma_228.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is not annihilated by $p$. If $D$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, then $D$ contains an element $x$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^{p}\in k$.
lemma_228.proof:
Let $\varphi:(L,G,c)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }D$ be a $k$-algebra isomorphism, and, to lighten notation, identify $D$ with $A:=(L,G,c)=\bigoplus_{g\in G}Lu_g$ through $\varphi$; thus $u_g\lambda=g(\lambda)u_g$ and $u_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}$ for all $\lambda\in L$, $g,h\in G$, and $\{u_g\}_{g\in G}$ is an $L$-basis of $A$. Since $A\cong D$ is a division ring, every nonzero element of $A$ is invertible; in particular each $u_g\neq0$ is invertible.

Step 1: $L$ is a Galois maximal subfield of $D$ with group $G$.  Apply lemma_133 (Spark) with $n=p^{2}$: since $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ with $|G|=p^{2}$, $L$ is a field and its image in $D$ is a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$. Hence $[L:k]=|G|=p^{2}$ and $L^{G}=k$.

Step 2: $G$ is abelian, so $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$ or $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$.  Write the class equation for the conjugation action of $G$ on itself: $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i[G:C_G(g_i)]$, where $g_i$ runs over representatives of the conjugacy classes with more than one element. Each index $[G:C_G(g_i)]$ divides $|G|=p^{2}$ and is $>1$ (it equals $1$ exactly for central elements), so each is divisible by $p$. As $p\mid |G|=p^{2}$, the class equation gives $p\mid|Z(G)|$, so $|Z(G)|\in\{p,p^{2}\}$. If $|Z(G)|=p$, then $G/Z(G)$ has order $p$ and is therefore cyclic, generated by some $gZ(G)$; every element of $G$ is then of the form $g^{i}z$ with $z\in Z(G)$, and for two such elements $g^{i}z\cdot g^{i'}z'=g^{i+i'}zz'=g^{i'}z'\cdot g^{i}z$ (centrality of $z,z'$ and commutativity of powers of $g$), so $G$ would be abelian, forcing $|Z(G)|=p^{2}$, a contradiction. Hence $|Z(G)|=p^{2}$ and $G$ is abelian. By the structure theorem for finite abelian groups, $G\cong C_{p^{2}}$ or $G\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}$ (the only abelian groups of order $p^{2}$).

Step 3: the case $G\cong C_p\times C_p$ is impossible.  In that case Step 1 gives a maximal subfield of $D$ that is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $C_p\times C_p$, and lemma_166 (Spark) then implies that the class $[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is annihilated by $p$, contradicting the hypothesis on $D$. Therefore $G$ is cyclic of order $p^{2}$; fix a generator $\sigma$, so that $L/k$ is cyclic Galois of degree $p^{2}$ with generator $\sigma$, and $L^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=L^{G}=k$.

Step 4: the powers of $v:=u_{\sigma}$ are $L$-linearly independent, up to exponent $p^{2}-1$.  We claim by induction on $i\geq 1$ that $v^{i}=\gamma_i u_{\sigma^{i}}$ with $\gamma_i\in L^{\times}$, where $\gamma_1=1$ and $\gamma_{i+1}=\gamma_i\,c(\sigma^{i},\sigma)$. Indeed $v^{1}=u_{\sigma}$ gives $\gamma_1=1$, and if $v^{i}=\gamma_i u_{\sigma^{i}}$ then $v^{i+1}=\gamma_i u_{\sigma^{i}}u_{\sigma}=\gamma_i c(\sigma^{i},\sigma)u_{\sigma^{i+1}}$, with $\gamma_i c(\sigma^{i},\sigma)\in L^{\times}$ because $c$ takes values in $L^{\times}$. Now take $0\le i\le p^{2}-1$: since $\sigma$ has exact order $p^{2}$ in $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ (the action is faithful because $L/k$ is Galois with group $G=\langle\sigma\rangle$ of order $p^{2}$), the group elements $1,\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{p^{2}-1}$ are pairwise distinct, so the summands $Lu_{\sigma^{i}}$ are pairwise distinct members of the direct-sum decomposition $A=\bigoplus_{g\in G}Lu_g$. If $\sum_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}a_i v^{i}=0$ with $a_i\in L$, then $a_0\cdot 1+\sum_{i\ge1}a_i\gamma_i u_{\sigma^{i}}=0$ is a relation whose summands lie in pairwise distinct direct summands (using $1\in Lu_1$); hence each summand vanishes, giving $a_0=0$ and $a_i\gamma_i=0$ for $i\ge1$, so $a_i=0$ since $\gamma_i\in L^{\times}$. Thus $1,v,\dots,v^{p^{2}-1}$ are $L$-linearly independent. (Note that no minimal-polynomial argument is used here: independence comes purely from the direct-sum decomposition, exactly as required.)

Step 5: the parameter $b:=v^{p^{2}}$ lies in $k^{\times}$.  First, $u_1\in L^{\times}$: from $u_1u_1=c(1,1)u_1$ with $u_1\neq0$, multiplying on the right by $u_1^{-1}$ in the division ring $A$ gives $u_1=c(1,1)\in L^{\times}$; hence $Lu_1=L\cdot 1_A$. By Step 4 with $i=p^{2}$ and $\sigma^{p^{2}}=1$, we get $b:=v^{p^{2}}=\gamma_{p^{2}}u_{1}=\gamma_{p^{2}}c(1,1)\in L^{\times}$, where $\gamma_{p^{2}}=c(\sigma,\sigma)c(\sigma^{2},\sigma)\cdots c(\sigma^{p^{2}-1},\sigma)\in L^{\times}$. Next, conjugation by $v$ restricts to $\sigma$ on $L$: indeed $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in L$ and $v$ is invertible, so $v\lambda v^{-1}=\sigma(\lambda)$. Since $v$ commutes with its own power $b=v^{p^{2}}$, we obtain $\sigma(b)=v b v^{-1}=b$, i.e. $b\in L^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=k$; together with $b\in L^{\times}$ this gives $b\in k^{\times}$.

Step 6: $D$ is the cyclic algebra $(L,\sigma,b)$.  The $L$-span $\sum_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}Lv^{i}$ is a direct sum of $p^{2}$ one-dimensional $L$-lines by Step 4, hence has $k$-dimension $p^{2}\,[L:k]=p^{2}\cdot p^{2}=p^{4}$. Since $D$ is a division algebra of degree $p^{2}$, $\dim_k D=(p^{2})^{2}=p^{4}$; so the span equals all of $D$, and by construction the defining relations are $v^{p^{2}}=b\in k^{\times}$ and $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in L$. Thus $D\cong\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}Lv^{i}$ is exactly the cyclic algebra attached to the cyclic Galois extension $L/k$ of degree $p^{2}$, generator $\sigma$, and parameter $b\in k^{\times}$.

Step 7: $x:=v^{p}$ is $p$-central.  By lemma_cyclic_p2_has_pcentral (Spark), applied to the cyclic Galois extension $L/k$ of degree $p^{2}$ with generator $\sigma$, the parameter $b\in k^{\times}$, and the algebra $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}Lv^{i}$ with $v^{p^{2}}=b$ and $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$, one has $v^{p}\notin k$ and $(v^{p})^{p}\in k$. Setting $x=v^{p}$ gives the required element. For completeness we verify these two facts directly inside $D$. (i) $x^{p}=v^{p^{2}}=b\in k$. (ii) $x\notin k$: since $\sigma$ has exact order $p^{2}$, $\sigma^{p}\neq\mathrm{id}_{L}$; choose $\lambda\in L$ with $\sigma^{p}(\lambda)\neq\lambda$. Iterating $v\mu=\sigma(\mu)v$ gives $x\mu=v^{p}\mu=\sigma^{p}(\mu)v^{p}=\sigma^{p}(\mu)x$ for all $\mu\in L$, so $x\lambda=\sigma^{p}(\lambda)x\neq\lambda x$, the inequality holding because $(\sigma^{p}(\lambda)-\lambda)x\neq0$ in the division ring $D$ (both factors are nonzero). But every element of $k=Z(D)$ commutes with $\lambda$; hence $x\notin k$. Thus $x\notin k$ and $x^{p}\in k$, i.e. $D$ contains a $p$-central element, which is the claim. (This also shows, consistently, that the earlier minimal-polynomial route was both unnecessary and unsound: it is the crossed-product relation $v^{p^{2}}=b\in k^{\times}$, not any minimal polynomial, that yields $x^{p}\in k$.)

lemma_exp_laurent_series_injective.statement: Let $F$ be a field and let $A$ be a central simple $F$-algebra. Then the class of $A$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ and the class of $A\otimes_F F((u))$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F((u)))$ have the same order.
lemma_exp_laurent_series_injective.proof:
Let $K:=F((u))$ and, for a finite-dimensional $F$-algebra $R$, write $R_K:=R\otimes_F K$.

=== 0. Preliminaries (standard facts, with proofs recalled) ===

(P1) Wedderburn--Artin. Every central simple algebra over a field $E$ is isomorphic to $M_r(D)$ with $D$ a central division $E$-algebra; $M_r(D)$ is central simple (its only two-sided ideals come from those of $D$, and $Z(M_r(D))=Z(D)=E$).

(P2) Descent of central simplicity. Let $R$ be a finite-dimensional $F$-algebra and $L/F$ a field extension. If $R\otimes_F L$ is central simple over $L$, then $R$ is central simple over $F$. Indeed, $L$ is a free (hence faithfully flat) $F$-module. Simplicity: for a nonzero two-sided ideal $I\triangleleft R$, flatness gives an injection $I\otimes_F L\hookrightarrow R\otimes_F L$, whose image is a two-sided ideal (since $(R\otimes L)(I\otimes L)\subseteq RI\otimes L=I\otimes L$); it is nonzero because $L\cong\bigoplus_{b\in\mathcal B}F$ for a basis $\mathcal B$ gives $I\otimes_F L\cong\bigoplus_{\mathcal B}I\neq 0$. Simplicity of $R\otimes_F L$ forces $I\otimes_F L=R\otimes_F L$, i.e. $(R/I)\otimes_F L=0$, and again freeness of $L$ forces $R/I=0$, so $I=R$. Center: $Z(R)$ is the equalizer of the two $F$-linear maps $\alpha,\beta:R\to\mathrm{Hom}_F(R,R)$, $\alpha(r)(x)=rx$, $\beta(r)(xr)=xr$; i.e. $0\to Z(R)\rightrightarrows R$ is an equalizer. Flatness of $L$ preserves equalizers, and since $R$ is finite free over $F$ the natural map $\mathrm{Hom}_F(R,R)\otimes_F L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Hom}_L(R\otimes_F L,R\otimes_F L)$ is an isomorphism carrying $\alpha\otimes 1,\beta\otimes 1$ to left and right multiplication on $R_L$. Hence $Z(R)\otimes_F L\cong Z(R\otimes_F L)=L$ as $L$-algebras, so $\dim_F Z(R)=\dim_L(Z(R)\otimes_F L)=1$, i.e. $Z(R)=F\cdot 1$.

(P3) Existence of splitting fields. Let $A$ be a central simple $F$-algebra, $A\cong M_s(\Delta)$ with $\Delta$ central division. Choose a subfield $P\subseteq\Delta$ maximal among subfields of $\Delta$ (exists since $\dim_F\Delta<\infty$). Then $P\subseteq C_\Delta(P)$; if $t\in C_\Delta(P)\setminus P$, then $P(t)$ is a commutative finite-dimensional $F$-domain, hence a field, properly containing $P$, contradiction. So $C_\Delta(P)=P$, and by the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) $P$ is a maximal subfield of $\Delta$, with $[P:F]\cdot[C_\Delta(P):F]=\dim_F\Delta$, so $[P:F]=\deg\Delta$. By ref_5 (maximal subfield $\iff$ splitting), $\Delta\otimes_F P\cong M_{\deg\Delta}(P)$, hence $A\otimes_F P\cong M_{s\deg\Delta}(P)$: $P$ splits $A$.

=== 1. The ring $\Delta((u))$ for $\Delta$ central division over $F$ ===

Let $\Delta$ be a central division $F$-algebra, $d:=\dim_F\Delta$ (so $d=(\deg\Delta)^2$). Define
$$\Delta((u)):=\Big\{\textstyle\sum_{i\ge m}\delta_i u^{i}\;:\; m\in\mathbb Z,\ \delta_i\in\Delta\Big\}$$
with coefficientwise addition and multiplication given by $(\sum_i\delta_i u^i)(\sum_j\varepsilon_j u^j)=\sum_n\big(\sum_{i+j=n}\delta_i\varepsilon_j\big)u^n$; the inner sums are finite because $\delta_i=0$ (resp. $\varepsilon_j=0$) for $i\ll0$ (resp. $j\ll0$). Associativity holds because the coefficient of $u^n$ in both $ (xy)z$ and $x(yz)$ equals $\sum_{i+j+k=n}\delta_i\varepsilon_j\zeta_k$; $1=1_\Delta u^0$ is a unit; and $u$ is central by definition.

**Claim 1(a).** The map $\Phi:\Delta\otimes_F K\to\Delta((u))$ given on elementary tensors by
$$\Phi\Big(\delta\otimes\sum_{i\ge m}a_i u^i\Big):=\sum_{i\ge m}(a_i\delta)u^i$$
is a well-defined isomorphism of $K$-algebras.

*Well-definedness and linearity.* The expression $f=\sum_{i\ge m}a_iu^i$ has unique coefficients $a_i\in F$, so $B(\delta,f):=\sum_i(a_i\delta)u^i$ defines a function $B:\Delta\times K\to\Delta((u))$. It is $F$-bilinear: additivity in each variable is coefficientwise; for $\lambda\in F$, the $u^i$-coefficient of $B(\lambda\delta,f)$ is $a_i(\lambda\delta)=(a_i\lambda)\delta=(\lambda a_i)\delta=\lambda(a_i\delta)$, since $a_i\in F\subseteq Z(\Delta)$. By the universal property of $\otimes_F$ there is a unique $F$-linear $\Phi$ with $\Phi(\delta\otimes f)=B(\delta,f)$; this is the displayed formula.

*Construction of the inverse using a basis.* Let $e_1,\dots,e_{d'}$ be an $F$-basis of $\Delta$ ($d'=\dim_F\Delta$). For $x=\sum_{i\ge m}\delta_i u^i\in\Delta((u))$ write each coefficient uniquely as $\delta_i=\sum_{j=1}^{d'}\lambda_{ij}e_j$ with $\lambda_{ij}\in F$, and set
$$\Psi(x):=\sum_{j=1}^{d'}e_j\otimes\Big(\sum_{i\ge m}\lambda_{ij}u^i\Big).$$
This is legitimate: whenever $\delta_i=0$ all $\lambda_{ij}=0$, so $\lambda_{ij}=0$ for all $i<m$, and each inner series lies in $K$; the outer sum has only $d'$ terms. Uniqueness of the $\delta_i$ and of the coordinates $\lambda_{ij}$ makes $\Psi$ a genuine function, and it is plainly $F$-linear.

*$\Phi\circ\Psi=\mathrm{id}$.* $\Phi(\Psi(x))=\sum_{j}\Phi\big(e_j\otimes\sum_i\lambda_{ij}u^i\big)=\sum_j\big(\sum_i(\lambda_{ij}e_j)u^i\big)=\sum_i\big(\sum_j\lambda_{ij}e_j\big)u^i=\sum_i\delta_iu^i=x$, where the interchange is valid because addition in $\Delta((u))$ is coefficientwise and the sum over $j$ is finite.

*$\Psi\circ\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ on elementary tensors.* Let $\delta=\sum_j\lambda_je_j$ and $f=\sum_ia_iu^i$. Then $\Phi(\delta\otimes f)=\sum_i\big(\sum_j\lambda_ja_ie_j\big)u^i$, whose $u^i$-coefficient is $\delta_i=\sum_j(\lambda_ja_i)e_j$, so the coordinates are $\lambda_{ij}=\lambda_ja_i$. Hence
$$\Psi\Phi(\delta\otimes f)=\sum_je_j\otimes\Big(\sum_i\lambda_ja_iu^i\Big)=\sum_je_j\otimes(\lambda_jf)=\sum_j\lambda_j(e_j\otimes f)=\Big(\sum_j\lambda_je_j\Big)\otimes f=\delta\otimes f.$$
Since $\Psi\circ\Phi$ and $\mathrm{id}$ are $F$-linear maps $\Delta\otimes_FK\to\Delta\otimes_FK$ agreeing on the spanning set of elementary tensors, they are equal. Thus $\Phi$ is bijective with inverse $\Psi$. (Note that nowhere was $F((u))$ written as an algebraic direct sum of the lines $F\cdot u^i$; the argument uses only the finite-dimensionality of $\Delta$ over $F$.)

*Multiplicativity.* The maps $(X,Y)\mapsto\Phi(XY)$ and $(X,Y)\mapsto\Phi(X)\Phi(Y)$ are $F$-bilinear on $(\Delta\otimes K)^2$, so it suffices to check elementary tensors. With $f=\sum_ia_iu^i$, $g=\sum_jb_ju^j$ one has $fg=\sum_n\big(\sum_{i+j=n}a_ib_j\big)u^n$, hence
$$\Phi\big((\delta\otimes f)(\varepsilon\otimes g)\big)=\Phi(\delta\varepsilon\otimes fg)=\sum_n\Big(\sum_{i+j=n}a_ib_j\Big)(\delta\varepsilon)u^n,$$
while
$$\Phi(\delta\otimes f)\,\Phi(\varepsilon\otimes g)=\sum_n\Big(\sum_{i+j=n}(a_i\delta)(b_j\varepsilon)\Big)u^n=\sum_n\Big(\sum_{i+j=n}a_ib_j\,\delta\varepsilon\Big)u^n,$$
because $b_j\in F=Z(\Delta)$ gives $(a_i\delta)(b_j\varepsilon)=a_i(\delta b_j)\varepsilon=a_i(b_j\delta)\varepsilon=(a_ib_j)(\delta\varepsilon)$. The two expressions agree, and $\Phi(1\otimes1)=1$. So $\Phi$ is a unital ring isomorphism (and $\Psi$ is then automatically a ring homomorphism as well).

*$K$-linearity.* $K$ acts on $\Delta\otimes_FK$ by multiplication on the second factor, and on $\Delta((u))$ by multiplication by the series with coefficients in $F\subseteq\Delta$ (which is legitimate since those coefficients are central). For $X\in\Delta\otimes_FK$ and $g\in K$, multiplicativity gives $\Phi(X\cdot(1\otimes g))=\Phi(X)\,\Phi(1\otimes g)=\Phi(X)\cdot g$, and $\Phi(1\otimes g)=g$ as a series. Thus $\Phi$ is an isomorphism of $K$-algebras.

**Claim 1(b).** $\Delta((u))$ is a division ring. Let $x=\sum_{i\ge m}\delta_iu^i\neq0$ and $y=\sum_{j\ge s}\varepsilon_ju^j\neq0$, so $\delta_m\neq0\neq\varepsilon_s$. The $u^{m+s}$-coefficient of $xy$ is the single product $\delta_m\varepsilon_s$, which is nonzero because $\Delta$ is a division ring ($\delta_m\varepsilon_s=0$ with $\delta_m\neq0$ would give $\varepsilon_s=\delta_m^{-1}\cdot0=0$). Hence $xy\neq0$: there are no zero divisors.
For inverses, write $x=u^m\delta_m(1+z)$ with $z=\sum_{i\ge1}\delta_m^{-1}\delta_{m+i}u^i\in u\Delta[[u]]$ (valid since $u$ is central and $\delta_mz=\sum_{i\ge1}\delta_{m+i}u^i$). The series $w:=\sum_{j\ge0}(-z)^j$ is well defined coefficientwise: $(-z)^j\in u^j\Delta[[u]]$, so the coefficient of $u^i$ in $w$ involves only $0\le j\le i$. For each $J\ge0$ one has the telescoping identity $(1+z)\sum_{j=0}^{J}(-z)^j=1-(-z)^{J+1}$. Fix $i\ge0$; for $J\ge i$ the coefficient of $u^i$ in $\sum_{j=0}^J(-z)^j$ equals that in $w$, and multiplication by the fixed element $1+z$ involves only coefficients of degree $\le i$, so the $u^i$-coefficient of $(1+z)w$ equals that of $1-(-z)^{J+1}$ for any $J\ge i+1$; and $(-z)^{J+1}\in u^{J+1}\Delta[[u]]\subseteq u^{i+1}\Delta[[u]]$ makes that coefficient equal to the $u^i$-coefficient of $1$ (which is $1$ if $i=0$, $0$ otherwise). Thus $(1+z)w=1$; the same argument on the right gives $w(1+z)=1$. Therefore $x^{-1}:=w\,\delta_m^{-1}u^{-m}$ satisfies $xx^{-1}=u^m\delta_m(1+z)w\delta_m^{-1}u^{-m}=u^m\delta_m\delta_m^{-1}u^{-m}=1$ and $x^{-1}x=w(1+z)=1$, using centrality and invertibility of $u$. So every nonzero element is invertible.

**Claim 1(c).** $Z(\Delta((u)))=F((u))=K$. Let $c=\sum_ic_iu^i\in Z(\Delta((u)))$. For each $\delta\in\Delta$, comparing the coefficients of the constant series $\delta$ in $c\delta$ and $\delta c$ (legitimate because expansions in $\Delta((u))$ have unique coefficients) gives $c_i\delta=\delta c_i$ for all $i$, so $c_i\in Z(\Delta)=F$. Conversely, if $c=\sum_ic_iu^i$ with all $c_i\in F$ and $x=\sum_j\delta_ju^j$, the $u^n$-coefficient of $cx$ is $\sum_{i+j=n}c_i\delta_j=\sum_{i+j=n}\delta_jc_i$, which is the $u^n$-coefficient of $xc$. Hence $c$ is central.

**Claim 1(d).** $\dim_K\Delta((u))=\dim_F\Delta=d$. By Claim 1(a), $\Phi$ is a $K$-linear bijection, so $\dim_K\Delta((u))=\dim_K(\Delta\otimes_FK)$; and since $\{e_j\}$ is an $F$-basis of $\Delta$, $\{e_j\otimes1\}$ is a $K$-basis of $\Delta\otimes_FK$: it spans because $\delta\otimes\mu=\sum_je_j\otimes(\lambda_j\mu)$ for $\delta=\sum_j\lambda_je_j$, and it is independent because applying $\varphi_i\otimes\mathrm{id}_K$ for the dual functionals $\varphi_i:\Delta\to F$ sends $\sum_je_j\otimes\mu_j$ to $\mu_i$. Thus $\dim_K\Delta((u))=d'=\dim_F\Delta$.

Combining (a)--(d): $\Delta((u))$ is a central division $K$-algebra with $\dim_K\Delta((u))=d$, hence $\deg\Delta((u))=\deg\Delta$.

=== 2. Base change of $A$ ===

Write $A\cong M_s(\Delta)$ with $\Delta$ central division over $F$. Using $M_r(F)\otimes_F B\xrightarrow{\sim}M_r(B)$, $\sum E_{ij}\otimes b_{ij}\mapsto(b_{ij})$ (an algebra isomorphism, since $(E_{ij}\otimes x)(E_{kl}\otimes y)=\delta_{jk}E_{il}\otimes xy$ corresponds exactly to matrix multiplication), we obtain
$$A\otimes_FK\;\cong\;M_s(F)\otimes_F\Delta\otimes_FK\;\cong\;M_s(F)\otimes_F(\Delta\otimes_FK)\;\cong\;M_s(\Delta((u))).$$
By Claim 1, $\Delta((u))$ is a central division $K$-algebra, so by (P1) $A\otimes_FK$ is a central simple $K$-algebra; its class in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$ is therefore defined, and its division part is $\Delta((u))$.

=== 3. Tensor powers commute with base change ===

For central simple $F$-algebras $A,B$ there is a $K$-algebra isomorphism
$$\beta:(A\otimes_FK)\otimes_K(B\otimes_FK)\xrightarrow{\sim}(A\otimes_FB)\otimes_FK,\qquad (a\otimes\lambda)\otimes(b\otimes\mu)\longmapsto(a\otimes b)\otimes\lambda\mu.$$
The map $((a\otimes\lambda),(b\otimes\mu))\mapsto(a\otimes b)\otimes\lambda\mu$ is $F$-bilinear and $K$-balanced ($(a\otimes\lambda g)\otimes(b\otimes\mu)$ and $(a\otimes\lambda)\otimes(gb\otimes\mu)$ both go to $(a\otimes b)\otimes\lambda g\mu$, using commutativity of $K$), so $\beta$ is well defined; it is an algebra homomorphism because multiplication in both sides is componentwise on elementary tensors. Its inverse is $\alpha:(a\otimes b)\otimes\lambda\mapsto(a\otimes\lambda)\otimes(b\otimes1)$: $\beta\alpha=\mathrm{id}$ is immediate, and $\alpha\beta((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes(b\otimes\mu))=(a\otimes\lambda\mu)\otimes(b\otimes1)=(a\otimes1)\otimes\lambda\mu(b\otimes1)=(a\otimes1)\otimes(b\otimes\lambda\mu)=(a\otimes\lambda)\otimes(b\otimes\mu)$, using the balancing relations over $K$. By induction,
$$(A^{\otimes_F n})\otimes_FK\;\cong\;(A\otimes_FK)^{\otimes_K n}\qquad\text{for all } n\ge1. \tag{$\ast$}$$

=== 4. Equality of the sets of splitting exponents ===

Let $S(A):=\{n\ge1: A^{\otimes_F n}\ \text{is split over }F\}$ and $S_K(A):=\{n\ge1:(A\otimes_FK)^{\otimes_Kn}\ \text{is split over }K\}$.

*First, $A^{\otimes_Fn}$ is central simple over $F$.* By (P3) there is a field $P/F$ with $A\otimes_FP\cong M_m(P)$. By $(\ast)$ (with $P$ in place of $K$), $(A^{\otimes n})\otimes_FP\cong M_m(P)^{\otimes_Pn}\cong M_{m^n}(P)$, which is central simple over $P$ by (P1); (P2) then gives that $A^{\otimes_F n}$ is central simple over $F$. Hence by (P1) there is a central division $F$-algebra $\Delta$ and $r\ge1$ with
$$A^{\otimes_F n}\cong M_r(\Delta).$$
Combining Section 2's identification with $(\ast)$,
$$(A\otimes_FK)^{\otimes_K n}\;\cong\;(A^{\otimes_Fn})\otimes_FK\;\cong\;M_r(\Delta)\otimes_FK\;\cong\;M_r(\Delta\otimes_FK)\;\cong\;M_r(\Delta((u))),$$
and $\Delta((u))$ is a central division $K$-algebra by Claim 1.

*($\Rightarrow$)* If $n\in S(A)$, i.e. $A^{\otimes n}\cong M_r(F)$, then by $(\ast)$, $(A\otimes_FK)^{\otimes n}\cong M_r(F)\otimes_FK\cong M_r(K)$, so $n\in S_K(A)$.

*($\Leftarrow$)* Suppose $n\in S_K(A)$: $M_r(\Delta((u)))\cong M_N(K)$ as $K$-algebras, where $N=n\deg A$. We use the following corner argument. Let $D$ be any central division $K$-algebra, $r\ge1$, and suppose $\varphi:M_r(D)\xrightarrow{\sim}M_N(K)$ is a (unital) ring isomorphism. Put $e=E_{11}\in M_r(D)$; then $eM_r(D)e=\{\text{matrices supported in position }(1,1)\}\cong D$ via $d\mapsto$ the matrix with $d$ in position $(1,1)$, a ring isomorphism carrying $1_D$ to $e$. Set $\varepsilon:=\varphi(e)$, an idempotent of $M_N(K)=\mathrm{End}_K(K^N)$. Then $\varepsilon$ restricts to the identity on its image $V:=\mathrm{im}(\varepsilon)$ and to $0$ on $W:=\ker\varepsilon$, and $K^N=V\oplus W$ since $v=\varepsilon v+(v-\varepsilon v)$ with $\varepsilon v\in V$, $v-\varepsilon v\in W$. Choosing a basis of $K^N$ adapted to this decomposition, conjugation by the corresponding invertible matrix $P$ is an automorphism $X\mapsto PXP^{-1}$ of $M_N(K)$ carrying $\varepsilon$ to $e_0:=\mathrm{diag}(I_t,0)$ with $t=\dim_KV$, hence restricts to a ring isomorphism $\varepsilon M_N(K)\varepsilon\cong e_0M_N(K)e_0\cong M_t(K)$. Therefore $D\cong eM_r(D)e\cong\varepsilon M_N(K)\varepsilon\cong M_t(K)$. Since $D$ is a division ring and $M_t(K)$ has non-invertible nonzero elements (e.g. $E_{11}$) whenever $t\ge2$, we must have $t=1$, and $D\cong K$.
Applying this with $D=\Delta((u))$ gives $\Delta((u))\cong K$, hence $\dim_F\Delta=\dim_K\Delta((u))=1$ by Claim 1(d). A division $F$-algebra of dimension $1$ is $F\cdot1$, so $\Delta\cong F$ and $A^{\otimes_Fn}\cong M_r(F)$ is split, i.e. $n\in S(A)$.

Thus $S(A)=S_K(A)$.

=== 5. Conclusion ===

The order of $[A]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is $\min S(A)$ and the order of $[A\otimes_FF((u))]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F((u)))$ is $\min S_K(A)$; these sets are equal, so the two orders are equal. (Both sets are non-empty, so the orders are finite: by (P3) a splitting field $P/F$ of $A$ exists, and one may take $n=[P:F]$ once $P$ is taken Galois, since $[A]$ then lies in $\mathrm{Br}(P/F)=H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(P/F),P^\times)$, which is annihilated by $|\mathrm{Gal}(P/F)|$; equivalently one may invoke the classical theorem $\exp(A)\mid\mathrm{ind}(A)\mid\deg(A)$. In any case, with the convention that the order is $\infty$ when $S(A)=\varnothing$, the equality of the sets gives the equality of orders unconditionally.)

In particular, taking $n=\mathrm{ord}[A]$ shows that $[A\otimes_FF((u))]=0$ forces $[A]=0$: the scalar-extension map $\mathrm{Br}(F)\to\mathrm{Br}(F((u)))$ is injective (Amitsur). No Grothendieck purity/localisation input was used.

lemma_230.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a field complete for a discrete valuation of characteristic $p>2$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ and perfect residue field. Then for every $c\in k$ there exists $\lambda\in k$ such that, for $c'=c-(\lambda^{p}-\lambda)$, either $v(c')\ge 0$, or $v(c')<0$ and $p\nmid v(c')$.
lemma_230.proof:
Notation. Write $\wp(t)=t^{p}-t$ for the Artin--Schreier map; since $\operatorname{char} k=p$, the map $\wp$ is additive: $\wp(x+y)=\wp(x)+\wp(y)$ for all $x,y\in k$ (Frobenius $x\mapsto x^{p}$ is additive). Let $\mathcal O=\{x\in k:v(x)\ge 0\}$ be the valuation ring, $\mathfrak m=\{x:v(x)>0\}=\{x:v(x)\ge 1\}$ its maximal ideal, and $x\mapsto\bar x$ the residue map $\mathcal O\to\bar k=\mathcal O/\mathfrak m$. Since $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$, there is a uniformiser $\pi\in k$ with $v(\pi)=1$, and every $x\in k^{\times}$ can be written uniquely as $x=\pi^{v(x)}u$ with $u\in\mathcal O^{\times}$. We use the convention $v(0)=+\infty$, so that $v(0)\ge 0$.

We prove the following auxiliary claim, then deduce the lemma by strong induction on $m=-v(c)$.

**Claim (one cancellation step).** Let $c\in k$ with $v(c)=-m<0$ and suppose $p\mid m$; write $m=pn$ with $n\ge 1$. Then there exists $\lambda_{0}\in k$ with $v(\lambda_{0})=-n$ such that
$$v\big(c-\wp(\lambda_{0})\big)\ \ge\ -m+1\ >\ -m=v(c).$$

*Proof of the claim.* Write $c=\pi^{-pn}u$ with $u\in\mathcal O^{\times}$ (possible because $v(c)=-pn$). The residue field $\bar k$ is perfect, so the Frobenius $\bar k\to\bar k$, $t\mapsto t^{p}$, is surjective; hence there is $\bar a\in\bar k$ with $\bar a^{\,p}=\bar u$. Note $\bar u\ne 0$ because $u$ is a unit, so $\bar a\ne 0$. Choose a lift $a\in\mathcal O$ of $\bar a$; then $a\in\mathcal O^{\times}$ and $v(a)=0$. Since $\bar u-\bar a^{\,p}=\bar u-\overline{a^{p}}=0$ in $\bar k$, the element $u-a^{p}$ lies in $\mathcal O$ with zero residue, i.e. $u-a^{p}\in\mathfrak m$, so
$$v(u-a^{p})\ \ge\ 1. \tag{1}$$
Set $\lambda_{0}=a\,\pi^{-n}$. Then $v(\lambda_{0})=v(a)-n=-n$, and by the Frobenius,
$$\lambda_{0}^{p}=a^{p}\pi^{-pn},\qquad\text{so}\qquad c-\lambda_{0}^{p}=\pi^{-pn}\big(u-a^{p}\big),$$
whence by (1)
$$v\big(c-\lambda_{0}^{p}\big)=-pn+v(u-a^{p})\ \ge\ -pn+1=-m+1. \tag{2}$$
Moreover
$$-n\ \ge\ -pn+1 \iff n(p-1)\ge 1,$$
which holds since $n\ge 1$ and $p\ge 2$ (indeed $p>2$ gives $n(p-1)\ge 2$). Thus $v(\lambda_{0})=-n\ge -m+1$. Finally,
$$c-\wp(\lambda_{0})=c-\lambda_{0}^{p}+\lambda_{0},$$
so by the ultrametric inequality together with (2) and $v(\lambda_{0})\ge -m+1$,
$$v\big(c-\wp(\lambda_{0})\big)\ \ge\ \min\{\,v(c-\lambda_{0}^{p}),\,v(\lambda_{0})\,\}\ \ge\ -m+1.$$
This proves the claim. $\square$

**Proof of the lemma.** Let $c\in k$. We argue by strong induction on the positive integer $m=-v(c)$, in the case $v(c)<0$; the case $v(c)\ge 0$ (which includes $c=0$, where $v(0)=+\infty\ge 0$) is settled by taking $\lambda=0$, since then $c'=c$ and $v(c')\ge 0$.

Assume henceforth $v(c)=-m<0$.

*Base case.* If $p\nmid m$, take $\lambda=0$. Then $c'=c$ satisfies $v(c')=-m<0$ and $p\nmid v(c')$, as required.

*Inductive step.* Suppose $p\mid m$; write $m=pn$ with $n\ge 1$. By the claim there is $\lambda_{0}\in k$ with
$$v(c_{1})\ \ge\ -m+1,\qquad\text{where } c_{1}:=c-\wp(\lambda_{0}).$$
If $v(c_{1})\ge 0$, we are done with $\lambda=\lambda_{0}$, since $c'=c-\wp(\lambda_{0})=c_{1}$ has $v(c')\ge 0$.

Otherwise $v(c_{1})<0$; write $v(c_{1})=-m_{1}$ with $m_{1}\ge 1$. From $-m_{1}=v(c_{1})\ge -m+1$ we get $m_{1}\le m-1<m$. By the strong induction hypothesis applied to $c_{1}$ (whose valuation is negative and whose associated integer $m_{1}$ is strictly smaller than $m$), there exists $\lambda_{1}\in k$ such that $c_{1}-\wp(\lambda_{1})$ either has valuation $\ge 0$, or has negative valuation not divisible by $p$.

Set $\lambda=\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{1}$. By additivity of $\wp$,
$$\wp(\lambda)=\lambda^{p}-\lambda=\big(\lambda_{0}^{p}-\lambda_{0}\big)+\big(\lambda_{1}^{p}-\lambda_{1}\big)=\wp(\lambda_{0})+\wp(\lambda_{1}),$$
hence
$$c-\wp(\lambda)=c-\wp(\lambda_{0})-\wp(\lambda_{1})=c_{1}-\wp(\lambda_{1}),$$
which, by the choice of $\lambda_{1}$, either has valuation $\ge 0$, or has negative valuation prime to $p$. This is exactly the required conclusion for $c$.

The induction is well founded on $\mathbb Z_{>0}$, so the statement holds for every $c\in k$: there exists $\lambda\in k$ such that $c'=c-(\lambda^{p}-\lambda)$ satisfies $v(c')\ge 0$, or $v(c')<0$ and $p\nmid v(c')$.

(Remark: the argument is a finite descent — each cancellation step strictly increases the valuation while it stays negative and divisible by $p$, and a strictly increasing sequence of negative integers terminates — so only the existence of a uniformiser and the perfection of $\bar k$ were used; the hypotheses that $v$ is complete and discrete with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$ are more than sufficient, and the assumption $p>2$ is more than the inequality $n(p-1)\ge1$ needs.)

lemma_229.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ complete for a discrete valuation $v$ with $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$, let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, and let $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)=\bigoplus_{\gamma}D^{\ge\gamma}/D^{>\gamma}$ be the associated graded ring with $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ viewed as a graded subring. Suppose every homogeneous element $y\in\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ satisfying $y^{p}\in\mathrm{gr}(k)$ already lies in $\mathrm{gr}(k)$. Then $D$ contains no element $x$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^{p}\in k$.
lemma_229.proof:
We argue by contradiction; the argument is valid for every prime $p$ (including $p=2$) and uses only the multiplicativity of the valuation on the division ring, the completeness of $k$, and the stated hypothesis on homogeneous elements of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$.

NOTATION. For $\gamma\in\mathbb{Q}$ write $D^{\ge\gamma}=\{z\in D: w(z)\ge\gamma\}$, $D^{>\gamma}=\{z\in D: w(z)>\gamma\}$, $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_\gamma=D^{\ge\gamma}/D^{>\gamma}$; for $0\neq z\in D$ let $\mathrm{in}_w(z)$ denote the class of $z$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{w(z)}$. We use the analogous notation $k^{\ge\gamma},k^{>\gamma},\mathrm{in}_v$ for $k$. Since $w|_k=v$, $k\cap D^{>\gamma}=k^{>\gamma}$, so $k^{\ge\gamma}/k^{>\gamma}\hookrightarrow D^{\ge\gamma}/D^{>\gamma}$, and $\mathrm{gr}(k)=\bigoplus_{\gamma}k^{\ge\gamma}/k^{>\gamma}$ is the graded subring of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ mentioned in the hypothesis. Because $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$ is discrete, for $\gamma\notin\mathbb{Z}$ one has $k^{\ge\gamma}=k^{>\gamma}$ (a value in $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\ge\gamma$ iff it is $>\gamma$), hence $\mathrm{gr}(k)_\gamma=k^{\ge\gamma}/k^{>\gamma}=0$ for $\gamma\notin\mathbb{Z}$.   (∗)

STANDING PROPERTIES OF $w$. Since $w$ is a valuation on the division ring $D$ (equivalently, $\mathcal{O}_w=\{z:w(z)\ge0\}$ is a valuation ring of $D$), the map $w\colon D^{\times}\to w(D^{\times})$ is a group homomorphism:
(1)  $w(z_1z_2)=w(z_1)+w(z_2)$ for all $z_1,z_2\in D^{\times}$.
Consequently $w(z^n)=n\,w(z)$ for all $n\ge1$, and initial forms multiply: if $z_1,z_2\ne0$ then $\mathrm{in}_w(z_1z_2)=\mathrm{in}_w(z_1)\mathrm{in}_w(z_2)$ in $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{w(z_1)+w(z_2)}$, because by (1) the product of the classes of $z_1$ and $z_2$ has degree $w(z_1z_2)$ and is nonzero (a representative is $z_1z_2$ itself, whose value equals that degree, so its class in $D^{\ge w(z_1z_2)}/D^{>w(z_1z_2)}$ is nonzero and equals both products).
We also use the ultrametric inequality with its standard sharpening:
(2)  $w(u+v)\ge\min\{w(u),w(v)\}$, with equality whenever $w(u)\neq w(v)$.
Indeed, if $w(u)<w(v)$ and $w(u+v)>w(u)$, then $w(u)=w((u+v)-v)\ge\min\{w(u+v),w(v)\}>w(u)$, a contradiction.

REDUCTION. Suppose some $x\in D\setminus k$ satisfies $x^p\in k$. Put $x_0:=x$ and $c_0:=x_0^p\in k$. Since $0\in k$, $x_0\neq0$; since $D$ is a division ring, $c_0=x_0^p\neq0$. Thus $c_0\in k^{\times}$.

CLAIM. There is a sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $k^{\times}$ such that, defining inductively $x_{n+1}:=x_n-a_n$ and $c_{n+1}:=x_{n+1}^p$, the following hold for all $n\ge0$:
(i) $x_n\neq0$, $c_n\in k^{\times}$, and $x_n^p=c_n$;
(ii) $\gamma_n:=w(x_n)\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $v(a_n)=\gamma_n$;
(iii) $\gamma_{n+1}>\gamma_n$.

Proof of the claim, by induction on $n$. Assume $x_n\neq0$ and $x_n^p=c_n\in k^{\times}$ (for $n=0$ this is the reduction).
Step 1 (values). By (1) and $w|_k=v$: $v(c_n)=w(c_n)=w(x_n^p)=p\,w(x_n)=p\,\gamma_n$. In particular $p\gamma_n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Step 2 (initial form). The element $y_n:=\mathrm{in}_w(x_n)\in\mathrm{gr}_w(D)_{\gamma_n}$ is nonzero, and by the multiplicativity of initial forms proved above,
$y_n^{\,p}=\mathrm{in}_w(x_n^p)=\mathrm{in}_w(c_n)=\mathrm{in}_v(c_n)\in\mathrm{gr}(k)_{p\gamma_n}$,
the last identification being the inclusion of $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ into $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$. Thus $y_n$ is a homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$ whose $p$-th power lies in $\mathrm{gr}(k)$; by the hypothesis of the lemma, $y_n\in\mathrm{gr}(k)$.
Step 3 (choice of $a_n$). Being a nonzero element of the graded ring $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ which is homogeneous of degree $\gamma_n$ (as an element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(D)$, hence of the subring), $y_n$ lies in $\mathrm{gr}(k)_{\gamma_n}=k^{\ge\gamma_n}/k^{>\gamma_n}$, which is therefore nonzero; by (∗) this forces $\gamma_n\in v(k^{\times})=\mathbb{Z}$. Pick $a_n\in k^{\ge\gamma_n}$ mapping to $y_n$; since $y_n\neq0$, $a_n\notin k^{>\gamma_n}$, so $v(a_n)=\gamma_n$. Moreover $a_n-x_n\in D^{>\gamma_n}$, i.e. $w(x_n-a_n)>\gamma_n$.
Step 4 (the next term). Set $x_{n+1}:=x_n-a_n$; then $\gamma_{n+1}:=w(x_{n+1})>\gamma_n$, proving (iii). Since $a_n\in k=Z(D)$ and $\mathrm{char}(k)=p$, the binomial theorem gives $x_{n+1}^p=(x_n-a_n)^p=x_n^p-a_n^p=c_n-a_n^p\in k$; call it $c_{n+1}$. If $x_{n+1}=0$, then $x=a_0+\cdots+a_n\in k$, contradicting $x\notin k$; hence $x_{n+1}\neq0$ and consequently $c_{n+1}=x_{n+1}^p\neq0$. This gives (i) for $n+1$, and the induction is complete.

PASSAGE TO THE LIMIT. By (ii) and (iii), $(\gamma_n)$ is a strictly increasing sequence of integers, so $\gamma_n\ge\gamma_0+n\to+\infty$; and $v(a_n)=\gamma_n\to+\infty$. Since $k$ is complete for $v$, the series $s:=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n$ converges in $k$. Let $s_n:=a_0+\cdots+a_{n-1}$; telescoping the relations $x_{i+1}=x_i-a_i$ gives $x-s_n=x_n$ for every $n$. For $m>n$, $s_m-s_n=\sum_{i=n}^{m-1}a_i$ has $v$-value equal to $\min_{n\le i<m}v(a_i)=v(a_n)=\gamma_n$ by (2) (the minimum is attained at the single index $i=n$). Since $s_m\to s$, we have $v(s_m-s)\to\infty$; choosing $m$ with $v(s_m-s)>\gamma_n$ and applying (2) to $s-s_n=(s_m-s_n)+(s-s_m)$ gives $v(s-s_n)=\gamma_n$. As $s-s_n\in k$, $w(s-s_n)=v(s-s_n)=\gamma_n$. Hence by (2),
$w(x-s)\ge\min\{w(x-s_n),\,w(s_n-s)\}=\min\{\gamma_n,\gamma_n\}=\gamma_n$ for every $n$.
Since $\gamma_n\to+\infty$, this forces $w(x-s)=+\infty$, and by the axiom $w(z)=\infty\iff z=0$ we get $x-s=0$. Thus $x=s\in k$, contradicting $x\notin k$.

The contradiction shows that no element $x\in D\setminus k$ with $x^p\in k$ exists, which is exactly the claim of the lemma. $\blacksquare$

lemma_matrix_over_cyclic_degree_p_crosse.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p$. If $D$ contains a maximal subfield $K$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p$, then the matrix algebra $M_{p}(D)$ is isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_matrix_over_cyclic_degree_p_crosse.proof:
We write G0 = Gal(K/k) = <sigma>, a cyclic group of order p, and G = C_p x C_p = G0 x G0, so |G| = p^2 (this is the group whose order we must produce).

STEP 1: K is a maximal subfield of D and C_D(K) = K.
Since deg(D) = p we have dim_k D = p^2, and [K:k] = p = deg(D). By the double-centralizer/maximal-subfield criterion (ref_1), a subfield of a central simple algebra whose k-dimension equals deg(A) is maximal and satisfies C_D(K) = K.

STEP 2: D is the cyclic algebra (K/k, sigma, a).
The subalgebra K subset D is commutative, dim_k K = p = deg(D), and K is a G0-Galois algebra in the sense of the definitions: K/k is finite separable, hence etale; G0 = Gal(K/k) acts by k-automorphisms; dim_k K = p = |G0|; and K^{G0} = k by Galois theory. Hence ref_3 applies to A = D, L = K, G = G0: there are units u_g in D^x (g in G0), with u_1 = 1, such that
  u_g lambda u_g^{-1} = g(lambda) for all lambda in K,   D = (+)_{i=0}^{p-1} K u_{sigma^i},   u_g u_h = f(g,h) u_{gh}
for a normalized 2-cocycle f: G0 x G0 -> K^x. Put v := u_sigma; v is a unit and v lambda = sigma(lambda) v for all lambda in K.
Write u_{sigma^i} = d_i v^i with d_i in K^x, proved by induction: d_0 = 1 works for i = 0; and from u_{sigma^{i+1}} = f(sigma, sigma^i)^{-1} u_sigma u_{sigma^i} we get d_{i+1} = f(sigma,sigma^i)^{-1} sigma(d_i) in K^x, using v d_i = sigma(d_i) v. Thus D = (+)_{i=0}^{p-1} K v^i.
Now consider v^p. For lambda in K, v^p lambda v^{-p} = sigma^p(lambda) = lambda, so v^p in C_D(K) = K by Step 1.
