Moreover v v^p v^{-1} = v^p, and conjugation by v restricts to sigma on K, hence sigma(v^p) = v^p; therefore v^p in K^{<sigma>} = k. Since v is a unit, a := v^p is a nonzero element of k, so a in k^x. Consequently
  D = (+)_{i=0}^{p-1} K v^i,   v lambda = sigma(lambda) v,   v^p = a in k^x,
i.e. D is the cyclic algebra (K/k, sigma, a).

STEP 3: The split cyclic algebra (K/k, sigma, 1) is M_p(k).
Let B := (+)_{i=0}^{p-1} K w^i with multiplication determined by w lambda = sigma(lambda) w and w^p = 1; by ref_22(i) (the cyclic-algebra calculus) B is a central simple k-algebra of degree p, dim_k B = p^2. Define a k-linear map psi: B -> End_k(K) on the basis {w^i} by psi(sum_i lambda_i w^i) := sum_i m_{lambda_i} o sigma^i, where m_mu denotes multiplication by mu on K. This is an algebra homomorphism: using sigma^i m_mu = m_{sigma^i(mu)} sigma^i (both sides send x to sigma^i(mu x)),
  psi(lambda w^i) psi(mu w^j) = m_lambda sigma^i m_mu sigma^j = m_{lambda sigma^i(mu)} sigma^{i+j},
while psi(lambda w^i * mu w^j) = psi(lambda sigma^i(mu) w^{i+j}); the two agree also when i+j >= p because then w^{i+j} = w^{i+j-p} (as w^p = 1) and sigma^{i+j} = sigma^{i+j-p} (as sigma^p = id). Also psi(1) = id_K, so psi is nonzero. Since B is central simple (ref_22(i)), ker psi is a proper two-sided ideal, hence 0; and dim_k End_k(K) = p^2 = dim_k B, so psi is an isomorphism. Choosing a k-basis of K identifies End_k(K) with M_p(k). Thus M_p(k) = psi(B) = (+)_{i=0}^{p-1} psi(K) psi(w)^i is a C_p-crossed product whose Galois algebra is psi(K) with action sigma( psi(lambda) ) := psi(sigma(lambda)); note (psi(K))^{C_p} = psi(K^{<sigma>}) = psi(k) = k and dim_k psi(K) = p = |C_p|.

STEP 4: M_p(D) = D tensor_k M_p(k).
The standard map Theta: D tensor_k M_p(k) -> M_p(D), Theta(x tensor (b_{ij})) = (b_{ij} x), is a k-algebra isomorphism (it sends the k-basis {x tensor E_{ij}} bijectively onto {x e_{ij}}, and it is multiplicative because entries b_{ij} lie in k, which is central in D: (b_{ij}x)(b'_{kl}x') = sum_k b_{ik}b'_{kj} x x'). Composing id_D tensor psi: D tensor_k B -> D tensor_k M_p(k) with Theta gives a k-algebra isomorphism
  Theta': D tensor_k B  ~-> M_p(D),   x tensor y |-> x * psi~(y),
where psi~: B -> M_p(D) is psi followed by the inclusion of scalar matrices M_p(k) subset M_p(D); multiplicativity holds since psi~(y') has entries in k and hence commutes with every element of M_p(D).

STEP 5: L := K tensor_k K is a G-Galois k-algebra (G = C_p x C_p).
(a) Etale: K/k is finite separable, so K is etale over k; for an algebraic closure Omega of k, K tensor_k Omega ~ Omega^p, hence (K tensor_k K) tensor_k Omega ~ (K tensor_k Omega) tensor_Omega (K tensor_k Omega) ~ Omega^p tensor_Omega Omega^p ~ Omega^{p^2}, a product of copies of Omega. A finite-dimensional k-algebra that becomes a product of copies of Omega over Omega is etale, so L is etale.
(b) Dimension: dim_k L = [K:k]^2 = p^2 = |G|.
(c) Action: (sigma^m, sigma^n)(x tensor y) := sigma^m(x) tensor sigma^j(y) with j = n is well defined because for c in k, sigma^m(xc) tensor sigma^n(y) = sigma^m(x) c tensor sigma^n(y) = sigma^m(x) tensor sigma^n(cy); it is a k-algebra automorphism, and (m,n) |-> (x tensor y |-> sigma^m x tensor sigma^n y) is a group action since sigma^{m+m'} = sigma^m sigma^n-composition etc.
(d) Fixed ring: consider alpha: K tensor_k K -> F := Map(Gal(K/k), K), alpha(x tensor y)(g) = x g(y); alpha is a k-algebra homomorphism since g is a field automorphism. We show alpha is an isomorphism. As K/k is finite separable, K = k(theta) with minimal polynomial f of degree p. Then L = K tensor_k k[theta] ~ K[T]/(f). Since K/k is Galois, f splits in K as f = prod_{g in G0} (T - g(theta)) with pairwise distinct roots (f is separable), the ideals (T - g(theta)) are maximal and pairwise comaximal, so the Chinese remainder theorem gives K[T]/(f) ~ prod_{g in G0} K[T]/(T - g(theta)) ~ prod_{g in G0} K = F, the class of T going to (g(theta))_g and constants c in K to constant functions. The composite is exactly x tensor y |-> (g |-> x g(y)) = alpha(x tensor y); hence alpha is a k-algebra isomorphism.
Under alpha the G-action becomes: alpha((sigma^m,1)(x tensor y))(g) = sigma^m(x) g(y) = sigma^m(alpha(x tensor y)(g)), and alpha((1,sigma^n)(x tensor y))(g) = x (g sigma^n)(y) = alpha(x tensor y)(g sigma^n). Thus for phi in F,
  ((sigma^m,sigma^n) phi)(g) = sigma^m( phi(g sigma^n) ).
If phi is G-invariant, taking m = 0 gives phi(g sigma^n) = phi(g) for all g, n, i.e. phi is a constant function phi = c; then taking n = 0 gives sigma^m(c) = c for all m, so c in K^{G0} = k. Conversely constant functions with value in k are clearly invariant. Hence L^G = k * (1 tensor 1) = k.
So L is a Galois G-algebra over k in the sense of the definitions (etale, dim_k L = |G| = p^2, L^G = k). This is also the content of ref_10 in this special case: the tensor product of the C_p-crossed products D and M_p(k) carries the (C_p x C_p)-Galois algebra K tensor_k K.

STEP 6: The crossed product structure on D tensor_k B, hence on M_p(D).
Inside D tensor_k B let L = K tensor_k K (the two copies of K), and for g = (i,j) in {0,...,p-1}^2 set U_g := v^i tensor w^j. Then:
(i) U_1 = 1 tensor 1 = 1, and U_g is a unit (v^{p-1}a^{-1} tensor w^{p-1} inverts U_{(1,1)}; powers of units are units).
(ii) Direct-sum decomposition: D tensor_k B is spanned over k by (lambda v^i) tensor (mu w^j) = (lambda tensor mu)(v^i tensor w^j), so D tensor_k B = sum_{g in G} L U_g. The sum is direct: take a k-basis {e_a} of K; then {e_a v^i} is a k-basis of D and {e_b w^j} a k-basis of B, so {e_a v^i tensor e_b w^j} is a k-basis of D tensor_k B. If sum_{i,j} ell_{ij} U_{(i,j)} = 0 with ell_{ij} = sum_{a,b} c^{ij}_{ab}(e_a tensor e_b) in L, then sum c^{ij}_{ab} (e_a v^i tensor e_b w^j) = 0 forces all c^{ij}_{ab} = 0, hence all ell_{ij} = 0. Thus M_p(D) = (+)_{g in G} L U_g as a left L-module, with p^2 = |G| summands.
(iii) Twisting relation: for x tensor y in L,
  U_{(i,j)} (x tensor y) = (v^i x) tensor (w^j y) = (sigma^i(x) v^i) tensor (sigma^j(y) w^j) = ((sigma^i,sigma^j)(x tensor y)) U_{(i,j)},
which is exactly u_g x = g(x) u_g for the G-action of Step 5(c); such elements span L, so the relation holds for all of L.
(iv) Cocycle: write i + i' = q p + r with 0 <= r < p, so q = floor((i+i')/p) in {0,1}. Then v^i v^{i'} = v^{i+i'} = (v^p)^q v^r = a^q v^r, and similarly w^j w^{j'} = (w^p)^{q'} w^{r'} = w^{r'} since w^p = 1. Hence, with the group law in G = C_p x C_p being addition mod p in each coordinate,
  U_{(i,j)} U_{(i',j')} = a^{q} U_{(r,r')} = a^{q} U_{(i,j)(i',j')}.
Define c: G x G -> L^x by c((i,j),(i',j')) := a^{floor((i+i')/p)} in k^x subset L^x. Then u_g u_h = c(g,h) u_{gh} for all g, h in G, as required.
(v) c is a 2-cocycle: c is normalized since floor((0+i)/p) = floor((i+0)/p) = 0 gives c(1,g) = c(g,1) = 1; and for g = (i,j), h = (i',j'), k = (i'',j'') both sides of the cocycle identity equal a^{floor((i+i'+i'')/p)}:
  c(g,h) c(gh,k) = a^{floor((i+i')/p)} * a^{floor(((i+i' mod p) + i'')/p)} = a^{floor((i+i'+i'')/p)} = c(h,k) c(g,hk).
(Equivalently, the identity is forced by associativity (U_g U_h)U_k = U_g(U_h U_k) together with the directness of the decomposition and invertibility of the U_g.)

CONCLUSION. Steps 4 and 6 give a k-algebra isomorphism
  M_p(D) ~ D tensor_k B = (+)_{g in G} L U_g,   U_g x = g(x) U_g,   U_g U_h = c(g,h) U_{gh},
where G = C_p x C_p is a group of order p^2, L = K tensor_k K is a G-Galois k-algebra (etale of k-dimension p^2 = |G| with L^G = k, Step 5), and c: G x G -> L^x is a normalized 2-cocycle (Step 6(v)). By the definition of a G-crossed product algebra, M_p(D) is isomorphic to the crossed product (L, G, c) with |G| = p^2. (Conceptually, Steps 5-6 are the explicit realisation, for this pair of algebras, of ref_10: the tensor product of a G1- and a G2-crossed product is a (G1 x G2)-crossed product with Galois algebra the tensor product of the Galois algebras.) Note that the argument uses only that K/k is cyclic of degree p; the hypothesis p > 2 is not needed beyond the standing assumption of the statement.

lemma_234.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$ with perfect residue field $\bar k$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$. Suppose $w(D^\times)=v(k^\times)$ and the residue division ring $\bar D$ is central of degree $p^2$ over $\bar k$. If $D$ contains a maximal subfield $L$ that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$, then $\bar D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $\bar k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$.
lemma_234.proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: (k,v) is henselian discretely valued of characteristic p>2 with perfect residue field \bar k; D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2 with (Krull) valuation w extending v; w(D^\times)=v(k^\times); the residue division ring \bar D = O_D/M_D is central of degree p^2 over \bar k; and L\subset D is a maximal subfield, Galois over k with Gal(L/k) cyclic of order p^2. We prove that the residue field \bar L is a maximal subfield of \bar D and that \bar L/\bar k is Galois cyclic of order p^2.

Step 1 (the valuation on L, and its basic properties). Write again w for the restriction of the valuation of D to L, and O_L = {x\in L : w(x)\ge 0}, M_L = {x\in L : w(x)>0}, \bar L = O_L/M_L. Since w extends v, the restriction of w to k is v, so O_k = O_D\cap k and M_k = M_D\cap k; hence the residue map O_k\to \bar L is exactly the residue map of k, and \bar k embeds in \bar L. Two standard facts about henselian valuations will be used: (a) every extension of a henselian valuation to an algebraic field extension is again henselian and is the unique extension (equivalently, henselianity of v means that v has a unique extension to a separable closure of k, and this unique extension restricts to a henselian valuation on each intermediate field); (b) Hensel's lemma holds for (L,w): if F\in O_L[T] is monic and \bar F = \bar g\,\bar h in \bar L[T] with \bar g,\bar h monic and coprime, then F = g h with g,h monic in O_L[T] reducing to \bar g,\bar h. Applying (a) to the finite extension L/k we see that (L,w) is henselian and that w is the unique extension of v to L. Consequently every \sigma\in Gal(L/k) preserves O_L and M_L: indeed w\circ\sigma is another extension of v to L, hence equals w by uniqueness, so w(\sigma(x))=w(x) for all x. Thus \sigma induces a \bar k-automorphism \bar\sigma of \bar L, and \sigma\mapsto\bar\sigma is a group homomorphism
    \rho : Gal(L/k) \longrightarrow Aut_{\bar k}(\bar L).

Step 2 (the ramification index of L/k is 1, and [\bar L:\bar k]=p^2). Because Gal(L/k) has order p^2 and L/k is Galois, [L:k]=p^2. The field (k,v) is henselian discretely valued and L/k is finite Galois, so by lemma_96 (triviality of the defect)
    [L:k] = [w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k].
Now k^\times\subseteq L^\times\subseteq D^\times, so v(k^\times)\subseteq w(L^\times)\subseteq w(D^\times)=v(k^\times) by hypothesis; hence w(L^\times)=v(k^\times) and [w(L^\times):v(k^\times)]=1. Therefore
    [\bar L:\bar k] = [L:k] = p^2.      (2.1)

Step 3 (\bar L is a maximal subfield of \bar D). The residue homomorphism O_D\to\bar D restricts to O_L\to\bar D; its kernel is O_L\cap M_D = M_L, so it induces an injective ring homomorphism \bar L\hookrightarrow \bar D, whose image is a subfield of the division ring \bar D containing \bar k (the latter because O_k\to\bar k is surjective, as noted in Step 1). By hypothesis \bar D is a central division \bar k-algebra of degree p^2. Applying the double centraliser theorem (ref_1) to the \bar k-subalgebra \bar L of \bar D, the centraliser C_{\bar D}(\bar L) is a central simple \bar L-algebra of degree deg(\bar D)/[\bar L:\bar k] = p^2/p^2 = 1 by (2.1); a central simple algebra of degree 1 over its centre is the centre itself, so C_{\bar D}(\bar L)=\bar L. By the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1 (K is a maximal subfield of A iff C_A(K)=K), \bar L is a maximal subfield of \bar D.

Step 4 (\bar L/\bar k is Galois). Since (k,v) is henselian with perfect residue field and L/k is finite Galois, lemma_183 gives that \bar L/\bar k is a finite Galois extension. Together with (2.1),
    |Gal(\bar L/\bar k)| = [\bar L:\bar k] = p^2,      (4.1)
and the image of \rho of Step 1 lies in Gal(\bar L/\bar k).

Step 5 (\rho is surjective). This is the only point where the cyclicity hypothesis is used, and we argue directly with Hensel's lemma.

(a) Since \bar L/\bar k is finite separable, choose \bar\alpha\in\bar L with \bar L=\bar k(\bar\alpha) (primitive element theorem). Let \bar f\in\bar k[T] be the monic minimal polynomial of \bar\alpha; deg\bar f = [\bar L:\bar k]=p^2 by (2.1), and \bar f is separable because \bar k is perfect. Since \bar L/\bar k is normal (Step 4), \bar f splits completely in \bar L; as it is separable it has exactly p^2 distinct roots in \bar L, namely the conjugates \bar\tau(\bar\alpha), \bar\tau\in Gal(\bar L/\bar k).

(b) Lift \bar f to a monic polynomial F\in O_k[T] of the same degree (possible because O_k\twoheadrightarrow\bar k is surjective), so \bar F=\bar f. Then F is irreducible over k: a monic factorisation F=GH in k[T] with 0<deg G,deg H<deg F would have G,H\in O_k[T] (the roots of F are integral over the DVR O_k, so the coefficients of G and H are integral over O_k and lie in k, hence in O_k), and reducing modulo M_k would factor \bar f, contradiction. Hence [k(\alpha'):k]=p^2 for every root \alpha' of F.

(c) For each root \bar\beta of \bar f in \bar L, apply Hensel's lemma in the henselian field (L,w) to the factorisation \bar F = (T-\bar\beta)\cdot(\bar f/(T-\bar\beta)) in \bar L[T]. The two factors are monic and coprime, because \bar\beta is a simple root of the separable polynomial \bar f. Hensel's lemma yields a factorisation F=(T-\alpha_\beta)\,h with \alpha_\beta\in O_L whose residue is \bar\beta. Distinct \bar\beta give distinct \alpha_\beta (their residues differ). Thus F has p^2 distinct roots \{\alpha_\beta\} in L, one above each root of \bar f; since deg F=p^2, F splits completely in L.

(d) Now fix \bar\tau\in Gal(\bar L/\bar k) and put \bar\beta=\bar\tau(\bar\alpha). Take \alpha:=\alpha_{\bar\alpha} and \alpha':=\alpha_{\bar\beta}, two roots of F in L. By (b), [k(\alpha):k]=[k(\alpha'):k]=p^2=[L:k], so k(\alpha)=L=k(\alpha'). Since \alpha and \alpha' have the same minimal polynomial F over k, there is a unique k-isomorphism \sigma:k(\alpha)\xrightarrow{\sim}k(\alpha') with \sigma(\alpha)=\alpha'; viewing it as a self-map of L we get \sigma\in Gal(L/k). Its induced residue automorphism satisfies \bar\sigma(\bar\alpha)=\bar{\sigma(\alpha)}=\bar{\alpha'}=\bar\beta=\bar\tau(\bar\alpha). Because \bar L=\bar k(\bar\alpha), two \bar k-automorphisms of \bar L that agree on \bar\alpha are equal; hence \bar\sigma=\bar\tau. So \rho is surjective.

Step 6 (conclusion on the Galois group). By Step 5, Gal(\bar L/\bar k) is a quotient of Gal(L/k), which is cyclic of order p^2; hence Gal(\bar L/\bar k) is cyclic of order dividing p^2. By (4.1) its order is exactly p^2, so Gal(\bar L/\bar k) is cyclic of order p^2 (and \rho is in fact an isomorphism, i.e. L/k is unramified).

Combining Step 3 and Step 6, \bar L is a maximal subfield of \bar D which is Galois over \bar k with cyclic Galois group of order p^2. This is exactly the required conclusion. \hfill\blacksquare

lemma_exp_p2_pcentral_iff_xpowp2.statement: Let $p>2$ be a prime and let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p$. Let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has order $p^{2}$. Then $D$ contains an element $x$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ if and only if $D$ contains an element $y$ with $y\notin k$ and $y^{p}\in k$.
lemma_exp_p2_pcentral_iff_xpowp2.proof:
Let char(k) = p > 2, let D be a central division k-algebra of degree p^2, and suppose the class [D] in Br(k) has order exactly p^2. We first record that [D] is not annihilated by p: if p[D] = 0 then the order of [D] would divide p, contradicting ord([D]) = p^2.

DIRECTION (<=). Assume D contains y with y notin k and y^p in k. Take x := y. Then x notin k, and x^{p^2} = (y^p)^p. Since y^p is an element of the field k and k is closed under multiplication, (y^p)^p lies in k. Thus x witnesses the existence of an element not in k whose p^2-th power is in k. (This direction uses neither the degree nor the exponent hypothesis.)

DIRECTION (=>). Assume D contains x with x notin k and x^{p^2} in k. Since 0 in k, we have x != 0; as D is a division ring it follows that x^{p^2} != 0. We argue by cases according to whether x^p lies in k.

Case 1: x^p in k. Then x itself is p-central, so y := x satisfies y notin k and y^p in k, and we are done.

Case 2: x^p notin k. The hypotheses of lemma_214 are now all satisfied: char(k) = p > 2; D is a central division k-algebra of degree p^2; [D] is not annihilated by p (shown above); x^{p^2} in k; and x^p notin k. By lemma_214, D contains a maximal subfield M that is Galois over k with cyclic Galois group of order p^2. Write G := Gal(M/k) = <sigma>, with sigma a generator; then G = {1, sigma, sigma^2, ..., sigma^{p^2-1}} and, by Galois theory, the fixed field M^{<sigma>} equals k.

Step A (crossed product realisation inside D). By lemma_106 applied to A = D and the Galois maximal subfield M/k with group G, D is a crossed product (M, G, c). We use this in the explicit form supplied by the crossed product criterion ref_3: M is a commutative k-subalgebra of D with dim_k(M) = p^2 = deg(D), M is a field hence etale over k, G acts on M by k-automorphisms with |G| = p^2 = dim_k(M), and M^G = k. Hence ref_3 yields units u_tau in D^x for tau in G, with u_1 = 1, such that
  (1) u_tau lambda u_tau^{-1} = tau(lambda) for all lambda in M and all tau in G,
  (2) D = direct sum over tau in G of M u_tau,
  (3) u_tau u_rho = f(tau, rho) u_{tau rho} for a normalized 2-cocycle f: G x G -> M^x, i.e. f(1, tau) = f(tau, 1) = 1.
Set u := u_sigma.

Step B (the p^2-th power of u lies in k^x). First, u^{p^2} != 0 because u is a unit of the division ring D. For lambda in M, conjugation by u restricts to sigma on M by (1); by induction, conjugation by u^i restricts to sigma^i on M for every i >= 0. Since sigma has order p^2, conjugation by u^{p^2} restricts to sigma^{p^2} = id_M. Thus u^{p^2} centralises M, i.e. u^{p^2} in C_D(M). By the double centralizer theorem ref_1 applied to the subfield M of the central simple algebra D: because dim_k(M) = p^2 = deg(D), M is a maximal subfield of D, and ref_1 gives C_D(M) = M. Hence u^{p^2} in M. (The same conclusion follows directly from the cocycle: an induction with u_{sigma^i} u_sigma = f(sigma^i, sigma) u_{sigma^{i+1}} gives u^i = a_i u_{sigma^i} with a_i in M^x for all i >= 0; for i = p^2 one has sigma^{p^2} = 1 and u_1 = 1, so u^{p^2} = a_{p^2} in M^x.) Now apply (1) with lambda = u^{p^2}, which we have just shown to lie in M: u u^{p^2} u^{-1} = sigma(u^{p^2}), while the left hand side is plainly u^{p^2}. Hence sigma(u^{p^2}) = u^{p^2}, so u^{p^2} in M^{<sigma>} = k. Since u^{p^2} != 0, we obtain b := u^{p^2} in k^x.

Step C (identification with the cyclic algebra (M, sigma, b)). Let B := direct sum_{i=0}^{p^2-1} M v^i be the k-algebra defined by v^{p^2} = b and v lambda = sigma(lambda) v for lambda in M. From the induction in Step B, M u^i = M u_{sigma^i} for every i >= 0; since {sigma^0, ..., sigma^{p^2-1}} = G, (2) gives D = direct sum_{i=0}^{p^2-1} M u^i, so each element of D is written uniquely as sum_i m_i u^i with m_i in M. Define the k-linear map Psi: B -> D by Psi(sum_i m_i v^i) = sum_i m_i u^i; it is a bijection and restricts to the identity on M (hence on k). It is multiplicative: for monomials, Psi(m v^i) Psi(m' v^j) = m u^i m' u^j = m sigma^i(m') u^{i+j} by (1) applied repeatedly. Write i + j = q p^2 + r with q >= 0 and 0 <= r < p^2; then u^{i+j} = (u^{p^2})^q u^r = b^q u^r in D by Step B, and v^{i+j} = (v^{p^2})^q v^r = b^q v^r in B by definition. Therefore Psi(m v^i) Psi(m' v^j) = m sigma^i(m') b^q Psi(v^r) = Psi((m v^i)(m' v^j)), so Psi is a k-algebra isomorphism B -> D, with Psi^{-1} fixing k elementwise.

Step D (producing the p-central element). Apply lemma_cyclic_p2_has_pcentral to the cyclic Galois extension M/k of degree p^2 with generator sigma, to the element b in k^x, and to the algebra B = direct sum_{i=0}^{p^2-1} M v^i with v^{p^2} = b and v lambda = sigma(lambda) v. Its conclusion is that v^p notin k and (v^p)^p in k. Define y := u^p = Psi(v^p) in D. Then y^p = u^{p^2} = b in k. Moreover y notin k: if y were in k, then v^p = Psi^{-1}(y) would lie in k because Psi^{-1} fixes k elementwise, contradicting v^p notin k. Hence y is an element of D with y notin k and y^p in k, as required.

The two cases exhaust all possibilities in the assumption 'x notin k and x^{p^2} in k', so in every case D contains a p-central element. Combined with the first direction, this proves the stated equivalence.

lemma_235.statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $F$-algebra. Let $k=F((u))$ with its $u$-adic valuation $v$. Then $D_k=D\otimes_F k$ is a central division $k$-algebra, the valuation $w$ extending $v$ satisfies $w(D_k^\times)=v(k^\times)$, its residue division ring is $D$, and the class of $D_k$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has the same order as the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$.
lemma_235.proof:
Let $n=\deg D$, so $\dim_F D=n^{2}<\infty$ and $Z(D)=F$. We write $\Lambda:=D((u))$ for the ring of formal Laurent series $x=\sum_{i\ge i_0(x)}d_i u^i$ with $i_0(x)\in\mathbb Z$, $d_i\in D$, where $u$ is a central indeterminate: addition is termwise and multiplication is given by the Cauchy product $c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}d_i e_j$, which is a finite sum because both supports are bounded below. Associativity, distributivity and the unit $1_D$ are checked exactly as for commutative Laurent series (all coefficients of $u^k$ on both sides of each identity are the same finite sums, since $u$ commutes with every $d\in D$). The field $k=F((u))$ embeds in $\Lambda$ through the scalar coefficients, which are central, so $\Lambda$ is a $k$-algebra.

Step 1 (the $k$-algebra isomorphism $D\otimes_F F((u))\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }D((u)$)). The map $\Phi\colon D\times F((u))\to\Lambda$, $(d,f)\mapsto df$ (i.e. $d\cdot\sum_i a_i u^i=\sum_i (a_i d)u^i$) is $F$-bilinear, so it induces an $F$-linear $\Phi\colon D\otimes_F F((u))\to\Lambda$, which is a ring homomorphism because $u$ is central. Fix an $F$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_N$ of $D$ with $N=n^2$. Every element of $D\otimes_F F((u))$ is uniquely of the form $\sum_{t=1}^{N} e_t\otimes f_t$ with $f_t=\sum_i a_{ti}u^i\in F((u))$, and
$$\Phi\Big(\sum_t e_t\otimes f_t\Big)=\sum_{i}\Big(\sum_t a_{ti}e_t\Big)u^i.$$
Conversely, given $\sum_i d_i u^i\in\Lambda$ with $d_i=\sum_t a_{ti}e_t$ uniquely, all $d_i$ (hence all $a_{ti}$) vanish for $i<i_0$, so each $f_t:=\sum_i a_{ti}u^i$ lies in $F((u))$, and $\sum_t e_t\otimes f_t$ maps to $\sum_i d_i u^i$. Thus $\Phi$ is bijective, an isomorphism of $k$-algebras; in particular $\dim_k\Lambda=\dim_F D=n^2$.

Step 2 (the Gauss valuation). For $x=\sum_i d_i u^i\ne 0$ set $w(x)=\min\{i:d_i\ne 0\}$, and $w(0)=\infty$. Then:
(a) $w(x)=\infty\iff x=0$ by definition.
(b) $w(x+y)\ge\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$, since all coefficients of $x+y$ of index $<\min\{w(x),w(y)\}$ vanish.
(c) Multiplicativity: let $m=w(x)$, $n=w(y)$, with leading coefficients $d_m\ne 0$, $e_n\ne 0$. Then $xy=\sum_{k\ge m+n}c_ku^k$ with $c_{m+n}=d_me_n$. Because $D$ is a division ring it has no zero divisors, so $d_me_n\ne 0$, and hence $w(xy)=m+n=w(x)+w(y)$. (This is the only place where the hypothesis that $D$ is a division ring is used; the case $D=F$, $n=1$, is covered since $F$ is a field.)
(d) $w$ extends $v$: for $a=\sum_i a_i u^i\in k^{\times}$ the coefficients in $\Lambda$ are $a_i\cdot 1_D$, which vanish exactly when $a_i=0$, so $w(a)=\min\{i:a_i\ne0\}=v(a)$. In particular $w(u)=1$.
Thus $w$ is a (Krull) valuation on the ring $\Lambda$ extending the $u$-adic valuation of $k$.

Step 3 (every nonzero element is a unit; the value group). Let $x\ne0$ in $\Lambda$ and put $m=w(x)$, so $x=\sum_{i\ge m}d_iu^i$ with $d_m\ne0$. Since $u$ is central,
$$x=u^{m}\Big(\sum_{n\ge0}d_{m+n}u^{n}\Big)=u^{m}d_m(1+z),\qquad z:=\sum_{n\ge1}d_m^{-1}d_{m+n}u^{n}\in uD[[u]].$$
We claim $1+z$ is a unit of $D[[u]]$ with two-sided inverse $s=\sum_{n\ge0}(-z)^n$. Well-definedness: $z\in uD[[u]]$ gives $z^{n}\in u^{n}D[[u]]$, so for each fixed index $i$ the coefficient of $u^i$ in the partial sum $s_N:=\sum_{n=0}^{N}(-z)^n$ is independent of $N$ once $N\ge i$; hence $s:=\lim_N s_N$ is a well-defined element of $D[[u]]$. Telescoping identity: for every $N$,
$$(1+z)s_N=\sum_{n=0}^{N}(-z)^n-\sum_{n=1}^{N+1}(-z)^n=1-(-z)^{N+1},$$
and likewise $s_N(1+z)=1-(-z)^{N+1}$.
Now fix an index $i$ and take $N\ge i$. Write $s=s_N+t_N$ with $t_N=\sum_{n>N}(-z)^n$. Each summand $(-z)^n$ lies in $u^{n}D[[u]]\subseteq u^{N+1}D[[u]]$, so $t_N\in u^{N+1}D[[u]]$. Then
$$(1+z)s=1-(-z)^{N+1}+(1+z)t_N,$$
where $(-z)^{N+1}\in u^{N+1}D[[u]]\subseteq u^{i+1}D[[u]]$, and $(1+z)t_N=t_N+zt_N\in u^{N+1}D[[u]]+u^{N+2}D[[u]]\subseteq u^{i+1}D[[u]]$. Hence the coefficient of $u^i$ in $(1+z)s$ equals the coefficient of $u^i$ in $1$, namely $\delta_{0i}$. As $i$ was arbitrary, $(1+z)s=1$; symmetrically $s(1+z)=1$. (Note the sign: the telescoping gives $1-(-z)^{N+1}$, which converges coefficientwise to $1$.)
Therefore $x$ is invertible, with
$$x^{-1}=(1+z)^{-1}d_m^{-1}u^{-m}=s\,d_m^{-1}u^{-m}\in\Lambda,$$
and indeed $x\,x^{-1}=u^{m}d_m(1+z)s\,d_m^{-1}u^{-m}=u^{m}d_md_m^{-1}u^{-m}=1$. So $\Lambda$ is a division ring. Consequently $w(\Lambda^{\times})=w(\Lambda\setminus\{0\})=\mathbb Z$ (every $m\in\mathbb Z$ occurs, e.g. $w(u^{m})=m$), and since $v(k^{\times})=\mathbb Z$ we obtain
$$w(\Lambda^{\times})=\mathbb Z=v(k^{\times}).$$

Step 4 (the centre; $D_k$ is central division over $k$). Let $x=\sum_i d_iu^i\in Z(\Lambda)$. For every $d\in D\subset\Lambda$, $0=xd-dx=\sum_i(d_id-dd_i)u^i$, so $d_id=dd_i$ for all $d\in D$, i.e. $d_i\in Z(D)=F$. Thus $x\in F((u))=k$, and the reverse inclusion $k\subseteq Z(\Lambda)$ holds by construction. Hence $Z(\Lambda)=k$. By Step 1, $\Lambda\cong D\otimes_F k$ and $\dim_k\Lambda=n^2<\infty$; combined with Step 3 ($\Lambda$ a division ring) and $Z(\Lambda)=k$, this says exactly that $D_k=D\otimes_F k$ is a central division $k$-algebra (of degree $n$), in particular a central simple $k$-algebra.

Step 5 (valuation ring, maximal ideal, residue division ring). By definition of $w$,
$$\mathcal O_w=\{x\in\Lambda:w(x)\ge0\}=D[[u]],\qquad \mathfrak M_w=\{x\in\Lambda:w(x)>0\}=uD[[u]].$$
$\mathfrak M_w$ is a two-sided ideal of $\mathcal O_w$: if $w(a)>0$ and $r\in\mathcal O_w$ then $w(ar)=w(ra)=w(a)+w(r)>0$ by Step 2(c), and sums of elements of positive value have positive value by Step 2(b). Moreover $\mathcal O_w\setminus\mathfrak M_w=\{x:w(x)=0\}=\mathcal O_w^{\times}$: if $w(x)=0$ then Step 3 with $m=0$ gives $x=d_0(1+z)$ with $d_0\in D^{\times}$, $z\in uD[[u]]$, and $x^{-1}=s\,d_0^{-1}\in D[[u]]=\mathcal O_w$; conversely, if $x,y\in\mathcal O_w$ with $xy=1$ then $0=w(1)=w(x)+w(y)$ with both terms $\ge0$, so $w(x)=0$. Thus $\mathcal O_w$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak M_w$, and its residue ring $\mathcal O_w/\mathfrak M_w$ is a division ring (the image of any nonzero element has value $0$, hence is a unit).
The constant-term map $\varepsilon\colon D[[u]]\to D$, $\sum_{i\ge0}d_iu^i\mapsto d_0$, is a surjective ring homomorphism (surjective because constant series map identically; multiplicative because the constant term of a Cauchy product is the product of the constant terms) with kernel $\{\sum_{i\ge0}d_iu^i:d_0=0\}=uD[[u]]=\mathfrak M_w$. Hence
$$\bar\Lambda:=\mathcal O_w/\mathfrak M_w\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ D.$$
Under this isomorphism the residue field of $k$, namely $\mathcal O_v/M_v=F[[u]]/(u)\simeq F$, maps to $F\cdot1_D\subset D$, which is precisely the map on residue rings induced by the inclusion $k\hookrightarrow\Lambda$. So the residue division ring of $(\Lambda,w)$ is $D$.
(Remark, not used below: $k=F((u))$ is complete, hence henselian, for $v$, and a henselian valuation on the centre of a division ring finite-dimensional over that centre admits a unique extension to the division ring; equivalently $w(x)=v(\mathrm{Nrd}_{\Lambda/k}(x))/n$. So the Gauss valuation of Step 2 is *the* extension of $v$ to $D_k$.)

Step 6 (order of the Brauer class). By Step 1 and Step 4, $D\otimes_F k=D\otimes_F F((u))$ is a central simple $k$-algebra. We apply the proved lemma \texttt{lemma\_exp\_laurent\_series\_injective} (Spark), whose statement with base field $F$ and central simple algebra $A=D$ reads: the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ and the class of $D\otimes_F F((u))$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F((u)))$ have the same order. Since $k=F((u))$ and $D_k=D\otimes_F F((u))$, the class $[D_k]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has the same order as $[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(F)$ (both orders being $1$ in the split case $D\cong M_n(F)$, which here forces $D=F$ and $D_k=k$).

Collecting the steps: Step 4 gives that $D_k$ is a central division $k$-algebra; Step 2(d) gives that $w$ extends $v$; Step 3 gives $w(D_k^{\times})=\mathbb Z=v(k^{\times})$; Step 5 identifies the residue division ring with $D$; Step 6 identifies the orders of the Brauer classes. This proves all the asserted claims. (The assumption $\operatorname{char}F=p>2$ is never used; the argument is valid in every characteristic.)

lemma_236.statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $F$-algebra containing no element $a\notin F$ with $a^p\in F$. Then $D\otimes_F F((u))$ contains no element $x\notin F((u))$ with $x^p\in F((u))$.
lemma_236.proof:
Let $k:=F((u))$ be the Laurent series field over $F$, with its $u$-adic valuation $v$: for $0\neq f=\sum_{n\ge n_0}\alpha_n u^n\in k$ (with $\alpha_{n_0}\neq 0$) set $v(f)=n_0$, and $v(0)=\infty$. Then $(k,v)$ is a discretely valued field with value group $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, of characteristic $p>0$.

Step 1: Identify $D\otimes_F k$ with the Laurent series ring $D((u))$.
Let $D((u))$ denote the ring of formal series $\sum_{n\ge n_0} d_n u^n$ with $d_n\in D$ and $n_0\in\mathbb Z$, added coefficientwise and multiplied by convolution; the indeterminate $u$ is declared central, so $u d=d u$ for all $d\in D$. Because exponents are bounded below, the convolution sums defining coefficients are finite, so this is an associative unital ring, and it is an $F$-algebra containing $D$ and $k$.
The $F$-bilinear map $D\times k\to D((u))$, $(d,f)\mapsto df=\sum_n (\alpha_n d)u^n$ (note $\alpha_n d=d\alpha_n$ since $\alpha_n\in F=Z(D)$), induces an $F$-linear $\Phi\colon D\otimes_F k\to D((u))$, which is plainly $k$-linear and a ring homomorphism. Fix an $F$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $D$ (possible since $\dim_F D=\deg(D)^2<\infty$). Every element of $D\otimes_F k$ is uniquely $\sum_{j=1}^r e_j\otimes f_j$ with $f_j\in k$, and $\Phi(\sum_j e_j\otimes f_j)=\sum_n(\sum_j \beta_{j,n}e_j)u^n$ where $f_j=\sum_n\beta_{j,n}u^n$. This is zero iff every $\sum_j\beta_{j,n}e_j=0$, iff all $\beta_{j,n}=0$ (basis), iff all $f_j=0$: $\Phi$ is injective. Conversely, given $g=\sum_n d_nu^n\in D((u))$, write $d_n=\sum_j\beta_{j,n}e_j$; then $g=\sum_{j=1}^r e_j\otimes(\sum_n\beta_{j,n}u^n)$, a finite sum, so $\Phi$ is surjective. Hence $A:=D\otimes_F k\cong D((u))$ as $k$-algebras.

Step 2: $A$ is a division ring.
Let $0\neq f=\sum_{n\ge m}d_nu^n\in D((u))$ with $d_m\neq0$. Then $f=u^m d_m(1-h)$ where $h=-\sum_{k\ge1}d_m^{-1}d_{m+k}u^k\in uD[[u]]$. Since $u$ is central, $h^j\in u^jD[[u]]$, so $\sum_{j\ge0}h^j$ is a well-defined element of $D[[u]]$ (the coefficient of $u^t$ receives contributions only from $h^0,\dots,h^t$), and it is the inverse of $1-h$ because the partial sums satisfy $(1-h)\sum_{j=0}^{N}h^j=1-h^{N+1}$ with $h^{N+1}\in u^{N+1}D[[u]]$. Thus $f^{-1}=(\sum_{j\ge0}h^j)d_m^{-1}u^{-m}$ exists. So $A$ is a division ring.

Step 3: The center of $A$ is $k$.
If $z=\sum_n z_nu^n$ is central, then for every $e\in D$, $\sum_n z_ne\,u^n=ze=ez=\sum_n e z_n\,u^n$, so $z_ne=ez_n$ for all $n$ and all $e\in D$, i.e. $z_n\in Z(D)=F$; hence $z\in F((u))=k$. The reverse inclusion is clear since $k$ is commutative and $u$ is central. Thus $A$ is a central division $k$-algebra (of degree $\deg D$, as $\dim_k A=\dim_F D$ by Step 1).

Step 4: The valuation $w$ on $A$.
Define $w\colon A\to\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\}$ by $w(0)=\infty$ and $w(f)=\min\{n:d_n\neq0\}$ for $f\neq0$. Then:
(i) $w(f)=\infty\iff f=0$.
(ii) $w(f+g)\ge\min\{w(f),w(g)\}$, clear from the definition.
(iii) $w(fg)=w(f)+w(g)$: writing $f=u^m(d_0+d_1u+\cdots)$, $g=u^n(e_0+e_1u+\cdots)$ with $d_0,e_0\neq0$ and using that $u$ is central, $fg=u^{m+n}(d_0e_0+(\text{terms of degree}\ge1))$, and $d_0e_0\neq0$ because $D$ is a division ring (no zero divisors). Hence $w(fg)=m+n$.
(iv) $w(1)=0$; $w(u)=1$, so $w(A^\times)=\mathbb Z$.
(v) $w$ extends $v$: for $0\neq f\in k$, $w(f)$ is the least index with nonzero coefficient, which is exactly $v(f)$.
Moreover $k$ is complete for $v$: given a $v$-Cauchy sequence $(f_s)$ in $k$, for each $n$ the coefficient of $u^n$ in $f_s$ is eventually constant (Cauchy with $N=n+1$), and the $f_s$ are eventually bounded below in valuation (Cauchy with $N=n_0$ gives $v(f_s)\ge\min(v(f_{s_0}),n_0)$ for $s\ge s_0$), so the coefficientwise limit $g=\sum_nc_nu^n$ is a legitimate Laurent series in $k$ with $f_s\to g$. Thus $(k,v)$ satisfies the field-theoretic hypotheses of lemma_229.

Step 5: The graded ring $\mathrm{gr}_w(A)$.
For $\gamma\in\mathbb Z$, $A^{\ge\gamma}/A^{>\gamma}$ is described by the map $\rho_\gamma\colon A^{\ge\gamma}\to D$, $\rho_\gamma(x)=d_0$ where $xu^{-\gamma}=\sum_{n\ge0}d_nu^n$; $\rho_\gamma$ is additive, surjective (take $x=du^\gamma$), with kernel $\{x:w(x)>\gamma\}=A^{>\gamma}$. For $\gamma\notin\mathbb Z$ the group $A^{\ge\gamma}/A^{>\gamma}$ is $0$. Since $u$ is central, $\rho_{\gamma+\delta}(xy)=\rho_\gamma(x)\rho_\delta(y)$: indeed $(xy)u^{-\gamma-\delta}=(xu^{-\gamma})(yu^{-\delta})$ and the leading coefficient of a product of two series in $D[[u]]$ is the product of the leading coefficients (valid as $D$ has no zero divisors). Hence, writing $U$ for the central homogeneous unit of degree $1$ given by the initial form of $u$, we have a graded isomorphism
$$\mathrm{gr}_w(A)\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\; D[U,U^{-1}],\qquad \overline{x}\,\ (\bmod A^{>\gamma})\ \longmapsto\ \rho_\gamma(x)\,U^{\gamma},$$
with multiplication $(dU^\gamma)(eU^\delta)=(de)U^{\gamma+\delta}$. Under this identification the graded subring $\mathrm{gr}_v(k)$, whose degree-$\delta$ piece is $\{aU^\delta:a\in F\}$, becomes $F[U,U^{-1}]$.

Step 6: Verification of the graded hypothesis of lemma_229.
Let $y\in\mathrm{gr}_w(A)$ be homogeneous with $y^p\in\mathrm{gr}(k)$. If $y=0$ there is nothing to prove, so write $y=dU^\gamma$ with $\gamma\in\mathbb Z$ and $0\neq d\in D$. Since $U$ is central and the characteristic is $p$,
$$y^p=(dU^\gamma)^p=d^pU^{p\gamma}.$$
This element is homogeneous of degree $p\gamma$ and lies in the graded subring $\mathrm{gr}(k)=F[U,U^{-1}]$; because $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ is a graded subring, a homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(A)$ belonging to $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ lies in its degree-$p\gamma$ piece, so $d^pU^{p\gamma}\in F\,U^{p\gamma}$, i.e. $d^p\in F$. By the hypothesis on $D$ (no element of $D$ outside $F$ has its $p$-th power in $F$), we must have $d\in F$. Therefore $y=dU^\gamma\in F\,U^\gamma\subset\mathrm{gr}(k)$. Thus every homogeneous element of $\mathrm{gr}_w(A)$ whose $p$-th power lies in $\mathrm{gr}(k)$ already lies in $\mathrm{gr}(k)$.

Step 7: Conclusion.
We have checked all hypotheses of lemma_229 (Spark) for the complete discretely valued field $(k,v)=(F((u)),u\text{-adic})$ with $v(k^\times)=\mathbb Z$, of characteristic $p>0$, for the central division $k$-algebra $A\cong D\otimes_F F((u))$ with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, and for the graded condition of Step 6. Lemma_229 yields: $A$ contains no element $x$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^p\in k$. Translating back through the isomorphism of Step 1, this says exactly that $D\otimes_F F((u))$ contains no element $x\notin F((u))$ with $x^p\in F((u))$, which is the claim.

(Remark on the mechanism, not needed for the logic: the graded condition of Step 6 is the shadow of the direct approximation argument — for $x^p=c\in k^\times$ one gets $p\,w(x)=v(c)$ from Step 4(iii), so $y=xu^{-w(x)}$ has $w(y)=0$ and $y^p\in\mathcal O_k^\times$ with residue $\bar y^{\,p}=\bar c\in F$, whence $\bar y=a_0\in F$ by the hypothesis on $D$; then $x_1=x-a_0u^{w(x)}$ satisfies $x_1^p\in k$ and $w(x_1)\ge w(x)+1$. Iterating produces a Laurent series $s\in F((u))$ with $w(x-s)=\infty$, i.e. $x=s\in k$.)

lemma_237.statement: Let $(k,v)$ be a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic $p>2$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, endowed with the valuation $w$ extending $v$, with residue division ring $\bar D$ and residue field $\bar k$. If $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\cdot[\bar D:\bar k]<p^{2}$, then $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$; in particular $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_237.proof:
We write the proof in full detail, checking every inclusion and every index.

**Notation.** Let $\mathcal O_D=\{x\in D: w(x)\ge 0\}$, $M_D=\{x\in D: w(x)>0\}$, so that $\bar D=\mathcal O_D/M_D$ is the residue division ring of the valued division ring $(D,w)$; similarly $\mathcal O_k=\{a\in k:v(a)\ge0\}=\mathcal O_D\cap k$, $M_k=\{a\in k:v(a)>0\}=M_D\cap k$ and $\bar k=\mathcal O_k/M_k$. Because $w$ extends $v$, $\mathcal O_k=\mathcal O_D\cap k$ and $M_k=M_D\cap\mathcal O_k$ hold by definition.

We record two elementary facts that will be used repeatedly.

(F1) $M_D$ is the unique maximal left (right) ideal of $\mathcal O_D$, and $\bar D$ is a division ring: indeed if $\bar x\in\bar D$ is non-zero with $x\in\mathcal O_D$, then $w(x)=0$ (since $w(x)>0$ would mean $x\in M_D$, i.e. $\bar x=0$), so $w(x^{-1})=-w(x)=0$ and $x^{-1}\in\mathcal O_D$, whence $\overline{x^{-1}}=\bar x^{-1}$. Also, since $k\subseteq Z(D)$, for $a\in\mathcal O_k$ and $x\in\mathcal O_D$ we have $ax=xa$, hence $\bar a\bar x=\bar x\bar a$ in $\bar D$; so the image of $\bar k$ lies in $Z(\bar D)$ and $\bar D$ is a $\bar k$-vector space, $[\bar D:\bar k]=\dim_{\bar k}\bar D$.

(F2) The hypothesis $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\cdot[\bar D:\bar k]<p^{2}$ forces both factors to be finite, since $[\bar D:\bar k]\ge 1$ and $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\ge 1$ (each factor being a positive integer or $\infty$; if one were $\infty$ the product would be $\infty$).

**Step 1: a Galois maximal subfield has degree $p^{2}$.** Suppose, for a contradiction, that $D$ contains a maximal subfield $L$ which is Galois over $k$. Since $L$ is a subfield of $D$ containing $k$, the double centralizer theorem (ref_1) says that $C_D(L)$ is a central simple $L$-algebra of degree $\deg(D)/[L:k]=p^{2}/[L:k]$, and that $L$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ if and only if $C_D(L)=L$. As $L$ is maximal by assumption, $C_D(L)=L$, which is an $L$-algebra of degree $1$; hence $p^{2}/[L:k]=1$, i.e.
$$[L:k]=p^{2}.$$

**Step 2: the residue field of $L$ embeds in $\bar D$ as a $\bar k$-subspace.** Give $L$ the restricted valuation $w|_L$, and put $\mathcal O_L=\{x\in L:w(x)\ge0\}=\mathcal O_D\cap L$ and $M_L=\{x\in L:w(x)>0\}$. Then:
- $M_L=\mathcal O_L\cap M_D$: indeed $\mathcal O_L\cap M_D=\{x\in L: w(x)\ge0\ \text{and}\ w(x)>0\}=\{x\in L:w(x)>0\}=M_L$.
- Hence the inclusion $\iota:\mathcal O_L\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_D$ satisfies $\iota(M_L)\subseteq M_D$ and induces an injective ring homomorphism $\bar\iota:\bar L=\mathcal O_L/M_L\hookrightarrow \mathcal O_D/M_D=\bar D$, $\bar x\mapsto\bar x$, whose kernel is $(\mathcal O_L\cap M_D)/M_L=0$.
- $\bar L$ is a field: if $0\ne\bar x\in\bar L$ with $x\in\mathcal O_L$, then $w(x)=0$ (otherwise $x\in M_L$ and $\bar x=0$), so $x^{-1}\in L$ has $w(x^{-1})=0$ and $\overline{x^{-1}}=\bar x^{-1}\in\bar L$.
- The structure maps compose: the canonical map $\bar k\to\bar L$ is injective (its kernel is $(\mathcal O_k\cap M_L)/M_k=0$, because $\mathcal O_k\cap M_L=\{a\in k: v(a)>0\}=M_k$), and the composite $\bar k\hookrightarrow\bar L\xrightarrow{\ \bar\iota\ }\bar D$ is the standard inclusion of (F1). Consequently $\bar\iota(\bar L)$ is a $\bar k$-linear subspace of the $\bar k$-vector space $\bar D$, and therefore
$$[\bar L:\bar k]=\dim_{\bar k}\bar L\ \le\ \dim_{\bar k}\bar D=[\bar D:\bar k].\qquad(1)$$
(Both sides are finite by (F2) and the inequality.)

**Step 3: comparison of value groups.** Since $k^{\times}\subseteq L^{\times}\subseteq D^{\times}$, we have a tower of abelian groups
$$v(k^{\times})\ \subseteq\ w(L^{\times})\ \subseteq\ w(D^{\times}),$$
and by (F2) the top index $[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]$ is finite. The tower formula for indices therefore gives
$$[w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]=[w(D^{\times}):w(L^{\times})]\cdot[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})],$$
with both factors positive integers, hence
$$[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\ \le\ [w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})].\qquad(2)$$

**Step 4: defectlessness of $L/k$ and the contradiction.** The field $k$ is henselian for the discrete valuation $v$, and $L/k$ is a finite Galois extension endowed with the valuation $w|_L$ extending $v$, with residue field $\bar L$. By lemma_96 (defectlessness of finite Galois extensions over a henselian discretely valued field),
$$[L:k]=[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k].$$
Combining this with $[L:k]=p^{2}$ from Step 1 and the inequalities (1) and (2), we obtain
$$p^{2}=[w(L^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\cdot[\bar L:\bar k]\ \le\ [w(D^{\times}):v(k^{\times})]\cdot[\bar D:\bar k]\ <\ p^{2},$$
an impossibility. Hence $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$.

**Step 5: the crossed-product consequence.** Suppose $D$ were isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, where $L$ is a $G$-Galois $k$-algebra (etale of dimension $|G|=p^{2}=\deg D$ with $L^{G}=k$) and $c:G\times G\to L^{\times}$ a $2$-cocycle. By lemma_133 (applied with $n=\deg D=p^{2}=|G|$), $L$ is a field, and its image in $D$ under such an isomorphism is a maximal subfield of $D$ which is Galois over $k$ with Galois group $G$. This contradicts the conclusion of Step 4. Therefore $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.

This completes the proof. (Note that no perfection hypothesis on $\bar k$ was needed; the argument covers in particular the immediate case $w(D^{\times})=v(k^{\times})$, $\bar D=\bar k$, where the product equals $1<p^{2}$.)

lemma_238.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$, write $\wp(k)=\{y^{p}-y:y\in k\}$, and let $c_1,c_2\in k$ whose images in the $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space $k/\wp(k)$ are linearly independent. Let $x_1,x_2$ lie in a common extension field of $k$ with $x_i^{p}-x_i=c_i$, and put $L=k(x_1,x_2)$. Then $L/k$ is a Galois extension of degree $p^{2}$ with Galois group isomorphic to $C_p\times C_p$, and the intermediate fields of $L$ of degree $p$ over $k$ are exactly the fields $k(a_1x_1+a_2x_2)$ with $(a_1,a_2)\in\mathbb{F}_p^{2}\setminus\{0\}$.
lemma_238.proof:
We write $\wp(t)=t^{p}-t$. The proof is self-contained and proceeds in seven steps.

STEP 0 (elementary properties of $\wp$). Since the characteristic is $p$, $(u+v)^{p}=u^{p}+v^{p}$, so $\wp$ is additive: $\wp(u+v)=\wp(u)+\wp(v)$; also $\wp(\lambda t)=\lambda^{p}t^{p}-\lambda t=\lambda(t^{p}-t)=\lambda\wp(t)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$, because $\lambda^{p}=\lambda$. The kernel of $\wp$ on any field of characteristic $p$ is exactly $\mathbb{F}_{p}$: $\wp(t)=0$ means $t^{p}=t$, and the polynomial $T^{p}-T$ has at most $p$ roots while all $p$ elements of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ are roots. Since $\wp(nt)=n\wp(t)$ for every integer $n$, we have $p\cdot\overline{t}=\overline{pt}=\overline{0}$ in $k/\wp(k)$, so $k/\wp(k)$ is an $\mathbb{F}_{p}$-vector space; the hypothesis says precisely that $\alpha_{1}c_{1}+\alpha_{2}c_{2}\in\wp(k)$ with $\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ forces $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0$. In particular $\overline{c}_{i}\neq0$, i.e. $c_{i}\notin\wp(k)$, and $c_{i}\neq0$ (as $0=\wp(0)\in\wp(k)$). Finally, if $z^{p}-z=a$ then the roots of $T^{p}-T-a$ are exactly the $p$ distinct elements $z+j$, $j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$, since $(z+j)^{p}-(z+j)=z^{p}-z+(j^{p}-j)=a$, and the derivative $-1\neq0$ makes them simple.

STEP 1 (irreducibility criterion over an arbitrary base). Let $K$ be any extension field of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $a\in K$. Then $T^{p}-T-a$ is irreducible over $K$ if and only if $a\notin\wp(K)$. If $a=\wp(u)$ with $u\in K$ the polynomial has the root $u$, so it is reducible. Conversely assume $a\notin\wp(K)$, let $\theta$ be a root in an extension field, and let $m\in K[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\theta$ over $K$, of degree $d\ge1$. Then $m\mid T^{p}-T-a$ in $K[T]$, so in a fixed algebraic closure the roots of $m$ are among $\{\theta+j:j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$. Put $S=\{j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:\theta+j \text{ is a root of } m\}$; then $0\in S$, $|S|=d$, and since $m$ is separable, $m(T)=\prod_{j\in S}(T-(\theta+j))$. The coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $m$ is $-(d\theta+\sum_{j\in S}j)\in K$. If $d<p$, then $d\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\subseteq K^{\times}$, and $\theta=-d^{-1}\cdot(\text{that coefficient})-d^{-1}\sum_{j\in S}j\in K$, whence $a=\wp(\theta)\in\wp(K)$, a contradiction. Thus $d=p$ and $T^{p}-T-a$ is irreducible over $K$.

STEP 2 (the key computation: $\wp(k(x))\cap k=\wp(k)+\mathbb{F}_{p}c$). Let $c\in k\setminus\wp(k)$, let $x$ satisfy $x^{p}-x=c$, and put $K=k(x)$. By Step 1 (with $K=k$), $[K:k]=p$. The field $K$ contains all roots $x+j$, $j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$, of the separable polynomial $T^{p}-T-c$, so $K/k$ is Galois with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)=\{\sigma_{j}\}_{j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}$, $\sigma_{j}(x)=x+j$; note $\sigma_{j}\sigma_{j'}=\sigma_{j+j'}$, so $j\mapsto\sigma_{j}$ is a group isomorphism $(\mathbb{F}_{p},+)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)$.
Now let $y\in K$ satisfy $\wp(y)\in k$. For each $j$, using that $\sigma_{j}$ fixes $k$ and that $\wp$ is additive and commutes with $\sigma_{j}$,
$\wp(\sigma_{j}(y)-y)=\sigma_{j}(y^{p}-y)-(y^{p}-y)=\sigma_{j}(\wp(y))-\wp(y)=0$,
so by Step 0, $\lambda(\sigma_{j}):=\sigma_{j}(y)-y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$. The map $\lambda:\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)\to(\mathbb{F}_{p},+)$ is a homomorphism: $\sigma\tau(y)-y=(\sigma\tau(y)-\tau(y))+(\tau(y)-y)=\lambda(\sigma)+\lambda(\tau)$. Write $\mu:=\lambda(\sigma_{1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$; then $\lambda(\sigma_{j})=\lambda(\sigma_{1}^{j})=j\mu$. If $\mu=0$, every $\sigma_{j}$ fixes $y$, so $y\in K^{\mathrm{Gal}(K/k)}=k$ (Galois correspondence). If $\mu\ne0$, then $\sigma_{j}(y-\mu x)=(y+j\mu)-(\mu x+\mu j)=y-\mu x$ for all $j$, so $y-\mu x\in k$, say $y-\mu x=b\in k$. In both cases $y=\mu x+b$ with $\mu\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$, $b\in k$, and then
$\wp(y)=\wp(\mu x)+\wp(b)=\mu\wp(x)+\wp(b)=\mu c+\wp(b)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}c+\wp(k)$.
This proves $\wp(K)\cap k\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{p}c+\wp(k)$. The reverse inclusion holds because $\wp(k)\subseteq\wp(K)\cap k$ and $\wp(\mu x)=\mu c$ for $\mu\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$. Hence $\wp(K)\cap k=\wp(k)+\mathbb{F}_{p}c$.

STEP 3 ($[L:k]=p^{2}$ and $x_{2}\notin k(x_{1})$). Apply Step 2 with $c=c_{1}$, $x=x_{1}$, $K=k(x_{1})$; then $[K:k]=p$ and $\wp(K)\cap k=\wp(k)+\mathbb{F}_{p}c_{1}$. If $x_{2}\in K$, then $c_{2}=\wp(x_{2})\in\wp(K)\cap k$, so $c_{2}=\wp(b)+\lambda c_{1}$ for some $b\in k$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$, i.e. $\overline{c}_{2}-\lambda\overline{c}_{1}=\overline{0}$ in $k/\wp(k)$; this is a nontrivial $\mathbb{F}_{p}$-linear relation between $\overline{c}_{1}$ and $\overline{c}_{2}$ (the coefficient of $\overline{c}_{2}$ is $1\neq0$), contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $x_{2}\notin K$; equivalently $c_{2}\notin\wp(K)$, and Step 1 applied over the base field $K$ gives $[L:K]=[K(x_{2}):K]=p$. Therefore $[L:k]=[L:K]\,[K:k]=p\cdot p=p^{2}$.

STEP 4 ($L/k$ is Galois with group $C_{p}\times C_{p}$). Every root of $T^{p}-T-c_{i}$ is $x_{i}+j$ with $j\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ (Step 0), hence lies in $L$; so $L$ is the splitting field over $k$ of the separable polynomial $f(T)=(T^{p}-T-c_{1})(T^{p}-T-c_{2})$ (separable because $f'$ has no common root with $f$: the derivative of each factor is $-1$). Thus $L/k$ is Galois and $|\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)|=[L:k]=p^{2}$. For $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$, $\sigma(x_{i})$ is again a root of $T^{p}-T-c_{i}$, so $\sigma(x_{i})=x_{i}+a_{i}$ with $a_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$. Since $L=k(x_{1},x_{2})$, $\sigma$ is determined by $(a_{1},a_{2})$, so
$\Phi:\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\longrightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2},\qquad \sigma\longmapsto(\sigma(x_{1})-x_{1},\ \sigma(x_{2})-x_{2})$
is injective. It is a homomorphism: $\sigma\tau(x_{i})-x_{i}=\sigma(x_{i}-\tau(x_{i})+\tau(x_{i}))$... explicitly, $\sigma\tau(x_{i})-x_{i}=\sigma(x_{i})-\sigma(x_{i})$... writing it out, $\sigma\tau(x_{i})=\sigma(x_{i}+b_{i})=\sigma(x_{i})+b_{i}=(x_{i}+a_{i})+b_{i}$ where $a_{i}=\sigma(x_{i})-x_{i}$, $b_{i}=\tau(x_{i})-x_{i}$, so $\Phi(\sigma\tau)=\Phi(\sigma)+\Phi(\tau)$. As $|\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)|=p^{2}=|\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}|$, the injective homomorphism $\Phi$ is a group isomorphism. Hence $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\simeq(\mathbb{F}_{p},+)\times(\mathbb{F}_{p},+)\simeq C_{p}\times C_{p}$. We denote by $\sigma_{(a,b)}$ the automorphism with $x_{1}\mapsto x_{1}+a$, $x_{2}\mapsto x_{2}+b$.

STEP 5 (the fields $k(a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2})$ have degree $p$). Let $v=(a_{1},a_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$ and $\theta_{v}=a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2}$. Using $a_{i}^{p}=a_{i}$ and additivity of $\wp$,
$\wp(\theta_{v})=a_{1}^{p}(x_{1}^{p}-x_{1})+a_{2}^{p}(x_{2}^{p}-x_{2})=a_{1}c_{1}+a_{2}c_{2}$.
This element is not in $\wp(k)$: if $a_{1}c_{1}+a_{2}c_{2}=\wp(b)$ for some $b\in k$, then $a_{1}\overline{c}_{1}+a_{2}\overline{c}_{2}=\overline{0}$ in $k/\wp(k)$, forcing $a_{1}=a_{2}=0$ by hypothesis, a contradiction. (In particular $\theta_{v}\notin k$, since $\theta_{v}\in k$ would give $\wp(\theta_{v})\in\wp(k)$.) The subgroup of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ fixing the field $k(\theta_{v})$ is
$\mathrm{Gal}(L/k(\theta_{v}))=\{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/k):\sigma(\theta_{v})=\theta_{v}\}=\{\sigma_{(a,b)}:a_{1}a+a_{2}b=0\}=\ker\varphi_{v}$,
where $\varphi_{v}:\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}$, $(a,b)\mapsto a_{1}a+a_{2}b$, is a nonzero $\mathbb{F}_{p}$-linear form (nonzero because $v\ne0$). Its kernel is a $1$-dimensional subspace of the $2$-dimensional space $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}$, hence has $p$ elements. By the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, $[L:k(\theta_{v})]=|\ker\varphi_{v}|=p$, so $[k(\theta_{v}):k]=[L:k]/[L:k(\theta_{v})]=p^{2}/p=p$, and $k(\theta_{v})=L^{\ker\varphi_{v}}$.

STEP 6 (every intermediate field of degree $p$ arises this way). Let $E$ be an intermediate field with $[E:k]=p$. By the Galois correspondence for the Galois extension $L/k$, $H:=\mathrm{Gal}(L/E)$ is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ with $[L:H]=[E:k]=p$, i.e. $|H|=p$, and $E=L^{H}$. Transporting by the isomorphism $\Phi$ of Step 4, $\Phi(H)$ is a subgroup of order $p$ of the $\mathbb{F}_{p}$-vector space $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}$; being closed under addition and under multiplication by scalars of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ (multiples are sums), it is a $1$-dimensional subspace. Every $1$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}$ is the kernel of a nonzero linear form: indeed, if $\Phi(H)=\mathbb{F}_{p}(a,b)$ with $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, take $(a_{1},a_{2}):=(b,-a)$ (which is nonzero) and $v:=(a_{1},a_{2})$; then $\varphi_{v}(a,b)=ba-ab=0$ gives $\Phi(H)\subseteq\ker\varphi_{v}$, and both sides have $p$ elements, so $\Phi(H)=\ker\varphi_{v}$. By Step 5, $k(\theta_{v})=L^{\ker\varphi_{v}}=L^{\Phi(H)}=L^{H}=E$. Thus $E=k(a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2})$ for some $(a_{1},a_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$. Combining with Step 5, the intermediate fields of $L$ of degree $p$ over $k$ are exactly the fields $k(a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2})$ with $(a_{1},a_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$.

STEP 7 (counting, for completeness). For $v,v'\ne0$, $k(\theta_{v})=k(\theta_{v'})$ if and only if $v'\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}v$: if $v'=\lambda v$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}$ then $\theta_{v'}=\lambda\theta_{v}$ and $\theta_{v}=\lambda^{-1}\theta_{v'}$, so the fields coincide; conversely, if the lines $\mathbb{F}_{p}v\ne\mathbb{F}_{p}v'$ are distinct then $\ker\varphi_{v}\ne\ker\varphi_{v'}$ (a $1$-dimensional space determines its kernel line bijectively, since $v\mapsto\ker\varphi_{v}$ is injective on lines by nondegeneracy of the dot product), and the Galois correspondence, being a bijection, gives $L^{\ker\varphi_{v}}\ne L^{\ker\varphi_{v'}}$. Hence there are exactly $(p^{2}-1)/(p-1)=p+1$ such intermediate fields.

Steps 3, 4, 5 and 6 give all the claims of the lemma: $L/k$ is Galois of degree $p^{2}$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)\simeq C_{p}\times C_{p}$, and its intermediate fields of degree $p$ over $k$ are precisely the $k(a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2})$, $(a_{1},a_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$. $\blacksquare$

lemma_239.statement: Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p>2$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has order $p^{2}$. Then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.
lemma_239.proof:
Let $k$ be perfect of characteristic $p>2$, and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ whose Brauer class $[D]$ has order exactly $p^{2}$. Thus $\dim_k D=p^{4}$, and in particular
$$(*)\qquad p\,[D]\neq 0\ \ \text{in } \mathrm{Br}(k).$$
We argue by contradiction: suppose there are a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, a $G$-Galois $k$-algebra $L$ and a $2$-cocycle $c:G\times G\to L^{\times}$ with $D\cong (L,G,c)$ as $k$-algebras.

**Step 1 (a cyclic maximal subfield).** Apply the proved lemma lemma_209 (Spark) to $D$: since $D$ is a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$ isomorphic to a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$, either
(a) $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$, or
(b) the class of $D$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is annihilated by $p$.
Alternative (b) contradicts $(*)$, because $[D]$ has order $p^{2}>p$. Hence (a) holds: there is a maximal subfield $M\subset D$ with $M/k$ Galois, cyclic of degree $p^{2}$. Fix a generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(M/k)$; then $\sigma$ has order $p^{2}$ and $\sigma^{p}\neq \mathrm{id}_{M}$. Note $\dim_k M=[M:k]=p^{2}=\deg D$, as befits a maximal subfield.

**Step 2 (writing $D$ as the cyclic algebra $(M,\sigma,b)$).**
(i) *Skolem--Noether for $\sigma$.* The field $M$ is a commutative \'etale $k$-subalgebra of the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ with $\dim_k M=\deg D$. By ref_2 (part (iv)), every $k$-algebra automorphism of $M$ is induced by an inner automorphism of $D$; hence there exists $u\in D^{\times}$ with
$$u\,m\,u^{-1}=\sigma(m)\qquad\text{for all } m\in M.$$
(ii) *Centralizer.* By ref_1 (double centralizer theorem, maximal-subfield criterion), since $M$ is a maximal subfield of $D$ we have $C_{D}(M)=M$.
(iii) *Linear independence claim.* The elements $1,u,\dots,u^{p^{2}-1}$ are linearly independent over $M$ on the left. Suppose some non-trivial relation $\sum_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1} m_i u^{i}=0$ with $m_i\in M$ exists, and choose one whose support $I=\{i:m_i\neq 0\}$ has minimal cardinality. Necessarily $|I|\ge 2$, since a one-term relation $m_i u^{i}=0$ forces $m_i=0$ (each $u^{i}$ is a unit). Choose $i_0\in I$ and $i_1\in I\setminus\{i_0\}$. Because $\sigma$ has order $p^{2}$ and $0\le i_0\neq i_1\le p^{2}-1$, the automorphisms $\sigma^{i_0}$ and $\sigma^{i_1}$ of $M$ are distinct; pick $\mu\in M$ with $\sigma^{i_1}(\mu)\neq\sigma^{i_0}(\mu)$ (then automatically $\mu\neq 0$). Right-multiplying the relation by $\mu$ and using $u^{i}\mu=\sigma^{i}(\mu)u^{i}$ gives $\sum_i m_i\sigma^{i}(\mu)u^{i}=0$; multiplying this by $\sigma^{i_0}(\mu)^{-1}\in M^{\times}$ and subtracting from the original relation yields
$$\sum_{i\in I} m_i\bigl(1-\sigma^{i}(\mu)\sigma^{i_0}(\mu)^{-1}\bigr)u^{i}=0.$$
The coefficient of $u^{i_0}$ in this relation is $0$, while the coefficient of $u^{i_1}$ is $m_{i_1}\bigl(1-\sigma^{i_1}(\mu)\sigma^{i_0}(\mu)^{-1}\bigr)\neq 0$. We thus obtain a non-trivial $M$-linear relation among the $u^{i}$ whose support is strictly contained in $I$, contradicting the minimality of $I$. The claim follows.
(iv) By (iii), $B:=\sum_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1} M u^{i}$ is an $M$-subspace of $D$ of dimension $p^{2}$, hence $\dim_k B=p^{2}\cdot p^{2}=p^{4}=\dim_k D$. Since $B\subseteq D$, we get $B=D$, the sum being direct: $D=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}M u^{i}$.
(v) *The parameter lies in $k$.* Conjugation by $u^{p^{2}}$ restricts to $\sigma^{p^{2}}=\mathrm{id}$ on $M$, so $u^{p^{2}}\in C_{D}(M)=M$ by (ii); trivially $u^{p^{2}}$ commutes with $u$. Since $D$ is generated as a $k$-algebra by $M$ and $u$ (by (iv)), $u^{p^{2}}\in Z(D)=k$. As $D$ is a division ring, $b:=u^{p^{2}}\in k^{\times}$. Conclusion: $D=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}M v^{i}$ with $v:=u$, $v\lambda=\sigma(\lambda)v$ for all $\lambda\in M$, and $v^{p^{2}}=b\in k^{\times}$; i.e. $D$ is the cyclic algebra $(M,\sigma,b)$.

**Step 3 (a $p$-central element).** Put $x:=u^{p}\in D$. Then
$$x^{p}=u^{p\cdot p}=u^{p^{2}}=b\in k.$$
Moreover $x\notin k$: if $u^{p}\in k=Z(D)$, then conjugation by $u^{p}$ on $M$ would be the identity, but that conjugation is $\sigma^{p}$, and $\sigma$ has order $p^{2}$, so $\sigma^{p}\neq\mathrm{id}_{M}$ — contradiction. Thus $D$ contains an element $x$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^{p}\in k$ (a $p$-central element).

**Step 4 (contradiction with perfectness of $k$).** By the proved lemma lemma_217 (Spark), a central division algebra over a perfect field of characteristic $p>0$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^{p}\in k$. For completeness we recall the one-line reason, which we verify here in full: write $x^{p}=c\in k$; since $k$ is perfect the Frobenius $k\to k$, $a\mapsto a^{p}$, is surjective, so $c=a^{p}$ for some $a\in k$. As $a\in k=Z(D)$ commutes with $x$, the binomial theorem in characteristic $p$ gives $(x-a)^{p}=x^{p}-a^{p}=c-c=0$. A division ring has no non-zero nilpotent elements, so $x-a=0$, i.e. $x=a\in k$, contradicting $x\notin k$. This contradicts Step 3.

**Conclusion.** The assumption of Step 1 that $D\cong (L,G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ is false. Since $G$ (and $L$, $c$) were arbitrary, $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$. $\hfill\blacksquare$

(Remark on the logic: the only place the hypothesis "$\operatorname{char}k=p>2$" is used beyond the standing assumptions is in the applicability of lemma_209, and the only place perfectness is used is Step 4; the hypothesis that $[D]$ has order $p^{2}$ is used exactly to rule out alternative (b) of lemma_209, which is the case of exponent $p$ where crossed products with group $C_{p}\times C_{p}$ do occur.)

lemma_240.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$. If $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^2$, then $D$ contains an element $x$ such that $x^{p^2}\in k$ and $x^p\notin k$.
lemma_240.proof:
Let $n:=p^{2}$. Thus $\dim_k D=n^{2}=p^{4}$, and $L\subset D$ is a maximal subfield with $L/k$ Galois and $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)=\langle\sigma\rangle$ cyclic of order $n$; in particular $[L:k]=|\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)|=n=p^{2}$, $\sigma$ has exact order $n$, and $L^{\langle\sigma\rangle}=k$.

Step 1 (the centralizer of $L$ is $L$). Since $L/k$ is Galois it is finite separable, hence $L$ is a commutative \'etale $k$-subalgebra of $D$ with $\dim_k L=p^{2}=\deg D$. By ref_2(iii) (equivalently, by the double centralizer theorem ref_1: $\dim_k C_D(L)=\dim_k D/\dim_k L=p^{4}/p^{2}=p^{2}$ and $L\subseteq C_D(L)$ because $L$ is commutative) we have
$$C_D(L)=L.$$

Step 2 (Skolem--Noether: $\sigma$ is inner on $D$). By ref_2(iv), every $k$-algebra automorphism of the \'etale subalgebra $L$ of $D$ is induced by an inner automorphism of $D$. Applying this to $\sigma$, there is a unit $v\in D^{\times}$ with
$$v\,\ell\,v^{-1}=\sigma(\ell)\qquad\text{for all }\ell\in L.$$
By induction on $i\ge 0$ it follows that
$$v^{i}\,\ell\,v^{-i}=\sigma^{i}(\ell)\qquad\text{for all }\ell\in L,$$
since $v^{i+1}\ell v^{-(i+1)}=v\,\sigma^{i}(\ell)\,v^{-1}=\sigma^{i+1}(\ell)$.

Step 3 ($v^{n}\in L$). Put $w:=v^{n}=v^{p^{2}}\in D^{\times}$. For every $\ell\in L$, using Step 2 with $i=n$ and the fact that $\sigma$ has order $n$,
$$w\,\ell\,w^{-1}=\sigma^{n}(\ell)=\ell.$$
Hence $w$ centralizes $L$, i.e. $w\in C_D(L)=L$ by Step 1.

Step 4 ($v^{p^{2}}\in k$). Since $w=v^{n}$ is a power of $v$, it commutes with $v$. Applying the defining relation of Step 2 to the element $w\in L$ (which lies in $L$ by Step 3) gives
$$\sigma(w)=v\,w\,v^{-1}=w,$$
so $w$ is fixed by the generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$, hence by all of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$. As $L/k$ is Galois, $L^{\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)}=k$; therefore $w\in k^{\times}\subset k$. Thus $x:=v$ satisfies $x^{p^{2}}=w\in k$.

Step 5 ($v^{p}\notin k$). Suppose for a contradiction that $v^{p}\in k$. Since $D$ is central over $k$, every element of $k$ is central in $D$, so $v^{p}\ell v^{-p}=\ell$ for all $\ell\in L$. On the other hand, Step 2 with $i=p$ gives $v^{p}\ell v^{-p}=\sigma^{p}(\ell)$. Hence $\sigma^{p}(\ell)=\ell$ for all $\ell\in L$, i.e. $\sigma^{p}=\mathrm{id}_{L}$. But $\sigma$ generates $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$, a cyclic group of order exactly $p^{2}$, so $\sigma^{p}\neq\mathrm{id}_{L}$ (as $p<p^{2}$ and the action of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ on $L$ is faithful). This contradiction shows $v^{p}\notin k$.

(As a byproduct one also gets $v\notin k$, since $v\in k$ would force $\sigma=\mathrm{id}_{L}$, contradicting $|\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)|=p^{2}>1$.)

Step 6 (structural remark; not needed for the conclusion). The $k$-subspace $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}Lv^{i}$ is a $k$-subalgebra of $D$: it contains $1$, and it is closed under multiplication because $v\ell=\sigma(\ell)v$ moves coefficients to the left and $v^{n}=w\in L$. The sum is direct: if $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\ell_i v^{i}=0$ were a relation with the minimal number $r\ge1$ of nonzero coefficients, then $r\neq1$ (as $D^{\times}$ has no zero divisors), and choosing $\mu\in L$ with $\sigma^{i_1}(\mu)\ne\sigma^{i_2}(\mu)$ for two indices $i_1<i_2$ occurring in the relation (possible because $\sigma^{i_1}\ne\sigma^{i_2}$, both exponents being $<n=\mathrm{ord}(\sigma)$), the relation $\sum_i\ell_i\,(\sigma^{i_1}(\mu)-\sigma^{i}(\mu))v^{i}=0$ obtained from $\sigma^{i_1}(\mu)\sum_i\ell_i v^{i}-\big(\sum_i\ell_i v^{i}\big)\mu=0$ has strictly fewer nonzero terms, contradicting minimality. Hence $\dim_k\big(\sum_{i}Lv^{i}\big)=n\cdot n=p^{4}=\dim_k D$, so $D=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}Lv^{i}$ is the cyclic algebra $(L,\sigma,w)$ with $w=v^{p^{2}}\in k^{\times}$.

Conclusion: the element $x=v\in D$ satisfies $x^{p^{2}}\in k$ and $x^{p}\notin k$, which is exactly the claim.

lemma_241.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^2$ whose class in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ has order $p^2$. If $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^{p^2}\in k$, then $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^2$.
lemma_241.proof:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>2$ and let $D$ be a central division $k$-algebra of degree $p^{2}$, with $[D]\in\mathrm{Br}(k)$ of order $p^{2}$. Assume, for a contradiction, that $D$ is isomorphic as a $k$-algebra to a crossed product $(L_{0},G,c)$ for some group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.

Step 1 (obtaining a cyclic Galois maximal subfield). The order of $[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(k)$ is $p^{2}$. If $p$ annihilated $[D]$, i.e. $p[D]=0$, then the order of $[D]$ would divide $p$, contradicting $\mathrm{ord}([D])=p^{2}\nmid p$. Hence $[D]$ is not annihilated by $p$. We may now apply lemma_209 (Spark) to $D$: since $D$ is a crossed product $(L,G,c)$ for a group $G$ of order $p^{2}$ over a field of characteristic $p>2$, either (a) $D$ contains a maximal subfield that is Galois over $k$ with cyclic Galois group of order $p^{2}$, or (b) $[D]$ is annihilated by $p$. Alternative (b) is excluded, so alternative (a) holds: there is a subfield $L\subset D$ which is a maximal subfield of $D$ and a Galois field extension of $k$ with
$$\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)=\langle\sigma\rangle\cong C_{p^{2}}$$
for some $\sigma$ of exact order $p^{2}$. Since $L/k$ is a Galois field extension, $[L:k]=|\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)|=p^{2}$, and $L$ is separable and normal over $k$, hence $L$ is a commutative \'etale $k$-algebra with $\dim_{k}L=p^{2}=\deg D$.

Step 2 (Skolem--Noether: realising $\sigma$ inner on $D$). View $L$ as a commutative \etale $k$-subalgebra of the central simple $k$-algebra $D$ with $\dim_{k}L=\deg D$. By ref_2(iii),(iv), every $k$-algebra automorphism of $L$ is induced by an inner automorphism of $D$. Applying this to $\sigma$, there exists a unit $v\in D^{\times}$ such that
$$v\,\lambda\,v^{-1}=\sigma(\lambda)\qquad\text{for all }\lambda\in L.$$

Step 3 ($v^{p^{2}}$ lies in $k$). First we record, by induction on $m\ge 1$, that
$$v^{m}\lambda v^{-m}=\sigma^{m}(\lambda)\quad\forall\lambda\in L.$$
For $m=1$ this is Step 2. If it holds for $m$, then $v^{m+1}\lambda v^{-(m+1)}=v\,(v^{m}\lambda v^{-m})\,v^{-1}=v\,\sigma^{m}(\lambda)\,v^{-1}=\sigma(\sigma^{m}(\lambda))=\sigma^{m+1}(\lambda)$, using Step 2 applied to the element $\sigma^{m}(\lambda)\in L$. Taking $m=p^{2}$ and using that $\sigma$ has order $p^{2}$, we get $v^{p^{2}}\lambda v^{-p^{2}}=\lambda$ for every $\lambda\in L$, i.e.
$$v^{p^{2}}\in C_{D}(L).$$
Since $L$ is a maximal subfield of the central simple algebra $D$, the maximal-subfield criterion in ref_1 (double centralizer theorem) gives $C_{D}(L)=L$. Hence $v^{p^{2}}\in L$.

Next, $v$ commutes with its own power $v^{p^{2}}$, so for every $\lambda\in L$,
$$\sigma(v^{p^{2}})=v\,v^{p^{2}}\,v^{-1}=v^{p^{2}},$$
where the first equality is Step 2 applied to the element $v^{p^{2}}\in L$. Thus $v^{p^{2}}$ is fixed by $\sigma$, and therefore by every power of $\sigma$, i.e. by all of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)=\langle\sigma\rangle$. By the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, $L^{\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)}=k$, so
$$b:=v^{p^{2}}\in k.$$
Moreover $b\neq 0$ since $v\in D^{\times}$, so $b\in k^{\times}$.

Step 4 ($v\notin k$). Suppose $v\in k$. Since $k$ is the center of $D$, conjugation by $v$ is the identity automorphism of $D$; then Step 2 gives $\sigma(\lambda)=v\lambda v^{-1}=\lambda$ for all $\lambda\in L$, so $\sigma=\mathrm{id}_{L}$. This contradicts the fact that $\sigma$ has exact order $p^{2}>1$. Hence $v\notin k$.

Step 5 (contradiction with the hypothesis). Steps 3 and 4 exhibit an element $x:=v\in D$ with $x\notin k$ and $x^{p^{2}}=b\in k$. This directly contradicts the hypothesis that $D$ contains no element $x\notin k$ with $x^{p^{2}}\in k$.

The contradiction shows that our assumption was false: $D$ is not isomorphic to a crossed product algebra $(L,G,c)$ for any group $G$ of order $p^{2}$.

(Remark on the logic: the only deep input is lemma_209, which upgrades "crossed product for some group of order $p^{2}$" to "cyclic Galois maximal subfield" whenever the Brauer class is not $p$-torsion; the rest is the formal Skolem--Noether/double-centralizer argument producing from a cyclic Galois maximal subfield an element $v$ with $v\notin k$, $v^{p^{2}}\in k$. No claim that $D=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^{2}-1}Lv^{i}$ is made or needed, so no linear-independence argument is required.)
